CENTRAL ELECTRICITY REGULATORY COMMISSION
NEW DELHI

Coram:

Date of Order 03.06.2026
In the matter of:
Petition under Regulation 41 (Power to Relax) and Regulation 42 (Power to Remove
Difficulty) of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Connectivity and General
Network Access to the Inter-State Transmission System) Regulations, 2022 seeking
extension of the Financial Closure of the 250 MW capacity Wind-Solar Hybrid Power Project
at Bidar, Karnataka, where the in-principle connectivity has been granted on 22.07.2024
And
In the matter of:
1. M/s Welspun Narmada Pvt. Ltd
D/8, BKT House, Trade World,

Parties Present:
Shri Avijeet Lala, Advocate, WNPL
Ms. Ashmita Narula, Advocate, WNPL
Ms. Tannishtha Chatterjee, Advocate, WNPL

Ms. Pallavi Saigal, Advocate, CTUIL

ORDER
M/s Welspun Narmada Pvt.Ltd has filed the instant Petition under Regulation 41
(Power to Relax) and Regulation 42 (Power to Remove Difficulty) of the Central
Electricity Regulatory Commission (Connectivity and General Network Access to the
Inter-State Transmission System) Regulations, 2022, seeking extension of the
Financial Closure of the 250 MW capacity Wind-Solar Hybrid Power Project at Bidar,
Karnataka, where the in-principle connectivity has been granted on 22.07.2024
2. The Petitioner has made the following prayers in the present Petition:
(a) Hold and declare that the Petitioner is entitled to an extension of Financial Closure in the
facts and circumstances detailed in the present Petition; and / or
(b) Pass such other orders that this Hon’ble Commission deems fit in the facts of this case
Interim Relief
(a) Restrain the Respondent No. 1 from taking any coercive steps against the Petitioner,
during the pendency of the present Petition.
Submissions of Petitioner
3. Petitioner has made the following submissions:
a) Petitioner M/s Welspun Narmada Pvt. Ltd is a subsidiary of Welspun Renewable
Energy Private Limited. The Petitioner is setting up a Wind-Solar Hybrid Power Project
of 250 MW capacity at Bidar in the State of Karnataka, which is proposed to be
evacuated at Bidar PS at 220 kV level.
b) On 16.04.2024, the Petitioner submitted an application seeking Connectivity to the
Inter-State Transmission System (ISTS) Bidar PS under CERC (Connectivity and
Order in Petition No. 815/MP/2025
Page 2

General Network Access to the inter-State Transmission System) Regulations, 2022
(GNA Regulations). Vide letters dated 22.04.2024 and 03.03.2025, the Petitioner
furnished a Land Bank Guarantee of Rs. 25,00,00,000/- issued on 15.04.2024 and
valid up to 30.04.2027.
c) Respondent No. 1 Central Transmission Utility of India Limited (CTUIL) conveyed the
in-principle grant of connectivity for 250 MW at Bidar PS to the Petitioner vide letter
dated 22.07.2024. Vide letter dated 21.08.2024, the Petitioner submitted the following
Connectivity Bank Guarantees:
S.No. BG No. Validity Date Amount (Rs.)
1. 13940100022530 31.03.2027 50,00,000/-
(CONN BG-1)
2. 13940100022531 31.08.2028 3,00,00,000/-
(CONN BG-2)
3. 13940100022532 31.08.2028 5,00,00,000/-
(CONN BG-3)
d) It is the responsibility of the Respondent No. 2 to construct the infrastructure for the
220 kV line bay at Bidar PS for the evacuation of power from the Generation Pooling
Station of the Petitioner. Respondent No. 2 has not undertaken any infrastructure work
or any work within the aforesaid defined scope.
e) As per the in-principle grant of connectivity, the Start Date of Connectivity is
28.02.2026. Under the GNA Regulations, the Petitioner is required to achieve
Financial Closure (FC) at least six (6) months prior to the Scheduled Commercial
Operation Date (SCOD) or the Start Date of Connectivity, whichever is later.
f) The Respondent No. 1 sent an email to the Petitioner on 27.08.2025, whereby it has
asked the Petitioner to confirm the date of achievement of the FC along with
supporting documents under Regulation 11A of the GNA Regulations.
g) Vide notification dated 31.08.2025, this Commission notified the Third Amendment to
the GNA Regulations, which materially altered the manner in which the project has to
be implemented, including the manner in which the FC has to be achieved. Further,
as per Clause 10.5 of the Amended GNA Regulations, the confirmation of the firm
Start Date of Connectivity shall be communicated by the Nodal Agency within six (6)
months of the final grant of connectivity, based on the SCOD of the Associated
Transmission System (ATS), terminal bays, and any augmentation, if required.
Order in Petition No. 815/MP/2025
Page 3

h) With respect to the grant of connectivity for 250 MW RE capacity at Bidar ISTS Sub-
station, the Petitioner has not yet received the issuance of the final grant of
connectivity, and consequently, a firm Start Date of Connectivity has also not been
communicated, in terms of the Amended Regulations.
i) As per proviso to Regulation 11A(2) of the GNA Regulations, the Petitioner was
required to submit proof of FC of the project by 11.09.2025. Given uncertainty about
whether the Bidar Sub-station would be ready on time, proceeding with FC at that
stage would have exposed the Petitioner to the risk of heavy financial loss.
j) Respondent No. 1 has erroneously assumed that SCOD means SCOD of only the
developers' proposed 250 MW RE plant, whereas the definition of SCOD includes
SCOD of both the 250 MW RE plant and the required evacuation infrastructure, along
with the associated ISTS substation required augmentation.
Hearing on 18.09.2025
4. During the hearing held on 18.09.2025, the Commission directed the issuance of
notice to the Respondents.
Hearing on 23.09.2025
5. RoP for hearing dated 23.09.2025 is as under:
…………
2. The Petitioner is directed to submit, on an affidavit within two days, (i) the present status
of its Dedicated Transmission Line (DTL), i.e., M/s Welspun Narmada Pvt. Ltd – Bidar PS
220 kV S/c line along with the line bay at the generation pooling station, which was under
the scope of the Petitioner and (ii) specify the date upto which the Petitioner is seeking
extension for the financial closure.
3. CTUIL was directed to submit the following information, on an affidavit, within two days:
(a) Present status of the Bidar sub-station.
(b) Status of 1 no. 220 kV line bay at Bidar PS, which is required for termination of the
dedicated line of the Petitioner.
Submissions of Respondent (Compliance of RoP dated 23.09.2025)
6. Respondent, CTUIL, vide affidavit dated 30.09.2025 has submitted that the Bidar
substation and the required 220 kV line bay at Bidar Substation for termination of
dedicated line of the petitioner falls under the scope of the ISTS scheme
“Transmission Scheme for Solar Energy Zone in Bidar (2500 MW), Karnataka” which
Order in Petition No. 815/MP/2025
Page 4

is under implementation by POWERGRID with the timeline of 24 months from SPV
transfer (SPV Transfer Date - 09.02.2024) with the SCOD of 09.02.2026 and
anticipated CoD of 30.06.2026 as per the latest information available with CTUIL.
Submission of Petitioner (Compliance of RoP dated 23.09.2025)
7. Petitioner vide affidavit dated 03.10.2025 has submitted that the transmission line
route survey has been completed, and the RoW negotiations are currently in progress.
Further, two contracts have been executed with land aggregators for 300 acres, and
the respective TSR has been completed. Out of the said 300 acres, the execution of
the Lease Deed is in process for 200 acres.
Submissions of the Respondent
8. Respondent CTUIL vide affidavit dated 29.10.2025 has submitted as below:
a) Transmission Licensee, i.e., Bidar Transmission Limited (POWERGRID), is
implementing the concerned Transmission scheme. As per the latest information
available with CTUIL, the anticipated COD of the Substation and line bay is as under:
S. No. Element SCOD Anticipated COD
Establishment of 765/400 kV
3x1500 MVA, 400/220 kV 5x500
1 09.02.2026 30.06.2026
MVA pooling station at a suitable
border location near Bidar.
Status of 1 no. 220 kV line bay at
2 09.02.2026 30.06.2026
Bidar PS.
Hearing on 30.10.2025
9. RoP for hearing dated 30.10.2025 is as under:
At the outset, the learned counsel for the Petitioner and the Respondent, CTUIL,
jointly submitted that the matter be reserved for order, with the parties permitted to file their
respective written submissions, if any.
2. Considering the above, the Commission permitted both sides to file their brief written
submissions, if any, within two weeks, with a copy to the other side. The interim direction
issued vide Record of Proceedings for the hearing dated 26.9.2025 shall continue until a
decision is taken in the matter.
3. The Commission further directed the Petitioner to file the following information, on an
affidavit, within two weeks:
(i) In compliance with the Record of Proceedings for the hearing dated 23.9.2025,
indicate the date up to which the Financial Closure extension is required and the reasons
for the same.
(ii) Project Progress Status as per the format annexed with this Record of Proceedings.
Order in Petition No. 815/MP/2025
Page 5

4. CTUIL was directed to file the following information/clarification, on an affidavit, within
two weeks:
(i) Project Progress Status as per the format annexed with this Record of Proceedings
(ii) Clarify the reasons for non-intimation of final grant of connectivity to the Petitioner
within 15 days of receipt of Conn BG-2 as per the GNA Regulations, along with a copy
of intimation of final grant, if issued.
5. Subject to the above, the matter was reserved for order.
Submissions of Petitioner
10. Petitioner vide written submission dated 18.11.2025 has reiterated its earlier
submission and has additionally submitted as below:
a) Despite the absence of the final grant of Connectivity and the Connectivity Agreement,
the Petitioner has achieved FC through internal financing from group entities on
13.11.2025. The Petitioner has submitted proof of achieving FC to the Respondent
on 14.11.2025 along with supporting documents, to which the Respondent has not
responded. The Petitioner reserves the right to initiate further proceedings and/or take
recourse to remedies available under law, if so necessitated with respect to the same.
b) Petitioner furnished the status of the Project.
Submissions of the Respondent
11. Respondent CTUIL vide affidavit dated 23.12.2025 has submitted as below:
a) A meeting was held on 14.09.2024 at the Ministry of Power (MoP) to discuss the
issues of Solar & Wind Power Developers in commissioning their projects, wherein it
was emerged that the quantum of connectivity for wind-solar hybrid projects shall be
decided by CTU based on analysis/simulation of maximum possible power injection
into the grid. Accordingly, CTU issued an advisory regarding the submission of the
study analysis report by co-located hybrid power projects for the identification of the
Connectivity quantum to all RE Connectivity applicants/grantees, implementing co-
located hybrid projects, viz. Wind & Solar.
b) Vide email dated 03.07.2025, CTU had again requested the Petitioner for submission
of analysis/simulation of maximum possible power injection into the grid. The
petitioner has submitted the report vide email dated 08.07.2025; however, the same
was reverted by CTUIL on account of the wrongly considered installed capacity of
solar and wind quantum. Subsequently, vide emails dated 28.07.2025, 30.07.2025
and 28.08.2025, CTU again requested the submission of a revised report.
Order in Petition No. 815/MP/2025
Page 6

c) Petitioner vide email dated 29.08.2025, shared the Excel file for the generation profile
towards maximum power injection into the grid. CTU, vide email dated 10.09.2025,
informed the Petitioner that the total maximum generation (Solar and Wind) in the
shared Excel file is 198.6 MW, which is less than the connectivity quantum, i.e., 250
MW. Therefore, the Petitioner was requested to confirm the same and submit the
report in proper format so that intimation for final grant could be issued.
d) Subsequently, vide communication dated 10.11.2025, the Petitioner has informed
CTU that based on its in-depth system study and on-site technical survey the
Petitioner has found that Wind is not feasible option at Bidar site and has requested
to change source of RE from earlier submitted i.e. Solar (100 MW) & Wind (150 MW)
to Solar (250 MW) & BESS (125 MW/ 750 MWh).
12. Respondent CTUIL vide additional affidavit dated 16.02.2026 has submitted as below:
a) The final grant could not be issued on account of the study report that ought to be
submitted by the Petitioner showing maximum power injection into the grid.
b) M/s Welspun Narmada Pvt. Ltd. vide letter dated 19.01.2026 has requested the
withdrawal of application no. 2200000716 for 250 MW (granted at Bidar PS) under
Regulation 3.7.3 of the GNA Regulations.
c) Due to the subsistence of status-quo direction in the subject matter and the fact that
this Commission’s Order will adjudicate on the treatment/ administration of the
application, the subject development [request for withdrawal of application received
from applicant] is brought on record.
Hearing on 17.04.2026
13. RoP for hearing dated 17.04.2026 is as under:
At the outset, the learned counsel for the Petitioner submitted that the present
Petition had been filed seeking an extension of time for the Financial Closure of the 250
MW capacity Wind-Solar Hybrid Power Project at Bidar, Karnataka. The learned counsel
further submitted that the matter was reserved by the Commission after hearing the parties
at length. However, the Respondent, CTUIL, subsequently mentioned the matter for
rehearing. The learned counsel further submitted that, vide its application dated
19.1.2026, the Petitioner requested CTUIL to allow withdrawal of its application for
the grant of connectivity in terms of Regulation 3.7.3 of the GNA Regulations.
Accordingly, nothing survives for adjudication in the present matter. The learned
counsel further sought a week’s time to file an affidavit placing the aforesaid
aspects/developments on record.
Order in Petition No. 815/MP/2025
Page 7

2. In response, the learned counsel for the Respondent, CTUIL, submitted that the
Petitioner’s application dated 19.1.2026 seeking withdrawal of its application for the grant
of connectivity in terms of Regulation 3.7.3 of the GNA Regulations shall be dealt with in
accordance with the applicable Regulations. The learned counsel further submitted that
the Petitioner has achieved financial closure, albeit belatedly, and the consequences of
such delay shall also be addressed in terms of the GNA Regulations.
3. After hearing the learned counsel for the parties, the Commission directed the
Petitioner to file its affidavit, as above, within a week, with a copy to the Respondent.
4. Subject to the above, the matter was reserved for order.
Submissions of Petitioner
14. Petitioner vide affidavit dated 29.04.2026 has submitted as below:
a) On 19.01.2026, the Petitioner filed an application before the Respondent, CTUIL,
seeking withdrawal of its connectivity, which is a right available to the Petitioner under
Regulation 3.7.3 of the GNA Regulations. The Petitioner is willing to exercise the
option, under Regulation 3.8 of the GNA Regulations, to pay the equivalent amount
through online payment in lieu of encashment of applicable Bank Guarantees, and
CTUIL can return the Bank Guarantees in accordance with the GNA Regulations, if
any.
b) CTUIL with submission dated 16.02.2026 stated that it would not be able to process
the Petitioner’s application for withdrawal in view of the directions of this Commission
vide ROPs dated 26.09.2025 and 30.10.2025 to maintain status quo, and accordingly,
the said application would remain subject to the outcome of the present Petition.
c) The application to withdraw connectivity is an independent right available under the
GNA Regulations, and the outcome of the present proceedings has no bearing on the
exercise of such right. The directions issued by this Commission vide ROPs dated
26.09.2025 and 30.10.2025 directing CTUIL to maintain the status quo were limited
only to the issue of financial closure and did not extend to the withdrawal of
connectivity. The said direction does not impose any embargo on CTUIL from
processing such a withdrawal as per the GNA Regulations.
d) That during the pendency of the captioned Petition for extension of time to achieve
FC, the Petitioner has achieved financial closure on 13.11.2025, albeit with a delay of
77 days, and that this remains the sole issue for consideration before this Commission
as on date. The proof of achieving financial closure, along with supporting documents,
was submitted to CTUIL/ Respondent No. 1 on 14.11.2025. In view thereof, it is prayed
Order in Petition No. 815/MP/2025
Page 8

that this Commission may be pleased to consider the same and pass appropriate
orders, as deemed fit.
Analysis and Decision
15. We have considered the submissions of the Petitioner, Respondent and perused the
facts available on record.
16. Petitioner has submitted that it is setting up a Wind-Solar Hybrid Power Project of 250
MW capacity at Bidar in the State of Karnataka. On 16.04.2024, the Petitioner
submitted its application under the Land BG route, seeking Connectivity to the ISTS
Bidar PS under GNA Regulations, stating SCOD of the project to be 28.02.2026.
Respondent No. 1 CTUIL conveyed the in-principle grant of connectivity for 250 MW
at Bidar PS to the Petitioner vide letter dated 22.07.2024 with a start date of
28.02.2026, requiring Financial closure to be furnished by 11.09.2025.
17. Petitioner filed the instant petition seeking an extension to furnish financial closure
documents. Petitioner has submitted that the DTL route survey has been completed
and the RoW negotiations are currently in progress. Also, two contracts have been
executed with land aggregators for 300 acres, and the respective TSR has been
completed. Out of the said 300 acres, the execution of the Lease Deed is in process
for 200 acres. Subsequently, Petitioner furnished financial closure documents to
CTUIL on 14.11.2025. Final Grant of Connectivity has not been issued to the
Petitioner.
18. On 19.01.2026, the Petitioner filed an application before Respondent CTUIL seeking
withdrawal of its connectivity, under Regulation 3.7.3 of the GNA Regulations and is
willing to exercise the option under Regulation 3.8 of the GNA Regulations to pay the
equivalent amount through online payment in lieu of encashment of applicable Bank
Guarantees, and CTUIL can return the Bank Guarantees in accordance with the GNA
Regulations, if any.
19. CTUIL with submission dated 16.02.2026 stated that it would not be able to process
the Petitioner’s application for withdrawal in view of the directions of this Commission
vide ROPs dated 26.09.2025 and 30.10.2025 to maintain status quo, and accordingly,
the said application would remain subject to the outcome of the present Petition.
20. We have considered the submissions of the Petitioner and Respondent.
Order in Petition No. 815/MP/2025
Page 9

21. We note that the Petitioner have already filed the withdrawal application dated
19.01.2026 to CTUIL and has requested to avail its option to pay the equivalent
amount through online payment in lieu of encashment of applicable BGs. Relevant
extract of the letter dated 19.01.2026 is as under:
As per the above, Petitioner has submitted the withdrawal application to CTUIL under
Regulation 3.7.3 of the GNA Regulations. Further, the Petitioner has stated that
although in-principle connectivity was granted and required bank guarantees and FCs
Order in Petition No. 815/MP/2025
Page 10

were submitted, the final grant of connectivity and execution of the Connectivity
Agreement were not completed, and there remained uncertainty regarding
transmission infrastructure readiness and confirmed commercial operation timelines.
Due to these delays and the resulting commercial non-viability of the project, the
Company’s Board decided not to proceed and accordingly withdrew the connectivity
application under the GNA Regulations. The Petitioner also requested CTUIL to allow
payment in lieu of encashment of bank guarantees as per Regulation 3.8 of the GNA
Regulations and sought their return, while confirming that it has no claims against
CTUIL.
22. Regulation 3.7.3 and 3.8 of the GNA Regulation are as under:
3.7.3 If any application for the grant of Connectivity is withdrawn after the in-principle grant
of Connectivity and before the final grant of Connectivity, the Nodal Agency shall deal with
such cases in the following manner:
(a) 100% of the application fee shall be forfeited.
(b) 5% of the BG submitted in terms of clause (vii)(c) or clause (xi)(c) of Regulation
5.8 of these regulations, as the case may be, shall be forfeited and the balance 95%
of the BG shall be returned to the Applicant within 15 days of withdrawal of the
application.
(c) If Conn BG1, and Conn-BG3, as applicable, have been furnished, Conn BG-1 shall
be encashed and Conn-BG3 shall be returned to the Applicant within 15 days of
withdrawal of the application.
(d) If Conn-BG2 has been furnished and ATS or terminal bay(s) have been awarded
for implementation, as on the date of withdrawal, Conn-BG2 shall be encashed. For
cases where ATS or terminal bay(s) have not been awarded for implementation, as
on the date of withdrawal, Conn-BG2 shall be returned within 15 days of withdrawal
of the application.
(e) Application shall be closed within 15 days from the date of withdrawal of the
application, with intimation to the Applicant.
……….
3.8 An applicant whose Bank Guarantee (BG) is required to be encashed, shall have
the option to pay the equivalent amount through online payment mode, in lieu of such
encashment of BG under these regulations and seek the return of the BG, subject to
the condition that online payment is made on or before the date of revocation by the
Nodal Agency. In such cases(s), the Nodal Agency shall return the BG within 15
working days of confirmation of receipt of the equivalent amount through an online
payment mode
As per the above, if any application for the grant of Connectivity is withdrawn after the
in-principle grant of Connectivity and before the final grant of Connectivity, the Nodal
Agency shall deal with such cases in terms of the above-quoted clauses. Further,
Regulation 3.8 permits an applicant to pay the equivalent amount through online
payment, in lieu of encashing the BG under these regulations, and to seek the return
Order in Petition No. 815/MP/2025
Page 11

of the BG. In such cases(s), the Nodal Agency shall return the BG within 15 working
days of confirmation of receipt of the equivalent amount through an online payment
mode.
23. Since the petitioner has already requested the withdrawal of its Connectivity
application, we are of the view that the issue of submission of financial closure no
longer survives. We direct CTUIL to process the withdrawal application in terms of
Regulation 3.7.3 of the GNA Regulation and permit the petitioner to furnish the cash
in lieu of BG. CTUIL is directed to inform the Petitioner of the amount to be deposited
in terms of Regulation 3.7.3 within a period of 10 days from the issue of this Order.
Petitioner is required to furnish the amount communicated by the CTUIL within a
period of 10 days thereafter, failing which CTUIL shall encash the amount from the
BGs. CTUIL shall close the application on receipt of the required amounts in terms of
the GNA Regulations and return the BG within 15 working days of receipt of the
required amount.
24. Accordingly, Petitioner No.815/MP/2025 is disposed of in terms of the above.
Sd/ Sd/ Sd/ Sd/
(Ravinder Singh Dhillon) (Harish Dudani) (Ramesh Babu V.) (Jishnu Barua)
Member Member Member Chairperson

ORDER
Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Limited has filed the instant Petition under Sections
79(1)(b) and (f) read with Sections 11, 29 and other applicable provisions of the
Electricity Act, 2003, seeking directions against Tata Power Company Limited (“TPCL”
or the “Respondent No. 1”) for compliance with the directions issued by the Ministry of
Power (“MoP”) under Section 11 of the Act dated 20.2.2023 and under Section 142
Order in IA Numbers 79/IA/2023, 86/IA/2024 and 87/IA/2024 in Petition No. 117/MP/2023 Page 2 of 39

and 146 of the Electricity Act, 2003 (“Act”) and with reference to the Power Purchase
Agreement (“PPA”) dated 22.4.2007 executed between the parties.
2. The Petitioner has alleged that despite the operation of the MoP directions
requiring generation and supply of power from imported coal-based plants during the
notified period, TPCL failed to supply power in accordance with its contractual and
statutory obligations, resulting in financial loss to GUVNL. The Petitioner has made
the following prayers in the instant Petition:
“a. Direct that the Respondent No. - 1 Tata Power Company Limited is obligated to
generate and supply electricity to Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Limited in terms of the
directions of the Ministry of Power, Government of India dated 20.02.2023 under
Section 11 of the Electricity Act, 2003;
b. Direct Tata Power to declare availability to Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Limited
against the contracted capacity of 1805 MW and WRLDC to schedule the
requirement of GUVNL in terms of the directions of the Central Government,

Petition was limited to TPCL’s alleged non-compliance with the directions of the
MoP dated 20.2.2023 under Section 11(1) of the Act. Through the present
amendment, the Petitioner seeks to convert the statutory enforcement Petition
into one for monetary claims and contractual damages exceeding ₹600 crore.

factual narratives, internal correspondence, availability data, and market
calculations are introduced, none of which formed part of the original pleadings.
These additions fundamentally alter the dispute and give rise to contested factual
issues that would require detailed evidentiary hearings, contrary to the nature of
a Section 11 enforcement proceeding. The attempt to introduce contractual
claims within a statutory compliance Petition is beyond the jurisdiction and intent
of the original filing.
b. The original cause of action was confined to statutory obligations under
Section 11. However, the amendment now seeks to create a hybrid cause
combining contractual and statutory remedies. Such a change in legal character
is impermissible under settled law and must be rejected. The application also
fails the requirement of due diligence under Regulation 38 of the Central
Electricity Regulatory Commission (Conduct of Business) Regulations, 2023
(hereinafter “2023 COB Regulations”), and Order VI Rule 17 CPC. The Petitioner
had full knowledge of the facts and data now relied upon when the Petition was
filed in April 2023, and no justification is provided for the belated inclusion of
these monetary claims.
c. Regulation 38 of the 2023 COB Regulations and Order VI Rule 17 CPC
permit amendment of pleadings only when such amendment is necessary to
determine the real issue in controversy and when the party demonstrates that,
despite due diligence, the matter could not have been raised earlier. The
amendment now sought does not clarify or supplement existing pleadings.
Instead, it introduces a new cause of action based on contractual entitlement to
availability-linked compensation and quantified monetary reliefs. Such a shift in
the nature of the Petition falls squarely within the category of impermissible
amendments identified by the Supreme Court in Revajeetu Builders [(2009) 10
SCC 84 and LIC v. Sanjeev Builders (2022) 16 SCC 1].
d. The proposed amendment changes the essential nature of the proceedings
from statutory enforcement under Section 11 to a contractual dispute under the
PPA. This is legally untenable because the Petition was never conceived as one
for adjudicating damages or availability-based claims. Permitting the amendment
would therefore violate the jurisdictional contours of Section 11 proceedings and
convert them into a monetary claim adjudication. The amendment also runs
counter to the principle that a pleading cannot be recast to set up a new and
independent case that could have been pursued separately. The Petitioner’s

proposed changes introduce fresh factual matrices, new calculations, and
contractual interpretations unrelated to the original lis. Accordingly, the
amendment is beyond the permissible scope of Regulation 38 and Order VI Rule
17 and must be rejected.
e. Without prejudice to the above objections, the claims advanced by the
Petitioner are misconceived and contractually unsustainable. The PPA
comprehensively provides for the consequences of non-supply or reduced
availability under Schedule 7, and the Petitioner has already made deductions in
accordance therewith. No additional compensation can therefore be sought. The
non-supply between 15.3.2023 and 15.4.2023 occurred solely because the
Petitioner failed to establish and maintain valid Letters of Credit (LCs), in a timely
manner, which is a mandatory precondition for scheduling and dispatch under
the PPA. In the absence of a valid LC, TPCL could not be expected to operate
or schedule generation, and the resultant shortfall is entirely attributable to the
Petitioner. During 2023-24, operations at the Mundra UMPP were also affected
by force majeure conditions, including Cyclone Biparjoy and the technical
overhaul of 5th Unit (Unit 40), duly notified to the MoP, CEA, and all procurers.
The directions of 20.2.2023 were to be implemented subject to technical
feasibility. Hence, the obligation to operate “to full capacity” must be read in light
of normative availability.
f. The term “full capacity” in the Section 11 directions must be harmoniously
interpreted with the PPA, where 80 per cent annual normative availability entitles
full recovery of fixed charges. Coal-based plants are not designed for continuous
100 per cent PLF operation. Therefore, compliance with the Section 11 directions
is satisfied when the generating station maintains normative availability
consistent with the PPA and the Ministry’s clarifications issued under the earlier
Section 11 directions. The Petitioner’s assertion that TPCL was bound to
maintain continuous 100 per cent generation is contrary to the PPA framework
and to the MoP’s own clarification dated 20.5.2022, which states that “full
capacity” means normative availability. Availability and procurement are
reciprocal. If the Petitioner insists on a 100 per cent declaration, it must
correspondingly schedule and procure 100 per cent of its contracted share.
Frequent instances of partial scheduling and alternate sourcing by the Petitioner
have resulted in commercial loss to TPCL. Such selective enforcement of
obligations cannot be sustained. Further, implementation of the Section 11
Order in IA Numbers 79/IA/2023, 86/IA/2024 and 87/IA/2024 in Petition No. 117/MP/2023 Page 10 of 39

directions and compensation thereunder is the subject matter of Petition No.
179/MP/2023 pending before the Commission. The present proceedings cannot
be used to pre-empt or duplicate those adjudications.
g. Reliance is placed on Revajeetu Builders & Developers v. Narayanaswamy
& Sons (2009) 10 SCC 84 to submit the settled principles governing amendment,
including that amendments changing the nature of the case must be rejected.
Reliance is placed on LIC v. Sanjeev Builders (P) Ltd. (2022) 16 SCC 1 to
contend that amendments introducing a new cause of action or altering the
nature of the proceedings are liable to be disallowed.

26. Before examining the permissibility of the amendment sought by the Petitioner,
it is necessary to refer to the statutory and regulatory framework governing the
amendment of pleadings before this Commission. The issue of amendment of
pleadings in proceedings before the Commission is governed by Regulation 38 of the
2023 COB Regulations, which provides the procedural basis for alteration or
amendment of pleadings in petitions filed before the Commission.
27. Regulation 38 of the 2023 COB Regulations is reproduced below:
“38. Amendment of Pleadings
The Commission may, at any stage of the proceedings in a petition, allow either party
to alter or amend its pleadings in such manner and on such terms as may be
considered appropriate, and all such amendments shall be made as may be necessary
for the purpose of determining the real issues in controversy between the parties:
Provided that no application for amendment shall be allowed after
commencement of the final hearing of the petition, unless the Commission is of the
opinion that, in spite of due diligence, the party could not have raised the matter before
the commencement of the final hearing:
Provided further that no application for amendment shall be entertained after
the conclusion of the final hearing and order is reserved in the petition.”
28. The above provision makes it clear that while the Commission possesses
discretion to permit amendment of pleadings, such amendment can be allowed only
when it satisfies the following conditions:
(a) the amendment must be necessary for determining the real issues in
controversy between the parties; and
(b) where the proceedings have progressed substantially, the party seeking
amendment must demonstrate that, despite due diligence, the matter could not
have been raised earlier.
Order in IA Numbers 79/IA/2023, 86/IA/2024 and 87/IA/2024 in Petition No. 117/MP/2023 Page 24 of 39

29. The above Regulation is materially identical in wording and intent to Order VI
Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (CPC), which deals with the amendment
of pleadings. Rule 17 provides as follows:
“17. Amendment of pleadings.
The Court may at any stage of the proceedings allow either party to alter or amend his
pleadings in such manner and on such terms as may be just, and all such amendments
shall be made as may be necessary for the purpose of determining the real questions
in controversy between the parties:
Provided that no application for amendment shall be allowed after trial has
commenced, unless the court comes to the conclusion that inspite of due diligence,
the party could not have raised the matter before commencement of trial.”
Thus, both Regulation 38 of the 2023 COB Regulations and Order VI Rule 17
CPC recognise a liberal approach towards amendment of pleadings, but such
amendments cannot be permitted where they introduce an entirely new cause of
action or fundamentally alter the nature of the proceedings originally instituted.
30. The principles governing amendment of pleadings have been comprehensively
explained by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Revajeetu Builders & Developers v.
Narayanaswamy & Sons, wherein the Court laid down certain guiding factors which
must be considered while deciding an application for amendment of pleadings. In the
case of Revajeetu Builders and Developers Vs. Narayanswamy (2009) 10 SCC 84),
the Supreme Court enunciated the following principles for allowing the amendment:
“Whether amendment necessary to decide the real controversy
58. The first condition which must be satisfied before the amendment can be allowed
by the court is whether such amendment is necessary for the determination of the real
question in controversy. If that condition is not satisfied, the amendment cannot be
allowed. This is the basic test which should govern the court’s decision discretion in
grant or refusal of the amendment.
No prejudice or injury to other party
59. The other important condition which should govern the discretion of the court is
potentiality of prejudice or injustice which is likely to be caused to the other side.
Ordinarily if the other side is compensated with costs, then there is no injustice but in
practice hardly any court grants actual costs to the opposite side. The Courts have
very wide discretion in the matter of amendment of pleadings but the Court’s powers
must be exercised judiciously and with great care.”

“Factors to be taken into consideration while dealing with the application for
amendment
63. On critically analyzing both the English and Indian cases, some basic principles
emerge which ought to be taken into consideration while allowing or rejecting the
application for amendment:
(1) Whether the amendment sought is imperative for the proper adjudication of
the case;
(2) Whether the application for amendment is bonafide or malafide;
(3) The amendment should not cause such prejudice to the other side which
cannot be compensated adequately in terms of money;
(4) Refusing amendment would in fact lead to injustice or lead to multiple
litigation;
(5) Whether the proposed amendment constitutionally or fundamentally
changes the nature or character of the case; and
(6) As a general rule, the court should decline amendments if a fresh suit on
the amended claims would be barred by limitation on the date of application.
These are some of the important factors which may be kept in mind while dealing with
the application filed under Order 6 Rule 17. These are only illustrative and not
exhaustive.
64. The decision on an application made under Order 6 Rule 17 is a very serious
judicial exercise and the said exercise should never be undertaken in a causal manner.
We can conclude our discussion by observing that while deciding applications for
amendments the courts must not refuse bona fide, legitimate, honest and necessary
amendments and should never permit mala fide, worthless and/or dishonest
amendments.”
31. The Hon’ble Supreme Court has clarified that while a liberal approach is
generally adopted in permitting amendments, amendments which introduce a new
and independent cause of action or fundamentally alter the nature of the proceedings
ought not to be permitted.
32. In the light of the above principles, the amendment sought by the Petitioner is

between the parties; and (ii) whether the Petitioner has demonstrated due diligence
in seeking such amendment. These requirements operate as substantive limitations
on the otherwise broad discretion of the Court or tribunal to permit amendment of

a) First factor - Whether the amendment is imperative for proper and
effective adjudication of the case?
The original Petition was instituted seeking enforcement of the directions
issued by the MoP under Section 11 of the Act, and for initiation of
proceedings under Sections 142 and 146 of the Act for alleged non-
compliance with such statutory directions. The amendments now sought to
introduce extensive monetary claims relating to alleged financial losses
incurred by the Petitioner due to the procurement of electricity from
alternate sources, as well as claims based on contractual provisions of the
PPA. Such claims are not necessary for determining whether the
Respondent complied with the statutory directions issued under Section 11
Order in IA Numbers 79/IA/2023, 86/IA/2024 and 87/IA/2024 in Petition No. 117/MP/2023 Page 29 of 39

introducing monetary claims and contractual issues which were not part of
the original lis. Even in the absence of demonstrable prejudice, such a
fundamental shift in the nature of the proceedings cannot be permitted
within the framework of the present Petition.
d) Fourth factor - Whether refusal of amendment would lead to
injustice or multiplicity of proceedings?
The refusal of the amendment would not result in any injustice to the
Petitioner. The Petitioner remains free to pursue its monetary claims, if
otherwise permissible in law, through appropriate independent
proceedings. While such a course may give rise to separate proceedings,
this consequence flows from the fact that the monetary claims sought to be
introduced are distinct from the regulatory enforcement issues raised in the
original Petition. Permitting the amendment within the present proceedings
would effectively deviate from the nature and scope of the original lis and
convert the proceedings for adjudication of monetary restitution claims.
We note that the Petitioner had earlier filed Petition No. 107/MP/2023, inter
alia, seeking adjudication of disputes arising out of alleged non-supply/
short supply of power by TPCL under the PPA dated 22.4.2007. The said
petition involves the same parties and arises from the same PPA, and
broadly concerns issues relating to the supply of power, compliance with
the Section 11 directions, declaration of availability, scheduling, and
consequential claims for compensation for non-supply. The Petitioner has
therein contended that TPCL failed to make available the contracted
capacity of 1805 MW, necessitating procurement of power from alternate
sources at higher rates and resulting in financial loss. The said Petition was
earlier adjudicated by this Commission and, upon challenge before APTEL,
Order in IA Numbers 79/IA/2023, 86/IA/2024 and 87/IA/2024 in Petition No. 117/MP/2023 Page 31 of 39

we are of the view that the proposed amendment does fundamentally alter
the nature and character of the present proceedings.
f) Sixth factor - Whether a fresh proceeding on the amended claims
would be barred by limitation?
The Commission notes that the monetary claims sought to be introduced
through the proposed amendment pertain to events that occurred in the
recent past and are based on operational and financial data relating to the
period subsequent to the issuance of the Section 11 directions. The
Petitioner has not demonstrated that such claims would be barred by
limitation if pursued through independent proceedings. It is further observed
that the Petitioner in Petition No. 107/MP/2023 has claimed compensation
and damages for non-supply of electricity as per the PPA dated 22.4.2007
“from 13.2.2023 onwards”, which could also include the compensation
claims made in the instant petition for the period beyond March, 2023. In
these circumstances, the question of the Petitioner being deprived of its
remedy on account of limitation does not arise, and therefore, this factor
also does not justify permitting the amendment within the present
proceedings.
38. In view of the above analysis, we are of the considered opinion that although
the amendment application cannot be said to be mala fide, the proposed amendment
fails to satisfy the governing principles laid down in Revajeetu Builders. In particular,
the amendment is not imperative for adjudication of the original controversy and
would fundamentally alter the nature of the proceedings by introducing monetary
restitution claims within a petition primarily concerned with regulatory enforcement of
statutory directions.
Order in IA Numbers 79/IA/2023, 86/IA/2024 and 87/IA/2024 in Petition No. 117/MP/2023 Page 33 of 39

cause of action and alters the nature of the original petition. The distinction between
a “continuing cause” and a “new cause” was lucidly explained in State of A.P. v.
Pioneer Builders, (2006) 12 SCC 119, where the Supreme Court held that
subsequent events may be pleaded only when they are integrally connected with the
existing lis. In the present matter, the subsequent financial computations do not flow
as a mere extension of the statutory non-compliance but as an independent
contractual dispute. Allowing such an amendment would conflate enforcement
proceedings under Section 142 with adjudicatory proceedings under Section 79(1)(f),
which is impermissible. Further, a proceeding under Section 142 is in the nature of
quasi-penal enforcement, meant to secure compliance with statutory directions. Its
scope is limited to determining whether a contravention occurred and, if so, to
imposing a penalty.
42. The proposed amendments are retrospective in orientation; they seek
adjudication and recovery of alleged financial losses already suffered in the past on
account of short-supply/ non-supply during periods that had already elapsed by the
time the IA was filed. The amendment shifts the focus from prospective enforcement
and future compliance (the original character of the Petition) to the retrospective
determination of liability, the quantification of damages, and the recovery of
compensation for past events. This shift is not merely incidental but transformative:
where the original Petition invoked the Commission's regulatory authority to compel
ongoing statutory adherence under Section 11(1), the amendment pivots to invoking
its adjudicatory powers under Section 79(1)(f) for settling contractual accounts and
enforcing monetary restitution, effectively seeking monetary compensation on what
was conceived as a quasi-penal enforcement mechanism.
Order in IA Numbers 79/IA/2023, 86/IA/2024 and 87/IA/2024 in Petition No. 117/MP/2023 Page 36 of 39

43. We also find that the causes of action involved are distinct and cannot co-exist
within the framework of Section 142. The cause of action in the original Petition was
singular and self-contained, namely, alleged non-compliance with statutory
directions issued under Section 11(1). In contrast, the cause of action now sought to
be introduced pertains to non-supply of power and resultant financial loss under the
PPA, which falls within an entirely different legal domain.
44. The Petitioner had initially filed IA No.79/IA/2023 seeking to place certain
additional particulars on record and to introduce an additional monetary prayer
limited to the period up to 18.4.2023, quantified at ₹112.83 crore. Subsequently, by
way of IA No. 86/IA/2024, the Petitioner has sought a comprehensive amendment of
the Petition incorporating expanded pleadings, extended computation up to
31.5.2024 and beyond, and additional monetary reliefs aggregating to over ₹600
crore. The reliefs and computations sought in IA No.79/IA/2023 stand subsumed
within and overtaken by the broader amendment sought in IA No. 86/IA/2024.
45. In effect, IA No. 79/IA/2023 does not survive as an independent application.
The monetary claims and additional pleadings originally sought through IA
No.79/IA/2023 have been merged into the comprehensive amendment proposed in IA
No.86/IA/2023. Accordingly, IA No. 79/IA/2023 has become infructuous and is
disposed of accordingly.
46. In view of the above discussion, the amendments sought in IA No. 86/IA/2024
are impermissible and not maintainable and do not meet the requirements under Order
VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, read with Regulation 38 of the 2023
CoB Regulations. Therefore, IA No. 86/IA/2024 filed by the Petitioner is dismissed as
not maintainable and is disposed of. Issue No.1 is accordingly decided.
Order in IA Numbers 79/IA/2023, 86/IA/2024 and 87/IA/2024 in Petition No. 117/MP/2023 Page 37 of 39

Issue No.2: Whether the interim reliefs sought in IA No. 87/IA/2024 are
allowable?
47. We have also considered the prayers and submissions of the Petitioner and
TPCL in IA No. 87/IA/2024. The reliefs sought in the said application are in the nature
of interim directions permitting adjustment of substantial monetary claims, including
alleged compensation towards alternate procurement cost and reduction in capacity
charges. The claims pressed in IA No. 87/IA/2024 are purely monetary and
compensatory in nature. The alleged injury pertains to quantifiable financial loss
arising from the procurement of alternate power and the computation of availability
under the PPA. Such claims, if ultimately found admissible, are capable of being
adjudicated and compensated at the stage of final determination, and no irreparable
harm, incapable of restitution, has been demonstrated.
48. Further, the interim relief sought is intrinsically linked to the monetary claims
sought to be introduced through IA No. 86/IA/2024. In view of our finding that such
claims are not maintainable in the present proceedings, the interim reliefs founded
thereon cannot be entertained. Permitting adjustment or deduction of amounts at this
stage would, in effect, amount to granting final relief in respect of disputed claims and
would pre-judge issues relating to the interpretation of the Section 11 directions, the
applicability of PPA provisions, and the quantification of alleged losses, all of which
require detailed adjudication.
49. The Petitioner is, however, at liberty to pursue such monetary claims in
accordance with law, including in Petition No. 107/MP/2023, which is presently
pending adjudication before this Commission. Accordingly, the interim relief sought in
IA No. 87/IA/2024 is not allowable and is therefore dismissed as not maintainable.
Issue No.2 is accordingly decided.
Order in IA Numbers 79/IA/2023, 86/IA/2024 and 87/IA/2024 in Petition No. 117/MP/2023 Page 38 of 39

50. The Petitioner is, however, at liberty to pursue its monetary claims,
restitutionary reliefs, and adjudication of its contractual rights in accordance with law.
51. Accordingly, IA Nos. 79/IA/2023, 86/IA/2024 and 87/IA/2024 are disposed of.
The main petition shall be listed for a hearing on the merits in due course.

submissions made in the Petition and submitted that the Petitioner satisfies all the

trading licence, if granted.

make an application to the Commission for grant of licence in the manner

************

(6) The Applicant shall file its reply before the Commission within 30 days

(7) The Commission after consideration of the objections or suggestions
received in response to the notice published by the Applicant and its reply
may reject the application or may propose to grant licence.
(8) When the Commission proposes to grant licence, it shall publish a notice
of its proposal in two daily newspapers, as the Commission may consider
appropriate, stating the name and address of the person to whom it proposes
to issue the licence and with such other details as the Commission considers
appropriate, to invite further objections or suggestions to its proposal.”
5. The Petitioner has submitted the application, as per Form I, along with the
requisite fees.
6. The Petitioner has uploaded the application for the grant of a trading licence
on its website in terms of Clause (3) of Regulation 6 of the Trading Licence
Regulations, 2020, and further placed on record the relevant copies of the
newspapers in original in which notice of its application has been published. As per

required to publish notices of its application within 7 days of filing, in two daily

period is on account of the replacement of the components/equipment in the

A. Replacement of 400 kV Pneumatic Operated Circuit Breakers at Bhiwadi
Substation (6 Nos.):
Circuit Breakers (CBs) of CGL make under this project are of the pneumatic-
operated type. These CBs will complete 25 years of their useful life by March
2028. Due to ageing, these CBs frequently face maintenance issues such as
pneumatic drive failures and air leakages from various parts of the mechanism,
leading to prolonged outages and causing unstable grid operation. The OEM
is taking longer to supply spares and deploy service engineers due to the
outdated model, resulting in extended outages. Since these breakers have
surpassed their useful life, it is prudent to replace these old CBs with new,
technologically advanced, and simple spring-operated CBs in a timely manner
to prevent failures that could cause consequential damage to the system.
Therefore, it is proposed to replace these old CGL CBs to ensure efficient and
secure grid operation.
B. Replacement of Old and Obsolete 400 kV and 220 kV (Make: Elpro)
Isolators at Bhiwadi (42 Sets):
The existing Elpro make isolators will complete 25 years of service by March
2028. They face issues such as frequent misalignment, jamming, improper
closing and opening, and over-traveling due to aging. Wear and tear, along
with heavy current passing during faults, have weakened the copper contacts,
causing frequent hotspots. These outdoor isolators are exposed to various
Page 24 of 64
Order in Petition No. 580/TT/2025

weather conditions like rain, fog, and summer heat. After long use, many MOM
boxes have rusted, impairing their function, which prevents motorised
operation. This results in incorrect indications, control problems, interlock
failures, and unsafe remote operation. The ageing TBs inside the MOM boxes
have become brittle, causing terminals to contact the boxes and generate DC
earth faults—damaging the control and protection systems. The deteriorating
condition of the isolators, especially their interlock and drive mechanisms,
makes them unstable during storms and high winds, sometimes causing them
to open under load, which is hazardous to the system and personnel. OEMs
are not providing spares or support due to the outdated models, and current
spares are exhausted. Consequently, it is proposed to replace 42 sets of
isolators at Bhiwadi Substation (400 kV: 12, 220 kV: 30).
C. Replacement of Old and Obsolete 400 kV and 220 kV “CGL/TELK” Make
Porcelain CTs at Bhiwadi Substation (45 Nos.):
The existing Current Transformers (CTs) are going to complete 25 years of
their useful life in March 2028. There have been oil leakages observed from
various points such as secondary terminals, primary terminals, domes, oil sight
glass, and others in many of these CTs. These oil leakages are beyond repair.
Over time, such leaks may cause low oil levels, moisture ingress, and eventual
failure. Since the CTs are hermetically sealed equipment, major repairs on-site
are not advisable. Additionally, moisture ingress necessitates the complete
replacement of active insulation parts at the manufacturer's facility, which is
not economically or technically feasible, as the manufacturer has ceased
production and repair of these types of CTs. Failure of these CTs could lead to
consequential damage to surrounding equipment and potentially cause
Page 25 of 64
Order in Petition No. 580/TT/2025

instability in grid operations. Therefore, it is proposed to replace 45 CTs at
Bhiwadi Substation (400 kV: 21, 220 kV: 24).
D. Replacement of Old and Obsolete 400 kV and 220 kV CVTs at Bhiwadi
Substation (8 Nos.):
The existing CVTs are going to complete 25 years of their useful life by March
2028. CVTs are used for protection and metering purposes. Leakage or
seepage from various points, such as the EMU tank, oil level glass, and
secondary terminal boxes, has been observed due to ageing, which has
altered the capacitance of the CVTs caused by internal failure of the capacitor
elements, leading to disruptions in secondary voltage. Since CVT secondary
output is utilised for metering and protection systems, its accuracy is crucial.
Variations in secondary voltage can result in inaccurate metering and
malfunction of protection relays on transmission elements. These CVTs are
hermetically sealed; however, moisture ingress necessitates complete
replacement of the active insulation part at the manufacturer's facility, which is
neither technically nor economically feasible. Consequently, these aged CVTs
are unreliable for their intended performance and are susceptible to failure at
any moment, risking forced outages of critically loaded feeders. Failure of
these CVTs could cause consequential damage to surrounding equipment and
destabilise grid operations. Therefore, it is proposed to replace 8 CVTs at
Bhiwadi Substation (400 kV: 4, 220 kV: 4).
E. Replacement of Old Bushings in Transformers at Bhiwadi Substation (14
Nos.):
The Petitioner operates and maintains over 3800 transformers and reactors,
many of which have been in service for more than 25 years. A significant failure
Page 26 of 64
Order in Petition No. 580/TT/2025

mode in transformers/reactors is the failure of bushings. The following are the
main inputs compiled from various CIGRE Technical Brochures as well as
industry practices.
➢ According to CIGRE TB 642, bushing failure is the third most common
reason for transformer failure worldwide, after winding and OLTC failure.
In the Indian context, failures due to bushings are even more significant
owing to manufacturing issues observed in certain makes of bushings.
➢ CIGRE TB 887 (Life Extension of Oil-Filled Transformers and Shunt
Reactors) recommends the strategic replacement of bushings, which can
positively impact transformer reliability and potentially extend the
transformer's lifespan. It also offers a general guideline that bushings
should be replaced once during the transformer's operational life.
➢ CIGRE TB 755 (Transformer Bushing Reliability) states that an incipient
bushing fault can develop into failure either rapidly (within 1 ms) or
gradually (over 10 years), and no diagnostic method, whether online or
offline, exists that can prevent such quickly developing incipient failures.
➢ From 2015 onwards, Resin Impregnated Paper/Synthetic (RIP/RIS)
bushings have been specified in PGCIL instead of Oil Impregnated Paper
(OIP) bushings. The Central Electricity Authority (CEA) has also mandated
the use of RIP/RIS bushings (HV & IV) for 400 kV transformers and
reactors, and OIP/RIP/RIS bushings for LV. This is due to lower
consequential damage if RIP/RIS bushings fail. Domestic manufacturing
of RIP/RIS bushings has recently begun under the Make in India initiative.
In view of the above, we may conclude that older bushings, which have been
in service for more than 25 years and are nearing the end of their useful life,
Page 27 of 64
Order in Petition No. 580/TT/2025

pose a potential hazard to the transformer/reactor. Additionally, these bushings
are all OIP type, which can cause transformer/reactor failure. In the past,
bushing failures have resulted in transformer failures at many substations.
Therefore, it is advisable to take pre-emptive action to replace such bushings.
Consequently, it is proposed to replace 14 transformer bushings at Bhiwadi
Substation, which will exceed their useful life during the current 2024-29 tariff
period.
F. Supply and Installation of 400 kV Bus Bar Protection, LBB and A/R Relays
at Bhiwadi Substation:
These relays are going to complete 25 years of their useful life by March, 2028.
They are of electro-magnetic/static type and obsolete. The OEMs have phased
out these models of relays, and there is no spare support. In case of non-
availability of healthy spares, the relays are to be kept out of service to avoid
mal-operation, and the only option is replacement. Due to ageing, mal-
operation or non-operation occurs because of stuck contacts and coil issues.
These relays are not IEC 61850 compliant and lack built-in DR and time
synchronisation features, leading to challenges in fault analysis. These relays
do not have remote access facilities, causing difficulty in remote operation. In
view of the above, it is proposed to replace these old relays with numerical
relays.
G. Renovation of Firefighting System at Bhiwadi Substation:
The pipelines in the current firefighting systems are laid underground, and due
to ageing, the anti-rusting coating on the pipes has worn out, causing rust and
frequent, persistent leaks. Identifying and fixing these leaks is a tedious, time-
consuming process, often taking the systems out of service for extended

periods, which risks fire protection for ICT/Reactor. Additionally, because of
their long service life, components such as pumps, motors, deluge valves, and
sluice valves are experiencing wear, rust, and failure, resulting in unreliable
operation. The existing firefighting and fire alarm systems will reach 25 years
of service by March 2025. Since the equipment is very old, the design has
become outdated, and spare parts are no longer available. Given the
importance of the fire protection system, it is crucial to keep it operational at all
times with minimal maintenance. Therefore, it is proposed to replace the old,

units following the latest specifications.
H. Replacement of 220V and 48V Battery Charger at Bhiwadi Substation (4
Nos.):
The 220V system is used for control and protection, while the 48V is used for
the PLCC system; both play a vital role in the protection system. The battery
chargers are the main source to keep the DC system healthy. These battery
chargers are going to complete 25 years of their useful life by March, 2028. A
lot of issues are being faced with chargers because of their obsolete design,
and timely spare parts and service support are not available. Due to unreliable
charger service, the protection system always remains at risk, especially during
an outage of auxiliary power. Furthermore, due to ageing, the TBs of the
charger panels have become brittle and prone to DC leakages. For the proper
functioning of the protection system, the health of the 220V and 48V battery
charger system is essential. Hence, in view of the above, it is proposed to
replace the old and obsolete battery chargers with new, latest battery chargers
at Bhiwadi Substation.

I. Replacement of OLD DG Sets at Bhiwadi Substation:

Regulations 25(2)(a) and 25(2)(c) of the 2024 Tariff Regulations. Regulation 25(2) of the
2024 Tariff Regulations provides as follows:
“(a) Assets whose useful life is not commensurate with the useful life of the project and such
assets have been fully depreciated in accordance with the provisions of these regulations;
(b) The replacement of the asset or equipment is necessary on account of a change in law or
Force Majeure conditions;
(c) The replacement of such asset or equipment is necessary on account of obsolescence of
technology; and
(d) The replacement of such asset or equipment has otherwise been allowed by the
Commission.

(e) The additional expenditure, excluding recurring expenses covered in O&M expenses,
involved in relation to the renewal of lease of lease hold land on case to case basis.”
Provided that any claim of additional capitalisation with respect to the replacement of assets under
the original scope and on account of obsolescence of technology, less than Rs. 20 lakhs shall not
be considered as part of Capital cost and shall be met through normative O&M expenses.”
52. We think it proper here to refer to Regulations 3(24) and 3(62) of the 2024 Tariff
Regulations, which provide as follows:
Regulation 3(24) of the 2024 Tariff Regulations
“(24) 'Element' means an asset which has been distinctively defined under the scope of the
transmission project in the Investment Approval, such as transmission lines, including line bays
and line reactors, substations, bays, compensation devices, Interconnecting Transformers which
can be put to use.”
Regulation 3(62) of the 2024 Tariff Regulations
“62) 'Project' means:
i) in the case of a thermal generating station, all components of the thermal generating station
and including an integrated coal mine, biomass pellet handling system, pollution control system,
and effluent treatment plan, as may be required;
ii) in the case of a hydro generating station, all components of the hydro generating station
including the dam, intake water conductor system, power generating station, as apportioned to
power generation; and
iii) in case of transmission, all components of the transmission system, including the
communication system;”
53. As per the proviso under Regulation 25(2) of the 2024 Tariff Regulations, any ACE
with respect to the replacement of assets under the original scope on account of the
obsolescence of technology of less than ₹20 lakh shall not be considered as part of the
capital cost. In the instant case, the Petitioner is replacing certain substation equipment and
components on account of the obsolescence of technology.
54. The Petitioner has claimed the ACE under the head of a “New Element.” However,
as discussed above, it is observed that in the present Petition, the Petitioner has only
proposed the replacement of certain equipment of the existing transmission asset, not the
replacement or creation of an entire transmission asset as a separate element. Therefore,
the ACE claimed by the Petitioner cannot be classified as a “New Element.” Accordingly,
the said expenditure shall be regarded as ACE related to the existing transmission asset

and will be examined in accordance with the applicable provisions of the Tariff Regulations
governing ACE for Existing Assets.

CENTRAL ELECTRICITY REGULATORY COMMISSION
NEW DELHI

Date of Order: 2nd June, 2026
In the matter of:
Petition under Sections 79(1)(c) and 79(1)(k) of the Electricity Act, 2003 read with
Regulation 19(3) of the CERC (Indian Electricity Grid Code) (First Amendment)
Regulations, 2024 (seeking extension of time for infirm power injection); and Regulation
57 of the CERC (Indian Electricity Grid Code) Regulations, 2023 read with Regulation 65
of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Conduct of Business) Regulations, 2023,
seeking relaxation/extension of the time prescribed for filing the present petition.
And in the matter of:
JSW Renew Energy Ltd.
JSW Centre, Bandra Kurla Complex,
Bandra (E), Mumbai – 400051 ……Petitioner
Versus
