Bangalore – 560009
2. Solar Energy Corporation of India Limited (SECI)
6th Floor, Plate-B, NBCC Office, Block Tower 2,
East Kidwai Nagar, Kidwai Nagar, New Delhi, Delhi – 110023
.…Respondents
Parties Present: Shri Aman Anand, Advocate, JSWREL
Shri Aman Dixit, Advocate, JSWREL
Order in Petition No. 178/MP/2026 Page 1

Ms. Natasha Debroy, Advocate, JSWREL
Ms. Srishti Gupta, Advocate, JSWREL
Shri Nadim Ahmad, SRLDC
Shri Suresh Raj, SRLDC
Shri Phanindra, SRLDC
Shri Alok Mishra, SRLDC
Ms. B S Shruthi, SRLDC
ORDER
The present Petition has been filed by the JSW Renew Energy Ltd. (hereinafter
referred to as the “Petitioner”) seeking extension of time for injection of infirm power under
Regulation 19(3) of the CERC (Indian Electricity Grid Code) Regulations, 2023, for
conducting PPC testing and commissioning in respect of 10 Wind Turbine Generators
(WTGs) (27 MW) forming part of its 270 MW wind power project and relaxation of the time
prescribed for filing the present petition. The Petitioner has made the following prayers:
(a) Grant extension of time for injection of infirm power in respect of the balance 10 WTG Nos.
LOT-5 Req Id (DPM-064, DPM-065, DPM-066, DPM-067, DPM068, DPM-069, DPM-070,
DPM-072, DPM-073, DPM-074) for conducting PPC (Power Plant Controller) Testing of the
Petitioner's wind power project; and permit 30 days to the petitioner to commission the said
WTGs;
(b) Direct the SRLDC to permit injection of infirm power during the extended period for the purpose
of conducting PPC Testing and commissioning;
(c) Condone the delay, of 67 days, in filing the present Petition;
(d) Pass any order(s) that it may deems fit in the interest of justice.
Submission of the Petitioner:
2. The Petitioner has mainly submitted as under:
(a) The Petitioner is developing a wind power project of an aggregate capacity of 270 MW
in the State of Tamil Nadu.
(b) CTUIL granted LTA to the Petitioner for 100 MW and 170 MW, respectively, for the
injection of power at Karur PS, Tamil Nadu, on 03.02.2022 and 14.02.2023. CTUIL
issued final connectivity to the Petitioner on 29.11.2024 for 150 MW of exportable
capacity. The total capacity to be commissioned in this phase is 189 MW (70 * 2.7
MW).
(c) Out of the total capacity of 189 MW, 162 MW (60*2.7 MW) has been commissioned
after successfully trial run tests. Out of 70 WTGs in the present phase, 60 WTGs are
Order in Petition No. 178/MP/2026 Page 2

commissioned.
(d) The Petitioner was granted FTC approval by SRLDC for the 10 WTGs in question as
part of FTC approval for the larger quantum of 91.8 MW (34 * 2.7 MW) on 17.09.2025.
The Petitioner was permitted infirm power injection for pre-commissioning testing for a
period of 45 days, i.e. up to 01.11 .2025. The said WTGs were put under trial operation;
however, the commercial operation declaration for the subject 10 WTGs could not be
completed. During PPC functionality testing, a critical piece of imported equipment,
i.e., the 4th sub-controller, failed, rendering the test incomplete and invalid.
(e) The replacement of the sub-controller was received only by the 3rd week of January
2026. After importing the PPC replacement equipment and integrating it with the
system, the Petitioner vide letter dated 13.03.2026 requested SRLDC for an extension
of infirm power injection for a period of 30 days, since the stipulated date had expired
on 01.11.2025.
(f) The SRLDC vide email dated 18.03.2026 pointed out that the power to grant extension
for injection of infirm power during the pre-commissioning and testing phase is
available with SRLDC for a maximum period of 135 days (i.e. expired on 30.01.2026),
beyond which it is only this Commission that can permit infirm power injection in the
pre-commissioning and testing phase.
(g) In terms of proviso (b) of Regulation 19(3) of the Grid Code, the present Petition should
have been filed 15 days prior to expiry of the earlier approved period of infirm injection,
i.e. on 15.01.2026. The present Petition is being filed on 24.03.2026 after a delay of
67 days, and the Petitioner therefore seeks condonation of the delay in filing the instant
petition under the Commission's power to relax.
(h) The delay in completion of energisation activities for the balance WTGs has occurred
due to uncontrollable factors, which were entirely beyond the control of the Petitioner.
The Petitioner has successfully commissioned the majority of the Project capacity,
remobilised resources at the site, and is fully ready to energise the remaining WTGs
and complete all pre-commissioning and commissioning activities within the extended
period sought, i.e., 30 days.
(i) The denial of extension for injection of infirm power would result in stranding of 27 MW
of wind capacity only due to procedural constraints, which would neither serve grid
Order in Petition No. 178/MP/2026 Page 3

security nor be in the interest of consumers, the transmission system or the renewable
energy sector. Grant of the limited extension sought would, on the other hand, facilitate
orderly commissioning of the balance WTGs and enable achievement of Commercial
Operation.
Hearing dated 22.04.2026:
3. The extracts of the Record of Proceedings for the hearing dated 22.04.2026 are as
under:
“Learned senior counsel for the Petitioners submitted that the present petition has been filed
seeking extension of time for Infirm Power Injection and for relaxation/ extension of the time
prescribed for filing the present Petition. Learned counsel further submitted that, in the first
phase, 70 WTGs were to be commissioned, and out of those, 60 WTGs have been
commissioned. However, the remaining 10 WTGs could not be commissioned as one sub-
controller of the power plant controller system failed. Learned counsel further pointed out that
SRLDC does not have the power to grant an extension for infirm power injection beyond 135
days and requested the Commission for an extension of 30 days to conduct tests and
commission the said capacity.
2. Learned counsel for SRLDC accepted the notice and further submitted that SRLDC has
already granted the extension within its purview as per the Grid Code and that the Commission
may consider the prayer for further extension as deemed fit.
3. Considering the submissions made by the learned counsel and the representative for the
parties, the Commission directed as under:
(a) The Petitioner to implead SECI as party to the Petition and to file revised memo of parties
within two days.
(b) Admit and issue notice.
(c) The Respondents, including SECI were directed to file their respective replies within two
weeks with an advance copy to the Petitioner who may file its rejoinder, if any, within a
week thereafter
(d) The Petitioner to file the following information, on an affidavit, within a week:
(i) The date when the PPC functionality testing for the 10 WTGs (27 MW) failed and
also the date when the PPC replacement and integration was completed along with
supporting documents.
(ii) COD Certificate in respect of 162 MW capacity out of 189 MW.”
Submissions of the Petitioner in Compliance to the RoP for hearing dated
22.04.2026:
4. The Petitioner has impleaded SECI as a party to the present Petition and furnished the
COD certificate of 162 MW capacity. Petitioner has also submitted that the PPC
Order in Petition No. 178/MP/2026 Page 4

functionality testing for the 10 WTGs (27 MW) failed on 27.09.2025. Thereafter, the
purchase order for replacement was placed on 27.11.2025. The replacement sub-
controller was received on 25.01.2026, and validation was completed only on
28.02.2026.
Hearing dated 12.05.2026:
5. The learned counsel for the Petitioner submitted that the Petitioner has complied with
the directions issued vide the Record of Proceedings dated 22.4.2026 and furnished
the additional information sought therein, and none of the Respondents has filed any
reply. Considering the submissions made by the Petitioner, the Commission reserved
the matter for orders.
Analysis and Decision:
6. The Petitioner has submitted that it is developing a 270 MW wind power project in Tamil
Nadu. Out of 270 MW, 189 MW is being developed in this phase. While 162 MW
capacity has been successfully commissioned following successful trial runs, the
remaining 27 MW (10 WTGs x 2.7 MW) could not achieve its COD, as during PPC
functionality testing, a critical, i.e. imported 4th sub-controller failed on 27.09.2025. FTC
approval by SRLDC for the 10 WTGs in question, as part of FTC approval for the larger
quantum of 91.8 MW, was issued on 17.09.2025. The Petitioner was permitted infirm
power injection for pre-commissioning testing for a period of 45 days, i.e. up to
01.11.2025. The replacement equipment was received on 25.01.2026, and its
validation was completed on 28.02.2026.
7. The Petitioner is seeking an extension of time to inject infirm power for a period of 30
days. Further, the Petitioner has submitted that in terms of proviso (b) of Regulation
19(3) of the Grid Code, the present Petition should have been filed 15 days prior to
expiry of the earlier approved period of infirm injection, i.e. on 15.01.2026. The present
Petition was, however, filed on 24.03.2026, with a delay of 67 days; therefore, the
Petitioner seeks condonation of the delay in filing the instant petition.
8. We have considered the submissions of Petitioner and documents placed on the
record.
9. The issue that arises for our consideration is as under:
Order in Petition No. 178/MP/2026 Page 5

Issue 1: Whether the delay in filing the instant Petition can be condoned?
Whether the Petitioner can be granted an extension of time for the injection of
infirm power for testing and commissioning of 10 WTGs (10*2.7 MW)?
10. The above issue is dealt with in subsequent paragraphs.
11. The relevant extracts of the 2023 Grid Code are as under:
“19. DRAWAL OF START UP POWER AND INJECTION OF INFIRM POWER
(1) A unit of a generating station including unit of a captive generating plant that has been
granted connectivity to the inter-State Transmission System in accordance with GNA
Regulations shall be allowed to inter-change power with the grid during the
commissioning period, including testing and full load testing before the COD, after
obtaining prior permission of the concerned Regional Load Despatch Centre:
Provided that the concerned Regional Load Despatch Centre while granting such
permission shall keep grid security in view.
(2) The period for which such inter-change shall be allowed shall be as follows:
(a) Drawal of start-up power shall not exceed 15 months prior to the expected date of
first synchronization and one year after the date of first synchronization; and
(b) Injection of infirm power shall not exceed one year from the date of first
synchronization for generating stations other than REGS and ESS (except Hydro
PSP ESS).
(c) Injection of infirm power shall not exceed 45 (forty-five) days from the date
of first time energization and integration (FTC) approval for REGS and ESS
(except Hydro PSP ESS)
(3) Notwithstanding the provisions of clause (2) of this Regulation, the Commission may
allow extension of the period for inter-change of power beyond the stipulated period on
an application made by the generating station at least two months in advance of the
completion of the stipulated period:
Provided that for REGS and ESS (except Hydro PSP ESS), extension of period for
injection of infirm power beyond the stipulated period may be allowed (a) for a
period up to three months by respective RLDC on an application(s) made by such
generating station or ESS(except Hydro PSP ESS) to respective RLDC along with
detailed reasons, at least 10 days in advance of the completion of the stipulated period,
(b) for a period beyond three months, by the Commission on an application(s)
made by such generating station or ESS(except Hydro PSP ESS) along with
detailed reasons, at least 15 days in advance of the completion of the stipulated
period.”
As per the above, in case of REGS, injection of infirm power is allowed for 45 (forty-
five) days from the date of FTC approval. Beyond a period of 45 days, an extension of
up to three months may be granted by the concerned RLDC. Extension beyond three
months may be allowed by the Commission, and the application for such a request is
to be made 15 days in advance of the completion of the three-month extension period
Order in Petition No. 178/MP/2026 Page 6

under the purview of RLDC.
12. We observe that in the present case, the FTC approval for 10 WTGs (10*2.7 MW) was
granted by SRLDC on 17.09.2025, and in terms of Regulation 19(2)(c) of the Grid Code,
the Petitioner was permitted for injection of infirm power for 45 days, i.e. up to
01.11.2025. We observe that Petitioner, vide its letter dated 13.03.2026, approached
the SRLDC seeking extension of the infirm power injection. The relevant extract is as
under:
“This is with reference to the FTC approval dated 17.09.2025 for 10 WTGs, for which the
infirm injection validity was up to 01.11.2025.
We would like to apprise that, Project had already obtained TOC for 60 WTGs of each
2.7MW Senvion Make and subsequently TOC application made for last 10 WTGs of
Senvion Make 2.7MW capacity each. Successful Trial Operation was performed and Power
Corroboration Test and requisite details was submitted to SRLDC FTC portal by dated 26-
Sep-25. However, PPC testing could not be completed due to some unavoidable
circumstances.
As per Clause 19.3 of the Indian Electricity Grid Code (IEGC) 2023 (and subsequent
amendments), RLDC is empowered to grant an extension of up to three months for infirm
injection. In this regard, we request SRLDC to kindly grant an extension of the infirm
injection period for next 30 days to complete the pending PPC testing and if any requirement
from SRLDC with 189MW installed capacity comprises of 70 WTGs (60 Commissioned and
10 Under Trial Operation).”
As per the above, Petitioner requested SRLDC for an extension of the infirm injection
period by 30 days to complete the pending PPC testing.
13. We also observe that in response to the Petitioner’s letter dated 13.03.2026, SRLDC
vide e-mail dated 18.03.2026 responded as follows:
“It is to inform that the provisions governing the injection of infirm power are specified
under Clause 2(c) and Clause 3 of Regulation 19 of the IEGC Regulations 2023 and
are as follows
…..
In accordance with the above provisions, SRLDC had permitted the injection of infirm
power from 17-09-2025 to 01-11-2025 i.e for 45 days from the issuance of FTC
approval. Subsequently, no request was received from JSW Renew Energy Limited
seeking extension of the infirm power injection. It is pertinent to mention that, had such
a request been submitted, SRLDC could have considered granting an extension up to
30.01.2026 (i.e., up to 135 days from FTC approval). However, as per the prevailing
regulations, extension of the infirm injection period beyond 135 days does not fall within
the purview of SRLDC and requires approval from the Commission.
As per the above, SRLDC did not grant permission, considering that the Petitioner
approached SRLDC on 13.03.26, which is beyond 30.1.2026 (3 months from the expiry
of the 45-day period).
Order in Petition No. 178/MP/2026 Page 7

14. The Petitioner has prayed for the condonation of the delay in filing the instant Petition,
invoking the Commission's power to relax under Regulation 57 of the Grid Code. We
note that the Petitioner should have approached RLDC 10 days prior to 1.11.2025, as
per the Grid Code, seeking an extension of the period if it was envisaged that it would
not be able to achieve COD by the stipulated period. PPC testing failed on 27.9.2025,
well before 21.10.2025, when the Petitioner should have approached the RLDC.
However, Petitioner approached RLDC as late as March 2026. We are of the
considered view that the Petitioner, once having obtained FTC from RLDC, should have
informed RLDC about its inability to complete the commissioning within the stipulated
period. Petitioner is directed to keep RLDC informed of any such event and the tentative
time by which it expects to resolve the issue.
15. Keeping in view that the Petitioner is in the advanced stage of commissioning of its
project, we condone the delay in filing the instant Petition. Further, we permit the
Petitioner an extension of the period for injection of infirm power for a period of 30 days
from the date of issuance of this Order under Regulation 19(3) of the Grid Code. The
events impacting commissioning activities are acknowledged only to allow extension of
the infirm of power under the Grid Code, and not otherwise.
16. Petition No. 178/MP/2026 stands disposed of in terms of the above.

(e) Pass such other orders as this Hon’ble Commission deems fit.”
3. The Petitioners further filed Interlocutory Application No. 55/IA/2022 along with
the petition seeking a stay on levy and recovery of the transmission charges raised by
CTUIL and issuance of appropriate directions to CTUIL to not take any coercive steps
against the Petitioners during the pendency of the present petition. The Commission,
vide the Record of the Proceedings (RoP) dated 24.1.2023, directed the Petitioners to
pay 10% of the outstanding transmission charges to CTUIL within a week and directed
CTUIL not to take any coercive measures until the next date of hearing. Accordingly,
the IA No. 55/IA/2022 was disposed of.
4. The Petitioners have also filed IA No. 18/IA/2025 on 19.2.2025 to place on
record the subsequent developments and permit the Petitioners to make oral
submissions. The same was allowed by the Commission, and the said IA was
disposed of vide RoP dated 7.8.2025.
5. ReNew AP2, Petitioner No.1, is a generating company incorporated for the
supply of contracted capacity of 100 MW to SECI from its proposed wind-based power
Project to be set up in Kutch, Gujarat (“100 MW Project”). RPPL, Petitioner No. 2, is
the parent company of ReNew AP2 and has executed the LTAA Tranche 1 dated
29.1.2018 and LTAA Tranche 2 dated 6.9.2018 with PGCIL for a total quantum of 100
MW for the evacuation of power from the proposed 100 MW Wind Power Project.
6. CTUIL, Respondent No.1, is the Central Transmission Utility within the meaning
of Section 38 of the Act, undertaking transmission of electricity through the Inter-State
Transmission System and discharging inter alia, functions of planning and
coordination relating to ISTS with all concerned authorities. PGCIL, Respondent No.
Order in Petition No. 227/MP/2022
Page 3 of 46

2, is a deemed transmission licensee under the Act and was also performing the
functions of CTU under Section 38 of the Act till the formation of CTUIL. SECI,
Respondent No. 3, is a Government of India enterprise under the Ministry of New and
Renewable Energy ("MNRE") having the main objective to assist MNRE and function
as the implementing and facilitating arm of the National Solar Mission ("NSM") for
development, promotion and commercialisation of solar energy technologies in the
country.
7. The instant petition was admitted on 20.10.2022, and notices were issued to
the Respondents. CTUIL filed its reply to the petition vide affidavit dated 29.12.2022,
to which the Petitioners filed a rejoinder dated 8.2.2023. In compliance with the
directions in Record of Proceedings (RoP) dated 24.1.2023, the Petitioners have filed
an affidavit dated 20.2.2023, and CTUIL filed an affidavit dated 1.4.2023. CTUIL has
also filed an affidavit dated 13.10.2023 in compliance with RoP dated 13.9.2023. The
Petitioners have filed an affidavit dated 1.11.2023 in compliance with RoP dated
9.10.2023. CTUIL has filed an additional affidavit dated 10.5.2024 in compliance with
RoP dated 19.4.2024, and an additional affidavit dated 17.1.2025 in compliance with
RoP dated 13.1.2025. CTUIL has also filed Written Submissions dated 6.2.2025. The
Petitioners have filed Written Submissions dated 28.8.2025.
8. The Petitioners, ReNew AP2 and RPPL, have made the following submissions:
a) On 15.4.2016, RPPL applied for connectivity for 400 MW for the proposed
wind power-based projects in Bhuvad, Kutch District, Gujarat. PGCIL granted
connectivity to RPVPL on 29.7.2016, for 400 MW at PGCIL’s 400/220 kV
Bhachau Sub-station, and the same was to be made effective from 15.12.2017.
Further, on 12.1.2018, SECI issued a Request for Selection (“RfS”) for the
setting up of 2000 MW ISTS-Connected Wind Power Projects (“SECI Tranche
III”). As per clause 3.17 of the RfS, the project was required to be commissioned
within 18 months from the effective date of the PPA.
Order in Petition No. 227/MP/2022
Page 4 of 46

on 8.3.2019, GoG issued a clarification stating that revenue land would be
allotted to companies that have won wind bids, whether by GUVNL, SECI, or
other agencies of the Government of India, and supported by a letter to that
effect from GEDA.
l) On 7.8.2019, ReNew AP2 sought an extension in SCOD from SECI till
December 2020, for the entire 400 MW project due to delay in attaining FC on
account of delay in land allotment by GoG. On 22.10.2019, MNRE issued a
letter recognising the delays the developers faced in procuring land and held
that the period between the date of application and the grant of approval for
land, minus 90 days, should be considered for the extension of SCOD. On
27.11.2019, ReNew AP2 again requested an SCOD extension from SECI. On
9.12.2019, ReNew AP2 submitted a note to SECI seeking a 15-month
extension of SCOD, i.e., up to February 2021, stating that it had applied for the
requisite land on 2.6.2018 and that the allotment remained pending due to
delays in GoG’s land allocation process. On 3.2.2020, SECI granted an
extension of SCOD for the 400 MW Project from 24.11.2019 to 31.3.2021.
m) On 15.1.2021, to address the mismatch between extensions granted for
SCOD and commencement/ operationalisation of LTA, MoP issued directions
to the Commission under Section 107 of the Act to amend the Central Electricity
Regulatory Commission (Sharing of Inter-State Transmission Charges and
Losses) Regulations, 2020 (“2020 Sharing Regulations”) so as to provide
exemption to the eligible projects impacted by force majeure, from payment of
transmission charges. On 15.1.2021, MoP also issued an order in supersession
of its previous orders dated 13.2.2018, 9.11.2019 and 5.8.2020 providing that
(i) no ISTS charges will be levied on transmission of the electricity generated
from solar or wind power plants for a period of 25 years from the date of
commissioning for all plants commissioned up to 30.6.2023 and (ii) where a
renewable energy generation capacity which is eligible for ISTS waiver in terms
of the extant orders, is granted extension in COD by the competent authority on
account of force majeure, the commencement and the period of the LTA shall
also get extended accordingly, and it will be deemed that the period of ISTS
waiver is extended by the said period. This position was again clarified by MoP
vide orders dated 23.11.2021 and 30.11.2021.
n) Further, the Ministry of Finance, vide OM dated 19.2.2020, designated
COVID-19 as a ‘Natural Calamity’. On 20.3.2020, MNRE issued an OM
directing agencies such as NTPC and SECI to treat delays in project
construction or commissioning caused by supply chain disruptions resulting
from the Covid-19 outbreak in China or elsewhere as force majeure events. On
24.3.2020, the Ministry of Home Affairs imposed a nationwide lockdown till
14.4.2020, which was extended vide orders dated 15.4.2020, 1.5.2020,
17.5.2020 and 30.5.2020.
Order in Petition No. 227/MP/2022
Page 7 of 46

s) Further, ReNew AP2 acted in a prudent manner by applying for the Project
sites well in advance in terms of GoG’s 2004 Land Policy. However, due to a
change in GoG policy, land for the 100 MW Project has not been provided. In
Vaayu Renewable Energy (Kaveri) Pvt. Ltd. v. CERC & Ors., it was held that
the delay in performance of obligations under the respective 100 MW PPAs, on
account of a change in the GoG Land Policy, was not under the control of the
WPDs. Further, the cases of MD, Army Welfare Housing Organisation v.
Sumangal Services (P) Ltd.; Commissioner of Customs (Imports) v. Tullow
India Operation Ltd. are relevant in the matter.
t) Due to the change in GoG’s land policy in April 2018, all pending allotments
were halted, compelling ReNew AP2 to reapply for 39 sites. Despite timely
action, by 6.2.2022, only 29 of 103 locations had been allotted, resulting in an
over 40-month delay in securing the requisite land for the 100 MW Project.
Further, the Hon’ble Supreme Court has recognised the concept of frustration
and impossibility of performance under Section 56 of the Indian Contract Act in
the cases of Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur & Co. and Anr (AIR 1954
SC 44); Mugneeram Bangur and Co. v. Gurbachan Singh, (1965) 2 SCR 630;
Naihati Jute Mills Ltd Versus Khyaliram Jagannath, (AIR 1968 SC 522);
Managing Director, Army Welfare Housing Organisation v. Sumangal Services
(Pvt) Ltd. (2004) 9 SCC 619; Energy Watchdog v. Central Electricity Regulatory
Commission, (2017) 14 SCC 80.
u) Through MoP orders dated 15.1.2021, 23.11.2021, and 30.11.2021, and
MoP directions to the Commission dated 15.1.2021 under Section 107 of the
Act, the timelines under the LTAA and the PPA were interconnected and it was
directed that whenever a renewable energy project is granted an extension of
its SCOD by the competent authority (such as SECI) on the ground of force
majeure, the commencement and duration of its LTA should also be extended.
Further, in Appeal Nos. 260 and 261 of 2022 (ACME Deoghar Solar Power Ltd.
& Ors. v. CERC & Ors.), APTEL granted a stay on the recovery of transmission
charges from the solar developer and observed that due effect must be given
to the MoP’s orders and Section 107 directions dated 15.1.2021 linking LTA
timelines with SCOD extensions.
v) The force majeure events continued even after 31.8.2021 (i.e., the extension
granted by SECI on account of force majeure) since the land was not made
available to ReNew AP2 by GoG. Therefore, since the force majeure events
continued, relief under MoP’s Section 107 directions dated 15.1.2021 should
not be limited to revised SCOD; rather, it should be directed that RPPL is not
liable to pay the transmission charges on account of continued force majeure.
Other relevant case law in the matter is Dhanrajamal Gobindram v. Shamji
Kalidas & Co., (1961) 3 SCR 1020; Appeal No. 17 of 2019, titled NRSS XXXI(B)
Transmission Ltd. v. CERC & Ors.
Order in Petition No. 227/MP/2022
Page 9 of 46

w) As per Regulation 13(1)(c) of the 2020 Sharing Regulations, no transmission
charges and losses for the use of ISTS are payable by generating companies
for the generation of power from solar and wind power resources that are
commissioned up to 31.12.2022. Further, under Regulation 13(3) of the said
Regulations, solar or wind generating stations are liable to pay transmission
charges only if the COD of the generating station is delayed and the associated
transmission system has been commissioned. SECI acknowledged that the
delays were beyond ReNew AP2’s control and granted an extension of SCOD
to 31.8.2021 from the original SCOD of 24.11.2019.
x) Even assuming that CTUIL could levy transmission charges, such liability
could arise only after the revised SCOD of 31.8.2021, as the commencement
of LTA was deemed extended up to that date as per MoP’s orders and Section
107 Directions dated 15.1.2021. The issue of aligning LTA commencement with
SCOD is presently under consideration before APTEL in ACME Deoghar Solar
Power Pvt. Ltd. (Appeal No. 261/2022), ACME Phalodi Solar Energy Pvt. Ltd.
(Appeal No. 260/2022), and Sprng Renewable Energy Pvt. Ltd. (Appeal No.
236/2022), where the Tribunal has stayed CTUIL’s recovery of transmission
charges. Given the identical issue, the Commission should similarly stay the
recovery of such charges in the present case pending final adjudication.
y) Moreover, CTUIL has computed transmission charges for the period of
November 2019 to October 2020 based on the 2010 Sharing Regulations,
which is incorrect and contrary to law, as it ought to have been computed as
per the law existing as on the date of raising the bills, i.e., 2020 Sharing
Regulations.
9. The gist of the submissions made by CTUIL in its reply is as follows:
a) In Petition No.195/MP/2019, Vivid Solaire Energy Private Limited v. PGCIL
& Ors.; Petition No. 525/MP/2020, Sprng Renewable Energy Private Limited v.
CTUIL & Ors. and Petition Nos. 103/MP/2021 and Ors., ACME Deoghar Solar
Power Private Limited v. PGCIL & Ors., the Commission has held that: (i) there
is no linkage between a PPA and the LTAA/ BPTA and the rights/obligations
arising out of a PPA cannot affect the obligations under the LTAA (ii) since the
start date of LTA is fixed as per the request of the LTA applicant, it is the
responsibility of the LTA grantee to match the commissioning under the LTAA
(iii) notwithstanding that the provisions of the TSA become operative only upon
operationalisation of the LTA, in the absence of a notice of force majeure under
clause 14 of the TSA, no relief on that account can be claimed by either party
to the TSA (iv) the waiver of transmission charges as per MoP’s OMs and the
provisions of the Sharing Regulations is only applicable after commencement
of power supply i.e. after the COD of the generating station. For the period when
LTA is operationalised but the generation project has not yet been declared
Order in Petition No. 227/MP/2022
Page 10 of 46

commercial, the generating company is liable to bear the applicable
transmission charges until its COD, as per the applicable Sharing Regulations.
However, the orders of the Commission in Sprng Renewable Energy Private
Limited v. CTUIL & Ors. and ACME Deoghar Solar Power Private Limited v.
PGCIL & Ors. have been challenged before APTEL in Appeal No 236/2022
[against order dated 23.5.2022] and Appeal Nos. 260/2022 and 261/2022
[against order dated 8.6.2022], and APTEL has directed that no precipitative
actions be taken by both parties till further orders.
b) The aforesaid directions of APTEL are prima facie observations, and the
orders passed by the Commission continue to have a binding force in law till
the Appeals filed against the same are decided, and the orders are quashed/set
aside by APTEL. Further, at the 24th JCC Meeting held on 25.6.2019, CTUIL
informed the Petitioners that the 300 MW LTA had become effective w.e.f.
1.5.2019, and the Petitioners are liable for payment of transmission charges. In
the 25th JCC Meeting held on 26.9.2019, the Petitioners were once again
informed by CTUIL that the LTA of 50 MW was to be operationalised w.e.f.
23.11.2019.
c) With the operationalisation of the 50 MW LTA w.e.f. 23.11.2019 and the 300
MW w.e.f. 1.5.2019, ReNew AP2 and RPPL were required to bear the
transmission charges for the same till the COD of their generation projects, and
thereafter, in terms of the waiver of transmission charges for RE-based
generation projects, no transmission charges were payable by them.
Accordingly, upon the operationalisation of the said LTAs, CTUIL raised the
invoices till the billing period of November, 2022.
d) The said charges were computed by CTUIL in accordance with the 2010
Sharing Regulations for the period prior to November, 2020 and in terms of the
2020 Sharing Regulations w.e.f. November, 2020. The said methodology is in
accordance with the order dated 23.5.2022 passed by the Commission in
Petition No.525/MP/2020, whereunder, the Commission had approved the
methodology of computation of transmission charges from the
operationalisation of LTA till COD of its generating station in two parts, i.e., the
period falling under the 2010 Sharing Regulations, and the period falling under
the 2020 Sharing Regulations.
e) RPPL contended, vide letter dated 2.8.2022, that CTUIL had wrongly levied
the transmission charges as the Transmission Agreements were frustrated on
account of the termination of the PPA. However, the Petitioners neither sought
to surrender the connectivity nor to relinquish the LTA. Further, the obligations
of RPPL and ReNew AP2 under the PPAs were independent of their obligations
under the Transmission Agreements, which were separate and distinct
agreements.
Order in Petition No. 227/MP/2022
Page 11 of 46

f) The Transmission Agreements between the Petitioners and CTUIL relate to
the transmission system arrangement, its implementation and servicing through
payment of transmission charges and the respective rights and obligations of
the parties. The said Agreements do not contain any reference to the supply
arrangements (PPAs) between the generator and its beneficiaries, and none of
the obligations thereunder is subject to the due performance of obligations
under the supply agreements. The supply agreements (PPAs) and the
Transmission Agreements may record their own separate force majeure
clauses, and each of these force majeure clauses operates within its agreed
sphere, and the occurrence of a force majeure event under the supply
agreement cannot have a cascading effect upon the obligations under the
Transmission Agreements or vice versa.
g) Further, under Section 10(3) of the Act, a generator is required to coordinate
with the CTU/STU for transmission of electricity generated by it. Section 38(2)
of the Act enjoins CTUIL to ensure the development of ISTS lines and to provide
open access on payment of transmission charges.
h) Further, while granting regulatory approval for the development of several
high-capacity corridors across the country, the Commission, in its order dated
25.2.2010 in Petition No.233/2009, held that the existence of PPAs with
beneficiaries is not a condition precedent for network expansion. In an order
dated 18.7.2017 in Petition No.293/MP/2015, Jaiprakash Power Ventures
Limited v. PGCIL, it was held that the inability to enter into PPAs cannot be
considered as a ground for not performing the obligations under the BPTA with
PGCIL. These findings apply mutatis mutandis when existing PPAs are
terminated or frustrated.
i) The context and facts of the case of Ameet Lalchand Shah v. Rishabh
Enterprises are inapplicable to the present case. Further, the Commission, vide
order dated 30.1.2020 in Petition Nos. 56/MP/2019, 57/MP/2019 and
58/MP/2019 have rejected the plea of force majeure by a renewable power
generator on account of issues concerning land allotment. The said order was
challenged before APTEL in Appeal Nos. 26/2020, 27/2020 and 28/2020,
wherein APTEL has held that in case of failure of construction of a dedicated
line by a grantee, the penal provision, i.e. clause 11.2, must be construed strictly
and upon lapse of such time, the said penal provisions must be given effect to.
Thus, the Petitioners have misconstrued the said judgment.
j) Neither the Connectivity Regulations/ Detailed Procedure nor the
Transmission Agreements signed by the Petitioners provides for “extension” of
the LTA commencement date.
Order in Petition No. 227/MP/2022
Page 12 of 46

k) The MoP’s directions dated 15.1.2021 under Section 107 of the Act, to the
Commission, act as a guiding factor and such directions are required to be
incorporated in Regulations framed by the Commission. In the present case, no
such modification or amendment has been notified in the applicable
Regulations. In this regard, reliance is placed on Zilla Vyavasayadarula
Sangham v. Andhra Pradesh State Electricity Board [(2001) 1 SCC 396];
judgment dated 31.1.2011 in Appeal Nos. 41, 42 and 43 of 2010: Polyplex
Corporation v. Uttarakhand Electricity Regulatory Commission; judgment dated
4.10.2012 in Appeal No.200/2011: M/s Maruti Suzuki India Ltd. v. Haryana
Electricity Regulatory Commission and Ors.
l) As per the case of Andhra Pradesh v. P. Laxmi Devi [(2008) 4 SCC 720], in
the statutory hierarchy, policy or executive directions issued by the government
are subordinate to statutory regulations framed as delegated legislation. Thus,
the MoP’s order dated 15.1.2021 issued under Section 107 of the Act cannot
override the 2010 Sharing Regulations and 2020 Sharing Regulations. Further,
the Transmission Agreements are statutory contracts and are thus immune
from the general pleas of frustration of contract under Section 56 of the Indian
Contract Act, 1872. It has been held in Mary v. State of Kerala [(2014) 14 SCC
272] that, though the doctrine of frustration excludes further performance in
cases of impossibility of performance, the said principle is not applicable to a
statutory contract. Further, as in Alopi Parshad and Sons Ltd. v. Union of India
[AIR 1960 SC 588], mere termination or non-existence of PPAs cannot affect
the operation of the Transmission Agreements.
m) Further, Regulation 8 of the 2010 Sharing Regulations provides that in case
the transmission elements are identified for an LTA grantee, the said grantee is
liable to pay the transmission charges under Regulation 8(6) prior to its COD.
10. The Petitioners, in their rejoinder dated 8.2.2023, to the reply filed by CTUIL,
reiterated the submissions made in the petition, besides the following submissions:
a) The MoP orders dated 23.11.2021 and 30.11.2021 have been passed under
Section 3(3) of the Act read with Para 6.4(6) of the Tariff Policy, 2016 and Rule
5(12) of the Electricity (Transmission System Planning, Development and
Recovery of Inter-State Transmission Charges) Rules, 2021. Being a statutory
document, the Tariff Policy 2016 and all orders issued thereunder will be
binding on the Petitioners and CTUIL. The purpose of the MoP orders is that,
when SCOD is extended by SECI under the PPA, the operationalisation of the
LTA ought also to be aligned with the revised SCOD.
b) CTUIL’s reliance on Petition No. 293/MP/2015, Jaiprakash Power Ventures
v. PGCIL, is misplaced because in this case, the Commission had held that the
Order in Petition No. 227/MP/2022
Page 13 of 46

generator was not impacted by any force majeure event and thus was not
absolved of its obligations under the BPTA.
c) The operative part of the judgment in Ameet Lalchand Shah v. Rishabh
Enterprises case applies squarely to inter-linked agreements such as the
Transmission Arrangement and the PPA. Further, the solar and wind power
developers should not be burdened with transmission charges when delays
arise from force majeure events beyond their control. CTUIL suffers no financial
impact as transmission system costs are not recovered from developers or
purchasers of renewable energy, and CTUIL continues to recover full charges.
Moreover, in this case, LTA was granted on the existing system margins without
any augmentation, resulting in no loss to CTUIL, thereby justifying the levy of
transmission charges.
d) Imposing transmission charges on solar and wind developers for delays in
commissioning amounts to a penalty, and it is well settled in the cases of J.K
Synthetics Ltd. v. Commercial Taxes Officer: (1994) 4 SCC 276; Commissioner,
Central Excise and Customs v. ITC Ltd., (2007) 1 SCC 62 that penalty
provisions must be construed strictly. Further, the MoP direction dated
15.1.2021 under Section 107 of the Act should be considered binding, being an
integral instrument that interlinks the PPA and the Transmission Arrangement.
e) The test to be applied for frustration of contract under Section 56 of the Indian
Contract Act is whether the changed circumstances altogether destroyed the
fundamental basis of the agreement and its underlying object. In the present
case, it is physically impossible to perform the obligations without land.
f) Regulation 26(1) of the 2020 Sharing Regulations states that the 2010
Sharing Regulations stand repealed. In terms of Regulation 26(2) of the 2020
Sharing Regulations, any action taken under the repealed 2010 Sharing
Regulations shall be deemed to have been taken under the 2020 Sharing
Regulations. Therefore, transmission charges, if any, can only be levied in
accordance with Regulation 13(7) of 2020 Sharing Regulations, i.e., at the rate
of 10% of the transmission charges payable per MW.
11. The Commission in RoP of the hearing dated 24.1.2023 gave the following
directions:
“(a) The Petitioners to pay 10% of outstanding transmission charges to CTUIL within
a week.
(b) The Petitioners and CTUIL to convene a meeting to clarify and confirm the details
of the billing. Thereafter, the Petitioners shall file an affidavit within a week, giving the
details of the minutes of meeting and the details of the bills raised.
Order in Petition No. 227/MP/2022
Page 14 of 46

effective on 23.11.2019. It was further stated therein that the said 2 Nos. of LTA were
granted for utilization by the 100 MW generating units of RPPL and form the subject
matter of the present petition. Further, against the LTA for 300 MW, only 230.1 MW of
generation capacity has been commissioned in a staggered manner from 18.5.2019

23.5.2022 in Petition No. 525/MP/2020, held that it is the responsibility of the LTA
grantee to seek the start date of LTA as per its assessment, and the LTA Agreement
does not provide for any matching with the SCD of the Project. The relevant portions
of the order dated 23.5.2022 are as follows:
“28. Thus, it is clear that the LTA has been granted on existing transmission system
and the start date of LTA has been recorded as 30.11.2019. We note that LTA
Order in Petition No. 227/MP/2022
Page 33 of 46

agreement has no clause with respect to date from which supply under PPA is
anticipated or alignment of such date with LTA start date. The start date of LTA has
solely been based on Petitioner’s assessment, requirement and as agreed by the
Petitioner. LTA agreement does not contain any stipulation in regard to
commencement of LTA in phases. We also note that CTU operationalized the said LTA
for 300 MW from 30.11.2019, as has been noted in CTU’s letter dated 5.11.2019 and
5.12.2019. Thus, we observe that RfS/PPA and LTA Agreement are two entirely
different and distinct agreements and the liabilities and obligations contained therein
are also different. The obligation of the Petitioner arising out of the PPAs is
independent of its obligation to meet the timeline which the Petitioner has sought under
the LTA application and LTA Agreement. There is no reference of PPA clauses in the
LTA Agreement and deferment of start date of LTA is provided neither in LTA
Agreement nor in any Regulation. Therefore, the Petitioner cannot contend that CTU
should have matched the SCOD in the PPA and the date of operationalization of LTA.
It was the sole responsibility of the Petitioner to correctly assess and inform the correct
start date of LTA.
29. We observe that similar issue was dealt by the Commission in the order dated
5.2.2019 in Petition No.195/MP/2019 as under:
“24. The Petitioner has also referred to Regulation 15B of the 2009 Connectivity
Regulations to argue that dates of PPAs and LTA should be aligned. The Petitioner
has further submitted that under Section 28(3)(a) of the Act, Regional Load
Despatch Centre (“RLDC”) has the responsibility of optimum scheduling and
dispatch of electricity, strictly in accordance with the contracts entered into with
the licensee or the generating companies. It has submitted that non-alignment of
PPAs with operationalization of grant has led to non-optimal scheduling.
25. The PGCIL has submitted that the Petitioner has requested 31.07.2019 as the
start date while submitting applications for Stage-I Connectivity, StageII
Connectivity as well as LTA. The Petitioner signed Transmission Agreement dated
07.08.2018 and LTA Agreement dated 20.09.2018 wherein the stipulated start
date of 31.07.2019 was again endorsed. In the present case, LTA has been
granted to the Petitioner without any system augmentation and, therefore, the start
dates of Petitioner’s Connectivity/ LTA is as requested by the Petitioner in its
respective applications. PGCIL has submitted that the Petitioner was at liberty to
suitably apply for LTA in terms of its consequent contractual/ bidding obligations.
The Petitioner was also at liberty to make separate LTA applications with different
quantum and start dates. It is the LTA applicant, who comes up with the date from
which it requires the Connectivity and Long-term Access. Accordingly, it is the
responsibility of the LTA applicant to synchronize between the two sets of
agreements i.e. PPAs and LTA agreements.
26. PGCIL has submitted that in terms of third proviso to Regulation 12(1) of the
2009 Connectivity Regulations, the relevance of PPA is limited to firming up the
drawal or injection point (as the case may be) and is not at all determinative of the
start date or date of effectiveness of LTA and that LTA is solely determined as per
the applicable Regulations of the Commission, LTA application, LTA grant letter
and LTA agreement. It has further submitted that it is only when Connectivity or
LTA is granted with system augmentation that the start date of Connectivity or LTA
is dependent on the commissioning of the identified transmission elements
required for Connectivity/ LTA. In such cases, Connectivity/ LTA is granted with
‘availability of the requirement transmission elements/ system or the start date,
whichever is later’.”
Order in Petition No. 227/MP/2022
Page 34 of 46

“28. Thus, the Petitioner was fully aware of all the relevant dates and was a party
to the grant of LTA. It was the Petitioner at whose behest the date of LTA was
decided as 31.07.2019. In our view, the Petitioner cannot now contend that CTU
should have matched the dates of SCOD in the PPAs and the operationalization
of LTA. It was the responsibility of the Petitioner to assess and inform the correct
dates from when it required LTA, specially, when there is no system augmentation
involved and LTA is granted on existing system. The Petitioner has itself submitted
that there were incentives attached for early commissioning and, therefore, it
cannot be ruled out that the Petitioner wanted to commission its project earlier
than SCOD and for that purpose, it sought LTA from 31.07.2019. This is also borne
out from JCC meetings where the Petitioner had stated that it was expected to
Commission 150 MW by 31.7.2019. Therefore, PGCIL cannot be faulted for
operationalizing the LTA from the date it was sought by the Petitioner.”
30. Thus, we observe that LTA is granted to the Petitioner based on its application and
the start date of Petitioner’s LTA is as requested by the Petitioner itself in its
application. The Petitioner is at liberty to suitably apply for LTA in terms of its
contractual/bidding obligations and for the same the Petitioner can make separate LTA
applications with different quantum and start dates.
31. Therefore, we are of the view that it is the responsibility of the LTA applicant to
synchronize and match the dates between the two sets of agreements i.e. PPA and
LTA Agreement, as it is the LTA applicant which signs both the sets of the
agreements.”
49. In the instant case, we have already held under Issue No. 1 that the PPA
executed between the Petitioner and SECI on 23.5.2018 and the Transmission
Arrangement (LTA Agreements dated 29.1.2018 and 6.9.2018 and TSA dated
29.1.2018 executed between Petitioner No. 2 and CTUIL) are distinct agreements in
the instant case and the liabilities and obligations arising therefrom are independent.
The obligations of the Petitioners under the PPA are independent of their obligation to
meet the timeline sought in the LTA applications and LTA Agreements. The LTA
Agreements do not specify or provide for the dates from which the supply under the
PPA is anticipated nor do they address the alignment of those dates with the LTA start
date. The start date of LTAs is based solely on the Petitioner’s assessment, request
and agreement. It is the Petitioner's responsibility to correctly assess the SCOD of the
Project and, accordingly, seek the LTA. There is no reference to the PPA clauses in
the LTA Agreement, and deferment of the start date of LTA is not provided either in
the LTA Agreement or in any of the regulations. Thus, the Petitioners cannot claim
Order in Petition No. 227/MP/2022
Page 35 of 46

that the dates of operationalisation of LTAs must match the revised SCOD of the
Project. Moreover, as the Petitioners did not relinquish the LTA after terminating the
PPA dated 23.5.2018, we hold that the Petitioners are liable to pay the transmission
charges from the respective dates of operationalisation of LTA Tranche 1 and LTA
Tranche 2. Issue No. 2 is answered accordingly.
Issue No. 3: Whether the Petitioner is eligible for waiver of transmission charges
in accordance with MoP’s orders dated 15.1.2021, 23.11.2021 and 30.11.2021
etc.?
50. The Petitioners have contended that the MoP orders dated 15.1.2021,
23.11.2021 and 30.11.2021 and the directions issued by MoP to the Commission
under Section 107 of the Act expressly provide that whenever a renewable energy
project receives an extension of SCOD from the competent authority (SECI) on
account of force majeure, the commencement and duration of the corresponding LTA
must also be extended, and the waiver period for transmission charge is deemed to
be extended for the same duration. Since SECI has extended the SCOD of the Project
to 31.8.2021 on account of force majeure events, the LTAs for both Tranches 1 and 2
stood automatically extended to that date, and therefore, no transmission charges
could be levied before 31.8.2021. Further, the Petitioners have submitted that because
the force majeure events continued even beyond 31.8.2021 (as land was still not
allotted), no transmission charges are leviable, and that CTUIL’s insistence on
recovering charges from 1.5.2019 and 23.11.2019 is contrary to the binding MoP
orders and directions.
51. Per contra, CTUIL has submitted that the MoP’s orders and directions under
Section 107 cannot override the 2020 Sharing Regulations and the Transmission
Agreements. The MoP directions are merely guiding factors that must be incorporated
into the Regulations framed by the Commission, and since no such amendments have
Order in Petition No. 227/MP/2022
Page 36 of 46

been notified, the existing regulatory provisions continue to govern the matter. It has
also been stated by CTUIL that under the applicable Regulations, once LTA has been
operationalised and the associated transmission system has achieved COD,
transmission charges are mandatorily payable by the generator irrespective of the
project progress or delays, and Regulation 13(3) does not contemplate consideration
of reasons for delay in generation.
52. We have considered the submissions of the Petitioners and CTUIL. We have
also perused the MoP orders referred to by the Petitioners. The MoP order dated
15.1.2021 is as follows:
“Subject: Waiver of Inter-State Transmission charges and losses on

the Solar Energy Corporation of India/ NTPC Limited or other Project Implementing
Agencies on behalf of Government of India for reasons of Force Majeure or delays on
the part of the transmission provider or inaction / delays on the part of Government
Agency; and it had been represented that in such cases the eligible renewable power
projects should not be deprived of the waiver of inter-state transmission charges and
losses. It was also considered that provisions related to applicability of ISTS charges
and losses waiver to all obligated entities needs a relook.

Ministry of Power's earlier order No 23/12/2016-R&R dated 13.2.2018, Order No.

transmission charges will be levied on transmission of the electricity generated from

a) Power plants using solar and wind sources of energy, including solar wind

for sale to distribution licensees, irrespective of whether this power is within RPO
or not, provided that the power has been procured competitively under the

“51. We observe that above quoted MOP Orders are issued under paragraph 6.4(6) of

to be levied for the purpose of “sale”. Further, the subject of all the above quoted MOP
Orders is “Waiver of inter-state transmission charges and losses on transmission of the
electricity generated from solar and wind sources of energy under para 6.4(6) of the
revised Tariff Policy, 2016”. Therefore, it is abundantly clear that waiver of transmission
charges is on “electricity generated.
53. Further, the MOP Orders including the Order dated 13.2.2018 have been
incorporated in 2010 Sharing Regulations and 2020 Sharing Regulations including the
modalities of its implementation. Regulation 13 of the 2020 Sharing Regulations
provides as under:
“13. Treatment of transmission charges and losses in specific cases (1) No

(b) generation based on solar or wind power resources for a period of 25 years

(i) Such generation capacity has been awarded through competitive bidding;
and
(ii) Such generation capacity has been declared under commercial operation
during the period from 1.7.2017 to 12.2.2018 for solar based resources or
during the period from 30.9.2016 to 12.2.2018 for wind based resources; and

(c) generation based on solar or wind power resources, for a period of 25 years
from the date of commercial operation, fulfilling the following conditions:
(i) Such generation capacity has been awarded through competitive bidding

and

during the period from 13.2.2018 to 31.12.2022; and
(iii) Power Purchase Agreement(s) have been executed for sale of such

54. The 2020 Sharing regulations clearly provide that waiver of transmission charges is

“a) Power plants using solar and wind sources of energy, including solar-wind
hybrid power plants with or without storage commissioned upto 30th June, 2023
for sale to distribution licensees, irrespective of whether this power is within RPO

plants may also be used for charging of storage including Hydro pumped storage

ORDER
The Petitioner, Lanco Kondapalli Power Limited (in short ‘LKPL’), has filed the
instant Petition under Section 79(1)(f) of the Electricity Act, 2003 (‘the Act’), seeking the
following reliefs:
(a) Allow the Present Petition and direct that the pleadings in OP No. 42 of 2009
(renumbered as OP No. 28/2015) as filed before the Andhra Pradesh Electricity
Regulatory Commission be taken on record by this Hon’ble Commission;
(b) Declare/hold that the Petitioner is entitled for reimbursement of Finance and
Procurement Costs as per Article 3.3 of Power Purchase Agreement dated 31.3.1997
and consequently direct the respondents 1 to 6 to reimburse an amount of Rs. 10.79
Crores as claimed vide Bill Nos. 01 to 15 and supplementary bill no. FPA/01 billed for
the period from 22.06.2000 to 10.08.2001;
(c) Declare/hold that the Petitioner is entitled for interest of Rs. 10,90,92,073/- from
10.08.2001 till the date of filing of this Petition on account of delay in reimbursement of
Finance and Procurement Costs in terms of Article 3.3 of Power Purchase Agreement
dated 31.3.1997 and consequently direct the respondents 1 to 6 pay the same;
(d) Declare/hold that the Petitioner is entitled for further interest from the original date of this
Petition till realization; and
(e) Pass any other or further order/reliefs which this Commission may deem fit and proper
in light of justice, equity and good conscience.
Background of the case
2. The Petitioner, LKPL, is a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956,
inter alia, engaged in the generation and sale of electricity. It has set up a 368.144 MW
Combined Cycle Power Project located in the Kondapalli Industrial Development Area,
Krishna District, Andhra Pradesh. It is a short-gestation power plant completed on time
out of the six projects awarded through Tariff-Based International Competitive Bidding
Order in Petition No. 250/MP/2022 Page 2 of 34

by the Government of Andhra Pradesh (GoAP) / Andhra Pradesh State Electricity Board
(APSEB). LKPL executed a Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) with the erstwhile
APSEB (presently APTRANSCO) on 31.3.1997 for the purchase of all the available
capacity, in accordance with the terms and conditions of the said PPA. LKPL
implemented the project. The first generating unit was tested from 22.6.2000 to
27.6.2000, and its Commercial Operation Date (COD) of the first unit was declared on
26.7.2000. Similarly, the COD of the second generating unit was declared on 24.9.2000,
after testing. Subsequently, LKPL demonstrated its total capacity of the project as per
the provisions of the PPA on 25.10.2000, in the presence of APTRANSCO and NTPC
officials (deputed by APTRANSCO) and the COD of the project was declared on
25.10.2000. Thereafter, vide G.O.Ms. No. 59 dated 7.6.2005, Respondent No. 1 Andhra
Pradesh Power Corporation Committee (APPCC), was constituted to advise and guide
the other four distribution companies in the discharge of their functions.
3. As disputes arose between the parties due to the failure of the Respondent AP
Discoms to make the payments to LKPL for finance and procurement of Naphtha
payable upto September 2001, and the efforts to settle the same amicably, was not
responded to by the Respondents, LKPL issued notice on 26.3.2004, nominating
Justice B.P. Jeevan Reddy, as its arbitrator and requested the Respondents to
nominate their arbitrator. As the Respondents failed to settle the disputes through
negotiation or arbitration, LKPL filed an application before the Hon’ble Andhra Pradesh
High Court (AA No. 31/2004) for the appointment of an arbitrator. However, the Hon’ble
High Court disposed of the said application on 18.3.2009, granting liberty to LKPL to
approach the Andhra Pradesh Electricity Regulatory Commission (APERC) for
appropriate relief. Accordingly, LKPL filed O.P. No. 42/2009 before the APERC, seeking
the reliefs (b) to (d), as in para 1 above. However, the APERC, in other similar petitions
vide order dated 13.6.2011, dismissed the said Petition holding that the period spent by
Order in Petition No. 250/MP/2022 Page 3 of 34

LKPL in the arbitration proceedings could not be excluded under Section 14(2) of the
Limitation Act, 1963. Aggrieved by this order, LKPL filed Appeal Nos. 128 and 129/2011
before the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL) and the APTEL, after examining
the issue of limitation held vide judgment dated 2.7.2012, that the claim of LKPL cannot
be said to be barred by limitation and directed the refund of the capacity charges along
with interest, in terms of its findings. It was also directed that the APERC pass
consequential orders in terms of the said judgment. Against this judgment, the
Respondents filed Civil Appeal No. 6036/2012 before the Hon’ble Supreme Court, and
the Hon’ble Supreme Court, without going into the merits of the claims, rejected the said
appeal filed by the Respondents, vide its judgment dated 16.10.2015, thereby upholding
the APTEL judgment on the question of limitation.
4. Pursuant to the Andhra Pradesh Reorganization Act, 2014 (w.e.f. from 1.3.2014),
apart from the AP Discoms (Respondents 4 & 6), the Telangana Discoms (Respondents
3 & 5) succeeded the rights and obligations under the PPA to the part contracted
capacity, viz., 335 MW. These Respondents are collectively referred to as ‘Respondent
Discoms’, in this order. Subsequently, this Petition (O.P. No. 42/2009) was renumbered
as O.P. No. 28/2015. The Respondents filed their counter-affidavit on 2.2.2013, and
thereafter the Petitioner filed its Rejoinder, and the pleadings were completed on
21.6.2013. During the pendency of this Petition, the Hon’ble Supreme Court in C.A. Nos.
3788-3790/2019 (APEPDCL & anr v GMRVPGL & ors) vide order dated 4.2.2020,
upheld the jurisdiction of the Central Commission to decide the cases involving the
disputes between the Respondent Discoms and the Generating Company. In terms of
the said order, the Telangana State Electricity Regulatory Commission (TSERC), vide
its order dated 29.5.2021, transferred the various Petitions to this Commission, in
addition to the Petition O.P. No. 28/2015. Thereafter, this Commission, vide letter dated
10.8.2021, called upon the Petitioner to file the Petition along with the filing fees in terms
Order in Petition No. 250/MP/2022 Page 4 of 34

of this Commission's Conduct of Business Regulations. In this background, the present
Petition has been filed by LKPL on 17.12.2021, seeking the reliefs, as mentioned in para
1 above. The Petitioner has submitted that it was admitted to the Corporate Insolvency
Resolution Process (CIRP) vide order dated 23.4.2019 and thereafter, admitted into
liquidation vide NCLT (Hyd. Bench) order dated 16.4.2021.
Submissions of the Petitioner
5. LKPL, in support of the reliefs sought, has submitted the following:
(i) As per Article 3 of the PPA, the Respondent Discoms are liable to pay
Energy charges to LKPL. Article 3.3 of the PPA specifically provides the
mechanism for computation of such Energy Charges and stipulates that the same
include the cost of fuel. Article 3.3(a)(i) expressly provides that the “cost of fuel”
encompasses finance and procurement costs. Therefore, reimbursement of
finance and procurement costs incurred in relation to fuel procurement forms an
integral part of the Energy Charges payable under the PPA.
(ii) In compliance with the directions of the Respondents, LKPL procured
naphtha from Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Limited (HPCL) from time to
time, at its own cost, for the generation of electricity. Such procurement involved
substantial finance and procurement costs, as well as bank guarantee charges.

32. At the outset, it is necessary to examine the relevant contractual framework.

Order in Petition No. 250/MP/2022 Page 24 of 34

naphtha was procured and used by LKPL for the generation of electricity in accordance
with the PPA and the directions of the Respondent Discoms. Naphtha, therefore,
squarely falls within the contractual definition of “Fuel”.
35. Article 3.3 of the PPA provides the complete mechanism for the computation of
Energy Charges payable by the Respondent Discoms. The Energy Charge is formula-
based, and one of the essential variables in the formula is “C”, which is defined as “the
cost of Fuel in Rs. per unit of Fuel; as delivered at the Fuel metering point at the site”.
The expression “cost of Fuel” is not left undefined or vague. On the contrary, the proviso
to Article 3.3(a) expressly stipulates how such cost is to be computed. The proviso
clearly mandates that the cost of Fuel “C” shall equal the sum of: (i) the basic weighted
average cost of Fuel in case of indigenous fuel and, in case of imported fuel, the
weighted average CIF value, plus in each case, finance and procurement costs; (ii)
taxes, duties, cesses and other Government Agency levies; and (iii) handling, storage,
transportation and importation charges. The language employed in the proviso is
explicit, unambiguous and admits of no alternative interpretation. Finance and
procurement costs are expressly enumerated as a component of fuel cost and are not
made conditional upon any further qualification, save and except that they form part of
the cost of fuel as delivered at the site.
36. The Respondent Discom's contention that finance and procurement costs are not
payable or are subsumed elsewhere in the tariff structure cannot be accepted in view of
the express contractual stipulation. The PPA explicitly separates Capacity Charges from
Energy Charges. While working capital requirements may be a factor in determining
Capacity Charges, the Energy Charge mechanism under Article 3.3 independently
recognises that the procurement of fuel may entail financing costs and procurement-
related expenses, which are to be recovered as part of the fuel cost itself. To read Article
Order in Petition No. 250/MP/2022 Page 26 of 34

3.3 otherwise would render the express words “plus in each case, finance and
procurement costs” otiose, which is impermissible in contractual interpretation.
37. Further, the contractual scheme indicates that the fuel is to be supplied at the
generator’s end, and the cost recoverable is the cost of fuel “as delivered at the Fuel
metering point at the site”. This necessarily includes all costs intrinsically linked to
making the fuel available at the site, including financing costs incurred due to credit
terms, letters of credit, bank guarantees, and procurement arrangements with the fuel
supplier. These costs are not extraneous or collateral expenses but are directly and
inextricably connected to the procurement of fuel for electricity generation.
38. The Respondent Discom's reliance on policy guidelines or a general assertion that
fuel risk lies with the generator cannot override the express terms of the PPA. The PPA
is a concluded contract between the parties, and unless any clause is shown to be
contrary to law or unenforceable, the parties are bound by its terms. No provision has
been brought to our notice which nullifies or dilutes the specific stipulation in Article 3.3
regarding the inclusion of finance and procurement costs in fuel costs.
39. The billing provisions under Article 5 further reinforce this conclusion. Article 5.2
contemplates monthly tariff bills including Energy Charges “duly supported by
supporting data”, while Article 5.5 permits supplementary bills for “any other
adjustments or payments due to the Company hereunder”. Read together, these
provisions indicate that where fuel-related costs, including finance and procurement
costs, are incurred and are payable under Article 3.3, such costs are recoverable
through the billing mechanism prescribed under the PPA. The structure of Article 5 does
not curtail the substantive entitlement under Article 3.3 but only regulates the manner of
billing and payment.
Order in Petition No. 250/MP/2022 Page 27 of 34

40. We also find merit in the Petitioner’s submission that the Respondents themselves
have, for subsequent periods, accepted and reimbursed finance and procurement costs
under the same contractual framework. While such conduct cannot create an
entitlement contrary to contract, it lends support to the interpretation that both parties
understood Article 3.3 as permitting recovery of such costs as part of the fuel costs.
41. In view of the clear and categorical language of Article 3.3, read with the definition
of “Fuel” under Article 1.1(27) and the billing provisions under Article 5, we hold that
finance and procurement costs incurred for procurement of fuel are an integral
component of “Fuel Cost” and are contractually recoverable as part of Energy Charges
under the PPA dated 31.3.1997, subject to proof of actual incurrence and compliance
with the billing requirements stipulated therein. Issue No. (C) is disposed of accordingly.
Issue No. (D): Whether LKPL has furnished sufficient evidence in support of its
claim?
42. The claim of LKPL seeking reimbursement of finance and procurement costs for
the period from 22.6.2000 to 10.8.2001 has been strenuously opposed by the
Respondent Discoms on the principal ground that LKPL has allegedly failed to place on
record adequate documentary material to demonstrate actual incurrence and payment
of such costs, as purportedly required under Article 5.2 of the PPA. It is therefore
necessary to examine whether the evidentiary requirements under the contractual
framework are duly satisfied in the facts of the present case.
43. At the outset, it must be noted that the claim under consideration is not in the
nature of a claim for damages or compensation, but arises out of the tariff mechanism
itself, being a reimbursement claim embedded within the Energy Charge formulation
under Article 3.3(a)(i) of the PPA. As we have already held, while deciding Issue No.
(C), that finance and procurement costs constitute an integral component of “Fuel Cost”
under the PPA, the scope of inquiry is limited to ascertaining whether LKPL has
Order in Petition No. 250/MP/2022 Page 28 of 34

produced sufficient material to establish that such costs were incurred in connection
with the procurement of fuel and were billed in accordance with the contractual
provisions.
44. The Respondents have placed reliance on Article 5.2 of the PPA and the
judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Tata Iron & Steel Co. Ltd. v. Union of India
to contend that reimbursement necessarily presupposes strict proof of prior payment,
including production of bank statements evidencing remittance of interest and LC
charges. We are unable to accede to this contention in the facts and circumstances of
the present case for more than one reason. Article 5.2 of the PPA merely stipulates that
monthly tariff bills shall be supported by “relevant supporting data”. The provision neither
prescribes a rigid nor exhaustive list of documents nor mandates production of bank
statements or lender confirmations as a condition precedent for raising or honouring
tariff bills. The expression “supporting data” must, therefore, be construed contextually,
keeping in view the nature of the claim, prevailing industry practice, contemporaneous
conduct of the parties and the overall contractual scheme.
45. In support of its claim, LKPL has placed on record contemporaneous billing and
operational material, including energy bills and supplementary bills raised for the
relevant period wherein finance and procurement costs were expressly included as part
of the fuel cost computation; invoices, laboratory test reports and delivery documents
issued by HPCL evidencing actual supply of naphtha; the Fuel Supply Agreement dated
19.1.1998 executed with HPCL, which was duly reviewed and approved by the Fuel
Supply Committee constituted under Schedule I of the PPA and comprising
representatives of the Respondents; detailed computation statements and bill-wise
break-ups furnished pursuant to directions of the Commission; and records
demonstrating uninterrupted supply of naphtha during the disputed period, which
Order in Petition No. 250/MP/2022 Page 29 of 34

necessarily presupposes adherence to the commercial terms of HPCL, including those
relating to interest and letters of credit.
46. It is significant that the Respondent Discoms have not disputed the factum of
supply of naphtha, the quantities consumed, or the applicability of HPCL’s credit terms
requiring interest and bank guarantees. Their objection is confined solely to the alleged
absence of proof of actual payment of interest and LC charges. In our view, such an
objection is overly technical and ignores commercial realities. In long-term fuel supply
arrangements, particularly with public sector oil companies, continued and uninterrupted
supply on credit is itself a strong indicator that the purchaser has complied with the
financial obligations attached to such supplies. The evidentiary standard applicable to
tariff proceedings before a regulatory commission cannot be equated with that
applicable to a civil suit for recovery of money. The Commission is required to adopt a
pragmatic and purposive approach, particularly where the claim flows from a concluded
contractual tariff mechanism and is supported by contemporaneous billing records and
operational evidence.
47. It is also of relevance that the Respondent Discoms did not invoke the dispute
resolution mechanism under Article 5.7 of the PPA within the stipulated period of sixty
days in respect of the bills raised for the disputed period. Under the contractual
framework, such inaction results in the bills attaining finality, subject only to adjudication
of legal issues. Having failed to raise any contemporaneous objection regarding
insufficiency of documentation, the Respondent Discoms cannot be permitted to raise
such objections belatedly after a lapse of more than two decades, particularly when
similar documentation was accepted for subsequent periods.
48. This conclusion is further reinforced by the conduct of the Respondent Discoms
themselves. The APPCC Negotiating Committee constituted by Respondent No.1
Order in Petition No. 250/MP/2022 Page 30 of 34

examined identical claims of LKPL for a subsequent period, based on documentation of
the same nature, and approved payment of finance and procurement costs as well as
bank guarantee charges. The Respondents have failed to demonstrate any material
distinction in the nature or quality of the documentation furnished for the earlier period
presently under consideration. The plea of insufficiency of evidence thus appears to be
an afterthought raised solely to evade liability.
49. The reliance placed by the Respondents on the judgment of the Hon’ble
Supreme Court in Tata Iron & Steel Co. Ltd. v. Union of India is misplaced. The said
decision was rendered in the context of a statutory customs duty refund claim governed
by a distinct legal regime and cannot be mechanically applied to tariff reimbursement
claims arising under a negotiated PPA, where reimbursement is an in-built component
of the tariff formula itself.
50. We also find merit in the submission of LKPL that the PPA does not require
production of bank statements or lender certificates as a precondition for reimbursement
of finance and procurement costs. To import such a requirement into the contract would
amount to rewriting the terms of the PPA, which is impermissible in law.
51. In light of the foregoing discussion, we are satisfied that LKPL has placed on
record sufficient, credible and contemporaneous material to substantiate its claim for
reimbursement of finance and procurement costs for the period from 22.6.2000 to
10.8.2001. The evidentiary material adduced meets the contractual and regulatory
standards applicable to tariff claims under the PPA. Issue No. (D) is disposed of
accordingly.
Issue No. (E): Whether the Respondents are liable to pay the interest of Rs.
10,90,92,073/- from 10.8.2001 till the original date of filing of this Petition on
account of delay in reimbursement of finance & procurement costs in terms of
Article 3.3 of the PPA dated 31.3.1997?
Order in Petition No. 250/MP/2022 Page 31 of 34

52. The claim of LKPL for interest is founded squarely on the contractual framework
of the PPA. Article 5.7 expressly provides that any amount payable by the Respondents
and not paid within the stipulated period shall carry interest at the applicable working
capital rate from the date the amount becomes due until the date of actual payment.
When Article 5.7 is read in conjunction with Article 3.3, it is evident that the PPA not only
obligates the Respondents to reimburse finance and procurement costs as part of fuel
cost, but also contemplates compensation to the generator for the time value of money
in the event of delayed payment. Consequently, once it is held under Issue Nos. (C) and
(D) that finance and procurement costs are recoverable under Article 3.3 and that LKPL
has duly substantiated the incurrence of such costs, the liability of the Respondent
Discoms to pay interest follows as an automatic and necessary contractual
consequence.
53. The contention of the Respondent Discoms that interest is not payable on the
ground that the principal claim itself was disputed and allegedly unsupported by
evidence cannot be accepted. The record clearly establishes that LKPL had raised Bills
Nos. 01 to 15 and Supplementary Bill No. FPA/01 for the period from 22.6.2000 to
10.8.2001, claiming reimbursement of finance and procurement costs. These bills were
admittedly received by the Respondents and were neither rejected nor disputed within
the time stipulated under Article 5.7 of the PPA. In the absence of any contemporaneous
dispute being raised in the manner prescribed under the contract, the amounts claimed
attained finality and became due and payable. The due date for payment having expired
on 10.8.2001, the liability to pay interest commenced from that date, and subsequent
objections or disputes raised by the Respondents cannot retrospectively nullify the
contractual default that had already occurred.
54. It is also significant that LKPL cannot be accused of having acquiesced in the
non-payment or having slept over its rights. The material on record demonstrates that

Hon’ble High Court, and eventually before the State Commission and this Commission.
The entire period spent in bona fide prosecution of these remedies has been held to be
excludable for the purpose of limitation by the APTEL, a view that has been affirmed by
the Hon’ble Supreme Court. In such circumstances, where the Respondents have
withheld payment of the principal amount for over two decades, they cannot seek
immunity from interest liability merely because the adjudicatory process was prolonged.
Interest in the present case is compensatory in nature and not penal.
55. The objection of the Respondent Discoms that the interest claimed exceeds the
principal amount and is therefore barred by the rule of damdupat is equally untenable.
The rule of damdupat is a doctrine of Hindu law primarily applicable to money-lending
transactions and is irrelevant to commercial contracts governed by express contractual
terms. In the context of infrastructure and power sector PPAs, where the rate and
incidence of interest are expressly stipulated, such provisions are enforceable unless
shown to be unconscionable or contrary to statutory mandate. No such case has been
established by the Respondents.
56. As regards the applicable rate of interest, LKPL has placed on record a certificate
issued by its working capital banker, State Bank of India, certifying the relevant working
capital rates for the period in question. The Respondents have neither disputed the
authenticity of this certificate nor produced any evidence to suggest that a different rate
was contractually applicable. We are, therefore, satisfied that the computation of interest
has been made strictly in accordance with Article 5.7 of the PPA.
57. Finally, even on equitable considerations, the claim for interest merits
acceptance. The Respondent Discoms, though public utilities, cannot rely on their
Order in Petition No. 250/MP/2022 Page 33 of 34

public-undertaking character to justify withholding payments that were contractually
payable to the generator. To deny interest in such circumstances would amount to
permitting unjust enrichment, as the Respondents enjoyed the benefit of electricity
supplied while depriving LKPL of timely reimbursement of fuel-related costs. Equity,
therefore, reinforces LKPL’s contractual entitlement to interest on the delayed payment,
as per the provisions of the PPA.
58. Accordingly, Petition No. 250/MP/2022 is disposed of in terms of the above
discussions and findings.

(Ravinder Singh Dhillon) (Harish Dudani) (Ramesh Babu V.) (Jishnu Barua)

Parties Present:
Shri Gopal Jain, Sr. Advocate, JSL
