Shri Raghav Tandon, Advocate, Odisha SLDC
ORDER
Through the instant Petition, the Petitioner, Jindal Steel Limited, has sought
direction to Odisha SLDC to grant Standing Clearance under the NOAR/ Grant of
Temporary General Network Access (T-GNA) framework for its Angul plant without
insisting on DISCOM consent, under Section 79(1)(c) and (f) of the Electricity Act, 2003
(in short ‘the Act’) read with the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Connectivity
and General Network Access to the inter-State Transmission System) Regulations,
2022. The Petitioner has made the following prayers in the present Petition:
a) Hold and declare that the insistence on DISCOM consent/ NOC as a mandatory
pre-condition for the grant of Standing Clearance/ T-GNA to the Petitioner is
ultra vires the CERC GNA Regulations and the NOAR Procedure, and hence
unsustainable;
b) Direct Respondent No. 3 to process and give effect to the Petitioner’s Standing
Clearance request for the month of May 2026 without insisting on DISCOM
consent as pre-condition;
Order in Petition No. 191/MP/2026 Page 2

c) Set aside the conditions imposed by Respondent No. 1 as pre-condition to
grant of its consent as arbitrary, unreasonable and illegal;
d) Direct Respondent No. 1 not to withhold its NOC/ consent for May 2026 and
subsequent months on the basis of the non-fulfilment of the extraneous
conditions put forth in its email dated 31.03.2026, i.e., (i) execution of the
pending agreements for providing a new connection of 20 MVA to JSOL; and
(ii) arrangement of emergency power supply for ACPP-II; and
e) Pass such other order(s) as this Hon’ble Commission may deem fit in the facts
and circumstances of the present case.”
Interim Relief prayers in the main Petition:
a) Direct that the Petitioner’s request for Standing Clearance for the month of May
2026 be processed and allowed in view of the Standing Clearance already
granted by Respondent No. 4, pending disposal of the present Petition; and
b) Pass any other order or direction as this Hon’ble Commission may deem fit in
light of facts and circumstances of the present Petition.
2.The Petitioner has filed an IA No. 67/2026 for urgent listing seeking the following prayers:
a) Urgent listing of the Petition bearing Diary No. 256 of 2026 (filed on 21.04.2026)
at the earliest date subject to convenience of this Hon’ble Commission.
b) An ex-parte ad interim direction to the Respondents to process, allow and give
effect to the Standing Clearance dated 10.04.2026 already granted by
Respondent No. 4 for the month of May 2026 without insisting on consent from
Respondent No. 1 as a per-condition, pending disposal of the captioned Petition.
Submissions of the Petitioner
2. The Petitioner has mainly submitted as under:
(a) The Petitioner owns and operates two captive generation facilities at Angul, Odisha
(ACPP-I and ACPP-II) and participates in short-term exchange-based/open access-
based power trading through the framework governed by the CERC (Connectivity
and General Network Access to the inter-State Transmission System) Regulations,
2022 (CERC GNA Regulations), and the NOAR Procedure.
(b) The Petitioner holds an existing connectivity and contract demand of 90 MVA with
Respondent No. 1 (as Extra High Tension (EHT) consumer) for start-up and auxiliary
power requirements, connected at 400 kV via Respondent No. 2’s Meramandali
substation in Odisha.
Order in Petition No. 191/MP/2026 Page 3

(c) Jindal Steel Odisha Limited (JSOL), a wholly owned subsidiary of the Petitioner,
which is also located in the same premises at Angul, Odisha, draws captive power
from the Petitioner’s CGPs per the Electricity Rules 2005 (as amended from time to
time) (Rules 2005), through a wholly owned, dedicated 400 kV private transmission
system operating entirely behind the meter, without utilising the State transmission or
distribution network of Respondents No. 1 and 2.
(d) Respondent No. 4 issued a Standing Clearance to the Petitioner on 10.04.2026 for
the month of May 2026, for an injection request of 700 MW and a drawal request of
300 MW on a 24-hour basis.
(e) On an application made by the Petitioner on the NOAR platform for the grant of
Standing Clearance for grant of Temporary General Network Access (T-GNA),
Respondent No. 3, in operating the NOAR platform, indicated that a No Objection
Certificate (NOC)/ consent from Respondent No. 1 would be mandatory for the grant
of Standing Clearance by an email dated 13.04.2026 issued to the Petitioner.
(f) The Petitioner vide e-mail dated 15.04.2026 informed Respondent No.1/TPCODL
that the Petitioner has cleared all its electrical dues pertaining to the month of March,
2026 and accordingly, requested Respondent No.1 to issue the no dues certificate /
NOC in order to facilitate the Petitioner to undertake its power trading activities.
(g) Respondent No. 1, while providing a conditional consent for the grant of Standing
Clearance for the April 2026 to the Petitioner by email dated 31.03.2026, has
baselessly and arbitrarily made the NOC conditional, subject to the compliance of the
two, entirely unconnected, conditions by the end of April 2026, namely (i) execution
of the pending agreements for providing a new connection of 20 MVA to JSOL (which
pertinently is not required by JSOL); and (ii) arrangement of emergency power supply
for ACPP-II. While issuing the NOC dated 31.03.2026, Respondent No. 1 has
explicitly threatened that in case of non-compliance with the two conditions, the NOC
for subsequent months may not be issued.
(h) In the circumstances, the Petitioner is facing the imminent threat of its application
made at NOAR for the grant of the Standing Clearance for May 2026 being rejected,
directly impairing its ability to engage in monthly short-term trading, resulting in grave
prejudice to the Petitioner, disabling it from availing T-GNA for May 2026 (as also,
subsequent periods). The Petitioner would be faced with immediate consequences,
including but not limited to loss of the opportunity to monetise surplus power, possible
Order in Petition No. 191/MP/2026 Page 4

backing down or inefficient utilisation of its captive generating stations, disruption of
monthly trading schedules that operate on strict regulatory timelines, and
corresponding financial prejudice on account of lost market revenue and stranded
generation.
(i) The regulatory framework governing the grant of the T-GNA, i.e., the CERC GNA
Regulations, read with the Procedure for Grant of Temporary General Network
Access (T-GNA) to the inter-State Transmission System through National Open
Access Registry (NOAR) (NOAR Procedure), must be applied strictly in determining
the grant of T-GNA to an applicant.
(j) The CERC GNA Regulations, by virtue of Regulation 29.7(A)(ii) contained therein,
make clear that, in the case of an intra-State entity, the relevant statutory checkpoint
for access into the inter-State short-term regime is the grant of Standing Clearance by
the concerned SLDC. The purpose of such Standing Clearance is narrow and
technical: namely, to confirm the existence of (i) the necessary infrastructure for time-
block-wise energy metering and accounting, (ii) the appropriate communication
system, and (iii) availability of transmission capacity in the intra-State network. Thus,
the CERC GNA Regulations identify the precise parameters on which Standing
Clearance rests.
(k) Regulation 31.3 provides that the refusal of Standing Clearance is permissible only
in two specific and limited circumstances: (i) non-existence of necessary
infrastructure; or (ii) unavailability of surplus transmission capacity in the intra-State
transmission network. Pertinently, the Petitioner has already obtained the necessary
Standing Clearance from Respondent No. 4 for previous periods, on satisfaction of
the above conditions. Without prejudice, the CERC GNA Regulations do not provide
for the Discom's consent/NOC to be an independent substantive statutory condition
for the grant of T-GNA.
(l) The NOAR Procedure, in Clause 6, expressly provides that the applications for
Standing Clearance shall be processed in accordance with Regulation 31 of the
CERC GNA Regulations. It similarly recognises refusal only on the grounds of the
non-existence of necessary infrastructure or the unavailability of surplus transmission
capacity in the intra-State transmission network and requires that reasons be
furnished. Clause 6(e) of the NOAR Procedure states that for intra-State entities, “the
consent of DISCOM, if any, shall be uploaded in the NOAR by SLDC or the T-GNA
applicant, as per practice in the host state.” The use of the words “if any” establishes
Order in Petition No. 191/MP/2026 Page 5

that the consent of Discom is not a mandatory condition, and regardless, cannot be
predicated on conditions completely alien to the CERC GNA Regulations and the
NOAR Procedure.
(m)No right can be said to be available to the DISCOMs to sit in judgment over, veto, or
override the SLDC’s satisfaction on the matters expressly entrusted to it under
Regulation 29.7(A)(ii) and Regulation 31 of the CERC GNA Regulations. Clause 6(e)
of the NOAR Procedure must be read harmoniously and in the context of Regulation
31 of the CERC GNA Regulations. A procedure cannot expand the substantive
grounds of refusal beyond what the parent regulations permit. Accordingly, even if
there is a host-state practice of uploading DISCOM consent, such practice cannot be
treated as conferring an independent and un-canalised power on the DISCOM to
block access on grounds foreign to Regulation 31.
(n) Therefore, the insistence on NOC/ consent from Respondent No. 1 as a mandatory
condition for processing the Petitioner’s T-GNA/ Standing Clearance request is ultra
vires the CERC GNA Regulations and the NOAR Procedure and hence, is liable to
be set aside.
(o) Consent of the DISCOM is not statutorily mandatory; the conduct of Respondent No.
1 shows an attempt to abuse the process as a coercive instrument to compel the
Petitioner to accede to unrelated commercial and connectivity demands. Such
demands have no connection to the statutory requirements for the grant of Standing
Clearance, and are hence vexatious and illegal. Respondent No. 1’s conduct in
threatening to withhold its consent on non-compliance with unrelated and
unwarranted conditions is contrary to the express provisions of the CERC GNA
Regulations, antithetical to regulatory certainty and undermines the non-
discriminatory access regime envisaged by the Act and the CERC GNA Regulations.
(p) In any event and without prejudice to the above, the two conditions sought to be
imposed on the Petitioner by Respondent No. 1 are unsustainable. This is because:
(i) Respondent No. 1 has sought execution of pending agreements for a new 20 MVA
connection to JSOL (a wholly owned subsidiary of the Petitioner herein). This
condition proceeds on the erroneous premise that, in order for JSOL to consume
power from the Petitioner’s CGPs (under the captive framework provided under the
Act and the Rules 2005), JSOL, being a separate legal entity, must independently
connect to the OPTCL/ TPCODL network and take a separate contract demand.
Order in Petition No. 191/MP/2026 Page 6

(q) The Central Electricity Authority (CEA), by its clarification dated 10.04.2026, has
categorically clarified that ACPP-I, ACPP-II, the Petitioner’s load and JSOL’s load can
collectively be treated as a Captive Generating Plant. CEA has further clarified that,
in such a configuration, no separate metering or connectivity at JSOL’s end is
warranted, and that the system can be treated as one integrated captive complex;
and (ii) Respondent No. 1 has attempted to mandate the Petitioner to arrange an
emergency power supply for ACPP-II as a precondition to NOC. In this regard, the
CEA has clarified that where ACPP-I, ACPP-II and the associated loads form part of
an integrated captive generation complex, separate connectivity for start-up power
for ACPP-II is not required.
(r) Accordingly, the Petitioner is constrained to approach this Commission by way of the
present Petition, impugning the arbitrary conduct of Respondent No. 1 in imposing
extraneous conditions and the threat of withholding of consent for subsequent months
and the imposition of a non-statutory requirement of the DISCOM’s consent, as a
mandatory requirement, by Respondent No. 3 in the grant of the Standing Clearance
to the Petitioner.
Submissions vide IA 67/2026
3. The Petitioner vide IA 67/2026 dated 21.04.2026 has reiterated submissions already
made vide Petition. In addition, the Petitioner has prayed for urgent listing of the Petition.
Hearing dated 30.04.2026
4.The relevant extracts of the hearing are as below:
“Learned senior counsel for the Petitioner, JSL submitted that the present Petition has been filed
under Section 79(1)(c) and 79(1)(f) of the Electricity Act read with GNA Regulations, 2022 and the
Procedure for Grant of T-GNA to ISTS through National Open Access Registry (NOAR) for seeking
grant of Open Access/ Standing Clearance under the National Open Access Registry (NOAR)/
Grant of Temporary General Network Access (T-GNA) framework for its Angul plant for the month
of May 2026 and for future periods, in compliance with the applicable regulations and without being
subjected to extra-regulatory insistence on DISCOM’s consent or conditional NOCs founded on
issues wholly unrelated to open access eligibility, dues clearance, metering, communication, or
grid security. Learned senior counsel, while pressing on the IA as well as the main Petition, mainly
submitted as under:
(a) JSL owns and operates two captive generation facilities at Angul, Odisha (ACPP-I and ACPP-
II) and participates in short-term exchange-based/ open access-based power trading through the
framework governed by the GNA Regulations and the NOAR Procedure.
(b) As per Regulation 29.7(A)(ii) of the GNA Regulations, in the case of an intra State entity, the
relevant statutory checkpoint for access into the inter-State short-term regime is the grant of
Order in Petition No. 191/MP/2026 Page 7

Standing Clearance by the concerned SLDC. The purpose of such Standing Clearance is narrow
and technical: namely, to confirm the existence of (i) the necessary infrastructure for time-block-
wise energy metering and accounting, (ii) the appropriate communication system, and (iii)
availability of transmission capacity in the intra-State network.
(c) Regulation 31.3 of the GNA Regulations provides that the refusal of Standing Clearance is
permissible only in two specific and limited circumstances: (i) non-existence of necessary
infrastructure; or (ii) unavailability of surplus transmission capacity in the intra-State transmission
network. In fact, Clause 6 of the NOAR procedure expressly provides that the applications for
Standing Clearance shall be processed in accordance with Regulation 31 of the GNA Regulations.
(d) The GNA Regulations do not provide for consent/ NOC of distribution companies to be an
independent substantive statutory condition for the grant of TGNA. Thus, the distribution
companies have no role to play in the grant of the standing clearance and cannot be involved in
the matter expressly entrusted to SLDC under Regulation 29.7 (A)(ii) and Regulation 31 of the
GNA Regulations.
(e) Vide email dated 31.3.2026, TPCODL has arbitrarily made the NOC conditional, subject to the
compliance with the following two, entirely unconnected, conditions by the end of April 2026: (i)
execution of the pending agreements for providing a new connection of 20 MVA to JSOL (which
pertinently is not required by JSOL); and (ii) arrangement of emergency power supply for ACPP-
II.
(f) CEA vide clarification dated 10.04.2026, has categorically clarified that ACPP-I, ACPP-II, the
Petitioner’s load and JSOL’s load can collectively be treated as a Captive Generating Plant. CEA
has further clarified that, in such a configuration, no separate metering or connectivity at JSOL’s
end is warranted, and that the system can be treated as one integrated captive complex. Further,
it was also clarified that where ACPP-I, ACPP-II and the associated loads form part of an
integrated captive generation complex, separate connectivity for start-up power for ACPP-II is not
required.
(g) On 10.4.2026, the Respondent, Odisha SLDC, issued a Standing Clearance to the Petitioner
for the month of May 2026, for an injection request of 700 MW and a drawal request of 300 MW
on a 24-hour basis. Thereafter, JSL applied for the grant of Standing Clearance for the grant of T-
GNA on the NOAR platform managed by the Respondent, Grid India. Vide email dated 13.4.2026,
it was intimated to the Petitioner that a NOC from TPCODL would be mandatorily required for the
grant of Standing Clearance.
(h) Vide mail dated 15.4.2026, JSL informed TPCODL that it has cleared all its dues pertaining to
March 2026 and accordingly, requested TPCODL to issue NOC. However, TPCODL, vide email
dated 28.4.2026, has again asked the Petitioner to comply with the requirements of NOC as
already mentioned in the earlier communications.
(i) The ad-interim ex-parte directions may be issued to the Respondents to process, allow and give
effect to the standing clearance dated 10.4.2026 for the month of May 2026 without insisting on
consent from TPCODL as a precondition pending the disposal of the main matter. Otherwise, the
Petitioner’s right to participate in the short-term power market for May 2026 will be extinguished
permanently once the trading window for that month closes.
2. After hearing the learned senior counsel for the Petitioner, the Commission directed as under:
(a) Issue notice on IA as well as Petition on both counts, maintainability as well as merits;
(b) The Respondents to file their replies to IA, if any, within three days, with a copy to the Petitioner,
who may file its rejoinder, within 2 days thereafter.
(c) The Respondents to file their replies to the Petition, if any, within two weeks with a copy to the
Petitioner, who may file its rejoinder, within two weeks thereafter.”
Submissions of the Petitioner
Order in Petition No. 191/MP/2026 Page 8

5. The Petitioner, JSL vide affidavit dated 04.05.2026, has submitted some factual
corrections in pleadings and subsequent developments after filing the Petition as below:
(a) The Petitioner, on 28.03.2026, intimated Respondent No. 1 that it has cleared all
the energy dues for the month of February 2026. Accordingly, Respondent No. 1
was requested to grant consent or no objection to power trading in April 2026, in
accordance with the ST5 form. On 30.03.2026, Respondent No. 1 wrote to the
Petitioner directing it to (i) execute the pending agreements for providing a new
connection of 20 MVA to M/s. JSOL; and (ii) take an emergency power supply for
ACPP-II for issuance of open access NOC.
(b) Further, the Petitioner, on 30.03.2026, objected to Respondent No. 1’s email dated
30.03.2026, clarifying that all financial dues for February 2026 had already been
cleared, that JSOL’s power requirement was unrelated to the Petitioner’s power
trading issue, and that ACPP-I generation was sufficient to meet JSOL’s
requirement.
(c) Subsequently, on 31.03.2026, Respondent No. 1, in providing a conditional consent
for the grant of Standing Clearance for April 2026 to the Petitioner, has baselessly
and arbitrarily made the NOC conditional, subject to the compliance of the following
two, entirely unconnected, conditions by the end of April 2026:
(i)execution of the pending agreements for providing a new connection of 20
MVA to JSOL (which pertinently is not required by JSOL); and
(ii)arrangement of emergency power supply for ACPP-II.
In issuing the NOC dated 31.03.2026, Respondent No. 1 has explicitly
threatened that, in the event of non-compliance with the two conditions, the
NOC for subsequent months may not be issued.
(d) Pursuant to letters dated 02.02.2026 and 30.03.2026, on 10.04.2026, the Petitioner
sought clarification on issues arising from the demands raised by Respondent No.
1. The CEA clarified that:
(i)JSL’s load, JSOL’s load, ACPP-I and ACPP-II can collectively be treated as
a Captive Generating Plant;
(ii)Separate connectivity for start-up power for ACPP-II is not required.
Order in Petition No. 191/MP/2026 Page 9

(iii)metering point may be considered at the STU end, treating the entire
complex as a single complex, and no separate metering or connectivity at
JSOL’s end is warranted.
(e) On 10.04.2026, the JSL applied to Respondent No. 4 on the NOAR platform for
issuance of STOA for the month of May 2026 (01.05.2026 to 31.05.2026) for an
injection request of 700 MW and a drawal request of 300 MW on a 24-hour basis.
The application dated 10.04.2026 was inadvertently mentioned as the standing
clearance granted by SLDC, Odisha, in the Petition, whereas it is actually the
Application filed to seek the issuance of standing clearance from Respondent No.
4/SLDC, Odisha.
(f) On 13.04.2026, Respondent No. 3 indicated that a No Objection Certificate (NOC)/
consent from Respondent No. 1 would be mandatory for the grant of Standing
Clearance. On 15.04.2026, the JSL informed Respondent No. 1 that all electrical
dues pertaining to March 2026 had been cleared and requested the issuance of a
no-dues certificate/NOC to facilitate power trading activities. On 15.04.2026, a
detailed communication was addressed to Respondent No. 1 in response to the
conditions imposed in relation to power trading and connectivity arrangements. No
response was received from Respondent No. 1, and on 21.04.2026, the Petition
was filed.
(g) Subsequent to the filing of the Petition, on 28.04.2026, Respondent No. 1 refused
to grant NOC for sale of 700 MW and stated that the same would be provided after
compliance of the conditions mentioned in the last month open access NOC;
however, NOC was granted for purchase of 300 MW power through inter/ intra state
short term open access for the period from 01.05.2026 to 31.05.2026.
(h) Pursuant to partial NOC, on 29.04.2026, Respondent No. 4 partially approved the
application and granted Standing Clearance for the purchase of 300 MW power
through inter/ intra state short-term open access for the period from 01.05.2026 to
31.05.2026. On 30.04.2026, during the hearing, an interim application I.A. No. 67 of
2026 was pressed seeking ex-parte ad interim directions to direct processing and
grant of standing clearance for the entire quantum of power, including 700 MW
outward supply for the month of May 2026, pending disposal of the Petition. On
Order in Petition No. 191/MP/2026 Page 10

30.04.2026, discussions were ongoing with Respondent No. 1 to resolve the issues,
including the grant of an NOC within a week.
(i) Respondent No. 4 approved and granted Standing Clearance for the balance sale/
export of 700 MW power through inter/ intra-State short-term open access for the
period from 01.05.2026 to 31.05.2026.
Hearing dated 06.05.2026
6.The relevant extracts of the hearing are as below:
“At the outset, learned senior counsel for the Respondent, TPCODL, submitted that the Petitioner,
JSL, has not mapped the ID of TPCODL on the e-filing portal; therefore, TPCODL was unable to
access the main Petition and the accompanying IAs. Accordingly, he prayed for additional time to
file the reply on maintainability and merits in respect of the Petition and IA No. 67/2026.
2. Learned senior counsel for the Petitioner, JSL, while objecting to the above contentions,
submitted that TPCODL was duly mapped on the e-filing portal and thus, the service was deemed
to be completed on TPCODL in terms of the Conduct of Business Regulations, 2023. He further
submitted that JSL has filed an affidavit dated 4.5.2026 for placing on record certain factual
corrections and subsequent developments in the matter, which occurred after the filing of the
Petition.
3. Considering the above, the Commission permitted TPCODL to file its reply to the IA as well as
the Petition on both counts, maintainability as well as merits, within a week, with a copy to the
Petitioner, who may file its rejoinder to the same, if any, within two days thereafter.”
Submissions of Respondent No.1, TP Central Odisha Distribution Limited (TPCODL)
7.TPCODL, vide affidavit dated 18.05.2026, has submitted as under:
(a) The present Petition is not maintainable, and this Commission does not have
jurisdiction to adjudicate the present Petition since the underlying issue pertaining to
the grant of NOC in favour of the Petitioner is governed by the OERC (Terms and
Conditions for Intra-State Open Access) Regulations, 2020 (“OA Regulations”). As per
Regulation 15 of the OA Regulations, the procedure for the grant of short-term open
access is provided, and the proviso to Regulation 15(1) specifically states that in
respect of a consumer connected to the distribution system seeking inter-State short-
term open access, the SLDC shall require the consumer to submit consent of the
concerned distribution licensee before giving consent to RLDC.
(b) Regulation 16(1) of the OA Regulations stipulates that in case of an applicant

ACPP-II, as arbitrary and illegal for T-GNA applications.
8. The Petitioner vide IA No. 67/2026 has prayed for the grant of an ad interim direction to the
Respondents, to grant the Standing Clearance for the month of May, 2026, pending
disposal of the instant Petition.
9. The Odisha SLDC has submitted that the Petitioner is an entity embedded within the intra-
State transmission and distribution network of Odisha by virtue of its connectivity with
Meramundali Grid Sub-Station of OPTCL at 400 kV level and also maintains contract
demand with Respondent No. 1/ TPCODL for auxiliary, emergency, and start-up power
requirements.
10. The Respondents have contested that the matter in the captioned Petition for the grant of
Standing Clearance by SLDC primarily comes under the jurisdiction of Odisha Electricity
Regulatory Commission (OERC). Therefore, the Petition is liable to be rejected on the
ground of maintainability, as the Appropriate Commission is the Odisha Electricity
Regulatory Commission to deal with the Standing Clearance for Open Access to the
Petitioner and the conditions therein.
11. The Petitioner has argued that the GNA Regulations stipulated grounds of refusal of
Standing Clearance, either the non-existence of necessary infrastructure or the
unavailability of surplus transmission capacity. The conditions imposed by the DISCOM
to deny consent/ NOC are extraneous, leading to a dispute between the parties; therefore,
this Commission has jurisdiction to adjudicate the matter. It has further been submitted
that, since the matter relates to ISTS open access, not intra-state open access, governed
by the GNA Regulations and the procedures therein, this Commission has the power to
adjudicate and provide interim relief, as prayed for.
12. I We have considered the submissions of the Petitioner and Respondents and perused
the documents available on record. It is well-settled that the issue of maintainability, going
to the jurisdiction of this Commission, must be decided as a threshold question before
Order in Petition No. 191/MP/2026 Page 31

embarking on the merits of the dispute. The first and foremost issue that arises for our
consideration is ‘Whether this Commission has jurisdiction to adjudicate the dispute
in the instant Petition related to non-grant of Standing Clearance by the Odisha
SLDC for an intra-State entity, for transactions under T-GNA?
13. The Schematic diagram of JSL, Angul, as submitted by the Petitioner, is as under:
A perusal of the above connectivity diagram reveals that the Petitioner’s Steel plant,
along with the ACPP-II and ACPP-I generating stations, is directly connected to the intra-
State transmission system, at the 400kV level at OPTCL’s Meramandali Substation.
14. The relevant extracts of the GNA Regulations are as under:
“30. Grant of T-GNA
Order in Petition No. 191/MP/2026 Page 32

working days from the date of receipt of the application for the new grid
connected entity and within 3 (three) working days from the date of receipt
of the application for an existing grid connected entity.
g) In case the host SLDC/RLDC finds that the application for standing
clearance is incomplete or defective in any respect, it shall communicate
the same to the entity within 2 (two) working days from the date of receipt
of such application.
As per the above, the consent of DISCOM, if any, is also required to be uploaded
in the NOAR portal by SLDC or the T-GNA Applicant, as per the practise in the host
State.
16. Under the GNA Regulations, 2022, Standing Clearance is obtained through the NOAR
Procedure. Clause 6(e) of the NOAR Procedure, dealing with the documentation to be
submitted, provides that DISCOM consent, “if any, shall be uploaded as per the practice
in the host state.” It is clarified that SLDC issues Standing Clearance for intra-State entities
through the NOAR Portal. Hence, when issuing standing clearance, if the SLDC requires
the discom consent to be uploaded, it indicates this in the comments, as was done in the
instant case. The expression “as per the practice in the host state” is a deliberate and
conscious regulatory choice. This Commission, in framing the GNA Regulations and the
NOAR Procedure, expressly recognized and referred to the host state’s regulatory
framework for standing clearance to be issued by SLDC after DISCOM consent, as
applicable.
17. Indisputably, the concerned State Commission, i.e., OERC, has notified the Open Access
Regulations 2020 in exercise of its powers conferred under Section 42 read with Sections
39, 40, 86 and 181 of the Act. Regulation 2 thereof also clearly stipulates that the said
Regulations shall apply to open access for the use of intra-State transmission and
distribution systems in the State, including when such systems are used in conjunction
with the inter-state transmission system. Clause 6(e) is not an overriding provision
displacing the OERC OA Regulations; it is a facilitative clause that acknowledges and
incorporates the host State’s practice.
18. Significantly, under the GNA Regulations, 2022, there is no dispute resolution provision
for disputes between embedded consumers and their Distribution Licensees relating to
NOC. This is in marked contrast to Regulation 26 of the erstwhile CERC Open Access
Regulations, 2008, which expressly conferred upon this Commission dispute-resolution
jurisdiction for open access disputes (subject to the proviso that matters within the State
Commission jurisdiction would be referred to the State Commission). Applications made
Order in Petition No. 191/MP/2026 Page 35

As per the above, for the injection point in the intra-State transmission system,
consent from SLDCs and the Distribution licensee, as applicable, is a requirement for the
grant of Open Access.
19. We note that the Petitioner is an intra-State entity, and the OERC (Terms and Conditions
of intra-State Open Access) Regulations, 2020, are applicable to regulate intra-State open
access-related matters, such as in the instant case of the grant of Standing Clearance.
Pertinently, the APTEL in judgment dated 28.7.2016 passed Appeal Nos. 231 of 2025 and
Anr. has held that the UPERC Open Access Regulations shall be applicable for applying
for open access for use of intra-State transmission system and/or the distribution systems
of licensees within the State, including, when such system is used in conjunction with an
inter-State transmission system, and consequently, any dispute arising due to non-
issuance of NOC by UPSLDC/UPPTCL for use of intra-State transmission system for open
access has to be brought before the State Commission.
20. On the above principles, this Commission has also decided a similar issue in its order
dated 07.07.2025 in Petition No. 223/MP/2023 (Tadas Wind Energy Private Limited v.
KPTCL and Ors.), wherein the Commission inter alia held as under:
“30. Further, Section 86 of the Act provides as under:
“Section 86. (Functions of State Commission): --- (1) The State Commission shall discharge
the following functions, namely: -
………..
(c) facilitate intra-State transmission and wheeling of electricity:
………….
(f) adjudicate upon the disputes between the licensees, and generating companies and to
refer any dispute for arbitration:
……………….”
As per the above, the matter to facilitate intra-State transmission and wheeling of electricity,
and adjudication upon the disputes between the licensees, generating companies, fall under
the jurisdiction of the State Commission.
31.The question of whether the State Commission will have jurisdiction in case of inter-State
open access where the intra-State transmission system and the distribution systems are used
was considered by the Appellate Tribunal in Appeal No. 231/2015 and 251/2015 (UPPCL v
UPERC & Ors) where the question was whether dispute arising out of denial of no objection
by the SLDC for inter-State open access shall be subject to jurisdiction of the Central
Commission or the respective State Commission. The Appellate Tribunal in its judgment dated
28.7.2016 held that UPERC shall have the jurisdiction in case of disputes involving non-
issuance of NOC by UPSLDC/ UPPTCL for use of the Intra-State transmission system for
open access transactions. The relevant portion of the judgment of the Appellate Tribunal is
extracted as under:
“13. (r)….the current matter under consideration is consisting of two transactions,
one where Inter-state open access was sought for supply of power from shree
cement Rajasthan plant to Pali substation and the other where Intra-State open
access is required for using UPPTCL transmission system. After considering all the
Order in Petition No. 191/MP/2026 Page 37

relevant provisions of Electricity Act and the provisions of regulations of Central
commission and the State Commission, we are of the considered view that the
UPERC Open access regulations shall be applicable for applying for open access
for use of intra state transmission system and/ or the distribution system of licensees
within the State, including, when such system is used in conjunction with inter-state
transmission system. Hence any dispute arising due to non-issuance of NOC by
UPSLDC/ UPPTCL for use of Intra- State transmission system for open access
transactions has to be brought before the State Commission which in this case is
UPERC. Hence on this issue of jurisdiction we hold that in the present case the
UPERC‟s jurisdiction is attracted.”
As per the above judgment, any dispute due to non-issuance of NOC by SLDC for use of intra-
State transmission system/network and distribution system, including when such system is
used in conjunction with inter-State transmission system, would be adjudicated by the
concerned State Commission.
32. Regulation 14 of the Karnataka Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and conditions for
Open Access) Regulations, 2004, as amended from time to time, provides as under:
“16. Dispute Resolution:(1) All disputes and complaints relating to open access shall be
raised before the SLDC, which may investigate and endeavour to resolve he grievance.
(2) If the SLDC is unable to redress the grievance, after giving opportunity to the open
access applicant, shall pass orders referring the matter to the Commission for resolution.
The open access applicant may file a Petition before the Commission within a period of thirty
days from the date of receipt of order from the nodal agency, namely SLDC.”
As per the above Regulations of the State Commission, any dispute arising due to non-
Issuance of NOC by Respondent No. 1 has to be brought before the State Commission, which
in this case is KERC, and for the same reason, KERC's jurisdiction is attracted.
33. Considering the above discussion, we are of the considered view that the issue
involved under this Petition, i.e. grant of standing clearance to the Petitioner to use
of the intra-State transmission network of the KPTCL, is related to the intra-State
transmission network. Thus, we are not in agreement with the Petitioner claims
that the instant Petition falls under the jurisdiction of this Commission in terms
of Section 79(1)(c), Section 79(1)(f), and Regulation 26 of the CERC (Open
Access in inter-State Transmission) Regulations, 2008. We are of the view that,
in terms of Section 86 of the Act, the issue under this Petition falls under the
jurisdiction of the State Commission. Therefore, the Petitioner is directed to
approach the concerned State Commission for adjudication of the issues
under this Petition.”
As per the above, it was held that the grant of standing clearance to the Petitioner
for use of the intra-State transmission network is within the jurisdiction of the State
Electricity Regulatory Commission.
21. The above conclusion, in our view, is also supported by the recent decision of the Hon’ble
Supreme Court in Ramayana Ispat Pvt. Ltd. and Anr. v. State of Rajasthan and Ors., 2025
INSC 424, wherein the Hon’ble Supreme Court has, while rejecting the claim that only
CERC has the authority to regulate the inter-State open access, held that RERC/State
Commission retains the jurisdiction over intra-State aspects of open access transactions
Order in Petition No. 191/MP/2026 Page 38

even if the power originates from another State. The relevant extracts of the said judgment
read as under:
I. Whether the RERC had the jurisdiction to regulate inter-state open access under the Act
of 2003?
44. The primary contention of the appellants regarding the jurisdiction of the RERC to regulate
inter-state open access is without any merit. The Act of 2003 establishes a clear distinction
between the regulatory functions of the CERC and State Commissions. While inter-state
transmission falls within the domain of the CERC under Section 79(1)(c), the power of the State
Commission to regulate intra-state transmission and distribution under Section 86(1)(c) is well
established. Furthermore, the appellants’ argument that the Regulations of 2016 have an
extraterritorial effect is misplaced. The Regulations of 2016 do not seek to regulate inter-state
transmission per se but rather ensures that transactions impacting the Rajasthan grid remain
under the oversight of the State Commission.
45. Section 79(1)(c) of the Act of 2003, defines the regulatory authority of the CERC over inter-
state transmission of electricity. However, this provision does not strip State Commissions,
including RERC, of their jurisdiction over intra-state aspects of open access. Section 42(2) of the
Act of 2003 expressly empowers State Commissions to regulate open access within their
respective states, ensuring fair and non-discriminatory access to transmission and distribution
networks within the state. Further, Section 42(3) of the Act of 2003 provides that whenever a
consumer, with premises within the area of supply of a distribution licensee, requires supply of
electricity from a generating company other than such distribution licensee, such transmission
and supply shall be in accordance with the regulations made by the State Commission.
46. The respondents have, in their submissions, drawn a relevant and appropriate parallel with
the regulation of National Highways in the country, which also run across state borders. It has
been rightly analogised by the RERC that even though National Highways falls under Entry 23
of List I of the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution of India and is a central subject, nevertheless
when it passes through the respective states it is subject to tolls under the respective state laws
as per Entry 59 of List II of the Seventh Schedule. Therefore, when ‘Electricity’ which is a subject
matter of Entry 38, List III is wheeled from outside the state and distributed within the state, the
regulations governing such distribution within the state cannot, by any stretch, be termed to be
suffering from any excess of jurisdiction.
47. The key determinant is not the source of power but its delivery, end-user, and consumption
within Rajasthan's intra-state grid. The Act of 2003 provides a framework for demarcating
responsibilities between CERC and State Commissions, ensuring that intrastate aspects of
electricity regulation remain within the purview of State Commissions. The appellants’
interpretation would render Section 42 redundant and contradict the legislative intent behind
decentralizing regulatory authority to the State Commissions. Thus, the claim that only CERC
has the authority to regulate inter-state open access cannot be accepted in light of the legislative
intent behind the Act of 2003. Therefore, RERC retains jurisdiction over intra-state transactions
even if the power originates from another state.
48. Further, Section 2(47) of the Act of 2003 defines open access as non-discriminatory access
to transmission and distribution systems, encompassing both interstate and intra-state
transactions. The respondents argue that the statute does not differentiate between them for
regulatory purposes, meaning that State Commissions naturally retain authority over open
access within their jurisdictions. This interpretation aligns with Section 42, which explicitly grants
State Commissions the power to regulate open access for consumers in their states. Additionally,
Section 2(15) of the Act of 2003 defines a “consumer” as any person who receives electricity
from a licensee or whose premises are connected to a distribution system. Since distribution
licensees operate within state boundaries, the regulation of open access for consumers falls
squarely within the State Commission’s jurisdiction. Section 2(17) further strengthens this
position by defining a “distribution licensee” as an entity authorized to distribute electricity within
Order in Petition No. 191/MP/2026 Page 39

a specific area, reinforcing the role of State Commissions in regulating transactions that
ultimately facilitate electricity supply to consumers within the state.
49. Section 181 of the Act of 2003 empowers State Commissions to frame regulations necessary
for implementing the provisions of the Act of 2003. This includes establishing conditions for open
access, determining charges, and ensuring fair access to intra-state transmission and distribution
networks. By granting State Commissions the authority to introduce and regulate open access,
the legislature has clearly vested regulatory oversight with RERC in Rajasthan. The omission of
any reference to CERC’s jurisdiction over open access consumers in Section 42 of the Act further
reinforces the respondents’ argument. Section 79, which delineates CERC’s functions, does not
extend its authority to the regulation of end consumers or the supply of power via distribution
licensees. This omission is indicative of the legislature’s intent to keep such matters under State
Commissions’ oversight, ensuring that electricity consumers and distribution networks within a
state remain subject to state-level regulation.
50. Thus, the respondents’ argument is well-founded in statutory provisions, legislative intent,
and the structural framework of the Act of 2003. RERC’s authority to regulate intra-state aspects
of open access transactions, even when electricity is sourced from another state, aligns with the
Act’s objectives and ensures effective regulatory oversight….”
The Petitioner has sought to distinguish the aforesaid judgment by contending that the
sole issue in the said judgment was a constitutional/statutory challenge to RERC’s own
subordinate legislation and the key determinant for the Hon’ble Supreme Court therein was
that the end use and consumption is within Rajasthan’s intra-state grid, which is not the
case with the Petitioner, who is seeking the T-GNA for access to ISTS under a bilateral
transaction. However, we do not find any merit in such contentions put forth to distinguish
the present case. Once it has been held that the State Commission retains authority to
regulate intra-state aspects of open access transactions, even when the electricity is
sourced from another state (or sourced to another State as is in this case), the regulatory
jurisdiction of the State Commission gets attracted, either exercised under Section 86(1)(c)
or by way of delegated legislation under Section 181 of the Act, and consequently, any
dispute arising in terms of the use of the intra-state network, even when to be used in
conjunction with ISTS, would fall within the jurisdiction of the State Commission. As already
noted above, the Petitioner is connected to the intra-State network of the State, thereby an
intra-State entity and is also an EHT consumer of the distribution licensee/Respondent
No.1, and as the requirement of consent/NOC from the distribution licensee would be
governed by the provisions of the OERC Regulations, the dispute arising therefrom also
must be held to lie before the OERC only.
22. Based on the foregoing, we are of the view that the matter under the present Petition is
beyond the jurisdictional power of this Commission. Accordingly, the Petition as well as
the related Interlocutory Application are rejected. The Petitioner may approach the
Appropriate Commission for adjudication of the issues under the instant Petition.
Order in Petition No. 191/MP/2026 Page 40

ORDER
The Petitioner, R.K.M. Powergen Private Limited (in short ‘RKMPPL’), has filed
the present Petition seeking the following relief(s):
“a) Hold and declare that the notification dated 07.12.2015 issued by the Ministry of
Environment Forest and Climate Change (MoEF&CC), requiring installation of Flue Gas
Desulphurizer (FGD) and associated systems, constitutes as a change in law event,
within the meaning of Article 10 of the PPA dated 15.03.2016, executed between the
Petitioner and the Respondent No.1;
b) Allow in-principal approval for the proposed expenditure to be incurred towards the
Change in Law event in relation to procurement, installation, commissioning, operation
& maintenance of Flue Gas Desulphurizer (FGD) and associated systems, along with
carrying costs as per the provisions of PPA, subject to true up;
(c) Device a methodology for the purpose of recovery of the amount incurred/ to be
incurred by the Petitioner, in installing the FGD and associated systems, along with the
methodology towards calculating tariff in relation to the estimated increase in O&M
Expenses, other operating norms like Auxiliary Power Consumption and SHR, spares,
water charges, landed cost of reagents, gypsum disposal cost etc., with corresponding
increase in Capacity Charges and energy charge rate (ECR), as a result of complying
with the change in law event of installation of FGD and associated systems such that
the Petitioner is restored to the same economic position as if such Change in Law event
had not occurred;
(d) While considering prayers (b) and (c) above, issue directions for exclusion of the
period of shutdown (required for installation of FGD) for the purposes of calculating the
Availability of the power project of the Petitioner, in order to ensure full recovery of
Capacity Charges due to such shutdown;
(e) Grant liberty to the Petitioner to approach this Hon’ble Commission, after installation
of the FGD equipment, for the purpose of true up/ reimbursement of the actual amount,
Order in Petition No.191/MP/2024 Page 2 of 4

and to claim any other amount not included in the present petition, along with applicable
carrying cost/ interest cost, if any;
(f) Approve and grant carrying costs/ interest costs to the Petitioner from the effective
date of the change in law events as claimed in the present petition;
(g) Direct UPPCL, in future, to continue to make any payments, which will be accruing
in favour of the Petitioner, on account of the change in law events, as prayed in the
present Petition;
(h) pass any other order as this Hon’ble Commission may deem fit in the facts and
circumstances of the present case and in the interest of justice.”
2. The Petitioner, a company registered under the Companies Act, 1956, has set
up a 4x360 MW coal-based thermal generating station at Ucchpinda Village, Janjgir-
Champa District, Chhattisgarh. Pursuant to the competitive bidding process conducted
by the Respondent, UPPCL, the bid submitted by the Petitioner for the supply of 350
MW power was accepted, and thereafter, a PPA dated 15.3.2016 was executed
between the parties, for a term of 25 years.
3. The Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEF&CC) issued a
notification on 7 December 2015 requiring thermal power plants to install additional
emission control systems, including Flue Gas Desulphurization (FGD) units, to meet
the revised environmental standards. To comply with the said direction, the Petitioner
conducted a feasibility study and selected wet limestone-based FGD technology. The
Petitioner issued a Change in Law notice to UPPCL on 1st September 2018, relying on
the directions of the Ministry of Power and relevant regulatory orders supporting
recovery of FGD-related costs. Pursuant to the notification of the Electricity (Timely
Recovery of Costs due to Change in Law) Rules, 2021, the Petitioner issued a fresh
notice on 30 December 2021 and the same was rejected by the Respondent, UPPCL,
on 20 January 2022. In terms of the APTEL judgment in related matters, the Petitioner
Order in Petition No.191/MP/2024 Page 3 of 4

again issued a Change in Law notice on 28 November 2023, but UPPCL rejected the
same as well on 21 December 2023.
4. In this background, the Petitioner filed the instant Petition. During the first
hearing on 7.10.2024, notice was issued, subject to just exceptions and parties were
directed to complete the pleadings. Respondent UPPCL, in its reply dated 6 November
2024, challenged the Petition on various grounds, including limitation, maintainability,
and non-compliance with the Change in Law provisions of the PPA.
Hearing dated 25.5.2026
5. During the course of the hearing, the learned counsel for the Petitioner submitted
that in terms of the MoEFCC notification dated 11.7.2025, the generating station of the
Petitioner stands classified under Category ‘C’, pursuant to which the requirement of
the FGD systems is no longer required. Therefore, upon instructions, the learned
counsel for the Petitioner requested to withdraw the present Petition. The learned
counsel appearing for the Respondents did not object to the said request.
6. In view of the submissions made by the learned counsel for the Petitioner and
in the absence of any objection from the Respondents, the prayer for withdrawal of the
instant Petition is allowed.
7. Accordingly, Petition No. 191/MP/2024 is disposed of as ‘withdrawn’.

ORDER
The instant Petition is seeking compensation for capital assets that are required
to be replaced or taken out of service when the Utility is undertaking the same as
per the decisions and approval of statutory planning agencies. The Petitioner has
made the following prayers vide the instant Petition:
a)Admit the Petition and initiate the proceedings to consider the aspects raised by

never raised the issue that these works have at any time led to redundancy,
non-usability, or obsolescence of certain assets/parts of the assets, and to
consequential decapitalization and under-recovery of investment. Therefore,
the Petitioner is required to explain the manner in which the issues of
decapitalization were being addressed in such cases till now.
(j)In case of upgradation/modification involving Part-B works, i.e., replacement of
conductor and converting line into a higher voltage line with multiple circuits,
there is a definite issue of stranded cost on account of decapitalization. The
Petitioner states that the stranded cost is on account of compensation devices,
foundations, tower parts, tower accessories like insulators, hardware and
substation equipment etc. In this connection, it was stated as hereunder:-
i. Initial cost estimates of the Petitioner are prepared based on works/supplies
made under old contracts, high level of IDC, IEDC and contingency charges.
The Commission, in its several orders, has observed that the cost estimates
of the Petitioner are on the higher side. Therefore, the cost of said
assets/parts/equipment cannot be derived from these estimates.
Order in Petition Number 61/MP/2022 Page 12

ii.The scope of the project is generally split by the Petitioner into more than one
package, and bids are invited on a turnkey basis. The cost of the said
assets/parts/equipment cannot be found out from the price discovered through
bids.
iii.Section 61 of the Electricity Act, 2003 mandates that the tariff should reflect
the actual cost of supply. Therefore, it is necessary that the cost of
assets/parts/equipment becoming redundant, unusable, or obsolete must be
found as of the date of their being put into commercial use.
iv.The prayer of the Petitioner to allow it to continue serving such
assets/parts/equipment as part of the capital cost of the upgraded and new
system is contrary to Section 61 of the Act, 2003, which mandates that the
tariff should reflect the actual cost of supply and also safeguards the interest
of consumers. The prayer is not based on actual cost nor safeguards the
interests of consumers as such, and cannot be allowed.
v.Alternatively, the Petitioner has prayed to allow it to recover the “balance
unrecovered depreciation” and dismantling cost on a one-time basis on
decapitalization of the existing assets in its gross block. The Petitioner has not
submitted a mathematical model in support of this prayer. Even for this
purpose, actual historical cost of assets/parts/equipment becoming
redundant, unusable, or obsolete would be needed for the computation of
“balance uncovered depreciation”; as such, it cannot be allowed, contrary to
the provisions of Section 61 of the Act, 2003.
vi.The dismantling cost cannot be a case of “one-time decapitalization” and
should not be allowed. The dismantling cost is a matter of work related to
upgradation/modification, and such costs should be claimed under the cost of
such works.

Analysis and Decision
23. The Petitioner has submitted that if existing assets are not being used after being
upgraded or modified in accordance with approved schemes and for reasons other
than any default or failure attributable to the transmission licensee, the
Transmission Licensee may be permitted to continue servicing the value of such
assets as part of the capital cost of the upgraded and new system. Alternatively,
the Transmission Licensee may be permitted to recover the remaining unrecovered
depreciation and dismantling costs on a one-time basis upon de-capitalization of
the existing assets in its gross block. The Petitioner has further stated that there will
be financial repercussions for the investment made by the transmission licensees,
including Power Grid, if the same is prohibited because such assets are no longer
utilized in the system. Petitioner has prayed for permission to grant the said
dispensation under the Power to relax and the Power to remove difficulty under the
Tariff Regulations.
24.Respondents have opposed the prayer of the petitioner, stating that the issues can
be addressed by amendments to the current Regulations. Further the transmission
licensee may be compensated for the uncovered cost due to decapitalization of
assets rendered redundant, unusable or obsolete only when there are remote
chances of their use in future provided, (i) it is not on account of inefficiency or
negligence of the transmission licensee and (ii) it is done on the recommendations
of RPC/Standing Committee or any statutory Body, Court and Government
instrumentality competent to issue directions of the nature involved in the present
matter. The Commission’s power to remove difficulties can only be invoked to
facilitate smooth implementation and cannot alter the basic structure or essential
provisions of the statute. This stance has been stipulated in the judgment of the
Hon’ble Supreme Court in MU Sinai v. Union of India, (1975) 3 SCC 765, which
holds as follows:
“The existence or arising of a difficulty is the sine qua non for the exercise of power.
If this condition precedent is not satisfied as an objective fact, the power under this
Order in Petition Number 61/MP/2022 Page 30

clause cannot be invoked at all. Again, the “difficulty” contemplated by the clause
must be a difficulty arising in giving effect to the provisions of the Act and not a
difficulty arising aliunde, or an extraneous difficulty. Further, the central
Government can exercise the power under the clause only to the extent it is
necessary for applying or giving effect to the Act etc., and no further. It may slightly
tinker with the Act to round off angularities, and smoothen the joints or remove
minor obscurities to make it workable, but it cannot change, disfigure or do violence
to the basic structure and primary features of the Act. In no case, can it, under the
guise of removing a difficulty change the scheme and essential provisions of the
Act.”
25. Respondents have submitted that Petitioner has wrongfully placed reliance upon
Section 61 of the Act while seeking the present relief. Once tariff regulations are
framed under Section 61 of the Act, the Commission is bound to act in conformity
with them.
26.We have considered the submissions of the Petitioner as well as the Respondents.
The issue which arises for consideration in the present Petition is
ISSUE 1: Whether the unrecovered depreciation of the decapitalised/
removed assets can be recovered as per the Tariff Regulations, 2019?
ISSUE 2: Whether the Commission can exercise power to relax for the
evolution of an appropriate methodology to effectively compensate the
transmission licensees, such as POWERGRID, in regard to financial
implications arising out of upgradation/modification of assets?
The above issues are addressed in the subsequent paragraphs.

29.Keeping in view the above discussions, we are of the considered view that recovery
of unrecovered depreciation for assets decapitalised is beyond the scope of
provisions of Tariff Regulations, 2019. We have also perused Tariff Regulations,
2024, which provides as under:
“
35. De-Commissioning
(1) In case a generating station or unit thereof, or a transmission system including
communication systems or element thereof after it is certified by CEA or CTU or any other
statutory authority, that any asset cannot be operated or needs to be replaced on account
of environmental concerns or safety issues or system upgradation or a combination of
these factors not attributable to generating company or a transmission licensee, the
unrecovered depreciable value may be allowed to be recovered on a case-to-case basis
Order in Petition Number 61/MP/2022 Page 35

after duly adjusting the salvage value or realisation value, whichever is higher, post
disposal of such project.
Provided that the manner of recovery, including a number of instalments in which such
unrecovered depreciation will be allowed, shall be specified by the Commission on a case-
to-case basis.
Provided further that no carrying cost shall be allowed on any delay associated with
such recovery.”
As per the above, the recovery of unrecovered depreciation has been covered. We
note that any items listed under Paragraph 27 and decommissioned in 2024-2029
would be covered by the above-quoted Regulations.
30.The Petitioner, in support of its contention, has submitted that in terms of the
Hon'ble Supreme Court judgment in the case of PTC India Ltd. v. CERC, (2010) 4
SCC 603, the Commission retains residuary powers to address gaps in regulations
through appropriate orders. Both the Tariff Regulations, 2014 and 2019, expressly
vest the Commission with the "power to relax" and "power to remove difficulties”,
enabling deviations from strict regulatory provisions, which were justified.
31.Per contra, the Respondents have opposed the invocation of powers to relax and
remove difficulties on the ground that the treatment of decapitalised assets is
specifically governed by the Tariff Regulations. UPPCL has submitted that the
methodology relating to decapitalisation is specifically provided under the Tariff
Regulations and, therefore, the relief sought by the Petitioner cannot be granted
by invoking the powers to relax or remove difficulty. MPPMCL has contended that
the power to relax can be used for applying the muster of ‘public interest’ and there
cannot be any relaxation contrary to the public interest. BSES has submitted that
the power to relax is a judicial discretion which cannot be invoked for profit motive
or for the grant of an unreasonable tariff, and that invocation of the powers to relax
and remove difficulty in the present case would alter the existing tariff framework
and create a tariff recovery mechanism not contemplated under the Regulations.
CSPDCL has argued that the power to remove difficulty is intended only to facilitate
implementation of the Regulations and cannot be invoked to address financial
hardship arising from the operation of the Regulations themselves. The
Respondents have, therefore, collectively submitted that the relief sought by the
Petitioner can only be provided through amendment of the Tariff Regulations and
not through exercise of the powers to relax or remove difficulty. MPPMCL, BSES
and CSPDCL have also relied upon the judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in
M.U. Sinai v. Union of India to contend that the powers to relax and remove
Order in Petition Number 61/MP/2022 Page 36

difficulty are limited powers intended to facilitate implementation of the Regulations
and cannot be exercised in a manner that alters the scheme of the Regulations or
creates substantive rights not contemplated therein.
32.We have considered the parties' submissions. In PTC India Ltd. v. CERC, the
Hon'ble Supreme Court, vide judgment dated 15.3.2010, held that the Commission
is not precluded from exercising its statutory powers under Section 79 of the Act in
the absence of regulations. However, the Hon'ble Supreme Court also held that
where regulations have been framed under Section 178 of the Act, the measures
undertaken by the Commission under Section 79 are required to be in conformity
with such regulations. Therefore, while the Commission may exercise its powers
in areas not governed by regulations, such powers cannot be exercised in a
manner contrary to the express provisions contained in the regulations. The
relevant excerpt of the judgment dated 15.3.2010 is as follows:
“As stated, if there is a regulation, then the measure under Section 79(1) has
to be in conformity with such regulation under Section 178. This principle flows
from various judgments of this Court which we have discussed hereinafter. For
example, under Section 79(1)(g) the Central Commission is required to levy
fees for the purpose of the 2003 Act. An Order imposing regulatory fees could
be passed even in the absence of a regulation under Section 178. If the levy is
unreasonable, it could be the subject matter of challenge before the Appellate
Authority under Section 111 as the levy is imposed by an Order/decision
making process. Making of a regulation under Section 178 is not a pre-condition
to passing of an Order levying a regulatory fee under Section 79(1)(g).
However, if there is a regulation under Section 178 in that regard then the Order
levying fees under Section 79(1)(g) has to be in consonance with such
regulation. Similarly, while exercising the power to frame the terms and
conditions for determination of tariff under Section 178, the Commission has to
be guided by the factors specified in Section 61. It is open to the Central
Commission to specify terms and conditions for determination of tariff even in
the absence of the regulations under Section 178. However, if a regulation is
made under Section 178, then, in that event, framing of terms and conditions
for determination of tariff under Section 61 has to be in consonance with the
regulation under Section 178.
….”
33.Accordingly, in the present case, the treatment of decapitalised assets and
depreciation thereon was specifically governed by Regulations 19 and 33 of the
2019 Tariff Regulations. Therefore, the relief sought cannot be granted by invoking
residuary powers in a manner contrary to the regulatory framework then in force.
34.Further, the Hon’ble Supreme Court in judgment dated 7.11.1974 in Mahendra
Upendra Sinai Etc. v. Union of India & Ors., 1975 SCR (2) 640, observed that there
Order in Petition Number 61/MP/2022 Page 37

must be a “difficulty” in giving effect to the provisions for exercising the Power to
Remove Difficulty and that the “difficulty” must not be extraneous. The relevant
extract of the said judgment dated 7.11.1974 is as follows:
“Now let us turn to Clause (7) of the Regulation. It will be seen that the power
given by it is not uncontrolled or unfettered. It is strictly circumscribed, and its
use is conditioned and restricted. The existence or arising of a "difficulty" is the
sine qua non for the exercise of the power. If this condition precedent is not
satisfied as an objective fact, the power under this Clause cannot, be invoked
at au. Again, the "difficulty" contemplated by the Clause must be a difficulty
arising in giving effect to the provisions of the Act and not a difficulty arising
aliunde, or an extraneous difficulty. Further, the Central Government can
exercise the power under the Clause only to the extent it is necessary for
applying or giving effect to the Act etc., and no further. It may slightly tinker with
the Act to round off angularities, and smoothen the joints or remove minor
obscurities to make it workable, but it cannot change, disfigure or do violence
to the basic structure and primary features of the Act. In no case, can it, under
the guise of removing a difficulty, change the scheme and essential provisions
of the Act.”
As per the above judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court, the condition precedent
for invoking the Power to remove Difficulty is the existence of “difficulty”. In the
instant case, there is no “difficulty” in the implementation of the 2019 Tariff
Regulations as there is no provision to allow recovery of unrecovered depreciation.
For the same reason, the Commission cannot invoke ‘power to relax’ in the
absence of a Regulation with regard to recovery of unrecovered depreciation. In
our considered view, the prayer of the Petitioner to exercise the power of
relaxation/removal of difficulty for recovery of unrecovered depreciation would
have the effect of amending the said Regulations, which is not permissible. Under
the guise of relaxation or removing the difficulty, the Petitioner cannot seek the
introduction of a new provision, i.e. an amendment to the said regulations.
35.In light of the above discussions, we find no reason to allow the prayer of the
Petitioner for recovery of unrecovered depreciation for the control period 2019-24,
as there is no case to exercise the Power of relaxation/Removal of difficulty in the
present case.
36.We note that, considering the submissions of the Petitioner, the required provisions
have been incorporated into the Tariff Regulations, 2024. Since the provision of
recovery of unrecovered depreciation was not there in the Tariff Regulations 2019
and considering the submissions of respondents opposing the prayer of the
Petitioner, we are of the considered view that the prayers of the Petitioner cannot
be permitted for the period prior to the Tariff Regulations 2024.
Order in Petition Number 61/MP/2022 Page 38

37.Accordingly, the prayers of the Petitioner for the items listed under Paragraph 27,
which are decommissioned during the period prior to Tariff Regulations 2024, are
rejected.
38.Petition No 61/MP/2022 is disposed of in terms of the above.
Sd/ Sd/ Sd/
(Harish Dudani) (Ramesh Babu V.) (Jishnu Barua)
Member Member Chairperson
