Road, Gulbarga– 585102, Karnataka.
44. Hubli Electricity Supply Company
Navanagar, PB Road, Hubli- 580025, Karnataka .... Respondents
Parties Present:
Ms. Swapna Seshadri, Advocate, NTPC
Shri M Karthikeyan, Advocate, NTPC
Shri S. Vallinayagam, Advocate, TANGEDCO
Shri Anup Jain, Advocate, MSEDCL
Shri Vyom Chaturvedi, Advocate, MSEDCL
ORDER
The Petitioner, NTPC Limited, (hereinafter referred to as ‘Petitioner’ or ‘NTPC’)
has filed the present Petition under Sections 62 and 79 (1) (a) of the Electricity Act, 2003
(‘the Act’), seeking the determination of the Input price of coal of Pakri Barwadih Mine
(West & East) for the period from 1.4.2019 to 31.3.2024, as per Regulation 9 of the
Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations
2019 (in short ‘Tariff Regulations 2019’), as amended vide Central Electricity Regulatory
Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) (Second Amendment) Regulations, 2021
(in short ‘Second Amendment Regulations 2021’). The Petitioner has made the following
prayers:
a) Approve input price of coal of Pakri Barwadih mine for the tariff period 1.4.2019 to
31.3.2024;
b) Allow mine closure expenses as submitted in the petition;
c) Allow the Petitioner to provisionally bill input price of coal as per this Petition until
Order in Petition No.60/MP/2022 Page 4 of 105

the time the present Petition is disposed off with permission for retrospective
adjustment;
d) Allow relaxation in ATQ for the year 2020-21 as submitted in the Petition;
e) Allow the reimbursement of expenditure towards filing fees and any other
expenditure incurred by the Petitioner in relation to filing the present Petition before
the Hon’ble Commission in terms of the Tariff Regulation 2019 as amended from
the beneficiaries;
f) Condone any error/omission in the Petition and to grant an opportunity to the
Petitioner to rectify the same;
g) Permit the Petitioner to make such further submission(s), addition(s) and
alteration(s) to this Petition as may be necessary from time to time;
h) Pass any other order as it may deem fit in the circumstances as above.
Background of the case:
2. The Petitioner, NTPC, is a company incorporated under the provisions of the
Companies Act, 1956 and is a Government Company within the meaning of Section 2(45)
of the Companies Act, 2013. NTPC is also a “Generating Company” as defined under
Section 2(28) of the Act. The tariff for the sale of electricity generated at the generating
stations of NTPC is regulated by the Commission in terms of Section 79(1)(a) of the Act
read with Sections 61, 62 and 64 of the Act and the Regulations notified thereunder.
3. NTPC has been allocated integrated coal mines, including captive and basket-type
mines, for the supply of coal to its specified end-use generating stations, whose tariff is
determined by the Commission. Pakri Barwadih is one such integrated coal mine located
in the Hazaribagh district of the State of Jharkhand. The said mine has been allocated to
NTPC as a basket-type mine, and coal from the mine can be supplied to any of NTPC’s
generating stations depending on operational requirements.
4. The Pakri Barwadih mine is being operated under the Mine Developer and Operator
(MDO) mode, and the Letter of Award (LOA) for appointment of the MDO was issued to
M/s Thriveni-Sainik JV on 30.9.2015. The mine achieved its Commercial Operation Date
(COD) on 1.4.2019, and the coal extracted from the mine is used for the generation of
electricity at NTPC’s end-use generating stations for supply to the beneficiaries.
Order in Petition No.60/MP/2022 Page 5 of 105

5. The Commission notified the Tariff Regulations, 2019, which came into force on
1.4.2019 and provided the framework for the tariff determination for the period 2019–24.
Subsequently, the Commission notified the Second Amendment Regulations, 2021 on
13.9.2021, which stipulate the methodology and terms for the determination of the input
price of coal supplied from integrated mines to linked generating stations. In terms of
Regulation 2(1)(a) of the Tariff Regulations, 2019, as amended, the provisions apply where
a generating company has an arrangement for the supply of coal from integrated mines
allocated to it for one or more specified end-use generating stations whose tariff is
determined by the Commission. Further, Regulation 9(4) of the Tariff Regulations, 2019,
as amended, requires the generating company to file a Petition for the determination of the
input price of coal from the integrated mine(s) within sixty days from the date of commercial
operation of the mine or from the date of notification of the Regulations, whichever is later.
6. In terms of the above provisions, the present Petition has been filed by NTPC for the
determination of the input price of coal supplied from the Pakri Barwadih mine for the
period from 1.4.2019 to 31.3.2024. NTPC has also submitted that a certain delay occurred
in filing the Petition due to disruptions caused during the COVID-19 pandemic, including
the closure of offices and the loss of personnel involved in coal mining operations, and has
sought condonation of the delay.
7. The revised mining plan of the Pakri Barwadih was approved by the competent
authority on 21.9.2023. As per the approved mining plan, the mine is projected to reach
its peak rated capacity of 19MTPA by FY 2032-33. The salient features of the Pakri
Barwadih coal mine are as under:
Characteristics
Peak rated capacity 19 MTPA (to be achieved by FY 2032-33)
Location Hazaribagh, Jharkhand
Extractable Reserves (Opencast) 503.38 MT
Project Area 4209.84 Hectare
Average stripping ratio 1:4.17
Type of mining Open cast
Order in Petition No.60/MP/2022 Page 6 of 105

Committee (VDAC) in accordance with the National Policy on Resettlement and
Rehabilitation (NPRR) of Project Affected Families (PAF), 2003 and NTPC’s
Resettlement and Rehabilitation policy. The process was further complicated by
the introduction of the Jharkhand Rehabilitation and Resettlement Policy, 2008,
which required preparation, consultation and approval of a detailed R&R plan by
the State Government. Although a comprehensive R&R plan and compensation
package were eventually approved by the Government of Jharkhand in February
2013, land acquisition continued to face resistance due to demands for higher
compensation and other benefits. In addition, issues relating to the beneficiary
identification , encroachment on forest and government land, agitation by
villagers, and security concerns hindered progress. Despite continuous
engagement with district authorities, State Government officials and Central
Government ministries, the project suffered delays which were beyond the
control of the Petitioner.
(c) The Mining operations could not commence immediately, even after statutory
approvals were obtained, due to persistent protests and obstruction of site
activities by local groups, which also resulted in threats to NTPC personnel and
damage to equipment. Various communications were addressed by NTPC and
the Ministry of Power (MOP) to the State Government seeking intervention to
restore law and order and facilitate land acquisition. Eventually, following
revisions in compensation packages and engagement with the district
administration, the revised compensation scheme was approved, and
development activities were initiated after the appointment of an MDO in 2015.
The mine touched coal on 7.12.2016, and commercial operations of the Pakri
Barwadih mine were declared on 1.4.2019.
(d) With regard to tariff determination, the capital cost of the Pakri Barwadih mine
as on COD is Rs. 1252.50 crore on a cash basis, along with liabilities of Rs.
640.79 crore and notional Interest During Construction (IDC) of Rs. 51.63 crore.
The input price of coal has been computed in accordance with the Tariff
Regulations, 2019, as amended. The calculations have been based on a
normative debt-equity ratio of 70:30 and a base rate of return on equity of 14%.
Equity in excess of the normative level has been treated as a normative loan in
terms of Regulation 19(2)(b) of the Tariff Regulations, 2019, and the notional
IDC has been included as part of the capital cost. The rate of interest on the loan
has been considered based on the actual weighted average rate of interest for
the project. Depreciation has been calculated on a straight-line basis in
accordance with the asset life specified in Appendix IA to the Tariff Regulations.
Operation and maintenance (O&M) expenses have been claimed based on
actual expenditure for the year 2019-20 with an escalation of 3.5% for
subsequent years, subject to truing up. Statutory charges, including GST
applicable on coal, have also been considered in accordance with prevailing
regulations.
Order in Petition No.60/MP/2022 Page 8 of 105

(e) Mining operations at Pakri Barwadih are carried out through an MDO and the
mining fee payable to the MDO has been claimed as part of the input price in
accordance with the Tariff Regulations, 2019. The mining fee has been
calculated based on the base mining charge specified in the LOA along with the
escalation linked to input costs such as machinery, fuel, explosives, power, tyres
and labour. The escalation is determined as per the formula provided in the
MDO agreement, and the actual escalation factors paid to the MDO have been
considered in the computation. The liquidated damages of Rs. 23.62 per tonne
are being recovered from the MDO due to non-completion of certain
transportation facilities, and the corresponding loading and transportation work
has been awarded to a third party. Accordingly, the mining fee claimed has been
reduced by the amount of liquidated damages recovered, while the cost incurred
for alternative transportation has been included in the transportation charges.
The adjustments relating to stripping ratio, as provided under the Tariff
Regulations, 2019, would be accounted for at the time of truing up.
(f) As per the approved mining plan, the coal from the mine was to be transported
to the loading point through a Coal Handling Plant (CHP) comprising cross-
country conveyor belts and silo loading systems. The capital cost of installing
the CHP has been borne by NTPC, while its O&M will be carried out by the MDO.
However, due to delays arising from land acquisition and law-and-order issues,
the CHP could not be capitalised before COD. Therefore, coal transportation
was temporarily carried out through trucks from the mine mouth to the loading
point through competitively awarded contracts. The transportation charges for
this interim period have been claimed on the basis of actual payment made to
the transport contractors in accordance with Regulation 36I of the Tariff
Regulations, 2019. After commissioning the CHP, transportation charges would
include O&M charges payable to the MDO, as well as the capital cost of the
infrastructure.
(g) Regulation 36C (2) of the Tariff Regulations, 2019 provides that where crushing,
transportation, handling or washing activities are within the scope of the MDO,
no additional charges shall be admitted as such costs are deemed to be
recovered through the mining charges. However, in the present case, the fixed
infrastructure for coal transportation and loading has been developed and
funded by NTPC and the cost of such infrastructure is not included in the MDO
charges. Accordingly, strict application of the regulation would result in non-
recovery of the capital investment incurred by NTPC for the creation of such
infrastructure. Therefore, the Commission may exercise its powers under
Regulation 76 (Power to Relax) and Regulation 77 (Power to Remove Difficulty)
of the Tariff Regulations, 2019 and allow recovery of the capital cost of the CHP
infrastructure, along with the O&M charges payable to the MDO.
Order in Petition No.60/MP/2022 Page 9 of 105

(h) Regulation 36K of the Tariff Regulations, 2019, provides that the treatment of
such expenses. In the case of Pakri Barwadih mine, progressive mine closure
activities are within the scope of the MDO and their cost of such activities is
already included in the mining fee. The total estimated mine closure amount,
including both progressive and final closure components, is required to be
deposited in an escrow account as per the mining plan. Since progressive
closure expenses are included in the MDO fee, the Petitioner requested that the
difference between the borrowing cost on the portion of the escrow deposit
attributable to progressive closure and the interest received from the escrow
account be allowed as mine closure expenses. For the remaining portion relating
to final mine closure activities undertaken by NTPC, the amount deposited in the
escrow account should be allowed as part of the input price of coal in
accordance with Regulation 36K (1).
(i) The Annual Target Quantity (ATQ) for the Pakri Barwadih mine for the year
2020-21, as specified in the approved mining plan, is 95 lakh tonnes. However,
during the year 2020-21, the mine could achieve production of only 70.69 lakh
tonnes and dispatch of 66.37 lakh tonnes. This shortfall was primarily due to the
impact of the COVID-19 pandemic and suspension of mining operations caused
by protests and road blockades by nearby villagers. although mining activities
were exempted from lockdown restrictions, operations were severely affected
by a shortage of manpower, disruptions in the supply of spare parts and
machinery, and other operational constraints arising from the pandemic. In
addition, mining operations were completely halted for 94 days due to protests
and obstruction by villagers, who blocked access roads and prevented supply of
diesel, explosives and manpower to the mine site. These circumstances were
beyond its control and despite efforts made by NTPC and intervention by district
authorities and law-enforcement agencies, the disruption resulted in significant
loss of production.
(j) In view of these circumstances, the Commission mayexercise its powers under
Regulation 3(4)(a) of the Tariff Regulations, 2019, which permits relaxation of
the ATQ where supply of coal is prevented due to reasons not attributable to the
generating company. The Commission also possesses inherent powers under
Regulations 76 and 77 to relax the provisions of the regulations or remove
difficulties where strict application would cause hardship. In support of this
contention, the Petitioner relied upon judicial precedents including Hari Singh v.
State of Rajasthan, 1992 SCC OnLine Raj 210; Haryana Power Purchase
Centre v. Haryana Electricity Regulatory Commission, (Appeal Nos. 107 and
117 of 2015) decided on 21.03.2018; Tata Power Company Ltd. v. Jharkhand
State Electricity Regulatory Commission, Appeal No. 189 of 2011 decided on
20.09.2012; BSES Yamuna Power Ltd. v. CERC & Ors., Appeal Nos. 55 of 2013
and connected matters; and Ratnagiri Gas and Power Pvt. Ltd. v. CERC, Appeal
No. 130 of 2009 decided on 25.03.2011. These judgments recognise that the
Order in Petition No.60/MP/2022 Page 10 of 105

power to relax may be exercised where strict application of regulations causes
hardship and the circumstances leading to such hardship are beyond the control
of the party seeking relief.
(k) Accordingly, the Commission may relax the ATQ for the year 2020-21 and
consider the actual dispatch quantity of 66.37 lakh tonnes for the purpose of
computation of input price. Until the determination of input price is completed, it
is presently billing the coal supplied from Pakri Barwadih at the notified price of
Coal India Limited (CIL) for the corresponding grade of coal supplied to the
power sector in accordance with the Tariff Regulations, 2019. However, since
the input price claimed in the present Petition differs from the currently billed
price, the Petitioner may be permitted to provisionally bill the input price of coal
in accordance with the claim made in the Petition until the Commission finally
determines the input price.
(l) Petitioner has requested for recovery of the filing fee and publication expenses
directly from the beneficiaries in terms of Regulation 70(1) of the Tariff
Regulations, 2019.
Hearing dated 28.6.2022
10. The Petition was admitted on 28.6.2022, after hearing the learned counsel for the
Petitioner. The Petitioner was directed to furnish certain additional information, and
parties were directed to complete the pleadings. The Petitioner had filed additional
information vide affidavit dated 21.7.2022, and the Respondents MSEDCL, TANGEDCO,
BSPHCL and MPPMCL filed their replies vide separate affidavits dated 23.6.2022,
4.8.2022, 4.8.2022 and 5.8.2022, respectively. Thereafter, the Petitioner filed separate
rejoinders to the respective replies of the Respondents.
Reply of the Respondent No. 27, MSEDCL
11. The Respondent MSEDCL, in its reply, has mainly submitted as under:
(a) The land acquisition process for the mine commenced in 2008 but was
concluded only in 2015, after revision of the compensation package for
villagers, resulting in an inordinate delay of about seven years in securing land
for mining operations. Therefore, such a delay is unjustifiable, particularly
when the State Government’s compensation policies were already in place. It
is further pointed out that the Petitioner approached the State Government
only in 2011 and the Central Government only in 2013, whereas such
intervention could have been sought much earlier, especially since the
Order in Petition No.60/MP/2022 Page 11 of 105

(g) In terms of proviso (b) to Regulation 36K (1) of the Tariff Regulations, 2019,
the amount lying in the escrow account cannot be considered for
determination of input price. Accordingly, the claim for treating the Escrow
deposit as part of the input cost is liable to be disallowed.
(h) For FY 2020–21, coal production stood at 70.69 lakh tonnes against the target
of 95 lakh tonnes. The reasons indicated for the shortfall requires a prudence
check to ascertain whether such factors were valid and beyond the Petitioner’s
control. Any relaxation of ATQ must therefore be granted strictly in accordance
with the regulations. It is well settled through consistent precedents that the
power to relax must be exercised sparingly, based on sufficient justification,
and only where non-exercise would result in hardship, injustice, or an
inequitable outcome.
(i) The billing should continue under the existing methodology, i.e., at the CIL
notified price for the corresponding grade of coal. Any billing based on the
claim raised in the present Petition, without prior approval of the Commission
and contrary to the prevailing regulations, is impermissible and liable to be
rejected.
Rejoinder to the Reply filed by MSEDCL
12. The Petitioner, in its rejoinder, to the reply of the Respondent MSEDCL, has mainly
submitted as under:
(a) NTPC took all possible steps to expedite land acquisition; however, the delay in
achieving COD occurred due to uncontrollable factors such as delay in approval of
the Rehabilitation Action Plan (RAP), issues in identification of beneficiaries,
encroachment and forest land. Regulation 22 of the Tariff Regulations, 2019
expressly treats land acquisition as an uncontrollable factor, and the settled
principles laid down by the APTEL in its judgments dated 27.4.2011 in Appeal No.
72 of 2010 (MSPGCL v. MERC & Ors.) and 1.8.2017 in Appeal No. 35 of 2016
(GMR Kamalanga Energy Ltd. v. CERC & Ors.) recognize that delays beyond the
control of the generator, including delay in handing over possession of land, warrant
condonation of time overrun. As NTPC has duly substantiated the uncontrollable
nature of the delay and the mitigation measures undertaken, the same deserves to
be condoned.
(b) A detailed breakup of the capital cost is provided in Form B. Reasons for the delay
in the development of mine have been described in detail in the Petition, and all the
reasons were beyond the control of the Petitioner.
(c) Escalation in mining fee is mainly because of an increase in the price of diesel,
explosives and an increase in the minimum wages of workers. Relevant extracts of
the MDO agreement clearly indicating the formula of escalation and weightage of
Order in Petition No.60/MP/2022 Page 13 of 105

the constituents have been submitted along with the Petition.
(d) Any excess or shortfall in overburden removal for FY 2019–20 is adjustable up to
FY 2022–23, which is presently underway. The actual overburden removal figures,
along with the requisite adjustment calculations, will be furnished at the time of
truing up. All necessary efforts are being undertaken to ensure removal in
accordance with the approved mine plan, and no shortfall is anticipated.
(e) CHP system of the Pakri Barwadih mine could not be capitalised prior to COD due
to reasons beyond the Petitioner’s control, including land acquisition and law and
order issues, as detailed in the Petition. In view of these constraints, the MOC, in
the revised mine plan approved in January 2016, permitted surface transportation
of coal until commissioning of the CHP. During this interim period, no CHP O&M
charges have been paid to the MDO, and instead, coal transportation has been
undertaken through competitively bid truck contracts, and the actual transportation
charges so incurred have been claimed in accordance with Regulation 36I(3) of the
Tariff Regulations, 2019.
(f) In respect of the Pakri Barwadih mine, NTPC has incurred capital expenditure
towards the creation of fixed coal transportation and loading infrastructure (CHP),
while its O&M is undertaken by the MDO and is not included in the MDO cost. The
interpretation suggested by MSEDCL would result in non-recovery of NTPC’s
legitimate fixed cost incurred for such infrastructure. Accordingly, the Commission
may allow recovery of the capital investment as well as the O&M charges paid to
the MDO for the CHP, by exercising its powers under Regulations 76 and 77 of the
Tariff Regulations, 2019.
(g) In terms of the contract executed with the MDO, NTPC is required to deposit mine

these replies have been filed by the Petitioner vide affidavits dated 18.12.2023.

22. The Petitioner, in compliance with the directions issued by the ROP of the hearing
dated 6.9.2023, has submitted its additional information as under:

(c) In view of the confidentiality provision of the MDO agreement, a copy of the
Order in Petition No.60/MP/2022 Page 26 of 105

agreement is being submitted in a sealed envelope.
(d) Soft copy of the revised tariff forms is uploaded on the e-filing portal.
(e) Interest on working capital has been claimed in terms of Regulations 36(J)(1) of

& on a projection basis for the future period.

Replies of the Respondents TANGEDCO and BSPHCL to the IA No. 1/2023
23. Respondent 38, TANGEDCO, in its reply to the IA, has mainly submitted as under:
(a) Revised claims filed through the IA reflect a substantial increase in the Run of
Mine (ROM) cost compared to the original petition.
(b) NTPC’s request for relaxation of the ATQ for FY 2021–22 from 10 MT to 8.86
MT on the grounds of COVID-19 and excess rainfall is unjustified, as mining

(d) The absence of the MDO agreement in the public domain, along with the

24. Respondent 1, BSPHCL, in its reply to the IA, has mainly submitted as under:
(a) IA seeks to introduce revised tariff filing forms based on actual additional
capitalisation and O&M expenses for the period 2019–2022, and also seeks
Order in Petition No.60/MP/2022 Page 27 of 105

relaxation of ATQ for FY 2021–22. The revised submissions reflect substantial

25. The Petitioner, in its rejoinders to the respective replies of Respondents TANGEDCO
and BSPHCL in IA No. 1/2023, has mainly submitted as under:
(a) The objections raised by BSPHCL and TANGEDCO are misconceived and

Hearing dated 12.1.2024
26. During the hearing, the learned counsel for the Petitioner made detailed submissions

its claims had been placed on record. It was further submitted by the learned counsel for

27. After reserving order in the Petition, the Commission directed the Petitioner to file

Additional Submissions of the Petitioner
28. The Petitioner, in its additional submissions, has mainly submitted as under:
(a) The year-wise comparison of the RoM cost and input price of coal from the Pakri
Barwadih mine with the notified price of coal by CIL has been furnished, however,
such a comparison cannot be made on a strict like-for-like basis as each coal mine

mine has a higher stripping ratio and is a relatively new mine that has not yet

West quarry were not available at the time of declaration of COD of the mine on

(c) NTPC further furnished auditor-certified tariff forms, capital cost break-ups, and
Order in Petition No.60/MP/2022 Page 30 of 105

Commission may direct NTPC to furnish the correct computation of escalation
factors duly certified by an authorised auditor.
(f) The Commission may direct NTPC to furnish all relevant details and undertake
a detailed scrutiny of the claims, and the matter be listed for hearing again
before the final order is issued.
Rejoinders to the Replies filed by PCKL and TANGEDCO
30. The Petitioner, in its respective rejoinders to the respective replies of the

(a) The Petition has been filed under Sections 62 and 79(1)(a) of the Act, seeking
approval of the input price of coal supplied from the Pakri Barwadih coal mine
for the period from its COD (1.4.2019) to 31.3.2024 in accordance with the

Proceedings has been duly furnished through additional affidavits and

(b) With regard to the allegation of delay in filing the Petition, the proviso to
Regulation 9(4) of the Tariff Regulations, 2019 was introduced through the
Second Amendment Regulations notified in the Gazette on 13.9.2021.
Accordingly, the timeline for filing the Petition has to be computed from the
date of notification of the amendment, which is later than the COD of the mine.
Therefore, the Petition cannot be treated as delayed. The COVID-19
pandemic severely disrupted normal functioning, with closure of offices and
manpower constraints, which also contributed to the delay in filing the petition
and deserves condonation.
(c) The Pakri Barwadih coal block, though allotted as a single block, consists of
different quarries—East, West and North-West. The East and West quarries
were initially explored and covered under the approved mining plan, whereas
the North-West portion was unexplored at the time of allocation and was
subsequently developed after further geological exploration. Accordingly, the
present petition pertains to the East and West parts of the mine, while a
separate petition would be filed for the North-West quarry.
(d) On the issue of delay in achieving COD and project execution, the delay was
primarily due to land acquisition issues, resistance from local inhabitants,
rehabilitation and resettlement matters, and law-and-order constraints, which
were beyond its control. NTPC continuously pursued the matter with the
District, State and Central authorities and took all necessary steps to resolve
the issues. In terms of Regulation 22 of the Tariff Regulations, 2019, land
Order in Petition No.60/MP/2022 Page 33 of 105

production was adversely affected due to manpower shortages, supply chain
disruptions, and work stoppages caused by local issues. These circumstances
were beyond NTPC’s control and warrant regulatory relaxation.
Hearing dated 17.9.2024
31. Since the order in the Petition (which was reserved on 12.1.2024) could not be issued

to file an additional affidavit revising the forms/documents pertaining to the year 2023-24
and to place the same on record. The learned counsels for the Respondents TANGEDCO
and MSEDCL sought time to file their replies to the additional affidavit to be submitted by
the Petitioner.
32. The Commission, after hearing the parties, reserved order in the Petition with
direction to the Petitioner to file information on the status of commissioning of CHP &
associated cost incurred year-wise and directed Respondents to file their replies &
Petitioner its rejoinder, if any. In compliance with the said direction, the Petitioner, vide
affidavit dated 1.10.2024, has filed additional submissions after serving a copy on the
Respondents. Replies have been filed by the Respondents MSEDCL and BSPHCL vide
affidavits dated 16.10.2024 and 17.10.2024, respectively. Rejoinders to these replies have
been filed by the Petitioner vide affidavits dated 22.10.2024.
Additional Submissions of the Petitioner
33. The Petitioner, in its additional submissions, has mainly submitted as under:
(a) In terms of the revised mine plan, the peak rated capacity of the Pakri
Barwadih (East-West Block & North-West Block) has been revised to 22
MTPA as against 18 MTPA, which was the earlier peak rated capacity. The
primary change is that for the East-West Block, against the peak rated
capacity of 15 MTPA, the figure has now been revised to 19 MTPA.
(b) The prime modification as a result of the above is that for FY 2023-24, the
ATQ stands revised from 10 MTPA to 15.5 MTPA. This would have a direct
bearing on the per-unit cost determined by this Commission for FY 2023-24.
Considering that the increased ATQ results in a decrease in the per tonne
Order in Petition No.60/MP/2022 Page 35 of 105

relevant authorities.
39. Per contra, the Petitioner has submitted that the delay in commencement of
production was primarily due to challenges encountered in the process of land acquisition,
which were beyond its control. The Petitioner explained that a significant portion of the
project land, approximately 2520 hectares out of the total 4695 hectares (around 53%),
comprised privately owned land. The acquisition of such land faced considerable
resistance from the local villagers and project affected families, resulting in prolonged
delays in the process. The Petitioner has further submitted that the procedural framework
governing the land acquisition and rehabilitation significantly contributed to the delay. In
accordance with the NPRR 2003, VDACs were constituted in July 2006 by the State
Government under the chairmanship of the District Collector, with representatives from the
State Government, NTPC and the affected families. While the consultation process
regarding the Rehabilitation Action Plan was underway, the Government of Jharkhand
notified a new Resettlement and Rehabilitation (R&R) Policy in July 2008. The notification
of this policy necessitated realignment of the ongoing process of finalising the R&R plan
in accordance with the procedures prescribed under the new policy.
40. We have considered the submissions of the parties. It is noted that the revised policy
required several procedural steps, including the preparation of a draft R&R scheme
following surveys and censuses of affected persons, publication of the draft scheme,
approval by the State Government, and subsequent disbursement of compensation.
Pursuant to extensive consultations with the Project Affected Families, the draft R&R plan
was approved by the District Administration on 23.8.2009, and thereafter, the Petitioner’s
Board approved the detailed Rehabilitation Action Plan on 11.9.2009. The comprehensive
R&R plan was subsequently approved by the District Administration on 8.2.2010 and
forwarded to the Government of Jharkhand for approval.
Order in Petition No.60/MP/2022 Page 39 of 105

41. It is noticed that there was a considerable delay in obtaining approval of the R&R
plan from the State Government. The Petitioner has placed on record the documentary
evidence, including communications and minutes of meetings between officials of the
District Administration and NTPC, indicating that the matter remained under consideration
of the State Government from February 2010 until February 2013. Eventually, the
Government of Jharkhand approved the compensation package and R&R plan for land
acquisition in February 2013. Despite such approval, the process of land acquisition
continued to face difficulties due to persistent demands from villagers for higher
compensation, repeated agitations, encroachment on acquired land and deterioration of
the law and order situation in the project area. In support, the Petitioner has placed on
record the copies of various newspaper reports, copies of FIRs filed by project authorities
and communications addressed to State Authorities highlighting the law and order issues
affecting the project.
42. The Petitioner has demonstrated that it undertook sustained efforts to resolve these
issues by approaching various authorities at the State and Central levels. Communications
were addressed to several senior authorities, including the Secretary (Power), MOP, GOI,
the Advisor to the Governor of Jharkhand, the Chief Secretary of the Government of
Jharkhand, the Principal Secretary to the Prime Minister and the Minister of State
(Independent Charge) for Power, Government of India, requesting intervention to facilitate
the resolution of land acquisition and law and order issues. Subsequently, after prolonged
consultations and negotiations with stakeholders, the Jharkhand administration approved
a revised Compensation-cum-R&R package in March 2015. Immediately thereafter, the
Petitioner’s Board also approved the revised compensation package on 25.3.2015.
Following the resolution of these issues, mining activities progressed, and the mine
touched coal in the following year, with production commencing on 7.12.2016.

ORDER
M/s Datta Power Infra Private Limited has filed the Petition under Section 79(1)(c)
and 79(1)(f) of the Electricity Act, 2003 read with Regulation 41 (Power to Relax) and
Regulation 42 (Power to Remove Difficulty) of the CERC (Connectivity and General
Network Access to the Inter-State Transmission System) Regulations, 2022 seeking
extension of the timeline for achieving Financial Closure and extension of the start
date of connectivity in respect of its 162 MW ISTS-connected Wind-Solar Hybrid
Power Projects (Hybrid-1 and Hybrid-2) in Madhya Pradesh
2. The Petitioner has made the following prayers in the present Petition:
(a) Allow the present Petition;
(b) Grant an extension of the timeline for achieving Financial Closure and Start Date of
Connectivity as prescribed under Regulation 11A(2) and Regulation 11A(2A) of the GNA
Regulations, in respect of the Petitioner’s connectivity granted under Application No.
2200001582, for an aggregate capacity of 162 MW, until November 2027 as the tentative
SCOD, and such extended SCOD after the execution of the PPA;
(c) Direct that the timeline for achieving Financial Closure be aligned with the SCOD as
determined in the PPA once executed, in order to ensure consistency with the project
development framework under the projects in question and in the meantime, align the
Financial Closure with a tentative SCOD of November 2027;
(d) Direct Respondent No.1 to maintain the in-principle connectivity approval dated
01.07.2025 (Ref: CTU/WR/Conn-INT-1A/2200001582) as valid and subsisting during the
pendency of the present proceedings and until the extended Financial Closure and
SCOD timelines as may be approved by this Hon’ble Commission;
(e) Pass any such order and further reliefs as this Hon’ble Commission deems just and
proper in the nature and circumstances of the present case.
Interim Relief
(a) Direct that no coercive action be taken by Respondent No.1 against the Petitioner during
the pendency of the present Petition, including but not limited to, revocation of
connectivity, forfeiture or encashment of any Connectivity Bank Guarantees (Conn-BG1,
Order in Petition No. 1015/MP/2025 and IA No. 5/2026
Page 2

BG2, or BG3), or any other adverse measures;
(b) Injunct the Respondent No.1 from allocating the connectivity quantum granted to the
Petitioner to any other developer, till pendency of the present proceedings;
3. The Petitioners have filed the IA No. 5/IA/2026 seeking the following reliefs:
(a) Direct that no coercive action be taken by Respondent CTUIL against the Petitioner
during the pendency of the present Petition, including but not limited to, revocation of
connectivity, forfeiture or encashment of any Connectivity Bank Guarantees (Conn-BG1,
BG2, or BG3), or any other adverse measures;
(b) Pass such other and further orders as this Hon’ble Commission may deem fit and proper
in the facts and circumstances of the present case and in the interest of justice.
4. The Petitioners have filed the IA Dy No. 96/2026 seeking the following reliefs:
(a) Take on record the subsequent event, namely the revocation letter dated 11.02.2026
issued by Respondent No.1;
(b) Direct that the operation and effect of the revocation letter dated 11.02.2026 be kept in
abeyance pending pronouncement of the order in Petition No. 1015/MP/2025 and IA No.
5/2026;
(c) Pass such other and further orders as this Hon’ble Commission may deem fit and proper
in the facts and circumstances of the present case and in the interest of justice.
IA (Diary) No. 96/2026 was disposed of vide RoP for hearing held on 19.02.2026.
Submissions of Petitioner
5. Petitioner has made the following submissions:
a) DPIPL participated in competitive bidding processes conducted by SJVN Limited
under Hybrid-1 and Hybrid-2 schemes and was issued Letters of Award dated
06.03.2024 and 26.06.2024 aggregating to 120 MW capacity, subsequently amended
on 19.12.2024. Pursuant to the LOAs, Petitioner applied for a grant of ISTS
connectivity through the LOA route on 19.12.2024 for an aggregate capacity of 162
MW covering both projects. In-principle grant of ISTS Connectivity was issued by
CTUIL on 01.07.2025 for 162 MW.
b) DPIPL furnished requisite Connectivity Bank Guarantees on 31.07.2025, namely
Conn-BG1 of ₹50,00,000, Conn-BG2 of ₹3,00,00,000 and Conn-BG3 of ₹3,24,00,000.
CTUIL reflected 30.12.2025 as the deadline for submission of proof of Financial
Closure.
Order in Petition No. 1015/MP/2025 and IA No. 5/2026
Page 3

c) PPA pursuant to the LOAs has not been executed by Respondent No.2, and execution
of PPA forms the foundational precondition for the determination of SCOD and for
securing project financing. Financial institutions have conveyed their inability to
process or sanction project financing in the absence of executed PPAs, rendering it
practically impossible to achieve Financial Closure within the stipulated timeline. The
delay in the execution of PPAs is attributable to the Renewable Energy Implementing
Agency and to downstream arrangements with Buying Entities, and is beyond the
DPIPL's control.
d) DPIPL addressed communications dated 26.09.2025 and 03.11.2025 to Respondents
seeking alignment of Financial Closure and Start Date of Connectivity timelines with
execution of PPAs; no final decision has been communicated. National Solar Energy
Federation of India, vide representation dated 26.09.2025, highlighted sector-wide
difficulties in meeting Financial Closure timelines, given that PPAs remain unsigned,
and sought a uniform extension.
e) Fixed deadline of 30.12.2025 for Financial Closure has been mechanically computed
from the date of in-principle connectivity without considering the linkage between
SCOD and PPA execution under the bidding documents. Obligation under Regulation
11A (2) cannot operate in isolation when SCOD remains indeterminate due to non-
execution of PPA. The imposition of the Financial Closure deadline in the prevailing
circumstances is arbitrary, unreasonable and contrary to the regulatory intent
underlying the GNA framework.
f) Revocation of connectivity and encashment of Connectivity Bank Guarantees in such
circumstances would cause irreparable prejudice despite compliance with all
procedural requirements. The present case constitutes a regulatory difficulty
warranting the exercise of powers under Regulation 41 and Regulation 42 of the GNA
Regulations, 2022, to relax and remove the difficulty in the implementation of
Regulation 11A.

consequently, the deadline to achieve the Financial Closure (FC), in terms of Regulation
11A(2), works out to 28.8.2027, (v) regardless, the Petitioner will achieve the FC by
31.12.2026 and has already taken various measures towards setting up of the project, (vi)
in such circumstances, CTUIL ought to be retrained from taking any coercive steps against
the Petitioner. Whereas, the learned counsel for the Respondent, CTUIL, mainly submitted
that (i) the deadline for achieving the FC was communicated to the Petitioner way back in
August 2025, (ii) admittedly, the final grant of connectivity was communicated on
29.12.2025, (iii) since the firm start date of connectivity is 30.6.2026, the deadline for
achieving the FC works out to 30.12.2026, (iv) the e-mails of SJVN extending the SCOD
on tentative basis do not meet the criteria specified in the concerned Regulations, nor has
CTUIL considered such tentative extensions in other similar cases, (v) the delay in
conveying the final grant of connectivity was on account of CTUIL being engaged in giving
effect and implementing the provisions of Third Amendment to the GNA Regulations and
CTUIL will be filing its compliance affidavit to the Record of Proceedings dated 19.12.2025
wherein similar queries have been posed.
2. At the request of the learned senior counsel and learned counsel for the parties, the
Commission also permitted both sides to file their respective written submissions within
two days with a copy to the other side.
3. Since the parties argued the matter on the merits, the Commission deemed it appropriate
to reserve the matter itself for the order.”
Submissions of the Respondent
8. Respondent CTUIL vide Written Submissions dated 16.01.2026 has submitted as
below:
a) On 07.06.2022, this Commission notified the GNA Regulations, 2022. On 19.06.2024,
this Hon’ble Commission issued the Second Amendment to the GNA Regulations
whereby Regulation 11A(2) provided that an applicant to whom in-principle grant of
connectivity has been issued shall achieve financial closure for the capacity of such
connectivity latest by six months prior to the scheduled date of commercial operation
Order in Petition No. 1015/MP/2025 and IA No. 5/2026
Page 5

or start date of connectivity, whichever is later, and submit proof of financial closure to
CTU within fifteen days of achieving the same.
b) On 19.12.2024, the Petitioner filed an application before CTUIL seeking connectivity
of 162 MW Wind Solar Hybrid (120 MW Solar and 42 MW Wind) at Dhule ISTS sub-
station in terms of the GNA Regulations and mentioned the commissioning schedule
and date from which connectivity is required as 30.06.2026 under the LOA/PPA route
and provided copies of LOAs issued by SJVN Limited. On 01.07.2025, CTUIL issued
an intimation for the in-principle grant of connectivity to the Petitioner, with a likely start
date of connectivity as 30.06.2026.
c) On 06.08.2025, CTUIL issued an email to the Petitioner seeking Financial Closure
documents for compliance of Regulation 11A(2) specifying SCOD as per application
as 30.06.2026, connectivity start date (in-principle) as 30.06.2026 and due date for
submission of Financial Closure documents as 30.12.2025 and further stating that in
case of non-submission within the due date suitable action will be taken as per
Regulation 11B(2) of the GNA Regulations.
d) On 31.08.2025 (effective from 09.09.2025), this Commission issued the Third
Amendment to the GNA Regulations. On 29.12.2025, CTUIL intimated the Final grant
of connectivity to the Petitioner, specifying SCOD as 09.02.2026, the firm start date of
connectivity as 30.06.2026 and providing that effectiveness shall be subject to the
availability of the Common Transmission System.
e) CTUIL had already intimated the Petitioner on 06.08.2025 that the due date of
Financial Closure is 30.12.2025 in terms of Regulation 11A(2), which mandates that
an applicant who has been issued an in-principle grant shall achieve Financial Closure
latest by six months prior to the scheduled date of commercial operation or start date
of connectivity, whichever is later.
f) Since the Petitioner itself specified the SCOD and start date of connectivity as
30.06.2026 in the connectivity application, applying Regulation 11A(2) to the said date
resulted in the outer limit for achieving Financial Closure being 30.12.2025. Even after
the coming into force of the Third Amendment to the GNA Regulations with effect from
09.09.2025, the cut-off date for achieving Financial Closure remained unchanged, and
Order in Petition No. 1015/MP/2025 and IA No. 5/2026
Page 6

under the amended Regulation 11A(2), the connectivity grantee shall achieve
Financial Closure at the latest by six months prior to the scheduled date of commercial
operation or firm start date of connectivity, whichever is later.
g) In the present case, the firm start date of connectivity as per the final grant issued by
CTUIL continues to be 30.06.2026 and therefore, even applying the amended
Regulation 11A(2), the outer limit for achieving Financial Closure remains 30.12.2025.
CTUIL does not possess any discretion under the GNA Regulations to alter the start
date of connectivity as applied for by the Petitioner or the statutory timeline for
achieving Financial Closure linked thereto, and is statutorily bound to implement the
Regulations as notified without dilution on equitable or commercial considerations.
h) The Petitioner cannot seek to resile from the start date of connectivity voluntarily
sought in the connectivity application in order to indirectly extend the statutory timeline
for achieving Financial Closure, and permitting such an approach would defeat the
object and scheme of Regulation 11A, which was introduced to ensure seriousness
and certainty in transmission planning. The second proviso to Regulation 11A(2)
contemplates extension of the Financial Closure timeline only where the SCOD is
validly extended by the Renewable Energy Implementing Agency and the Petitioner
has failed to demonstrate that any extension of SCOD has been granted by SJVN
Limited.
i) The Petitioner has relied on an email dated 02.01.2026 from SJVN, which only refers
to a tentative timeline for execution of the PPA and tentative SCSD as 28.02.2026,
and the said communication merely refers to a tentative timeline and no PPA has been
entered. Under the GNA Regulations, only a duly recognised and finalised SCOD or
firm start date of connectivity reflected in the connectivity grant issued by CTUIL can
have any bearing on the computation of Financial Closure timelines and Regulation
11A(2) second proviso is attracted only on extension of SCOD by REIA and not for
delay in signing of the PPA.
j) Any tentative or indicative dates communicated by the REIA cannot constitute an
extension within the meaning of Regulation 11A(2), and the email dated 02.01.2026 is
irrelevant for determining the due date of Financial Closure and cannot be relied upon
to claim any extension or deferment of obligations.
Order in Petition No. 1015/MP/2025 and IA No. 5/2026
Page 7

k) The Petitioner could have resorted to the second proviso to Regulation 11A(2) only
before expiry of the cut-off date and not thereafter, and since the outer limit for
achieving Financial Closure expired on 30.12.2025, the Petitioner stood in clear non-
compliance with Regulation 11A(2), attracting statutory consequences under the GNA
Regulations. The Petitioner’s contention that CTUIL would be unjustly enriched on
encashment of Bank Guarantees is incorrect since any consequence for failure to
submit Financial Closure documents before the due date arises strictly in terms of the
GNA Regulations, and CTUIL is a revenue-neutral body, and therefore the contention
of unjust enrichment is denied.
Submissions of the Respondent
9. Respondent CTUIL vide affidavit dated 21.01.2026 filed compliance to ROP for
hearing held on 19.12.2025 and has submitted as below:
a) Intimation of final grant of connectivity has been issued to the Petitioner vide letter
dated 29.12.2025.
b) Transmission scheme for evacuation of power from Dhule 2 GW REZ has been
identified for grant of connectivity to M/s Datta Power Infra Private Limited, comprising
establishment of 4×500 MVA, 400/220 kV Pooling Station near Dhule and Dhule PS
Dhule (BDTCL) 400 kV D/c line with Quad ACSR/AAAC/AL59 Moose equivalent
conductor. It has been stated that the above system is presently under implementation
by M/s Dhule Power Transmission Limited, a subsidiary of IndiGrid 2 Limited, with
SCOD of 09.02.2026 and as per the status reported during the 50th WR JCC meeting
held on 24.12.2025, the system is expected by June 2026. It has also been highlighted
that since the firm start date of connectivity for the Petitioner is June 2026, while the
start date of connectivity for other developers is December 2026 or later, the
transmission system would remain idle from June 2026 to December 2026 if the
Petitioner does not materialise in a timely manner.
c) It has further been stated that the due date for compliance with Financial Closure in
terms of Regulation 11A(2) was 30.12.2025; no documents have been submitted by
the Petitioner, and therefore, CTUIL is in the process of taking suitable actions in
accordance with the GNA Regulations, 2022.
Submissions of Petitioner
Order in Petition No. 1015/MP/2025 and IA No. 5/2026
Page 8

10. Petitioner DPIPL vide affidavit dated 29.01.2 2025 has submitted as below:
a) The final grant of connectivity was issued on 29.12.2025, i.e., after the hearing before
the Commission and after the Commission had specifically directed Respondent No.1
to clarify the status of final grant of connectivity, status of implementation of
transmission system for the connectivity and the due date for Financial Closure, and
the said action was arbitrary and effected in a manner that left the DPIPL with no
meaningful opportunity to comply with any alleged Financial Closure requirement, the
final grant having been issued only a few hours prior to the deadline of 30.12.2025
which itself was under challenge before this Hon’ble Commission.
b) Respondent No.1 has sought to justify its position by referring to the status of
implementation of the transmission system and by contending that in the event the
DPIPL does not materialise, the transmission corridor may remain underutilised;
however such contention is misplaced and contrary to the governing regulatory
framework under the CERC (Connectivity and General Network Access to the Inter-
State Transmission System) Regulations, 2022 which expressly contemplate
extension and realignment of timelines where the Scheduled Commercial Operation
Date is extended by the Renewable Energy Implementing Agency, particularly in
projects granted connectivity through the Letter of Award route.
c) The applicable regulatory framework independently mandates extension of the SCOD
in the present case in terms of the second proviso to Regulation 11A(2) of the GNA
Regulations which provides that where connectivity is granted under the LOA route,
the SCOD for the purposes of Regulation 11A(2) shall be the SCOD as extended by
the REIA subject to the condition that the corresponding extension for achieving
Financial Closure shall not exceed twelve months from the original timeline linked to
the initial SCOD, and Regulation 11A(2) read with its proviso does not condition such
extension upon execution of a PPA.
d) The REIA has communicated an extended SCOD of 28.02.2028 and accordingly even
in the absence of an executed PPA the SCOD is required to stand extended with the
Financial Closure timeline correspondingly falling no earlier than 30.12.2026 and upon
execution of the PPA the SCOD and Financial Closure would necessarily stand
aligned with the SCOD stipulated therein and/or in the absence of PPA in accordance
with amended regulatory framework, if any.
Order in Petition No. 1015/MP/2025 and IA No. 5/2026
Page 9

e) In light of the above regulatory position, any contention raised by Respondent No.1
regarding the transmission corridor remaining underutilised is immaterial and legally
untenable, and Respondent No.1 is bound to act strictly in accordance with the GNA
Regulations, which expressly provide for extension and realignment of SCOD and
Financial Closure timelines in such cases. Considerations of alleged underutilisation
of transmission infrastructure cannot override or dilute the mandatory operation of the
statutory regulatory framework, nor can they be relied upon to justify coercive action
contrary to the express provisions of the Regulations.
f) Without prejudice to the rights and contentions of the DPIPL, even assuming that there
is any temporary mismatch between the readiness of the transmission assets and the
commissioning of the generating project, the regulatory framework under the CERC
(Sharing of Inter-State Transmission Charges and Losses) Regulations, 2020
provides a complete and self-contained mechanism for treatment of transmission
charges during such period and considerations relating to alleged idling of
transmission infrastructure cannot be invoked as a ground to deny extension of
timelines or to initiate coercive action under the GNA Regulations.
g) The DPIPL has acted bona fide at all times and has complied with all obligations within
its control, and the present difficulty arises solely due to non-execution of the Power
Purchase Agreements, which is beyond the control of the DPIPL and the affidavit filed
by Respondent No.1 does not dislodge this position nor address the regulatory
interdependence between PPA execution, determination of SCOD and achievement
of Financial Closure.
h) In view of the foregoing, the affidavit filed by Respondent No.1 does not justify initiation
or continuation of any coercive action against the DPIPL and does not warrant any
adverse inference in the pending proceedings.
Submissions of Petitioner vide IA Dy No. 96/2026 dated 11.02.2026
11. Petitioner DPIPL has submitted as below:
a) DPIPL has filed the present IA to place on record subsequent developments arising
during the pendency of the main Petition, particularly the revocation of its connectivity
by CTUIL vide letter dated 11.02.2026, after the matter had already been heard and
Order in Petition No. 1015/MP/2025 and IA No. 5/2026
Page 10

reserved for orders. The Petitioner has submitted that such action has been taken on
the same grounds which are under adjudication, including the issue of Financial
Closure timeline and permissibility of coercive action, and therefore amounts to pre-
empting the decision of this Hon’ble Commission and undermining the adjudicatory
process. It has been contended that the said revocation renders the pending
proceedings infructuous and defeats the reliefs sought in the Petition.
b) DPIPL has further submitted that, without prejudice to its rights, it has deposited an
amount equivalent to the Connectivity Bank Guarantee under protest to avoid
encashment, and has requested CTUIL to keep coercive steps in abeyance. It has
been stated that the revocation has serious consequences, including risk of
encashment of Bank Guarantees, loss of connectivity, and impact on investments
already made. Accordingly, the Petitioner has sought that the revocation letter dated
11.02.2026 be taken on record and its operation be kept in abeyance pending final
decision in the main Petition.
Hearing on 19.02.2026
12. RoP for hearing dated 19.02.2026 is as under:
“Learned senior counsel for the Petitioner, DPIPL, submitted that the present IA has been
filed inter alia seeking direction to the Respondent, CTUIL, to keep the revocation letter
dated 11.2.2026 in abeyance pending orders of the Commission in Petition No.
1015/MP/2025. The learned senior counsel further submitted that the filing of the present
IA became necessitated owing to the fact that the Respondent, notwithstanding that the
matter had been fully heard and reserved for orders by the Commission, has proceeded to
revoke the Petitioner’s connectivity vide email dated 11.2.2026, without awaiting the
decision of the Commission. The learned senior counsel submitted that the very grounds
forming the basis of the said revocation are identical to those which are under consideration
in the pending proceedings, and that the action of the Respondent in revoking the
Petitioner’s connectivity during the period when the matter stood reserved for orders is ex
facie arbitrary and thereby rendering the main Petition infructuous and defeating the reliefs
sought therein. The learned senior counsel added that, pursuant to the issuance of the
revocation notice, the Petitioner, in compliance with Regulation 3.8 of the GNA
Regulations, has deposited an amount equivalent to the Connectivity Bank Guarantee
under express protest and solely with a view to securing the Connectivity Bank Guarantee
from encashment.
2. In response, the learned counsel for the Respondent, CTUIL, fairly submitted that the
Commission has, in similar cases, restrained the creation of third-party rights over the
revoked quantum pending the pronouncement of the order, and CTUIL has no objection if
a similar dispensation is adopted in this case too.
3. Considering the submissions made by the learned senior counsel and learned counsel
for the parties, the Commission directed CTUIL not to re-allocate the quantum
corresponding to the Petitioner’s 162 MW connectivity at Dhule PS to any third parties till
the pronouncement of the order in the Petition. With this, IA (Diary) No. 96/2026 was
disposed of.”
Order in Petition No. 1015/MP/2025 and IA No. 5/2026
Page 11

Analysis and Decision
13. We have considered the submissions of the Petitioner, Respondent and perused the
facts available on record. The following issues arise for our consideration:
Issue No.1: Whether the timeline for achieving Financial Closure in terms of
Regulation 11A(2) of the GNA Regulations and the start date of Connectivity in
terms of Regulation 11A(2A) is required to be aligned with the tentative SCOD
under the prospective Power Purchase Agreement for projects granted
connectivity under the LOA route?
Issue No. 2: Whether the revocation of connectivity vide communication dated
11.02.2026 issued by the CTUIL is liable to be set aside?
The above issues are addressed together and dealt with in the succeeding
paragraphs.
14. The Petitioner has been issued an in-principle grant of connectivity using the LOA
issued by SJVN for 162 MW Wind Solar Hybrid (120 MW Solar and 42 MW Wind) at
Dhule ISTS sub-station on 01.07.2025, specifying the likely start date of connectivity
as 30.06.2026.
15. CTUIL intimated that the due date for submission of Financial Closure documents is
30.12.2025 in terms of Regulation 11A(2) of the GNA Regulations. The Petitioner
submitted that execution of Power Purchase Agreements has not taken place, and
Financial Closure cannot be achieved in the absence of an executed PPA. Petitioner
has submitted that the second proviso to Regulation 11A(2) provides that where
connectivity is granted under the LOA route, the SCOD shall be the SCOD as
extended by the REIA, subject to the condition that the corresponding extension for
achieving Financial Closure shall not exceed twelve months from the original timeline
linked to the initial SCOD, and that the REIA has communicated an extended SCOD
of 28.02.2028, and accordingly, the SCOD is required to stand extended with the
Financial Closure timeline correspondingly falling no earlier than 30.12.2026.
16. CTUIL has submitted that the second proviso to Regulation 11A(2) contemplates
extension of the Financial Closure timeline only where the SCOD is validly extended
by the Renewable Energy Implementing Agency, and the Petitioner has failed to
demonstrate that any extension of SCOD has been granted by SJVN Limited and that
Order in Petition No. 1015/MP/2025 and IA No. 5/2026
Page 12

the email dated 02.01.2026 from SJVN merely refers to tentative timeline for execution
of the PPA and tentative commencement of supply and no PPA has been entered.
17. Petitioner has submitted that the final grant of connectivity was issued on 29.12.2025,
after the hearing before the Commission and only a few hours prior to the deadline of
30.12.2025, leaving the Petitioner with no meaningful opportunity to comply with the
alleged Financial Closure requirement.
18. We have considered the submissions of the Petitioner and Respondent. We have
perused the provisions of the GNA Regulations quoted as under:
“11A…
(2) An applicant which is REGS (other than Hydro generating station), ESS (excluding
PSP) or Renewable power park developer to which an in-principle grant of connectivity
has been issued, shall have to achieve the financial closure for the capacity of such
Connectivity, latest by 6 months prior to the scheduled date of a commercial operation or
firm start date of Connectivity of such applicant, whichever is later:
Provided that such an applicant shall submit proof of Financial Closure of the project (with
copy of loan sanction letter or proof of first disbursal of loan amount) or copy of board
resolution (if internal funding is planned for 100% of the project cost) to CTU within 15
days of achieving the financial closure:
Provided further that in case of REGS (other than Hydro generating station) or ESS
(excluding PSP) which has been granted Connectivity under sub-clause (a) of Clause (xi)
of Regulation 5.8, the scheduled date of commercial operation for the purpose of this
Clause shall be considered as the SCOD, as extended by REIA or a distribution licensee
or an authorized agency on behalf of distribution licensee from time to time, subject to the
condition that any extension in the timeline to achieve the milestone of Financial Closure
due to extension in SCOD shall not be allowed more than 12 months from the original
timeline as per initial SCOD:
Provided also that entities which have been granted Connectivity under sub-clause (b) or
(c) of Clause (xi) of Regulation 5.8 and are subsequently covered under sub-clause (a) of
Clause (xi) of Regulation 5.8 shall be required to achieve financial closure for the capacity
of such Connectivity, latest by 6 months prior to the firm start date of Connectivity of such
applicant”
Clause (2) of Regulation 11B of these Regulations is as follows:
“(2) If the Connectivity grantee fails to achieve the financial closure within the
stipulated time or fails to submit the copy of financial closure within the stipulated
time as per Clause (2) of Regulation 11A of these regulations, Connectivity shall be
revoked, Bank Guarantee submitted under sub-clause (c) of Clause (vii) or sub-
clause (c) of Clause (xi) of Regulation 5.8 of these regulations shall be encashed,
and Conn-BG1, Conn-BG2 and Conn-BG3 shall be treated in terms of Regulation
24.2 or Regulation 24.3 of these regulations, as applicable.”
As per above, financial closure is required to be achieved at the latest 6 months prior
to the scheduled date of commercial operation or the firm start date of Connectivity for
such applicant, whichever is later.
Order in Petition No. 1015/MP/2025 and IA No. 5/2026
Page 13

19. We have perused the connectivity application and grant of connectivity for the
Petitioner as under:
(a) Connectivity application under the GNA Regulations applied on 19.12.2024 and
reapplied on 8.1.2025
(b) In-principle grant of Connectivity by the CTUIL dated 1.7.2025
Order in Petition No. 1015/MP/2025 and IA No. 5/2026
Page 14

Order in Petition No. 1015/MP/2025 and IA No. 5/2026
Page 15

As per the above, in-principle Connectivity was intimated with no ATS, and augmentation
was identified and is already under implementation with the SCOD of augmentation as
9.2.2026. The likely start date for connectivity is indicated as 30.6.2026.
(c ) Final Grant of Connectivity issued on 29.12.2025
20. As per the above, the firm start date of Connectivity is provided as 30.6.2026
21. Petitioner has stated that its SCOD should be taken as February 2028, and
accordingly, the last date of achieving FC should be calculated. Let us peruse as to
whether the SCOD of February 2028 can be considered. SJVN vide email dated
30.12.2025 stated as under:
Order in Petition No. 1015/MP/2025 and IA No. 5/2026
Page 16

As per the above, SJVN stated that the PSA has yet to be signed, and accordingly,
the PPA is also yet to be signed. Assuming the PPA signing date falls in February
2026, SCOD will be February 2028.
22. Petitioner, based on the above-quoted email of SJVN dated 30.12.2025, wrote to
CTUIL as under:
Order in Petition No. 1015/MP/2025 and IA No. 5/2026
Page 17

As per the above, Petitioner requested that CTUIL consider SCOD as 28.2.2028, stating
that it is as per the PPA.
23. CTUIL has submitted that the second proviso to Regulation 11A(2) contemplates
extension of the Financial Closure timeline only where the SCOD is validly extended
by the Renewable Energy Implementing Agency.
24. We have perused the Regulations, SCOD furnished by the petitioner in the
Connectivity application, the firm start date of Connectivity and extension of SCOD as
claimed by the Petitioner. We are of the considered view that the tentative SCOD,
based on the tentative PPA that is yet to be signed, is not a valid document for the
extension of the SCOD. Hence, such a date of February 2028 cannot be considered
for the purpose of Regulation 11A. Hence, the last date to achieve Financial Closure
Order in Petition No. 1015/MP/2025 and IA No. 5/2026
Page 18

comes out as 31.12.2025, calculated as the later of 6 months prior to the firm start
date of connectivity (which is 30.6.2026) or SCOD (which is 30.6.2026).
25. We note that CTUIL intimated final grant of Connectivity, including the firm start date
as late as 29.12.2025, even when the augmentation was already under
implementation, and CTUIL issued in-principle connectivity on 1.7.2025. CTUIL has
stated that it could not issue a final grant because it was engaged in the
implementation of the third amendment to the GNA Regulations.
26. We note that Petitioner furnished Conn-BGs on 31.07.2025. Regulation 9.1 of the
GNA Regulations provides as under:
“
9. Final Grant of Connectivity by the Nodal Agency
9.1. Within 15 days of receipt of Conn-BG1, Conn-BG2 and Conn-BG3, as applicable, the
Nodal Agency shall intimate the final grant of Connectivity to the entity that has been
intimated the in-principle grant of Connectivity. The intimation shall contain, inter alia, the
following: ..”
As per the above, CTUIL was required to issue the final grant of Connectivity by
15.8.2025. We note that the third amendment to the GNA regulations was issued
on 31.8.2025 and is effective from 9.9.2025, which is much later than the timeline
by which the final grant should have been issued by the CTUIL.
27. We note that CTUIL issued the final grant as late as 29.12.2025, with the last date to
achieve FC stated by CTUIL as 30.12.2025.
28. We observe that the delay on the part of CTUIL cannot be justified, and CTUIL should
have been more prudent, being the implementing agency of Connectivity of ISTS. A
casual approach in not issuing a final grant for reasons of work that has not even
started cannot be accepted. CTUIL is the body responsible for planning and open
Access under the Act and should be more prudent in handling the applications. We
are not imposing any financial penalty for now, considering that CTUIL shall act more
prudently in future cases. We direct CTUIL to process all pending final grants of
connectivity despite submission of requisite Conn-BGs by applicants, and where there
is no issue in planning the augmentation within a period of 30 days from the issue of
this Order, and submit to a compliance report to the commission.
Order in Petition No. 1015/MP/2025 and IA No. 5/2026
Page 19

29. We note that CTUIL issued the revocation of connectivity vide letter dated 11.02.2026
quoted as under :
Order in Petition No. 1015/MP/2025 and IA No. 5/2026
Page 20

As per the above, Connectivity was revoked on 11.2.2026 due to the failure to submit
FC.
30. Petitioner submitted during the hearing held on 19.2.2026 that it had deposited an
amount equivalent to the Connectivity Bank Guarantee under express protest and
solely with a view to securing the Connectivity Bank Guarantee from encashment.
During the hearing held on 19.2.2026, the Commission directed CTUIL not to re-
allocate the quantum corresponding to the Petitioner’s 162 MW connectivity at Dhule
PS to any third parties till the pronouncement of the order in the Petition.
31. Petitioner has prayed the Commission to exercise their powers under Regulation 41
and 42 of the GNA Regulations and grant an extension of the time to submit the
Financial Closure document by the Petitioner.
32. We have considered the submissions of the Petitioner and the revocation carried out
by the CTUIL. We note that, as per the GNA Regulations, Petitioner was required to
achieve FC by 31.12.2025 and furnish the documents within 15 days thereafter, failing
which Connectivity was to be revoked. Hence, CTUIL has rightly revoked the
Petitioner's Connectivity. However, we have also noted that CTUIL delayed the
issuance of the final grant of Connectivity by ~4.5 months without any justifiable
reason. Accordingly, we are of the view that the Petitioner should be given some time
to furnish the Financial Closure document. We note that the petitioner’s SCOD stands
as 30.6.2026.
33. In light of the above discussions, we exercise our powers under Regulations 41 and
42 of the GNA Regulations and permit 30 days’ time from the date of issuance of this
Order to the petitioner to furnish a financial closure document in terms of
Regulation11A(2) of the GNA Regulations. Accordingly, the revocation letter dated
11.2.2026 is set aside. Further, submission of FC documents after expiry of the
granted 30 days within a period of 60 days thereafter shall attract a delay penalty of
5% of the Conn-BGs amount. Non-submission of FC beyond 90 days from the date of
issuance of this order shall be dealt with by CTUIL in terms of Regulation 11B(2) of
GNA regulation. Petitioner shall restore the Conn-BGs within a period of 10 days from
issuance of this Order, if not already subsisting. The cash deposited by the Petitioner
in lieu of Conn-BGs shall be returned by the CTUIL within 7 days of restoration of
Conn-BGs by the Petitioner or 7 days of issuance of this Order (if Conn-BGs are
subsisting).
Order in Petition No. 1015/MP/2025 and IA No. 5/2026
Page 21

34. The Petition No. 1015/MP/2025, along with IA.No.5/2026, is disposed of in terms of
the above.
Sd/ Sd/ Sd/
(Harish Dudani) (Ramesh Babu V.) (Jishnu Barua)
Member Member Chairperson

Order in Petition No. 1015/MP/2025 and IA No. 5/2026

ORDER
The present Petition has been filed by the Petitioner, Damodar Valley Corporation
(DVC) under Section 79(1)(f) of the Electricity Act, 2003 (hereinafter referred to as “the
Act”) seeking a declaration that DVC is entitled to appropriate payment made by BSES
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Order in Petition No. 319/MP/2019 Page 1 of 46

Yamuna Power Limited (BYPL) first towards Late Payment Surcharge (LPSC) and
thereafter towards principal dues, along with consequential relief for payment of the
outstanding LPSC. The Petitioner has made the following prayers:
“(a) Adjudicate and declare that DVC shall be entitled to adjust and was right in
adjusting all payments made by BYPL from time to time in the past and also in the
future first towards all amounts of outstanding late payment surcharge in full before
adjusting any amount of the principal;
(b) hold that DVC is entitled to recover as on 31.8.2019, a sum of Rs.535.00
crore towards principal and Rs.94.54 crore towards outstanding late payment
surcharge (LPSC) along with future late payment surcharge on the outstanding
principal till full payment and discharge of the liabilities of BYPL to DVC;
(c) direct that late payment surcharge shall be payable by BYPL to DVC at the
rates provided in the Tariff Regulations notified by the Hon’ble Commission from
time to time for the relevant tariff control period;
(d) award cost of the present petition including the court fees paid by DVC;
and
(e) pass such further order or orders as this Commission may deem just and proper
in the circumstances of the case.”
Submissions of the Petitioner
2. The Petitioner has mainly submitted as under:
(a) On 24.8.2006, the Delhi Transco Limited (DTL) entered into a Power

was required to make payment to the Petitioner as per the tariff determined by this
Commission for its various generating stations and in case, of delay in payment of

(b) Order dated 3.7.2014 passed by the Hon’ble Supreme Court: The Hon’ble

(c) Judgments relied upon by DVC specifically pertain to the decretal amount:

(d) The PPA is silent as regards adjustment methodology: Admittedly, the
original PPA between DVC and DTL, dated 24.8.2006, which was later assigned
to the Respondent in terms of re-assignment order dated 31.3.2007 (and
subsequent re-assignment dated 27.2.2014), does not provide for any
methodology for adjustment of dues.
(e) The Petition is barred by the contract between the parties itself, as also the
Doctrine of Past Practice: On 11.1.2017, when the Joint Reconciliation Statements
were signed, all the payments made by the Respondent were adjusted firstly
towards principal amount and thereafter towards LPSC. The Joint Reconciliation
Statement is itself a contract between the parties. As such, the appropriation of
dues has to be done in accordance with the terms and conditions mutually agreed
between the parties under the PPA, read with the contract between the parties in
the form of the Joint Reconciliation Statement executed between them. In the
present case, DVC and Respondent have specifically agreed to the Joint
Reconciliation Statement, which is itself a contract between the parties. The
Hon’ble Supreme Court, in a catena of judgments, has held that the conduct of the
parties is a relevant factor in the construction of contracts. Further, DVC itself has
admitted the said fact in the instant Petition (Para 30); therefore, DVC is bound by
the same and cannot now unilaterally renege on it thereafter.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

(f) After 2017, when payment was made to DVC, since there was no specific
clause, one way or another, in the PPA and in accordance with the Joint
Reconciliation Statement of 2017, the Respondent had clearly intimated to DVC
that all such payments made were towards the principal amount of energy dues.
Under the Contract Act, this was the right and prerogative of the Respondent to do
so. In accordance with the exercise of such right by the Respondent, all payments
made after 2017 have, first, to be credited to the principal dues and not towards
the LPSC.
(g) Unilateral Change in methodology of adjustment cannot be done: In the
present case, the Respondent is not agreeable with the methodology as sought by
DVC for adjustment of dues, and DVC cannot unilaterally change the same as it
would amount to novation of contract for which parties have to mutually agree as
per Section 62 of the Indian Contract Act, 2003 and not otherwise.
(h) DVC indirectly changing the terms of PPA, which cannot be done: The
commercial terms once agreed mutually cannot be changed without the consent
of the parties. The Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (the APTEL) in its judgment
dated 24.1.2013 in Appeal No. 82 of 2012 has held that commercial terms, viz.,
Letter of Credit, and Dues etc., have to be mutually decided between the parties,
and it is not open to the parties to question the same after entering into the PPA
and acting as per the same.

Since the Hon`ble Supreme Court did not prescribe how payment should be

(c) Tariff orders as a decretal basis: The tariff orders of CERC determine the
final amount payable by BYPL, which functions like a decretal order. In the
absence of any clause in the PPA on payment adjustment, the general Principal
applies-payment is first adjusted against LPSC, then against principal dues.
(d) Ad hoc adjustment not a waiver: The temporary arrangement post
11.1.2017 reconciliation, where DVC accepted fixed payment towards LPSC, was
only provisional and does not amount to waiver of the DVC’s rights. BYPL itself
never agreed to this arrangement (as seen in the 18.4.2018 reconciliation).
Further, BYPL's reliance on Sections 59, 60, and 61 of the Indian Contract Act,
1872, is misplaced and has no application to the facts of the present case. The
present case relates to the appropriation of the amount paid by BYPL to DVC for
the same transactions, by apportioning it between the LPSC and the principal
amount.
(e) No unilateral change: There is no unilateral change in the adjustment of
methodology or violation of the PPA. It maintains that the general rule of
appropriation governs payment adjustments in the absence of any mutually agreed
method.

(k) In present Petition, DVC has failed to appreciate that the KSEB judgment,
far from supporting DVC’s case, actually goes completely against it. The Hon’ble
Supreme Court, while dealing with the aforesaid judgments, has inter alia observed
that “appropriation of money is the indication of an intention that money should be
applied in a particular way” and if a party has indicated the manner in which the
appropriation is to be made, the creditor has no choice but to appropriate the
payment in that manner. Thereby, the conduct and actions of DVC are in the teeth
of the findings of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the KSEB Judgment. Gurpreet
Singh and BHEL Judgments deal with the issue of appropriation of amount payable
under a money decree and/or an order in the nature of a decree, i.e., decretal
amounts. However, in the present case, between the parties, no decree has been
passed by any court against BYPL and in favour of DVC.

Section 2(2) of Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (“CPC”) (amended from time to
time) defines “decree” to mean “the formal expression of an adjudication which, so
far as regards the Court expressing it, conclusively determines the rights of the
parties with regard to all or any of the matters in controversy in the suit and may
be either preliminary or final…” The Hon’ble Supreme Court in a catena of

paid towards principal amounts first and is therefore, contrary to the mandate of

the Constitution Bench of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Gurpreet Singh vs.

“20. … It was also held that the general rule of appropriation towards a decretal

“31. From what has been stated in the said decision, the following Principles

31.1. The general rule of appropriation towards a decretal amount was that such
