on the transmission service at present, we are of the view that the Petitioner’s prayer
on this count is premature.
Security Expenses, Insurance and Capital Spares
80. The Petitioner has submitted that, as per Regulation 36(3)(d) of the 2024 Tariff
Regulations, the security expenses and capital spares of more than ₹10 lakh for the
transmission system will be allowed separately after a prudence check.

of the 2024 Tariff Regulations. According to the Petitioner, the security expenses
regarding the transmission asset are not claimed in the instant Petition.

the instant Petition and has submitted that it will file a separate Petition for claiming the

actual insurance expenses incurred by it for FY 2023-24 after escalating the same at

26, 2026-27, 2027-28, and 2028-29.

the instant Petition for the 2024-29 tariff period. According to the Petitioner, it will file

on an actual basis for the 2024-29 tariff period as per the 2024 Tariff Regulations. The
Petitioner has also submitted that it has filed Petition No. 45/MP/2024, claiming therein
capital spares for the 2019-24 tariff period as per the 2019 Tariff Regulations.

We deem it proper here to refer Regulation 36(3)(d) of the 2024 Tariff Regulations,
which provides as follows:
“36(3)
(d) The Security Expenses, Capital Spares individually costing more than Rs. 10 lakh
and Insurance expenses arrived through competitive bidding for the transmission
system and associated communication system shall be allowed separately after
prudence check:
Provided that in case of self-insurance, the premium shall not exceed 0.12% of
the GFA of the assets insured;
Provided that the transmission licensee shall submit the along with estimated
security expenses based on assessment of the security requirement, capital spares
and insurance expenses, which shall be trued up based on details of the year-wise
actuals along with appropriate justification for incurring the same and along with
confirmation that the same is not claimed as a part of additional capitalisation or
consumption of stores and spares and renovation and modernization.
Provided that the self-insurance premium shall be transferred to a separate
fund for utilization to meet the claims, and the expenditure incurred or amount utilized
from the self-insurance fund shall be made available to the Commission as and when
directed.”
85. On the perusal of Regulation 36(3)(d) of the 2024 Tariff Regulations and
considering the Petitioner’s submissions, the Petitioner is allowed to file a single
consolidated Petition comprising of security expenses, capital spares individually
costing more than ₹10 lakh and insurance expenses on an estimated basis in terms of
the 2024 Tariff Regulations for the 2024-29 tariff period.

“82. The Commission vide order dated 31.1.2017 in Petition No. 558/TT/2014 held as

आदेश/ ORDER
The Petitioner, India Power Corporation Limited (IPCL), is a distribution licensee under
Section 2 (17) of the Electricity Act, 2003, duly licensed by the West Bengal Electricity
Regulatory Commission (WBERC), and operates in the Asansol-Raniganj area of West
Bengal, with 12 MW of embedded generation. The Petitioner supplies power to various
consumer categories in the said area. In addition to conventional power sourcing, the
Petitioner also sources power from a 2 MWp Solar PV project in West Bengal Green Energy
Development Corporation Ltd. and a long-term 100 MW RE (Wind-Solar Hybrid) PPA with
Solar Energy Corporation of India Ltd. (SECI).
2. The Respondent, National Load Dispatch Centre (NLDC), operated by Grid-India, is
designated as the Central Agency under the CERC REC Regulations, 2022 and is entrusted
with the functions of granting registration and issuance and monitoring of RECs as per the
said REC Regulations.
3. The Petitioner, IPCL filed the present petition under Section 66 of the Electricity Act, 2003
read with Regulation 17 of the CERC (Terms and Conditions for Renewable Energy
Certificates for Renewable Energy Generation) Regulations, 2022 (REC Regulations, 2022)
and related provisions, seeking directions against the Respondent, National Load Despatch
Centre (NLDC), regarding the issuance of reduced Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs) to
the Petitioner for the FY 2024-25 based on the Renewable Energy Consumption Obligation
(RCO) targets notified by the Ministry of Power (MoP), in contravention of the statutory
framework established by the Commission. For FY 2024-25, the Petitioner claimed eligibility
for the issuance of 4,40,119 RECs based on excess RE procurement over the RPO targets
specified by the WBERC. However, the Respondent, while processing the Petitioner’s
Order in Petition No. 841/MP/2025 Page 2 of 11

application for REC issuance, computed the eligibility on the basis of the provision in the
Detailed REC Procedure amended with the RCO targets notified by the MoP Notification No.
S.0.4617 (E) dated 20.10.2023 and consequently issued only 3,20,826 RECs, resulting in a
shortfall of 1,19,293 RECs.
4. The Petitioner has made the following prayers:
(a) Admit the Petition;
(b) Issue appropriate practice directions under Regulation 17 of the CERC REC Regulations,
2022, clarifying that the issuance of RECs to eligible entities shall be strictly in
accordance with the REC Regulations and shall not be curtailed, reduced, or otherwise

Submission by the Petitioner, IPCL
5. The Petitioner submitted the following:
(a) The WBERC vide Regulation 3.1 of WBERC (Cogeneration and Generation of
Electricity from Renewable Source of Energy) (First Amendment), 2020 (issued on
21.12.2020) specified that the RPO targets for FY 2022-23 (in %) of total consumption
from renewable energy (RE) sources was 6% for solar and 11% for non-solar, cumulative
to 17%.
(b) WBERC vide its Suo-Moto Order in Case No. SM-37/23-24 dated 30.10.2023 decided
that the RPO target for FY 2022-23 would continue till further order of the WBERC in
view of the decision of the High Court of Calcutta in MAT No. 568 of 2022 and in MAT
No. 569 of 2022. Accordingly, the RPO targets for 2024-25 remained the same as those
of 2022-23.

(c) During the FY 2024-25, IPCL was able to procure RE power in excess of the aforesaid
RPO target specified by WBERC as indicated in the following table:

correspondence accepted the reduced REC under protest without any prejudice to the

(k) Subsequently, the Respondent issued the reduced RECs to the Petitioner on 09.07.2025
pursuant to the payment of fees and charges as per Regulations 15 of the CERC REC
Regulations, 2022 by the Petitioner.
(l) The Respondent also revised the procedure for “Implementation of REC Mechanism” in
compliance with REC Regulations, 2022, on 07.03.2024, without prior approval from the
Commission and without any public stakeholders’ consultation, as such changes
materially affected the stakeholders.
(m) Further, the Commission vide its letter dated 15.10.2020 issued a statutory advice to
MoP, specifically mentioned that one of the avowed objectives of the Electricity Act,
2003 was to distance the regulatory responsibilities from the Government and vest it in
the Regulatory Commissions. Therefore, the directions issued by the MoP or any
executive authority cannot override regulations issued by the State Commission under a
statutory framework.
(n) Accordingly, the Petitioner requested the Commission to exercise its power to give

RECs in favour of the Petitioner.
Hearing dated 04.11.2025
6. During the course of the hearing, the counsel for the Petitioner submitted that the issue in
the present matter was related to the question as to whether the Respondent, while issuing
Order in Petition No. 841/MP/2025 Page 5 of 11

the RECs, needed to abide by the CERC REC Regulations or the Revised REC Procedure
based on the RCO obligations issued by the MoP. After hearing the counsel for the
Petitioner, the Commission admitted the Petition and directed the Respondents to file
their reply and the Petitioner to file the rejoinder, if any.
Submissions of the Respondent, NLDC, on 03.12.2025 in compliance with the Record of
Proceedings (ROP) of the hearing dated 04.11.2025
7. The Respondent, NLDC, submitted the following:
(a) REC entitlement is determined by surplus over State RPO, and in accordance with the
REC Regulations read together with the applicable Detailed REC Procedure.
(b) Further, under Section 166 read with Section 176 of the Electricity Act, the Forum of
Regulators Rules (FOR Rules) were notified on 16.02.2005 and subsequently amended on
08.09.2022. Rule 3(c) of the FOR Rules provides that renewable compliance monitoring
will be based on the higher of the State-notified obligation or the Central-notified target.
(c) Subsequent to the above, the MoP issued the statutory RCO trajectory dated 20.10.2023,
prescribing an obligation of 29.91% for FY 2024-25 for obligated entities. The RCO was
issued under statutory authority and required that renewable compliance reflect the higher
national target.
(d) In order to ensure consistency and alignment between the REC mechanism, the FoR
Rules and the RCO trajectory notified by MoP, NLDC addressed a communication dated
08.03.2024 to the Commission, submitting that REC issuance under the REC
Regulations, 2022, required harmonisation with the national obligation trajectory to
prevent differential treatment of obligated entities and REC market distortion. Along with
this letter, NLDC placed before the Commission a Draft Revised Detailed REC Procedure
(Revision-3) (Revised REC Procedure) for public consultation. Upon receipt and
consideration of stakeholder submissions, NLDC issued a communication dated
28.03.2024 to the Commission, enclosing the Final Revised REC Procedure and stating
that the procedure aligned with the Rules and the RCO Notification. The said letter
informed that the Revised Procedure would come into effect from 01.04.2024, and the
same was implemented accordingly.
(e) Further, the Petitioner submitted the REC application dated 29.06.2025, claiming
4,40,119 RECs. Upon scrutiny of the Petitioner’s, NLDC issued an email dated
02.07.2025 and informed the Petitioner that eligibility for surplus RECs for FY 2024-25
Order in Petition No. 841/MP/2025 Page 6 of 11

would be computed as per the Revised REC Procedure w.e.f. 01.04.2024 updated based
on the Revised REC Detailed Procedure with MoP RCO Target of 29.91% for FY 2024-
25. The REC-eligible surplus was accordingly recalculated as 3,20,826 units. Upon
completion of fee payment, NLDC issued 3,20,826 RECs on 09.07.2025.
(f) NLDC submitted that it acted in accordance with the statutory FoR framework and the
RCO Notification dated 20.10.2023.
Rejoinder by the Petitioner, IPCL, dated 02.01.2026, on the Reply submitted by the
NLDC
8. The Petitioner submitted the following:
(a) The Respondent’s reliance on Rule 3(c) of the FoR Rules,2025 was misplaced, as the
scope of the said Rule remained confined to the “monitoring of renewable purchase
compliance” by distribution licensees, captive generators, and open access consumers
and did not confer any authority upon FoR or its implementing agencies including
NLDC to alter, recalibrate, or reinterpret the statutory parameters governing REC
eligibility, including RPO or excess procurement.
(b) The action of NLDC in recalculating the eligible surplus was alleged to be ultra vires of
the REC Regulations, 2022, and the FoR Rules could not override or modify the
statutory REC Regulations framed by CERC.
(c) The MoP’s Notification S.O. 4617(E) dated 20.10.2023, issued under clauses (n) and (x)
of Section 14 of the Energy Conservation Act, 2001, which prescribed RCO targets
including 29.91% for FY 2024-25 for designated consumers, could not in law override,
amend, modify, or displace the REC mechanism framed under the Electricity Act, 2003.
(d) Further, the revised REC Procedure (Rev-3) relied upon by NLDC did not possess legal
sanctity without CERC approval.
Hearing dated 15.01.2026
9. During the course of the hearing, at the request of the counsels for the parties, the
Commission permitted them to file their respective written submissions, if any. Subject to
this, the matter was reserved for order.
Submissions by the Petitioner, IPCL, on 25.01.2026 in compliance with the ROP of the
hearing dated 15.01.2026.
Order in Petition No. 841/MP/2025 Page 7 of 11

10. The Petitioner, in its submissions dated 25.01.2026, reiterated the contentions made in the
Petition as well as in the rejoinder and further made the following submissions:
(a) Section 66 of the Electricity Act, 2003 vested the jurisdiction to deal with the market
instruments like RECs with the ‘Appropriate Commissions’ and not with the ‘Central
Government’. Such statutory jurisdiction could not be taken away from the
‘Appropriate Commissions’ unless such provision is amended by following due
process.
(b) In exercise of the powers under Section 66 read with Section 178 of the Electricity
Act, 2003, the Commission framed the REC Regulations, 2022, which provided that
under Regulation 4(4), RECs are to be issued considering the RPO targets set by the
respective State Commissions.
(c) The MoP Notification dated 20.10.2023 was issued under the Energy Conservation
Act, 2001 and not under the Electricity Act, 2003. The said notification only
mandated the targets for ‘consumption/purchase’ of RE by the Obligated Entities and
did not relate to the issuance of ‘RECs’, a matter statutorily vested in the ‘Appropriate
Commission’ under Section 66 of the Electricity Act, 2003.
(d) In terms of Section 173 read with Section 174 of the Electricity Act, 2003, the
provisions of the Electricity Act, 2003 have an over-riding effect on inconsistent
provisions contained in any other law except the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 or
the Atomic Energy Act, 1962 or the Railways Act, 1989. The Energy Conservation
Act, 2001, does not contain such an ‘overriding/ notwithstanding’ clause similar to
Section 173 or Section 174 of the Electricity Act, 2003.
(e) Accordingly, the issuance of RECs for FY 2024-2025 and the subsequent period is to
be in accordance with Regulation 4(4) of the CERC REC Regulations 2022 (based on
RPO targets set by the State Commission) and not on the RCO targets fixed by the
MoP under the Energy Conservation Act, 2001.
Analysis and Decision
11. The Commission has heard the learned counsels for the Petitioner and the Respondent
and has carefully perused the records.
12. Brief facts of the case: The Petitioner, IPCL which is a distribution company (DISCOM)
in the state of West Bengal, filed the present petition under Section 66 of the Electricity
Act, 2003 read with Regulations 17 of the CERC REC Regulations, 2022 and related
Order in Petition No. 841/MP/2025 Page 8 of 11

provisions, to seek directions against the Respondent, NLDC, regarding the issuance of
reduced RECs to the Petitioner for the FY 2024-25. For FY 2024-25, the Petitioner
claimed eligibility for issuance of 4,40,119 RECs on account of procurement of RE in
excess of the RPO targets specified by the WBERC. However, the Respondent, NLDC,
computed the eligible RECs based on the Revised Detailed REC procedure, as amended
by the RCO trajectory notified by the Ministry of Power vide Notification No. S.O.
4617(E) dated 20.10.2023 and issued only 3,20,826 RECs, thereby resulting in a shortfall
of 1,19,293 RECs. Aggrieved by the reduction in the number of RECs issued, the
Petitioner approached this Commission and submitted that NLDC's action in applying the
RCO targets notified by the MoP is contrary to the statutory framework under the
Electricity Act, 2003, and the REC Regulations, 2022. NLDC, in its response, submitted
that the eligibility of DISCOMs for issuance of RECs is determined based on surplus RE
procurement over and above the higher of the RPO specified by the concerned State
Commission or the RCO trajectory notified by the MoP vide Notification dated
20.10.2023, in terms of the Forum of Regulators Rules and as provided under the
Detailed Procedure for implementation of the REC mechanism.
13. In view of the above submissions and pleadings, the Commission notes that the only issue
that arises for the adjudication is whether the Petitioner is entitled to the issuance of
4,40,119 RECs as claimed by it or only 3,20,826 RECs as issued by the Respondent,
NLDC.
14. We observe that the REC Regulations, 2022, provide the eligibility for issuance of
certificates for the Distribution Licensee. The extract of the relevant provision is as
follows:
“4. Eligibility for Issuance of Certificates
………………..
(4) An obligated entity being a distribution licensee or an open access consumer,
which purchases electricity from renewable energy sources in excess of the renewable
purchase obligation as determined by the concerned State Commission shall be
eligible for issuance of Certificates to the extent of purchase of such excess electricity
from renewable energy sources.”
Order in Petition No. 841/MP/2025 Page 9 of 11

15. We also observe that the REC Regulations, 2022, provide the provision for application
for issuance of Certificates by the Distribution Licensee. The extract of the relevant
provision is as follows:
“10. Issuance of Certificates
..…..
(3) Application for issuance of Certificates shall be made by an eligible entity being a
distribution licensee or an open access consumer within three months from the end of a
financial year, along with a copy of certification from the concerned State Commission
about purchase of electricity from renewable energy sources in excess of the renewable
purchase obligations as determined by the concerned State Commission:
Provided that no Certificate shall be issued in case the application is made beyond
the period of three months from the end of the financial year.”
16. From the above, we observe that as per the provisions of REC Regulations 2022, a
distribution licensee becomes eligible for issuance of RECs only to the extent of RE
procured in excess of the RPO specified by the concerned State Commission and such
eligible entity is required to apply for issuance of Certificates within three months from
the end of the financial year along with certification from the concerned State
Commission regarding such excess RE procurement.
17. The Commission observes that, as per the submission on record, the WBERC on
26.06.2025, certified the quantum of 440.127 MU of excess RE procured by the
Petitioner, IPCL, for FY 2024-25. Based on such certification, the Petitioner submitted its
application for the issuance of RECs within the stipulated time under Regulation 10(3) of
the REC Regulations, 2022.
18. The Commission notes that the Respondent, NLDC, in its submissions, stated that it has
acted in accordance with the Forum of Regulators Rules, notified on 16.02.2005 and
subsequently amended on 08.09.2022, which provide that RPO compliance monitoring
shall be based on the higher of the State-notified obligation or the Central-notified target.
19. The relevant extract of the said notification is as follows:
“3. In the said rules, in rule 4,
Order in Petition No. 841/MP/2025 Page 10 of 11

…
(c) Monitoring of renewable purchase compliance- (i) The compliance of
targets, by each of the distribution licensees, captive consumption and
consumers procuring power through open access, for purchase of electricity
from renewable sources as determined by the Central Government or by
State Commission, whichever is higher, in accordance with the provisions of
the Act and rules, regulations, guidelines made thereunder.”
20. The Commission observes that the aforesaid provisions of the Forum of Regulators Rules
are confined to monitoring RPO compliance of obligated entities. Under the REC
Regulations, 2022, eligibility for the issuance of RECs is linked solely to the procurement
of renewable energy in excess of the RPO, as determined and certified by the “concerned
State Commission”.
21. The Commission notes that, in terms of Regulation 4(4) of the CERC REC Regulations,
2022, the Petitioner, IPCL, being an eligible obligated entity, is entitled to the issuance of
RECs corresponding to its procurement of RE in excess of the RPO as determined and
certified by the concerned State Commission, i.e. WBERC. We observe that, as per the
certification issued by WBERC, the Petitioner is entitled to 4,40,119 RECs for FY 2024-
25; however, the Respondent, in processing the Petitioner’s REC application, issued only
3,20,826 RECs.
22. We also note that the Petitioner, being an eligible distribution licensee, is entitled to
4,40,119 RECs as certified by the SERC in accordance with Regulation 4(4) of the REC
Regulations, 2022. In our view, the issuance of the REC is procedural in nature and is not
likely to prejudice any stakeholders, including the Respondent. Accordingly, we direct
NLDC to issue the remaining 1,19,293 RECs to the Petitioner.
23. Petition No. 841/MP/2025 is disposed of in terms of the above.

याचिका संख्या / Petition No 338/MP/2025
कोरम/ Coram:

आदेश चदनांक/ Date of Order 25th of May, 2026
In the matter of
Petition under Section 66 of the Electricity Act, 2003 read with Regulation 25 and 19 of the
CERC (Power Market) Regulations, 2021, for approval of the revision in Green Contracts
at Indian Energy Exchange Ltd. to align them with the Renewable Energy (RE) consumption
framework as per the Ministry of Power Notification dated 20.10.2023.
And
In the matter of
Indian Energy Exchange Limited (IEX)
9th Floor, Max Towers, Sector 16 B,
Gautam Buddha Nagar, Uttar Pradesh – 201301 … Petitioner
Vs
National Load Despatch Centre (NLDC)
B-9 (1st Floor), Qutab Institutional Area,
Katwaria Sarai, New Delhi 110016 … Respondent
Parties present
Shri Gaurav Maheshwari, IEX
Shri Saurabh Srivastava, IEX
Shri Subhendu Mukherjee, NLDC
Shri Ashok Ranjan, NLDC
Shri Debajyoti Majumdar, NLDC
Order in Petition No. 338/MP/2025 Page 1 of 23

Ms. Himani Dutta, NLDC
ORDER
The Petitioner, Indian Energy Exchange Limited (IEX), has filed the petition under
Section 66 of the Electricity Act, 2003, (hereinafter referred to as “the Act”), read with
Regulations 25 and 19 of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Power Market)
Regulations, 2021 (hereinafter referred to as “PMR 2021”) for approval of the revision in
Green Contracts at IEX to align them with Renewable Energy (RE) consumption framework
as per the Ministry of Power notification dated 20.10.2023 (alternatively also referred to as
“the MoP Notification”). The Petitioner has made the following prayers:
a) Accord approval for revision in Green Contracts to align them with the RE source
classification as per the RE consumption framework prescribed in the Ministry of
Power Notification dated 20.10.2023 & its amendment time to time.
b) Accord approval to the modifications proposed in the Business Rules and contract
specifications to incorporate the above RE classification.
c) Issue appropriate directions to NLDC to make provisions in the T-GNA procedures
for issuance of appropriate standing clearance endorsing the RE category type for
participation in the contracts.
d) Pass such further order or orders as may be considered.
Initial submission of the Petitioner (dated 10.01.2025)
2. The Petitioner, IEX, is a company incorporated under the provisions of the
Companies Act, 1956 and having its corporate office at Plot No. C-001/A/1, 9th Floor, Max
Towers, Sector 16 B, Noida, Gautam Buddha Nagar, Uttar Pradesh – 201301.
3. The Hon’ble Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (hereinafter referred to as
the “Commission" or “CERC”) was pleased to grant permission to IEX to set up, operate
Order in Petition No. 338/MP/2025 Page 2 of 23

and commence power exchange operations by its orders dated 31.08.2007 and 09.06.2008.
IEX has been in operation since 27.06.2008.
4. IEX is presently operating Integrated Day Ahead Market (IDAM), Intra-Day Market
(ITD), Day Ahead Contingency Market (DAC), Term Ahead Market (TAM), Real Time
Market (RTM), Green Intra-Day Market (G-ITD), Green Day Ahead Contingency Market
(G-DAC) and Green Term Ahead Market (G-TAM) in electricity segment and Renewable
Energy Certificate (RECs) and Energy Savings Certificates (ESCerts) Market, in accordance
with the byelaws, rules and business rules of IEX and Regulations and approvals of the
Commission. The electricity transactions at IEX are governed by PMR 2021 and
Connectivity and GNA Regulations and Procedures issued thereof.
5. IEX has been providing a transparent, demutualised and automated trading platform
for physical delivery of electricity, enabling competition, efficient price discovery and
counter-party risk management for its participants in all market segments.
6. With a strong policy support from the Government of India (GoI) and an enabling
regulatory framework, the capacity addition of RE sources has seen phenomenal growth in
recent times. Major impetus has been provided by the national-level Renewable Purchase
Obligation (RPO) trajectory notified by the Ministry of Power (MoP), wherein RPO targets
have been set for obligated entities, to be fulfilled at the state level by purchasing RE power
or RECs. The latest RE consumption targets were issued by the MoP on 20.10.2023 and
subsequently on 27.09.2025 under Section 14 of the Energy Conservation Act, 2001
(alternatively referred to as “the EC Act”).
7. IEX has been aiding obligated entities in meeting their RPO compliance by providing
its platform for trading of RECs since February 2011. IEX introduced its first RE-specific
Order in Petition No. 338/MP/2025 Page 3 of 23

segment G-TAM, in August 2020, tenure for which was extended to provide delivery up to
3 months of trade of RE power based on the CERC order dated 07.06.2022 in petition no.
219/MP/2021. Subsequently, G-DAM was introduced in October 2021, providing additional
options for procuring RE power.
Need for revision in Green Contracts
8. The RPO trajectory has historically been categorised as “Solar” and “Non-solar”
based on the type of sources, viz., solar, and other than solar, viz., wind, small hydro,
bagasse, etc.
9. Green Contracts at IEX were initially provided for “Solar” and “Non-solar” RPO
categories for the fulfilment of RPO compliance of the obligated entities. Following the GoI
Office Memorandum (OM) dated 08.03.2019 to promote the hydropower sector, large
hydropower projects (LHPs > 25 MW capacity) were notified separately as an RE source for
HPO obligation. The MoP notified the trajectory for HPO vide OM dated 29.01.2021.
Following the MoP order and the Commission's approval vide order dated 24.02.2022 in
petition no. 169/MP/2021, IEX introduced Hydropower contracts in G-TAM, providing
obligated entities with the option to fulfil their HPO. Further, the hydropower contracts were
amended to a duration beyond T+11 in pursuance of the Commission’s order dated
07.06.2022 in petition no. 219/MP/2021. Similarly, hydropower projects (HPPs) eligible to
fulfil HPO of obligated entities were implemented in the G-DAM segment of IDAM at IEX.
10. The MoP vide its order dated 22.07.2022 and 19.09.2022 re-classified the then
prevailing RPO framework (Solar/Non-Solar/HPO) to a new RPO framework wherein RPO
was categorised as Wind RPO (projects with COD after 31.03.2022), HPO (projects with
COD after 08.03.2019) and other RPO (for all RE sources).
Order in Petition No. 338/MP/2025 Page 4 of 23

11. Following the MoP notification dated 20.10.2023, the RPO category was revised to
Wind (for Wind Power Projects- WPPs with COD after 31.03.2024), Hydro (for Hydro
Power Projects- HPPs, including pump storage projects and small hydro projects with COD
after 31.03.2024), Other RE (all other RE sources) and Distributed RE (RE projects < 10
MW capacity). Distributed RE to include solar installations under all configurations (net
metering, gross metering, virtual net metering, group net metering, behind-the-meter
installations, etc).
12. Following the MoP notification dated 20.10.2023, seven (7) states have aligned their
trajectory by amending state regulations, while six (6) states have issued draft regulations to
align their trajectory. With changes to RPO classification and states aligning their
trajectories, it has become necessary to modify Green Contracts on the IEX platform.
Framework of the revised Green Contracts
13. The proposed re-classification of RPO does not require any major modification in
Green Contracts, except that the underlying asset, viz. “Wind/Hydro/DRE/Other RE” will
be available for trade to obligated entities in place of “Solar/Non-solar/Hydro”.
14. The eligibility conditions for participation of sellers in respective segments of Green
Contracts shall be as per the MoP notification dated 20.10.2023 or its subsequent
amendments. Also, as per existing practice, sellers shall provide NOC/ standing clearance
specifying the category as “Wind/Hydro/DRE/Other”. All other conditions and
specifications will remain the same. A certificate will be issued by IEX detailing the trades
undertaken by buyers in each category, which may be used to meet the relevant RE
consumption target/ RPO compliance. The proposed changes would be available in the
following contracts:
Order in Petition No. 338/MP/2025 Page 5 of 23

a. Green Day Ahead Market (G-DAM)
b. Green Day-Ahead Contingency Contract (G-DAC)
c. Green Intra-day Contracts (G-IDC)
d. Green Daily Contracts (G-Daily)
e. Green Weekly Contracts (G-Weekly)
f. Green Monthly Contracts (G-Monthly)
g. Green Any Day(s) Single Sided Contracts (G-ADSS)
15. Further, the minimum volume quotation in G-IDC and G-DAC has been proposed to
be modified from 0.220 MW to 0.1 MW to align it with other Green Contracts in G-DAM
and G-TAM segments at IEX and Green Energy Open Access Rules of MoP.
16. Further, with the introduction of the proposed “Other RE” category, all RE sources,
including solar, wind, hydro, etc., will be traded in a single contract. To ensure uniformity
across all Green Contracts, it is proposed that all G-TAM contracts be traded in “MWh”.
17. In view of proposed modifications in the existing contracts, a copy of the revised
business rules of IEX incorporating proposed amendments is submitted for the consideration
of the Commission. It is submitted that the Commission may kindly accord its approval to
the proposed modifications to the Business Rules.
18. IEX has filed a petition no. 277/MP/2024 dated 12.07.2024 for the introduction of
G-RTM at IEX. Any changes to the classification of RE sources for Green Contracts at IEX
may be applicable mutatis mutandis to G-RTM as and when approved by the Commission.
Proceedings before the Commission
Commission hearing dated 21.05.2025
19. The Petitioner submitted that the Petition has been filed seeking approval of the
Commission to revise Green Contracts at IEX to align them with the Renewable Energy
Order in Petition No. 338/MP/2025 Page 6 of 23

(RE) consumption framework as per the MoP notification dated 20.10.2023.
20. Considering the submission, the Commission directed as follows: (a) Admit and
issue notice to the Respondent, subject to just exceptions; (b) The Respondent to file its
reply, if any, within four weeks, with a copy to the Petitioner, who may file its rejoinder, if
any, within three weeks thereafter.
21. Further, considering the aspects involved in the matter, the Commission considered
it appropriate to list the present matter along with Petition Nos. 277/MP/2024 and
446/MP/2025.
Commission hearing dated 12.08.2025
22. The Petitioner submitted that the Petition has been filed seeking approval of the
Commission to revise the Green Contracts at IEX to align them with the Renewable Energy
(RE) consumption framework as per the MoP notification dated 20.10.2023.
23. In response to the specific query of the Commission as to whether Grid India (NLDC)
has filed its reply/ response to the instant Petition, Grid India replied in the negative.
However, Grid India submitted that it has no objection to the prayers as made by the
Petitioner.
24. Considering the submissions made by both parties, the Commission directed the
Respondent, NLDC, to file its reply within two weeks, with a copy to the Petitioner, who
may file its rejoinder, if any, within two weeks thereafter.
25. The Petitioner and the Respondent were directed to clarify, on an affidavit, within
two weeks, the fungibility provision contained in the notification and submit their views on
possible options for incorporating this provision into Green Contracts, along with the
Order in Petition No. 338/MP/2025 Page 7 of 23

respective advantages and disadvantages of each option.
Submission of the Respondent (dated 01.09.2025)
26. The Respondent, National Load Despatch Centre (NLDC), Grid India, filed its reply
in compliance with the RoP for hearing dated 12.08.2025.
27. The proposed amendment to the Green Contracts by the Petitioner is intended to align
them with the RPO trajectory set forth by the MoP notification dated 20.10.2023 and
amendments thereof, and to revise the current classifications of Solar, Non-Solar, and Hydro
to the updated categories of Wind, Hydro, Distributed Renewable Energy (DRE), and
Others.
28. It is pertinent to mention that the MoP has issued a revised “draft” Renewable
Consumption Obligation (RCO) notification on 05.08.2025, which provides full fungibility
among Wind, Hydro, and Other RE components such that any deficiency in one component
may be offset by surplus in another.
29. Further, the Power Exchanges certify RPO to the corresponding buyer precisely to
the specific source of the cleared trade executed through the bilateral mode. Hence, for
bilateral contracts, a change in the existing arrangement of Solar/Non-Solar/Hydro segments
to Wind, Hydro, DRE and Others yields benefits limited to nominal re-designation, as the
underlying market-clearing mechanism and all other functionalities remain unchanged.
30. In the “draft” RCO notification dated 05.08.2025, the policy intent is to ensure actual
physical deployment of less than 10 MW installations (rooftop, behind-the-meter, group
metering, etc.) as DRE, to directly serve the consumers at the distribution level. This is also
reinforced by the non-fungibility clause and the relaxation provided to the hilly and North-
Order in Petition No. 338/MP/2025 Page 8 of 23

Eastern States/Union Territories (where DRE obligation is halved and the balance merged
into Other RE, recognising their geographical constraints). It transpires that DRE is
specifically intended to drive physical installation, and its shortfall cannot be substituted
through fungible categories. Accordingly, it is submitted that DRE obligations can be met
by the actual consumption of energy generated from qualifying distributed installations.
Therefore, the introduction of a DRE contract on the Power Exchange may be deemed
appropriate by the Commission.
31. If the Commission considers it appropriate for the re-classification of the Green
Contracts, there will be a requirement to replace the existing designation of renewable type
(Solar/Non-Solar/Hydro) with the proposed categories of Wind, Hydro, DRE, and Others.
Such modifications to the Standing Clearance format, as well as corresponding changes to
the NOAR portal, shall be implemented by NLDC in compliance with the Commission's
directions.
32. There is a lack of visibility in the nature of power, i.e. RE or non-RE, from where
state DISCOMs are selling through portfolio sale, this was mentioned by Grid-India in its
Reply in the Petition No. 25/MP/2019. The Commission vide order dated 17.10.2021 in the
Petition No. 146/MP/2021 has provided direction on the same, which is reproduced as
follows:
“26. We observe that this issue has already been dealt by the Commission in order
dated 17.05.2020 in Petition No. 25/MP/2019 while approving the proposal of the
Petitioner to introduce GTAM. Relevant extract of the order is reproduced
hereunder:
“36. POSOCO has expressed concern that in case of portfolio sale by a RE-rich
State, the power sold is from a mix of generators and it is not possible to identify
Order in Petition No. 338/MP/2025 Page 9 of 23

and tag this power as green power. Hence, such sale of power cannot be used for
fulfilment of RPO by the buyer. The Petitioner, in its reply, has submitted that the
sellers participating in the G-TAM Contracts will have to produce NOC from
RLDC/SLDC indicating the source of generation which would establish that the
power to be sold is truly RE and that it will go towards the fulfilment of RPO
compliance of the buyer.
37. We observe that POSOCO in its reply has submitted that the details of source,
quantum etc. are already being mentioned in the NOCs issued to RE generators by
the SLDCs/RLDCs. Accordingly, any seller transacting through a portfolio shall
ensure that the source of generation (solar or non-solar) is indicated in the NOC
clearly for being able to participate in solar or non-Solar segment of GTAM.
In line with the above-quoted order, any Discom transacting through a portfolio
under GDAC shall ensure that the source of generation (solar or non-solar) is
indicated in the NOC/ Standing Clearance.”
Grid-India, in its response, had submitted to mention the source of generation, which would
establish that the power to be sold is truly RE and that it will go towards the fulfilment of
the buyer's RPO compliance. But presently, Power Exchanges are providing source of
generation as ‘solar or non-solar’. Therefore, it is submitted that, in the case of portfolio sale
by DISCOMs, the names of the RE plants may be mentioned to ensure visibility of RE
power.
33. In view of the response shared above, it is prayed that the Commission may be
pleased to pass such order as the Commission may deem fit and proper in the circumstances
of the case.
Order in Petition No. 338/MP/2025 Page 10 of 23

Additional information filed by Petitioner (dated 01.09.2025)
34. The Petitioner, IEX, filed additional information in compliance with the RoP for the
hearing dated 12.08.2025.
Existing Green contracts at IEX and the corresponding RPO categories
35. The RPO trajectory has historically been classified as “Solar” & Non-solar”, where
Solar RPO is met by procurement of solar power and Non-solar RPO is met through all the
other sources, viz. Wind, Small Hydro, Bagasse, etc.
36. Green Contracts at IEX initially provided only “Solar” & “Non-solar” RPO
categories for the fulfilment of compliance of the obligated entities. Subsequently, the GoI
approved measures to promote the hydropower sector vide OM dated 08.03.2019, the key
among which were the declaration of the capacity of Large Hydropower Projects (LHPs)
(>25 MW) as an RE source and the notification of HPO as a separate obligation for all
entities, which can be fulfilled through LHPs commissioned after 08.03.2019. The MoP
notified the trajectory of HPO vide OM dated 29.01.2021.
37. In pursuance of the MoP order dated 29.01.2021 and based on the approval granted
by the Commission vide order dated 24.02.2022 in Petition No. 169/MP/2021, IEX
introduced the Hydropower Contract in G-TAM for trade in hydropower and to provide
options to obligated entities to fulfil their HPO.
38. Later, the aforesaid was also implemented in G-DAM such that, in addition to the
existing eligible “Solar” and “Non-solar” category RE sellers in G-DAM, the HPPs eligible
to fulfil HPO were eligible to participate in G-DAM under I-DAM.
Order in Petition No. 338/MP/2025 Page 11 of 23

Fungibility provision in the RCO notification dated 20.10.2023
39. MoP vide its notification dated 22.07.2022 and 19.09.2022 re-classified the then
prevailing RPO framework (Solar/Non-Solar/HPO) to a new RPO framework wherein RPO
was categorised as - Wind RPO (for projects with COD after 31.03.2022), HPO (for projects
with COD after 08.03.2019) and Other RPO (for all other RE sources).
40. Subsequently, the MoP vide notification dated 20.10.2023, revised the RPO
categories as:
i. Wind (for wind projects with COD after 31.03.2024)
ii. Hydro Power projects
1. For hydro projects, including PSPs and SHPs with COD after 31.03.2024
2. Free power from Hydro Projects with COD after 31.03.2024
3. Hydro Projects located outside India, as approved by the Central
Government on a case-by-case basis
iii. Other RE (all the other renewable energy sources).
iv. Distributed RE (RE projects with size <10 MW)
41. As per the MoP notification, the following can be stated with respect to the
fungibility of components:
i. Shortfall & surplus of ‘wind renewable energy’ & ‘hydro renewable energy’
components against the respective targets are fungible between each other.
Surplus left under the ‘wind renewable energy’ or ‘hydro renewable energy’
component after the above adjustments can be used for the ‘other renewable
energy’ component.
ii. Surplus of ‘Other renewable energy’ component is fungible with the shortfall in
Order in Petition No. 338/MP/2025 Page 12 of 23

‘Wind renewable energy’ or ‘Hydro renewable energy’ components.
iii. Designated consumers who are open access consumers or Captive can fulfil their
obligation as per the specified total RE target, regardless of the individual
component level target.
Evidently, fungibility is among the sources of surplus consumption for each component, not
the overall consumption. Thus, each component needs to exist separately.
42. Since the MoP notification dated 20.10.2023, thirteen (13) states/UTs have aligned
their trajectory with MoP by amending their regulations, while five (5) states have issued
draft regulations to align their trajectory. A few states (2) have also notified full fungibility
among the RE sources against the targets. Even otherwise, MoP has clarified that the
obligated entities need to comply with the RCO targets provided in the MoP notification.
43. Thus, it is imperative that Green Contracts available at the IEX platform reflect the
RCO components provided in the MoP notification. The entities can buy RE power under
the proposed categories through IEX to fulfil their corresponding RCO target as per their
requirements. Additionally, to align with evolving policy needs, IEX would update the RCO
components in response to amendments as and when notified by the MoP. The same will be
incorporated with intimation to the Commission.
44. In view of the above and considering the overall development of the RE market, it is
submitted that the Commission may consider the present submission and pass such orders
as may be deemed fit.
Further proceedings before the Commission
Commission hearing dated 02.09.2025
45. The Petitioner submitted that in compliance with the direction of the Commission
Order in Petition No. 338/MP/2025 Page 13 of 23

vide RoP for the hearing dated 12.08.2025, the Petitioner has filed an affidavit dated
01.09.2025, furnishing its views on the fungibility provisions contained in RCO notification
and the possible options for incorporating this provision into green contracts. IEX further
submitted that the MoP has vide notification dated 20.10.2023, revised the RPO categories
into (i) Wind (for Wind Projects with COD after 31.3.2024), (ii) Hydro Power Projects,
including PSPs and SHPs with COD after 31.3.2024, free power from Hydro Projects with
COD after 31.3.2024 and hydro projects located outside India, as approved by Central Govt.,
(iii) Other RE (all other renewable energy sources), and (iv) Distributed RE (RE Project with
size < 10 MW). Further, as per the said notification, fungibility is among the surplus
consumption of each component, not in the overall consumption and thus each component
needs to exist separately in the green contracts available on its Platform to reflect the RCO
components provided in the aforesaid Notification.
46. The Respondent, NLDC, submitted that it has already filed its reply in the matter.
NLDC further pointed out that the MoP issued a revised draft RCO Notification on
05.08.2025, which provides for full fungibility among the Wind, Hydro, and Other RE
components, such that any shortfall in one component may be offset by a surplus in another.
NLDC also submitted that, insofar as the DRE is concerned, the policy intent, as per the
aforesaid draft RCO Notification, appears to ensure that the actual physical installations and
their shortfall cannot be substituted through fungible categories. Accordingly, the
Commission may appropriately consider introducing a DRE contract on the Power
Exchanges.
47. Considering the submissions made by the representatives of the parties, the
Commission reserved the matter for Order.
Order in Petition No. 338/MP/2025 Page 14 of 23

Analysis and Decision
48. The Petitioner seeks approval of the Commission for revision in Green Contracts at
its platform to align them with the Renewable Energy (RE) consumption framework as per
the MoP notification dated 20.10.2023 and its subsequent amendments. The Petitioner also
seeks approval to incorporate the revised RE classification into its Business Rules and
contract specifications. In addition, the Petitioner seeks the Commission’s direction to
NLDC to make provisions in T-GNA procedures for issuing appropriate standing clearance
endorsing the RE category.
49. Regulations 25 and 19 of PMR 2021 provide as follows:
“25. Approval or Suspension of Contracts by the Commission
(1) The Commission may, on its own or on an application made in this behalf,
permit any Power Exchange to introduce new contracts as specified in clause
(1) of Regulation 4 of these regulations:
…..
19. Bye-laws, rules and business rules of Power Exchange
…...
(2) No amendment to the bye-laws, rules and business rules shall be carried out
without prior approval of the Commission:
Provided that the Commission may, through a separate order, dispense with the
requirement of prior approval for amendment of certain provisions of the bye-
laws, rules and business rules;
Provided further that such amendments shall be required to be approved by the
Board of Directors of the Power Exchange.”
Order in Petition No. 338/MP/2025 Page 15 of 23

50. Section 86(1)(e) of the Act mandates State Electricity Regulatory Commissions
(SERCs) to specify a minimum share of total consumption from RE sources of energy for
their state. While states have come up with their RPO Regulations, the Government of India
(GoI) has also set a national RPO trajectory for the states. Since 2010-11, the GoI has been
relying on RPO as an instrument to promote RE deployment in the country.
51. Until 2020, RPO was specifically categorised as “Solar” and “Non-solar”. The non-
solar category included sources such as wind, hydro, and bagasse. With the Commission’s
approval and following the dual classification of RPO categories, the Petitioner permitted
trading of Green Contracts on its platform categorising them as “Solar” and “Non-solar”,
allowing the obligated entities to fulfil their RPO compliance.
52. In March 2019, the MoP conceptualised Hydro Power Obligation (HPO) as a
specific category for obligated entities to fulfil their HPO compliance. This was supported
by the HPO trajectory introduced by the MoP in January 2021. Based on the MoP order, the
Petitioner approached the Commission through formal petitions and introduced
Hydropower-based contracts for trading through Green segments - GTAM and GDAM for
entities to fulfil their HPO compliance.
53. In 2022, the categorisation of sources was further revised to Wind RPO, HPO and
Other RPO, along with a new energy storage category. However, the categories were soon
revised vide MoP notification dated 20.10.2023 to Wind, Hydro, Distributed RE and Other
RE. Year-wise RCO targets as specified in the MoP notification for the period 2024-2030
are tabulated.

54. Lately, the MoP issued a “draft” RCO notification on 05.08.2025. Following
stakeholders’ feedback, the MoP released “final” RCO notification on 27.09.2025 (herein
after referred to as “the RCO notification”) enlisting the same targets as notified by the MoP
in their notification dated 20.10.2023 and minor changes in other terms and conditions. The
minimum share of electrical energy from RE sources, as a percentage of total electrical
energy consumption by designated consumers and a few key provisions provided in the RCO
notification are as follows.

Order in Petition No. 338/MP/2025 Page 18 of 23

“Note1*: For hilly and North-Eastern States and Union territories, namely,
Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim,
Tripura, Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Union territory of Jammu and Kashmir
and Union territory of Ladakh, the Distributed renewable energy obligation shall
be 50% of the level specified in the Table. For distribution licensees serving
exclusively urban consumers, the Distributed renewable energy obligation shall be
75% of the specified level. The remaining Distributed renewable energy component
obligation for these States and Union territories shall be included in the Other
renewable energy component.
Note 2: The obligation under the Wind energy component shall be met by energy
produced from Wind Power Projects commissioned after 31st March, 2024.
Note 3: The obligations under the Hydro energy component shall be met by energy
produced from Hydro Power Projects, commissioned after 31st March, 2024:
Provided that the obligation under the Hydro energy component may also be
met out of the free power being provided to the State or distribution licensee from
such Projects:
Provided further that the obligation under the Hydro energy component may
also be met from Hydro Power Projects located outside India, as approved by the
Central Government, on a case- to-case basis.
Note 4: The obligation under the Distributed renewable energy component shall be
met from the energy generated from renewable energy projects that do not exceed
10 MW in size and shall include solar installations under all configurations (net
metering, gross metering, virtual net metering, group net metering, behind the
meter installations and any other configuration) and Other renewable energy
sources notified by the Central Government:
Provided that the compliance against Distributed renewable energy obligation
shall ordinarily be considered in terms of energy (kilowatt hour units):
Provided further that in case the designated consumer is unable to provide
generation data against Distributed renewable energy installations, the reported
capacity shall be converted into Distributed renewable energy generation in terms
of energy by a multiplier of 4-kilowatt hour per kilowatt per day (kWh/kW/day).
Note 5: The obligation under the Other renewable energy component may be met
by electrical energy produced from any renewable energy project other than
Order in Petition No. 338/MP/2025 Page 19 of 23

specified in Notes 2, 3 and 4. Other renewable energy shall include, but not limited
to, electrical energy generated from all,
(i) Wind Power Projects;
(ii) Hydro Power Projects, including free power, commissioned before 1st
April, 2024; and
(iii) Co-firing of biomass pellets and charcoal produced from Municipal Solid
Waste.
3. Obligations under Wind, Hydro, and Other renewable energy components are fungible
(shortfalls in one may be met by surpluses from others), while Distributed renewable energy
is non-fungible for its shortfall but its surplus may offset other components.
4. For all the designated consumers, the Renewable Consumption Obligation shall exclude
electricity consumed from Nuclear Power Sources.
5. Open access consumers and captive users specified as designated consumers shall meet
the specified total Renewable Consumption Obligation, from any renewable energy source.
6. For open access consumers specified as designated consumers, Renewable Consumption
Obligation shall include electrical energy consumption at the point of drawal from the grid.
8. For designated consumers who are distribution licensees, the Renewable Consumption
Obligation shall be calculated based on the electrical energy supplied to consumers within
the periphery of the distribution licensee. This supply shall not include the consumption of
open access users from the sources other than the distribution licensee and the electricity
generated and self- consumed by captive users. (An illustrative example is provided in
Annexure –I attached to this notification.)
9. Designated consumers may fulfil the specified Renewable Consumption Obligation
through one or more of the following methods, namely:
(i) consumption of renewable electricity, either directly or through an energy storage
system;
(ii) purchased or self-generated Renewable Energy Certificates issued in accordance
with regulations notified by the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission
including Renewable Energy Certificates acquired under Virtual Power Purchase
Agreements; and
(iii) payment of the buyout price specified by the Central Electricity Regulatory
Commission….
13. Any shortfall in meeting the Renewable Consumption Obligation shall be treated as non-
Order in Petition No. 338/MP/2025 Page 20 of 23

compliance and penalty may be imposed in accordance with the provisions under sub-
section (3) of section 26 of the Act.
14. In case of a non-compliance of this notification including but not limited to shortfall in
meeting the Renewable Consumption Obligation, non-submission of required information,
or submission of incorrect information, the Bureau or the State designated agency may
process for imposing penalty, in accordance with the provisions of the Act and the rules
made thereunder.”
55. The Commission has taken note of the submissions made by Petitioner and
Respondent, and the latest RCO notification issued by the MoP. The Commission observes
that reclassification of Green Contracts on the Power exchanges, as per the recent
notification by the MoP dated 27.09.2025 and its subsequent amendment, is required to
facilitate RPO/RCO compliance by the obligated entities. Accordingly, the Commission
decides that the Petitioner be allowed to make changes in Green Contracts on its platform,
in accordance with the classification provided in the RCO notification dated 27.09.2025 and
subsequent amendments thereto, and the Commission’s directions in the subsequent
paragraphs of this order.
56. The Petitioner is directed to make suitable changes in its platform with respect to
the classification criteria for Wind/Hydro/DRE/Other RE sources as per the RCO
notification dated 27.09.2025. The eligibility conditions for sellers' participation in the
respective sub-segments of Green Contracts shall be in line with the RCO notification and
any subsequent amendments thereto. Further, the underlying market-clearing mechanism
and all other functionalities shall remain unchanged. The Petitioner will issue a certificate
detailing the trades undertaken by buyers in each category, which may be used by buyers to
meet RE consumption targets and RPO compliance.
57. Further, as per the existing practice, the seller shall be required to provide NOC/
Order in Petition No. 338/MP/2025 Page 21 of 23

standing clearance specifying the category as Wind/Hydro/DRE/Other RE, with all other
conditions and specifications remaining the same. We direct NLDC to make the
corresponding changes to the NOAR portal and suitable changes to T-GNA procedures for
issuing standing clearance endorsing RE category as per the RCO notification dated
27.09.2025 and submit a compliance report to the Commission within four weeks of this
order.
58. In case of portfolio sale by DISCOMS, the Petitioner is directed to include the name
and source (viz. Wind/Hydro/DRE/Other RE) of RE plants in order to ensure true visibility
of RE power.
59. The fungibility conditions among Wind, Hydro, DRE, and Other RE components
shall be strictly as per RCO Notification dated 27.09.2025 and its amendments thereof.
60. The Commission has taken a note of Petitioner’s request for modifying the
minimum volume quotation in Green-Intra Day and Green-DAC Contracts from 0.220 MW
to 0.1 MW in order to align them with Green Contracts in G-DAM and G-TAM segment at
IEX and Green energy open access rules of the MoP. The changes requested by the Petitioner
are permitted to maintain the uniform structure of Green Contracts.
61. We hereby direct the Petitioner to make appropriate changes in its software and to
align its Business Rules, Rules and Bye-laws in accordance with the approval granted in this
order and in line with the RE classification as per the RCO notification dated 27.09.2025
and amendment thereto. We further direct the Petitioner to submit a compliance report of the
same on affidavit within two weeks after the changes by NLDC in the NOAR Portal and T-
GNA procedures. The Petitioner is also directed to upload the revised Business Rules, Rules
and Bye-laws on its website. Further, if any discrepancy is noticed, or it appears that the
Order in Petition No. 338/MP/2025 Page 22 of 23

revised Business Rules, Rules and Byelaws do not conform to the Regulations and/or
directions contained in this order and the RE classification as per the RCO notification dated
27.09.2025, the Commission will issue necessary directions for such compliance.
62. Petition No. 338/MP/2025 is disposed of in terms of the above.

ORDER
The Petitioner, TP Gopalpur Transmission Limited (hereinafter referred to as
“TPGTL”), has filed the present Petition under Section 63 of the Electricity Act, 2003
(hereinafter referred to as “the Act”) for the adoption of transmission charges to
establish the Inter-State Transmission System for “the Transmission Licence to
“Eastern Region Expansion Scheme-XXXIX Power Transmission Limited”
(hereinafter referred to as “the Project”) on a Build, Own, Operate and Transfer Basis
(hereinafter referred to as “BOOT Basis”). The Petitioner has made the following
prayers:

Expansion Scheme – XXXIX” comprising of the elements/ assets as detailed
in the executed Transmission Service Agreement dated 14.11.2024;
(b) Approve the Transmission Service Agreement dated 14.11.2024 and other

(c) Condone any inadvertent errors/ omissions/ shortcomings and permit the
Petitioner to add/change/modify/alter these filings and make further

Background
3. The present Petition is a consequence of the earlier Petition No. 514/AT/2024
filed by the Petitioner seeking adoption of transmission charges for the Project. Vide
order dated 7.1.2026 in Petition No. 514/AT/2024, the Commission observed that
the Petition was premature, in relation to the order in the related licence matter
(Petition No. 514/AT/2024) which referred the scheme back to the National
Committee on Transmission (NCT) to address concerns regarding potential
redundant assets. The Commission further observed that no purpose would be
Order in Petition No. 124/AT/2026
Page 3

served to adopt the transmission charges prior to the NCT's reconsideration, and
granted the Petitioner liberty to file a fresh adoption Petition after the NCT renders its
decision. The relevant extract of the order is as under:
“17. It is noted that the Petitioner had filed a separate application along with
the instant Petition for the grant of a transmission licence for the subject
transmission system. The Commission, vide its order dated 18.12.2025 in
Petition No. 513/TL/2024, has observed that it is premature to consider the
grant of a transmission licence for the instant transmission scheme, as it
does not fulfil the requirement prescribed under Section 38(2)(c) of the Act,
and accordingly, referred the matter to NCT for reconsideration on the basis
of its likely utilization and impact on the consumers, in the absence of any
application for its use by the bulk consumers.
18. In view of the above, the question of adoption of transmission charges of
the subject transmission scheme does not arise at this stage, and no
purpose would be served to keep the instant adoption Petition pending any
further when the decision of the NCT is pending in the subject transmission
scheme. Accordingly, the Petition is disposed of, with liberty to the Petitioner
to approach the Commission for the adoption of transmission charges after
the NCT takes a decision on the subject transmission scheme. The filing fee
paid in the instant Petition shall be adjusted against the adoption Petition, if
any, to be filed by the Petitioner for the subject transmission scheme in
future.”
4. Subsequently, the transmission scheme was discussed in the 36th Meeting of
the National Committee on Transmission (NCT) held on 30.12.2025. After
deliberation, NCT strongly recommended the early start of work of the ERES-39
Scheme, upon grant of licence by CERC, so that the line is completed within the
scheduled time frame, as our period now is only about 24 months. Accordingly, the
Petitioner has approached the Commission for the adoption of transmission charges
in terms of the liberty granted by the Commission vide order dated 7.1.2026 in
Petition No. 514/AT/2024.
Hearing dated 18.3.2026

Analysis and Decision
6. We have considered the submissions of the Petitioner, BPC, and CTUIL and
perused the documents available on record. Section 63 of the Act provides as under:
“Section 63: Determination of tariff by bidding process: Notwithstanding
anything contained in section 62, the Appropriate Commission shall adopt the
tariff if such tariff has been determined through transparent process of bidding
in accordance with the guidelines issued by the Central Government.”
7. The Ministry of Power, Government of India, has notified the “Tariff based
Competitive Bidding Guidelines for Transmission Service” and “Guidelines for
Encouraging Competition in Development of Transmission Projects‟ (hereinafter
referred to as “the Guidelines‟) under Section 63 of the Act vide Resolution No.
15/1/2017-Trans dated 10.8.2021, as amended from time to time. The salient
features of the Guidelines are as under:
(a) The Guidelines are applicable for the procurement of transmission
services for transmission of electricity through tariff based competitive bidding
Order in Petition No. 124/AT/2026
Page 5

for selection of the Transmission Service Provider (TSP) for new transmission
system on a Build, Own, Operate and Transfer basis.
(b) For procurement of the transmission services required for any inter-
State transmission Project, the Central Government shall notify the CTUIL or
any Central Government Organisation/ Central Public Sector Undertaking or its
wholly owned subsidiary (Special Purpose Vehicle) to be the Bid Process
Coordinator (BPC), who would be responsible for the coordinating the bid
process.
(c) The BPC shall prepare the bid documents in accordance with the
Guidelines and obtain approval of the Appropriate Government, or alternatively,
the BPC can use the Standard Bid Documents notified by the Ministry of
Power. Any material deviation from the Standard Bidding Documents shall be
made only with the prior approval of the Appropriate Government. Intimation
about initiation of the bidding process shall be sent by the BPC to the
Appropriate Commission.
(d) For the procurement of the transmission services under the guidelines,
BPC shall adopt a single stage two envelope tender process featuring Request
for Proposal (RfP). The entire bidding process shall be conducted online
through electronic medium under e-reverse bidding framework.
(e) The RfP notice should be published in at least two national
newspapers, website of the BPC, and preferably in trade magazines also, so as
to accord it wide publicity. The bidding shall necessarily be by way of the

International Competitive Bidding (ICB). For the purpose of issue of the RfP,
minimum conditions to be met by the bidder shall be specified in the RfP.
(f) Standard documentation to be provided in the RfP shall include
definitions of requirements including brief description of the Project,
commissioning milestones to be achieved by the bidders, qualification
requirements to be met by the bidders including, minimum net worth, etc. with
necessary proof of the same, as outlined in the bid documents, Specified target
dates/months for commissioning and commercial operations, Standard
Transmission Service Agreement (TSA), agreement(s) under the Central
Electricity Regulatory Commission (Sharing of Inter State Transmission
Charges and Losses) Regulations as amended from time to time, period of
validity of offer of bidder, TSA proposed to be entered with the SPV including
amendments, bid evaluation methodology to be adopted by the BPC,
specification regarding bid bond as well as the Contract Performance
Guarantee to be furnished by the bidders, proposed indemnification agreement
between the TSP and the Nodal Agency, liquidated damages that shall apply in
the event of delay in start of providing the transmission services and technical,
operational and safety criteria to be met by the bidder/TSP and requirement of
obtaining transmission licence from the Appropriate Commission.
(g) The TSP, on the date of acquisition of the SPV from the BPC will enter
into a Transmission Service Agreement with the Nodal Agency.
(h) To ensure competitiveness, the minimum number of qualified bidders
shall be two. For inter-State transmission system, bids shall be opened in the

office of the CEA by a bid committee comprising of at least one member from

Further, in case project is inter-regional, there shall be at least one

(i) The BPC is required to complete e-reverse bidding after opening of the

(j) The TSP shall make an application for the grant of a transmission
licence to the Appropriate Commission within five (5) working days from the
date of execution of the Share Purchase Agreement for acquisition of the SPV.
(k) The BPC shall make the final result of evaluation of all bids public. The
final TSA, along with the certification by the bid evaluation committee, shall be

Order in Petition No. 124/AT/2026
Page 17

a) Lowest annual transmission charges of Rs. 2,897.29 million
discovered through electronic reverse auction is 24.43% lower than the
estimated annual transmission charges of Rs. 3,833.69 million which is
computed based on the estimated cost Rs. 2828.33 Crore (Rupees Two
Thousand Eight Hundred Twenty-Eight Crore Thirty-Three Lakh) as
communicated by cost committee and as per prevailing CERC norms.
b) As per provisions of RFP Document, successful bidder i.e., M/s The
Tata Power Company Limited has submitted original hard copies of
Annexure-3 and Annexure-14 and the same are found to be in order.
c) The entire bid process has been carried out in accordance with the
"Tariff based Competitive Bidding Guidelines for Transmission Service"
and "Guidelines for encouraging competition in development of the
Transmission Projects" issued by Ministry of Power, Govt, of India
under Section 63 of the Electricity Act, 2003 as amended from time to
time.
7. After detailed discussions on the evaluation report prepared by BPC
(Annexure 2), the Bid Evaluation Committee observed the following:
a) M/s The Tata Power Company Limited, with the lowest annual
transmission charges of Rs. 2,897.29 million, is the successful Bidder
after the conclusion of the electronic reverse auction.
b) The transmission charges discovered after electronic reverse auction
is lower than the transmission charges estimated by BPC para 6(a) and
is acceptable.
8. In view of para 7 above, BEC recommended to issue the Letter of Intent
(LOI) to M/s The Tata Power Company Limited.
9. The certificate by BEC to be forwarded to CERC for adoption of tariff in
terms of Section 63 of the Electricity Act, 2003 is attached at Annexure 3.”
25. Bid Evaluation Committee (BEC), vide its certificate dated 8.10.2024, certified
as under:
“It is certified that:
a. The entire bid process has been carried out in accordance with the "Tariff
based Competitive Bidding Guidelines for Transmission Service" and
"Guidelines for encouraging competition in development of the
Transmission Projects" issued by Ministry of Power, Govt, of India under
Section 63 of the Electricity Act, 2003 as amended from time to time.

b. M/s The Tata Power Company Limited, with the lowest annual
transmission charges of Rs. 2,897.29 Million, emerged as the successful
Bidder after the conclusion of electronic reverse auction.
c. The transmission charges of Rs. 2,897.29 Million discovered after
electronic reverse auction is acceptable.”
26. In the light of the discussions in the preceding paragraphs, it emerges that the
selection of the successful bidder and the discovery of the annual transmission
charges of the Project have been carried out by the BPC through a transparent
process of competitive bidding in accordance with the Guidelines issued by the
Ministry of Power, Government of India, under Section 63 of the Act. BEC has
certified that the process is in conformity with the Ministry of Power Guidelines. The
BEC, in its certificate dated 8.10.2024, has certified that The Tata Power Company

auction with the lowest transmission charges of Rs. 2,897.29 million. It is noted that
the quoted tariff of Rs. 2,897.29 million is lower (~ 24.43% lower) than the estimated

CENTRAL ELECTRICITY REGULATORY COMMISSION

and Conditions for Grant of Trading Licence and other Related Matters) Regulations,
2020, for grant of an inter-state trading licence.

ORDER
The Petitioner, EKI Energy Service Limited (hereinafter referred to as “the
Petitioner”), incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956 has made the present
Application under Sections 14 and 15 (1) of the Electricity Act, 2003 (hereinafter
referred to as “the Act”) read with Regulation 6 of the Central Electricity Regulatory
Order in Petition No. 92/TD/2026
Page 1 of 6

Commission (Procedure, Terms and Conditions for the Grant of Trading Licence and
other related matters) Regulations, 2020 (hereinafter referred to as “the Trading
Licence Regulations”), amended from time to time, for the grant of a Category ‘IV’
trading licence for inter-State trading in electricity across India.
2. In accordance with sub-Section (2) of Section 15 of the Act read with Clause
(4) of Regulation 6 of the Trading Licence Regulations, notices were published by
the Petitioner on 6.2.2026 in all India edition of the ‘Business Standard’
(Ahmedabad, Bengaluru, Bhopal, Bhubaneshwar, Chandigarh, Chennai, Delhi,
Hyderabad, Jaipur, Kochi, Kolkata, Lucknow, Mumbai and Pune) and ‘Indian
Express’ (Ahmedabad, Delhi, Jaipur, Kolkata, Lucknow and Nagpur). The Petitioner
has submitted that no objections have been received in response to the public
notices.
3. In accordance with Regulation 3(3) of the Trading Licence Regulations, a
person applying for a Category 'IV' trading licence should have a net worth of Rs.
Ten crore and should have maintained a minimum current ratio and liquidity ratio of
1:1 as on the date of the Audited Special Balance Sheet accompanying the
application. As per the Audited Balance Sheet submitted by the Petitioner as on
13.12.2025, the Petitioner possesses the required net worth, current ratio and
liquidity ratio for the grant of a Category 'IV' trading licence. The Commission, vide its
order dated 4.5.2026, concluded that the Petitioner is prima facie qualified for the
grant of a Category “IV” licence for inter-State trading in electricity.
4. On the above consideration, the Commission, vide its order dated 4.5.2026,
had proposed to grant a Category 'IV' inter-State trading licence to the Petitioner.
Order in Petition No. 92/TD/2026
Page 2 of 6

The relevant portions of the said order dated 4.5.2026 are extracted as under:
“14. In accordance with Clause (2) of Regulation 3 of the Trading Licence
Regulations, the Petitioner should have at least one full-time professional
possessing qualifications and experience in power system operation and the
commercial aspects of power transfer, including finance, commerce and
accounts. With regard to full-time professionals, the Petitioner vide its affidavit
dated 29.1.2026 has submitted that Shri Manish Dabkara, Chairman of the
Applicant, has over 16 years of experience in power and carbon
management, with expertise in power trading, energy management, climate
change, carbon markets, renewable energy, and ESG advisory. He holds a
B.E. in Electrical & Electronics Engineering (2005) from Oriental Institute of
Science & Technology, Bhopal, and an M.Tech. in Energy Management
(2008) from the School of Energy & Environmental Studies, DAVV; Shri
Ramakrishna Patil, President Operations, has over 20 years of experience in
the power sector, with expertise in power trading and energy risk
management. He holds a B.E. in Mechanical Engineering (2001) from PVPIL,
Budhgaon, Sangli, and an M.Tech in Energy Management (2004) from the
School of Energy and Environmental Studies, Indore. Shri Mohit Kumar
Agarwal, Chief Financial Officer of EKIESL, has over 17 years of experience
in finance, commerce, and accounts. He holds a B.Com. (Hons) from B.R.A.
Bihar University, Muzaffarpur, and pursued M.Com. from DAVV University,
Indore, and is a Chartered Accountant (ICAI, 2008). Accordingly, as per the
information submitted by the Petitioner, it fulfils the requirements of Clause (2)
of Regulation 3 of the Trading Licence Regulations.
15. On consideration of the above facts, after a preliminary examination,
we find that the Petitioner meets the requirements as specified in the Trading
Licence Regulations for the grant of a Category 'IV' trading licence. In view
thereof, the Commission proposes to grant a Category 'IV' trading licence to
the Petitioner. We direct that a notice under Clause (a) of Sub-section (5) of
Section 15 of the Act be issued inviting further suggestions or objections to
the proposal of the Commission.”
5. In line with the above mentioned order dated 4.5.2026, notice under Clause
(a) of sub-Section (5) of Section 15 of the Act was published in all editions of the
Times of India (English) and Dainik Jagran (Hindi) on 8.5.2026. No suggestions or
objections have been received in response to the Commission’s notice.
6. The case was called out for the hearing on 19.5.2026. During the course of
the hearing, the learned counsel for the Petitioner submitted that no objection had
Order in Petition No. 92/TD/2026
Page 3 of 6

been received in response to the public notice published by the Commission under
sub-Section (5) of Section 15 of the Act. He further submitted that the Petitioner’s
company would comply with the requirements specified in the Trading Licence
Regulations during the subsistence of the trading licence, i.e., till 25 years, if granted.
7. Clause (9) of Regulation 6 of the Trading Licence Regulations provides as
under:
“(9) On consideration of further objections or suggestions received and the
reply of the applicant thereto, if any, the Commission may grant the licence or
reject the application, for reasons to be recorded in writing if the application
does not confirm to the provisions of the Act, the rules or regulations or
provisions of any other law for the time being in force:
Provided that no application shall be rejected, unless the applicant has been
given an opportunity of being heard.”
8. On consideration of the materials on record, we are satisfied that the
Petitioner company meets the requirements of the Act and the Trading Licence
Regulations for the grant of an inter-State trading licence for a Category 'IV'.
9. The grant of the trading licence to the Petitioner (hereinafter referred to as
“the licensee”) is subject to the fulfilment of the following conditions throughout the
period of subsistence of the licence:
(a) The licensee shall comply with the provisions of the Act, the Rules, and
the Regulations, particularly Trading Licence Regulations, orders, and
directions issued by the Commission, from time to time, and any other law in
force;
(b) The licensee shall comply with orders and directions issued by the
Commission from time to time;
Order in Petition No. 92/TD/2026
Page 4 of 6

(c) The licensee shall not engage in the business of transmission of
electricity during the period of subsistence of the trading licence, i.e., till 25
years;
(d) The licensee shall charge trading margin strictly in accordance with the
Trading Licence Regulations, as amended from time to time;
(e) The licensee shall maintain the net worth as mentioned in the order
dated 31.8.2025, and current & liquidity ratio, as prescribed in the Trading
Licence Regulations, at all times.
(f) The licensee shall continue to be governed by the qualifications and
disqualifications specified in Chapter 2 of the Trading Licence Regulations
during the subsistence of the licence;
(g) The licensee shall continue to abide by the terms and conditions of the
licence specified in Chapter V of the Trading Licence Regulations, as
amended from time to time;
(h) The licensee shall regularly pay the annual licence fee in accordance
with the provisions of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Payment
of Fees) Regulations, 2012, as amended from time to time or any subsequent
enactment thereof;
(i) Non-compliance with the provisions of the Act, Rules, Regulations, and
the provisions of the Trading Licence Regulations shall make the licence of
the Petitioner liable for revocation;
Order in Petition No. 92/TD/2026
Page 5 of 6

(j) If the licensee fails to undertake trading in electricity within a year from
the date of the licence, the licence shall be liable for revocation in accordance
with the provisions of the Act and the Trading Licence Regulations; and
(k) The licensee shall submit all such reports or information as may be
required under Trading Licence Regulations or any other regulations of the
Commission or as per the directions of the Commission as may be issued
from time to time.
10. An extract of a copy of this order be sent to the Central Government (the
Ministry of Power) and the Central Electricity Authority in terms of sub-Section (7) of
Section 15 of the Act for their information and record.
11. Petition No. 92/TD/2026 is allowed in terms of the above.
Sd/- sd/- sd/- sd/-
(Ravinder Singh Dhillon) (Ramesh Babu V.) (Harish Dudani) (Jishnu Barua)

Page 6 of 6
