items.pdf_text:
CENTRAL ELECTRICITY REGULATORY COMMISSION
NEW DELHI
Petition No. 346/MP/2020
Coram:
Shri Jishnu Barua, Chairperson
Shri Ramesh Babu V., Member
Shri Harish Dudani, Member
Shri Ravinder Singh Dhillon, Member
Date of Order: 13.05.2026
In the matter of:
Petition under Section 79(1)(f) of the Electricity Act, 2003, for adjudication of disputes
between DVC and PSPCL and for directions.
And
In the matter of:
Damodar Valley Corporation,
DVC Towers, VIP Road,
Kolkata-700054 …Petitioner
Vs
Punjab State Power Corporation Limited,
PSEB, Head Office,
The Mall, Patiala,
Punjab-147001 …Respondent
Parties Present:
Shri Venkatesh, Advocate, DVC
Shri Shivam Kumar, Advocate, DVC
Shri Mohit Gupta, Advocate, DVC
Ms. Suparna Srivastava, Advocate, PSPCL
Ms. Sunidhi Singh, Advocate, PSPCL
INTERIM ORDER
Damodar Valley Corporation (in short ‘DVC’) has filed the instant petition under
Section 79(1)(f) of the Electricity Act, 2003 (in short ‘Act’) for adjudication of disputes
between DVC and Punjab State Power Corporation Limited (in short, ‘PSPCL’),
seeking the following relief(s):
(a) “Declare that PSPCL is liable to pay to DVC towards the fixed charges for BTPS-
A for the period 23.2.2017 to 25.3.2018, a sum aggregating to Rs 340.04 crores
Order in Petition No.346/MP/2020 Page 1 of 22

towards principal and delayed payment surcharge as on 31.1.2020 and further
interest at the rate specified in the Hon’ble Commission’s Regulations till full
payment and discharge of all the outstanding;
(b) Direct PSPCL to pay the amount due to DVC in terms of the prayer (a) above
within 30 days from the date of the order together with interest as per the delayed
payment surcharge for the period till due payment and discharge of the amount
outstanding by PSPCL;
(c) Pass an interim order directing PSPCL to pay on an ad-hoc basis 85% of the
amount claimed by DVC subject to further adjustments on the passing of the final
order;
(d) Allow DVC to file the duly affirmed affidavit to the Petition and the annexures to
the Petition as and when the restrictions imposed due to Covid-19 are lifted;
(e) pass such further order or orders as this Hon’ble Commission may deem just and
proper in the circumstances of the case.”
Background
2. DVC is constituted under the Damodar Valley Corporation Act, 1948 and
controlled by the Central Government and operates as a generating company. DVC
entered a Power Purchase Agreement (in short ‘PPA’) on 7.11.2006 with PSPCL to
supply 200 MW of electricity from one of its generating stations, Bokaro Thermal
Power Station (in short 'BTPS-A'), in accordance with the terms and conditions
contained in the PPA.
3. Clauses 4.4 and 4.5 of the PPA required PSPCL to seek long-term open access
from Power Grid Corporation of India Ltd (PGCIL) and coordinate the necessary
transmission system for power evacuation from DVC's delivery points. As per Article
5.10 of the PPA and applicable tariff regulations, PSPCL was obligated to pay tariffs,
including fixed and energy charges, for the scheduled quantum of power from BTPS-
A. PSPCL remained liable for fixed charges for power that DVC was prepared to
generate and deliver, even if PSPCL did not schedule it for delivery.
Submissions of DVC
4. In the above background, DVC has submitted the following:
Order in Petition No.346/MP/2020 Page 2 of 22

a. As per the PPA and applicable regulations, DVC was capable of generating
and supplying electricity from the Commercial Operation Date (COD) of BTPS-
A. Although DVC informed PSPCL about the arrangements required for power
delivery, PSPCL did not complete the necessary formalities and failed to finalise
the Long-Term Access (LTA) Agreement within the timeline prescribed by
PGCIL. As a result, the LTA initially granted was revoked. On 16.8.2016, DVC
informed PSPCL that the COD of BTPS-A was expected by September 2016.
After this declaration, PSPCL was required to start scheduling power up to 200
MW under the PPA. DVC requested PSPCL to obtain approval from PGCIL for
LTA to enable the delivery of power. On 23.2.2017, DVC declared the COD of
BTPS-A and asked PSPCL to confirm the status of the LTA. DVC also informed
PSPCL that non-drawal of power would result in liability to pay fixed charges.
Despite repeated reminders, PSPCL delayed signing the LTA Agreement. Due
to this delay, PGCIL revoked the granted LTA. This inaction by PSPCL directly
affected DVC’s ability to supply power under the PPA.
b. DVC informed PSPCL that DVC had filed a tariff petition for BTPS-A before the
Commission. Pending the tariff order, DVC proposed fixed charges of
₹1.6853/kWh and energy charges of ₹1.95/kWh. PGCIL notified PSPCL
regarding 200 MW LTA, subject to signing the LTA Agreement within 30 days.
PGCIL also requested that PSPCL sign the LTA Agreement and Transmission
Service Agreement (TSA) to share transmission charges in accordance with
the applicable Tariff Regulations. DVC repeatedly urged PSPCL to complete
the LTA formalities so that power from BTPS-A could be scheduled without
delay. DVC also requested PGCIL to allow the immediate commencement of
the 200 MW supply. PSPCL, instead, asked DVC to relinquish its 200 MW
share from Durgapur TPS, another DVC generating station, stating that the
power was no longer required. PSPCL further proposed terminating the PPA
for that station after July 2017, so that the capacity could be allocated to another
utility.
c. Despite several requests from DVC, PSPCL continued to delay signing the LTA
Agreement. PGCIL granted an additional 15 days for execution of the
agreement. PSPCL then sought a further extension of two months, stating that
the matter was under consideration by its management. In a meeting held on
Order in Petition No.346/MP/2020 Page 3 of 22

25.9.2017, PSPCL suggested three options, including scheduling power from
multiple stations and reducing the fixed costs of Durgapur Steel TPS.
d. The PPA covered round-the-clock power supply from DVC’s three generating
stations- BTPS-A, Durgapur Steel TPS, and Raghunathpur TPS. PSPCL’s
attempt to unilaterally terminate the PPA for 200 MW from Durgapur Steel TPS
was disputed by DVC. The PPA was valid for 25 years and could be reviewed
only after five years. DVC requested PSPCL to sign the LTA for BTPS-A
independently without linking it to the dispute relating to Durgapur TPS. DVC
also stated that, as discussed in the meeting held on 18.9.2017, it was willing
to reduce the fixed charges of Durgapur Steel TPS. The matter was escalated
to the Secretary, Ministry of Power, seeking intervention due to the financial
losses suffered by DVC because of PSPCL’s delay in signing the LTA
Agreement for BTPS-A. PSPCL was warned that action would be taken under
the PPA if the agreement was not signed by 17.11.2017.
e. PSPCL proposed that it would sign the LTA Agreement for BTPS-A only after
a reduction of 20 paise in the fixed charges of Durgapur Steel TPS. DVC
responded that fixed charges for BTPS-A were payable from 23.2.2017, being
the COD, and that the reduction of fixed charges for Durgapur Steel TPS was
still under consideration. On 4.12.2017, PSPCL was informed that DVC had
agreed to reduce the fixed charges of Durgapur Steel TPS by 20 paise. DVC
reiterated that PSPCL must pay fixed charges for BTPS-A as per the PPA and
the Commission’s Tariff Regulations, and that PSPCL had never raised
objections earlier. DVC rejected PSPCL’s request to pay fixed charges only
from the scheduling date and pointed out that PSPCL’s failure to sign the LTA
Agreement amounted to default. Due to continued delays, PGCIL revoked the
LTA earlier granted. PSPCL thereafter requested revival of the 200 MW LTA
and confirmed its acceptance of the reduction in fixed charges of Durgapur
Steel TPS, along with a request for a supplementary agreement. PGCIL
informed PSPCL that the revoked LTA could not be restored and directed to file
a fresh online application. PSPCL submitted a new application, and PGCIL
indicated that LTA could again be granted for 200 MW, subject to signing the
agreement within 30 days.
f. Power supply from BTPS-A to PSPCL commenced on 26.3.2018 after PSPCL
confirmed scheduling and requested execution of the supplementary
Order in Petition No.346/MP/2020 Page 4 of 22

agreement for the reduction of fixed charges of Durgapur Steel TPS. DVC again
reiterated its entitlement to fixed charges from the COD of BTPS-A and invited
PSPCL to resolve the issue. DVC also shared sample calculations showing the
reduced fixed charges for Durgapur Steel TPS, effective from the scheduling
date of BTPS-A. It was emphasised that PSPCL must pay fixed charges for the
period during which power from BTPS-A was not scheduled. PSPCL thereafter
shared its own sample calculations relating to Durgapur Steel TPS fixed
charges. An amount of ₹86.74 crore was jointly reconciled at PSPCL’s Patiala
office on 1st and 2nd August 2019, and confirmed in writing by DVC. After this
reconciliation, PSPCL was requested to place the matter before its competent
authority and communicate its decision regarding the balance fixed charges of
BTPS-A amounting to ₹188.68 crore, after adjusting the gain-sharing amount
of ₹86.74 crore. As a goodwill gesture, DVC adjusted ₹86.74 crore from the
original claim of ₹275.42 crore, reducing the outstanding amount to ₹188.68
crore.
g. PSPCL refused to pay the balance amount of ₹188.68 crore and maintained
that fixed charges were payable only from 26.3.2018. By its letter dated
7.2.2020, PSPCL denied liability for the period from 23.2.2017 to 25.3.2018 due
to non-scheduling of power. In response, DVC, by letter dated 3.3.2020, stated
that PSPCL was now liable to pay the entire principal amount of ₹275.42 crore
along with late payment surcharge, totalling ₹340.04 crore as on 31.1.2020.
DVC objected to PSPCL’s unilateral adjustment of the entire gain amount and
asserted that PSPCL was bound by the agreed 50% gain-sharing arrangement.
Discussions were held on gain sharing for power supplied by BTPS-A and
adjustment against PSPCL’s liability for the period from 23.2.2017 to 25.3.2018.
PSPCL requested reconciliation of its 50% share amounting to ₹86.74 crore,
which was jointly verified. However, PSPCL continued, through
communications dated 15.10.2019 and 7.2.2020, to refuse to pay the remaining
amount of ₹188.68 crore and insisted on paying fixed charges only from
26.3.2018. Consequently, DVC asserted that PSPCL is liable for the full amount
of ₹275.42 crore including the applicable late payment surcharge.
5. PSPCL filed, vide its reply on 23.10.2020 and submitted its arguments on
merits, to which a rejoinder was filed by the Petitioner on 19.3.2021.
Order in Petition No.346/MP/2020 Page 5 of 22

Hearings in the matter
6. The matter was admitted on 25.8.2020, and the parties were directed to
complete their pleadings. Thereafter, on 14.3.2023, the Commission sought additional
information and directed completion of pleadings. PSPCL filed IA No.24/IA/2024 on
23.2.2024 seeking interim protection against coercive recovery by DVC, and it was
heard along with the Petition on 18.3.2024. The Commission reserved the order in
the matter and directed that no precipitative action shall be taken by any party during
the pendency of the Petition. However, the order could not be issued before two
Members of the Coram demitted office. Therefore, the matter was again heard on
5.9.2024, 14.11.2024, 21.1.2025, 25.3.2025 and 13.5.2025. At that stage, since the
issue of arbitrability of disputes was pending consideration in batch matters before the
Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL), the Petition was adjourned to be listed after
the decision in those batch matters. After APTEL delivered its judgment dated
28.8.2024 in Appeal No.309 of 2019 (MPPMCL v. DVC), which was affirmed by the
Hon’ble Supreme Court on 23.9.2024, and the subsequent final judgment of the
APTEL on 25.2.2026 in Appeal Nos.348, 371 & 400 of 2025 (Mundra UMPP batch)
having settled the law on arbitrability, the Commission directed the parties to file
written submissions on the issue of arbitrability. The matter was also listed on
19.8.2025, and the oral arguments on the issue of arbitrability on behalf of the
Petitioner were concluded. PSPCL contended that the Commission ought to first
determine whether liability pertained to ‘scheduled power’ or ‘contracted power’ before
deciding arbitrability. Owing to paucity of time, the hearing remained inconclusive and
the matter was adjourned. The matter was finally heard on 30.9.2025, when detailed
oral arguments were advanced by the learned counsel for both parties on the question
of arbitrability. The learned counsel for the Petitioner submitted that the dispute was
contractual in nature and qualified as a non-tariff dispute referable to arbitration as per
Order in Petition No.346/MP/2020 Page 6 of 22

the APTEL judgment dated 28.8.2024. The learned counsel for PSPCL opposed the
same, contending that the issue related to fixed charges determined under Tariff
Regulations and constituted a tariff dispute falling within the Commission’s jurisdiction.
The Commission, after hearing the Parties, reserved its order on the question of
arbitrability of the dispute on 30.9.2025.
Interlocutory Application
7. During the pendency of the Petition, PSPCL has filed Interlocutory Application
No. 24/IA/2024 on 23.2.2024 (IA), seeking directions restraining DVC from taking any
coercive action, for removal and stay of the Supplementary Invoice dated 5.1.2024
from the PRAAPTI Portal, and for protection against enforcement of any invoices
relating to the disputed period prior to 26.3.2018. The Commission, after hearing the
learned counsel for the parties on 18.3.2024, directed the Petitioner not to take any
precipitative action against PSPCL with regard to the invoices raised in the PRAAPTI
portal till final disposal of the present Petition.
Written submissions by DVC
8. The Petitioner has filed Written Submissions dated 12.7.2025 on the question
of arbitrability of the disputes and has mainly submitted the following:
a. The dispute between the parties arises out of the PPA and is rooted in the
rights and obligations flowing from the contractual framework agreed between
the parties, including obligations relating to the scheduling of power, the
application for LTA, and payment of fixed charges for declared capacity. The
nature of the dispute is one of contractual breach, inasmuch as the claim arises
from non-performance of obligations under the PPA and enforcement of payment
obligations stipulated therein, and therefore the dispute is required to be
characterised as a “non-tariff dispute”.
b. The classification of disputes into “tariff” and “non-tariff” stands conclusively
settled by the judgment of MPPMCL v. DVC dated 28.8.2024, wherein disputes
Order in Petition No.346/MP/2020 Page 7 of 22

arising out of contractual breach, which do not have any bearing on tariff either
directly or indirectly, have been categorised as non-tariff disputes. The aforesaid
judgment stands affirmed by the DVC Supreme Court Order dated 23.9.2024,
thereby attaining finality and binding precedential value, particularly in light of the
distinction drawn between Sections 79(1)(f) and 86(1)(f) of the Act.
c. Disputes relating to termination or breach of contract, including disputes
concerning performance of obligations under a PPA and recovery of dues arising
therefrom, do not fall within the scope of tariff regulation and are therefore
required to be treated as non-tariff disputes, mandatorily referable to arbitration
where an arbitration agreement exists.
d. Tariff disputes are confined to matters having a bearing on tariff, such as a
change in law, delay in project completion, force majeure events, or other
regulatory issues impacting tariff determination, whereas disputes arising purely
from contractual non-performance, including non-scheduling and payment
defaults, fall outside the regulatory domain. The present dispute does not involve
any determination, revision, or regulation of tariffs, either directly or indirectly,
and is limited to the enforcement of contractual payment obligations, namely the
recovery of fixed charges and interest arising from breach of the PPA. The mere
fact that the claim relates to fixed charges does not render the dispute a tariff
dispute, as the claim arises out of breach of contractual obligations under the
PPA and not out of any exercise of tariff determination by this Commission.
e. The PPA contains an arbitration clause, which evidences the clear intention
of the parties to resolve disputes arising out of contractual obligations through
arbitration, and such contractual intent is required to be given full effect.
f. Section 79(1)(f) of the Act contemplates both adjudication of disputes and
reference of disputes to arbitration, and the legislative scheme, read with Section
158 of the Act, envisages that disputes not falling within the regulatory domain
are to be referred to arbitration. The expression “and to refer any dispute for
arbitration” appearing in Section 79(1)(f) cannot be rendered redundant, and
must be given a meaningful interpretation so as to give effect to the statutory
mandate of referring non-tariff disputes to arbitration.
g. The principles laid down in the DVC APTEL Judgment clearly delineate the
scope of jurisdiction of this Commission and identify the category of disputes
Order in Petition No.346/MP/2020 Page 8 of 22

which must necessarily be referred to arbitration, including disputes arising out
of contractual breach.
h. A clear commonality exists between the dispute involved in the DVC APTEL
case and the present case, inasmuch as both cases involve PPAs containing
arbitration clauses, disputes arising out of performance and obligations under
such PPAs, and reliefs relating to payment of fixed charges or damages for non-
performance.
i. The reliefs sought in the present Petition, being recovery of fixed charges and
interest on account of non-performance of contractual obligations, are in the
nature of damages arising out of breach of contract and do not involve any issue
of tariff determination or regulation.
j. The DVC APTEL Judgment, having been affirmed by the Hon’ble Supreme
Court, is binding on this Commission under Article 141 of the Constitution of
India, and is required to be followed in the interest of judicial discipline. By
application of the doctrine of merger, the APTEL judgment stands merged with
the order of the Hon’ble Supreme Court, and the law laid down therein constitutes
the prevailing and enforceable law governing the field. The law declared by the
Hon’ble Supreme Court applies retrospectively to all pending proceedings, and
therefore governs the present dispute irrespective of the stage of the
proceedings.
k. Jurisdiction is a matter of law and goes to the root of the matter; in the absence
of jurisdiction, any adjudication by this Commission would be without authority
and would render the proceedings a nullity. Jurisdiction cannot be conferred by
the parties' consent, and where the dispute falls outside the Commission's
statutory jurisdiction, it cannot be adjudicated merely because the Petition has
been filed before this forum.
l. Objections relating to lack of jurisdiction and arbitrability can be raised at any
stage of the proceedings, including collateral proceedings, and are required to
be examined at the threshold.
m. The present dispute, being one arising out of breach of PPA and claim for
damages and interest thereon, is purely contractual in nature, does not have any
impact on tariff, and squarely falls within the category of non-tariff disputes. Once
the dispute is held to be non-tariff in nature, the Commission inherently lacks
Order in Petition No.346/MP/2020 Page 9 of 22

jurisdiction to adjudicate it and is bound, in terms of Section 79(1)(f) read with
Section 158 of the Electricity Act, to refer the dispute to arbitration.
Reply to Written Submissions of the Petitioner by PSPCL
9. PSPCL, in its response dated 14.8.2025 filed to the Written Submissions filed
by the Petitioner dated 12.7.2025 on the question of arbitrability of the disputes, has
mainly submitted the following:
a. The Petitioner had itself, during the hearings held on 21.1.2025 and
25.3.2025, requested that the present matter be taken up after the decision in
batch matters concerning arbitrability of tariff and non-tariff disputes, and
subsequently sought time on 13.5.2025 to file Written Submissions on
arbitrability, which indicates that the issue is not settled in the manner sought to
be projected by the Petitioner.
b. The reliance placed by the Petitioner on the judgment of MPPMCL v. DVC and
the affirmation thereof by the DVC Supreme Court Order is misplaced and
requires proper appreciation in the context of the facts and issues involved in the
present case. The said judgment deals with the issue of arbitrability in the context
of disputes relating to termination of PPA and the applicability of Section 8 of the
Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, in proceedings under Section 79(1)(f) of
the Act, and lays down the distinction between tariff and non-tariff disputes.
c. A dispute which directly or indirectly impacts tariff is required to be treated as
a “tariff dispute” falling squarely within the jurisdiction of the Commission under
Section 79(1)(f) of the Act, whereas only those disputes which arise purely out of
breach or termination of contract without any bearing on tariff can be categorised
as non-tariff disputes referable to arbitration. The ratio of the DVC APTEL
Judgment is confined to disputes concerning termination of PPA, where the core
issue relates to the legality and validity of termination, which has no bearing on
tariff, and therefore such disputes were held to be non-tariff and arbitrable. The
present dispute, however, is fundamentally distinct, inasmuch as it pertains to
liability for payment of fixed charges, which are not merely contractual in nature
but are an integral component of the tariff determined under the applicable
regulatory framework.
Order in Petition No.346/MP/2020 Page 10 of 22

d. Under the 2014 Tariff Regulations, the tariff for a generating station comprises
capacity charges and energy charges, and fixed charges correspond to capacity
charges forming part of the tariff structure. In view of the above statutory scheme,
any dispute relating to fixed charges inherently relates to tariff and therefore falls
within the exclusive regulatory and adjudicatory jurisdiction of the Commission
under Section 79(1)(f) of the Act.
e. The contention of the Petitioner that disputes relating to fixed charges can be
treated as non-tariff disputes is erroneous, as fixed charges are inseparable from
tariff and cannot be viewed in isolation as purely contractual claims. The
comparison sought to be drawn by the Petitioner between the present case and
the DVC APTEL case is incorrect and misleading, inasmuch as the primary issue
in the DVC APTEL case pertained to the termination of the PPA, whereas the
present case concerns the payment of fixed charges forming part of the tariff.
f. A bare perusal of the prayer clauses in the DVC APTEL case demonstrates
that the principal relief sought therein was a declaration regarding invalid
termination of the PPA, with consequential reliefs relating to payment, whereas
in the present case, the sole dispute is with respect to payment of fixed charges.
The Petitioner has selectively relied on certain portions of the prayer clause in
the DVC APTEL case while omitting the crucial aspect relating to termination of
PPA, thereby attempting to create a false equivalence between two factually
distinct cases.
g. The ratio of a judgment can be treated as binding precedent only when the
material facts and issues involved are substantially similar, and in the absence
of such similarity, reliance on such precedent is misplaced and legally untenable.
h. The doctrine of stare decisis requires application of precedent only in cases
which are materially alike, and does not permit mechanical or blind application of
a judgment without examining the factual matrix and legal context of the case at
hand. In the present case, the dispute relating to payment of fixed charges, being
part of the tariff, is clearly distinguishable from disputes relating to termination of
PPA, and therefore, the ratio laid down in the DVC APTEL Judgment, as affirmed
by the Hon’ble Supreme Court, is not applicable to the present case.
i. Since the dispute directly relates to tariff, it squarely falls within the jurisdiction
of the Commission and cannot be referred to arbitration under the guise of being
a non-tariff dispute.
Order in Petition No.346/MP/2020 Page 11 of 22

Analysis and Decision
10. We have examined the rival contentions. Petitioner’s contention is that the
dispute is contractual in nature and it constitutes a non-tariff dispute; on the contrary,
PSPCL’s contention is that the present dispute is a tariff dispute and has to be
adjudicated by the Commission. Thus, the limited issue before us at this stage is
whether the dispute raised by the Petitioner in the present Petition constitutes a tariff-
related dispute or a non-tariff dispute and whether the same falls under the
adjudicatory jurisdiction of the Commission under Section 79(1)(f) of the Act?
11. PSPCL has contended that it is necessary to first determine whether PSPCL’s
liability towards fixed charges pertained to ‘scheduled power’ or ‘contracted power’
before deciding on its arbitrability. We are of the view that the issue raised by PSPCL
is on ‘merits’ and it will be considered after deciding the issue of ‘arbitrability’ and
hearing both parties.
12. The core dispute in the present Petition is whether PSPCL is liable to pay the
fixed/ capacity charges component of the tariff for the period from 23.2.2017 to
25.3.2018, even though power was not scheduled by PSPCL during this period.
13. We now proceed to examine whether PSPCL’s liability to pay the fixed charges
for the period from 23.2.2017 to 25.3.2018 is a tariff-related dispute or a non-tariff
dispute. It is necessary to examine the statutory contours of the jurisdiction vested in
the Commission under Section 79 of the Act. Clauses (a) to (d) of Section 79(1) confer
upon the Commission the power to regulate the tariff of generating companies and to
regulate and determine the tariff for inter-State transmission of electricity. Clause (f) of
Section 79(1) empowers the Commission to adjudicate disputes involving generating
companies or transmission licensees only in regard to matters connected with clauses
Order in Petition No.346/MP/2020 Page 12 of 22

(a) to (d) or, in the alternative, to refer such disputes to arbitration. Thus, the
Commission's jurisdiction to adjudicate disputes is not plenary but statutorily
circumscribed, and is invoked only when the dispute has a demonstrable nexus with
tariff regulation.
14. Section 79(1) of the Act provides as follows:
“Section 79. Functions of Central Commission: ---
(1) The Central Commission shall discharge the following functions, namely: -
(a) to regulate the tariff of generating companies owned or controlled by the
Central Government;
(b) to regulate the tariff of generating companies other than those owned or
controlled by the Central Government specified in clause (a), if such generating
companies enter into or otherwise have a composite scheme for generation and
sale of electricity in more than one State;
(c) to regulate the inter-State transmission of electricity;
(d)to determine tariff for inter-State transmission of electricity;
(e) to issue licenses to persons to function as transmission licensee and
electricity trader with respect to their inter-State operations;
(f) to adjudicate upon disputes involving generating companies or transmission
licensee in regard to matters connected with clauses (a) to (d) above and to refer
any dispute for arbitration;
(g) to levy fees for the purposes of this Act;
(h) to specify Grid Code having regard to Grid Standards;
(i) to specify and enforce the standards with respect to quality, continuity and
reliability of service by licensees;
(j) to fix the trading margin in the inter-State trading of electricity, if considered,
necessary;
(k) to discharge such other functions as may be assigned under this Act.”
15. The dispute pertains to the period from 23.2.2017 to 25.3.2018, i.e. the 2014-
19 tariff period, governed by the 2014 Tariff Regulations. As per Regulation 20(1) of
the 2014 Tariff Regulations, the tariff for a thermal generating station is based on a
two-part structure comprising capacity charges and energy charges. The capacity
charges shall be derived on the basis of the annual fixed charges consisting of the five
components as provided in Regulation 21 of the 2014 Tariff Regulations. Regulation
20(1) and Regulation 21 of the 2014 tariff Regulations, which provide as follows:
“20. Components of Tariff:
(1) The tariff for supply of electricity from a thermal generating station shall comprise
two parts, namely, capacity charge (for recovery of annual fixed cost consisting of the
Order in Petition No.346/MP/2020 Page 13 of 22

components as specified in Regulation 21 of these regulations) and energy charge
(for recovery of primary and secondary fuel cost and limestone cost where
applicable).
……”
“21. Capacity Charges: The Capacity charges shall be derived on the basis of
annual fixed cost. The annual fixed cost (AFC) of a generating station or a
transmission system including communication system shall consist of the following
components:
(a) Return on equity;
(b) Interest on loan capital;
(c) Depreciation;
(d) Interest on working capital; and
(e) Operation and maintenance expenses:
……”
16. Further, Regulation 42 of the 2014 Tariff Regulations provides for the raising of
monthly bills and recovery of capacity charges and energy charges determined as per
the Regulations from the beneficiaries as a percentage share of the installed capacity
of the generating station. Regulation 42 of the 2014 Tariff Regulations provides as
follows:
“42. Billing and Payment of charges:
(1) Bills shall be raised for capacity charge, energy charge and the transmission charge
on monthly basis by the generating company and the transmission licensee in
accordance with these regulations, and payments shall be made by the beneficiaries
or the long-term transmission customers/ DICs directly to the generating company or
the transmission licensee, as the case may be.
(2) Payment of the capacity charge for a thermal generating station shall be shared by
the beneficiaries of the generating station as per their percentage shares for the month
(inclusive of any allocation out of the unallocated capacity) in the installed capacity of
the generating station. Payment of capacity charge and energy charge for a hydro
generating station shall be shared by the beneficiaries of the generating station in
proportion to their shares (inclusive of any allocation out of the unallocated capacity)
in the saleable capacity (to be determined after deducting the capacity corresponding
to free energy to home State as per Note 3 herein.
…..”
17. The PPA also recognises that the tariff for the sale of power by DVC to PSPCL
will be determined by the Commission from time to time in accordance with the terms
and conditions of tariff specified in the tariff regulations, which provides for a two-part
Order in Petition No.346/MP/2020 Page 14 of 22

tariff structure as the basis for tariff determination of thermal generating stations.
Clause 4.1 of the PPA provides as follows:
“4.1. Subject to the provisions of this agreement, DVC shall supply the energy at the
delivery point on scheduled basis and PSEB shall pay to DVC for the scheduled
energy as per REA prepared by ERPC. Tariff for such sale of power by DVC to PSEB
at DVC Periphery will be determined by CERC from time to time in accordance with
CERC regulation on terms and conditions of tariff including capital cost.
DVC shall file its Tariff Petition before CERC at least 2 months in advance to expected
date of commissioning of the Unit. In case the tariff as provided above is not
determined/approved by CERC/other competent authority prior to commencement of
commercial operation of the unit, the same would be worked out by DVC based on
the above provision and the guidelines for tariff as applicable from time to time and
within capital cost as approved by CEA/ other competent authority for the project.
This would be mutually discussed between the bulk power customers and DVC and
if not agreed within one month from date of the unit commissioning, the same shall
be billed by DVC on provisional basis subject to retrospective adjustment as and
when the tariff is determined/approved by CERC/ other competent authority.”
18. Clause 6 of the PPA provides for a dispute resolution mechanism, and it is as
follows:
"6. DISPUTE RESOLUTION MECHANISM:
6.1 All differences or disputes between the parties arising out of or in connection with
these presents save any question or matter of dispute which falls within the scope
and purview of the statutory arbitration under the provisions of the Electricity Act,
2003 as amended shall be settled through arbitration as provided herein.
6.2 In the event of such differences between the parties and failing settlement of the
same through mutual discussions amongst parties concerned, if the disputes are not
settled within three months, any party may by a written notice of 30 (thirty) days to
the other party or parties request for appointment of a Sole Arbitrator, to be decided
mutually by parties concerned and in case of disagreement, shall be guided by the
provisions of the Arbitration Act, 1996 and any statutory modification thereto. The
Sole Arbitrator shall give a speaking and reasoned award. The decision of the Sole
Arbitrator shall be final and binding on the parties. The venue of the arbitration and
meetings shall be at Kolkata. The Sole Arbitrator shall decide his fees with the
consent of the parties and it will be shared equally.
6.3 In the event that PSEB or its successor entity disputes any bill or part thereof as
raised by DVC, it shall pay 95% of the disputed amount forthwith and refer the dispute
for Arbitration in accordance with Law. The amount exceeding/beneath the said 95%
that is finally awarded shall be paid/ adjusted with interest @ 15% per annum, to be
calculated from the date on which the amount in dispute was payable/refundable.
6.4 The court of Kolkata shall be the jurisdiction in all matters relating to this
Agreement between DVC and PSEB.”
Order in Petition No.346/MP/2020 Page 15 of 22

19. Under clauses (a) to (d) of sub-section 1 of Section 79 of the Act, the
Commission is required to regulate the tariff of the generating stations owned or
controlled by the Central Government and the tariff of the generating stations which
have composite scheme for generation and sale of electricity in more than one State,
to regulate the inter-state transmission of electricity and determine the tariff of inter-
State transmission system. Under Section 79(1)(f) of the Act, the Commission has the
power to adjudicate the disputes involving a generating company or transmission
licensee in respect of the matters connected with clauses (a) to (d) of sub-Section 1
of Section 79 of the Act or refer to arbitration. In other words, the jurisdiction of the
Commission for adjudication of the dispute or to refer to arbitration is invoked if the
dispute involves either a generating company or a transmission licensee, and the
dispute pertains to the regulation of tariffs.
20. The Petitioner has contended that the dispute is purely contractual in nature
and arises out of breach of obligations under the PPA, and therefore constitutes a non-
tariff dispute liable to be referred to arbitration. Reliance has been placed on the
judgment of MPPMCL v. DVC as affirmed by the DVC Supreme Court Order. The
Respondent, PSPCL, on the other hand, has consistently contended that the present
dispute pertains to payment of fixed charges arising under the tariff framework
determined by the Commission and constitutes a tariff-related dispute falling within the
exclusive adjudicatory jurisdiction of the Commission under Section 79(1)(f) of the Act.
PSPCL has emphasised that the claim directly involves the fixed/ capacity charge
component of the two-part tariff approved by the Commission and cannot be treated
as a pure contractual money claim.
21. PSPCL has submitted that under the 2014 Tariff Regulations, the tariff for a
generating station is structured as a two-part tariff comprising capacity charges and
Order in Petition No.346/MP/2020 Page 16 of 22

energy charges. The fixed charges claimed by the Petitioner correspond to the
capacity charge component of the tariff and are therefore an integral and inseparable
part of the tariff framework determined by the Commission. It has been contended that
capacity charges are statutorily recognised components of tariff, designed to enable
recovery of the annual fixed costs of the generating station, including return on equity,
interest on the loan, depreciation, operating and maintenance expenses, and working
capital. Accordingly, any dispute relating to such fixed charges necessarily arises
within the tariff regime and cannot be treated as a standalone contractual claim. Since
fixed charges form part of the tariff determined under the applicable regulations, any
claim for payment or recovery thereof inherently involves issues relating to tariff
determination and application. Therefore, disputes concerning entitlement to fixed
charges fall squarely within the Commission's regulatory jurisdiction under Section
79(1)(f) of the Act.
22. Hon’ble Supreme Court in Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Limited v. Essar Power
Limited (2008) 4 SCC 755 has held that disputes pertaining to tariff or matters
intrinsically connected with tariff determination under the Act fall within the exclusive
domain of the Regulatory Commission and cannot be ousted by an arbitration clause.
The Commission is therefore empowered to adjudicate disputes involving generating
companies in regard to matters connected with tariff regulation.
23. We observe the following position emerges from the DVC APTEL Judgment
dated 28.8.2024 (affirmed by the Hon’ble Supreme Court on 23.9.2024):
“22. Thus, it is seen that the concept of arbitration is not alien to the disputes arising under
various provisions of Electricity Act, 2003 and in appropriate cases, where a valid
arbitration agreement exists between the parties and the dispute does not concern the
regulatory functions of the Commission, the Commission would be not only justified but
also bound to refer the dispute for arbitration.
…
25. At this juncture, we would again revert to Section 79(1) of the Electricity Act, 2003.
Section 79(1) empowers the Commission to adjudicate upon the disputes relating to
Order in Petition No.346/MP/2020 Page 17 of 22

regulation of tariff for the generating companies as well as inter-state transmission of
Electricity and to determine tariff inter-state transmission of electricity as provided under
clause (1) to (d) therein. We wonder how the dispute relating to termination of PPAs would
be regarded as a dispute relating to tariff or regulation of tariff of the generating companies,
as held by the Commission in the impugned order. To understand this aspect, it is
necessary to determine what constitutes tariff and non-tariff disputes. In our considered
opinion, all the matters which would have a bearing upon the tariff for a generating
company would constitute “tariff disputes” namely disputes related to Change in Law,
delayed completion of projects, invocation of Force Majeure events etc. Such matters
impact the tariff for a generating company directly and, therefore, fall solely within the
jurisdiction of the Central Commission under Section 79(1) of the Electricity Act, 2003.
However, the disputes related to termination or breach of contract which do not impact the
tariff either directly or indirectly, can be considered as non-tariff related disputes referable
to arbitration.
26. Perusal of the prayer clauses in the two petitions filed before the Commission reveals
that primary and main relief sought by 1st Respondent is the declaration that Appellant
shall not be entitled to treat the PPAs having been terminated. All other reliefs are ancillary
or consequential in nature. Thus, the main issue would be whether or not have been the
PPAs legally and validly terminated. Essentially, the dispute relating to termination of a
PPA is confined to the legality and validity of the termination of PPA and does not relate
to tariff or regulation of tariff.
…
37. In the instance case, there is undisputedly a valid and subsisting arbitration clause
contained in the PPAs. We have already held that the dispute between the parties primarily
relates to the termination of the PPAs which is a non-tariff dispute and thus, referable to
arbitration.”
24. The above findings of APTEL have subsequently been affirmed by the Hon’ble
Supreme Court under the DVC SC Order, wherein it was held as follows:
“We do not find any good ground and reason to interfere with the impugned judgment in
view of the difference of language in Section 79(1)(f) of the Electricity Act, 2003, from
Section 86(1)(f) of the 2003 Act. The power of the Central Electricity Regulatory
Commission under Section 79(1)(f) is different from the discretion exercised by the State
Electricity Regulatory Commission under Section 86(1)(f) of the 2003 Act.”
25. It follows that any dispute that bears a direct or indirect nexus with a tariff must
be characterised as a “tariff dispute” and falls within the adjudicatory domain of the
Commission under Section 79(1)(f) of the Act. In contrast, disputes arising purely from
contractual breach or termination, without any linkage to tariff, are to be treated as
“non-tariff disputes” and would be amenable to resolution through arbitration in
accordance with the agreed dispute resolution mechanism.
Order in Petition No.346/MP/2020 Page 18 of 22

26. The controversy in the DVC APTEL case was centred around termination of the
PPA, whereas the present dispute pertains to the obligation to pay fixed charges as
determined under the regulatory framework. As per Regulation 20 of the 2014 Tariff
Regulations, the tariff for a thermal generating station is based on a two-part structure
comprising capacity charges and energy charges. Fixed charges, thus, representing
the capacity charge component under the said framework, are statutorily embedded
within the tariff structure determined by the Commission and cannot be segregated
from it.
27. We observe from the judgment of APTEL dated 25.2.2026 in Appeal Nos. 348
of 2025, 371 of 2025 and 400 of 2025 (Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Limited & Ors. v.
Tata Power Company Limited & Ors. – Mundra UMPP batch) that disputes relating to
payment or recovery of fixed charges/ capacity charges even in the context of alleged
contractual defaults, non-scheduling, or diversion of power are tariff-related disputes
falling squarely within the adjudicatory jurisdiction of the Central Commission. The
relevant portions of the said judgment are extracted below:
“It is clear that the disputes which relate to the regulatory functions of the CERC and
which impact tariff, either directly or indirectly cannot be referred to arbitration, as
such disputes are non-arbitrable. As noted hereinabove, the power conferred on the
Central Commission, under Section 79(1)(f), is with respect to disputes involving
generating companies (i) in regard to, (ii) matters connected with, Clauses (a) to (d)
of Section 79(1)”
…
“(x) In the light of the law declared by this Tribunal, in the DVC Judgement, it must be
held that disputes, including those which fall within the ambit of the regulatory
functions of the Commission, or which impact tariff either directly or indirectly, are
non-arbitrable and, notwithstanding an arbitration agreement in existence and the
tests stipulated in Section 8(1) of the 1996 Act being satisfied, cannot be referred to
arbitration.”
28. In this regard, it is apposite to refer to the observations of the APTEL in its
judgment dated 27.3.2025 in Appeal No. 134/2024 (NPCIL v GUVNL & anr), wherein
the scope of Section 79(1)(a) and Section 79(1)(f) of the Act has been examined.
Order in Petition No.346/MP/2020 Page 19 of 22

APTEL has clarified that the jurisdiction of the Commission under Section 79(1)(f) is
attracted where the dispute involves a generating company and is in regard to matters
connected with the Commission’s power to regulate tariff under Section 79(1)(a). The
same has also been reiterated by the Commission in an order dated 28.1.2026 in
Petition No. 91/MP/2018 & batch. Relevant portions of the above-referred APTEL
judgment are extracted below:
“(iii) SECTION 79(1)(f): ITS SCOPE:
Section 79(1)(f) of the Electricity Act requires the Central Commission to discharge
the function of adjudication of disputes involving generating companies or
transmission licensees in regard to matters connected with clauses (a) to (d) of
Section 79(1), and to refer any dispute for arbitration.
The power conferred on the Central Commission to adjudicate disputes is confined
only to those disputes involving (1) generating companies or (2) transmission
licensees. As long as the dispute involves a generating company or a transmission
licensee, and even if the other parties to the dispute are neither generating
companies nor transmission licensees, the Central Commission would have
jurisdiction to adjudicate disputes.
xxx
The jurisdictional facts, necessary for the CERC to exercise its powers of adjudication
of the dispute under Section 79(1)(f) read with Section 79(1)(a), is firstly that the
dispute involves a generating company owned or controlled by the Central
Government; secondly that the dispute is in regard to matters connected with the
power of the CERC to regulate the tariff of such a generating company.
xxx
By use of the words ‘in regard to’, in Section 79(1)(f), Parliament has made it clear
that the disputes, to which a generator is a party to, can be adjudicated by the CERC
only ‘for the purposes of’ clauses (a) to (d) of Section 79(1), and not otherwise. By
use of the words “connected with”, in Section 79(1)(f), Parliament has stipulated that
the dispute should be really incidental or in close proximity to clauses (a) to (d) of
Section 79(1).”
29. We note the observations of the Commission in order in Petition No.
91/MP/2018 & batch, wherein, while examining the scope of jurisdiction under Section
79(1)(f) read with Section 79(1)(b) of the Act, it has been held that the exercise of
adjudicatory jurisdiction is contingent upon the existence of certain jurisdictional facts,
namely: (i) the dispute involves a generating company having a composite scheme,
and (ii) the dispute is in regard to matters connected with regulation of tariff. The
Commission has also observed that the term “tariff” is of wide import and includes not
Order in Petition No.346/MP/2020 Page 20 of 22

only the fixation of rates but also the regulatory framework governing such
determination.
30. In view of the above, since the issue raised in the present proceedings relates
to fixed/ capacity charges, which constitute a component of the tariff, it falls within the
regulatory domain of the tariff. We take note of the submission of the Petitioner that
disputes arising out of alleged contractual breaches under the PPA, which do not
impact tariff determination or regulation, fall outside the adjudicatory jurisdiction of the
Commission, while relying on the judgment of the APTEL in MPPMCL v. DVC.
However, in light of the subsequent judgment in the Mundra UMPP batch, the earlier
reliance placed on the judgment dated 28.8.2024 in MPPMCL v. DVC no longer
advances the case of the Petitioner. The law now stands clarified that disputes relating
to the regulatory functions of the Commission, or which impact tariff either directly or
indirectly, are non-arbitrable, notwithstanding an arbitration agreement. It is also
observed that though the Petitioner has characterised the dispute as arising from non-
scheduling of power and consequent contractual breach, the nature of the relief sought
is determinative. Even though non-scheduling may arise from contractual conduct, the
consequence sought, namely the recovery of fixed/capacity charges, is governed by
tariff principles and forms an integral part of the tariff framework regulated by the
Commission.
31. In the present case, the dispute pertains specifically to fixed charges, which
constitute one of the two fundamental components of the tariff under the recognised
two-part tariff structure. Fixed charges, being capacity charges, are designed to
compensate the generating company for making capacity available and are governed
by availability-based tariff principles. Therefore, any dispute concerning entitlement to
fixed charges necessarily involves the interpretation and application of tariff
Order in Petition No.346/MP/2020 Page 21 of 22

regulations. The present dispute is not merely about recovery of a sum arising out of
an alleged contractual breach, but concerns the entitlement to recover capacity
charges within the framework of a tariff determined under the applicable regulations.
Applying the aforesaid principles to the facts of the present case, the Commission
finds that the adjudication of the present dispute necessarily involves examination of
the entitlement to recover such charges, the regulatory framework governing such
recovery, and the interplay between the PPA and the Tariff Regulations.
32. In view of the foregoing analysis, the Commission holds that the present
Petition raises a tariff-related dispute falling squarely within the adjudicatory
jurisdiction of the Commission under Section 79(1)(f) of the Act. The Commission is
empowered and duty-bound to adjudicate the dispute on the merits and is not required
to refer it to arbitration.
33. The Petition will be listed for hearing ‘on merits’ in due course.

ORDER
The Petitioners, Adani Energy Solutions Limited (hereinafter referred to as
“AESL”) and KPS III HVDC Transmission Limited (SPV), has filed the present Petition
under Section 63 of the Electricity Act, 2003 (hereinafter referred to as “the Act”) for
the adoption of transmission charges to establish the Inter-State Transmission System
for “Transmission System for Evacuation of Power from potential renewable energy

Energy India Limited (vide letters dated 30.05.2023 and 27.12.2024), provided
estimates regarding the equipment cost of the "2500 MW, ±500 kV KPS3

(HVDC) [VSC] Terminal Station". Further, factors such as inflation, import
taxes and duties, and additional pile foundation requirements in the Khavda
region were added in the cost of equipment. The Cost Committee decided that
the lowest of the two cost estimates shall be considered after taking into

b) Post conclusion of the e-Reverse Auction process, the Bid Evaluation

Analysis and Decision
11. We have considered the submissions of the Petitioner, BPC, and CTUIL and
perused the documents available on record. Section 63 of the Act provides as under:
“Section 63: Determination of tariff by bidding process: Notwithstanding
anything contained in section 62, the Appropriate Commission shall adopt the
tariff if such tariff has been determined through transparent process of bidding
in accordance with the guidelines issued by the Central Government.”
12. The Ministry of Power, Government of India, has notified the “Tariff based
Competitive Bidding Guidelines for Transmission Service” and “Guidelines for
Encouraging Competition in Development of Transmission Projects‟ (hereinafter
referred to as “the Guidelines‟) under Section 63 of the Act vide Resolution No.
15/1/2017-Trans dated 10.8.2021, as amended from time to time. The salient features
of the Guidelines are as under:
Order in Petition No. 28/AT/2026
Page 7

(a) The Guidelines are applicable for the procurement of transmission
services for transmission of electricity through tariff based competitive bidding for
selection of the Transmission Service Provider (TSP) for new transmission
system on a Build, Own, Operate and Transfer basis.
(b) For procurement of the transmission services required for any inter-State
transmission Project, the Central Government shall notify the CTUIL or any
Central Government Organisation/ Central Public Sector Undertaking or its
wholly owned subsidiary (Special Purpose Vehicle) to be the Bid Process
Coordinator (BPC), who would be responsible for the coordinating the bid
process.
(c) The BPC shall prepare the bid documents in accordance with the
Guidelines and obtain approval of the Appropriate Government, or alternatively,
the BPC can use the Standard Bid Documents notified by the Ministry of Power.
Any material deviation from the Standard Bidding Documents shall be made only
with the prior approval of the Appropriate Government. Intimation about initiation
of the bidding process shall be sent by the BPC to the Appropriate Commission.
(d) For the procurement of the transmission services under the guidelines,
BPC shall adopt a single stage two envelope tender process featuring Request
for Proposal (RfP). The entire bidding process shall be conducted online through
electronic medium under e-reverse bidding framework.
(e) The RfP notice should be published in at least two national newspapers,
website of the BPC, and preferably in trade magazines also, so as to accord it
wide publicity. The bidding shall necessarily be by way of the International
Order in Petition No. 28/AT/2026
Page 8

Competitive Bidding (ICB). For the purpose of issue of the RfP, minimum
conditions to be met by the bidder shall be specified in the RfP.
(f) Standard documentation to be provided in the RfP shall include
definitions of requirements including brief description of the Project,
commissioning milestones to be achieved by the bidders, qualification
requirements to be met by the bidders including, minimum net worth, etc. with
necessary proof of the same, as outlined in the bid documents, Specified target
dates/months for commissioning and commercial operations, Standard
Transmission Service Agreement (TSA), agreement(s) under the Central
Electricity Regulatory Commission (Sharing of Inter State Transmission Charges
and Losses) Regulations as amended from time to time, period of validity of offer
of bidder, TSA proposed to be entered with the SPV including amendments, bid
evaluation methodology to be adopted by the BPC, specification regarding bid
bond as well as the Contract Performance Guarantee to be furnished by the
bidders, proposed indemnification agreement between the TSP and the Nodal
Agency, liquidated damages that shall apply in the event of delay in start of
providing the transmission services and technical, operational and safety criteria
to be met by the bidder/TSP and requirement of obtaining transmission licence
from the Appropriate Commission.
(g) The TSP, on the date of acquisition of the SPV from the BPC will enter
into a Transmission Service Agreement with the Nodal Agency.
(h) To ensure competitiveness, the minimum number of qualified bidders
shall be two. For inter-State transmission system, bids shall be opened in the
Order in Petition No. 28/AT/2026
Page 9

office of the CEA by a bid committee comprising of at least one member from the
CEA and one member from BPC. For inter-State transmission system, CEA shall
constitute a committee for evaluation of the bids with at least one representative
from the CEA and not less than two representatives from the concerned Regional
Power Committees and one independent member. Further, in case project is
inter-regional, there shall be at least one representative from every concerned
RPC. The technical bids shall be examined to ensure that the bids submitted
meet minimum eligibility criteria set out in the bid documents on all the technical
evaluation parameters. Only the bids that meet all elements of the minimum
technical criteria set out in the bid documents shall be considered for further
evaluation on the transmission charges bids. The online initial price bids shall be
electronically opened by the bid opening committee in the presence of the bid
evaluation committee. The bidder, who has quoted the lowest transmission
charge as per the evaluation procedure, shall be considered for the award.
(i) The BPC is required to complete e-reverse bidding after opening of the
initial offer within 75 days. The procurer may give extended time frame indicated
herein based on the prevailing circumstances, and such alterations shall not be
construed to be deviation from these guidelines.
(j) The TSP shall make an application for the grant of a transmission licence
to the Appropriate Commission within five (5) working days from the date of
execution of the Share Purchase Agreement for acquisition of the SPV.
(k) The BPC shall make the final result of evaluation of all bids public. The
final TSA, along with the certification by the bid evaluation committee, shall be
Order in Petition No. 28/AT/2026
Page 10

forwarded to the Appropriate Commission for the adoption of tariff discovered
from the quoted annual transmission charges during the e-reverse bidding
process in terms of Section 63 of the Act.
13. Therefore, we have to examine whether the Guidelines issued by the Central
Government have been followed in the present case in a transparent process of
bidding.
14. The Ministry of Power, Government of India, vide its Gazette Notification No.

for Evacuation of Power from potential renewable energy zone in Khavda area of

through a tariff-based competitive bidding process.
15. KPS III HVDC Transmission Limited was incorporated on 18.1.2024 under the
Companies Act, 2013, as a wholly owned subsidiary of PFCCL with the objective of
establishing the inter-State Transmission System for “Transmission System for
Evacuation of Power from potential renewable energy zone in Khavda area of Gujarat
under Phase-V (8 GW): Part C” and to act as the Transmission Service Provider after
being acquired by the successful bidder. The main objectives of the Petitioner

“To develop Power system network, To plan, promote and develop an
integrated and efficient power transmission system network in all its aspects
including planning, investigation, research, design and engineering,
preparation of preliminary, feasibility and definite project reports, construction,
operation and maintenance of transmission lines, sub-stations, load dispatch
stations and communication facilities and appurtenant works, coordination of
Order in Petition No. 28/AT/2026
Page 11

integrated operation of regional and national grid system, execution of turn-key
jobs for other utilities/organizations and wheeling of power in accordance with
the policies, guidelines and objectives laid down by the Central Government
from time to time”.
16. BPC prepared the bidding document (RfP) in accordance with the Standard Bid
Documents issued by the Ministry of Power, Government of India.
17. The BPC started the process of selection of the successful bidder with the

21. The RfP was issued on 26.7.2024. At the RfP (Technical and Financial) stage,

attributable to the BPC, the said activities are not completed by the Selected Bidder

extended the date up to 12.12.2025 for completion of all activities by the successful
bidder. The selected bidder furnished the Contract Performance Guarantee in favour
of the Nodal Agency (CTUIL) for an amount of Rs. 553.73 crore on 9.12.2025 and

after execution of the Share Purchase Agreement. As per clause 2.15.4 of the RfP,
TSP is required to apply to the Commission for the adoption of transmission charges

within five working days of the issuance of the acquisition of the SPV to the successful
bidder. The successful bidder, namely Adani Energy Solutions Limited, acquired the
SPV on 12.12.2025. Accordingly, the TSP has filed the instant Petition through e-filing
for the adoption of transmission charges on 4.12.2025.

a grant of transmission licence. The Commission, vide order dated 9.5.2026 in Petition
No. 27/TL/2026, on being satisfied that the Petitioner, prime facie, qualifies for the grant
of a transmission license as prayed for, directed publication of notices under clause (a)
of sub-section (5) of Section 15 of the Act, inviting suggestions/ objections to the
proposal of the Commission.
29. In accordance with the Guidelines, BEC has to certify that the tariff has been
discovered through a transparent process of bidding and the tariff discovered is in line
with prevailing market prices. In the minutes of the fifth Meeting of the Bid Evaluation
Committee meeting held on 12.11.2025, the following have been recorded:
“1. The fifth meeting of the Bid Evaluation Committee (BEC) for the evaluation
of the Final Offer (Financial Bid) for the transmission scheme "Transmission
System for Evacuation of Power from potential renewable energy zone in
Khavda area of Gujarat under Phase-V (8 GW): Part C" was held on
November 12, 2025, at 15:00 hrs (IST) through Video Conferencing (VC).
2. During the previous BEC meeting held on 18.09.2025 (MoM is enclosed at
Annexure-A), the BEC decided the following:
i. Considering the discovered tariff (Rs. 23,917.69 million per annum)
post e-RA is significantly higher than the estimated CERC Levelised
Tariff, the matter may be referred to the Cost Committee for reviewing
the cost of the project.
ii. The decision of the Cost Committee to be put up before the BEC for
further decision in the matter.
3. The BPC informed the BEC that, in line with the decision of the BEC, the
BPC had approached the Cost Committee for a review of the project's cost
Order in Petition No. 28/AT/2026
Page 18

estimates. Accordingly, a Cost Committee meeting was held on 10.11.2025,
wherein the estimated project cost was reviewed and reassessed.
4. BPC informed to BEC that based on the revised project cost approved by
the Cost Committee, the CERC tariff was again calculated. The Transmission
Charges discovered through the e-RA i.e. Rs.23,917.69 million per annum is
around ~12% higher than levelised tariff worked out as per CERC Tariff
Regulations (Annexure-B).
5. After taking into consideration the above, BEC deliberated on the following:
i. the subject scheme is based on Voltage Source Converter (VSC)
technology, which is the first project to be developed though the TBCB
route in India, and the higher price quoted by the bidder may be partially
attributable to the risk associated with adoption of this advanced
technology.
ii. the quoted tariff is discovered through the e-reverse bidding process
and through a competitive bidding process based on Guidelines issued
by MoP and may be considered as reasonable;
iii. Adani Energy Solutions Limited may be considered as the successful
bidder, and Letter of Intent (Lol) may be issued to the successful bidder.
6. Based on the discussions, the BEC recommended the following:
i. Adani Energy Solutions Limited is the successful bidder after the
conclusion of the e-reverse auction process with the lowest Quoted
Transmission Charge of Rs.23,917.69 million per annum;
ii. The quoted tariff discovered through the e-reverse bidding process is
acceptable;
iii. In view of (i) and (ii) above, Adani Energy Solutions Limited may be
issued Lol.
The BEC has also issued a separate certificate in this regard (Annexure-C).”
30. Bid Evaluation Committee (BEC), vide its certificate dated 12.11.2025, certified
as under:
“It is hereby certified that:
1. The entire bid process has been carried out in accordance with the "Tariff
based Competitive Bidding Guidelines for Transmission Service" and
"Guidelines for encouraging competition in development of the Transmission
Order in Petition No. 28/AT/2026
Page 19

Projects" issued by Ministry of Power, Govt., of India under Section 63 of the
Electricity Act, 2003 and as amended from time to time.
2. Adani Energy Solutions Limited emerged as the Successful Bidder after the
conclusion of e-reverse bidding process with the lowest Quoted Transmission
Charges of Rs.23,917.69 million per annum.
3. The quoted tariff is higher than the Levelised Tariff calculated based on CERC
norms considering the Capital Cost for the Project 'Transmission System for
Evacuation of Power from potential renewable energy zone in Khavda area of
Gujarat under Phase-V (8 GW): Part C' as assessed by Cost Committee. The
quoted tariff discovered through e-reverse bidding process is acceptable.”
31. In the light of the discussions in the preceding paragraphs, it emerges that the
selection of the successful bidder and the discovery of the annual transmission charges
of the Project have been carried out by the BPC through a transparent process of
competitive bidding in accordance with the Guidelines issued by the Ministry of Power,
Government of India, under Section 63 of the Act. BEC has certified that the process
is in conformity with the Ministry of Power Guidelines. BEC, in its certificate dated
12.11.2025, has certified that Adani Energy Solutions Limited has emerged as the
successful bidder after the conclusion of the e-reverse auction with the lowest
transmission charges of Rs. 23,917.69 million per annum. It is noted that the quoted
tariff is higher by approximately ~12% than the estimated CERC levelised tariff based
on the revised project cost approved by the Cost Committee. The BEC, in its meeting
held on 12.11.2025, observed that the subject scheme is based on Voltage Source
Converter (VSC) technology, which is the first project to be developed through the
TBCB route in India, and the higher price quoted by the bidder may be partially
attributable to the risk associated with the adoption of this advanced technology. The
BEC further observed that the quoted tariff has been discovered through a transparent
e-reverse bidding process based on Guidelines issued by the Ministry of Power and
may be considered reasonable. Accordingly, based on the BEC certification, we
Order in Petition No. 28/AT/2026
Page 20

approve and adopt the annual transmission charges of Rs. 23,917.69 million per
annum as per the final offer of the successful bidder, subject to the grant of
transmission licence to KPS III HVDC Transmission Limited company. The
transmission charges shall remain valid throughout the period covered in the TSA.
32. The sharing of the transmission charges by the designated ISTS customers
(DICs) shall be governed by the provisions of the Central Electricity Regulatory
Commission (Sharing of inter-State Transmission Charges and Losses) Regulations,
2020, as amended from time to time.
33. Extract copy of this order shall be sent to the Nodal agency, CTUIL.
34. Petition No. 28/AT/2026 is disposed of in terms of the above.

13. Section 14 of the Act provides that the Appropriate Commission may, on an
application made under Section 15 of the Act, grant a licence to any person to transmit
electricity as a transmission licensee in any area as may be specified in the licence.
The word “person” has been defined in Section 2 (49) of the Act to include any
company or body corporate or association or body of individuals, whether incorporated
or not, or artificial juridical person. The Petitioner has been incorporated under the
Companies Act, 2013. The main objective of the Petitioner Company is as under:
“To develop Power System Network, To plan, promote and develop an
integrated and efficient power transmission system network in all its aspects
including planning, investigation, research, design and engineering, preparation
of preliminary, feasibility and definite project reports, construction, operation
and maintenance of transmission lines, sub-stations, load dispatch stations
and communication facilities and appurtenant works, coordination of integrated
operation of state, regional and national grid system, execution of turn-key jobs
for other utilities/organizations and wheeling of power in accordance with the
policies, guidelines and objectives laid down by the Central Government from
time to time”
14. Section 15 (1) of the Act provides that every application under Section 14 of
the Act shall be made in such manner and in such form as may be specified by the
Appropriate Commission and shall be accompanied by such fees as may be prescribed
Order in Petition No. 131/TL/2026
Page 11

by the Central Government. The Commission has specified Transmission Licence
Regulations in this regard. Regulation 4 (1) of the Transmission Licence Regulations
provides that eligibility for the grant of a licence for inter-State transmission of electricity
is contingent upon the entity being selected either through the competitive bidding
process under Section 63 of the Electricity Act, 2003 or by the Central Government or
its authorized agency to implement a project under the regulated tariff mechanism.
Regulation 10 (1) of the Transmission Licence Regulations provided that, in case the
licensee has been selected for implementation of the project in accordance with the
competitive bidding guidelines, the transmission tariff in terms of the Transmission
Service Agreement shall be adopted by the Commission under Section 63 of the Act.
The Project under consideration has been identified for development under competitive
bidding by a competent authority, and the selection of the Project developer has been
certified to have been made in accordance with the Guidelines for competitive bidding.
15. Regulation 5 of the Transmission Licence Regulations, 2024 provides for the
procedure for granting of a transmission licence as under:
“(1) The application for the grant of licence shall be made to the Commission
in Form-I appended to these regulations and shall be accompanied by such
fee as may be prescribed by the Central Government from time to time under
sub-section (1) of section 15 of the Act.
(2) The application shall be supported with an affidavit in accordance with
Regulation 17 of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Conduct of
Business) Regulations, 2023.
(3) The applicant shall submit the original application in electronic form along
with enclosures on the e-filing portal of the Commission and electronically
serve a copy of such application on all the concerned DICs of the project and
the Central Transmission Utility. The application shall be served through e-mail
on the concerned DICs of the project who are not registered on the e-filing
portal of the Commission.
(4) The applicant shall also upload the complete application along with
annexures on its website, in English. The applicant shall also upload on its
website, the details as per Form-I and Form-II appended to these regulations

the project or concerned transmission line is situated or proposed to be

notice of its application in Form-II appended to these regulations in at least two
leading daily digital newspapers, one in English language and another in the
Indian language of the State or Union Territory where an element of the project

(7) In the notice published in the digital newspapers and on the applicant’s

at email id: registry@cercind.gov.in. Any suggestion or objection received in

(8) The applicant shall within 3 working days from the date of publication of the

i) Govt. of India has set a target for establishing 500 GW capacity from
non-fossil energy sources by 2030. In this direction, various RE
Potential zones had been identified and declared in Madhya
Pradesh. Morena area of Madhya Pradesh is one among the
identified zones with RE Potential of about 3.9 GW.
ii) As per potential identified by MNRE, Morena district of Gujarat is a
Renewable Energy (RE) zone with potential of 3.9 GW (Phase I –
2.5 GW by Dec-27 & Phase II-1.4 GW by Dec-30). As per
information provided by RUMSL, Morena Solar Park (600 MW with
BESS) is planning to connect to STU & Morena Solar Park (1400
MW without BESS) is planning to connect to ISTS network near
south of Sabalgarh area in 2027-28 timeframe. Moreover, other

(New) S/s for Strengthening In-ISTS network for which MPPTCL
have requested for ISTS in-feed for feeding power to 400/220 kV
Sabalgarh (New) S/s.
iii) For evacuation of this 2.5 GW capacity (Phase-I) from Morena
district of Madhya Pradesh & for feeding power to 400/220 kV
Sabalgarh (New) S/s of MPPTCL, establishment of 765/400 kV
Morena PS near South of Sabalgarh is proposed with 3X1500 MVA,
765/400kV, 2X500 MVA, 400/220 kV ICTs & Morena OS- Karera
(near Datia) 765 kV D/c line. The scheme will facilitate integration
of 2.5 GW RE injection into the ISTS network as well as
development of ISTS in Sabalgarh area. The scheme would also

proviso to Clause 2.15.2 of the RfP provides that “if for any reason attributable to the

extended, on a day-to-day basis till the end of the Bid validity period”. As per the above
provision, the selected bidder was required to complete all the activities, including the
acquisition of the SPVs, by 17.11.2025. Though the LoI was issued on 7.11.2025, BPC,
vide its letter dated 2.2.2026, in terms of Clause 2.15.2 of the RfP, extended the date
up to 3.2.2026 for completion of all activities by the successful bidder. The selected
bidder furnished the Contract Performance Guarantee in favour of the Nodal Agency
(CTUIL) for Rs. 52.00 crore on 3.2.2026 and acquired a hundred per cent equity-
holding in the applicant company on 3.2.2026 after execution of the Share Purchase
Agreement. As per clause 2.15.4 of the RfP, TSP is required to apply to the
Commission for the grant of a transmission licence within five working days of the
issuance of the acquisition of the SPV to the successful bidder. The successful bidder,
namely Enerica Infra 1 Private Limited, acquired the SPV on 3.2.2026. Accordingly,
the TSP filed the instant Petition through e-filing for the grant of a transmission licence
on 6.2.2026.
21. Considering the material on record, we are prima facie of the view that the
Petitioner satisfies the conditions for the grant of an inter-State transmission licence
under Section 15 of the Act, read with the Transmission Licence Regulations for
construction, operation, and maintenance of the transmission system as described in
para 1 of this order. We, therefore, direct that a public notice in two daily digital

provisions of the TSA, the applicable provisions of the Electricity Act, 2003, and the

expense, shall be responsible for designing, constructing, erecting, testing, and
commissioning each element of the Project by scheduled COD in accordance with the
various regulations of the Central Electricity Authority regarding Technical Standards
and Grid Standards, Prudent Utility Practices and other applicable laws. Further, Article
5.4 of the TSA provides that the TSP shall ensure that the Project is designed, built
and completed in a good workman-like manner using sound engineering and
construction practices and using only materials and equipment that are new and of
international utility-grade quality such that the useful life of the Project will be till the
expiry date. Further, the design, construction, and testing of all equipment, facilities,
components, and systems of the Project shall be in accordance with Indian Standards
and Codes issued by the Bureau of Indian Standards. In this regard, the Petitioner has
submitted that it will implement the Project in accordance with the provisions of the
TSA. It is expected that while carrying out the survey, the Petitioner has complied with
the provisions of clause 2.5.7.3, clause 2.5.7.4, and clause 2.5.7.5 of the RfP. The
Petitioner will comply with the bidding documents and the TSA for the commissioning
of the Project within the SCOD.

Competitive Bidding Guidelines for Transmission Service” (hereinafter referred to as

the Bid Process Coordinator (hereinafter referred to as “BPC”) for the purpose of

“TSP”) to establish the Inter-State transmission system for “Transmission system
strengthening for integration of additional RE potential at Davanagere (0.25 GW) and

and completed the same on 12.2.2026 in accordance with the Guidelines. Power Grid

to the beneficiaries of the transmission system.

four bidders, namely, (i) Power Grid Corporation of India Limited; (ii) H G Infra Engg.
Limited; (iii) Resonia Ltd. and (iv) Adani Energy Solutions Limited submitted their
offers. The RfP (Technical) bids were opened by the Bid Opening Committee at the
Central Electricity Authority on 8.12.2025 in the presence of a representative of the

11. Consequent to its selection as the lowest bidder, a Letter of Intent (hereinafter
referred to as “LoI”) was issued to Power Grid Corporation of India Limited on 7.1.2026,
which was accepted by Power Grid Corporation of India Limited. Under the terms of
RfP and the Letter of Intent, the successful bidder is obligated to accomplish the
following tasks:
a) Provide Contract Performance Guarantee in favour of Central Transmission
Utility of India Limited (CTUIL);
