Filing of Petition under Regulation 77 of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission
(Terms and Conditions for Tariff determination from Renewable Energy Sources)
Regulations, 2024 and Clause 5.1. of Part A- ‘Scope’ of the Tariff Based Competitive
Bidding Guidelines for Procurement of Storage Capacity/ Stored Energy from Pump
Storage Plants by Ministry of Power dated 6th February 2025 for seeking approval of
Tender Documents with the deviations for Long Term Procurement of 500 MW (For 6
Hours discharge with maximum 4 Hours continuous discharge per day) Power for 40
Years from ISTS Connected Pump Storage Plant/s through Competitive Bidding.
And
In the matter of:
1

1. Madhya Pradesh Power Management Company Limited (MPPMCL)
Shakti Bhawan, Rampur, Jabalpur, MP
2. Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Limited (UPPCL)

Shri Aditya Singh, Advocate, MPPMCL
Shri Dhiraj Munia, MPPMCL
ORDER
The Petitioners, M P Power Management Company Limited (hereinafter
‘MPPMCL’) and Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Limited (UPPCL) have filed the
present petition seeking approval of tender documents with the deviations for Long
Term Procurement of 500 MW (for 6 Hours discharge with maximum 4 Hours
continuous discharge per day) power for 40 years from ISTS connected pump storage
plant/s through competitive bidding, under Regulation 77 of the Central Electricity
Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions for Tariff determination from
Renewable Energy Sources) Regulations, 2024 and Clause 5.1. of Part A- ‘Scope’ of
the Tariff Based Competitive Bidding Guidelines for Procurement of Storage Capacity/
Stored Energy from Pump Storage Plants by Ministry of Power dated 06.02.2025.
2. The Petitioners have made the following prayers:
a. Admit the present Petition;
b. To accord approval for initiation of competitive bidding process for procurement
of power from ISTS Connected Pump Storage Plant/s through Competitive
Bidding;
c. To allow MPPMCL to conduct single stage two envelope tendering process;
2

d. To approve the Tender Documents prepared for procurement of power from
ISTS Connected Pump Storage Plant/s;
e. To approve the deviations sought from the Standard Bidding Guidelines;
f. Permit the petitioner to initiate the bidding process i.e. float the Tender
incorporating proposed deviations and the deviations in the Bidding Documents
shall all be subject to approval of the Commission;
g. Condone any inadvertent omissions/ errors/ shortcomings and permit the
Petitioner to add/ change/ modify/ alter portion(s) of this filing and make further
submissions as may be required at a later stage; and
h. Pass such other and further orders as are deemed fit and proper in the facts and
circumstances of the case.
Submissions of the Petitioners
3. The Petitioners have submitted that:
a. On 10.04.2023, MoP issued Guidelines to promote the development of Pump
Storage Projects (PSP). Further, on 06.02.2025, MoP has issued tariff-based
competitive bidding guidelines for the procurement of storage capacity/ stored
energy from pump storage plants with the objective of promoting the
development of pump storage plants (PSPs) and to provide a transparent, fair,
standardised procurement framework based on open competitive bidding with
appropriate risk-sharing between various stakeholders.
b. The assessment of electricity demand & supply in the state of Madhya Pradesh
for future years (till FY 2030) was carried out, and the requirement for energy
storage capacity was identified based on the demand pattern of the State.
However, the requirement is expected to be limited to the Rabi months (Nov-
April). Hence, a storage solution with other states having complementary
demand (May-Oct) was explored to maximise the use of storage resources
and reduce procurement costs. In this regard, the Petitioner No. 2, UPPCL,
expressed its interest in collaborating on storage solutions in response to the
Petitioner’s letter dated 24.01.2023, thereby jointly procuring storage solutions
and reducing the cost burden on each state.
c. Accordingly, the procurement of power through Pump Storage Projects as
envisaged in this Petition falls under composite scheme as sub-section (1)(b)
3

of Section 79 of the Electricity Act, 2003 wherein the generation and sale are
envisaged to take place in more than one state, by the virtue of the Section 79
of Electricity Act 2003, this Commission becomes the appropriate Commission
under the Act.
d. In the backdrop of the above facts and circumstances, the present Petition is
being made by MPPMCL & UPPCL for approval of the Tender documents with
the deviations for long-term procurement of 500 MW (For 6 Hours discharge
with maximum 4 Hours continuous discharge per day) power for 40 Years from
ISTS connected pump storage plants through competitive bidding.
e. Further, as regards the determination of tariff through the Competitive Bidding
process, Section 63 of the Electricity Act, 2003 provides as under:
“Section 63: Determination of tariff by bidding process: Notwithstanding
anything contained in section 62, the Appropriate Commission shall adopt the
tariff if such tariff has been determined through a transparent process of
bidding in accordance with the guidelines issued by the Central Government.”
f. In terms of Section 63 of the Act, the appropriate Commission is required to
adopt the tariff, on being satisfied that the transparent bidding process, in
accordance with the guidelines issued by the Central Government, has been
followed in determining such tariff.
g. The Petitioners are seeking approval of the Commission on the Tender
documents that have been prepared in accordance with the above-mentioned
guidelines.
h. The Petitioners have submitted the detailed provisions of the proposed power
procurement process, which are consistent with the Guidelines issued for the
procurement of Storage Capacity/ Stored Energy from Pump Storage Plants,
except for the deviations mentioned.
4. According to the Petitioners, the proposed tender is unique and the first of its
kind in India. With this complementary mechanism, wherein the storage facility/ project
will be utilised/ allocated to the First State for a particular period of the year, and for
the balance period of the year, it will be utilised/ allocated to State 2. The project will
make firm-despatchable power available to meet the Petitioners' peak-hour demand
patterns, thereby strengthening peak power supply capacity and power system
stabilisation measures in the states.
4

5. The salient features of the proposed Tender Document include Invitation of Bids
for Pump Storage Plant Developer/s to provide long-term energy storage capacity of
500 MW (for 6 hours discharge with a maximum of 4 hours continuous discharge per
day) from Pump Storage Plant/s (PSP/s) through a Competitive Bidding Process on a
"Build-Own-Operate" (BOO) basis, from projects commissioned or to be developed
anywhere in India, for a period of 40 years from the date of Commercial Operation
(COD). The minimum bid capacity is 100 MW against the total project capacity of 500
MW. The cycle operations shall entail 6 hours of discharge with a maximum of 4 hours
of continuous discharge per day, while the hours of charge and discharge shall remain
flexible.
6. The agreement shall be structured as a Tripartite Pump Storage Plant Power
Agreement (PSPPA) between MPPMCL, UPPCL, and the Developer, with both
MPPMCL and UPPCL acting as procurers on a complementary basis. The period of
supply shall be divided between the two procurers, with MPPMCL responsible for the
period from November to April (181 days) and UPPCL for the period from May to
October (184 days).
7. The selection of the bidder shall be carried out through an E-Reverse Auction
on a Bucket Filling basis. The project location is Pan-India, and the model type is BOO
(Build Own Operate). The charging/ pumping energy required for the operation of the
plant shall be provided by the Procurer.
8. The Petitioners have also submitted the details such as eligibility criteria for
bidders, selection process of bidders, letter of awards and signing of agreements, etc.,
as prescribed in the Tender document.
9. The Petitioners have prayed to approve the proposed Tender Documents
(Tender and Draft PSPPA) prepared for procurement from ISTS Connected Pump
Storage Plant/s through Global Competitive Bidding.
5

10. The Petitioners have submitted deviations (in tabular format) from the Standard
Bidding Guidelines (SBD) for the Pump Storage project as follows:

18. We have heard the learned counsels for the Petitioner and have carefully
perused the records.
19. The brief facts of the petition are that the Ministry of Power (MoP), Government
of India (GoI) vide order dated 22.07.2022 has issued a revised Trajectory for
Renewable Power Purchase Obligation (RPO) and Energy Storage Obligation (ESO).
A corrigendum to this trajectory has also been issued by MoP, GoI on 19.09.2022 and
20.10.2023. The Energy Department, Government of Madhya Pradesh (GoMP) vide
order no. F-03-24/2011/XII dated 22.09.2022 constituted a committee comprising
15

senior officers of Madhya Pradesh Power Companies, namely MPPMCL, MPPTCL,
MPPGCL, & MPSLDC, to analyse the technical feasibility, operational stability, and
other factors relating to the RPO trajectory notified by the Ministry of Power (MoP).
The assessment of electricity Demand & Supply in the State for future years (till FY
2030) was carried out, and the Committee identified the requirement for energy
storage capacity based on the State's demand pattern. However, the requirement was
envisaged to be limited to the Rabi months of the year (Nov-April). Hence, a storage
solution with other States having complementary demand (May-Oct) was explored to
maximise the use of storage resources and reduce the procurement cost. Uttar
Pradesh Power Corporation Limited (UPPCL) expressed its interest in collaborating
on storage solutions in response to MPPMCL’s letter dated 24.01.2023, thereby jointly
procuring storage solutions and reducing the cost burden on each state. On
10.04.2023, MoP issued Guidelines to Promote Development of Pump Storage
Projects (PSP). Further, on 06.02.2025, MoP issued Tariff-Based Competitive Bidding
Guidelines for the Procurement of Storage Capacity/ Stored Energy from Pump
Storage Plants with the objective of promoting the development of Pump Storage
Plants (PSPs) and to provide a transparent, fair, standardised procurement framework
based on open competitive bidding with appropriate risk-sharing between various
stakeholders.
20. We observe that the Petitioners have filed the petition under Regulation 77 of
the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions for Tariff
determination from Renewable Energy Sources) Regulations, 2024 and Clause 5.1.
of Part A- ‘Scope’ of the Tariff Based Competitive Bidding Guidelines for Procurement
of Storage Capacity/ Stored Energy from Pump Storage Plants by Ministry of Power
dated 06.02.2025 for seeking approval of Tender Documents with the deviations for
Long Term Procurement of 500 MW (for 6 Hours discharge with maximum 4 Hours
continuous discharge per day) Power for 40 Years from ISTS Connected Pump
Storage Plant/s through Competitive Bidding.
21. We observe that Regulation 77 of the Central Electricity Regulatory
Commission (Terms and Conditions for Tariff determination from Renewable Energy
Sources) Regulations, 2024 stipulates as under:
77. Power to remove difficulty
16

If any difficulty arises in giving effect to the provisions of these Regulations, the

3. Applicability
3.1. These Guidelines are issued under Section 63 of the Electricity Act,
2003, for the procurement of storage capacity /stored energy from
Pumped Storage Plants (PSPs) through competitive bidding.
3.2. The provisions of these Guidelines shall be applicable on the following
entities:
a. Developers,
b. Procurers (End Procurers or Intermediary Procurers)
3.3. These Guidelines are applicable for the procurement of storage
capacity or stored energy by the Procurers from existing, under-
construction or new PSP projects.

e. “Appropriate Commission” shall have the same meaning as defined in

23. Further, relevant Sections of the Electricity Act, 2003 stipulate as under:
Section 63: Determination of tariff by bidding process: Notwithstanding
anything contained in section 62, the Appropriate Commission shall adopt the
tariff if such tariff has been determined through transparent process of bidding
in accordance with the guidelines issued by the Central Government.
Section 79. (Functions of Central Commission): --- (1) The Central Commission
shall discharge the following functions, namely:-
(a) to regulate the tariff of generating companies owned or controlled by the
Central Government;
(b) to regulate the tariff of generating companies other than those owned or
controlled by the Central Government specified in clause (a), if such
generating companies enter into or otherwise have a composite scheme
for generation and sale of electricity in more than one State;
(c) to regulate the inter-State transmission of electricity;
(d) to determine tariff for inter-State transmission of electricity;
(e) to issue licenses to persons to function as transmission licensee and electricity
trader with respect to their inter-State operations;
(f) to adjudicate upon disputes involving generating companies or
transmission licensee in regard to matters connected with clauses (a) to
(d) above and to refer any dispute for arbitration;
(g) to levy fees for the purposes of this Act;
(h) to specify Grid Code having regard to Grid Standards;
(i) to specify and enforce the standards with respect to quality, continuity and
reliability of service by licensees;
(j) to fix the trading margin in the inter-State trading of electricity, if considered,
necessary;
(k) to discharge such other functions as may be assigned under this Act.
18

24. The issue of the composite scheme has been dealt with in detail by the Hon’ble
Supreme Court in the Energy Watchdog Case. The relevant extract of the said
judgment is extracted as under:
“22. The scheme that emerges from these Sections is that whenever there is
inter-State generation or supply of electricity, it is the Central Government that
is involved, and whenever there is intra-State generation or supply of electricity,
the State Government or the State Commission is involved. This is the precise
scheme of the entire Act, including Sections 79 and 86. It will be seen that
Section 79 itself in Subsections (c), (d) and (e) speaks of inter-State
transmission and inter-State operations. This is to be contrasted with Section
86 which deals with functions of the State Commission which uses the
expression "within the State" in Sub-clauses (a), (b), and (d), and "intra-state"
in sub-clause (c). This being the case, it is clear that the PPA, which deals with
generation and supply of electricity, will either have to be governed by the State
Commission or the Central Commission. The State Commission's jurisdiction
is only where generation and supply takes place within the State. On the other
hand, the moment generation and sale takes place in more than one State, the
Central Commission becomes the appropriate Commission under the Act.
What is important to remember is that if we were to accept the argument on
behalf of the Appellant, and we were to hold in the Adani case that there is no
composite scheme for generation and sale, as argued by the Appellant, it would
be clear that neither Commission would have jurisdiction, something which
would lead to absurdity. Since generation and sale of electricity is in more than
one State obviously Section 86 does not get attracted. This being the case, we
are constrained to observe that the expression "composite scheme" does not
mean anything more than a scheme for generation and sale of electricity in
more than one State.
23. This also follows from the dictionary meaning [(Mc-Graw-Hill Dictionary of
Scientific and Technical Terms (6th Edition), and P.Ramanatha Aiyar‟s
Advanced Law Lexicon (3rd Edition)] of the expression “composite”:
(a) “Composite” – “A re-recording consisting of at least two elements. A material
that results when two or more materials, each having its own, usually different
19

characteristics, are combined, giving useful properties for specific applications.
Also known as composite material.”
(b) “Composite character‟ – “A character that is produced by two or more
characters one on top of the other.”
(c) “Composite unit” – “A unit made of diverse elements.”
The aforesaid dictionary definitions lead to the conclusion that the expression
“composite” only means “consisting of at least two elements”. In the context of
the present case, generation and sale being in more than one State, this could
be referred to as “composite”.
24. Even otherwise, the expression used in Section 79(1)(b) is that generating
companies must enter into or otherwise have a "composite scheme". This
makes it clear that the expression "composite scheme" does not have some
special meaning-it is enough that generating companies have, in any manner,
a scheme for generation and sale of electricity which must be in more than one
State.
******************************************
26. Another important facet of dealing with this argument is that the tariff policy
dated 6th June, 2006 is the statutory policy which is enunciated under Section
3 of the Electricity Act. The amendment of 28th January, 2016 throws
considerable light on the expression “composite scheme”, which has been
defined for the first time as follows:
“5.11 (j) Composite Scheme: Sub-section (b) of Section79(1) of the Act
provides that Central Commission shall regulate the tariff of generating
company, if such generating company enters into or otherwise have a
composite scheme for generation and sale of electricity in more than one
State. Explanation: The composite scheme as specified under
section79(1) of the Act shall mean a scheme by a generating company
for generation and sale of electricity in more than one State, having
signed long-term or medium-term PPA prior to the date of commercial
operation of the project (the COD of the last unit of the project will be
20

deemed to be the date of commercial operation of the project) for sale of at
least 10% of the capacity of the project to a distribution licensee outside the
State in which such project is located.”
27. That this definition is an important aid to the construction of Section 79(1)(b)
cannot be doubted and, according to us, correctly brings out the meaning of
this expression as meaning nothing more than a scheme by a generating
company for generation and sale of electricity in more than one State. Section
64(5) has been relied upon by the Appellant as an indicator that the State
Commission has jurisdiction even in cases where tariff for inter-State supply is
involved. This provision begins with a non-obstante clause which would indicate
that in all cases involving inter-State supply, transmission, or wheeling of
electricity, the Central Commission alone has jurisdiction. In fact this further
supports the case of the Respondents. Section 64(5) can only apply if, the
jurisdiction otherwise being with the Central Commission alone, by application
of the parties concerned, jurisdiction is to be given to the State Commission
having jurisdiction in respect of the licensee who intends to distribute and make
payment for electricity. We, therefore, hold that the Central Commission had
the necessary jurisdiction to embark upon the issues raised in the present
cases.”
25. From the above, we observe that Regulation 77 of the Central Electricity Regulatory
Commission (Terms and Conditions for Tariff determination from Renewable Energy
Sources) Regulations, 2024, is attracted only in the cases which fall under section 62
of the Electricity Act, 2003, where the determination of tariff is undertaken by the
Commission. However, under Section 63 of the Electricity Act, 2003, the Commission
is required to adopt the tariff upon being satisfied that the transparent bidding process,
in accordance with the guidelines issued by the Central Government, has been
followed in determining such tariff. We further observe that Clause 5 of Part A- ‘Scope’
of the Tariff Based Competitive Bidding Guidelines for Procurement of Storage
Capacity/ Stored Energy from Pump Storage Plants by the Ministry of Power, dated
06.02.2025, mandates that the Procurer shall seek prior approval of the Appropriate
Commission for deviations from the process defined in the Guidelines before
the initiation of the bidding process itself. However, for the purpose of clarity, if the
Procurer, while preparing the Bid Documents and other Project Agreements, provides
21

detailed provisions that are consistent with these Guidelines, such detailing shall not
be considered as deviations from these Guidelines. In the instant petition, we observe
that MPPMCL is seeking approval for Tender Documents with deviations for long-
term procurement of 500 MW (for 6 Hours discharge with maximum 4 Hours
continuous discharge per day) Power for 40 Years from ISTS-connected Pump
Storage Plant/s through Competitive Bidding. We are of the view that the procurement
of power through Pump Storage Projects, as envisaged in this petition, is a composite
scheme in terms of Section 79 (1) (b) of the Electricity Act, 2003, wherein the
generation and sale are envisaged to take place in more than one State. Accordingly,
by virtue of the above-mentioned section of the Electricity Act 2003, this Commission
is the appropriate Commission. Further, we observe that the Hon’ble Supreme Court
has clearly held that the expression “composite scheme” used in Section 79(1)(b) of
the Act does not have some special meaning, and it is enough that generating
companies have, in any manner, a scheme for the generation and sale of electricity in
more than one State. It has also been clearly held that the moment when generation
and sale take place in more than one State, the jurisdiction of the Central Commission
is attracted.
26. The present Petition was first heard on 26.08.2025, wherein the Commission admitted
the Petition subject to just exceptions and initially directed the matter to be listed for
further hearing on 09.10.2025. Subsequently, to ensure broad stakeholder
participation, the Commission issued a Public Notice on 07.10.2025 inviting
comments, suggestions, and objections by 17.10.2025 and rescheduled the hearing.
Following this, the Petitioners undertook an extensive stakeholder consultation
process to ensure that the proposed bidding architecture remained transparent,
competitive, and commercially viable for prospective Pump Storage Plant developers.
On 15.01.2026, the Petitioners filed an additional affidavit. to bring on record the
exhaustive comments and representations received from various industry
stakeholders, the Petitioners' detailed responses and the Petitioners’ rebuttals to those
queries.
27. The matter was listed for its final hearing on 03.03.2026. During this hearing, the
Petitioners presented a detailed exposition of the commercial and technical
22

imperatives driving the deviations. After giving due consideration to the oral
submissions, the documentary evidence, and the statutory provisions, the
Commission reserved the matter for its final order.
28. With this background, the Commission is dealing with the prayers made jointly
by MPPMCL and UPPCL in the present Petition. In terms of Prayer (a), (b), (c), (d)
and (f), the Petitioners have submitted that while the proposed Tender Documents
(RfS and PSPPA) are broadly harmonised with the Ministry of Power's Guidelines for
Pump Storage Plants dated 06.02.2025, the unique inter-state seasonal
complementarity model, combined with the geotechnical realities of executing hydro
projects, demands specific deviations from the Standard Bidding Document (SBD).
29. The Petitioners have approached this Commission under Regulation 77 of the
CERC (Terms and Conditions for Tariff determination from Renewable Energy
Sources) Regulations, 2024, and Clause 5.1 of Part A of the Tariff-Based Competitive
Bidding Guidelines for Pumped Storage Plants dated 06.02.2025, praying for the
approval of the Tender Documents along with the proposed deviations. However, the
Commission notes that the prayer seeking approval of the tender documents is beyond
the scope of Part A - Clause 5.1 of the Guidelines, which mandates the prior approval
of the Appropriate Commission exclusively for deviations from the process defined in
the Guidelines prior to the initiation of the bidding process, and not for the approval of
the tender document itself. Accordingly, the Commission’s scrutiny and approval in the
present order are strictly limited to the specific deviations sought by the Petitioners
from the standard MoP Guidelines. The Commission has examined the six specific
deviations sought by the Petitioners. The issue-by-issue analysis, detailing the original
SBD mandate, the proposed deviation, the Petitioners' underlying rationale, and
findings of the Commission, is hereinunder:
30. Deviation 1: Timeline for the Adoption of Tariff
SBD Mandate (Part C, Clause 1.6): The standard guidelines prescribe that the
Procurer or Intermediary Procurer shall approach the Appropriate Commission for the
formal adoption of the tariff under Section 63 of the Act within thirty (30) days of the
issuance of the Letter of Award (LoA).
23

Proposed Tender Clause (2.12 ): The Petitioners request to amend this timeline,
stating that the Procurer shall approach the Appropriate Commission for tariff adoption
within sixty (60) days of the issuance of the LoA. The Petitioners argued that, since
this is a one-of-a-kind complementarity-based procurement, after the issuance of the
LoA, both states would require appropriate internal approvals, which would be time-
consuming. Therefore, a 60-day period would be required to approach the commission
post-issuance of LoAs.
Stakeholder Comments: Some stakeholders enquired if the Procurers will have to
approach CERC or SERC within 60 days of LOA, and that delays will not affect the
Financial Closure timeline, and provided the rationale as bankability concern - lenders
need assurance of timely tariff adoption. The Petitioners responded that the procurers
will file a petition before CERC for tariff adoption.
Commission’s Decision: The Commission observes that the 30-day timeline in the
SBD is designed for standard, single-procurer contracts to ensure market momentum.
However, the Commission acknowledges the administrative complexity introduced by
a dual-state procurement model. The extension to 60 days is a pragmatic
administrative cushion that does not materially harm the selected developer's interests
or the sanctity of the bid. Accordingly, the Commission approves the deviation to
extend the timeline for filing the tariff adoption petition to 60 days from the issuance of
the LoA.
31. Deviation 2 (A): Instruments Permitted for Bid Security (EMD)
SBD Mandate (Part B-A 7.2 d): The MoP guidelines permit developers to submit the
Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) using a wide array of financial instruments. These
include Bank Guarantees, Payment on Order instruments/ Letters of Undertaking,
Insurance Surety Bonds (payable unconditionally, similar to a Bank Guarantee), or
any other instrument approved by the Ministry of Finance.
Proposed Tender Clause (4.1 c): The Petitioners propose to strictly limit the
acceptable instruments. It is proposed that the Bidder/s shall provide the Bid Security
only in the form of a bank guarantee issued by a scheduled or nationalised bank.
Stakeholder Comments: Some stakeholders suggested that the Bidder/s be allowed
to submit EMD/PBG in the form of Insurance Surety Bonds or Payment on Order
24

Instrument (Pol) as an eligible instrument for Performance Guarantee, and that a
format for the same, similar to what is provided under Bid Security/EMD. This is in line
with "Tariff-based competitive bidding guidelines for procurement of storage capacity/
stored energy from pumped storage plants" released by MoP dated 26 June 2025.
The Petitioners submitted that since the functioning of insurance surety bonds is
unclear, they have not been included as an option for payment security. Also, for
Payment on Order instruments to be viable, an agreement among MPPMCL, REC,
PFC, and IREDA is required. Since such an agreement is not yet in place, the Payment
on Order instrument has not been included as an option either.
Commission’s Decision: The Commission recognises the Ministry of Power's intent
to diversify financial instruments to reduce developer’s working capital burden.
However, the Petitioners' paramount concern is the immediate enforceability and
liquidity of the security deposit. The restriction on Scheduled/ Nationalised Bank
Guarantees ensures foolproof financial indemnification against frivolous bidding.
Accordingly, the Commission approves the deviation that restricts the submission of
Bid Security (EMD) to Bank Guarantees only.
Deviation 2 (B): Instruments Permitted for Performance Bank Guarantee (PBG)
SBD Mandate (7.3 b): Similar to the EMD provisions, the standard guidelines allow
the Performance Guarantee (PG)—submitted at the time of PPA signing—to take the
form of Bank Guarantees, Payment on Order instruments, Insurance Surety Bonds, or
other approved instruments.
Proposed Tender Clause (6.11): The Petitioners reiterate the restriction, stating that
they shall accept the PBG strictly in the form of an unconditional and irrevocable Bank
Guarantee.
Stakeholder Comments: Some stakeholders suggested that the proposed PSPPA
4.5 (a) Performance Security be modified to also allow the provision of an Insurance
Surety Bond for providing Performance. The Petitioners have not accepted the change
25

suggested. The rationale provided is identical to Deviation 2 (A) and is not being
repeated here for the sake of brevity.
Commission’s Decision: The Commission's reasoning for the EMD applies equally
to the Performance Bank Guarantee (PBG). The PBG and Additional PBG represent
substantial financial leverage intended to ensure the developer's adherence to the
construction timeline and to the subsequent operational performance. However, the
Petitioner should provide the modalities of Additional PBG in the Tender Document.
As such, the Commission approves the amendment proposed in this context.
32. Deviation 3: Liquidated Damages and Contract Termination for Delay in
Commencement
SBD Mandate (Part C-A 9.6): The Petitioners have argued that the standard
guidelines impose an aggressive penalty and termination structure for commissioning
delays. For delays up to 6 months beyond the Scheduled Commencement of Supply
Date (SCSD), the Performance Guarantee is encashed on a per-day basis. Crucially,
if the delay extends beyond six months from the SCSD, the contracted storage
capacity is automatically and permanently reduced to whatever capacity has
commenced supply. The PPA for the balance capacity not commissioned is
immediately terminated.
Proposed Tender Clause (5.15.1 - 5.15.4): The Petitioners have rewritten this Clause
as follows:
a. Instead of terminating at 6 months, the developer is allowed a grace period
extending up to 10 Years from the Effective Date (i.e., 48 months beyond the
72-month SCSD).
b. For delays up to the 8th year, the original PBG is encashed on a per-day, pro-
rata basis.
c. For delays entering into the 8th to 10th year, the developer must furnish an
Additional Performance Bank Guarantee equivalent to two full years of the
Annual Fixed Charge (2 × AFC), which is also subject to per-day encashment.
d. Only if the project fails to commence after the 10th year is the contract for the
balance capacity terminated and the default clauses applied.
26

The Petitioners have submitted that, considering the gestation period of pumped
storage and the possibility of geological surprises during construction , it would not
be prudent to terminate the partial capacity of the project. Further, such a condition
would not be reasonable or in the best interests of the Petitioners and the developer,
given the substantial investment already made to meet evolving national requirements.
Hence, providing extended time will motivate the developers and will increase
participation.
Commission’s Decision: The Commission finds merit in the Petitioners' technical
reasoning. The Commission notes that the Petitioners are not offering a free pass for
delays; the imposition of the Additional Performance Security, equivalent to two years
of AFC, ensures that the developer compensates the procurers for the lost capacity.
This structure aligns with the principles of risk-sharing and infrastructure facilitation.
Accordingly, the Commission approves the deviation to replace the 6-month
termination clause with the proposed staggered extension mechanism.
33. Deviation 4: Extension of Time due to Delay in Connectivity/Grid Access
SBD Mandate: The guidelines state a blanket rule that the SCSD for projects shall be
automatically adjusted to a date thirty (30) days after the readiness of the Delivery
Point, power evacuation infrastructure, and/or the operationalisation of the Grid
Access.
Proposed Tender Clause (5.14 c): The Petitioners have introduced strict
preconditions for this extension. It has been proposed that the delay in CTU/ISTS
connectivity operationalisation will only be treated as a delay beyond the control of the
developer (warranting an SCSD extension), provided that:
a. The developer has complied with the complete application formalities with the
CTU.
b. The developer has adhered to all applicable procedures notified by
CERC/CEA/CTU.
c. The delay is solely a factor attributable to the CTU. Furthermore, the decision
to grant this requisite extension shall be made by the Lead Procurer.
Stakeholder Comments :
Some stakeholders have argued that the 30-day period may be increased to 60 days,
as that is the minimum period required to complete grid-related compliance and
studies before the first time charging. Further, the Developer shall be compensated
27

with an Annual Fixed Charge (AFC) for the period of delay of the start date of
connectivity. The Petitioners have argued that it is imperative to validate the
developer’s efforts in meeting the requirements before providing such an extension.
Commission’s Decision: The Petitioners' modification merely codifies the standard
legal principle that relief is only available to a party that has acted diligently.
Establishing the Lead Procurer's right to verify compliance before adjusting the SCSD
ensures grid discipline and contractual accountability. Accordingly, the Commission
approves the deviation seeking to add preconditions for extensions related to grid
connectivity delays.
34. Deviation 5: Penalty for Under-Achievement of Target Availability.
SBD Mandate (Part-C B 5.2 a): For any deficiency in available capacity or energy,
the standard guidelines direct that the penalty amount shall be equal to one and a half
times (1.5x) the PPA tariff for the shortfall.
Proposed Tender Clause (5.12.1): The Petitioners seek to make an alternative
provision. If the Actual Annual Availability falls below 85%, the penalty is calculated
as: Penalty (Rs Lakh) = (Target Annual Availability % – Actual Annual Availability %)
× (AFC in Rs Lakh per MW per annum) × (Contracted Capacity in MW).
Stakeholder Comments on PSPPA: Some stakeholders sought clarifications on
availability, and the Petitioners provided the required clarifications.
Commission’s Decision: The Commission finds that the SBD’s 1.5x flat tariff penalty
is proposed for refinement to align with the specific financial contours of this contract.
Accordingly, the Commission approves the deviation that introduces an AFC-based
penalty formula for shortfalls in Target Availability.
35. Deviation 6: Stringency in Debarring and Blacklisting
SBD Mandate (7.2): The standard guidelines state that punitive measures, such as
forfeiture of the EMD or debarment, should be undertaken if the successful bidder
fails to execute the PPA within the stipulated time.
Proposed Tender Clause (Appendix I & IX): The Petitioners have proposed that
bidders must sign declarations confirming submission of unaudited balance sheets,
28

complete bank statements, and full disclosures of any ongoing litigation prior to signing
the agreements. If any submitted documents are found to be misleading, or if the
bidder hides pending litigation, or if the bidder withdraws/modifies the bid during the
validity period, the Petitioners are empowered to immediately forfeit the Bid
Security/PBG, reject the LOA, and explicitly blacklist the bidder and all its affiliates
from participating in any future MPPMCL tenders for a strict period of 2 years.
Stakeholder Comments on PSPPA: Some stakeholders submitted that the Bidder
will be selected based on Financial Capacity as demonstrated during the bidding
process. Post-selection of the bidder, a successful submission of unaudited financials
and other financial details is not required. The Bidder may submit its Audited Annual
Financials annually. Therefore, the same should be deleted. The Petitioners have not
accepted the suggestion. The Petitioners have reasoned that, to ensure the bidder
submits true information when submitting the bid, it is essential to obtain an
undertaking certifying the contents of the documents submitted.
Commission’s view: The Commission takes note of the mechanisms that preserve
the sanctity of the competitive bidding process under Section 63. Accordingly, the
Commission approves the deviation, enhancing the debarring, blacklisting, and
disclosure provisions.
36. In light of the analysis and findings recorded above, and in terms of Prayer (e),
the Commission hereby approves the deviations sought by the Petitioners from the
Standard Bidding Guidelines.
37. Petition No. 739/MP/2025, along with IA No. 27/2025, is disposed of in terms
of the above

ORDER
The Petitioner, Udupi Kasargode Transmission Limited (hereinafter referred to
as “UKTL”/ “the Petitioner”) has been granted transmission licence under Section 14
of the Electricity Act, 2003 (hereinafter referred to as ‘the Act’) to establish the 400
kV (UPCL) - Kasargode D/C Line on a Build, Own, Operate and Maintain (BOOM)
basis (hereinafter referred to as “the Project”), the details of which are specified in
the schedule attached to the licence issued vide order dated 24.1.2020 in Petition No.
335/TL/2019. Further, vide the Order dated 28.1.2020 in Petition No. 336/AT/2019,
the Commission adopted the competitively discovered levelised tariff of Rs. 847.44
million per annum for the Project.
2. The Petitioner has filed the present Petition for approval for the creation and
perfection of a Security Interest in terms of Financing Document through the
hypothecation/ mortgage/ charge/ pledge /assignment (as applicable), over all assets,
and all the movable and immovable assets, Transmission Project accounts, Project
Documents (including assignment of transmission licence) etc., both present and
future, in favour of Respondent No. 1, namely Catalyst Trusteeship Limited, for the
benefit of lenders i.e. Societe Generale acting through its GIFT City Branch
Order in Petition No. 87/MP/2026 Page 3

(Respondent No. 2) and Clifford Capital Credit Solutions Pte. Ltd. (Respondent No.
3) (collectively referred to as the “Lenders”), including their respective successors,
transferees, novatees, and assignees for an amount of USD 95,000,000/- or, if lower,
the USD equivalent of Rs. 790 crore in accordance with Clause 5.4.3 of the Facility
Agreement dated 12.11.2025. The Petitioner has made the following prayers:
“(a) admit and list the instant Petition for an urgent hearing;
(b) approve the creation of the security interest by the Petitioner by way of
hypothecation/ mortgage/ charge/ pledge/ lien/ assignment etc. (as
applicable) over all the assets, including the movable and immovable assets,
Project accounts, Project documents (including the transmission license) etc.
of the Petitioner in favour of Respondent No. 1/ Security Trustee (or its
replacement or successor) to secure the Petitioner’s obligations towards
Respondent Nos. 2-3 (the Lenders) under the Facility Agreement dated
12.11.2025;
(c) approve the creation of Security Interest by way of hypothecation/
mortgage/ charge/ pledge/ lien/ assignment etc. over all the assets, including
the movable and immovable assets, Project accounts, Project documents
(including the transmission license) etc. of the Petitioner in favour of
Respondent No. 1/ Security Trustee (or its replacement or successor) to
secure the Petitioner’s obligations towards Respondent Nos. 2-3 (the Lenders)
under the Facility Agreement dated 12.11.2025 and for their subsequent
transferees, assigns, novatees and substitutes thereof in respect to the
Project; and
(d) pass any such other relief as the Commission deems fit and appropriate in
the facts and circumstances of the case.”
Background
3. The Petitioner, for the purpose of refinancing the project, requested Lenders
for which the Lenders have agreed to provide the financial assistance to the tune of
USD 95,000,000/- or, if lower, the USD equivalent of Rs. 790 crore by way of term
loan facility for the Project. For this purpose, the Petitioner and Respondent No.2,
Société Générale and Respondent No.3, Clifford Capital Credit Solutions Pte. Limited
have appointed Respondent No. 1, namely, Catalyst Trusteeship Limited, as a
Security Trustee (hereinafter referred to as “the Security Trustee‟), who has agreed
Order in Petition No. 87/MP/2026 Page 4

to act as Security Trustee for the Lenders and has entered into the Security Trustee
Agreement dated 18.11.2025.
Submissions of the Petitioners
4. The Petitioner has mainly submitted as under:
a. The Petitioner, for the purpose of financing the project, had earlier
availed financial assistance of Rs. 580.05 crore in the form of a rupee term
loan facility from the previous lender, i.e., REC Limited, through a Rupee Term
Loan Agreement dated 9.4.2021. Pursuant to the Security Trustee Agreement
dated 9.4.2021, at the request of the Petitioner, the lender agreed to provide
a loan of Rs. 580.05 crore (including LoC limit of Rs. 406.035 crore) for the
Project on the terms and conditions contained in the Rupee Term Loan
Agreement and Security Trustee Agreement. The Commission, vide its order
dated 23.10.2021 in Petition No. 184/MP/2021, accorded in-principle approval
allowing the Petitioner to create a security interest in favour of Catalyst
Trusteeship Limited, by way of mortgage/hypothecation on the Project assets.
b. Subsequently, to refinance the Project more efficiently, the Petitioner has
now availed financial assistance from Respondent Nos. 2 and 3, as per the
terms and conditions contained in the Facility Agreement dated 12.11.2025
for a sum of USD 95,000,000/- or, if lower, the USD equivalent of Rs. 790
crore.
c. Catalyst Trusteeship Limited was appointed as the Security Trustee in
terms of the Security Trustee Agreement executed on 18.11.2025.
d. The Petitioner has fully prepaid its entire loan to REC Limited by raising
a loan from Lenders. REC Limited has issued a 'No Dues Certificate' dated
Order in Petition No. 87/MP/2026 Page 5

1.12.2025, certifying that the aforesaid loan facility has been repaid in full by
the Petitioner.
5. The Petitioner has submitted that pursuant to the terms of the Facility
Agreement, the secured obligations are secured by:
a) The Transaction Security will rank pari passu by way of first charge in
favour of the Finance Parties and any Other Hedge Counterparty with no
preference or priority amongst them.
b) On or prior to the date falling 45 days from the first Utilisation Date, the
Borrower shall procure that the Promoter shall create a Security Interest in
favour of the Security Trustee over the receivables pertaining to Shareholder
Loans pursuant to the terms of the Shareholder Loan Security Agreement in
relation to the Promoter and shall do all such things as are required to perfect
such Security Interest.
c) On or prior to the first Utilisation Date, the Borrower shall procure that
the Promoter shall execute the Pledge Agreement set out in paragraph (a) of
the definition of Pledge Agreement to create a Security Interest in favour of
the Security Trustee over the equity shares representing at least 100% of the
equity share capital of the Borrower (on fully diluted basis) and carrying at
least 100% (one hundred percent) voting rights in the Borrower pursuant to
the terms of that Pledge Agreement (other than the Nominee Shareholder).
d) On or prior to the date falling 45 days from the first Utilisation Date, the
Borrower shall (and shall procure that the Promoter shall) do all such things
to create and perfect the Security Interest over (a) the equity shares
representing at least 100% of the equity share capital of the Borrower (on fully
diluted basis) and carrying at least 100% (one hundred percent) voting rights
in the Borrower pursuant to the set out in paragraph (a) of the definition of
Pledge Agreement (other than the Nominee Shareholder); and (b) the
receivables pertaining to the Shareholder Loans pursuant to the terms of the
Shareholder Loan Security Agreement in relation to the Promoter.
e) On or prior to the date falling 8 months after the first Utilisation Date, the
Borrower shall obtain the approval under Section 17(3) of the Electricity Act
Order in Petition No. 87/MP/2026 Page 6

2003 from CERC/SERC in relation to the Security Interest set out in Clauses
23.13.6(A) to 23.13.6(D) below in a form and manner satisfactory to the
Agent. The Security Interest required to be created under the Security
Documents set out in Clause 23.13.6 shall be subject to terms approved
pursuant to this CERC/SERC approval.
f) On or prior to the date falling nine months after the first Utilisation Date,
the Borrower shall:
(A) Create a Security Interest in favour of the Security Trustee over all
the immovable properties (other than the Project Site), present and future,
of the Borrower pursuant to the terms of the Mortgage Document;
(B) Create a Security Interest in favour of the Security Trustee over all
the movables properties, including movable Project Assets, movable
plant and machinery, machinery spares, equipment, tools and
accessories, furniture, fixtures, vehicles, stocks and all other movable
assets, book debts, bills, monies, operating cash flows, receivables,
commissions, claims of all kinds, stocks including consumables and other
general stores, revenues of whatsoever nature and wherever arising,
present and future, intangibles, goodwill and uncalled capital, present and
future, of the Borrower pursuant to the terms of the Deed of
Hypothecation;
(C) create a Security Interest in favour of the Security Trustee over all
accounts of the Borrower, including, the Trust and Retention Account and
the Sub-Account(s) (excluding the Distribution Account), or any account
created for any reserve(s) to be created and maintained (or any account
in substitution thereof) that may be opened in accordance with the Trust
and Retention Account Agreement (other than the Distribution Account)
and the Financing Documents, or any of the other Project Documents and
all funds from time to time deposited therein, the receivables and all
Permitted Investments or other securities representing all amounts
credited to the Trust and Retention Account, any letter of credit and other
reserves of the Borrower present and future wherever maintained
pursuant to the terms of the Deed of Hypothecation;
(D) create a Security Interest in favour of the Security Trustee over:
Order in Petition No. 87/MP/2026 Page 7

(i) all the right, title, interest, benefit, claims and demand
whatsoever of the Borrower in the Project Documents (other
than leasehold rights pertaining to the Project Site, and including
the TSA to the extent permitted under the TSA);
(ii) all the rights, title, interest, benefits, claims and demands
whatsoever of the Borrower in the Project Authorizations, to the
extent permitted under Applicable Law;
(iii) all the rights titles, interest, benefits, licenses, claims and
demands, whatsoever of the Borrower in any letter of credit,
guarantee, performance bond, corporate guarantee and bank
guarantee provided by any party to the Project Documents in
relation to the Project; and
(iv) all the rights, title, interest, benefits, claims and demands
whatsoever of the Borrower in all insurance contracts and
Insurance Proceeds,
in each case, pursuant to the terms of the Deed of
Hypothecation; and do all such things to perfect the Security
Interest created pursuant to the Security Documents set out in
paragraphs (A) to (D) above (including the delivery to the Agent
of any relevant Notices of Assignment and Consents to
Assignment).
g) Subject to Legal Reservations, each of the Security Documents and the
Security Interests over the assets created thereunder in favour of the Security
Trustee for the benefit of the Finance Parties shall be in full force and effect
from and after the time of execution and delivery thereof.
h) The Borrower shall maintain and preserve the Security Interests created by
the Security Documents and the priority of such Security Interests and shall
do all things necessary to ensure that any Project Assets acquired by the
Borrower after the date of this Agreement are made subject to the Security
Documents promptly after they are acquired. So long as any monies remain
due and outstanding to the Lenders and/or the Hedge Counterparties, the
Borrower undertakes to promptly notify the Agent in writing of all its
acquisitions of immovable properties for the Project.
i) The Borrower shall undertake all necessary steps to ensure the perfection
and/or realization of such Security Interests in place from time to time,
including the execution of any transfer, conveyance, assignment, or
assurance of any Project Assets and the giving of notice, order or direction
Order in Petition No. 87/MP/2026 Page 8

and the making of any registration which the Security Trustee may require in
accordance with (and within the time periods required under) the terms of the
Finance Documents and Applicable Law.
j) The Borrower shall provide and/or procure all necessary Authorizations,
documents, opinions, assurances, and any other approvals or registration
including from the RBI, which the Security Trustee considers to be necessary
in connection with the creation and perfection of the Security Interests or
which are required to be obtained by the Borrower, the Sponsor and/or any
Shareholder (as the case may be) under applicable law.
Hearing dated 18.2.2026
6. The Petition was taken up for hearing on 18.2.2026 after notice to the
Respondents. Vide Record of Proceedings (hereinafter referred to as “RoP”) dated
18.2.2026, the Respondents were granted an opportunity to file their respective
replies, and the Petitioner was directed to file the information called for vide letter
dated 29.1.2026.
7. In compliance with the RoP dated 18.2.2026, the Petitioner has placed on
record the financial plan against the estimated project cost as on the date of filing of
the Petition, i.e., 10.1.2026.
Hearing dated 25.3.2026
8. During the course of the hearing, the learned counsel for the Petitioner
submitted that vide RoP dated 18.2.2026, notice was issued and an opportunity was
granted to the Respondents to file their respective replies. However, no reply has
been filed by any of the Respondents to date. The learned counsel further submitted
that pursuant to the directions issued vide the RoP dated 18.2.2026, the Petitioner
Order in Petition No. 87/MP/2026 Page 9

has complied with the said directions vide affidavit dated 16.2.2026. The learned
counsel accordingly prayed for appropriate directions in the matter.
9. Vide RoP dated 25.3.2026, it was noted that the Petitioner's response filed vide
affidavit dated 16.2.2026 to the Commission’s letter dated 29.1.2026 was insufficient.
Accordingly, the Petitioner was further directed to specifically comply with earlier
directions and submit a structured Financial Plan in the prescribed format.
10. In compliance with the RoP dated 25.3.2026, the Petitioner submitted the
requisite information called for by way of an affidavit dated 6.4.2026.
Analysis and Decision
11. We have considered the submissions made by the Petitioner and perused the
documents available on the record. The Commission, vide Order dated 23.10.2021 in
Petition No. 184/MP/2021, accorded in-principle approval allowing the Petitioner to
create a security interest in favour of Catalyst Trusteeship Limited for the benefit of
REC Limited. REC Limited has issued a 'No Dues Certificate' dated 1.12.2025,
certifying that the aforesaid loan facility has been repaid in full by the Petitioner. The
Petitioner approached the Lenders, namely, Societe Generale acting through its GIFT
City Branch (Respondent No. 2) and Clifford Capital Credit Solutions Pte. Ltd.
(Respondent No. 3), for the purpose of refinancing the Project. The lender has agreed
to grant financial assistance of USD 95,000,000/- or, if lower, the USD equivalent of
Rs. 790 crore only.
12. The Petitioner has submitted that it had appointed Catalyst Trusteeship Limited
as a Security Trustee, who agreed to act as a Security Trustee and had entered into
Order in Petition No. 87/MP/2026 Page 10

a Facility Agreement dated 12.11.2025 and a Security Trustee Agreement dated
18.11.2025. As per the Facility Agreement, the estimated cost of the Project is Rs.
1417 crore. In terms of the financing plan submitted by the Petitioner, the Project shall
be funded through debt of Rs. 790 crore and promoter contribution of Rs. 627 crore.
Breakup of Financing Plan is as under:
Estimated Project In Rs. Means of Finance In Rs.
Crore Crore
Equity 45.01
Promoter
CCDs 107.33
Estimated Project Cost 1417 Contribution
Unsecured 474.66
Loan
Project Debt 790
Total 1417
13. The Petitioner has submitted the details of sources and application of funds for
implementation of the Project as on 31.12.2025, duly supported by the affidavit and
the Chartered Accountant’s Certificate. As per the submissions, the total funds
deployed for the Project amount to Rs. 797.62 crore, which have been arranged
through Equity share capital, Promoters loan, Compulsory Convertible Debentures,
and funded Term Loan and have been utilized towards various components of the
Project.
14. The transmission projects are capital-intensive projects requiring huge capital
investment. These projects are financed through the equity of the project developer,
loans from financial institutions, and/or the issuance of debentures and/or the
issuance of Senior Secured Notes, which is a form of loan. It is a normal practice
followed by financial institutions/ the banking industry to ask for sufficient security from
the borrower to back the loan in order to mitigate the credit risk of the lenders. In the
instant case, the Commission, vide its order dated 23.10.2021 in Petition No.
Order in Petition No. 87/MP/2026 Page 11

184/MP/2021, had granted in-principle approval for the creation of a security interest
in favour of the Security Trustee, i.e., Catalyst Trusteeship Limited. The Petitioner,
Societe Generale acting through its GIFT City Branch (Respondent No. 2) and Clifford
Capital Credit Solutions Pte. Ltd. (Respondent No. 3) and Respondent No. 1 (the
Security Trustee) have executed a Facility Agreement dated 12.11.2025 and Security
Trustee Agreement dated 18.11.2025 for the loan of USD 95,000,000/- (USD Ninety-
Five Million Only) or if lower, the USD equivalent of Rs 790 crore only.
15. The Petitioner has submitted that, in terms of the Financing documents, the
Petitioner is required to create a Security Interest on a first-charge basis for the lender.
The Petitioner has submitted that under the Facility Agreements and on enforcement
of a security interest, it shall be lawful for the lender and its assigns, transferees, and
novates to enter into and take possession of the assets/properties
mortgaged/hypothecated/charges assigned for their benefits and substitute
themselves or any one of them or its nominees for the Petitioner under any or all of
the project document(s). Article 15.2.2 of the TSA provides as under:
“15.2.2 However, the TSP may create any encumbrance over all or part of the
receivables, or the Project Assets of the Project in favour of the Lenders or the
Lenders' Representative on their behalf, as security for amounts payable
under the Financing Agreements and any other amounts agreed by the
Parties.
Provided that:
(i) the Lenders or the Lenders' Representative on their behalf shall have
entered into the Financing Agreements and agreed in writing to the
provisions of this Agreement; and
(ii) any encumbrance granted by the TSP in accordance with this Article
15.2.2 shall contain provisions pursuant to which the Lenders or the
Lender's Representative on their behalf agrees unconditionally with the
TSP to release from such encumbrances upon payment by the TSP to
the Lenders of all amounts due under the Financing Agreements.”
Order in Petition No. 87/MP/2026 Page 12

In accordance with the above provision, the Transmission Service Provider has
been allowed to create an encumbrance over all or part of the receivables, Letters of
Credit, or other assets of the Project in favour of the lenders or the lenders’
representatives or their representatives, as security for amounts payable under the
Financing Agreements and any other amounts agreed by the parties.
16. Article 15.3 of the TSA provides as under:
“15.3 Substitution Rights of the Lenders:
15.3.1 The TSP would need to operate and maintain the Project under the
provisions of the Transmission License granted by the Appropriate
Commission and the provisions of this Agreement and can not assign the
Transmission License' or transfer the Project or part thereof to any person by
sale, lease, exchange or otherwise, without the prior approval of the
Appropriate Commission.
15.3.2 However, in the case of default by the TSP in debt repayments, the
Appropriate Commission may, on an application from, the Lenders, assign the
Transmission License to the nominee of the Lenders subject to the fulfilment
of the qualification requirements and provisions of the Central Electricity
Regulatory Commission (Procedure, terms and Conditions for grant of
Transmission License and other related matters) Regulations, 2009 or as
amended from time to time.”
17. Sub-sections (3) and (4) of Section 17 of the Act provide as under:
“17. (3) No licensee shall any time assign his licence or transfer his utility, or
any part hereof, by sale, lease, exchange or otherwise without the prior
approval of the Appropriate Commission.
(4) Any agreement relating to any transaction specified in sub-section (1) or
sub-section (3), unless made with the prior approval of the Appropriate
Commission, shall be void.”
As per the above provisions, a licensee is required to obtain Commission’s
approval for assigning its licence or transferring its utility or any part thereof by way of
sale, lease, exchange or otherwise, and entering into an agreement relating to any of
these transactions.
Order in Petition No. 87/MP/2026 Page 13

18. Accordingly, we accord approval for the substitution of new Lenders, who have
agreed to refinance the projects/ transmission assets and accord in-principle approval
for the creation of a security interest in favour of Security Trustee, namely, Catalyst
Trusteeship Limited, for the benefit of the Lenders. In this regard, the Petitioner has
placed on record the relevant documents pertaining to the involvement of Societe
Generale acting through its GIFT City Branch (Respondent No. 2) and Clifford Capital
Credit Solutions Pte. Ltd. (Respondent No. 3) as the new lenders and the creation of
a security interest in favour of Catalyst Trusteeship Limited, acting as the Security
Trustee on behalf of the new lenders, have been duly placed on record. The Petitioner
is directed to submit a signed copy of the Indenture of Mortgage for the Project
immediately after its execution.
19. This approval is being granted with the condition that the transmission licence
granted by the Commission to the Petitioner cannot be assigned in favour of the
Security Trustee or nominee of the lender without prior approval of the Commission
at the time of creating rights in favour of such a nominee. Before agreeing to the
assignment of the licence and the assets of the Petitioner to the nominee of the lender,
the Commission will evaluate such a nominee`s expertise in the development, design,
construction, operation, and maintenance of the transmission lines and their ability to
execute the Project and undertake the transmission of electricity. The licensee,
lender, security trustee, and nominee shall accordingly be jointly required to approach
the Commission to seek approval. This will allow the Commission to satisfy itself of
the circumstances necessitating such a transfer. This decision of ours is in
accordance with Regulation 8 of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission
(Procedure, Terms and Conditions for grant of Transmission Licence and other
related matters) Regulations, 2024, which reads as under:
Order in Petition No. 87/MP/2026 Page 14

“8. Assignment of Licence: In case of default by the licensee in debt repayment,
the Commission may, on an application made by the lenders, assign the
licence to a nominee of the lenders.”
20. In the event of a default by the licensee regarding debt repayment, the
Commission may, upon a joint application submitted by the licensee, lender, Security
Trustee, and their nominee, consider granting approval for the assignment of the
licence to a nominee, contingent upon the satisfactory completion of due diligence
procedures. Consequently, it is imperative to obtain explicit prior approval from the
Commission for the assignment of the licence to the nominee of the Security Trustee
or for the transfer of any assets to them. Finally, the Petitioner must submit the
financial documents and statements in accordance with the Commission's directives.
21. Petition No. 87/MP/2026 is disposed of in terms of the above.

The Petitioner, Airpower Windfarms Pvt. Ltd (AWPL), has filed an instant Petition
seeking direction to quash/ set aside the letter dated 03.09.2025 issued by the Central
Transmission Utility of India Limited (CTUIL), whereby the 175 MW connectivity granted
to the Petitioner has been revoked under Regulation 11B (1) of the Central Electricity
Regulatory Commission (General Network Access) Regulations 2022 amended from
time to time (in short, the ‘2022 GNA Regulations’).
2. The Petitioner has made the following prayers in the present Petition:
(a) Quash/ set aside the letter dated 03.09.2025 issued by the Central Transmission Utility of India
Limited to the Petitioner and direct the said Respondent to reinstate/ restore the connectivity of
175 MW of the Petitioner, in terms as stated in the present Petition;
(b) Direct the Respondent, Central Transmission Utility of India Limited to refund the amount of INR
4.00 Crores submitted by the Petitioner on 04.09.2025; and
(c) Pass such other or further order(s) as this hon’ble commission may deem fit in the facts
circumstances of the present case.
3. The Petitioner has also filed IA No.85/2025, with the following prayer(s):
(a) Direct CTUIL to stay the revocation of the connectivity granted to the Applicant/ Petitioner and to
not allocate or release the capacity of said connectivity to any other applicant(s);
(b) Direct CTUIL to not encash the Bank Guarantees bearing BG Nos. 15300100017196 amounting
to INR 50,00,000/- (INR Fifty Lakhs Only), BG No. 15300100017197 amounting to Rs.
3,50,00,000.00/- (INR Three Crores and Fifty Lakhs Only) and BG No. 15300100016715
amounting to INR 17,50,00,000/- (INR Seventeen Crores Fifty Lakhs Only), furnished by the
Applicant / Petitioner to the Respondent;
(c) Direct CTUIL to not take any coercive action in the context of revocation of the connectivity and/or
encashment of the BGs in any manner whatsoever, till the pendency of the present Petition;
(d) Permit the Petitioner to carry out all commissioning activities including, but not limited to First
Time Charging and Trial Run Operation in respect of their Project; and
(e) Pass such other or further order(s) as this Hon'ble Commission may deem fit in the facts and
circumstances of the present case.
4. Petitioner vide IA No. 86/2025 has made the following prayer(s):
(a) Allow the urgent listing of the accompanying Petition and Application seeking Interim Relief filed
by the Applicant; and
(b) Pass such other or further order(s) as this Hon'ble Commission may deem fit in the facts and
circumstances of the present case.
The above IA 86/2025 (Diary No. 464/2025), filed for urgent listing of matter, having
served its purpose, was disposed of vide ROP for hearing dated 09.09.2025.

7. The Petitioner, vide IA 85/2025 dated 05.09.2025, has reiterated the earlier submissions
and additionally has made the following submissions:
(a) CTUIL, vide its letter dated 03.09.2025, has erroneously stated that since the
timeline for submission of revised documents by the Applicant/ Petitioner was till
12.07.2025 and no rectified/ revised documents were submitted by the Applicant/
Petitioner till 12.07.2025, the 175 MW connectivity granted to the Applicant/

CTUIL if the present status quo prior to revocation is maintained.

Rejoinder by the Petitioner:
15. The Petitioner vide submission dated 30.01.2025 filed a rejoinder to the reply of CTUIL
in IA 9/2026 as under:
a) Since the status-quo order(s) passed by this Commission on 10.09.2025 and
16.10.2025, were passed “in the meantime” “until further order(s)”. The aforesaid
status quo direction was therefore continuing even after the present petition was
reserved for final orders on 11.11.2025. It is established law that such status quo
orders can only be understood to have been vacated if an order expressly vacating
the same was passed by this Hon’ble Commission. When this Commission issued
notice and granted ad-interim relief “in the meanwhile”, it is obvious that the ad-
interim relief was to operate till the order of stay was specifically vacated by this
Commission.

the contract is not a ground to restrain the enforcement of Bank guarantees or Letters
of Credit. However, this court made two exceptions for grant of an order of injunction
to restrain the enforcement of a Bank Guarantee or a Letter of Credit. (i) Fraud
committed in the notice of the bank which would vitiate the very foundation of
guarantee; (ii) injustice of the kind which would make it impossible for the guarantor to
reimburse himself.
Except under these circumstances, the courts should not readily issue injunction to
restrain the realization of a Bank Guarantee or a Letter of Credit. So far as the first
exception is concerned, i.e. of fraud, one has to satisfy the court that the fraud in
connection with the Bank Guarantee or Letter of Credit would vitiate the very
foundation of such a Bank Guarantee or Letter of Credit. So far as the second
exception is concerned, this court has held in that decision that it relates to cases
where allowing encashment of an unconditional bank guarantee would result in
irretrievable harm or injustice to one of the parties concerned. While dealing with the
case of fraud, this court in the case of U.P. Coop. Federation Ltd. Vs. Singh
Consultants and Engineers (P) Ltd. (1988) 1 SCC 174 held as follows:
The fraud must be of an egregious nature such as to vitiate the entire underlying
transaction. While coming to a conclusion as to what constitutes fraud, this court in the
above case quoted with approval the observations of Sir John Donaldson, M.R. in
Bolivinter Oil SA V/s. Chase Manhattan Bank (1984) 1 All ER 351 at p. 352 which is
as follows, The wholly exceptional case where an injunction may be granted is where
it is proved that the bank knows that any demand for payment already made or which
may thereafter be made will clearly be fraudulent. But the evidence must be clear both
Order in Petition No. 809/MP/2025 along with IA 85/2025 and IA 09/2026 Page 28

as to the fact of fraud and as to the bank’s knowledge. It would certainly not normally
be sufficient that this rests on the uncorroborated statement of the customer, for
irreparable damage can be done to a bank’s Credit in the relatively brief time which
must elapse between the granting of such an injunction and an application by the bank
to have it charged.”
As per the above, the status quo does not interdict the invocation of unconditional
bank guarantees unless the invocation is vitiated by fraud or special equities.
37. We note that in the instant case, Connectivity was revoked on 4.9.2025. ‘Status quo’ was
directed vide various ROPs. Considering the Order of the APTEL as well as the Hon`ble
Supreme Court, we are of the considered view that the encashment of LAND BG is not
unreasonable. We note that CTUIL has submitted that it inadvertently failed to encash
LAND BG, which was due for revocation as per CTUIL. When it revokes the Connectivity,
we are of the view that CTUIL should avoid such inadvertent errors and apply the
principles uniformly in all cases.
38. We have already directed under issue No 1 for the return of the amount deposited against
LAND BG and Conn BGs be returned after adjusting the compensation amount.
39. Issue No.2 is answered in terms of the above.
40. Other prayers of the Petitioner regarding non-coercive action against additional BGs are
addressed in light of the decisions above.
41. Petition No. 809/MP/2025, along with IA No. 85/2025 and IA No. 09/2026, is disposed of
in terms of the above.
Sd/- Sd/- Sd/- Sd/-
(Ravinder Singh Dhillon) (Harish Dudani) (Ramesh Babu V.) (Jishnu Barua)

CENTRAL ELECTRICITY REGULATORY COMMISSION
NEW DELHI

In the Matter Of:
Petition under Section 79(1)(c) and (f) of the Electricity Act read with Regulation 41
and 42 of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Connectivity and General
Network Access to the inter-State Transmission System) Regulations, 2022 seeking
appropriate directions to CTUIL for allowing the conversion of the Connectivity granted
under the Land-BG route to LOA/PPA route.
AND
In the Matter Of:
1. Ganeko One Energy Pvt. Ltd. (Ganeko-1)

IRCON International Tower, Tower 1,
