ORDER
The Petitioner, Tata Power Company Ltd. (“TPCL”), a generating
company, filed the petition for the determination of adverse financial impact
under Section 11(2) read with Section 79 of the Electricity Act, 2003 (“the Act”),
wherein the Petitioner also sought interim relief pending final adjudication. The
Respondent No.1, Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Ltd (“GUVNL”), represents the
interest of Gujarat Discoms. The Respondent No. 2, Punjab State Power
Corporation Ltd (“PSPCL”) is responsible for electricity distribution and
generation in Punjab. The Respondent No. 3, Maharashtra State Electricity
Distribution Company Ltd. (“MSEDCL”), is a distribution licensee responsible
for electricity distribution in Maharashtra. The Respondents Nos. 4 to 6 are the
distribution licensees of Rajasthan, and the Respondents Nos. 7 & 8 are the
distribution licensees of Haryana. The Respondent No. 9 represents the Central
Government through the Ministry of Power.
2. The Petitioner had filed this Petition on account of adverse financial impact
arising due to the implementation of the direction dated 20.2.2023 (“2023
directions”) issued by the Central Government under Section 11(1) of the Act
for the period between 1.3.2023 to 15.6.2023, and extended time to time. The
Order in Petition No. 179/MP/2023 Page 3 of 49

2023 directions are pari materia with the earlier directions on 5.5.2022 (“2022
directions”) wherein the Commission had decided the methodology for the
determination of adverse financial impact vide order dated 3.1.2023 in Petition
No. 128/MP/2022. During the operation of the 2023 directions, the petitioner
sought interim relief to make the payment of the Interim or Provisional Tariff in
respect of the 2023 directions. Since the Commission had already decided the
methodology of adverse financial impact in 2022 directions and the 2023
directions were pari materia to earlier directions, the interim relief was sought
by the petitioner based on the methodology decided by the Commission in its
final Order dated 3.1.2023 in respect of 2022 directions and also prayed to issue
a direction to Respondents 7 and 8 to furnish a revolving Letter of Credit. The
adverse financial impact under section 11(2) of the Act may involve other
components of the tariff. In the instant case, our scope is limited to the energy
charge rate (“ECR”) component.
Order of CERC dated 10.3.2025
3. On 10.3.2025, the Commission passed an order deciding the interim relief
in two parts. In the first part, the Commission dealt with the examination of the
powers of the Commission to grant the interim relief and fulfilment of the various
conditions for the grant of interim relief laid down by the Hon’ble Supreme Court
in Makers Development Services (P) Ltd. v. M. Visvesvaraya Industrial
Research & Development Centre, [(2012) 1 SCC 735]. Three conditions laid
down by the Hon’ble Supreme Court are: (i) whether the Petitioner has made
out a prima facie case, (ii) whether the balance of convenience is in favour of
Order in Petition No. 179/MP/2023 Page 4 of 49

the Petitioner, and (iii) whether the Petitioner would suffer irreparable injury if
interim relief is not granted. The Commission had examined these conditions
based on the submission placed on record by the parties. The Commission held
that all the tests for the grant of interim relief are satisfied in this case, and the
Petitioner is entitled to protection by way of interim relief.
4. After examination of admissibility of interim relief in the first part, the
Commission did not prefer to award the interim relief on ad hoc basis but went
into detailed computation for the purpose of interim relief and considered all the
arguments of the parties on each individual parameter, analysed elements of
the energy charge rate as submitted by the Petitioner and the submission of the
Respondents, and the basis of the rate notified by the Committee. In the
second part of the order, the Commission decided on the methodology for
quantifying the interim relief, wherein the Commission examined individual
parameters such as the GCV of blended coal, the loss of GCV during transit
and handling, ocean freight, and handling charges. Also, the direction to
Respondent Nos. 7 & 8, with regard to the opening of LC for fixed charges, were
issued.
APTEL Judgment dated 31.10.2025
5. Respondent Nos. 1, 2 and 4 to 6 have filed Appeal No. 122 of 2025 & IA No.
635 of 2025, 129 of 2025 & IA No. 703 of 2025 & 169 of 2025 & IA NO. 723 of
2025 before the APTEL challenging the order of the Commission dated
10.3.2025. Learned counsel for the Respondent No. 3 submitted that although
the Commission’s order dated 10.3.2025 is challenged, no interim directions or
Order in Petition No. 179/MP/2023 Page 5 of 49

stay have been granted by the APTEL, and the said appeal is currently pending
before the APTEL. In view of the same, Respondent No. 3 has complied with
the Commission’s order dated 10.3.2025 by paying the amount as per the
decision in the said order.
6. On 31.10.2025, the APTEL examined the order of the Commission in detail,
allowing the interim relief as decided by the Commission. The APTEL passed
an order of limited remand directing the CERC to compute the entitlement of
the Petitioner in accordance with its earlier order dated 10.3.2025. APTEL, in
its order, has examined the various aspects as follows:
a) Powers of the Commission u/s conferred under section 94(2) of the
Electricity Act, 2003, to grant interim relief, can be extended to
proceedings under section 11(2) of the Act.
b) Appellate power to interfere with an interim order passed by the
Commission, and whether the impugned order is in the nature of an
interim mandatory injunction;
c) Has the Petitioner failed to satisfy the tests for the grant of interim relief
by the CERC, and are there fallacies in the impugned order relating to
computation?;
d) Consideration of one cost element, namely ‘FOB cost of imported coal’,
to decide on the alleged adverse financial impact on Energy Charge Rate
(ECR) for the grant of interim relief.
e) Is the FOB cost supported by a Chartered Accountant’s certificate, and
has the Chartered Accountant examined the decision of the weighted
Order in Petition No. 179/MP/2023 Page 6 of 49

average method of GCV ?. APTEL also dealt with the issues of the
Petitioner’s entitlement to anything other than the PPA Tariff. APTEL
observed that in case any such contention is urged by GUVNL during
the hearing of the main petition, the CERC shall consider the same in
accordance with law.
f) Examined the issue of non-consideration of the counterclaims of the
GUVNL and their plea to set off. In this regard, the APTEL observed the
patent error in the tables in Para 65 (c) and 65 (e) of the order showing
the price of 13 shipments of imported coal in November, 2023 as its FOB
value, though 7 of them were on CFR basis and included freight, and
which ought to have been converted from CFR to FOB basis by
excluding freight therefrom in order to arrive at its FOB value, none of
the other objections taken on behalf of the Appellants, on the conclusion
of CERC that TPCL had made out a prima-facie case, are so grave as
to warrant interference in an appeal preferred against an interlocutory
order.
g) After dealing with the above aspects, the APTEL passed an order of
limited remand directing the CERC to compute the entitlement of TPCL,
in terms of its earlier order dated 10.3.2025 (wherein, among others, the
FoB price of imported coal was effectively determined at 84.90 USD/
MT), after hearing parties on either side in this regard.
7. The APTEL, vide order dated 31.10.2025, directed the Commission to
compute the Petitioner's entitlement, in terms of its earlier order dated
Order in Petition No. 179/MP/2023 Page 7 of 49

10.3.2025 (wherein, among others, the FoB price of imported coal was
effectively determined at 84.90 USD/MT), after hearing the parties on this
aspect. The relevant part is extracted below:
“XIII. CONCLUSION
…..
……
As noted hereinabove, a substantial portion of the interim relief sought, i.e. for
payment of interim/ Provisional Tariff towards ECR, represents the FOB price
of imported coal. The interim relief granted by the CERC is, effectively,
considering the FoB price of imported coal to be 84.90 USD/MT which is lower
than the FoB price as computed by GUVNL itself as 85.37 USD/MT. As what
has been granted as interim relief, by the impugned order of the CERC, is lower
than GUVNL’s computation of FoB price of imported coal, we see no reason to
direct the CERC to re-examine the afore-said issues, more so as the
Appellants’ interests are being adequately safeguarded on TPCL being directed
to furnish an unconditional bank guarantee as security for the amount which the
Appellants are required to pay them in terms of the impugned order.
We, therefore, pass an order of limited remand directing the CERC to compute
the entitlement of TPCL, in terms of its earlier order dated 10.03.2025 (wherein,
among others, the FoB price of imported coal was effectively determined at
84.90 USD/MT), after hearing parties on either side in this regard. We make it
clear that the hearing to be afforded is only with respect to computation of the
amounts payable in terms of the order dated 10.03.2025 for the period from
16.04.2023 till 10.03.2025, and not on merits. On the said amount being
computed and determined by the CERC, TPCL shall, in terms of its
submissions before this Tribunal, furnish unconditional bank guarantees from a
scheduled bank, for the entire amount determined by the CERC as payable to
it in terms of the order dated 10.03.2025. Further, the said Bank Guarantees
shall be renewed periodically and kept alive during the pendency of the main
Petition before the CERC. The Appellants shall, within two weeks of receipt of
the unconditional bank guarantees, make payment of the amounts, determined
by CERC, to TPCL.
……”
8. The APTEL, in its order, clarified that the hearing to be afforded shall be
limited only with respect to the computation of the amounts payable in terms of
the order dated 10.3.2025 for the period from 16.4.2023 till 10.3.2025, and not
on merits. Accordingly, in terms of the APTEL judgment dated 31.10.2015, the
Order in Petition No. 179/MP/2023 Page 8 of 49

matter is taken up by the Commission for the computation of entitlement by
determining the FoB price of imported coal.
Remand Proceedings before the Commission:
Submission by the Petitioner
9. The Petitioner, in its affidavit dated 27.11.2025, made a submission pursuant
to the liberty granted by this Hon’ble Commission vide Record of Proceedings
dated 25.11.2025, placing on record the detailed computation of ECR. The
Petitioner has also placed on record the order dated 31.10.2025 of the APTEL
in Appeal Nos. 122 of 2025, 129 of 2025, and 169 of 2025, computation of ECR
as per the methodology laid down by the Commission in its order, along with
shipment-wise and month-wise data, including weighted-average FOB prices
based on actual quantities for the relevant period. Also submitted the
voluminous data on month-wise total energy generated, energy scheduled by
the Procurers, energy sold at the exchange under the Real Time Market and
Day Ahead Market, revenue realised through sale of energy in short-term/
exchange and auxiliary power consumption. The Petitioner has made a further
submission vide affidavit dated 20.1.2026 pursuant to the liberty granted during
the hearing on 8.1.2026 to file a brief note, limited to addressing the objections
raised by the Respondents. Brief of the Petitioner’s submission is as under:
a) All relevant data/ documents/ information for the period 16.4.2023 to
31.8.2024, forming the basis of the Interim Order, are already on record.
The computation placed on record by way of the Affidavit dated
27.11.2025 is in strict conformity with the methodology laid down by this
Order in Petition No. 179/MP/2023 Page 9 of 49

Hon’ble Commission in its Order dated 3.1.2023 passed in Petition No.
128/MP/2022.
b) During Directions 2023, certain coal shipments were procured on a CIF
basis and not on an FOB basis. For such shipments, the freight
component is zero in the ECR computation. Accordingly, there is no
double calculation of freight, and ultimately, it is the CIF value which is
considered
c) Adverse financial impact in the order dated 3.1.2023 passed by this
Commission held that in case of shipments procured on FOB basis, the
transportation and insurance charges will be added to work out the CIF
cost in USD/MT. However, for shipments procured on a CIF basis, the
CIF cost of coal shall be considered. In the computation of ECR, whether
the coal cost is calculated as FOB + Freight & Insurance or as a single
consolidated CIF value is considered, the ECR remains the same.
d) GUVNL’s contention, vide affidavit dated 5.1.2026, primarily in relation to
the manner of treatment of FOB vis-à-vis CIF/CFR values for certain coal
shipments considered in the ECR computation.
e) APTEL’s remand is narrow and well-defined, and is confined exclusively
to an arithmetical and computational exercise, to determine the amounts
payable to the Petitioner strictly in terms of the methodology already laid
down in the Interim Order dated 10.3.2025.
f) On 16.1.2026, the Hon’ble Supreme Court dismissed both Civil Appeals
while refusing to interfere with the Hon’ble Tribunal’s Judgment.
Order in Petition No. 179/MP/2023 Page 10 of 49

g) This Commission has consistently recognised that where coal is procured
on an FOB basis, transportation and insurance charges are required to
be added to arrive at the CIF cost; and where coal is procured on a
CIF/CFR basis, the consolidated CIF cost of coal is to be considered
directly for the purpose of ECR computation.
h) GUVNL seeks to reopen issues on merits, expressly barred by the
Judgment dated 31.10.2025; or are premised on an incorrect reading of
the methodology already settled by this Hon’ble Commission in its Order
dated 3.1.2023, read with the Interim Order dated 10.3.2025.
i) Nothing further survives for consideration at this stage, except for the
computation and determination of the amounts payable to the Petitioner
for the period from 16.4.2023 to 10.3.2025, strictly in terms of the Interim
Order dated 10.3.2025.
Submission by Respondent No. 1
10. The Respondent No.1, in its affidavit dated 11.12.2025 and 20.1.2026,
submitted that they have filed an appeal under Section 125 of the Act, before
the Hon’ble Supreme Court, against the Order dated 31.10.2025 passed by the
Hon’ble Tribunal. The Respondent No.1 submits that the FOB of coal and the
Transportation charges are to be compared to the respective aspects
individually rather than collectively, as sought to be done by the Petitioner,
considering the CIF Value. The Respondent No. 1, vide its affidavit dated
5.1.2026, submitted the Statement of computation from April 2023 to March,
2025 (up to 10.3.2025), pursuant to the Record of Proceeding dated 20.1.2026.
Order in Petition No. 179/MP/2023 Page 11 of 49

Vide affidavit dated 6.2.2026, the Respondent No.1 filed a reply to the
Petitioner’s submission vide affidavit dated 27.11.2025. A brief of the
Respondent’s submission is as follows:
a) As per the APTEL Judgment, the Petitioner is required to provide the FOB
Cost of Coal in respect of each of the shipments involved for the imported
coal used for the generation and supply of electricity during the period from
16.4.2023 to 10.3.2025.
b) The CFR cost cannot be the consideration, and it is therefore incumbent on
the Petitioner to place the actual FOB Cost of Coal, which it claims to have
incurred, for consideration. In this regard, the Respondent No.1 referred to
the FOB cost of imported coal having GCV of 5000 kCal/kg considered by
the Committee appointed by the Central Government under Section 11(1) of
the Act, the APTEL Judgment, where para 82(e)(ii) of this Commission’s
order referred, FOB Cost of coal is the only relevant data.
c) The difference in the CIF Price cannot be claimed on an actual basis. The
Petitioner is required to arrange its affairs so that it will provide the FOB price
of coal for any adjustment in the cost of coal procurement. It is not open to
the Petitioner to claim that it will provide only the CFR/CIF Cost in the case
of a coal shipment described as a CFR shipment, and that the CIF cost
based thereon is sufficient to claim relief. Such a claim by the Petitioner is
contrary to (a) directions contained in para 82(e)(i) of the Order dated
10.3.2025.
d) The failure on the part of the Petitioner in not giving the FOB Cost actually
incurred by it in each of the shipments involved is in violation of the Orders
Order in Petition No. 179/MP/2023 Page 12 of 49

passed by this Commission and the Tribunal, adverse inference is to be
drawn against Tata Power and to the extent of the CFR Shipments, no relief
is to be granted to Tata Power.
e) The Respondent brought out inconsistencies in the claim made by the
Petitioner in the present proceedings in regard to the actual FOB cost of
coal, referring to the CA Certificates dated 15.3.2025, 18.4.2025 and
2.9.2025, indicating a different price.
f) The Petitioner cannot justify the non-furnishing of the FOB Cost of Coal on
the ground that the CFR Cost of Coal has been given, and therefore it will
not consider any shipping and transportation cost for such shipments, which
is against para 82(e)(ii) of the Order dated 10.3.2025. As per para 82(e)(ii)
of the Order dated 10.3.2025 of the Hon’ble Commission, the ‘transportation
and coal handling charges’ are to be in terms of the provisions of the PPA.
Schedule 11 of the PPA provides for the computation of transportation and
coal-handling charges, both escalable and non-escalable.
g) The CFR Price claimed in regard to various shipments has to be converted
to the FOB price. In the absence of any satisfactory data, the CFR Price
needs to be arrived at by excluding transportation costs, as per the published
indices for the shipment of coal from the country from which the coal has
been imported.
h) The Petitioner shall be entitled only to the FOB price so derived, which then
has to be capped as per the Order, and separately, the transportation and
coal handling charges also have to be capped as per the PPA. Tata Power

24. It may be observed that though the Commission has captured the FOB/
CFR price as $ 91.80 per MT in the table, the inference drawn by the
Commission is the FOB price worked out based on the nearest Argus ICI Index
and the findings in paragraph 6.3 of the order in 12/SM/2023. The Commission
was aware that some shipments were on a CFR basis; hence, the FOB price
worked out to compare with the index price or the Committee price may not
reflect the actual FOB price. This is clearly visible from the last column of the
table, wherein it was mentioned that the CFR value changed to FOB level i.e.
CFR value, wherever applicable, was considered to work out the consolidated
FOB price for comparison purposes. Para 64(g) and 64(h) of the order are
extracted below:
“g) The weighted average FOB price of blended coal of GCV 5291 kCal/kg has
been worked out as 81.39 $/MT with reference to the ICI3 index (applicable to
GCV of 5000 kCal/kg). This method does not capture the variation in index price
between high and low-quality coal. But if we consider the nearest Argus Index of
5800 GCV and 6400 GCV for higher quality coal, the weighted average FOB price
of blended coal of GCV 5291 kCal/kg has been worked out as 83.41 $/Ton.
h) The Commission, in para 6.3 of order in 12/SM/2023, has already recognized
the decoupling of high CV and mid-CV Coal in the International Coal index, i.e.,
Argus, Platts, etc. It implies that the rate of increase of International Index price
with an increase of quality is non-linear, and hence, the blending of coal based on
a weighted average of quantity and shipment-wise price of higher quality coal
leads to a higher weighted average coal price. The petitioner has used the higher
GCV blended coal of more than 5000 GCV due to technical requirements. Thus,
prima facie, there is a case for allowing ECR based on the higher FOB price of
the blended coal compared to the pro-rata FOB price of coal worked out by the
Committee with reference to the Argus ICI3 which is for 5000 GCV.”
25. As per Para 82(e)(i) of the order, fifty percent of the difference in the energy
charge rate on account of the FOB price of coal between the energy charge rate
as per the methodology decided in the CERC order dated 3.1.2023 and as
considered by the Committee, which was submitted by the Petitioner on a best
Order in Petition No. 179/MP/2023 Page 28 of 49

estimate basis. Since the Commission has mentioned the energy charge rate
on account of the FOB price only, and not including the CFR, the CFR price is
to be converted to the FOB price. Para 82(e)(i) of the order talks about the
difference in FOB price only, but not on account of the difference in other
parameters. It may be noted that if we consider the difference in ECR only on
account of FOB price, it represents only the difference in FOB Price as
explained below:
Scenario I II Difference
FOB Price 10000 12000 2000 Rs/MT
Specific Coal Consumption 0.47 0.47 0.47 Kg/kWh
Rs/Per Unit 4.70 5.64 0.94 Rs/kWh
( 2000 x0.47= 0.94 Rs per unit and 5.64 -4.70=0.94 Rs per unit )
26. The APTEL’s judgment is for limited remand of computation without
revisiting the merits of the order. The methodology adopted by the Commission
in its order dated 3.1.2023 addresses the energy charge rate computation for
coal procurement on the FOB price of coal as well as the CFR basis, given that
coal on a few instances was procured on a CFR basis. Since in the interim
relief granted in the order dated 10.3.2025, the Commission has allowed the
interim relief as a percentage of the FOB price as well as the energy charge
rate computation as per the methodology decided in the order dated 3.1.2023,
the deviation from any one of the above can lead to deviation from the interim
order dated 10.3.2025.
27. The issue herein is how to arrive at the FOB price where the coal is
procured on a CFR/CIF basis. We have perused the methodology decided by
Order in Petition No. 179/MP/2023 Page 29 of 49

the Commission in its order dated 3.1.2023 with regard to the coal procurement
on a CFR/CIF basis. Relevant para is extracted below:
“123. In light of the above, the summary of our decisions is as under:
….
….
(h) FOB cost of Indonesian coal for the purpose of offsetting of the adverse
financial impact under Section 11(2) should be taken as lower of the actual cost
of coal or the HPB based on the HBA index. Based on the said cost and the
transportation charges as per the PPA, the CIF cost in USD/MT shall be worked
out.
(i) In case of coal received from sources other than Indonesia, CIF cost of coal
shall be considered. Ocean freight shall not be admissible separately where the
ocean freight is included in CFR/DAP. Where the ocean freight is not included in
CFR/DAP, ocean freight charges on actual basis shall be considered to workout
the CIF cost.
(j) Thereafter, CIF cost as worked out in sub-paras (h) and (i) above shall be
converted into INR as per the applicable foreign exchange rate as per the
provisions of Clause 1.2.3 of Schedule 7 of the PPA. Landed cost of coal (LPPF)
shall be worked out by considering Port Handling Charges as per the PPA and
applicable taxes and duties.
(k) In case of coal sourced from countries other than Indonesia, the CIF price of
coal plus the mining profit per tonne (decided during the month in respect of
Indonesian coal per tonne) shall not be more than the CIF price of Indonesian coal
received during the said month.
…”
28. It may be observed from the above that where the coal is procured either
on FOB basis from Indonesia or on CFR/DAP basis from sources other than
Indonesia, the CIF cost is worked out in both cases. In both mechanisms, there
is a sufficient safeguard. As per methodology in the order dated 3.1.2023, the
coal sourced from Indonesia on FOB basis was compared with the HBA(HPB)
price to work out CIF basis, whereas the coal sourced from other than Indonesia
on CFR basis, the CIF price worked out shall be restricted to the Indonesian
coal price, i.e. HBA basis CIF price. In the instant case, the Petitioner has
Order in Petition No. 179/MP/2023 Page 30 of 49

worked out the energy charge rate in accordance with the order dated 3.1.2023
and compared it with the energy charge rate worked out by the Committee.
Subsequently, the Petitioner has reduced the difference in the energy charge
rate by 50% to raise the invoice. The coal procured by the Petitioner on a
CFR/CIF basis is restricted to the HBA(HPB) price as per the methodology
decided by the Commission, and hence, the interest of the Respondents is
protected in the existing mechanism.
29. We have considered the intent of the order dated 3.1.2023 and the decision
of the Commission as per the letter and spirit of the order dated 10.3.2025. In
Para 82(e) of the order dated 10.3.2025, we have referred only to the FOB
Price. The order of the Commission dated 3.1.2023 deals with procurement on
FOB Price as well as CFR/CIF basis, but the Commission has referred to the
FOB price in the interim order. This is consistent with the Directions 2023 of the
Respondent No. 9, which deal with the increase in price of imported coal
impacting the FOB price only, and hence, for the remaining components such
as freight & insurance, handling charges, etc., should be aligned with the PPA
except where these components have not been quoted separately. Paragraph
82(e) of the interim order refers to the admissibility of the energy charge rate
based on FOB Price only, and hence, it is imperative for the Petitioner to work
out the FOB Price or Energy charge rate corresponding to FOB Price only. The
illustrative example of November 2023 to ascertain the merit in the interim relief
for higher GCV, which is to be read distinctly from Paragraph 82(e) of the order.
Order in Petition No. 179/MP/2023 Page 31 of 49

30. We agree with the Respondent No. 1 that interim relief as per the order
dated 10.3.2025 shall be worked out by converting the CFR/CIF-based coal
price into FOB price and such FOB price then added with remaining
components such as admissible freight cost, handling charges, taxes and duties
and other charges, as applicable. Accordingly, we held that wherever coal is
procured on CFR or CIF price, it needs to be converted into FOB Price by
adjusting the freight & insurance per MT, as the case may.
Issue (II): If the coal price is to be converted to the FOB price, what will be
the freight and insurance charges to be adjusted from the CFR or CIF
price, i.e. as per the Index considered by the MoP’s Committee, S&P Index
or the PPA freight rate?
31. The Petitioner, in its calculation, submitted that when the coal is procured
on a CFR or CIF basis, the actual cost shall be considered to work out the
energy charge rate. Para 15 of the affidavit dated 20.1.2026 of the Petitioner is
reproduced as under:
“15. As per the said methodology, this Hon’ble Commission has consistently
recognised that: (a) where coal is procured on an FOB basis, transportation and
insurance charges are required to be added to arrive at the CIF cost; and (b)
where coal is procured on a CIF/CFR basis, the consolidated CIF cost of coal
is to be considered directly for the purpose of ECR computation.”
32. The Respondent No.1, in its calculation, considered the freight and
insurance to work out the FOB price as the higher of the S&P Index or actual
freight or freight as per PPA. Relevant column of the table submitted by the
Respondent vide affidavit dated 6.2.2026 is extracted below:
Order in Petition No. 179/MP/2023 Page 32 of 49

It may be observed from the above table that coal procured through shipment
at Sr No, 6 to 9 and 11 to 13 is on a CFR basis. The FOB price derived by
Respondent No.1 for shipment at Sr No. 7 is arrived at from the CIF price of $
85.02 per MT by subtracting the freight as per S&P Platts/ Argus for CFR
Vessels S&P Platts, i.e. $ 123.23 per MT – $ 38.21 per MT. Whereas admissible
ocean freight for the purpose of energy charge rate is considered as PPA.
33. On perusal of the submission of the Petitioner and the Respondent No.1, it
is understood that the Respondent have attempted to work out the value of FOB
price by removing the freight cost based on index price or as per PPA where
the coal is procured on CFR/CIF basis. The coal procurement on CFR (Cost
and Freight) is generally adopted by the buyer, which includes the consolidated
cost of coal plus shipping to the destination port, with the seller’s responsibility
Order in Petition No. 179/MP/2023 Page 33 of 49

for shipping logistics. We are not questioning the coal procurement modes, but
are concerned about the consideration of freight cost to work out the FOB price
of coal. The directions 2023 do not prescribe coal procurement on FOB basis,
and hence, it may not be appropriate to draw an adverse inference against the
petitioner, except to follow a prudent approach in procurement of coal. We have
observed a large variation in the freight index; hence, it may not be appropriate
to consider the specific index price. The directions of 2023 issued by the
Respondent No. 9 have an impact only on the FOB price, without altering the
other parameters, and hence, the remaining components shall be governed by
the PPA. The Petitioner has quoted the components of the energy charges
separately, i.e. fuel energy charges, and overseas transportation and handling
charges. We hold that if the coal is procured on a CFR or CIF basis, the FOB
Price of coal shall be worked out by adjusting the freight and insurance cost, as
applicable, which shall be reworked out from the quoted freight & insurance rate
and quoted handling charges, applicable to the year under consideration, and
the operational parameters as decided by the Commission in its interim order.
Issue (III): What will be the methodology for the computation of
entitlement as per the order of APTEL dated 31.10.2025 and computation
of the entitlement of interim relief thereof?
34. As discussed above, the Petitioner has claimed the energy charge rate
without deriving the FOB price of coal and 50% of the difference between the
actual FOB price of coal and the FOB price of coal as per the MOP’s committee.
But, it is observed from the Petitioner’s claim and the computation submitted
along with the invoice that the interim relief was worked out based on the 50%
Order in Petition No. 179/MP/2023 Page 34 of 49

of the difference between the energy charges as per the order dated 3.1.2023
in Petition 128/MP/2022 and billed as per the rate decided by the MoP’s
committee. Consequently, the difference in freight charges, handling charges
and taxes & duties, etc., is also reduced to 50%, which was not the intent of the
interim order. Prima facie, it appears that the Petitioner’s approach is not in
consonance with the decision of the Commission in the interim order.
35. Per contra, the Respondent No.1 has arrived at the FOB price of coal based
on the weighted average price of coal consumed during the month and
converting the CFR/CIF price into the FOB price. But while converting the
CFR/CIF price to the FOB price, the Respondent No.1 has considered the
freight rate based on the higher of the S&P Index, actual freight or PPA freight
rather than the quoted freight rate in the PPA. Further, to arrive at the difference
in FOB Price, the Respondent No.1 has considered the FOB Price based on
the 5000 GCV Index, which differs from the computation submitted by the
Petitioner on 18.4.2024 and as it is not adjusted to the actual GCV. In view of
the rival submission, we have proceeded to describe the methodology to work
out the entitlement to interim relief.
Methodology to work out the Entitlement
FOB Price of coal
36. We have held that the entitlement of interim relief requires computation of
the FOB price of coal every month. We have observed that the directions do
not mandate the requirement of the FOB price for the imported coal. The
Order in Petition No. 179/MP/2023 Page 35 of 49

petitioner has the liberty to procure the coal either on a CFR basis or FOB basis.
In these circumstances, the pass-through of the cost requires due diligence with
the market price or index price. Accordingly, the generating company shall work
out the FOB price using the available information only and by applying the
appropriate index as per the following methodology:-
a) Where the coal is procured on FOB basis (“P1”) at specific GCV (“Q1”),
the same shall be compared with the corresponding HBA(HPB) price to
arrive at the admissible FOB Price as under:
FOB price (P1) = Lower [ HBA(HPB) price, actual FOB price ]
b) Where the coal is procured on CFR or CIF basis (“C1”) at specific GCV
(“Q1”), the same shall be arrived at FOB basis (“P1”) by subtracting the
quoted freight or insurance cost or both, as the case may be.
Accordingly, the FOB Price worked out shall be compared with the
HBA(HPB) price to arrive at the admissible FOB Price as under:
FOB Price (P1) = CFR/CIF Price - [ Quoted Freight /Insurance
Tariff x GCV/ SHR) x (1-Aux%) x1000) ]
Admissible FOB Price (P1) = Lower [ HBA(HPB) price, Actual FOB
Price ]
This approach will address the interests of the Respondents. If the
petitioner has paid the cost of coal and freight above the market price,
it will be rationalised either through the freight as per the PPA or the
applicable HBA(HPB) price. The Respondent will not be burdened with
Order in Petition No. 179/MP/2023 Page 36 of 49

the cost of coal more than the agreed cost of freight and the market
price of coal.
c) FOB Price (P1) at specific GCV (Q1) worked out shall be compared with
the FOB price (“P2”) at specific GCV (“Q2”) considered by the
Committee. FOB price at specific GCV considered by the Committee to
be arrived on a pro-rata basis at GCV of coal procurer, i.e. P2x
GCV(Q1)/GCV(Q2) = P3. The admissible FOB price for the interim relief
would be as under:
FOB price (Pi) = P3 + (P1-P3)/2 at GCV (Q1)
d) We make it clear that at present, we are considering the HBA(HPB) index
in line with the order dated 3.1.2023, which will be reviewed in the final
order along with the admissibility of premium.
CIF Price of Coal
37. The energy charge rate shall be worked out from the landed price of coal
for entitlement of interim relief in terms of the order dated 10.3.2025. The
Landed Price of coal shall be worked out from the CIF price, i.e. the summation
of FOB price (Pi) and freight and insurance cost as under:
CIF Price = FOB Price (Pi) + [ Quoted Freight & Insurance
Tariff x (GCV/ SHR) x (1-Aux%) x1000]
Landed Price of Coal = CIF Price + [ Quoted handling x (GCV/ SHR)
x (1-Aux%) x1000] + Taxes and duties (as
applicable)
Energy Charge Rate
Order in Petition No. 179/MP/2023 Page 37 of 49

38. The energy charge rate (ECRi) shall be worked out based on the landed
price of coal and the operational parameters decided by the Commission in its
order dated 10.3.2025 by applying the following formula:
Energy Charge Rate ( ECRi in Rs/kWh ) = ( Station Heat Rate in kCal per
kWh / GCV of coal consumed in kcal per kg) X ( 1/ (1 –
Auxiliary Energy Consumption in %) x ( Landed Price of
Coal in Rs per MT /1000)
39. Net energy charges payable for interim relief shall be worked out for every
month, after excluding the mining profit as considered by the Committee from
the energy charge rate worked out above, and subtracting the energy charge
rate of the Committee (ECRc) from the energy charge rate worked out as per
above formula and scheduled energy certified in the Regional Energy Account
i.e. ( ECRi - ECRc) x (Scheduled Energy in kWh).
40. The Respondent No.1 submitted to the APTEL that the Commission did not
consider the entire gamut of computation for the period April 2023 to 10.3.2025
and rather left such computation for the Petitioner to undertake and to raise the
bills. APTEL also took cognizance of this submission and directed the
Commission to compute the entitlement of TPCL, in terms of the order dated
10.3.2025 (wherein, among others, the FoB price of imported coal was
effectively determined at 84.90 USD/ MT), as extracted below:
“We find force in the submission urged on behalf of GUVNL that the CERC
ought to have computed and quantified the entitlement of TPCL in terms of the
interim order passed by it, and ought not to have left it to TPCL to compute and
claim the said amounts. The aforesaid directions may, possibly, have been
issued by the CERC since the 2023 directions were still in force when it passed
the impugned order on 10.03.2025. As we have now made it clear that the
CERC could not have granted TPCL any interim relief, under Section 11(2) read
Order in Petition No. 179/MP/2023 Page 38 of 49

with Section 94(2) of the Electricity Act, for the period after it had passed the
impugned order on 10.03.2025, the interim relief which TPCL would be entitled
to is only for the period from 16.04.2023 till 10.03.2025, and not beyond.”
(Emphasis supplied)
41. The Commission, in terms of the order of APTEL and to avoid further
delay in interim relief, proceeded to determine the entitlement of interim relief,
subject to adjustment based on the outcome of the final order.
Computation of entitlement for Interim relief (from 16th April 2023 till 10th
March 2025)
42. We have considered the computation submitted by the Petitioner and
modified it by applying the above methodology as discussed in Para 35-38 of
this order. It is pertinent to note that the aforesaid methodology is consistent
with the submission of the Respondent No.1. Accordingly, interim relief is
worked out by considering the following aspects:-
a) The FOB Price of coal is worked out for each shipment by adjusting the
freight & insurance cost as per the PPA, where the coal is procured on
CFR or CIF basis, as the case may be, and comparing the FOB price of
coal with the applicable HBA(HPB) Index price as submitted by the
Petitioner for each shipment. This has replaced the CFR/CIF prices
considered by the Petitioner as the FOB Price. The taxes and duties have
been revised in accordance with the FOB price worked out.
b) From the FOB Price worked out as per para(a) above for each shipment,
the weighted average FOB cost of coal is worked out on a monthly basis
Order in Petition No. 179/MP/2023 Page 39 of 49

based on the coal consumed from shipments during the month. It is
observed that, apart from the adjustment of the freight issue, the
HBA(HPB) index considered by the Petitioner and the Respondent No.1
differ, and thereby the weighted average FOB Price of coal during the
month worked out is different. One of the reasons could be the difference
in the period considered by the Petitioner and the Respondent No.1. On
account of this, there is a marginal difference in the admissible FOB Price
of coal between the Petitioner and the Respondent No.1. This issue of
the consideration of the FOB Price of coal will be dealt with in the final
order. At present, for the purpose of interim relief, the FOB Price worked
out as per Para (a) above has been considered for the weighted average
FOB cost of coal on a monthly basis.
c) The weighted average FOB cost of coal is compared with the FOB price
considered by the Committee for the month. The revised FOB cost of coal
is worked out by adding 50% of the difference between the FOB cost of
coal and the FOB price considered by the Committee (adjusted for GCV).
We have observed from the submission of the computation by the
Respondent No.1 that the FOB Price considered by the Committee does
not match with the Petitioner’s submission dated 18.4.2024 for arriving at
the FOB price of the Committee through simulation till the month of
March, 2024. We do not find any objection from any of the Respondents
to the FOB Price of the Committee worked out by the Petitioner through
simulation. Ideally, we could have considered the FOB price considered
Order in Petition No. 179/MP/2023 Page 40 of 49

INTERIM ORDER
The instant petition has been filed by Power Grid Corporation of India Limited
for determination of tariff under Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms
and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2024 (hereinafter referred to as “the 2024 Tariff
Regulations”) of the period from COD to 31.3.2029 in respect of Asset-1: 1x1500
MVA, 765/400 kV ICT at POWERGRID Padghe Sub-station and Asset-2: 400 kV New
Navsari (GIS) - Magarwada (GIS) D/C line strung on multi circuit tower along with
associated 400 kV line bay (GIS) at New Navsari (GIS) Sub-station & Magarwada
(GIS) Sub-station, 400 kV Bus Reactor (1x125 MVAr) along with associated bay
(GIS) at New Navsari (GIS) Sub-station and 500 MVA, 400/220 kV ICT-1&2 along
with associated 400 kV & 220 kV ICT bays at New Navsari (GIS) Sub-station
(hereinafter referred to as the “transmission assets”) under the “Transmission
Network Expansion in Gujarat to increase ATC from ISTS, Part-B” (hereinafter
referred to as the “transmission system”) in the Western Region. The Petitioner has
also prayed for the grant of an interim tariff in accordance with Regulation 10(3) of the
2024 Tariff Regulations, for inclusion in the PoC charges.
Order in Petition No. 875/TT/2025 Page 2 of 26

2. Regulation 10(3) of the 2024 Tariff Regulations provides as follows:
“10. Determination of tariff
(3) If the information furnished in the petition is in accordance with these regulations,
the Commission may consider granting an interim tariff of up to ninety per cent (90%)
of the tariff claimed in the case of a new generating station or unit thereof or
transmission system, or element thereof during the first hearing of the application for
billing purposes till the final tariff is determined by the Commission:”
Provided that in case the final tariff determined by the Commission is lower than the
interim tariff by more than 10%, the generating company or transmission licensee shall
return the excess amount recovered from the beneficiaries or long term customers, as
the case may be, with simple interest at 1.20 times of the rate worked out on the basis
of 1 year SBI MCLR plus 100 basis points prevailing as on 1st April of the financial
year in which such excess recovery was made.”
3. As per Regulation 10(3) of the 2024 Tariff Regulations, if the information
furnished by the Petitioner is in accordance with the 2024 Tariff Regulations, the
Commission may grant an interim tariff up to 90% of the tariff claimed for the purpose
of billing up to the determination of the final tariff, which is subject to adjustment as per
the proviso to the said regulation.
4. In the instant case, the Petitioner has submitted the information required for the
determination of the tariff of the transmission assets as specified in Regulation 10(3)
of the 2024 Tariff Regulations. The Petitioner has also issued Public Notice of this
petition in the newspapers in accordance with Section 64(2) of the Electricity Act,
2003. No comments or suggestions have been received from the general public in
response to the aforesaid notice published in the newspapers by the Petitioner.
5. Thus, the Petitioner has complied with the requirements under Regulation 10(3)
of the 2024 Tariff Regulations and has also met the requirements under Section 64(2)
of the Electricity Act, 2003. Further, the issue of the final tariff order in the matter may
take some more time; therefore, we have decided to issue an interim tariff for the
transmission assets under Regulation 10(3) of the 2024 Tariff Regulations for billing
purposes, until the final order is issued.
Order in Petition No. 875/TT/2025 Page 3 of 26

Background
6. The brief facts of the case are as under:
(a) The ISTS scheme, which is a part of the “System Strengthening in Gujarat
associated with the integration of RE projects from Khavda potential REZ,”
was deliberated in the 5th NCT meeting held on 25.8.2021 and 2.9.2021.
(b) Subsequently, a Joint Study Meeting was held on 5.11.2021 amongst CEA,
CTUIL, POSOCO and GETCO to discuss the already planned scheme
based on updated inputs received from GETCO. In said meeting, it was
decided to phase the schemes already deliberated in the 5th meeting of
NCT, with minor modifications based on GETCO's ATC requirements and
system-strengthening requirements associated with the integration of RE
projects from the Khavda potential RE zone. Based on these deliberations,
CTUIL submitted the Transmission Scheme for the consideration of NCT.
(c) Meanwhile, in order to facilitate the development of RE power sources, the
Ministry of Power (MoP) vide letter dated 15.11.2021 directed the
Commission to modify its Regulation with regard to the requirement of
Regulatory Approval for the ISTS schemes approved by the MoP in
consultation with RPCs. Based on recommendations of CTUIL, the 7th NCT
meeting was held on 3.12.2021, during which NCT recommended the ISTS
Transmission Scheme to MoP to be implemented by POWERGRID
(implementing agency) through the RTM route.

scheme, i.e., 765 kV Navsari (New) - Padghe line and 765/400 kV ICTs at Navsari
(New) Sub-station, is yet to be commissioned. Therefore, there is no power flow in
Asset-2 on account of the delay of the Petitioner’s own asset, i.e. 765 kV Navsari Sub-
station and 765 kV Navsari (New) - Padghe Transmission Line and the downstream
system under the scope of GETCO during the period 20.3.2025 (date of deemed COD
claimed by the Petitioner) to 20.01.2026. As the Petitioner’s own transmission assets
are delayed and not ready, we do not find any merit in the Petitioner’s claim for
approval of the deemed COD of Asset-2 as 20.03.2025.
35. Further, as per the submission of the Petitioner, the 220 kV GETCO lines at
New Navsari Sub-station were successfully charged on 21.1.2026 and are presently
carrying a power of approximately 290 MW, utilising the Asset-2 of the Petitioner. This
indicates that upon commissioning of the 220 kV lines by GETCO, power from the
ISTS through Asset-2 could be facilitated in the Navsari area of South Gujarat, with
supply being routed from Magarwada to the Navsari/Sachin area through the 400/220
kV Navsari (New) Sub-station.
36. In view of the above, the Commission is of the considered view that the
Petitioner’s claim of deemed COD as on 20.3.2025 is not admissible. With the
Order in Petition No. 875/TT/2025 Page 23 of 26

commissioning of the downstream system under the control of GETCO on 21.1.2026,
Asset-2 has been put under regular use; accordingly, the COD of Asset-2 is approved
as 21.1.2026.
Capital cost
37. The Petitioner, vide affidavit dated 17.6.2025, has claimed the capital cost
incurred as on COD and the ACE projected to be incurred in respect of the
transmission asset and has placed on record a copy of the Auditor’s Certificate dated
5.6.2025 and 3.6.2025 in support of the same:
(₹ in lakh)

Cost Overrun
38. The total estimated completion cost of Asset-1 is ₹5898.39 lakh, which exceeds
the FR approved apportioned cost of ₹4379.07 lakh, and hence there is a cost over-
run of ₹1519.32 lakh. The estimated completion cost of Asset-2 is ₹106559.29 lakh,
which is within the FR apportioned approved cost of ₹122009.41 lakh.
39. After carrying out a preliminary prudence check of the AFC claimed by the
Petitioner and taking into consideration the time overrun and cost over-run in case of
Asset-1 and Asset-2, which will be dealt with in detail at the time of grant of the final
tariff order, we approve interim tariff of 80% of the AFC claimed by the Petitioner for
Asset-1 and Asset-2 from the date of COD to 31.3.2029 in terms of Regulation 10(3)
of the 2024 Tariff Regulations.
40. The details of the AFC claimed by the Petitioner and the AFC allowed for the
transmission assets are as follows:
Order in Petition No. 875/TT/2025 Page 24 of 26

A. Annual transmission charges claimed by the Petitioner in respect of the
transmission assets are as follows:

Sharing of Transmission Charges
41. The Petitioner has submitted that the tariff for the 2024-29 shall be recovered
on a monthly basis in accordance with Regulation 78 of the 2024 Tariff Regulations
and shall be shared by the beneficiaries and the long-term transmission customers in
accordance with the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Sharing of Inter-State
Transmission Charges and Losses) Regulations, 2020, as amended from time to time.
42. The Respondent, MSEDCL, has submitted that liability for sharing of
transmission charges under the POC mechanism presupposes a valid COD and
availability of transmission service in accordance with the CERC Tariff Regulations
and the Indian Electricity Grid Code. In the present case, the Petitioner has itself
admitted that due to non-readiness of the associated downstream 220 kV system, no
power flow has commenced through Asset-2, and the asset has merely been idling.
The mere depiction of Asset-2 as being “idle charged” does not confer any right upon
the Petitioner to recover transmission charges from the beneficiaries. In the absence
of operational readiness and actual availability of transmission service, no liability for
transmission charges can be fastened upon the beneficiaries, including MSEDCL.
Order in Petition No. 875/TT/2025 Page 25 of 26

MSEDCL has further submitted that non-availability of transmission service has arisen
solely due to non-readiness of the associated downstream 220 kV system, which was
to be developed by GETCO; hence, the liability, if any, for such charges ought to be
borne by the agency responsible for the said downstream system and not by the
beneficiaries. Therefore, the agency concerned, i.e., GETCO/ Respondent No. 7, may
be directed to bear the transmission charges for the period under consideration in the
present Petition, if so considered.
43. The Respondent, MPPMCL, has submitted that Asset-2 is non-operational and
no transmission charges are recoverable from beneficiaries for the relevant period;
MPPMCL further submitted that any liability arising due to non-readiness of
downstream systems be borne by the concerned entity and not by MPPMCL or other
beneficiaries.
44. We have considered the submissions of the Petitioner and the Respondents.
The Respondent’s contention that GETCO should bear the transmission charges for
the period of delay in commissioning of the transmission assets under the scope of
GETCO has become infructuous, as we have not approved the deemed COD of Asset-
2 as claimed by the Petitioner.
45. The COD of the Asset-1 and Asset-2 is approved as 3.7.2024 and 21.1.2026,
respectively. The transmission charges approved for the transmission assets in this
order shall be governed by the provisions of the 2020 Sharing Regulations as provided
in Regulation 78 of the 2024 Tariff Regulations.

याचिका संख्या / Petition No. 8/SM/2026
Coram:
Shri Jishnu Barua, Chairperson
Shri Ramesh Babu V., Member
Shri Harish Dudani, Member
Shri Ravinder Singh Dhillon, Member
आदेश चदनांक/ Date of Order: 28th April, 2026
In the matter of
Non-compliance of the provisions of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission
(Procedure, Terms and Conditions for grant of trading licence and other related
matters) Regulations, 2020.
And
In the matter of
Reneurja Power LLP,
C/o RAJM Automobiles
NR Katariya Auto Moto Mava
Kalawad Road, Rajkot– 360005, Gujarat. Respondent
ORDER
By order dated 31.7.2021, Reneurja Power LLP (hereinafter referred to as
“Respondent”), was granted inter-State trading licence for Category ‘V’ for trading in
electricity as an electricity trader in accordance with the Central Electricity Regulatory
Commission (Procedure, Terms and Conditions for grant of trading licence and other
related matters) Regulations, 2020 as amended from time to time (hereinafter
referred to as “Trading Licence Regulations, 2020”).
2. Regulations 7(4) and 11(2) of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission
Order in Petition No.8/SM/2026 Page 1 of 8

(Payment of Fees) Regulations, 2012, amended from time to time (hereinafter
referred to as “the Payment of Fees Regulations”) provide as under:
“7. Licence Fee
(4) Fees specified in this regulation shall be paid within thirty days of the
date of grant of licence and thereafter, annually by 30th April of each year
subject to proviso to clause (1) of this regulation.
11. Late payment surcharge
(2) Without prejudice to the liability for late payment surcharge, the
Commission may take any other action as may be considered appropriate for
non-compliance of these regulations if payment of fees is delayed beyond two
months from the due dates of payment as specified in these regulations.”
3. As per the above provisions of the Payment of Fees Regulations, the
Respondent was liable to pay the licence fee within thirty days of the grant of the
licence and thereafter, annually by 30th April of each year. However, the Respondent
has not paid its licence fee for Rs. 4.68 lakh for two consecutive financial years (2024
to 2026) due by 30th April of each year. A reminder was also served through vide
letter dated 17.4.2025.
4. Regulation 9 (15) of the Trading Licence Regulations, 2020 provides that:
“9. Obligations of the Trading Licensee:
(15) The Trading Licensee shall pay the licence fee by the stipulated date
specified by the Commission from time to time.”
As per Regulation 9 (15) of the Trading Licence Regulations, 2020, the
licensee is required to regularly pay the licence fee specified by the Commission,
from time to time.
5. Regulations 11(2), (4), (5) and (7) and Regulation 12(2) and (3) of Trading
Licence Regulations, 2020 provide as under:
“11. Submission of Information:
Order in Petition No.8/SM/2026 Page 2 of 8

(2) Furnish monthly information through Forms IV-A, IV-B, IV-C, IV-D, IV-E,
IV-F, IVG and IV-H in respect of inter-State trading, intra-State trading on the
basis of the inter-State trading licence, trading through power exchanges,
Banking of electricity, short-term, long-term trading and Cross Border Trade
of Electricity, so as to reach the Commission before 15th of the succeeding
month:
Provided that the information sent to the Commission, shall be posted on the
website of the Trading Licensee by 15th of the succeeding month, and such
report shall be available on the website for not less than five Years;
(4) Submit annual return of inter-State transactions detailing:
(a) total volume transacted (in MUs and Rupees) and the total trading
margin charged thereon,
(b) total volume transacted in intra-State transactions on the basis of the
inter-state trading licence (in MU and Rupees),
(c) total volume transacted on Power Exchange and the total trading
margin charged thereon,
(d) total volumes of Renewable Energy Certificates transacted,
(e) complete list of Buyers and Sellers in the above categories, certified by
Chartered Accountant or Cost Accountant by 31st May every Year as per
Form IV-J;
(5) Submit to the Commission copies of the Annual Reports including
Directors’ report, Auditors’ report, Balance Sheet and Profit and Loss Account
pertaining to inter-State and intra-State trading on the basis of the inter-State
trading licence, segment of the business along with all the Schedules and
notes to the accounts, not later than nine months after the close of the Year
to which they relate and shall keep them posted on its website or in any
authorized website for a period of at least five Years;
(7) Submit any report or information, as prescribed under Power Market
Regulations notified by the Commission from time to time;
12. Standards of Performance:
(2) Till such time the standards of performance are specified under clause
(1), the Trading Licensee shall furnish to the Commission the performance
details for each Year in the format prescribed by the Commission in Form V,
appended to these regulations by 30th April immediately following the Year
ending on 31st March.
Order in Petition No.8/SM/2026 Page 3 of 8

(3) The Trading Licensee shall display on its website (i) the volume of inter-
State and intra-State trading on the basis of the inter-State trading licence, if
any, on monthly basis; (ii) trading licences held by it; (iii) petitions filed before
the Commission and the orders including interim orders, if any, issued by the
Commission to ensure dissemination of information to its clients.”
6. It has been observed that the Respondent has defaulted in the payment of the
annual licence fee of Rs. 4.68 lakh for two consecutive financial years (2024 to 2026),
due by 30th April of each year. Further despite repeated reminder letters seeking
information vide letters/emails dated 24.3.2025, 17.4.2025, 5.6.2025, 10.7.2025,
17.7.2025, 18.8.2025 and 20.8.2025, the Respondent has failed to submit the
information in terms of Regulations 11(2), (4), (5) and (7) and Regulation 12(2) and
(3) of Trading Licence Regulations, 2020, as well as to ensure that the reports remain
available on the website for a period of not less than five years. However, the
Respondent has neither submitted the required information nor responded to the said
correspondence.
7. Regulation 9 (16) of the Trading Licence Regulations, 2020 provides as under:
“9 (16). The Trading Licensee shall not omit or neglect to undertake trading
activity.”
8. Regulations 17(5), (6), (7), (10), (11) and (12) of Trading Licence Regulations,
2020 enumerate specific acts constituting contravention and non-compliance by a
Trading Licensee as under:
“17 – Contravention by Trading Licensee
(5) Non-compliance of the orders of the Commission including the orders
issued for contravention of any regulation of the Commission;
(6) Non-payment of the licence fees and surcharge, if applicable within
the due date as specified in Central Electricity Regulatory Commission
(Payment of Fees) Regulations, 2012 or statutory re-enactment thereof;
Order in Petition No.8/SM/2026 Page 4 of 8

(7) Delay or non-submission of monthly transaction information sought
under clause (2) of Regulation 11;
(10) Non-submission or delay in submission of any report required to be
submitted by the Trading Licensee under any of the regulations
mentioned in clause (1) of this regulation;
(11) Delay in submission of any other information sought by the
Commission;
(12) Failure to make mandatory disclosures or reporting in accordance
with the provision to clause (2) of Regulation 11 of these regulations on
Trading Licensee’s website.”
9. Regulation 18 of the Trading Licence Regulations, 2020 provides for the
procedure for taking cognizance of the contraventions as under:
“18. Procedure for taking cognizance of the contraventions
(1) The Commission, on being satisfied on the basis of the information in its
possession or on basis of the information submitted by any person that a prima
facie case exists against any Trading Licensee with respect to any of the
provisions of Regulation 17, may initiate Suo-motu proceedings against the
Trading Licensee and may direct the Trading Licensee to submit such
information and explanation as may be considered necessary for the purpose
of the proceeding:
Provided that the proceedings for non-payment of fee shall be initiated if the
Trading Licensee fails to deposit the fees and surcharge, if any, within seven
days of the expiry of due date of payment as per the Central Electricity
Regulatory Commission (Payment of Fee) Regulations, 2012:
Provided further that the licence shall be deemed to be suspended after expiry
of fifteen days from the due date of payment and shall remain suspended till
the payment of fees and surcharge, if any, is made or suspension is withdrawn.
(2) No penalty shall be imposed on the Trading Licensee without giving it an
opportunity of being heard.
(3) The penalties, if any, shall be imposed in accordance with Regulation 19
of these regulations.
As per Regulations 9 (16), 17(5), (6), (7), (10), (11) and (12), and 18 of the
Trading Licence Regulations, 2020, the trading licensee shall not omit or neglect to
undertake trading activity. It has been brought to our notice by the office of the
Order in Petition No.8/SM/2026 Page 5 of 8

Commission that the Respondent has not undertaken any trading activity in the last
two years.
10. Section 19 of the Act provided that:
“19. Revocation of licence
(1) If the Appropriate Commission, after making an enquiry, is satisfied that
public interest so requires, it may revoke a licence in any of the following
cases, namely: -
(a) where the licensee, in the opinion of the Appropriate Commission,
makes wilful and prolonged default in doing anything required of him by or
under this Act or the rules or regulations made thereunder;
(b) where the licensee breaks any of the terms or conditions of his licence
the breach of which is expressly declared by such licence to render it liable
to revocation;
(c) where the licensee fails, within the period fixed in this behalf by his
licence, or any longer period which the Appropriate Commission may have
granted therefor –
(i) to show, to the satisfaction of the Appropriate Commission, that he
is in a position fully and efficiently to discharge the duties and
obligations imposed on him by his licence;
(ii) or to make the deposit or furnish the security, or pay the fees or other
charges required by his licence;
(d) where in the opinion of the Appropriate Commission the financial position
of the licensee is such that he is unable fully and efficiently to discharge the
duties and obligations imposed on him by his licence.
(2) Where in its opinion the public interest so requires, the Appropriate
Commission may, on application, or with the consent of the licensee, revoke
his licence as to the whole or any part of his area of distribution or
transmission or trading upon such terms and conditions as it thinks fit.
(3) No licence shall be revoked under sub-section (1) unless the Appropriate
Commission has given to the licensee not less than three months’ notice, in
writing, stating the grounds on which it is proposed to revoke the licence, and
has considered any cause shown by the licensee within the period of that
notice, against the proposed revocation.
(4) The Appropriate Commission may, instead of revoking a licence under
sub-section (1), permit it to remain in force subject to such further terms and
Order in Petition No.8/SM/2026 Page 6 of 8

conditions as it thinks fit to impose, and any further terms and conditions so
imposed shall be binding upon and be observed by the licensee and shall be
of like force and effect as if they were contained in the licence.
(5) Where the Commission revokes a licence under this section, it shall serve
a notice of revocation upon the licensee and fix a date on which the
revocation shall take effect.
(6) Where the Appropriate Commission has given notice for revocation of
licence under sub-section (5), without prejudice to any penalty which may be
imposed or prosecution proceeding which may be initiated under this Act, the
licensee may, after prior approval of that Commission, sell his utility to any
person who is found eligible by that Commission for grant of licence.”
Accordingly, in accordance with Section 19 of the Act read with the Trading
Licence Regulations, 2020, where the licensee, in the opinion of the Commission,
makes willful and prolonged default in doing anything required of him by or under the
Act or the Rules or the Regulations, the Commission may revoke the licence after
serving a notice of not less than three months.
11. The Respondent has not responded to the letters/emails dated 24.3.2025,
17.4.2025, 5.6.2025, 10.7.2025, 17.7.2025, 18.8.2025 and 20.8.2025 issued by the
office of the Commission for depositing the licence fee/seeking information. The
conduct of the licensee constitutes non-compliance and a contravention under the
provisions of the Trading Licence Regulations and Payment of Fees Regulations. In
our prima facie view, the licensee is not entitled to hold a licence when he has failed
to pay the licence fee and also neglected to undertake any trading activity in the last
two years, in violation of the regulations. Accordingly, we direct the Respondent to
file its response as to why its inter-State trading licence should not be revoked for
willful default in depositing the licence fee, as well as for not undertaking any trading
activity in the last two years. This order shall also be treated as notice under sub-
section (3) of Section 19 of the Act, and if no reply is received within three months
Order in Petition No.8/SM/2026 Page 7 of 8

and unless otherwise directed by the Commission, the licence of the licensee shall
stand revoked after expiry of the period of three months from the date of issue of this
order.
Sd/- Sd/- Sd/- Sd/-
(रच ंदर चसंह चिल्लो) (हरीश दुदानी) (रमेश बाबू .) (जिश्नु बरुआ)
सदस्य सदस्य सदस्य अध्यक्ष

“11. Submission of Information:
(2) Furnish monthly information through Forms IV-A, IV-B, IV-C, IV-D, IV-E,

Order in Petition No.7/SM/2026 Page 4 of 8

2020 enumerate specific acts constituting contravention and non-compliance by a

under clause (2) of Regulation 11;

mentioned in clause (1) of this regulation;

Commission;

with the provision to clause (2) of Regulation 11 of these regulations on

possession or on basis of the information submitted by any person that a prima
facie case exists against any Trading Licensee with respect to any of the
provisions of Regulation 17, may initiate Suo-motu proceedings against the
Trading Licensee and may direct the Trading Licensee to submit such
information and explanation as may be considered necessary for the purpose
of the proceeding:
Provided that the proceedings for non-payment of fee shall be initiated if the
Trading Licensee fails to deposit the fees and surcharge, if any, within seven
days of the expiry of due date of payment as per the Central Electricity
Regulatory Commission (Payment of Fee) Regulations, 2012:
Provided further that the licence shall be deemed to be suspended after expiry
of fifteen days from the due date of payment and shall remain suspended till
Order in Petition No.7/SM/2026 Page 5 of 8

the payment of fees and surcharge, if any, is made or suspension is withdrawn.
(2) No penalty shall be imposed on the Trading Licensee without giving it an
opportunity of being heard.
(3) The penalties, if any, shall be imposed in accordance with Regulation 19
of these regulations.”
As per Regulations 9 (16); 17(5), (6), (7), (10), (11) and (12) and 18 of the
Trading Licence Regulations, 2020, the trading licensee shall not omit or neglect to
undertake trading activity. It has been brought to our notice by the office of the
Commission that the Respondent has not undertaken any trading activity in the last
three years.
10. Section 19 of the Act provides for revocation of licence and reads as under:
“19. Revocation of licence
(1) If the Appropriate Commission, after making an enquiry, is satisfied that
public interest so requires, it may revoke a licence in any of the following
cases, namely: -
(a) where the licensee, in the opinion of the Appropriate Commission,
makes wilful and prolonged default in doing anything required of him by or
under this Act or the rules or regulations made thereunder;
(b) where the licensee breaks any of the terms or conditions of his licence
the breach of which is expressly declared by such licence to render it liable
to revocation;
(c) where the licensee fails, within the period fixed in this behalf by his
licence, or any longer period which the Appropriate Commission may have
granted therefor –
(i) to show, to the satisfaction of the Appropriate Commission, that he
is in a position fully and efficiently to discharge the duties and
obligations imposed on him by his licence;
(ii) or to make the deposit or furnish the security, or pay the fees or other
charges required by his licence;
(d) where in the opinion of the Appropriate Commission the financial position
of the licensee is such that he is unable fully and efficiently to discharge the
Order in Petition No.7/SM/2026 Page 6 of 8

duties and obligations imposed on him by his licence.
(2) Where in its opinion the public interest so requires, the Appropriate
Commission may, on application, or with the consent of the licensee, revoke
his licence as to the whole or any part of his area of distribution or
transmission or trading upon such terms and conditions as it thinks fit.
(3) No licence shall be revoked under sub-section (1) unless the Appropriate
Commission has given to the licensee not less than three months’ notice, in
writing, stating the grounds on which it is proposed to revoke the licence, and
has considered any cause shown by the licensee within the period of that
notice, against the proposed revocation.
(4) The Appropriate Commission may, instead of revoking a licence under
sub-section (1), permit it to remain in force subject to such further terms and
conditions as it thinks fit to impose, and any further terms and conditions so
imposed shall be binding upon and be observed by the licensee and shall be
of like force and effect as if they were contained in the licence.
(5) Where the Commission revokes a licence under this section, it shall serve
a notice of revocation upon the licensee and fix a date on which the
revocation shall take effect.
(6) Where the Appropriate Commission has given notice for revocation of
licence under sub-section (5), without prejudice to any penalty which may be
imposed or prosecution proceeding which may be initiated under this Act, the
licensee may, after prior approval of that Commission, sell his utility to any
person who is found eligible by that Commission for grant of licence.”
Accordingly, in accordance with Section 19 of the Act read with the Trading
Licence Regulations, 2020, where the licensee, in the opinion of the Commission,
makes willful and prolonged default in doing anything required of him by or under the
Act or the Rules or the Regulations, the Commission may revoke the licence after
serving a notice of not less than three months.
11. The Respondent has not responded to the letters/ emails dated 18.7.2024,
3.1.2025, 27.1.2025, 24.3.2025, 28.4.2025, 18.6.2025, 11.7.2025 and 10.7.2025
issued by the office of the Commission for depositing the licence fee/ seeking
information. The conduct of the licensee constitutes non-compliance and a
Order in Petition No.7/SM/2026 Page 7 of 8

contravention under the provisions of the Trading Licence Regulations and Payment
of Fees Regulations. In our prima facie view, the licensee is not entitled to hold a
licence when he has failed to pay the licence fee and also neglected to undertake any
trading activity in the last two years, in violation of the regulations. Accordingly, we
direct the Respondent to file its response as to why its inter-State trading licence
should not be revoked for willful default in depositing the licence fee, as well as for
not undertaking any trading activity in the last two years. This order shall also be
treated as notice under sub-section (3) of Section 19 of the Act, and if no reply is
received within three months and unless otherwise directed by the Commission, the
licence of the licensee shall stand revoked after expiry of the period of three months
from the date of issue of this order.

ORDER
By order dated 18.12.2008, Knowled ge Infrastructure Systems Private Limited

2. Regulations 7(4) and 11(2) of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission

“7. Licence Fee
(4) Fees specified in this regulation shall be paid within thirty days of the date
of grant of licence and thereafter, annually by 30th April of each year subject to
proviso to clause (1) of this regulation.
11. Late payment surcharge
(2) Without prejudice to the liability for late payment surcharge, the Commission may
take any other action as may be considered appropriate for non-compliance of these
regulations if payment of fees is delayed beyond two months from the due dates of
payment as specified in these regulations.”
3. As per the above provisions of the Payment of Fees Regulations, the licensees

the liability for late payment surcharge, the Commission is empowered to take any
Order in Petition No. 6/SM/2026 Page 2 of 8

other action it considers appropriate for non-compliance if payment of fees is delayed

4. Regulation 9 (15) of the Trading Licence Regulations, 2020 provides that:
“9. Obligations of the Trading Licensee:
(15) The Trading Licensee shall pay the licence fee by the stipulated date specified
by the Commission from time to time.”
As per Regulation 9 (15) of the Trading Licence Regulations, 2020, the
licensee is required to regularly pay the licence fee specified by the Commission,
from time to time.
5. Regulations 11(2), (4), (5) and (7) and Regulation 12(2) and (3) of the Trading
Licence Regulations, 2020 provide that:
“11. Submission of Information:
(2) Furnish monthly information through Forms IV-A, IV-B, IV-C, IV-D, IV-E, IV-F,

the Commission before 15th of the succeeding month:
Provided that the information sent to the Commission, shall be posted on the website
of the Trading Licensee by 15th of the succeeding month, and such report shall be

(4) Submit annual return of inter-State transactions detailing:

(b) total volume transacted in intra-State transactions on the basis of the inter-

IV-J;

12. Standards of Performance:
(2) Till such time the standards of performance are specified under clause (1), the

(3) The Trading Licensee shall display on its website (i) the volume of inter-State
and intra-State trading on the basis of the inter-State trading licence, if any, on
monthly basis; (ii) trading licences held by it; (iii) petitions filed before the
Commission and the orders including interim orders, if any, issued by the
Commission to ensure dissemination of information to its clients.”
6. It has been observed that the Respondent has defaulted in the payment of the
annual licence fee of Rs. 10.98 lakh for three consecutive financial years (2023 to
2026), due by 30th April of each year, in terms of the Payment of Fees Regulations
and Trading Licence Regulations, despite repeated reminder dated 12.11.2024,
12.12.2024, 3.1.2025, 13.1.2025, 27.1.2025, 12.2.2025, 21.2.2025, 4.3.2025,

has also defaulted in providing the information regarding the volume of electricity
transacted, revenues and expenses, and costs incurred due to default/delay in
contract payments during the last five years (2020-25), as sought vide letter dated
16.12.2024. Respondent has neither submitted the required information nor
responded to the said correspondence. As on 28.2.2026, the total outstanding
amount (with late payment surcharges) is Rs. 10.98 lakh.
Order in Petition No. 6/SM/2026 Page 4 of 8

7. Regulation 9 (16) of the Trading Licence Regulations, 2020 provides as under:
“9 (16). The Trading Licensee shall not omit or neglect to undertake trading
activity.”
8. Regulations 17(5), (6), (7), (10), (11) and (12) of the Trading Licence
Regulations, 2020 enumerate specific acts constituting contravention and non-
compliance by a Trading Licensee as under:
“17 . Contravention by Trading Licensee
(5) Non-compliance of the orders of the Commission including the orders issued
for contravention of any regulation of the Commission;
(6) Non-payment of the licence fees and surcharge, if applicable within the due
date as specified in Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Payment of
Fees) Regulations, 2012 or statutory re-enactment thereof;
(7) Delay or non-submission of monthly transaction information sought under
clause (2) of Regulation 11;
(10) Non-submission or delay in submission of any report required to be
submitted by the Trading Licensee under any of the regulations mentioned in
clause (1) of this regulation;
(11) Delay in submission of any other information sought by the Commission;
(12) Failure to make mandatory disclosures or reporting in accordance with the
provision to clause (2) of Regulation 11 of these regulations on Trading
Licensee’s website.”
9. Regulation 18 of the Trading Licence Regulations, 2020 provides for the
procedure for taking cognisance of the contraventions as under:
“18. Procedure for taking cognizance of the contraventions
(1) The Commission, on being satisfied on the basis of the information in its
possession or on basis of the information submitted by any person that a prima facie
case exists against any Trading Licensee with respect to any of the provisions of
Regulation 17, may initiate Suo-motu proceedings against the Trading Licensee and
may direct the Trading Licensee to submit such information and explanation as may
be considered necessary for the purpose of the proceeding:
Provided that the proceedings for non-payment of fee shall be initiated if the Trading
Licensee fails to deposit the fees and surcharge, if any, within seven days of the expiry
of due date of payment as per the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission
Order in Petition No. 6/SM/2026 Page 5 of 8

(Payment of Fee) Regulations, 2012:
Provided further that the licence shall be deemed to be suspended after expiry of

(2) No penalty shall be imposed on the Trading Licensee without giving it an
opportunity of being heard.
(3) The penalties, if any, shall be imposed in accordance with Regulation 19 of these
regulations.”
As per Regulations 9 (16), 17(5), (6), (7), (10), (11), and (12) and 18 of the
Trading Licence Regulations, 2020, the trading licensee shall not omit or neglect to
undertake trading activity. It has been brought to our notice by the office of the
Commission that the Respondent has not undertaken any trading activity in the last
three years.
10. Section 19 of the Act provides as under:
“19. Revocation of licence
(1) If the Appropriate Commission, after making an enquiry, is satisfied that public
interest so requires, it may revoke a licence in any of the following cases,
namely: -
(a) where the licensee, in the opinion of the Appropriate Commission, makes wilful

rules or regulations made thereunder;
(b) where the licensee breaks any of the terms or conditions of his licence the
breach of which is expressly declared by such licence to render it liable to
revocation;
(c) where the licensee fails, within the period fixed in this behalf by his licence, or
any longer period which the Appropriate Commission may have granted therefor –
(i) to show, to the satisfaction of the Appropriate Commission, that he is in a
position fully and efficiently to discharge the duties and obligations imposed
on him by his licence;
(ii) or to make the deposit or furnish the security, or pay the fees or other
charges required by his licence;
(d) where in the opinion of the Appropriate Commission the financial position of the
licensee is such that he is unable fully and efficiently to discharge the duties and
obligations imposed on him by his licence.
Order in Petition No. 6/SM/2026 Page 6 of 8

(2) Where in its opinion the public interest so requires, the Appropriate Commission
may, on application, or with the consent of the licensee, revoke his licence as to the
whole or any part of his area of distribution or transmission or trading upon such
terms and conditions as it thinks fit.
(3) No licence shall be revoked under sub-section (1) unless the Appropriate
Commission has given to the licensee not less than three months’ notice, in writing,
stating the grounds on which it is proposed to revoke the licence, and has considered
any cause shown by the licensee within the period of that notice, against the

(4) The Appropriate Commission may, instead of revoking a licence under sub-
section (1), permit it to remain in force subject to such further terms and conditions

(5) Where the Commission revokes a licence under this section, it shall serve a

(6) Where the Appropriate Commission has given notice for revocation of licence
