ORDER
Jhajjar Power Limited (JPL) owns and operates a 1,320 MW coal-based thermal
power plant comprising two units of 660 MW each at Jhajjar, Haryana, supplying power to
the State of Haryana and the National Capital Territory (NCT) of Delhi. Uttar Haryana Bijli
Vitran Nigam Limited and Dakshin Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Limited, the distribution
licensees, procure power through the Haryana Power Purchase Centre (HPPC), and Tata
Power Trading Company Limited (TPTCL), an inter-State trading licensee, sells power
procured from the Petitioner to Tata Power Delhi Distribution Limited (TPDDL) under
back-to-back arrangements.
2. JPL has filed the instant petition under Section 79(1)(b) read with Section 79(1)(f) of
the Electricity Act, 2003 (hereinafter referred to as “the Act”) inter alia, seeking
compensation on account of additional cost incurred/ to be incurred by the Petitioner due
to occurrence of certain Change in Law events, namely, (i) electrification of Railway
sidings in terms of Railway Electrification Notifications, and (ii) increase in water rates in
terms of Notification of Irrigation and Water Resources Department, Government of
Haryana, along with carrying cost thereon. It is noted that the Commission, vide order
dated 14.2.2022, had disposed of this petition directing the Petitioner to approach the
O rder in P etition N o . 5 6 2 / M P /2 0 2 0 pa g e 2 of 26

procurers for settlement of Change in Law claims among themselves in terms of the
Electricity (Timely Recovery of Costs due to Change in Law) Rules, 2021 (2021 Change
in Law Rules) and to approach the Commission only in terms of Rule 3(8) of the 2021
Change in Law Rules. The relevant portions of the said order are as follows:
“3. The matter was heard on 24.1.2022 through video conferencing. During the course of
the hearing, learned senior counsel for the Petitioner submitted that the Petitioner had
issued the notices regarding the occurrence of the aforesaid Change in Law events to the
Respondents. However, there is no agreement/ admission between the parties regarding
the aforesaid events being a Change in Law. In fact, the Respondents in their replies to the
Petition have already contested the Change in Law claims made by the Petitioner. Thus, the
entire matrix of the dispute is already before the Commission in the present case. Learned
senior counsel further submitted that at the time of filing of the present Petition on
22.6.2020, the Electricity (Timely Recovery of Costs due to Change in Law) Rules, 2021 (in
short 'the Change in Law Rules') were not in existence. The Change in Law Rules have
been notified only on 22.10.2021. However, the Commission, in its various recent decisions,
has taken a view that the Change in Law Rules are only procedural and, therefore, apply
retrospectively. However, the Petitioner having invoked the jurisdiction of the Commission
by way of filing the present Petition on 22.6.2020, the law applicable for the adjudication of
the Petitioner's claims is that prevailing as on the date of institution of the Petition. It is well
settled that the law applicable on the date of institution of the suit alone governs the suit. In
this regard, the reliance was placed on the decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in
Ramesh Chandra v. Additional District Judge and Ors., [(1992) 1 SCC 751]. Learned senior
counsel submitted that rather than disposing of the matter in view of the Change in Law
Rules, the Commission may consider adjourning the matter for 60 days or sine die, while
directing the parties to comply with the procedure prescribed in the Change in Law
Rules. Pursuant thereto, if the parties can reconcile the claims and resolve the issues, the
matter may be disposed of by way of an appropriate order. In the event, parties are not able
to resolve the issues, the Petitioner may be permitted to place on record the notice issued
under the Change in Law Rules and the response of the Respondents and thereafter, the
Commission can pass an effective order in the matter.”
“8. We consider that the process and methodology as prescribed in the Change in Law
Rules is simply a mechanism for time-bound settlement of claims in a deterministic manner,
and the Petitioner is not going to be prejudiced by adopting the said mechanism. We have
already held in our earlier orders (e.g. Order dated 06.12.2021 in Petition No. 228/MP/2021)
that since the Change in Law Rules is like procedural law and under the Change in Law
Rules, any substantive rights are not being taken away, it is to be applied retrospectively in
all pending proceedings.
9. In view of the foregoing discussions, the Petitioner may approach the procurers for
settlement of Change in Law claims among themselves in terms of the Change in Law
Rules and approach the Commission only in terms of Rule 3(8) of the Change in Law Rules.
The filing fees paid in the present Petition shall be adjusted against the Petition to be filed in
future in terms of Change in Law Rules.
10. Accordingly, the Petition No. 562/MP/2020 and IA No. 79/2021 are disposed of in terms
of the above.”
3. Subsequently, APTEL, vide order dated 5.4.2022 in OP No. 1 of 2022, observed
that several petitions seeking compensation on account of Change in Law events had
O rder in P etition N o . 5 6 2 / M P /2 0 2 0 pa g e 3 of 26

been disposed of by the Commission by directing the parties to follow the procedure
prescribed under the 2021 Change in Law Rules and directed the Commission to exercise
its review jurisdiction, suo motu, in all similarly placed claims for compensation founded on
change in law events where similar decisions were taken by the Commission after coming
into force of 2021 Change in Law Rules on 22.10.2021. APTEL further observed that if
such orders of the Commission are found to be inconsistent with the legal position clarified
by APTEL in the order dated 5.4.2022, or if those orders do not conform to the
interpretation given by APTEL, the Commission shall vacate the same and restore the
concerned claim cases to its file and complete the process of adjudication in accordance
with law. In pursuance of the APTEL order dated 5.4.2022, the Commission heard
together various petitions involving Change in Law claims, including Petition No.
562/MP/2020 and vide RoP dated 9.5.2022, decided to pass suo-motu orders applying the
2021 Change in Law Rules to Petitions previously disposed of by the Commission.
However, the Commission observed that for Petitions where APTEL had already set aside
the Commission’s dismissal orders, no suo-motu orders are needed. The Commission
further stated that it will decide on related requests as given in the following paragraphs by
APTEL in order dated 5.4.2022:
“72 - For the foregoing reasons, we find the impugned orders of the Central Commission
applying the CIL Rules to matters pending before it for adjudication under Section 79(1)(f)
of the Electricity Act on the date of coming into force of said rules wholly erroneous,
improper and bad in law. The said orders are thus set aside. In the result, the proceedings
in claim cases (in which impugned orders were passed – and that includes the orders dated
04.02.2022 in the Original Petitions) remain inchoate. The Central Commission is duty-
bound to consider each of them on the merits of the claims and adjudicate in accordance
with law on the dispute(s) in proper exercise of its jurisdiction under Section 79 of the
Electricity Act. It is directed to proceed to do so expeditiously.”
“74 - Such that the affected parties do not suffer on account of faulty approach of
adjudicatory authority, and this tribunal is not flooded by appeals raising identical issues
against such other decisions as above, rendered in similar fact-situation by the Central
Commission, it would be appropriate that it be asked to properly and fully perform its
statutory function by exercise of its review jurisdiction, suo motu, in all similarly placed
claims for compensation founded on change in law events where similar decisions have
been taken by the Central Commission after coming into force of CIL Rules on 22.10.2021
and, if such decisions are found running afoul of the view taken by this tribunal by this
judgment, to vacate the same and restore the concerned Claim cases to its file and
complete the process of adjudication thereupon in accordance with law. Needful action in
O rder in P etition N o . 5 6 2 / M P /2 0 2 0 pa g e 4 of 26

the above nature shall be initiated by the Central Commission within four weeks of this
judgment. Of course, a review can be undertaken even at the instance of the parties in
question, should they approach the Commission on their own. We may add that these
directions are without prejudice to the remedy, if any, already pursued or intended to be
pursued by the concerned parties vis-à-vis other such cases.”
4. The Petitioner filed I.A. No. 15/IA/2023 on 22.12.2022 to amend the petition to bring
on record certain developments that had taken place after the filing of the petition. In the
hearing dated 21.2.2023, the Petitioner stated that it had also filed IA No.79/IA/2021
earlier, seeking amendment to the pleadings/prayers to bring on record, the Ministry of
Railway’s Amendment No.5 to Circular No.2018/TC/(FM)/14/04 dated 23.6.2020 on
account of which the Petitioner had been required to bear the additional costs towards
maintenance of Over Head Equipment (OHE). The Commission, vide RoP dated
21.2.2023, had permitted the Petitioner to file a consolidated amended petition.
5. The prayers made by the Petitioner in the amended petition are as follows:
“(A) Admit the present Petition;
(B) Declare that the Railway Budget 2011-2012 (Electrification of the Line in the Pink Book),
Vision 2020 Blueprint dated 04.04.2011 and letter of Divisional Railway Manager dated
03.05.2012, qualify as events of 'Change in Law' in terms of the PPAs;
(B2) Declare that the Amendment No. 5 dated 23.06.2020 to Circular No. 2018/TC (FM)/14/04
issued by the Ministry of Railways, by way of which additional costs of maintenance of OHE
were imposed on the Petitioner, qualifies as an event of ‘Change in Law’ in terms of Article
13 of the PPAs;
(B3) grant in-principle approval to the Petitioner to recover the additional expenditure which may
be incurred by the Petitioner in future due to the issuance of Amendment No. 5 dated
23.06.2020 to circular no. 2018/TC (FM)/14/04 issued by the Ministry of Railways requiring
the Petitioner to bear the cost towards maintenance of OHE and the inspection charges
payable to NWR;
(B4) grant in-principle approval to the Petitioner to recover the additional expenditure which may
be incurred by the Petitioner in future due to issuance of Policy Circular on Private Sidings:
Freight Marketing Circular No. 99/TC(FM)/26/1/Pt.-II dated 22.08.2016 by Ministry of
Railways requiring the Petitioner to bear the cost towards inspection and supervision during
maintenance of S&T assets.”
(C) Declare that the costs due to increased operational expenses due to increased water
charges, to be compliant with Haryana Government Gazette notification no.08/04/2009-21W
dated 30.11.2018 issued by Irrigation and Water Resources Department, State Government
of Haryana, as intimated by the Engineer-in-Chief, IWRD, Government of India vide circular
no. 1541- 93/2R&CR/275/2011 dated 07.12.2018, qualifies as events of 'Change in Law' in
terms of the PPAs;
(D) Allow Carrying Cost and restore the Petitioner to the same economic condition before the
occurrence of the Change in Law Events by permitting the Petition and the amounts as per
the computations set out hereinabove or through a suitable mechanism to compensate the
Petitioner for the financial impact of the Changes in Law Events;
(E) Permit the Petitioner to recover an amount of INR 9,99,63,038 (Rupees Nine Crore Ninety
Nine Lakhs Sixty Three Thousand and Thirty Eight) paid by it to North Western Railway and
other additional costs that it may incur in future towards Electrification Costs of the Private
O rder in P etition N o . 5 6 2 / M P /2 0 2 0 pa g e 5 of 26

Railway Siding through a Supplementary Bill to be raised on the Respondents in accordance
with the provisions of the PPAs.
(F) Pass directions to allow the Petitioner to recover an amount of INR 39,10,33,433/- (Indian
Rupees Thirty Nine Crores Ten Lakh Thirty Three Thousand Four Hundred Thirty Three
Only) paid by it to IWRD for usage of water for the period of FY 2018 – 2019 till November
2022 through a Supplementary Bill to be raised on the Respondents in accordance with
provisions of the PPAs and any other additional costs that it may incur in future Contract
Years;
(FA) Declare that the Notification dated 15.07.2022 has no. 199/N/LA/HWRA/2022, issued by
the Haryana Water Resources Authority, qualifies as events of 'Change in Law' in terms of
the PPAs;
(FB) Pass directions to allow the Petitioner to recover the increased operational expenses
incurred by it to be compliant with the HWRA Notification;
(G) Declare that the Petitioner is entitled to recover carrying cost/ interest on all amounts
incurred/paid by the Petitioner for ensuring compliance with the Railway Electrification
Notifications and the Water Rate Notification from the date of incurrence/ payment of such
amounts by the Petitioner till such date as the Petitioner recovers such amounts in their
entirety;
(H) Allow necessary amendments to the PPAs to account for the aforementioned Change in Law
Events and direct the Respondents to execute such necessary amendments;
(I) Allow modification/ alternation/ amendment of the Petition/pleadings and/or provide additional
information in support of the Petitioner’s claim, if necessary; and
(J) Pass such further order(s) as this Hon'ble Commission may deem just and proper in the facts
and circumstances of the case.”
Hearing in the matter
6. The Petition was admitted on 6.4.2021, with directions for the impleadment of parties
and filing of replies and rejoinders. Thereafter, the matter was heard on several occasions
including, on 24.1.2022, 9.5.2022, 21.3.2023, 2.5.2023, 23.8.2023, 18.10.2023, 12.2.2024
and 7.5.2025 during which submissions were made on the Change in Law claims relating
to railway electrification and increase in water charges, and time was granted to the parties
for filing replies, rejoinders, amended pleadings, and additional affidavits to place
subsequent developments on record. The Commission, vide RoP of the hearing dated
12.2.2024, permitted the Petitioner to file an additional affidavit to bring on record the
details relating to the additional demands raised by the Railways upon the Petitioner
towards electrification of railway sidings. Final arguments were concluded on 30.7.2025,
and the matter was reserved for order by the Commission, with liberty to the parties to file
written submissions.
7. The gist of the submissions made by the Petitioner is as follows:
Additional cost incurred by the Petitioner towards railway electrification (railway Change in
O rder in P etition N o . 5 6 2 / M P /2 0 2 0 pa g e 6 of 26

Law events)
a) The Petitioner planned a private railway siding at Jharli station on the Rewari–
Manheru line, which was a single-line, non-electrified section during the bidding
stage. The proposal was developed in accordance with the Liberalisation of
Siding Rules Policy issued by the Railway Board vide Letter no. 99/TC (FM)/26/1
dated 31.3.2005, and the Indian Railways Code for the Engineering Department,
(Reprint 1999). The Chief Operations Manager (“COM”), NWR, vide letter
number T 5/PLG/423/Siding/Jharli/BKN Divn dated 10.9.2008, confirmed that no
separate Rail Traffic Clearance (“RTC”) would be required for putting up the
Private Railway Siding, but required submission of detailed plans for
examination. A feasibility study and conceptual plan were prepared, revised as
per the suggestions of the DRM and COM, and received in-principle approval.
Following this, a final location survey and Detailed Project Report were prepared,
estimating the non-electrified siding cost of at ₹32.65 crore. Construction began
in December 2009 and was completed in October 2011.
b) The Railway Board first announced the future electrification of the Alwar–Rewari–
Hissar–Jakhal route on 4.4.2011. Subsequently, on 3.5.2012, the DRM, Bikaner,
informed the Petitioner that electrification of the Rewari–Manheru section, where
the Petitioner’s siding is located, had been sanctioned, and under the 2012
Freight Policy, the Petitioner has to bear the OHE capital cost since the section
had been approved for electrification. The Petitioner was therefore asked to
submit an undertaking to bear these costs. A siding agreement was executed on
30.5.2012 (effective from 5.12.2011), and on 11.6.2012, the Petitioner consented
to bear the OHE capital cost. Later, Railways Vikas Nigam Limited (RVNL)
estimated the electrification cost at ₹8.63 crore, which was revised to ₹8.76 crore
on 14.10.2016. The Petitioner paid ₹8,76,50,872 in advance, which was
acknowledged by the Senior DRM on 6.2.2017. It was further clarified that
electrification had already been sanctioned in the Railway Budget 2011–12 as
part of the doubling work executed by RVNL.
c) The Private Railway Siding was originally planned and executed as an un-
electrified line, and the electrification requirement and resulting expenditure were
never envisaged in the bid or in the earlier in-principle approval of 23.12.2008.
The electrification decision came only in 2011, creating a substantial additional
financial burden. The advance payment was based on an estimated cost, and
there may be further demands if actual costs exceed the estimate.
O rder in P etition N o . 5 6 2 / M P /2 0 2 0 pa g e 7 of 26

d) Thereafter, on 23.6.2020, through the Amended Circular issued by the Ministry of
Railways, the additional costs towards maintenance of OHE were imposed on the
Petitioner. Therefore, in effect, contrary to the erstwhile position of 7 (seven) days
prior to Bid-Deadline, wherein the Railways were to bear such costs as per the
original circular bearing no. 99/TC (FM)/26/1 dated 31.3.2005 (“Original Circular”),
these additional costs were to be borne by the Petitioner. The relevant extract of
the Original Circular is as follows:
“4.3 Maintenance of OHE (Both new & existing siding): It has been decided that
OHE maintenance cost for existing as well as new sidings will be borne by the
Railways. Necessary amendment in the existing instructions as well as correction to
para 1826-E will be issued separately.”
e) Subsequently, on 23.6.2020, the Amended Circular was passed by the Ministry of
Railways, by way of which additional costs towards maintenance of OHE were
imposed on the Petitioner. The above position of payment to be made towards
OHE maintenance was altered from being payable by Railways to being payable
by the siding owner, i.e., the Petitioner in the present case. The relevant extract
of the Amended Circular is as follows:
“1.4 Para 9.3 Maintenance of OHE Para 9.3.1 – OHE maintenance cost for existing
as well as new sidings shall be borne by the siding owner in accordance with
Railways guidelines. Railway will carry out necessary inspection of maintenance
work in six months.”
f) The Ministry of Railways had issued Policy Circular Private Sidings: Freight
Marketing Circular No. 99/TC(FM)/26/1/Pt.-II dated 22.8.2016 (“2016 Policy
Circular”) in supersession of the Original Circular. However, this circular did not
alter the prevailing requirements for the payment of OHE maintenance charges as
provided under the Original Circular. However, vide the 2016 Policy Circular, under
Clause 9.6, a new provision for ‘Maintenance of signalling and telecom (S&T)
Assets’ was introduced. The relevant portion is reproduced below:
“9.6.3 Periodicity of inspection of equipments inside the siding shall be once a
quarter. Railway shall inspect the installation at the level of Sr. Section Engineer to
ensure safety and reliability aspects of the Signals and Telecom equipment. The
cost of such inspection & supervision shall be charged to the siding owner.”
g) As per the procedure specified in Article 13 of the PPAs, the Petitioner issued
requisite Change in Law notices dated 16.9.2021 to the Procurers, i.e., HPPC and

increase in rate of water charges. Therefore, this issue, i.e. Issue (B) is partially decided
against the Appellant i.e. increase in water charges, being input cost, not allowed as
compensation to the Appellant. However, levy of one time water allocation fee, being held
to be a change in law event, the same needs to be compensated to the Appellant.”
31. In view of the settled legal position, we are of the view that the increase in water
charges on account of the Government of Haryana notifications at (e) and (f) does not
qualify as a “change in law” event under Article 13 of the PPAs. Accordingly, the
Petitioner’s request for consequential relief because of the Government of Haryana
notifications is rejected.
B. Whether provisions with regard to notice in the PPA have been complied with
by the Petitioner?
32. We now proceed to examine the event relating to the electrification of the railway
siding with reference to the third criterion, i.e., issuance of notice to the beneficiaries as
provided under Article 13.3 of the PPAs. Article 13.3 of the Discoms PPA and TPTCL
PPA deals with the issue of notice in respect of “change in law” event, and it is as follows:
“13.3 NOTIFICATION OF CHANGE IN LAW
O rder in P etition N o . 5 6 2 / M P /2 0 2 0 pa g e 21 of 26

13.3.1 If the Seller is affected by a Change in Law in accordance with Article 13.2 and
wishes to claim a Change in Law under this Article, it shall give notice to the Procurers of
such Change in Law as soon as reasonably practicable after becoming aware of the same
or should reasonably have known of the Change in Law.
13.3.2 Notwithstanding Article 13.3.1, the Seller shall be obliged to serve a notice to all the
Procurers under this Article 13.3.2 if it is beneficially affected by a Change in Law. Without
prejudice to the factor of materiality or other provisions contained in this Agreement, the
obligation to inform the Procurers contained herein shall be material. Provided that in case
the Seller has not provided such notice, the Procurers shall jointly have the right to issue
such notice to the Seller.
13.3.3 Any notice served pursuant to this Article 13.3.2 shall provide, amongst other things,
precise details of:
(a) the Change in Law; and
(b) the effects on the Seller of the matters referred to in Article 13.2”.
TPTCL PPA also provides for a similar provision in Article 13.3.
33. The Haryana Utilities, vide affidavits dated 22.5.2023 and 18.8.2025, have submitted
that the Petitioner failed to issue “change in law” notices within the stipulated time under
Article 13.3.1 of the PPA. Per contra, the Petitioner vide affidavits dated 27.12.2025 has
submitted that the “change in law" events occurred after the cut-off date as defined under
the PPA and the notices were issued in compliance with Article 13.
34. We have considered the parties’ submissions. It has been noted that the Railway
Siding was conceptualised as an unelectrified siding. However, vide the Railway Budget
2011-12 (Electrification of the Line in the Pink Book) and Vision 2020 Blueprint dated
4.4.2011 (Railway Notifications), the electrification work on the Rewari-Manheru section
was sanctioned by the Railway Board. Subsequently, vide letter dated 14.10.2016
(having Reference No. 676-T/ Plan/RE/Sidings/II), the Petitioner was asked to deposit an
amount of ₹8,76,50,872 (Electrification Cost) in advance so that the electrification of the
Railway Siding can be executed simultaneously with the electrification of the Rewari-
Manheru section. The said amount was released by the Petitioner on 5.1.2017. The
Petitioner vide letter dated 9.8.2017 had issued a notice to HPPC and TPTCL under the
“change in law” event (Electrification of the Railway Siding). Further, Petitioner, vide
letter dated 16.9.2021, had issued an appropriate notice to HPPC and TPTCL, under the
O rder in P etition N o . 5 6 2 / M P /2 0 2 0 pa g e 22 of 26

“change in law” “Amendment No. 5 dated 23.06.2020 to Circular No. 2018/TC (FM)/14/04
issued by the Ministry of Railways”.
35. It is observed that Railways, for the first time, raised a demand on the Petitioner for
₹8,76,50,872 towards cost of electrification of the railway siding on 14.10.2016 and the
same was paid by the Petitioner on 5.1.2017 and the Petitioner issued a notice to the
procurers to this effect on 9.8.2017, much before the crystallisation of the actual cost of
the electrification on 6.2.2023. The above sequence of events shows that the Petitioner
had proactively issued the notice to the procurers much before the crystallisation of the
actual cost of electrification and thereby has complied with the requirement of serving the
notice regarding “change in law” in terms of Article 13.3 of the PPAs, satisfying the third
criterion of issue of notice regarding “change in law” event. Therefore, the events at (a),
(b), (c) and (d) mentioned above qualify as “change in law” events in terms of Article
13.1.1 of the PPA.
Issue No. 3: In-principle approval to recover the additional expenditure towards OHE
maintenance and S&T inspection charges.
36. The Petitioner has prayed for the grant of in-principle approval to recover the
additional expenditure incurred/to be incurred towards maintenance of OHE, inspection
charges, and costs towards inspection and supervision during maintenance of S&T
assets. On the contrary, the Haryana Discoms have submitted that OHE maintenance
and S&T inspection are operational in nature and are not a pass-through under Section
63 of the Act; therefore may not be allowed. TPDDL has submitted that the claims
relating to OHE maintenance under the 2020 Railway Circular are commercial and not
statutory in nature. We have considered the parties' submissions. On examination, we
observe that the PPA does not provide for the grant of any in-principle approval for the
recovery of such costs. Relief under “change in law” can be granted only upon
examination of actual expenditure incurred, subject to a prudence check and in
O rder in P etition N o . 5 6 2 / M P /2 0 2 0 pa g e 23 of 26

accordance with the applicable contractual and regulatory framework. Accordingly, the
Petitioner’s prayer seeking in-principle approval for OHE maintenance and S&T
inspections is denied.
Issue No.4: Allow carrying cost and restore the Petitioner to the same economic
condition before the occurrence of the “change in law” events.
37. The Petitioner has submitted that it is entitled to recover carrying cost/ interest on all
amounts incurred/ paid by the Petitioner for ensuring compliance with the Railway
Electrification Notifications and the Water Rate Notification from the date of incurring/
payment of such amounts by the Petitioner till it recovers the same from the procurers.
The Petitioner has also submitted that in both the PPAs, compensation for “change in
law” during the Operation Period is payable subject to the condition that increase/
decrease in revenues or costs to the Petitioner on account of the introduction of the
Railway Electrification Notifications and Water Rate Notifications is in excess of an
amount equivalent to one percent (1%) of the Letter of Credit (as defined in the relevant
PPA) in aggregate for a Contract Year. On the other hand, Haryana Discoms have
submitted that the Railway Electrification Notifications and Water Rate Notifications
issued by the Government of Haryana are not “change in law” events and hence, no
carrying cost is admissible.
38. We have already held that the Water Rate Notifications issued by the Government of
Haryana are not “change in law” events and therefore the Petitioner is not entitled to any
relief on account of the said notifications. We have also held that the Railway
Electrification Notifications are “change in law” events. It is noted that Rail Vikas Nigam
Limited (RVNL) raised a demand of ₹8,76,50,872 towards electrification of the railway
siding on 14.10.2016, and the Petitioner had paid the same, which was also
acknowledged by the Senior DRM on 6.2.2017. The Petitioner has also paid
₹1,23,12,166 towards S&T works. Subsequently, RVNL completed the electrification
work, informed the Petitioner of the final cost of ₹18,52,16,669 and raised a demand for
O rder in P etition N o . 5 6 2 / M P /2 0 2 0 pa g e 24 of 26

the balance amount of ₹8,52,53,631. On examination, we note that the additional cost
towards electrification of the private railway siding has arisen due to “change in law”
events occurring after the cut-off date. The said expenditure has been incurred pursuant
to the Railways' directions and was not contemplated at the time of bidding. It is also
noted that the Petitioner has issued notice to the procurers as required under Article 13.3
of the PPA. Accordingly, the Petitioner is entitled to recovery of the additional costs
incurred towards the electrification of the railway siding.
39. With regard to the carrying cost, it is a settled principle of law that carrying cost is
payable as per the provisions of the PPA to compensate the affected party for the time
value of money deployed on account of “change in law” events. If the PPAs contain a
restitution clause, the party is allowed to be restored to the same economic position as if
the “change in law” events had not occurred. This is in line with the Hon’ble Supreme
Court’s judgement in Uttar Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Anr. v. Adani Power Ltd. &
Ors dated 25.2.2019, wherein it was held that in case there is an in-built restitutionary
principle in the PPA, the affected party has to be put in the same economic position as if
such a “change in law” event had not occurred, i.e., the party must be given the benefit of
restitution as understood in civil law. Since in the present matter, both the PPAs have
inbuilt restitutionary principles, the Petitioner is entitled to the carrying costs on the
additional expenditure incurred due to the “change in law” event from the occurrence of
the “change in law” event.
40. We would like to state that we have not computed the threshold value for the
“change in law” compensation becoming payable during the Operation Period as per the
proviso to Article 13.2(b) of the PPAs. The “change in law” compensation as allowed
under this order shall become payable only if the impact due to them exceeds the
threshold value as provided in the aforesaid article.
Issue No. 5: Necessary amendments to the PPAs to account for the aforementioned
“change in law” events.
O rder in P etition N o . 5 6 2 / M P /2 0 2 0 pa g e 25 of 26

41. The Petitioner has requested to allow necessary amendments to the PPAs to
account for the aforementioned “change in law” events and to direct the Respondents to
execute such necessary amendments. The State Commission is vested with the
jurisdiction under Section 86(1)(b) of the Electricity Act, 2003, to regulate electricity
procurement, the procurement process and the price at which electricity is procured from
generating companies, licensees or other sources through PPAs. Further, under Article
18.1 of the PPA, the PPA may be amended or supplemented by a written agreement
between the parties, subject to the approval of the Appropriate Commission. Therefore,
we are of the considered opinion that the State Commission is the appropriate
Commission to examine the proposed amendments to the PPAs.
42. In this regard, we would refer to the Commission’s order dated 13.8.2025 in Petition
No. 65/MP/2024, wherein it was held that the State Commission is the Appropriate
Commission under the PPA to approve the amendments to the PPA and directed the
party to approach the State Commission. The relevant portion of the order dated
13.8.2025 is as follows:
“Further, in the present case, the tariff was determined under Section 63 of the Act and the
original tariff was adopted by the State Commission. It is the State Commission, which is
vested with ample power under Section 86(1) (b) to regulate the electricity purchase and
procurement process of distribution licensees, including the price at which electricity is being
purchased. Accordingly, the State Commission is the Appropriate Commission under Article
18.1 of the Act to approve amendments in the terms and conditions of the PPAs, including
the tariff.
40. Thus, we opine that this Commission does not have the necessary jurisdiction to deal
with the issues involved in the Petition, i.e., approval for SPPAs dated 28.2.2023.
Accordingly, the Petitioner is at liberty to approach the State Commission for appropriate
relief.”
43. Accordingly, the Petitioner may approach the State Commission for appropriate
relief.
44. Petition No. 562/MP/2020 is disposed of in terms of the above.

ORDER
This petition has been filed by the Petitioner, SJVN Limited (a joint venture of
Govt. of India and Govt. of Himachal Pradesh) for revision of tariff of Nathpa Jhakri
Power Station (6 x 250 MW) (in short, “the generating station” or “NJPS”) for the period
from 1.4.2019 to 31.3.2024 in accordance with the Central Electricity Regulatory
Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2019 (in short, “the 2019
Tariff Regulations”).
2. The generating station is located in the State of Himachal Pradesh, being a joint
venture between the Government of India (GoI) and the Government of Himachal
Pradesh, as a run-of-river project with pondage having six units of 250 MW each. The
dates of commercial operation (COD) of the different units of the generating station
are as under:

Respondents herein, as per the allocation order issued by MoP, GoI, as well as Power
Purchase Agreements (PPAs) signed with them.
4. The Petitioner had filed Petition No. 31/GT/2020 for the truing up the 2014-19
tariff of the generating station. Further, Petition No. 30/GT/2020 was filed by the
Petitioner for approval of the tariff for the period 2019-24, based on the projected

8. The Commission, vide technical validation letter (“TV Letter”) dated 2.5.2025,
had directed the Petitioner to submit clarifications with respect to the Petition filed. The
Petitioner, vide an affidavit dated 23.5.2025, had furnished additional information in
response to the TV letter dated 2.5.2025 and had served the same on the
Respondents. The Petition was heard on 27.5.2025, and parties were directed to
complete pleadings. The Respondent Punjab State Power Corporation Limited
(“PSPCL”), Respondent Rajasthan Urja Vitran Nigam Limited (“RUVNL”), Respondent
Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Limited (“UPPCL”), Respondent M.P. Power
Management Company Limited (“MPPMCL”), Respondent Tata Power Delhi
Distribution Limited (“TPDDL”), Respondent BSES Rajdhani Power Limited (“BRPL”),
Respondent BSES Yamuna Power Limited (“BYPL”), have preferred their respective
replies to the Petitioner, vide their affidavit dated 23.7.2025, 13.5.2025, 16.7.2025,
22.4.2025, 14.7.2025, 12.9.2025 and 5.8.2025 respectively and the Petitioner has filed

its rejoinder vide affidavits dated 5.8.2025, 11.7.2025, 4.8.2025, 21.5.2025, 23.7.2025,
1.10.2025 and 12.9.2025 respectively.
9. The Petition was further heard on 7.8.2025, wherein, after directing the
Petitioner to submit certain information, the order was reserved. In compliance with
the directions of the Commission, vide ROP (record of proceedings) of the hearing
dated 7.8.2025, the Petitioner has filed additional information vide affidavit dated
1.9.2025. Taking into consideration the submissions of the parties and documents
available on record, we proceed to examine the claims of the Petitioner, in this petition,
on a prudence check as stated in the subsequent paragraphs.
Capital Cost
10. Regulation 19(4) and 19(5) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations provides as under:
“(4) The capital cost in case of existing or new hydro generating station shall also
include:
(a) Cost approved rehabilitation and resettlement (R&R) plan of the project in
conformity with National R&R Policy and R&R package as approved; and
(b) Cost of the developer’s 10% contribution towards Rajiv Gandhi Grameen
Vidyutikaran Yojna (RGGVY) and Deendayal Upadhyaya Gram Jyoti Yojana
(DDUGJY) project affected area.
(5) The following shall be excluded from the capital cost of the existing and new
projects:
(a) The assets forming part of the project, but not in use, as declared in the tariff
petition;
(b) De-capitalised Assets after the date of commercial operation on account of
replacement or removal on account of obsolescence or shifting from one project to
another project:
Provided that in case replacement of transmission asset is recommended by
Regional Power Committee, such asset shall be de- capitalised only after its
redeployment;
Provided further that unless shifting of an asset from one project to another is
of permanent nature, there shall be no de-capitalization of the concerned assets.
(c) In case of hydro generating stations, any expenditure incurred or committed to be
incurred by a project developer for getting the project site allotted by the State
Government by following a transparent process;
(d) Proportionate cost of land of the existing project which is being used for generating
power from generating station based on renewable energy; and
(e) Any grant received from the Central or State Government or any statutory body or
authority for the execution of the project which does not carry any liability of
repayment.”
Order in Petition No. 54/GT/2025 Page 6 of 109

11. The Commission, vide order dated 6.9.2021 in Petition No. 31/GT/2020 (true-
up of tariff for the period 2019-24), had approved the capital cost of Rs. 886426.68
lakh as on 31.3.2019. The same capital cost was considered in the order dated
4.4.2023 in Petition No. 27/RP/2021 as on 1.4.2019. However, the Petitioner, in the
present Petition, has claimed the opening capital cost of Rs. 886448.26 lakh as on
1.4.2019, which also does not match the closing capital cost as on 31.3.2019 allowed
vide order dated 6.9.2021 in Petition No. 31/GT/2020. In response to a TV query, the
Petitioner, vide its affidavit dated 23.5.2025, had submitted that it had vide Appeal No.
340 of 2021 approached APTEL, regarding the issue of the variance in the opening
balance of the gross block.
12. Since the said appeal is pending disposal before APTEL, accordingly, the
capital cost of Rs. 886426.68 lakh as on 31.3.2019, in line with the order dated
6.9.2021 in Petition No. 31/GT/2020, has been considered as the opening capital cost
as on 1.4.2019, for the purpose of revision of tariff for the period 2019-24.
Additional Capital Expenditure:
13. Regulations 25 and 26 of the 2019 Tariff Regulations provide as under:
“25. Additional Capitalisation within the original scope and after the cut – off
date:
(1) The additional capital expenditure incurred or projected to be incurred in respect of
an existing project or a new project on the following counts within the original scope of
work and after the cut-off date may be admitted by the Commission, subject to
prudence check:
(a) Liabilities to meet award of arbitration or for compliance of the directions or order
of any statutory authority, or order or decree of any court of law;
(b) Change in law or compliance of any existing law;
(c) Deferred works relating to ash pond or ash handling system in the original scope of
work;
(d) Liability for works executed prior to the cut-off date;
(e) Force Majeure events;
(f) Liability for works admitted by the Commission after the cut-off date to the extent of
discharge of such liabilities by actual payments; and
(g) Raising of ash dyke as a part of ash disposal system.
Order in Petition No. 54/GT/2025 Page 7 of 109

(2) In case of replacement of assets deployed under the original scope of the existing
project after cut – off date, the additional capitalisation may be admitted by the
Commission, after making necessary adjustments in the gross fixed assets and the
cumulated depreciation, subject to prudence check on the following grounds:
(a) The useful life of the assets is not commensurate with the useful life of the project
and such assets have been fully depreciated in accordance with the provisions of these
regulations
(b) The replacement of the assets or equipment is necessary on account of change in
law or Force Majeure conditions;
(c) The replacement of such assets or equipment is necessary on account of
obsolescence of technology; and
(d) The replacement of such assets or equipment has otherwise been allowed by the
Commission.
26. Additional Capitalisation beyond the original scope
(1) The capital expenditure, in respect of existing generating station or the transmission
system including communication system, incurred or projected to be incurred on the
following counts beyond the original scope, may be admitted by the Commission,
subject to prudence check:
(a) Liabilities to meet award of arbitration or for compliance of order or directions of
any statutory authority, or order or decree of any court of law;
(b) Change in law or compliance of any existing law;
(c) Force Majeure events;
(d) Need for higher security and safety of the plant as advised or directed by
appropriate Indian Government Instrumentality or statutory authorities responsible for
national or internal security;
(e) Deferred works relating to ash pond or ash handling system in additional to the
original scope of work, on case to case basis:
Provided also that of any expenditure has been claimed under Renovation and
Maintenance (R&M) or repairs and maintenance under O&M expenses, the same shall
not be claimed under these Regulations;
(f) Usage of water from sewage treatment plant in thermal generating station.
(2) In case of de-capitalisation of assets of a generating company or the transmission
licensee, as the case may be, the original cost of such asset as on the date of
decapitalisation shall be deducted from the value of gross fixed asset and
corresponding loan as well as equity shall be deducted from outstanding loan and the
equity respectively in the year such de-capitalisation takes place with corresponding
adjustments in cumulative depreciation and cumulative repayment of loan, duly taking
into consideration the year in which it was capitalised.”
14. Regulations 25 and 26 of the 2019 Tariff Regulations, inter alia, provide that the
application for determination of tariff shall be based on admitted capital cost, including
any additional capital expenditure already admitted up to 31.3.2019 (either based on
actual or projected additional capital expenditure) and additional capital expenditure
for the respective years of the period 2019-24. The projected additional capital
Order in Petition No. 54/GT/2025 Page 8 of 109

expenditure allowed for the period 2019-24 in the Order dated 4.4.2023 in Petition No.
27/RP/2021, and the actual expenditure claimed in this petition are as under:
(Rs. in lakh)
2019-20 2020-21 2021-22 2022-23 2023-24
Projected additional capital 3863.49 206.72 250.00 63.60 0.00
expenditure allowed in Review
Petition No. 27/RP/2021*
Actual additional capital 4679.01 19700.55 1421.04 4651.01 853.43
expenditure claimed in this
petition**
*The projected additional capital expenditure allowed in the order dated 4.4.2023 is on a Cash basis.
**The actual additional capital expenditure claimed in the petition is on an accrual basis.
15. The Petitioner has submitted that there are certain capital expenditures, which
were not projected earlier, but had been incurred by the Petitioner, due to site-specific
requirements, for successful and efficient operation of the generating station, and the
same is required to be included as part of the capital base for the purpose of tariff.
16. The Respondents, PSPCL, RUVNL, UPPCL, BRPL, BYPL and MPPMCL have
submitted detailed replies with respect to the additional capital expenditure claimed
for the period 2019-24. Further, the Petitioner, vide its rejoinders, have provided
clarifications with respect to the claimed additional capital expenditure.
17. The matter has been considered. After assessing the submissions of Petitioner
and Respondents, and after exercising a prudence check, the claims with respect to
additional capitalisation are dealt with in the subsequent paragraphs.
Items Claimed under Regulation 25(2)(d) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations
18. It is observed that the Petitioner has claimed items like labyrinth seals, cover
wear rings, etc., for a total amounting to Rs. 861.33 lakh under Regulation 25(2)(d) of
the 2019 Tariff Regulations, quoting that these items have been claimed in order dated
16.9.2021 in Petition No. 30/GT/2020, and the same are to be considered at the time
of truing up. Further, the Petitioner has submitted that the expenditure is against the
items already decapitalized in previous tariff periods.

been reflected in the balance sheet, however the replacement has not been carried

procured".

Procurement of IT hardware and software claimed under Regulation 26(1)(b) of
the 2019 Tariff Regulations
20. The Petitioner has claimed additional capitalisation under provisions of
Regulation 26(1)(b) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations for the items corresponding to
procurement of IT hardware and software - desktop, laptops and other peripherals,
printers etc. amounting to 252.33 lakh and it is also stated that the expenditure has
been allowed on a projection basis for 2019-20 and 2020-21 amounting to 65 lakh and
20 lakh, respectively in the order dated 16.9.2021 in Petition No. 30/GT/2020. The
Petitioner has stated that the said procurement was undertaken by it in compliance
with the directions dated 31.8.2018 issued by the Ministry of Heavy Industries and
Public Enterprises. As per the Petitioner, the said direction was passed to provide
robust IT connectivity and digitisation, among other benefits. It is however, relevant to
point out that directions dated 31.8.2018 has not been placed on record and a bare
perusal of the petition inter alia reveals that the Petitioner has only placed on record,
Office Memorandum dated 21.7.2023 passed by Department of Expenditure, Ministry
of Finance, Government of India, which advises various departments and ministries to
purchase new laptops/ notebooks and similar devices for eligible officers. Further,
guidelines of the Ministry of Communication & IT, for condemnation & disposal of IT
Order in Petition No. 54/GT/2025 Page 10 of 109

equipment are also placed on record by the Petitioner, which are specifically
applicable to IT equipment installed in the Department of Telecommunication, Ministry
of Communications and IT, Government of India.
21. It is observed that the allowed expenditure towards the procurement of IT
hardware and software in the order dated 16.9.2021 in Petition No. 30/GT/2020 was
primarily towards the ERP requirement of the generating station. The Petitioner has
not submitted any proof that procurement of desktops, laptops and other peripherals,
etc. has been carried out to meet the ERP requirement. Instead, the Petitioner has
placed on record supply orders for the procurement of IT hardware and software,
including desktops, laptops, and other peripherals. It is pertinent to mention that the
claimed expenditure towards the procurement of laptops, etc., is of a minor nature and
cannot be allowed as part of the additional capital expenditure. Furthermore, the works
undertaken by the Petitioner to replace vintage computers and IT hardware with state-
of-the-art computers and other similar devices improve the efficiency and efficacy of
the workforce, thereby reducing the Petitioner's costs for various activities. Therefore,
the additional capitalisation sought against the procurement of IT hardware and
software is disallowed.

ORDER
M.P. Power Management Company Limited (MPPMCL), a Government-owned
company of the State of Madhya Pradesh, has filed Petition No.378/MP/2022 and
Petition No.220/MP/2022, under Sections 79(1)(f) and 94 of the Electricity Act, 2003
read with Regulations 74, 82, 111 and 112 of Central Electricity Regulatory Commission
Order in P e tition N o. 378/MP/2022 & 220/MP/2022
Page2 o f 4 0

(Conduct of Business) Regulations, 1999 for considering unit of water utilisation for
irrigation 'Q' from ‘BMQ’ or BM3 (Billion Cubic Meter) to 'MAFt' (Million Acre Feet) in the
tariff orders, in respect of Indira Sagar Hydro-electric Project (in short “ISHEP”) and
Omkareshwar Hydro-electric Project (in short OSP).
2. NHDC Ltd., Respondent No.1, is a joint venture company of NHPC Ltd. and the
Government of Madhya Pradesh (through Narmada Valley Development Authority
‘NVDA’) with equity participation of 51% and 49%, respectively.
3. MPPMCL has filed instant petitions pursuant to the corrigendum issued by
Central Electricity Authority (CEA) on 29.3.2022 to the Techno-Economic Clearance
(TEC) of the ISHEP (Petition No.378/MP/2022) of NHDC, stating that ‘BMQ’ may be
read as ‘MAFt’.
4. The Petitioner has made the following prayers in Petition No. 378/MP/2022:
“a) Admit and allow the instant petition filed by the Petitioner;
b) Revise and compute the Firm power (MW) and Design energy (MUs) from FY
2010-11 to FY 2023-24, as notified by the Commission in tariff orders dated
13.06.2012 in P. no. 154/2010, dated 26.05.2016 in P. no. 461/GT/2014, dated
31.05.2016 in P. no. 265/GT/2014 & dated 06.01.2022 in P.no. 106/GT/2020 in
accordance with the corrigendum dated 29.03.2022 issued by CEA, New Delhi; and
c) Pass such further or other orders as the Commission may deem just and proper
in the circumstances of the case.”
5. The Petitioner has made the following prayers in Petition No. 220/MP/2022:
“a) Admit and allow the instant petition filed by the Petitioner;
b) Revise the Firm power and Design energy in tariff orders dtd 09.05.2013 (P. no.
248/GT/ 2012), dtd 26.05.2016 (P no. 264/GT/2014), dtd 10.05.2016 (P no.
460/GT/2014) & dtd 11.03.2022 (P. no. 107/GT/2020) issued for the tariff period
2009-14, 2014-19 and 2019-24 in respect of Omkareshwar Hydro Electric Project,
from the commencement of stage-II of utilizable water for irrigation requirement
and reduced Reservoir level i.e., from 2010-11 onwards up to 2019 and for tariff
period 2019-24 in consonance with corrigendum issued by CEA in respect of Indira
Sagar Hydroelectric Project, TEC of Omkareshwar Hydro Electric Project issued
by CEA, NWDT award and NCA certificates & Reservoir level Daily Reports; and
c) Pass such further or other orders as the Commission may deem just and proper
in the circumstances of the case.”
Order in P e tition N o. 378/MP/2022 & 220/MP/2022
Page3 o f 4 0

6. The prayers made, and the relief sought in Petition No. 378/MP/2022 and Petition
No. 220/MP/2022 are similar, and the petitions are based on the corrigendum issued by
CEA on 29.3.2022 to the TEC of ISHEP. Therefore, both the said petitions are dealt with
together in the instant order.
7. After hearing the submissions of the Petitioner, the Commission admitted Petition
No. 220/MP/2022 on 11.12.2022 and Petition No. 378/MP/2022 on 11.4.2023 and
issued notice to the Respondents and directed the parties to complete the pleadings.
8. In Petition No. 220/MP/2022, NHDC Limited (NHDC) filed replies dated 9.3.2023
and 20.11.2023, and the Petitioner filed the rejoinders vide affidavit dated 1.5.2023 and
14.12.2023. The Petitioner filed an additional affidavit dated 30.11.2023. NHDC filed a
written submission dated 5.4.2024 and 19.8.2025, and the Petitioner filed a written
submission dated 7.11.2025.
9. In Petition No. 378/MP/2022, NHDC Limited filed replies dated 2.5.2023 and
20.11.2023. The Petitioner filed the rejoinders vide affidavit dated 19.5.2023 and
14.12.2023. The Petitioner filed an additional affidavit dated 30.11.2023. NHDC filed a
written submission dated 5.4.2024 and 19.8.2025, and the Petitioner filed a written
submission dated 7.11.2025.
10. The final hearing in these matters was held on 17.10.2025, and the order was
reserved. This order is being passed on the basis of the submissions made by the
Petitioner vide affidavits dated 9.3.2023, 1.5.2023, 2.5.2023, 19.5.2023, 30.10.2023,
201.11.2023, 14.12.2023, 5.4.2024, 19.8.2025 and 7.11.2025.
Submissions of the Petitioner in Petition No. 378/MP/2022
11. The gist of the submissions made by the Petitioner in the case of ISHEP in
Petition No.378/MP/2022 are as follows:
Order in P e tition N o. 378/MP/2022 & 220/MP/2022
Page4 o f 4 0

(a) ISHEP (1000 MW of 8×125 MW) is a component of the Narmada Sagar
Multipurpose Project (Irrigation & Power) in the Narmada Basin, Madhya
Pradesh. The project acts as the mother reservoir for downstream projects and
provides regulated releases that benefit the Omkareshwar and Sardar Sarovar
projects. The project achieved Commercial Operation on 17.1.2005, and the
Government of India has allocated 100% of the power generated from Indira
Sagar HEP to the State of Madhya Pradesh, at a tariff to be determined by this
Commission.
(b) Prior to commissioning, CEA accorded TEC to the Indira Sagar Project on
22.5.1984, based on the final allocation of Narmada basin waters under the
Narmada Water Disputes Tribunal (NWDT) Award dated 12.12.1979. Under the
said Award, water allocation from the Narmada Basin was fixed at 18.25 MAFt -
Madhya Pradesh, 9.0 MAFt - Gujarat, 0.25 MAFt for Maharashtra and 0.50 MAFt
for Rajasthan, aggregating to a total of 28 MAF. On 31.3.1989, CEA granted
approval for TEC to RCE of Indira Sagar HEP.
(c) On the request made by the Petitioner and after examination with reference
to the NWDT Award, NVDA and NHDC records, CEA issued a corrigendum dated
29.3.2022 clarifying that the unit of total irrigation water utilisation in the TEC/RCE
of Indira Sagar Project was erroneously mentioned as BM³ and the correct unit is
MAF (Million Acre Feet). Accordingly, CEA directed that in Para 3.1 of the RCE
dated 31.3.1989, the unit “BM³” shall be read as “MAF”. The relevant portion of
the corrigendum dated 29.3.2022 is as follows:
“In view of above, following corrigendum is issued in CEA letter no. 3/112/89-
PAC/732 to 734 dated 31.03.1989 for Narmada Sagar MPP (Indira Sagar), in
table of para 3.1 (power benefit from the project) of revised cost estimate (‘unit’
of total irrigation utilization in basin):
‘BMQ’ (Billion Cubic Meter) may be read as ‘MAFt’ (Million Acre
Feet)”
(d) In view of the said corrigendum, it has become necessary to replace the unit
and corresponding numerical values of irrigation water utilisation ‘Q’ from BM³
to MAFt for computation of Firm Power and Design Energy, particularly under
Stage-II of irrigation development, in the tariff and truing-up orders passed by
the Commission for the tariff periods 2009-14, 2014-19 and 2019-24 in respect
of the ISHEP.
Order in P e tition N o. 378/MP/2022 & 220/MP/2022
Page5 o f 4 0

(e) The tariff orders in question were passed by relying upon the TEC of the
project, wherein the unit of total irrigation utilisation was inadvertently mentioned
as BM³, contrary to the NWDT Award, 1979, which allocates Narmada basin
water in MAFt.
(f) Certification of annual water utilisation (for irrigation, drinking and other uses)
from the Narmada Basin for the States of Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat,
Maharashtra and Rajasthan is issued by the NCA in terms of MCM and MAFt,
and such NCA-certified data has consistently been relied upon by the
Commission for determination of Firm Power and Design Energy in the tariff
orders of the ISHEP.
(g) Due to the incorrect unit being applied, Stage-II of irrigation development
was considered to have commenced prematurely, leading to reduced Firm
Power and Design Energy being adopted in the tariff determination from 2010-
11 onwards. This resulted in incorrect computation of design energy and
secondary energy, thereby artificially inflating the cost of hydel power and
imposing an unwarranted burden on end consumers.
(h) The salient features of Design Energy and Secondary Energy indicated in
the TEC dated 22.5.1984 issued by CEA are reproduced hereunder:
TEC dated 22.05.1984 of Indira Sagar Hydro Electric Project
“1.1 The Narmada a major west flowing river in the Country is an Inter State river
going through the States of Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra and Gujrat. The
question of sharing the water of Narmada was examined by the Narmada Water
Dispute Tribunal which determined 75% utilizable quantum of water as 28 MAFT
and allocated them as under:
Madhya Pradesh - 18.25 Maft
Gujrat - 9.0 Maft
Maharashtra - 0.25 Maft
Rajasthan - 0.50 Maft
The above utilization at 75% dependable year was on the basis of provision of
adequate storage in the basin. For utilizing its share of water of the Narmada Basin,
Madhya Pradesh has drawn up a master plan identifying the possible irrigation,
power and multipurpose project in the basin, their features, phasing of development
etc.………..”
“3. POWER BENEFITS FROM THE PROJECT
3.1 The detailed simulation studies have been carried out to determine the
benefits from Narmada Sagar Project in the 3 stages of irrigation development in
the Narmada basin in MP. These studies for each of the 3 irrigation development
stages have been carried out for the 31 year cycle from 1949 to 1980 for which
Order in P e tition N o. 378/MP/2022 & 220/MP/2022

(k) The Commission issued tariff and truing-up orders for the tariff periods
2009-14, 2014-19 and 2019-24 in Petition Nos. 154/2010, 461/GT/2014,

13.6.2012 are reproduced hereunder:
“Design Energy (Stage-wise) and Commencement of Stage-II of the generating
station
52. The petitioner has submitted that the Government of Madhya Pradesh (GoMP)
is executing Unit-II (Canal) of this multipurpose project and depending upon the
development of canal network and the irrigation command, the three Stages of power
generation for 90% dependable year have been defined in the Techno-Economic
Clearance of CEA for the generating station. Accordingly, in Petition No.119/2005
filed by the petitioner for determination of annual fixed charges for 2004-09 for the
generating station, the Commission had admitted the Design Energy of 1980 MU in
a 90% dependable year, with firm power of 226 MW during Stage-I of the project.
The firm power during 90% dependable year for Stage-II & III of the project shall
subsequently reduce to 125 MW and 100 MW, respectively and accordingly, the
corresponding Design Energy during 90% dependable year for Stages-II & III shall
be 1095 MU and 876 MU, respectively. The petitioner has further submitted that the
current Design Energy of the generating station as approved by the Commission is
1980 MU, corresponding to Stage–I. The respondent No. 2 Narmada Valley
Development Authority (NVDA) has already constructed substantial portion of main
canal and has commenced drawing water for irrigation purposes from Indira Sagar
Reservoir through canal head regulators. Accordingly, the generating station is now
heading towards Stage–II from Stage-I. Taking into consideration the above factors,
the petitioner, during the hearing on 11.10.2011, prayed that that the respondent
No.2, NVDA, be directed to notify the date of termination of Stage-I and the
commencement of Stage-II of the generating station. In reply, the respondent No.2
vide its affidavit dated 17.10.2011 has submitted as under:
"In the reservoir at present there is ample quantity of water available and full
utilization of water for irrigation in Stage-I is under development by NVDA. Also
the Generation achieved at the presently permitted filling level 260.0 M against
FRL 262.13 M for financial year 2009-10 & year 2010-11 are 2118.33 MU &
2197.77 MU respectively. The generation during the financial year 2011-12 is
Order in P e tition N o. 378/MP/2022 & 220/MP/2022
Page8 o f 4 0

expected to be more than 2500 MUs. Thus the generation is more than the
said design Energy of phase-I i.e. 1980 MU. In view of this, Hon'ble CERC is
requested to defer the notification regarding the date of termination of Stage-I
of Canal Development and commencement of Stage-II, till full utilization of
water for irrigation is made by NVDA".
53. In response, the petitioner by its affidavit dated 3.11.2011 has submitted that the
water yields during monsoon 2009 and 2010 were much more than the water yields
corresponding to 90% dependable year and had resulted in generation of extra
energy. However, monsoon 2008 had resulted in water yields less than 90%
dependable year and consequently generation during 2008-09 was less to an extent
of 400 MU with respect to design energy. As such the submissions of the respondent
that ample water is available in the reservoir and generating more than the design
energy does not hold good. It has also submitted that as substantial length of main
canal has been completed by respondent No.2, its Stage-II has already commenced.
Accordingly, the design energy of the generating station for the period 2009- 14
corresponding to Stage-II should be reckoned as 1095 MU.
54. Thereafter, by affidavit dated 10.1.2012 the petitioner has submitted as under;
"1. As per clause 3 of the Techno Economic Clearance, the power benefits from

considered by this Commission in various orders while approving tariff for the period
from 2010-11 to 2019-24 in case of ISHEP and OSP. The Commission has considered
the unit of water utilisation for irrigation ‘Q’ as BMQ or BM3 in the case of ISHEP and
OSP. CEA in paragraph 3.1 of its TEC dated 22.5.1984 in respect of ISHEP has
mentioned ‘Q’ as BM3, and accordingly, the Commission computed Firm Power and
Design Energy considering ‘Q’ as BM3 for ISHEP for the period from 2010-11 to 2019-

40. We have considered the submissions made by the Petitioner. In the case of a
hydro generating station, the Annual Fixed Charges (AFC) approved by the Commission
are recoverable in two components, namely, Capacity Charges (50% of AFC) and
Energy Charges (50% of AFC). The Energy Charges component gets fully recovered
upon generation of energy equivalent to the Saleable Design Energy (SDE), i.e., Design
Energy (DE) minus auxiliary consumption, and is payable at the Energy Charge Rate
(ECR), which is derived on the basis of the AFC approved by the Commission and the
SDE. When the actual saleable energy in a year exceeds the SDE, such excess
generation is treated as secondary energy and is payable at the rate specified under the
applicable Tariff Regulations. This mechanism operates as an incentive structure,
whereby the generating company recovers additional amounts over and above the
energy charge corresponding to energy generated beyond SDE/ DE, while the
beneficiaries receive such additional energy at a rate lower than the ECR.
41. On consideration of ‘Q’ as MAFt, there is an increase in Firm Power, which
correspondingly results in an increase in the Design Energy. However, there is no
change in the total actual energy generated during the disputed period. The effect is
limited to the reclassification of energy from secondary energy to SDE/ DE. Illustratively,
Order in P e tition N o. 378/MP/2022 & 220/MP/2022
Page3 6 o f 4 0

if the earlier Design Energy was 1000 MUs and the actual generation was 1100 MUs,
100 MUs would have been treated as secondary energy. Upon revision, if the Design
Energy increases to 1050 MUs, then out of the same 1100 MUs generated, 1050 MUs
would be treated as Design Energy and only 50 MUs as secondary energy. Thus, there
is no change in total generation, but only a shift in classification.
42. Consequently, the increase in SDE (payable at ECR) and the corresponding
reduction in secondary energy (payable at the rate specified under the Tariff
Regulations) result in a revision of the secondary energy charges for the disputed period.
Except for the years 2017-18 and 2018-19, when the actual generation was lower than
the revised Design Energy, leading to a shortfall in energy charge payment, the impact
would be in the nature of a refund of excess secondary energy charges. However, there
is no change in the approved AFC, Capacity Charges or Energy Charges when we
consider ‘Q’ as MAFt. The impact is confined only to the quantum of secondary energy
and the corresponding payments. Accordingly, the amount relating to energy generated
beyond SDE/ DE (secondary energy) shall be revised retrospectively from the
admissible date.

ORDER
Background
Petition No. 229/2010 was filed by the Petitioner, Aravali Power Company
Private Limited (in short, “APCPL”), seeking approval of the tariff of Indira Gandhi
Super Thermal Power Project, Stage-I (3x500 MW) (in short, “generating station”) for
the period from the date of commercial operation of Unit-I to 31.3.2014. The
Commission, vide Order dated 6.5.2015, determined the tariff from respective CODs
to 31.3.2014 in respect of Unit-I, Unit-II and Unit-III of the generating station.
2. The Petitioner, aggrieved by the Commission’s order dated 6.5.2015, filed
Review Petition No. 12/RP/2015 in Petition No. 229/2010. The Commission, vide order
dated 27.6.2016, while disposing of the said Review Petition, observed as under:
“13. It is observed that the petitioner has filed Petition No. 437/GT2014 for truing up
of tariff of the generating station for the period from 5.3.2011 to 2014 and the same is
pending for consideration by the Commission. Moreover, the petitioner has been
granted liberty in para 35 of the order dated 6.5.2015 to submit certain information. In
this background, we consider it prudent to revise the tariff of this generating station
considering the issues allowed in this order at the time of truing up of tariff in terms of
Regulation 6(1) of the 2009 Tariff Regulations.
14. Petition No. 12/RP/2015 is disposed of in terms of the above. Petition No.
437/GT2014 shall be listed for hearing on 28.7.2016.”
3. The Commission, vide order dated 17.1.2017 in Petition No. 437/GT/2014, read
with corrigendum dated 14.2.2017, trued up the tariff of 2009-14 tariff period in respect
of Unit-I, Unit-II and Unit-III of the generating station.
4. An Appeal No. 204 of 2016 was filed by the Petitioner before the Appellate
Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL), challenging the order dated 6.5.2015 passed by the
Commission in Petition No. 229 of 2010 on the following grounds:
Order in Petition No. 229/2010 (on Remand from APTEL) Page 2 of 26

(a) Consideration of zero date as the date of award of the main plant package instead
of the date of financial closure;
(b) Consideration of Scheduled Commissioning Date as per the schedule tied up with
the vendors instead of benchmark timelines provided in the Tariff Regulations, 2009;
(c) Non-consideration of justifications provided by the Appellant for delay in execution
of various works while circulating the IDC and IEDC;
(d) Disallowance of the additional return on equity of 0.5% as provided in Regulation
15 of the Tariff Regulations, 2009.
(e) Non-consideration of the fact that the hard costs of the project were within the
benchmark costs and there was no cost over-run;
(f) Non-consideration of IDC on the notional loan by virtue of equity deployed in
excess of normative.
5. APTEL vide judgment dated 22.7.2025 has remanded the matter back to the
Commission and vide para 24 to 28 of the said judgment, held as under:
“24. In view of these facts and circumstances of the case, we find that the Commission
was right in reckoning the SCOD of the power project from the date of award for main
plant package instead of date of financial closure, as contended by the Appellant, but
has erred in considering the period for commercial operation of the 1st unit of the
project as 35 months from the date of award of such contract. The Commission ought
to have determined the commissioning schedule as 45 months from the date of main
plant contract for the 1st unit of the project with the interval of six months thereafter
for the other two units as specified in the feasible report.
25. The contention of the Appellant that the SCOD of the power project should be
reckoned from the date of investment approval has no basis and is not borne out from
any document on record. Even the investment approval mentions that commercial
operation date for 1st unit would be 42 months from the date of main plant order, even
though the period of “42 months” has been recorded incorrectly therein as per the
erroneous information given by the GM of NTPC.
26. We have carefully perused the previous judgements of this Tribunal relied upon
by the Learned Counsels for respondents in this matter. In none of those judgements
has this Tribunal considered the commissioning period mentioned in the contract
between the generating company and the vendor for determining the SCOD of the
power project. In all those cases, this Tribunal has determined the SCOD of the power
projects from the date of investment approval. However, in this case, as already noted
herein above, the Commissioning schedule has been mentioned incorrectly in the
investment approval on the basis of a wrong information provided by the GM, NTPC.
Therefore, we find it appropriate to consider the commissioning schedule for power
project in question as specified in the feasibility report.
27. Hence, we direct that the SCOD of the three units of the power project of the
Appellant shall be reckoned as per the schedule given in the feasibility report i.e. 45
months from the date of main plant contract for unit-I with an interval of six months
thereafter respectively for unit-II and III. The impugned order is hereby set aside to
the above extent.
28. Accordingly, the case is now remanded back to the Commission for determining
the timelines for the power project afresh in terms of this judgment after hearing the
Order in Petition No. 229/2010 (on Remand from APTEL) Page 3 of 26

parties again. The Commission shall endeavour to pass the fresh order expeditiously
and not later than four months from the date of the judgment.”
Hearing dated 14.10.2025
6. Pursuant to APTEL order dated 22.7.2025, the matter was heard on 14.10.2025.
The learned counsel for the petitioner referred to the APTEL judgment dated
22.7.2025, and requested a fresh determination of the project timelines, after
hearing the parties in accordance with the said judgment. She further submitted
that once the Scheduled Commercial Operation Date (SCOD) of the Project is
determined, the other reliefs sought by the Petitioner, being consequential thereto,
may also be considered, and requested time to place on record certain additional
documents in the matter. The Commission permitted the Petitioner to submit said
additional information, and the parties were directed to file their written
submissions. In compliance, the Petitioner has filed its written submissions.
Submission of the Petitioner

(a) The APTEL, vide its judgment dated 22.7.2025, has directed that the SCOD

schedule given in the feasibility report, i.e., 45 months from the date of the
main plant contract for Unit-I, with intervals of six months thereafter,
respectively, for Unit-II and Unit-III and issued with specific directions to
determine the timelines afresh in terms of the said Judgment. Accordingly,
the timeline of the project, as per the schedule given in the feasibility report,
is given below:

WORKS WHILE CALCULATING IDC AND IEDC.
(d) In view of the determination of timelines afresh by the APTEL judgment
dated 22.7.2025, the time overrun occurred for reasons beyond the control
of the Petitioner, the presently claimed IDC and IEDC till the date of COD
of Unit-I, II and III are Rs. Rs. 30773, Rs. 65834, and Rs. 114701 lakhs,
respectively.
Order in Petition No. 229/2010 (on Remand from APTEL) Page 7 of 26

II. NON-CONSIDERATION OF THE FACT THAT THERE WAS NO
ESCALATION IN THE MAIN PLANT CIVIL PACKAGE ON ACCOUNT OF
TIME OVERRUN
(e) There was no cost escalation in the main plant civil package on account of
the time overrun; however, the Commission compared the actual
expenditure with the awarded contract price and disallowed the excess
amount on a pro rata basis corresponding to the time overrun determined
in the earlier order dated 6.5.2015. Therefore, in view of the fresh
determination of timelines, the Petitioner has submitted that the time
overrun occurred due to reasons beyond its control, and the disallowed
capital cost pertaining to the main plant civil package may be reconsidered
for inclusion in the capital cost.
III. DISALLOWANCE OF ADDITIONAL RETURN OF EQUITY OF 0.5%.
(f) The Commission had previously disallowed the claim for additional Return
on Equity (‘RoE’) under Regulation 15 of the 2009 Tariff Regulations, on the
ground that the said Regulation mandates commissioning of all units of the
generating station within the timeframe specified in Appendix-II of the said
Regulations. However, the Petitioner challenged this interpretation,
asserting that Regulation 15 applies to individual units, not to the entire
station collectively. In light of the fact that Unit-I was commissioned within
the prescribed timeline, as affirmed by the APTEL judgment dated
22.7.2025, the Petitioner submits that it is entitled to the additional RoE for
Unit-I, which amounts to a total of Rs. 681.1 lakh.
IV. NON-CONSIDERATION OF NOTIONAL IDC.
(g) The decision on this issue will depend upon the extent of time overrun
being considered for Unit-II and Unit-III by the Commission in the present
proceedings. However, it is submitted that the APTEL judgment dated
3.10.2019 in Appeal No. 231 of 2017 (Powerlinks Transmission Limited v.
Central Electricity Regulatory Commission & Ors.) and Appeal No. 212 of
2017 (NTPC Tamil Nadu Energy Company Limited v. A.P. Transmission
Corporation Limited & Ors.) has held that the grant of notional IDC is not
contingent upon the actual drawal of loans. Accordingly, a notional IDC of
Rs. 4475.65 lakhs has been claimed by the Petitioner.
Order in Petition No. 229/2010 (on Remand from APTEL) Page 8 of 26

V. NON-CONSIDERATION OF DEFERMENT OF DRAW-DOWN/
DEPLOYMENT OF DEBT
(h) The decision on this issue will depend on the view taken on the time
overrun by the Commission in the present proceedings. However, in the
order dated 6.5.2015, while computing the cost overrun, the Commission
had not factored in the deferment of drawdown and deployment of debt.
Instead, the cost overrun was calculated proportionally to the time
overrun. In view of the APTEL direction to reassess the SCOD based on
the feasibility report, the project timelines are now being determined
afresh.
(i) Accordingly, the issue of cost overrun warrants reconsideration, as the
revised SCOD will directly impact the quantum and timing of expenditure,
including debt deployment. The deferment of debt drawdown has a

Background
3. The brief facts of the case are as follows:
a. The Investment Approval (IA) for implementation of transmission assets
under the transmission project was accorded by Board of Directors (BoD)
of the Petitioner in its 272nd meeting dated 29.5.2012 vide Memorandum
No. C/CP/FO-SR, dated 6.6.2012 with an estimated cost of ₹17416.00
lakh, including IDC of ₹974.00 lakh based on February, 2012 price level.
The transmission project was scheduled to be put into commercial
operation within 30 months progressively from the date of IA.
b. Further, POSOCO vide letters dated 4.5.2012 and 16.8.2012, requested
for installation of reliable voice communication facilities (Hot Line Speech
Communication System for Grid Operation) due to the problem faced in
Order in Petition No. 634/TT/2025
Page 7 of 52

view of the expansion of power systems in terms of an increase in the
number of power plants, Sub-station, etc. that are reporting to RLDCs and
SLDCs. Due to limited capacity and functionality, it has not been possible
to accommodate the speech requirement of all power plants in the existing
telephone exchanges. During the grid disturbance on 30.7.2012 and
31.7.2012, the operators at the control centres faced many problems in
connecting the speech to other control centres and important stations due
to the non-availability of fast dialing, easy directory sorting and inter-
regional voice connectivity, etc., which consequently affected the grid
restoration process.
c. Accordingly, the competent authority accorded its approval on 31.8.2012
for the establishment of a “Hot Line Speech Communication system for
Grid Operation” as part of ULDC projects.
d. The transmission project was discussed and agreed in 17th SRPC meeting
held on 12.8.2011. Subsequently, it was also discussed in 24th SRPC
meeting held on 15.3.2014 and 25th SRPC meeting held on 26.7.2014.
e. The Revised Cost Estimate (RCE) for the transmission project was
accorded by Board of Directors of the Petitioner in its 347th meeting dated
8.12.2017 vide Memorandum No. C/CP/PA1718-12-0E-RCE005 dated
28.12.2017 with an estimated cost of ₹19474.00 lakh including IDC of
₹1233.00 lakh based on June, 2017 price level.

Capital Cost for 2019-24 Tariff Period
11. The capital cost of the transmission assets has been calculated in accordance
with Regulation 19(1) and 19(2) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations.
12. The Commission vide order dated 19.1.2024 in Petition No. 294/TT/2022 and
30.5.2024 in Petition No. 194/TT/2023 had allowed the capital cost as on 1.4.2019 /
COD of ₹15210.97 lakh and ₹511.18 lakh in respect of Combined Asset and Asset-13
respectively for the 2019-24 tariff period. The Petitioner in the instant true-up Petition
has claimed the capital cost of ₹15221.47 lakh and ₹511.18 lakh in respect of Combined
Asset and Asset-13, respectively for the 2019-24 tariff period.
13. The Petitioner has submitted that the variation of ₹10.51 lakh between the capital
cost as on 1.4.2019 allowed vis-à-vis the amount claimed in the instant Petition is on
Order in Petition No. 634/TT/2025
Page 15 of 52

account of the Initial Spares, which were earlier disallowed but have been added back
in the instant Petition based on the overall completion cost of the project, in accordance
with the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL) judgment in Appeal No. 74 of 2017.
14. We have considered the Petitioner’s submissions and noted that the
Commission, vide its Order dated 19.1.2024 in Petition No. 294/TT/2022, had
disallowed the amount of ₹10.51 lakh towards excess Initial Spares. We note that Asset-
“NCTPS (TNEB)-Tondiarpet (TNEB) (17.893 km) OPGW communication link” is yet to
be commissioned as submitted by the Petitioner. Therefore, all the assets under the
transmission project have not been commissioned.
15. Further, we observed that the APTEL in its judgement dated 14.9.2019 in Appeal
No. 74 of 2017 observed that the Commission for the purpose of prudence check may
restrict the Initial Spares to the cost of the individual asset and later at the time of truing
up allow initial spares as per the ceiling limits on the overall project cost. The relevant
portion of the said judgement is extracted here under:
“18.13. ……… We do not agree with this methodology of restricting initial spares
asset / element wise as adopted by the Central Commission. The Central
Commission to have a prudence check on the initial spares, being restricted based
on the individual asset wise cost initially, but subsequently ought to have allowed as
per the ceiling limits on the overall project cost basis during the true- up.”
16. In terms of the judgement, the initial spares are to be allowed as per the
prescribed norms on the overall project cost, which can ideally be determined only when
all the transmission assets are combined. However, Asset-“NCTPS (TNEB)-Tondiarpet
(TNEB) (17.893 km) OPGW communication link” is yet to be commissioned.
Accordingly, claim of additional Initial Spares of ₹10.51 lakh in respect of Combined
Asset (1 to 12) is not accepted at this stage. The same shall be reviewed once all the
assets under the project will be commissioned and combined.
