3. The BPC published the Request for Qualification (RfQ) on 21.12.2016 for
shortlisting of the bidders for the Project and subsequently issued the Request for
Proposal dated 6.6.2017 (‘RfP’) for selection of the TSP for executing the Project.
Pursuant to the bidding process, Sterlite Grid 5 Limited (‘SGL5’) emerged as the
successful bidder and the Petitioner company was acquired by it. The Petitioner was
granted a transmission licence under Section 14 of the Act by the Commission, vide
its order dated 13.7.2018 in Petition No. 95/TL/2018, to establish the Project. Further,
vide its Order dated 13.7.2018 in Petition No. 97/AT/2018, this Commission adopted
the competitively discovered levelized tariff of Rs. 1647.75 million/annum.
Subsequently, after seeking approval dated 2.11.2020 from Respondent No.2,
Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Company Limited (‘MSEDCL’), i.e., the Lead
Long-Term Transmission Customer (‘Lead LTTC’) in terms of Article 18.2 of the TSA,
SGL5 transferred its shareholding in the Petitioner to Sterlite Grid 29 Limited
(‘SGL29’).
4. During the execution of the Project, the Petitioner faced several uncontrollable
impediments and challenges in the form of Force Majeure events. The Project also
faced several Change in Law events which unavoidably escalated the cost of its
implementation. Accordingly, the Petitioner filed Petition No.239/MP/2021 seeking a
consequential adjustment in the tariff payable to the Petitioner in terms of Article 12 of
the TSA to offset the financial impact of various Change in Law events that impacted
the Project during its construction period. Further, the Petition also sought an
extension to the SCOD of the Project in view of the delay in implementation caused
by the various Force Majeure events described in the Petition, in terms of Article 11 of
the TSA. The matter was heard on 24.1.2022, and notice was issued to the
Order in IA No. 91/2025 in Petition No. 239/MP/2021
Page 5 of 33

Respondents. After hearing the learned counsel for the parties, the Commission
reserved the order on the admissibility of the matter. Subsequently, the Commission,
vide its order dated 8.2.2022, had disposed of this matter at the stage of admission
itself. With respect to the Petitioner’s Force Majeure claims, the Commission observed
that since the Project has not been commissioned by the Petitioner and there was
uncertainty about the likely Commercial Operation Date (COD), it would not be
appropriate to take any view of the extension of SCOD. Accordingly, the Petitioner
was granted the liberty to approach the Commission for Force Majeure events after
commissioning of the Project. Whereas, with respect to the Change in Law reliefs, the
Commission had directed the Petitioner to approach the LTTCs for settlement of its
Change in Law claims among themselves in terms of the Electricity (Timely Recovery
of Costs due to Change in Law) Rules, 2021 (‘Change in Law Rules’) and approach
the Commission only in terms of Rule 3(8) of the Change in Law Rules.
5. The above order was challenged by the Petitioner before the Appellate Tribunal
for Electricity (the APTEL) in Appeal No. 134 of 2022, inter alia, on the limited ground
that the Commission ought to have considered granting the declaratory reliefs on the
merits of Force Majeure and Change in Law events faced by the Petitioner. The
APTEL, by its order dated 1.5.2023, set aside the Commission’s order dated 8.2.2022
and remanded the matter for this Commission to consider the rival contentions on
merits and in terms of its judgment dated 5.4.2022 in OP Nos. 1 and 2 of 2022 and
Appeal No. 116 of 2022 & batch.
6. Subsequently, the matter was heard on 5.7.2023. During the hearing, the
learned counsel for the Petitioner reiterated the submissions made in the pleadings
and further prayed for leave of the Commission to file an IA to incorporate necessary
amendments to the Petition. Considering the submissions made by the learned senior
Order in IA No. 91/2025 in Petition No. 239/MP/2021
Page 6 of 33

counsel for the Petitioner, the Commission permitted the Petitioner to file a proper
application for amendment of the Petition. Thereafter, the matter was heard on
11.10.2023 & 19.2.2024, wherein the learned counsel for the Petitioner, keeping in
view the decision of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Civil Appeal Nos. 12234-35 of 2018
(Goa Foundation v. State of Goa and Ors.), sought extension of time to file the
amended Petition in terms of the liberty granted by the Commission.
7. The matter was again heard on 27.2.2025. During the course of the hearing
dated 27.2.2025, the learned counsel for the Petitioner submitted that in view of the
subsequent developments and in terms of liberty granted by the Commission vide
Record of Proceedings for the hearing dated 19.2.2024, the Petitioner had filed the IA
No. 107/2024 seeking amendment of the Petition by including the details and
documents in relation to the subsequent developments and certain Force Majeure and
Change in Law events that have additionally impacted the implementation of its
Project. The details of the Petitioner’s Force Majeure and Change in Law claims, as
indicated in the proposed amendment, are tabulated hereunder:

8. On 27.2.2025, the Commission allowed the IA No. 107/2024 filed by the
Petitioner, and consequently, the amended Petition was taken on record. The
Respondents were permitted to file their respective replies to the amended Petition.
Subsequently, the matter was heard on 22.5.2025 wherein the learned counsel for the
Petitioner submitted that, in its recent order dated 20.04.2025 in Petition No.
131/MP/2024 (Mumbai Urja Marg Limited v. MSEDCL and Ors.) (“MUML Order”), the
Commission has held, inter alia, that unless the events claimed as Change in Law are
either consented to by the beneficiaries of the region in which the transmission system
Order in IA No. 91/2025 in Petition No. 239/MP/2021
Page 8 of 33

is situated or are specifically adjudicated and allowed by the Commission, NLDC
and/or CTUIL shall not include such claims for recovery under the Sharing
Regulations, 2020. In light of this position, the Petitioner’s Change in Law recoveries,
arising after the Change in Law Rules, 2021, could not commence. Accordingly, the
learned counsel for the Petitioner sought permission to further amend the Petition to
incorporate its Change in Law claims arising on or after 1.10.2021. Considering the
above, the Commission permitted the Petitioner to file an appropriate application
seeking amendment(s) to the Petition, as prayed for. Accordingly, the Petitioner has
filed IA No.91/2024 seeking an amendment to the Petition previously filed to include
details and documents relating to the Change in Law events that have occurred on or
after 21.10.2021.
Submissions of the Petitioner
9. The Petitioner has mainly submitted that several crucial developments have
taken place in the present matter since the captioned Petition was originally filed,
which necessitate an amendment to the captioned Petition. By way of the present
amendment application, the Applicant seeks to bring on record the relevant
subsequent developments, which go to the root of the matter and are imperative for a
proper and effective adjudication on merits. These events were not included in the
earlier amended Petition, where the Petitioner expressly reserved its rights under the
Change in Law Rules to separately make claims for all Change in Law events that
occurred after 21.10.2021 in accordance with the statutory procedure stipulated
thereunder. However, in view of the Commission’s MUML Order, the Petitioner seeks
to amend the Petition, as previously amended vide IA No. 107/2024, to include the
details and documents in relation to the Change in Law events that have occurred on
or after 21.10.2021, i.e., the date of issuance of Change in Law Rules.
Order in IA No. 91/2025 in Petition No. 239/MP/2021
Page 9 of 33

10. Through the present IA, the Petitioner has sought to substitute Para 9 of the
Petition, deletion of Para 242 of the Petition and insertion of Para 288 in the Petition.
The Petitioner has also sought to substitute Paragraph 312, containing the prayer
clause of the Petition. The Change in Law events that the Petitioner has now sought
are as follows: For Xeldem Substation: (a) Additional expenditure due to change in
location and technology, (b) Change in Scope of Work- Protection Fund Requirement,
(c) Additional expenditure due to relocation orders issued by the District Magistrate,
South Goa. For the XX & XM Line : (a) Change in compensatory afforestation rates
and (b) Change in Net Present Value rates. Finally, for the NN the NN Line: (a) Change
in the route of the NN Line in the State of Karnataka, (b) Additional expenditure
incurred due to additional scope of work in NN Line route in Goa and Karnataka, (c)
Increase in compensatory afforestation rates applicable in the State of Karnataka, (d)
Additional expenditure incurred for acquiring RoW for implementing the NN Line in the
State of Karnataka, and (e) Increase in the Net Present Value rates.
Proceedings before the Commission
Hearing dated 26.8.2025
11. The matter was heard on 26.8.2025. During the hearing dated 26.8.2025, the
learned counsel for the Petitioner pointed out that, in pursuance of the permission
granted by the Commission vide Record of Proceedings for the hearing dated
22.5.2025, the Petitioner has filed the IA No. 91/2025 seeking amendment of the
Petition. The learned counsel also pointed out that so far only the Respondent, M.P.
Power Management Company Limited, had filed its reply to the said IA opposing the
said amendment, and the remaining Respondents had yet to file their replies to the
IA. Considering the above, the Commission granted the Respondents another
Order in IA No. 91/2025 in Petition No. 239/MP/2021
Page 10 of 33

opportunity to file their respective replies to the said IA, with a copy to the Petitioner,
who will file its rejoinder thereafter.
Replies of Respondents:
12. The Respondent, MPPMCL, vide reply dated 18.8.2025, opposed the
maintainability of the IA and mainly submitted as under:
(a) This Commission, while adjudicating applications for amendment under
Regulation 38 of the Conduct of Business Regulations, is guided by principles akin
to those under Order VI Rule 17 of the CPC, emphasising that amendments must
not prejudice the opposite party or change the fundamental character of the
proceedings. In this regard, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Basavaraj v. Indira &
Ors. [(2024 INSC 151)] has clearly enumerated key factors for consideration.
Applying this to the present IA, both prejudice and alteration of the Petition's
character are evident, warranting dismissal.
(b) The proposed amendments introduce expansive claims on additional force
majeure events (such as detailed sub-delays in forest and wildlife clearances for
the NN Line, XM Line, Xeldem Substation, and DT Line, including rerouting impacts
and technical issues) and Change in Law events (including escalated
compensatory afforestation rates, right-of-way compensation in Goa and
Karnataka, and post - 21.10.2021 expenditures on protection funds and tower
height increases). These additions, if allowed, would prolong the pendency of the
Petition, which was originally filed seeking extension of SCOD beyond 13.11.2021
due to Force Majeure, following remand by the APTEL. During the extended
pendency of the IA, interest on the Petitioner's unverified claims continues to accrue
under the Transmission Service Agreement, thereby directly impacting
transmission charges payable by LTTCs. As Madhya Pradesh is reliant on power
evacuation from the Raigarh (Tamnar) Pool, this recurring interest burden
translates into higher tariffs for consumers, causing irreversible financial prejudice
that cannot be adequately compensated, especially given the two-year delay since
the remand order dated 1.5.2023. Allowing the amendment would thus exacerbate
this prejudice, contrary to the Hon’ble Supreme Court's mandate to evaluate such
impacts before permitting changes at an advanced stage of proceedings.
Order in IA No. 91/2025 in Petition No. 239/MP/2021
Page 11 of 33

(c) The original Petition, post-remand, focused on core force majeure events like
the COVID-19 pandemic, and initial delays in forest clearances for key lines (NN
Line in Karnataka, Xeldem Substation conversion in Goa), alongside limited change
in law claims (e.g., compensatory afforestation rate hikes). The first amendment (IA
No. 107/2024, allowed on 27.2.2025) already expanded these modestly, with
pleadings completed thereafter on 20.5.2025. The present IA, however, sways
substantially from this framework by introducing a cascade of new sub-events and
claims—such as interplay between clearances, Supreme Court order
consequences, wildlife clearance delays post-rerouting, heavy rainfall impacts on
XM Line, LTTC interconnection delays for DT Line, and post-SC (SCOD) Change
in Law events like wildlife plans and NPV rate increases, effectively transforming
the Petition into a comprehensive re-litigation of the entire project implementation
history spanning multiple states (Goa, Karnataka, Chhattisgarh). This not only
dilutes the remanded scope limited to “rival contentions on merits” but also injects
fresh causes of action that could have been raised earlier with due diligence, post
the 5.7.2023 liberty granted for initial amendments. Such a shift fundamentally
alters the Petition's character from a targeted SCOD extension to an omnibus claim
aggregation; therefore, the amendment application is liable to be dismissed.
(d) The Petitioner employs dilatory tactics by delaying the first amendment for 15
months despite permissions, now seeking further changes after pleadings closure,
causing abuse of process, thus allowing the Petitioner to leverage unrelated rulings.
Additionally, with the trial commenced after rejoinders in May 2025, amendments
are barred under Order VI Rule 17 CPC unless due diligence is shown, and the
proposals would inconvenience Respondents, such as LTTCs.
(e) Further, the proposed insertions by way of amendment lack clarity, vaguely
detailing changes to force majeure (e.g., NN Line delays) and Change in Law
events (e.g., increased afforestation costs), failing to meet amendment standards.

16. The issue for consideration is whether the present IA for amendment of the
Petition is maintainable. The Respondents, MPPMCL and MSEDCL, have vehemently
argued that the present IA seeking amendment of the Petition is non-maintainable
mainly on the grounds of abuse of the process of law and dilatory tactics and further
that allowing such amendments would not only prejudice the beneficiaries but would

17. We have considered the submissions made by both sides. The limited issue
that arises for consideration is whether the instant IA seeking amendment of the
Petition is maintainable or not. Under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, the
Amendment of Pleadings is governed by Order VI Rule 17, which reads as follows:
“17. Amendment of pleadings. The Court may at any stage of the proceedings
allow either party to alter or amend his pleadings in such manner and on such
terms as may be just, and all such amendments shall be made as may be
necessary for the purpose of determining the real questions in controversy
between the parties:
Provided that no application for amendment shall be allowed after the trial has
commenced, unless the Court comes to the conclusion that in spite of due
diligence, the party could not have raised the matter before the commencement
of trial.”
Order in IA No. 91/2025 in Petition No. 239/MP/2021
Page 22 of 33

As per the above provision, pleadings can be amended at any stage of the
proceedings if, in the view of the Court, the amendments are necessary for the purpose
of determining the real questions in controversy between the parties. The proviso to
the said rule provides that no application for amendment shall be allowed after the trial
has commenced unless the Court comes to the conclusion that, in spite of due
diligence, the party could not have raised the matter before the commencement of the
trial.
18. Similarly, the provisions governing the powers of this Commission to allow the
Amendment of Pleadings are captured in Regulation 38 of its Conduct of Business
Regulations. The relevant extract of the said Regulation reads as follows:
“38. AMENDMENT OF PLEADINGS
The Commission may, at any stage of the proceedings in a petition, allow either
party to alter or amend its pleadings in such manner and on such terms as may
be considered appropriate, and all such amendments shall be made as may be
necessary for the purpose of determining the real issues in controversy
between the parties:
Provided that no application for amendment shall be allowed after
commencement of the final hearing of the petition, unless the Commission is of
the opinion that, in spite of due diligence, the party could not have raised the
matter before the commencement of the final hearing:
Provided further that no application for amendment shall be entertained after
the conclusion of the final hearing and order is reserved in the petition.”
As per the above, the Commission may allow either party to alter or amend its
pleadings, necessary for the purpose of determining the real issues in controversy, in
such a manner and on such terms as may be considered appropriate at any stage of
proceedings in a Petition. However, the first proviso stipulates that no application for
amendment shall be allowed after the commencement of the final hearing of the
Petition, unless the Commission is of the opinion that, in spite of due diligence, the
Order in IA No. 91/2025 in Petition No. 239/MP/2021

party could not have raised the matter before the commencement of the final hearing.
Whereas, the second proviso goes a step further and stipulates that no application for
amendment shall be entertained after the conclusion of the final hearing and reserving
of the order in the Petition. However, in the present case, the final hearing in Petition
No.239/MP/2021 has not yet commenced. Regulation 3(17) of the Conduct of
Business Regulations defines the ‘final hearing’ as the stage when, after completion
of pleadings, the Petition is taken up for hearing on the merits of the issues raised in
the Petition, including the issues framed by the Commission, if any. So far, the instant
Petition has not been taken up for hearing on the merits of the issues raised therein,
and as such, the restrictions imposed by these provisos in allowing the amendment
application are not attracted in this case.
19. The principles governing the amendment of Pleadings are now well settled, and
in the case of LIC vs. Sanjeev Builders Private Limited & Anr., 2022 SCC OnLine SC
1128, the Hon’ble Supreme Court, after considering the several precedents regarding
the amendment of Pleadings, have culled out the following principles:
“70. Our final conclusions may be summed up thus:
***************
(ii) All amendments are to be allowed which are necessary for determining the
real question in controversy provided it does not cause injustice or prejudice to
the other side. This is mandatory, as is apparent from the use of the word
“shall”, in the latter part of Order VI Rule 17 of the CPC.
(iii) The prayer for amendment is to be allowed
(i) if the amendment is required for effective and proper adjudication of the
controversy between the parties, and
(ii) to avoid multiplicity of proceedings, provided
(a) the amendment does not result in injustice to the other side,
(b) by the amendment, the parties seeking amendment does not seek to
withdraw any clear admission made by the party which confers a right on
the other side and
(c) the amendment does not raise a time barred claim, resulting in divesting
of the other side of a valuable accrued right (in certain situations).
Order in IA No. 91/2025 in Petition No. 239/MP/2021
Page 24 of 33

(iv) A prayer for amendment is generally required to be allowed unless
(i) by the amendment, a time barred claim is sought to be introduced, in
which case the fact that the claim would be time barred becomes a relevant
factor for consideration,
(ii) the amendment changes the nature of the suit,
(iii) the prayer for amendment is malafide, or
(iv) by the amendment, the other side loses a valid defence.
(v) In dealing with a prayer for amendment of pleadings, the court should
avoid a hypertechnical approach, and is ordinarily required to be liberal
especially where the opposite party can be compensated by costs.
(vi) Where the amendment would enable the court to pin-pointedly consider the
dispute and would aid in rendering a more satisfactory decision, the prayer for
amendment should be allowed.
(vii) Where the amendment merely sought to introduce an additional or a new
approach without introducing a time barred cause of action, the amendment is
liable to be allowed even after expiry of limitation.
(viii) Amendment may be justifiably allowed where it is intended to rectify the
absence of material particulars in the plaint.
(ix) Delay in applying for amendment alone is not a ground to disallow the
prayer. Where the aspect of delay is arguable, the prayer for amendment could
be allowed and the issue of limitation framed separately for decision.
(x) Where the amendment changes the nature of the suit or the cause of action,
so as to set up an entirely new case, foreign to the case set up in the plaint, the
amendment must be disallowed. Where, however, the amendment sought is
only with respect to the relief in the plaint, and is predicated on facts which are
already pleaded in the plaint, ordinarily the amendment is required to be
allowed.
(xi) Where the amendment is sought before commencement of trial, the court
is required to be liberal in its approach. The court is required to bear in mind the
fact that the opposite party would have a chance to meet the case set up in
amendment. As such, where the amendment does not result in irreparable
prejudice to the opposite party, or divest the opposite party of an advantage
which it had secured as a result of an admission by the party seeking
amendment, the amendment is required to be allowed. Equally, where the
amendment is necessary for the court to effectively adjudicate on the main
issues in controversy between the parties, the amendment should be allowed.
(See Vijay Gupta v. Gagninder Kr. Gandhi & Ors., 2022 SCC OnLine Del 1897)
…..”

trees and pillar costs in Chhattisgarh, additional expenditure towards RoW, and the
expenses on account of Covid-19 and the consequent restrictions imposed by the
Central & State Governments.
21. Thereafter, in view of the several developments after the filing of the Petition,
the Petitioner filed IA No. 107/2024 seeking amendment of the Petition to include the
details and documents in relation to these subsequent developments amounting to
Force Majeure and Change in Law events under the TSA. The Amended Petition inter
alia sought various consequential and declaratory reliefs in terms of Articles 11 and
12 of the TSA with respect to the Force Majeure and Change in Law events that
impacted the implementation of the transmission project. The additional Force Majeure
events sought to be included were mainly the delay due to change in the route of NN
Order in IA No. 91/2025 in Petition No. 239/MP/2021
Page 26 of 33

Line as per the direction of the Hon’ble Supreme Court, delay due to severe RoW
issues, delay due to heavy rainfall and flood in Goa, delay in provision of inter-
connecting facilities by LTTCs, delay in conversion of land for construction of Xeldem
S/s and consequent change in location of S/s, etc. Whereas, the revised Change in
Law claims sought to be included were an increase in CA rates in Chhattisgarh,
additional expenditure incurred in securing RoW in Goa, additional expenditure
incurred due to Covid-19, additional expenditure due to re-routing of XM Line pursuant
to orders of Deputy Collector, additional expenditure incurred due to implementation
of Wildlife & Avifauna Plan in Chhattisgarh, additional requirement of increase tower
height for DT Line, increase in expenditure due to inclusion of area subsequently
categorised as prospective private forest. In the said amendment, the Petitioner did
not include the Change in Law events that occurred after 21.10.2021 (i.e. the date of
notification of Change in Law Rules) and instead prayed for liberty to approach the
Commission by way of a separate Petition as per the Change in Law Rules. The said
IA was allowed on 27.2.2025, and consequently, the Amended Petition was taken on
record.
22. Now, by way of the present IA, the Petitioner has sought further amendment to
the Petition to include the details and documents in relation to the Change in Law
events that occurred on or after 21.10.2021, i.e., the date of notification of the Change
in Law Rules. The additional Change in Law events now sought to be incorporated are
additional expenditure due to change in location and technology of Xeldem S/s,
change in scope of work – Protection Function Requirement, change in CA rates,
change in NPV rates, requirement of change in route of NN Line, additional scope of
work for NN Line, and the additional expenditure incurred for securing RoW for NN
Line in Karnataka.
Order in IA No. 91/2025 in Petition No. 239/MP/2021
Page 27 of 33

23. On a careful examination of the IA, it clearly appears that the Petitioner has
sought the further amendment to the Petition merely to incorporate its claims of
Change in Law events that occurred on or after 21.10.2021, along with the
consequential reliefs arising therefrom. Pertinently, the Petition already seeks
recognition and declaration of various Force Majeure and Change in Law events that
affected the construction of the transmission project and permitting the Petitioner to
include the Change in Law events that occurred on or after 21.10.2021, would only
allow the effective adjudication of the Petitioner’s claims of Change in Law events that
affected the transmission project during the construction phase. Additionally, allowing
such an amendment would serve the dominant purpose of avoiding multiplicity of
proceedings, as the Petitioner would otherwise be required to file a separate Petition
to raise such claims, thereby leading to a fresh round of litigation between the parties
over Change in Law events.
24. The Respondents have, however, opposed the amendment application on
several counts. The Respondents have argued that allowing the amendment will
cause prejudice by prolonging the pendency of the Petition. They have also argued
that the Petitioner has employed dilatory tactics by delaying the first amendment for
15 months despite permissions, and seeks further changes after the completion of
pleadings, causing abuse of process and allowing it to leverage unrelated rulings.
Additionally, with the trial commenced after rejoinders in May 2025, amendments are
barred under Order VI Rule 17 CPC unless due diligence is shown, and the proposed
amendments would also cause inconvenience to LTTCs. It is also argued that during
the extended pendency of the IA itself, interest on the Petitioner's unverified claims
continues to accrue under the TSA, directly impacting transmission charges payable
by the long-term transmission customers (LTTCs).
Order in IA No. 91/2025 in Petition No. 239/MP/2021
Page 28 of 33

25. Per contra, the Petitioner has submitted that the present application seeking
amendment is being filed pursuant to this Commission’s Order dated 20.4.2025
(“MUML Order”) in Petition No. 131/MP/2024, titled Mumbai Urja Marg Limited v.
MSEDCL and Ors. Before the issuance of the MUML Order, and in terms of the
Change in Law Rules issued by the Ministry of Power on 22.10.2021, the proceedings
before this Commission were understood to be confined to the verification of Change
in Law claims. However, by way of the MUML Order, this Commission, for the first
time, held that it would exercise its adjudicatory jurisdiction while considering Change
in Law claims filed under the said Rules. The MUML Order further clarified that Rule
3(8) of the Change in Law Rules does not circumscribe or limit the Commission’s
power to adjudicate upon the validity or merits of a Change in Law event.
26. We have carefully considered the objections raised by the Respondents
regarding alleged prejudice, abuse of process, and the delay. The Petitioner has
primarily argued that the need for the proposed amendment arose only in view of the
change in the regulatory position brought about by the MUML Order. The Petitioner
has argued that the Commission, by the said Order, has clarified that no recovery of
compensation for Change in Law claims shall commence unless (i) there is express
consent from all the beneficiaries of the region, or (ii) the claims have been duly
approved by the Commission. As a consequence of this, the Change in Law events
that occurred on or after 21.10.2021, for which the Petitioner had earlier reserved its
right to file a separate Petition under the Change in Law Rules, are now sought to be
incorporated for the adjudication of the Commission in this Petition itself. However, we
do not agree with the above submission that the need for the present amendment was
triggered by the MUML Order. Noticeably, the position clarified in the MUML Order
that the Change in Law Rules do not cover a scenario where the parties are not in
agreement with each other as to whether the event constitutes a Change in Law event
Order in IA No. 91/2025 in Petition No. 239/MP/2021
Page 29 of 33

or not under the TSA is based on the earlier findings of the APTEL in the judgment
dated 5.4.2022 in OP No. 1 of 2022 and Ors., wherein the APTEL had examined the
scope/ scheme of the Change in Law Rules. As a corollary, the MUML Order further
clarifies that recovery of charges cannot commence unless the Change in Law claims
are consented to by the beneficiaries or specifically adjudicated and allowed by the
Commission. The said Order, in our view, does not mark any regulatory change as
averred by the Petitioner.
27. Be that as it may, the non-acceptance of the Petitioner’s submission on the
scope of the MUML Order would not preclude it from seeking the amendment of the
Petition to include its claims of Change in Law arising on or after 21.10.2021. As noted
above, the final hearing of the Petition has not yet commenced; the test of due
diligence does not apply to the present application for amendment. It is well settled
that the delay in applying for the amendment alone is not a ground to disallow such a
prayer. While the Respondents have emphasised the pendency of proceedings and
the timing of the amendment, we are not persuaded that the proposed amendment
would cause such prejudice as would warrant its rejection. We find that the Project in
question is admittedly still under construction and has not yet achieved commercial
operation. All claims sought to be incorporated through the present amendment
pertain to the same transmission project, arise out of the same TSA, and relate to
events allegedly impacting the implementation timeline, tariff period, and contractual
obligations under the TSA. Accordingly, allowing the amendment merely enables a
comprehensive adjudication of all project-related Change in Law claims and does not
confer any immediate financial or legal advantage upon the Petitioner. The
Respondents’ apprehension of prejudice is therefore premature, as any impact on
transmission charges or beneficiaries would arise only upon final adjudication on
merits, after due scrutiny of the admissibility, validity, and quantification of the claims.
Order in IA No. 91/2025 in Petition No. 239/MP/2021
Page 30 of 33

The Respondents shall have full liberty to contest each of the claims at the appropriate
stage. In these circumstances, no vested or accrued right of the Respondents is
defeated by permitting the amendment. Though none of the Respondents have raised
any concern regarding the limitation on the Change in Law claims as raised by the
Petitioner through this amendment, we find that these claims do not appear to be
barred by the limitation. These claims arise out of the same TSA and pertain to events
that occurred during the implementation of the Project, which took place after the
promulgation of the Change in Law Rules with effect from 21.10.2021. The causes of
action in respect of these Change in Law events, i.e., the occurrence of the event
coupled with the incidence of additional expenditure in terms thereof, do not appear to
be more than three years anterior to the date of filing of the amendment application,
i.e., 8.6.2025. Hence, we do not find that the Change in Law claims sought to be
incorporated by the Petitioner by way of amendment are prima facie barred by
limitation as on the date of filing of such amendment application. Moreover, the
question of limitation is not to be adjudicated at this stage, and the same shall be finally
decided after giving both parties an opportunity to make their submissions on the
merits.
28. The Respondents have also argued that allowing such amendments would alter
the basic nature of the Petition. However, in our view, the proposed amendment does
not alter the basic nature of the Petition. As noted above, the original Petition was, and
continues to remain, one seeking recognition of Force Majeure and Change in Law
events affecting the same transmission project, arising out of the same TSA dated
28.06.2017, and seeking consequential reliefs under Articles 11 and 12 thereof,
including extension of SCOD and tariff-related reliefs. The amendment merely brings
on record subsequent developments, additional facts, documents relating to Change
in Law events which occurred on or after 21.10.2021. Not only does the nature of
Order in IA No. 91/2025 in Petition No. 239/MP/2021
Page 31 of 33

reliefs remain the same as prayed in the original Petition, but the scope of dispute also
does not extend beyond the implementation, delay, and cost impact of the
transmission project. Thus, the proposed amendment does not, in any manner, alter
the basic or fundamental nature of the Petition and would allow the effective and
comprehensive adjudication of the Change in Law events that affected the
construction of the transmission project.
29. Similarly, the argument of the Respondents that allowing the amendment will
prolong litigation and lead to financial prejudice/ cost escalation of unverified claims is
also misplaced. Such prejudice, however, is not caused by the amendment, but by the
pendency of the main Petition itself, and can be adequately addressed by granting
opportunity to the Respondents to file replies, raise objections, or address the merits
at the stage of final adjudication. No irreparable prejudice that cannot be compensated
or addressed procedurally has been shown. If the present amendment is refused, the
Petitioner would then be required to file a fresh Petition in relation to the events
occurring on and after 21.10.2021. This would be contrary to the objective of avoiding
multiplicity of litigation. Moreover, as already discussed, the proposed amendment
neither seeks to change the Petition’s basic nature nor introduces time-barred claims.
In our view, the proposed amendment satisfies the legal tests under Order VI Rule 17
CPC, Regulation 38 of the Conduct of Business Regulations, and the well-established
principles governing the Amendment of Pleadings as culled out in Sanjeev Builders
(supra).
30. Based on the above findings, the present IA, seeking the amendment of the
Petition, is hereby allowed, and the amended Petition is taken on record. All the
Respondents are also granted an opportunity to file their replies on the amended
Order in IA No. 91/2025 in Petition No. 239/MP/2021
Page 32 of 33

Petition, if any, within six weeks, with a copy to the Petitioner, who may file its
rejoinder(s), if any, within four weeks thereafter.
31. The Petition No. 239/MP/2021 will be listed for hearing on merits in due course,
for which a separate notice will be issued.
32. The IA No. 91/2025 is disposed of in terms of the above findings.

customers, as applicable, in accordance with Regulation 94(1) of the 2024 Tariff
Regulations.
74. We have considered the Petitioner's submissions. The Petitioner is entitled to
reimbursement of the fees paid for filing the Petition and publication expenses incurred
on this account directly from the beneficiaries or long-term customers, as the case may
be.
Fees and Charges of Central Transmission Utility of India Limited (CTUIL)
75. The Petitioner has submitted that, according to Regulation 99 of the 2024 Tariff
Regulations, the fees and charges of the CTUIL may be allowed separately through a
separate regulation. The Petitioner has further submitted that, in the absence of such
a regulation, the CTUIL expenses will be borne by the Petitioner and recovered as
additional O&M Expenses through a separate Petition at the end of the tariff period.
Order in Petition No. 598/TT/2025
Page 33 of 37

76. It is apt here to refer to Regulation 99 of the 2024 Tariff Regulations which
provides as under:
“99. Special Provisions relating to Central Transmission Utility of India Ltd.
(CTUIL): The fee and charges of CTUIL shall be allowed separately by the
Commission through a separate regulation:
Provided that until such regulation is issued by the Commission, the expenses
of CTUIL shall be borne by Power Grid Corporation of India Ltd. (PGCIL) which shall
be recovered by PGCIL as additional O&M expenses through a separate petition.”
77. We have considered the Petitioner’s submissions and perused Regulation 99 of
the 2024 Tariff Regulations. In view of the explicit provision made under Regulation 99
of the 2024 Tariff Regulations, we permit the Petitioner, i.e., PGCIL, to bear the fees and
charges expenses of CTUIL and recover the same as additional O&M Expenses
through a separate Petition until such a regulation is notified and issued by the
Commission.
Licence Fee and RLDC Fees and Charges
78. The Petitioner has claimed reimbursement of the license fee, RLDC Fees and
Charges. The Petitioner is allowed the reimbursement of the license fee in accordance
with Regulation 94(4) of the 2024 Tariff Regulations for the 2024-29 tariff period. The
Petitioner is also allowed to recover the RLDC fee and charges from the beneficiaries
in terms of Regulation 94(3) of the 2024 Tariff Regulations for the 2024-29 tariff period.
Goods and Services Tax
79. The Petitioner has submitted that the transmission charges claimed herein are
exclusive of GST, and in case GST is levied in the future, the same shall be additionally
paid by the Respondents, and the Petitioner shall be allowed to charge and bill it
separately. Petitioner further prays that in case any additional taxes are paid by the
Petitioner on account of the demand from the Government/ statutory authorities, the
Order in Petition No. 598/TT/2025
Page 34 of 37

Commission may allow the same to be recovered from the beneficiaries.
80. We have considered the submissions of the Petitioner. Since GST is not levied
on the transmission service at present, we are of the view that the Petitioner’s prayer
on this count is premature.
Security Expenses, Insurance and Capital Spares
81. The Petitioner has submitted that, as per Regulation 36(3)(d) of the 2024 Tariff
Regulations, the security expenses and capital spares of more than ₹10 lakh for the
transmission system will be allowed separately after a prudence check.
82. As regards the security expenses of the transmission asset, the Petitioner has
submitted that it will file a separate Petition for the truing up of security expenses from
1.4.2019 to 31.3.2024 under Regulation 35(3)(c) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations and
recovery of security expenses from 1.4.2024 to 31.3.2029 under Regulation 36(3)(d)
of the 2024 Tariff Regulations. According to the Petitioner, the security expenses
regarding the transmission asset are not claimed in the instant Petition.
83. The Petitioner has also submitted that it has not claimed insurance expenses in
the instant Petition and has submitted that it will file a separate Petition for claiming the
overall insurance expenses and consequential IWC on the same, considering the
actual insurance expenses incurred by it for FY 2023-24 after escalating the same at
5.25% per annum to arrive at the estimated insurance expenses for FYs 2024-25, 2025-
26, 2026-27, 2027-28, and 2028-29.
84. The Petitioner has not claimed capital spares for the transmission asset in the
instant Petition for the 2024-29 tariff period. According to the Petitioner, it will file a
separate Petition for the capital spares consumed and consequential IWC thereon on
an actual basis for the 2024-29 tariff period as per the 2024 Tariff Regulations. The
Petitioner has also submitted that it has filed Petition No. 45/MP/2024, claiming therein
Order in Petition No. 598/TT/2025
Page 35 of 37

capital spares for the 2019-24 tariff period as per the 2019 Tariff Regulations.
85. We have considered the Petitioner’s submissions and have perused the record.
We deem it proper here to refer Regulation 36(3)(d) of the 2024 Tariff Regulations,
which provides as follows:
“36(3)
(d) The Security Expenses, Capital Spares individually costing more than Rs. 10 lakh
and Insurance expenses arrived through competitive bidding for the transmission
system and associated communication system shall be allowed separately after
prudence check:
Provided that in case of self-insurance, the premium shall not exceed 0.12% of
the GFA of the assets insured;
Provided that the transmission licensee shall submit the along with estimated
security expenses based on assessment of the security requirement, capital spares
and insurance expenses, which shall be trued up based on details of the year-wise
actuals along with appropriate justification for incurring the same and along with
confirmation that the same is not claimed as a part of additional capitalisation or
consumption of stores and spares and renovation and modernization.
Provided that the self-insurance premium shall be transferred to a separate
fund for utilization to meet the claims, and the expenditure incurred or amount utilized
from the self-insurance fund shall be made available to the Commission as and when
directed.”
86. On the perusal of Regulation 36(3)(d) of the 2024 Tariff Regulations and
considering the Petitioner’s submissions, the Petitioner is allowed to file a single
consolidated Petition comprising of security expenses, capital spares individually
costing more than ₹10 lakh and insurance expenses on an estimated basis in terms of
the 2024 Tariff Regulations for the 2024-29 tariff period.
Sharing of Transmission Charges
87. The Petitioner has submitted that truing-up of the tariff for the 2019-24 tariff
period will be recovered on a monthly basis in accordance with Regulation 57 of the
2019 Tariff Regulations and will be shared by the beneficiaries and long-term
transmission customers. Further, the tariff for the 2024-29 tariff period will be
recovered on a monthly basis in accordance with Regulation 78 of the 2024 Tariff
Regulations and will be shared by the beneficiaries and long-term transmission
Order in Petition No. 598/TT/2025
Page 36 of 37

customers as per the 2020 Sharing Regulations.
88. The billing, collection and disbursement of the transmission charges in respect
of the transmission asset shall be recovered in terms of the provisions of the 2020
Sharing Regulations as provided in Regulation 57 of the 2019 Tariff Regulations for
the 2019-24 tariff period and Regulation 78 of the 2024 Tariff Regulations for the 2024-
29 tariff period.

ORDER
The instant Petition has been filed by Power Grid Corporation of India Limited
(PGCIL) (hereinafter referred to as “the Petitioner”), a deemed transmission licensee,
for the truing up of the transmission tariff for the 2019-24 period under the Central
Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2019
(hereinafter referred to as “the 2019 Tariff Regulations”) and for the determination of the
transmission tariff for the 2024-29 period under the Central Electricity Regulatory
Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2024 (hereinafter referred to
as “the 2024 Tariff Regulations”) for the assets forming part of the Transmission System
associated with Bairasuil in the Northern Region (hereinafter referred to as “the
transmission system”).
2. The Petitioner has made the following prayers in the instant Petition:
“a) Approve the trued-up Transmission Tariff for 2019-24 block and transmission tariff
for 2024-29 block for the assets covered under this petition, as per para 13 & 14 above.
b) Admit the capital cost claimed, and additional capitalization incurred during 2019-24
and projected to be incurred during 2024-29.
c) Allow the petitioner to recover the shortfall or refund the excess Annual Fixed
Charges, on account of Return on Equity due to change in applicable Minimum
Alternate/Corporate Income Tax rate as per the Income Tax Act, 1961 (as amended
from time to time) of the respective financial year directly without making any application
before the Commission as provided in Tariff Regulations, 2019 and Tariff Regulations,
2024 as per para 13 & 14 above for respective block.
Further it is submitted that deferred tax liability before 01.04.2009 shall be recoverable
from the beneficiaries or long term customers / DIC as the case may be, as and when
the same is materialized as per Regulation 67 of Tariff Regulations, 2019 and Regulation
89 of Tariff Regulations, 2024. The petitioner may be allowed to recover the deferred
Order in Petition No. 541/TT/2025 Page 3 of 54

tax liability materialized directly without making any application before the Hon’ble
Commission as provided in the regulations.
d) Approve the reimbursement of expenditure by the beneficiaries towards petition filing
fee, and expenditure on publishing of notices in newspapers in terms of Regulation 94
(1) Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff)
Regulations, 2024, and other expenditure (if any) in relation to the filing of petition.
e) Allow the petitioner to bill and recover RLDC fees & charges and Licensee fee,
separately from the respondents in terms of Regulation 94 (3) and (4) Central Electricity
Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2024.
f) Allow the petitioner to bill and adjust impact on Interest on Loan due to change in
Interest rate on account of floating rate of interest applicable during 2024-29 period, if
any, from the respondents.
g) Allow the petitioner to file a separate petition before Hon’ble Commission for claiming
the overall security expenses and consequential IOWC on that security expenses as
mentioned at para 20 above.
h) Allow the petitioner to file a separate petition before Hon’ble Commission for claiming
the overall insurance expenses and consequential IOWC on that insurance expenses
as mentioned at para 20 above.
i) Allow the petitioner to file a separate petition before Hon’ble Commission for claiming
the overall capital spares at the end of tariff block as per actual as mentioned at Para
20 above.
j) Allow the petitioner to claim expenses of CTUIL borne by POWERGRID through a
separate petition as mentioned at para 21 above.
k) Allow the petitioner to bill and recover GST on Transmission Charges separately from
the respondents, if GST on transmission is levied at any rate in future. Further, any taxes
including GST and duties including cess etc. imposed by any statutory/Govt./municipal
authorities shall be allowed to be recovered from the beneficiaries.
and pass such other relief as Commission deems fit and appropriate under the
circumstances of the case and in the interest of justice.”
Background
3. The brief facts of the case are as follows:
a. The Central Government's approval for establishing the transmission system
related to the Baira-Suil Hydro Electric Project was given by the Ministry of
Power (MoP), through a letter dated 9.3.1979, for a total capital investment
of ₹10885.00 lakh, including an Interest During Construction (IDC) of
₹1663.00 lakh. Later, the MoP, through a letter dated 16.10.1981, approved
the Revised Cost Estimate (RCE) of the Baira-Suil Electric Project, which
Order in Petition No. 541/TT/2025 Page 4 of 54

included ₹662.52 lakh (including an IDC of ₹78.85 lakh on a pro-rata basis)
for the transmission system. Subsequently, the transmission system was
implemented by NHPC Limited and later transferred to the Petitioner.
b. The scope of work covered under the transmission system is as follows:
A. Transmission Lines:
i. 220 kV D/C Bairasuil – Jessore- Pong Transmission Line.
B. Substation (Pong):
i. 1 number of 220 kV bay at Bairasuil.
ii. 1 number of 220 kV bay at Jessore.
c. The entire scope of work is covered under the instant Petition.
d. The transmission system was put under commercial operation on 18.5.1980.
e. The transmission tariff for the 2009-14 period was trued-up, and the tariff for
the 2014-19 tariff period was determined vide order dated 18.3.2016 in
Petition No. 491/TT/2014.
f. The Commission, by order dated 29.11.2021 in Petition No. 712/TT/2020,
trued-up the Annual Fixed Charges (AFC) for the 2014-19 tariff period and
determined the AFC for the 2019-24 tariff period for the transmission system
covered under this Petition.
4. The Respondents are the distribution licensees, transmission licensees and
power departments, mainly the beneficiaries of the Northern Region, which are
procuring transmission services from the Petitioner.
5. The Petitioner has served a copy of the Petition on the Respondents, and notices
regarding the filing of this Petition have been published in newspapers in accordance
with Section 64 of the Electricity Act, 2003 (hereinafter referred to as “the Act”). No
comments or suggestions have been received from the general public in response to
the notices published in the newspapers by the Petitioner.
Order in Petition No. 541/TT/2025 Page 5 of 54

6. None of the Respondents has filed any reply to the Petition.
7. The hearing in the matter was held on 21.1.2026, and the order was reserved.
This order is issued considering the submissions made by the Petitioner vide affidavits
dated 20.12.2024, 13.10.2025 and 9.2.2026.
8. Having heard the representatives of the Petitioner and perused the material
available on record, we proceed to dispose of the Petition.

2019–24 tariff period pertains to the replacement of the substation equipment, as
approved by the Commission, vide order dated 29.11.2021 in Petition No. 712/TT/2020.
Order in Petition No. 541/TT/2025 Page 8 of 54

18. It is submitted that the Pong Substation is maintained by M/s Bhakra Beas
Management Board (BBMB), and there was an inadvertent error in the justification for
ACE provided in Petition No. 712/TT/2020, where Punjab State Transmission
Corporation Limited (PSTCL) was mentioned instead of BBMB. It is further submitted
that a letter from M/s BBMB, requesting the Petitioner to replace the old equipment and
communication from OEM for the replacement of isolators, has also been furnished in
support of the ACE claimed for the 2019-24 tariff period.
19. The Petitioner, vide affidavit dated 13.10.2025, submitted that the ACE incurred
during the 2019–24 tariff block is claimed under Regulations 25(2)(a) and 25(2)(c) of
the 2019 Tariff Regulations. It is submitted that Regulations 25(2)(a) and 25(2)(c) of the
2019 Tariff Regulations pertain to the ACE towards replacement of aged, deteriorated,
and obsolete assets that are critical for maintaining system reliability and grid
security/stability. It is further submitted that deterioration in the performance of various
equipment has been noticed due to ageing, including deviations in testing parameters
of Circuit Breakers (CBs), Current Transformers (CTs), isolators, leakages in Capacitor
Voltage Transformers (CVTs), rusting of panels, and brittleness of the cables.
Therefore, the replacement/retrofitting of such equipment has become necessary to
address the ageing-related issues and to ensure continued reliable operation of the
transmission system.

claimed for the 2019-24 tariff period, as submitted by the Petitioner, vide affidavit dated

replaced and actual cost details of the replaced equipment and cost details of the new
equipment sub-station wise at the time of truing up. It is observed that letter dated 6.11.2020
Order in Petition No. 541/TT/2025 Page 10 of 54

has been addressed by BBMB to the Petitioner about replacement of equipment of 220 kV

The Petitioner has submitted that, according to Regulation 33(8) of the 2024 Tariff
Regulations, the depreciation of ACE shall be recovered by equally spreading the
depreciable value over the remaining useful life of the asset or 10 years, whichever is
longer. It is further submitted that in the present Petition, the ACE is claimed for the FYs
2022-23 and 2023-24 within the 2019-24 tariff period, and for FY 2024-25 within the
2024-29 tariff period. It is further submitted that the weighted average useful life of the
Existing Assets was completed on 31.03.2016; therefore, as per Regulation 33(8) of the
2024 Tariff Regulations, the proposed ACE during the 2024-29 tariff period for the
transmission system is being recovered by equally spreading the amount over 10 years
starting from FY 2024-25.
34. Further, in respect of the ACE incurred during the 2019–24 tariff period, the
Petitioner has calculated the corresponding depreciation by spreading it retrospectively
in the FYs 2022-23 and 2023-24. This approach ensures that the total depreciation is
recovered within the stipulated 12-year period, consistent with Regulation 33(8) of the
2024 Tariff Regulations. The Petitioner also explained that the tariff computation is
divided into two parts: one for Existing Assets and the other for New Equipment. The
de-capitalization is being done in the Existing Assets, with the depreciation being
recovered according to the original weighted useful life. Meanwhile, the depreciation for

74. Regulation 32 of the 2024 Tariff Regulations provides as follows:
“32. Interest on loan capital: (1) The loans arrived at in the manner indicated in
Regulation 18 of these regulations shall be considered gross normative loans for
the calculation of interest on loans.
(2) The normative loan outstanding as on 1.4.2024 shall be worked out by deducting
the cumulative repayment as admitted by the Commission up to 31.3.2024 from the
gross normative loan.
(3) The repayment for each of the years of the tariff period 2024-29 shall be deemed
to be equal to the depreciation allowed for the corresponding year or period. In case
of decapitalization of assets, the repayment shall be adjusted by taking into account
cumulative repayment on a pro rata basis, and the adjustment should not exceed
cumulative depreciation recovered up to the date of de-capitalisation of such asset.
Order in Petition No. 541/TT/2025 Page 39 of 54

(4) Notwithstanding any moratorium period availed of by the generating company or
the transmission licensee, as the case may be, the repayment of the loan shall be
considered from the first year of commercial operation of the project and shall be
equal to the depreciation allowed for the year or part of the year.
(5) The rate of interest shall be the weighted average rate of interest calculated on
the basis of the actual loan portfolio or allocated loan portfolio:
Provided that if there is no actual loan outstanding for a particular year but
the normative loan is still outstanding, the last available weighted average rate of
interest of the loan portfolio for the project shall be considered;
Provided further that if the generating station or the transmission system, as
the case may be, does not have any actual loan, then the weighted average rate of
interest of the loan portfolio of the generating company or the transmission licensee
as a whole shall be considered;
Provided that the rate of interest on the loan for the installation of the
emission control system commissioned subsequent to date of commercial operation
of the generating station or unit thereof, shall be the weighted average rate of
interest of the actual loan portfolio of the emission control system, and in the
absence of the actual loan portfolio, the weighted average rate of interest of the
generating company as a whole shall be considered, subject to a ceiling of 14%;
Provided further that if the generating company or the transmission licensee,
as the case may be, does not have any actual loan, then the rate of interest for a
loan shall be considered as 1-year MCLR of the State Bank of India as applicable
as on April 01, of the relevant financial year.
(6) The interest on the loan shall be calculated on the normative average loan of the
year by applying the weighted average rate of interest.
(7) The changes to the terms and conditions of the loans shall be reflected from the
date of such re-financing.”
75. The WAROI on loans has been considered on the basis of the rate prevailing as
on 1.4.2024. The Petitioner has submitted that in the tariff calculations for the 2024-29
tariff period, the IoL has been calculated on the basis of the interest rates prevailing as
on 1.4.2024 for the respective loans and the change in the interest rate due to the
floating rate of interest applicable, if any, for the transmission system needs to be
claimed/ adjusted over the tariff block of 5 years directly from/with the beneficiaries.
76. We have considered the submissions of the Petitioner. The floating rate of
interest, if any, will be considered at the time of true-up. The IoL has been allowed in
accordance with Regulation 32 of the 2024 Tariff Regulations. The Petitioner has not

The instant Petition has been filed by the Power Grid Corporation of India
Limited, (hereinafter referred to as the ‘Petitioner/PGCIL’), for the truing up of the

(hereinafter referred to as the “transmission project”) in the Southern Region.

“a) Approve the trued-up Transmission Tariff for 2019-24 block and transmission tariff

g) Allow the petitioner to bill and adjust impact on Interest on Loan due to change in
Interest rate on account of floating rate of interest applicable during 2024-29 period, if
any, from the respondents.
h) Allow the petitioner to file a separate petition before the Commission for claiming the

mentioned at para 26 above.
i) Allow the petitioner to file a separate petition before the Commission for claiming the
overall insurance expenses and consequential IOWC on that insurance expenses as

l) Allow the petitioner initial spares amount re-claimed on project level computation.
m) Allow the Petitioner to bill and recover GST on Transmission Charges separately
from the respondents, if GST on transmission is levied at any rate in future. Further, any

statutory/Govt./municipal authorities shall be allowed to be recovered from the
beneficiaries and
Pass such other relief as the Commission deems fit and appropriate under the
circumstances of the case and in the interest of justice.”
Background
3. The brief facts of the case are as under:
Order in Petition No. 920/TT/2025 Page 4 of 60

a. The Investment Approval (the IA) for the implementation of the transmission
project was accorded by the Board of Directors (BoD) of the Petitioner in the

lakh, including IDC of ₹4997 lakh based on October, 2015 price level.
b. The Ministry of Power, Government of India, vide letter dated 8.1.2015

c. The Commission, vide Order dated 19.8.2016 in Petition No. 36/MP/2016,

Regulations, 2010, for execution of subject transmission system.
d. The scope of the transmission project was discussed and agreed in 39th and

to submit Form-7B for both the 2019-24 and 2024-29 tariff periods. The Petitioner vide
affidavit dated 2.2.2026 has submitted that Form-7B is prescribed specifically for
furnishing details of additional capitalisation claimed during the last five years preceding
the end of the useful life of the project. In the present case, the Petitioner has submitted
that the assets covered under the instant Petition were commissioned during the 2014-
19 tariff period, with an effective Date of Commercial Operation (COD) of 9.5.2018. As
per the applicable tariff regulations, the weighted average useful life of the subject
transmission assets is 32 years. Accordingly, the useful life of the instant assets shall
be completed by the FY 2050-51. As on the date of filing of the present Petition, the
assets are still at an early stage of their useful life, and the project has not entered into
the last five years of its operational life. In view of the above facts, it is submitted that
the requirement of furnishing Form-7B, which is applicable only for capitalization claims
made during the final five years of the useful life of an asset, does not arise in the
present case. Therefore, form-7B is not applicable to the instant assets.

60. We have considered the submissions of the Petitioner. As per the APTEL’s
judgment dated 14.9.2019 in Appeal No. 74 of 2017, Initial Spares are to be allowed as
per the ceiling on overall project cost. The APTEL vide judgement dated 14.9.2019 in
Appeal No. 74 of 2017 has held as follows:
“8.13……………We do not agree with this methodology of restricting initial spares
asset/element wise as adopted by the Central Commission. The Central Commission to
have a prudence check on the initial spares, being restricted based on the individual
asset wise cost initially, but subsequently ought to have allowed as per the ceiling limits
on the overall project cost basis during the true-up”
61. In terms of the above, Initial Spares are to be allowed as percentage of the
project cost as a whole. In the instant case, the assets are being combined in the 2024-
29 tariff period, hence APTEL’s judgment is applicable in the 2024-29 tariff period. Also,
Initial Spares claimed under Transmission Line and Sub-station head are within
permissible limit as compared to Initial Spares worked out. Initial spares amounting to

of prudence check, may restrict the Initial Spares to the cost of the individual asset
and later, at the time of truing-up, allow the Initial Spares as per the limit on the overall
project cost. The relevant portion of the judgment dated 14.9.2019 is extracted here
under:
“8.13. ……… We do not agree with this methodology of restricting initial spares asset
/ element wise as adopted by the Central Commission. The Central Commission to
have a prudence check on the initial spares, being restricted based on the individual
asset wise cost initially, but subsequently ought to have allowed as per the ceiling
limits on the overall project cost basis during the true- up.”

60. Regulation 25 of the 2024 Tariff Regulations provides as under:
“25. Additional Capitalization within the original scope and after the cut-off date:
(1) The additional capital expenditure incurred or projected to be incurred in respect of an
existing project or a new project on the following counts within the original scope of work
and after the cut-off date may be admitted by the Commission, subject to prudence check:
(a) Payment made against award of arbitration or for compliance with the directions or
order of any statutory authority, or order or decree of any court of law;
(b) Change in law or compliance with any existing law which is not provided for in the original
scope of work;
(c) Deferred works relating to ash pond or ash handling system or raising of ash dyke in the
original scope of work;
(d) Payment made towards liability admitted for works within the original scope executed
prior to the cut-off date;
(e)Force Majeure events;
(f)Works within original scope executed after the cut-off date and admitted by the
Commission, to the extent of actual payments made; and
(2) In case of replacement of assets deployed under the original scope of the existing
project after the cut-off date, the additional capitalization may be admitted by the
Commission, after making necessary adjustments in the gross fixed assets and the
cumulative depreciation, subject to prudence check on the following grounds:
(a) Assets whose useful life is not commensurate with the useful life of the project and such
assets have been fully depreciated in accordance with the provisions of these regulations;
(b) The replacement of the asset or equipment is necessary on account of a change in law
or Force Majeure conditions;
(c) The replacement of such asset or equipment is necessary on account of obsolescence
of technology; and
(d) The replacement of such asset or equipment has otherwise been allowed by the
Commission.
(e) The additional expenditure, excluding recurring expenses covered in O&M expenses,
involved in relation to the renewal of lease of lease hold land on case to case basis.
Provided that any claim of additional capitalization with respect to the replacement
of assets under the original scope and on account of obsolescence of technology, less than
Rs. 20 lakhs shall not be considered as part of Capital cost and shall be met through
normative O&M Expenses.”

basis points as on 1st April of the year, subject to a ceiling of 14%;

applicable for that financial year to the concerned generating company or the
transmission licensee by excluding the income of non-generation or non-transmission
business, as the case may be, and the corresponding tax thereon:
Provided that in case a generating company or transmission licensee is paying

Provided further that in case a generating company or transmission licensee

(2) The rate of return on equity shall be rounded off to three decimal places and shall
be computed as per the formula given below:
Rate of pre-tax return on equity = Base rate / (1-t)
(3) The generating company or the transmission licensee, as the case may be, shall
true up the effective tax rate for every financial year based on actual tax paid together
with any additional tax demand, including interest thereon, duly adjusted for any refund
of tax including interest received from the income tax authorities pertaining to the tariff
period 2024-29 on actual gross income of any financial year. Further, any penalty
arising on account of delay in deposit or short deposit of tax amount shall not be
considered while computing the actual tax paid for the generating company or the
transmission licensee, as the case may be:
Provided that in case a generating company or transmission licensee is paying

on equity at the end of every financial year with the applicable MAT rate including

Provided that in case a generating company or transmission licensee is paying

Background
3. The brief facts of the case are as follows:
a. The Investment Approval (IA) for implementation of the transmission
project was accorded by the Board of Directors (BoD) of the Petitioner on
22.10.2011 and communicated vide Memorandum Ref: C/CP/SRSS-XIII
dated 27.10.2011 at an estimated cost of ₹48749.00 lakh including an IDC
of ₹1940.00 lakh based on 2nd quarter, 2011 price level. Subsequently,
the BoD of the Petitioner accorded approval for the Revised Cost Estimate
(RCE) at an estimated cost of ₹63946.00 lakh including an IDC of
₹3667.00 lakh based on April 2015 price level.
b. Further the Revised Cost Estimate-II (RCE-II) in respect of the
transmission project was accorded by the BoD of the Petitioner vide
Memorandum Ref: C/CP/PA 1920-12-BG-RCE017 dated 31.3.2020, at an
estimated cost of ₹80066.00 lakh including an IDC of ₹4863.00 lakh,
based on December, 2019 price level.
c. The scope of the transmission project was discussed and agreed in the
28th SCM meeting dated 15.6.2009 and 10th and 11th SRPC meeting dated
2.7.2009 and 17.9.2009, respectively. Further, considering the severe
RoW problems and to further optimize the corridor, a decision was taken
in the 35th SCM meeting held on 4.1.2013 that instead of LILO of both
circuits of Nelamangala-Hoody D/C Line, only one circuit to be LILOed
using one D/C of the multi-circuit towers and balance D/C to be used for
400 kV Madhugiri-Yelahanka D/C quad line using high ampacity
conductor in the multi-circuit portion. This revised scope under SRSS-12
Order in Petition No. 921/TT/2025 Page 5 of 63

and SRSS-13 received approval from the Ministry of Power, Government
of India vide letter Ref: 11/14/2007-PG dated 7.8.2013.
d. The scope of work covered under the transmission project is as under:
Transmission Line:
i. Gooty-Madhugiri 400 kV D/C line;
ii. Madhugiri-Yelahanka 400 kV D/C (Quad) line with a small portion
to be strung on multi-circuit tower of the SRSS-XII scheme with
high ampacity conductor in Bengaluru Area;
Sub-station:
i. 400/220 kV Sub-station (New) at Madhugiri with 2X500 MVA
transformers with provision of establishing a 765/400 kV Sub-station
in future in the same switchyard;
ii. Extension of Gooty 400/220 kV Sub-station;
iii. Extension of Yelahanka 400/220 kV Sub-station;
Reactive Compensation:
i. 1X63 MVAR Bus Reactor at 400/220 kV Sub-station at Madhugiri.
e. As per the IA, the transmission assets were scheduled to be put into
commercial operation within 32 months from the IA, i.e., by 27.6.2014.
However, Assets-I, II, III, IV and V were put into commercial operation on
1.12.2015. Thus, there was a time over-run of 17 months (517 days) in
case of the transmission assets, and the Commission vide order dated
19.7.2016 in Petition No. 403/TT/2014 condoned the said delay.
f. The date of commercial operation (COD) of Asset-A, Asset-B, Asset-C is
1.12.2015 and Asset-D is 2.2.2020.

17.8.2019, whereas, the downstream system associated with Asset-C of the
instant Petition (220 kV line bays at Madhugiri for termination of 220 kV D/C
Madhugiri - Nittur line) is not ready yet.
h. The Commission vide order dated 4.2.2021 in Petition No. 17/TT/2020 trued-

Asset-A, Asset-B and Asset-C for 2019-24 period. The Commission vide
order dated 25.7.2022 in Petition No. 707/TT/2020 determined the tariff in

the record. We have noted that the entities covered under the MAT regime are paying
Income Tax as per the MAT rates notified for the respective financial year under the IT
Act, 1961, which is levied on the book profit of the entity computed as per Section 115
JB of the IT Act, 1961. Section 115 JB (2) defines book profit as net profit in the
statement of Profit and Loss prepared in accordance with Schedule-III of the Companies
Act, 2013, subject to some additions and deductions as mentioned in the IT Act, 1961.
Since the Petitioner has been paying the MAT rates of the respective financial year, the
notified MAT rates for the respective financial year shall be considered as an effective
tax rate for the purpose of grossing up the RoE for truing up the 2019-24 tariff period in
terms of the provisions of the 2019 Tariff Regulations. Interest imposed on any
additional income tax demand as per the Assessment Order of the Income Tax
Authorities shall be considered on the actual payment. However, the penalty (for default
on the part of the Assessee), if any, imposed shall not be taken into account for the
purpose of grossing up of the rate of RoE. Any under recovery or over-recovery of the
grossed-up rates on the RoE after truing up shall be recovered or refunded to the
beneficiaries or the long-term customers, as the case may be on a year-to-year basis.

24. We have considered the Petitioner’s submissions. The APTEL vide its judgment
dated 27.4.2011 in Appeal No. 72 of 2010, has laid down the following principles for
dealing with the issue of time overrun in the execution of projects:
“7.4. The delay in execution of a generating project could occur due to following
reasons:
i) due to factors entirely attributable to the generating company, e.g.,
imprudence in selecting the contractors/suppliers and in executing contractual
agreements including terms and conditions of the contracts, delay in award of
contracts, delay in providing inputs like making land available to the contractors,
delay in payments to contractors/suppliers as per the terms of contract,
mismanagement of finances, slackness in project management like improper
co-ordination between the various contractors, etc.
ii) due to factors beyond the control of the generating company e.g. delay
caused due to force majeure like natural calamity or any other reasons which
clearly establish, beyond any doubt, that there has been no imprudence on the
part of the generating company in executing the project.
iii) situation not covered by (i) & (ii) above.
In our opinion in the first case the entire cost due to time over run has to be
borne by the generating company. However, the Liquidated Damages (LDs)
and insurance proceeds on account of delay, if any, received by the generating
company could be retained by the generating company. In the second case the
generating company could be given benefit of the additional cost incurred due
to time over-run. However, the consumers should get full benefit of the LDs
recovered from the contractors/suppliers of the generating company and the
insurance proceeds, if any, to reduce the capital cost. In the third case the
additional cost due to time overrun including the LDs and insurance proceeds
could be shared between the generating company and the consumer. It would
also be prudent to consider the delay with respect to some benchmarks rather
than depending on the provisions of the contract between the generating
company and its contractors/suppliers. If the time schedule is taken as per the
terms of the contract, this may result in imprudent time schedule not in
accordance with good industry practices.”

attributable to the project developer (in the instant case, PGCIL), or its contractors, the
cost of such time overrun, i.e., IDC and IEDC, is required to be borne by the project
developer and any LD recovered may be retained by the Petitioner. The Commission,
vide its order dated 25.07.2020 in Petition No. 130/TT/2020, had disallowed IDC of
₹369.25 lakh and IEDC of ₹106.40 lakh, on account of the time overrun with respect to
Asset-1 and Asset-2 (part of the instant Combined Asset).
27. Accordingly, as stated above, where the time overrun is attributable to the project
developer, or its contractors, the cost of time overrun, i.e., IDC and IEDC has to be
borne by the project developer and any LD recovered may be retained by the Petitioner.

30. We have considered the Petitioner’s submissions and have also gone through the
record. We note that the entities covered under the MAT regime are paying Income Tax as
per the MAT rates notified for the respective financial year under the IT Act, 1961, which is
levied on the book profit of the entity computed as per Section 115 JB of the IT Act, 1961.
Section 115 JB (2) defines book profit as net profit in the Statement of Profit and Loss

observe that the Petitioner itself has acknowledged, that the “New Equipment”, i.e., the re-
conductoring works of the LILO of both circuits of the Siliguri–Dhalkhola 220 kV D/C line
along with the associated 220 kV bays at Kishanganj (GIS) considered under Part-B, does

not constitute a separate asset but merely an upgradation of the existing asset covered
under Part-A. Both components, namely Part-A (existing asset) and Part-B (re-
conductoring/upgradation), share the same balance and lapsed useful life and have been
consistently mapped as parallel streams of the same underlying asset for regulatory and
accounting purposes. Accordingly, we are of the view that where the expenditure pertains
to upgradation or modification of an existing asset and is required to be claimed as ACE of
that asset, maintaining two separate tariff streams for the same asset is not consistent with
the applicable regulatory and accounting treatments. The financial requirements arising
from such upgradations are required to be reflected within the tariff determination of the
existing asset itself.

“18. Debt-Equity Ratio: (1) For new projects, the debt-equity ratio of 70:30 as on date of

Provided that:
i. where equity actually deployed is less than 30% of the capital cost, actual equity shall be

ii. the equity invested in foreign currency shall be designated in Indian rupees on the date of
each investment:
iii. any grant obtained for the execution of the project shall not be considered as a part of
capital structure for the purpose of debt: equity ratio.
Explanation.-The premium, if any, raised by the generating company or the transmission
licensee, as the case may be, while issuing share capital and investment of internal
resources created out of its free reserve, for the funding of the project, shall be reckoned as
paid up capital for the purpose of computing return on equity, only if such premium amount
and internal resources are actually utilised for meeting the capital expenditure of the
generating station or the transmission system.
(2) The generating company or the transmission licensee, as the case may be, shall submit
the resolution of the Board of the company or approval of the competent authority in other
cases regarding infusion of funds from internal resources in support of the utilization made
or proposed to be made to meet the capital expenditure of the generating station or the

17. MPPMCL vide its affidavit dated 21.1.2026, has submitted that the earlier
disallowance of the Initial Spares of ₹13.3 lakh has been added to the cost as on
31.3.2019 based on the overall project cost, in line with the APTEL’s judgment in Appeal
No. 74 of 2017.
18. We have considered both the Petitioner and MPPMCL’s submission. The APTEL
vide its judgment dated 14.9.2019 in Appeal No. 74 of 2017 observed that the
Commission for the purpose of prudence check may restrict the Initial Spares to the
cost of the individual asset and later at the time of truing-up allow Initial Spares as per
the ceiling limit on the overall project cost. The relevant portion of the said judgment is
extracted here under:
“18.13. ……… The Central Commission to have a prudence check on the initial spares,
being restricted based on the individual asset wise cost initially, but subsequently ought
to have allowed as per the ceiling limits on the overall project cost basis during the true-
up.”
19. Accordingly, in accordance with the APTEL’s judgement dated 14.9.2019 in
Appeal No. 74 of 2017, the Initial Spares are required to be re-calculated based on the
overall project cost with respect to the Combined Asset. Further, it is observed that the
instant Combined Asset were commissioned having the cut-off date during the 2009-14
and 2014-19 tariff period. The capital cost with respect to the instant Combined Asset
