ORDER
The Petitioner, Maheshwaram Transmission Limited (now known as
Maheshwaram Transmission Private Limited), has filed the present Regulatory
Compliance Application seeking approval for the change in the name of the
Order in Petition No. 81/RC/2026 Page 2

Transmission Licensee from ‘Maheshwaram Transmission Limited’ to ‘Maheshwaram
Transmission Private Limited’. The Petitioner has made the following prayer:
“(a) Allow the present petition;
(b) Take on record the change in name of the transmission licensee/Petitioner
from “Maheshwaram Transmission Limited” to “Maheshwaram Transmission
Private Limited”;
(c) Direct that necessary endorsement be made on the transmission licensee
with regard to change of name of “Maheshwaram Transmission Limited” to
“Maheshwaram Transmission Private Limited”;
(d) Pass necessary orders to ensure that no prejudice is caused to the Petitioner
on account of the above name change; and
(e) Pass any such further/other orders that this Commission may deem fit in the
interest of equity and justice.”
2. By order dated 23.11.2015 in Petition No. 218/TL/2015, Maheshwaram
Transmission Limited (MTL) was granted an inter-State transmission license bearing
License No. 36/Transmission/2015/CERC, to establish the Transmission System for
“Connectivity Lines for Maheshwaram (Hyderabad) 765/400 kV Pooling sub-station”.
3. The Petitioner has submitted that an application under Section 14(1) of the
Companies Act, 2013 read with rule 41 of the Companies (Incorporation) Rules, 2014
was filed before the Regional Director (WR), Ministry of Corporate Affairs, Mumbai,
seeking approval for the conversion of the company into a Private Limited Company,
which was duly approved vide Order dated 4.6.2025 by the Regional Director.
Thereafter, the Regional Director sanctioned the alteration of Clause I of the
Memorandum of Association, wherein “Maheshwaram Transmission Limited” was
substituted with “Maheshwaram Transmission Private Limited”.
Order in Petition No. 81/RC/2026 Page 3

4. Subsequently, the Ministry of Corporate Affairs also issued a Certificate of
Incorporation dated 2.7.2025 consequent upon conversion to a private company, duly
recording the aforesaid conversion.
5. The Petitioner has submitted that, consequent to the change in name of the
transmission licensee, i.e., the Petitioner, there has been no change in the composition
or structure of the company.
Analysis and Decision
6. This Petition is being decided by way of circulation.
7. We have considered the submission of the Petitioner and perused the
documents available on record. The Petitioner was granted the transmission license
vide order dated 23.11.2015 in Petition No. 218/TL/2015.
8. Consequent to the issuance of the certificate dated 2.7.2025, by the Ministry of
Corporate Affairs, as noted above, we direct that the name of the Transmission Licensee
be changed from “Maheshwaram Transmission Limited” to “Maheshwaram
Transmission Private Limited” in the records of the Commission. It is further stipulated
that Maheshwaram Transmission Private Limited shall remain unequivocally bound by
the terms and conditions of the inter-State transmission licence originally granted to
Maheshwaram Transmission Limited, provisions of the Transmission Service
Agreement, Transmission Licence Regulations, and the Electricity Act.
9. We direct that the necessary endorsement be made on the transmission licence
with regard to the change of name of “Maheshwaram Transmission Limited” to
Order in Petition No. 81/RC/2026 Page 4

“Maheshwaram Transmission Private Limited”. Except for the name, there shall be no
change in the terms and conditions of the licence.
10. Let an extract copy of this order be sent to the Central Government (the Ministry
of Power), the Central Electricity Authority and the Central Transmission Utility of India
Limited in terms of sub-section (7) of Section 15 of the Electricity Act, 2003, for their
information and record.
11. Accordingly, the Petition No. 81/RC/2026 is allowed in terms of the above.

ORDER
The instant Petition has been filed by Power Grid Corporation of India Limited, a
deemed transmission licensee, for truing up of the transmission tariff for the 2019-24
tariff period under the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions
of Tariff) Regulations, 2019 (hereinafter referred to as “the 2019 Tariff Regulations”) and
determination of the transmission tariff under the Central Electricity Regulatory
Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2024 (hereinafter referred to
as “the 2024 Tariff Regulations”) for the 2024-29 tariff period in respect of the following
transmission assets (hereinafter referred to as the “Combined Asset”) forming part of
Combined Asset under Installation of STATCOMs in the Western Region:
Asset 1: ±300 MVAR STATCOM at 400 kV Aurangabad Sub-station;
Asset 2: ±200 MVAR STATCOM at 400 kV Gwalior Sub-station;
Asset 3: ±300 MVAR STATCOM at 400 kV Satna Sub-station; and
Asset 4: ±300 MVAR STATCOM at 400 kV Solapur Sub-station.
Order in Petition No. 502/TT/2025 Page 2 of 50

All the assets have been combined in 2019-24 tariff period with an Effective Commercial
Operation Date (E-COD) of 8.6.2018 and have been collectively referred to as
"Combined Asset" for the 2019-24 tariff period.
2. The Petitioner has made the following prayers in the instant Petition:
“a) Approve the trued-up Transmission Tariff for 2019-24 block and transmission tariff
for 2024-29 block for the assets covered under this petition, as per para 14 and 15
above.
b) Admit the capital cost claimed and additional capitalization incurred during 2019-24.
c) Allow the petitioner to recover the shortfall or refund the excess Annual Fixed
Charges, on account of Return on Equity due to change in applicable Minimum
Alternate/Corporate Income Tax rate as per the Income Tax Act, 1961 (as amended
from time to time) of the respective financial year directly without making any application
before the Commission as provided in Tariff Regulations 2019 and Tariff Regulations,
2024 as per para 14 and 15 above for respective block.
d) Approve the reimbursement of expenditure by the beneficiaries towards petition filing
fee, and expenditure on publishing of notices in newspapers in terms of Regulation 94
(1) Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff)
Regulations, 2024, and other expenditure (if any) in relation to the filing of petition.
e) Allow the petitioner to bill and recover RLDC fees & charges and Licensee fee
separately from the respondents in terms of Regulation 94 (3) and (4) Central Electricity
Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2024.
f) Allow the petitioner to bill and adjust impact on Interest on Loan due to change in
Interest rate on account of floating rate of interest applicable during 2024-29 period, if
any, from the respondents.
g) Allow the petitioner to file a separate petition before the Commission for claiming the
overall security expenses and consequential IOWC on that security expenses as
mentioned at para 21 above.
h) Allow the petitioner to file a separate petition before the Commission for claiming the
overall insurance expenses and consequential IOWC on that insurance expenses as
mentioned at para 21 above.
i) Allow the petitioner to file a separate petition before the Commission for claiming the
overall capital spares as per actual as mentioned at Para 21 above.
j) Allow the petitioner to claim expenses of CTUIL borne by POWERGRID through a
separate petition as mentioned at para 22 above.
k) Allow the Petitioner to bill and recover GST on Transmission Charges separately from
the respondents, if GST on transmission is levied at any rate in future. Further, any taxes
including GST and duties including cess etc. imposed by any statutory/Govt./municipal
authorities shall be allowed to be recovered from the beneficiaries.
And pass such other relief as the Commission deems fit and appropriate under the
circumstances of the case and in the interest of justice.”
Order in Petition No. 502/TT/2025 Page 3 of 50

Background
3. The brief facts of the case are as follows:
a. The Petitioner was entrusted with implementation of the transmission project
and its scope was discussed and agreed in the 36th meeting of the Standing
Committee on Power System Planning in the Western Region and 24th
meeting of the Western Regional Power Committee held on 29.8.2013 and
9.10.2013 respectively.
b. Investment Approval (the IA) for implementation of the transmission project
was accorded by the Board of Directors (BoD) of the Petitioner’s Company
(in its 311th meeting held on 4.3.2015) at an estimated cost of ₹107124.00
lakh including IDC of ₹5768.00 lakh (based on October 2014 Price Level) with
the broad scope of work as follows:

c. As per the I.A. dated 4.3.2015, the scheduled COD of the transmission assets
was 3.9.2017 against which COD of Asset 1, Asset 2, Asset 3, and Asset 4,
as approved by the Commission vide order dated 1.11.2019 in Petition No.
111/TT/2018 was 1.4.2018, 26.12.2018, 31.3.2018, and 15.4.2018
respectively. Further, vide the said order, the time over-run of 210 days, 479
days, 209 days, and 224 days in the respective commissioning of Asset 1,
Asset 2, Asset 3, and Asset 4 were not condoned. Vide the same order,
transmission tariff of Asset 1, Asset 2, Asset 3, and Asset 4 for the period
from their respective COD to 31.3.2019 was determined.
Order in Petition No. 502/TT/2025 Page 4 of 50

d. The true-up of transmission tariff for Asset-1, Asset-2, Asset-3, and Asset-4
from their respective CODs to 31.3.2019 and determination of transmission
tariff for the Combined Asset for the 2019-24 period was allowed in Petition
No. 481/TT/2020 vide order dated 18.1.2022.
e. The entire scope of work is completed as per the IA and is covered in this
Petition.
4. The Petitioner has filed the instant true-up Petition for truing up of Annual Filed
Charges for the 2019-24 Tariff Period and determination of Annual Fixed Charges for
the 2024-29 Tariff Period in respect of the Combined Asset.
5. The Respondents are distribution licensees, transmission licensees and power
departments, which are procuring transmission services from the Petitioner, mainly
beneficiaries of the Western Region.
6. The Petitioner has served a copy of the Petition on the Respondents and notice
regarding the filing of this Petition has been published in the newspapers in accordance
with Section 64 of the Electricity Act, 2003. No comments or suggestions have been
received from the general public in response to the aforesaid notices published in the
newspapers by the Petitioner. Madhya Pradesh Power Management Company Limited
(MPPMCL), Respondent No. 1, has filed its reply vide affidavit dated 9.12.2025 and has
raised the issues on determination of transmission tariff for 2024-29 period, Additional
capital expenditure (ACE) of both 2019-24 and 2024-29 tariff period, reimbursement of
the Petition filing fee & publication expenses, recovery of licensee fee and RLDC fees
& charges, Interest on Loan (IoL) for 2024-29 period, security expenses, capital spares,
expenses of CTUIL, and effect of CGST.
7. The hearing in this matter was held on 19.12.2025 and the order was reserved.
Order in Petition No. 502/TT/2025 Page 5 of 50

8. This order is issued considering the submissions made by the Petitioner vide
affidavits dated 30.11.2024, 31.7.2025 & 2.1.2026 and submission made by MPPMCL,
Respondent No. 1 vide affidavit dated 9.12.2025.
9. Having heard the representatives of the Petitioner and perused the material on
record, we proceed to dispose of the Petition.
Truing up of Annual Fixed Charges for 2019-24 tariff period
10. The details of the trued-up transmission charges claimed by the Petitioner in
respect of the Combined Asset are as follows:

12. The capital cost of the transmission project has been calculated in accordance
with Regulation 19(1) and 19(3) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations.
Order in Petition No. 502/TT/2025 Page 6 of 50

13. The Commission vide order dated 18.1.2022 in Petition No. 481/TT/2020 had
allowed the capital cost as on 31.3.2019 of ₹ 75559.10 lakh in respect of the Combined
Asset.
14. The Petitioner in the instant true-up Petition has claimed the capital cost as on
31.3.2019 of ₹ 75592.12 lakh in respect of the Combined Asset. The Petitioner has
submitted that the difference of ₹33.01 lakh (₹75592.12 lakh – ₹75559.10 lakh) is on
account of recovery of Liquidated Damages (LD) during FY 2018–19. The amount
recovered from the contractor has been added by the Petitioner to the capital cost as
on 01.04.2019.
15. We have considered the submissions of the Petitioner. We first proceed with the
treatment of LD recovered.
Treatment of Liquidated Damages
16. The Petitioner has submitted that LD has been recovered from the contractor
amounting to ₹33.01 lakh during FY 2018-19, ₹56.25 lakh during FY 2019-20 and
₹38.38 Lakh during FY 2023-24. As the Commission had already disallowed IDC/IEDC
on account of time over run in the instant project, the Petitioner is allowed to retain LD
to the extent of IDC and IEDC disallowed in line with APTEL judgment dated 27.4.2011
in Appeal No. 72/2010. Accordingly, Liquidated Damages (LD) recovered from the
executing agency(ies) and were reduced from the capital cost as per the accounting
procedures. Subsequently, the said LD recovered has been added back in the year of
recovery. Further, the details of the LD recovered from the contractor have been
certified by the Auditors in Auditor’s Certificates for Asset-3 and Asset-4.
17. We have gone through the submissions of the Petitioner in respect of LD
recovered. Regulation 21 (4) & (5) of 2019 Tariff Regulations provides as follows:
Order in Petition No. 502/TT/2025 Page 7 of 50

“21. Interest During Construction (IDC) and Incidental Expenditure during
Construction (IEDC)
xxxxxxxx
(4) If the delay in achieving the COD is not attributable to the generating company or the
transmission licensee, IDC and IEDC beyond SCOD may be allowed after prudence
check and the liquidated damages, if any, recovered from the contractor or supplier or
agency shall be adjusted in the capital cost of the generating station or the transmission
system, as the case may be.
(5) If the delay in achieving the COD is attributable either in entirety on in part to the
generating company or the transmission licensee or its contractor or supplier or agency,
in such cases, IDC and IEDC beyond SCOD may be disallowed after prudence check
either in entirety or on pro-rata basis corresponding to the period of delay not condoned
and the liquidated damages, if any, recovered from the contractor or supplier or agency
shall be retained by the generating company or the transmission licensee, as the case
may be.”
18. As per the Auditor’s Certificate, the Petitioner has recovered the LD ₹38.38 lakh
and ₹89.26 lakh in respect of Asset-3 and Asset-4 during 2018-19 and 2019-20 & F.Y.
2023-24 respectively. The Commission vide order dated 18.1.2022 in Petition No.
481/TT/2020 has disallowed the IDC & IEDC on account of time overrun ‘not condoned’
in respect of Asset-3 & Asset-4. The details of IDC and IEDC disallowed vide
aforementioned order and LD recovered in respect of Asset -3 & Asset-4 (part of the
Combined Asset) are as follows:

19. As can be seen from the above, an amount of LD recovered during 2018-19 is
₹33.01 lakh. However, the Petitioner has added back the same amount as on the capital
cost as on 1.4.2019. As this amount was already recovered in 2018-19 during 2014-19
tariff period which has already been trued order dated 18.1.2022 in Petition No.
481/TT/2020, the Petitioner has not furnished any reason or justification as to why the
Order in Petition No. 502/TT/2025 Page 8 of 50

Liquidated Damages (LD) amount of ₹33.01 lakh was not adjusted in 2018-19 in Petition
No. 481/TT/2020. The Petitioner has added the amount of LD recovered of ₹33.01 lakh
to the capital cost as on 1.4.2019. We are of the view that the Petitioner should have
disclosed this recovery of LD in 2018-19 at the stage of truing up of tariff of 2018-19 in
Petition no. 481/TT/2020. Therefore, we are not inclined to allow the addition of LD
recovered of ₹33.01 lakh in 2018-19 to the capital cost as on 1.4.2019.
20. Accordingly, the capital cost considered as on 1.4.2019 for the purpose of truing
up of transmission tariff for the 2019-24 period in accordance with Regulation 19 (3) (a)
of the 2019 Tariff Regulations is ₹75559.10 lakh.
21. Further, as per Regulation 21(5) of 2019 Tariff Regulations, the treatment of LD
as effected by the Petitioner, i.e., adding back the LD recovered during F.Y. 2019-20 &
F.Y. 2023-24 to ACE as certified by the Auditor (₹74.45 lakh which is net of LD
recovered of ₹33.01 lakh in respect of Asset-3 in F.Y. 2023-24 and ₹442.25 lakh which
is net of LD recovered of ₹56.25 lakh in respect of Asset-4 in F.Y. 2019-20) to arrive at
the gross ACE claimed for Tariff Period 2019-24 in respect of Combined Asset is in
order, as IDC and IEDC have already been deducted from the Capital cost as on COD

and run-of river hydro generating station and at the base rate of 16.50% for storage type
hydro generating stations, pumped storage hydro generating stations and run-of- river
generating station with pondage;
(3) Return on equity for new project achieving COD on or after 01.04.2024 shall be
computed at the base rate of 15.00% for the transmission system, including the
communication system, at the base rate of 15.50% for Thermal generating station and
run-of-river hydro generating station and at the base rate of 17.00% for storage type
hydro generating stations, pumped storage hydro generating stations and run-of-river
generating station with pondage;
Provided that return on equity in respect of additional capitalization beyond the
original scope, including additional capitalization on account of the emission control
system, Change in Law, and Force Majeure shall be computed at the base rate of one-
year marginal cost of lending rate (MCLR) of the State Bank of India plus 350 basis
points as on 1st April of the year, subject to a ceiling of 14%;
Provided further that:
i. In case of a new project, the rate of return on equity shall be reduced by 1.00%
for such period as may be decided by the Commission if the generating station
or transmission system is found to be declared under commercial operation

…….………”
“31. Tax on Return on Equity. (1) The rate of return on equity as allowed by the

to be paid estimated in line with the provisions of the relevant Finance Act applicable for

by excluding the income of non-generation or non-transmission business, as the case

71. We have considered the Petitioner’s submissions. As per clause (vi) of the
second proviso to Regulation 35(3)(a) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations, the O&M
Expenses of Static Synchronous Compensator, and Static Var Compensator shall be
worked out at @ 1.5% of the “original project cost” as on COD.
Order in Petition No. 477/TT/2025
Page 30 of 64

72. The “original project cost” has been defined in Regulation 3(46) of the 2019 Tariff
Regulations as the capital expenditure/cost within the original scope of the
transmission project up to the cut-off date. However, clause (vi) of the second proviso
to Regulation 35(3)(a) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations refers to the “original project cost”
of the STATCOM as on COD for the purpose of determining the O&M Expenses. To
address the said difference in the definition of “original project cost” in Regulation 3(46)
and clause (vi) of the second proviso to Regulation 35(3)(a) of the 2019 Tariff
Regulations, the Commission, vide order dated 18.10.2021 in Petition No.
658/TT/2020, while allowing the O&M Expenses for the STATCOM, relaxed clause (vi)
of the second proviso to Regulation 35(3)(a) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations by
exercising the powers conferred to it under Regulation 76 of the 2019 Tariff
Regulations and allowed the O&M Expenses for the STATCOM @1.5% of the Plant
and Machinery Cost (excluding IDC, IEDC, Land Cost, and Cost of Civil Works) of the
STATCOM as on the cut-off date. The relevant portion of the order dated 18.10.2021
in Petition No. 658/TT/2020 is extracted as follows:
“77. The clause (vi) of the second proviso to Regulation 35(3)(a) of the 2019 Tariff
Regulations provides for O&M Expenses @ 1.5% of the “original project cost” of the
STATCOM as on COD. “Original Project Cost” has been defined in Regulation 3(46)
of the 2019 Tariff Regulations as under:
“3(46) ‘Original Project Cost' means the capital expenditure incurred by the
generating company or the transmission licensee, as the case may be, within the
original scope of the project up to the cut-off date, and as admitted by the
Commission;”
78. While “Original Project Cost” as defined in Regulation 3(46) of the 2019 Tariff
Regulations covers capital expenditure/ cost within the original scope of the project
up to the cut-off date, clause (vi) of the second proviso to Regulation 35(3)(a) of the
2019 Tariff Regulations refers to the “original project cost” of the STATCOM as on
COD for the purpose of determining O&M Expenses.
79. We also observe that “original project cost” includes components of IDC, IEDC,
land cost and cost of civil works. However, as per Regulation 3(45) of the 2019 Tariff
Regulations extracted hereunder, the O&M Expenses are allowed for operation and
maintenance of the project or part thereof and includes the expenditure towards
manpower, maintenance, repairs and maintenance etc. but it excludes IDC, IEDC,
land cost and cost of civil works:
Order in Petition No. 477/TT/2025
Page 31 of 64

“(45) ‘Operation and Maintenance Expenses’ or ‘O&M expenses' means the
expenditure incurred for operation and maintenance of the project, or part thereof,
and includes the expenditure on manpower, maintenance, repairs and maintenance
spares, consumables, insurance and overheads and fuel other than used for
generation of electricity;”
80. Therefore, we are of the view that determination of O&M expenses on the basis
of Project cost (including IDC, IEDC Land cost and Cost of civil work) will not be
consistent with the provisions of the 2019 Tariff Regulations as extracted above.
81. Regulation 76 of the 2019 Tariff Regulations provides for relaxation of any of the
provisions of the 2019 Tariff Regulations by recording the reasons for the same. The
said Regulation provides as follows.
“76. Power to Relax: The Commission, for reasons to be recorded in writing, may
relax any of the provisions of these regulations on its own motion or on an application
made before it by an interested person.”
82. To address above issues arising out of the difference in the way in which “original
project cost” has been considered in clause (vi) of the second proviso to Regulation
35(3)(a) and Regulation 3(46) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations, we relax clause (vi) of
the second proviso to Regulation 35(3)(a) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations under
Regulation 76 of the 2019 Tariff Regulations and allow O&M Expenses for the
transmission assets @1.5% of the Plant and Machinery cost (excluding IDC, IEDC,
Land cost and cost of Civil works) of the STATCOM as on the cut-off date. The same
has been escalated at the rate of 3.51% to work out the O&M Expenses for the 2019-
24 tariff period.”

70(2) of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Conduct of Business)
Regulations, 2023 for the execution of order dated 25.11.2024 passed by the
Commission and directions and initiation of appropriate action against the Respondent
for non-compliance of the directions issued under order dated 25.11.2024 in Petition

In the matter of
Jindal India Power Ltd.

ORDER
Jindal India Power Limited (JIPL) has filed the present petition under Section
142 of the Electricity Act, 2003 read with Regulations 65 and 70(2) of the Central
Order in Petition No. 874/MP/2025 Page 1 of 11

Electricity Regulatory Commission (Conduct of Business) Regulations, 2023, seeking
execution and enforcement of the Commission’s order dated 25.11.2024 in Petition
No. 75/MP/2022, and initiation of appropriate action against BSES Rajdhani Power
Limited (BRPL/ Respondent No.1) for non-compliance with the directions issued
therein.
2. The Petitioner has made the following prayers in the instant Petition:
“(a) Execute the Order dated 25.11.2024 passed by this Hon’ble Commission in
Petition No.75/MP/2024;
(b) Direct BRPL to make payment of Rs. 15,114,117/- along with interest towards
amounts due and payable to JIPL in terms of Order dated 25.11.2024 in Petition
No.75/MP/2024;
(c) Direct BRPL to pay further interest/compensation on the amount mentioned in
prayer (b) till the date of actual payment;
(d) Pass an order of attachment, attaching to the extent of Rs. 15,114,117/- from the
bank account(s) belonging to the Respondent No.1/BRPL, pending disposal of the
Petition;
(e) Award costs of these proceedings against the Respondent and in favour of the
Petitioner; and
(f) Pass any other such Orders that this Hon’ble Commission may deem fit.”
Background
3. The Petitioner is a generating company engaged in the business of generation
of electricity through its 1200 MW coal-based thermal power plant located at Angul,
Odisha. BRPL is a distribution licensee in Delhi, and Respondent No.2, Tata Power
Trading Company Limited (TPTCL), is a trading licensee under Section 14(c) of the
Electricity Act, through whom power from the Petitioner was supplied to BRPL.
4. The dispute between the parties arises out of the procurement of short-term
power by BRPL pursuant to the Guidelines for Short-Term Procurement of Power
issued by the Ministry of Power on 30.3.2016. In pursuance of the said Guidelines,
BRPL issued a Request for Proposal on 17.12.2020 for the procurement of up to 700
MW of short-term power for the period 1.4.2021 to 30.9.2021.
Order in Petition No. 874/MP/2025 Page 2 of 11

5. Pursuant to the competitive bidding process conducted through the DEEP
portal, BRPL issued a Letter of Intent (LOI) dated 13.2.2021 to TPTCL for the
procurement of power, with the Petitioner being the identified source of supply. The
LOI, inter alia, provided for the quantum of power to be supplied, the delivery point,
payment terms, and provisions relating to Liquidated Damages (LD) for a shortfall in
power supply.
6. Disputes subsequently arose between the parties regarding the computation of
LD for the alleged shortfall in the supply of power. The Petitioner and TPTCL
contended that the deviation of 15% from the contracted energy was required to be
computed on a monthly basis, whereas BRPL calculated the LD on a fortnightly
basis, resulting in the deduction of excess amounts from the payments due to the
Petitioner.
7. In view of the disputes, the Petitioner, along with TPTCL, filed Petition No.
75/MP/2022 before this Commission, inter alia, seeking adjudication of the issues
relating to the computation of LD, levy of GST on LD, and wrongful withholding of
amounts by BRPL.
8. The Commission, vide order dated 25.11.2024 in Petition No.75/MP/2022, inter
alia held that the computation of LD by BRPL on a fortnightly basis was not
sustainable and that LD was required to be calculated on a monthly basis in terms of
Clause 7(b) of the LOI. Accordingly, BRPL was directed to refund the excess
amounts deducted due to erroneous computation of LD, along with applicable
interest, within 30 days from the date of the order.
Submissions of the Petitioner
9. The gist of the submissions made by Petitioner is as follows:
Order in Petition No. 874/MP/2025 Page 3 of 11

i. Despite the lapse of more than eight months from the date of the order
dated 25.11.2024, BRPL has failed to comply with the directions of the
Commission and has not refunded the excess amount deducted from the
payments due to the Petitioner. Following the issuance of the said order,
communications were addressed to BRPL through TPTCL requesting a refund
of the excess LD amount along with applicable interest in accordance with
Commission’s directions. However, the said amount has not been refunded till
date.
ii. Aggrieved by certain findings in the order dated 25.11.2024, BRPL
preferred Appeal No. 22 of 2025 before the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity
(APTEL), challenging inter alia the findings of the Commission regarding
computation of LD on a monthly basis and the consequential direction to refund
the excess amount deducted from the payments due to the Petitioner. Along
with the said Appeal, BRPL also filed I.A. No. 2102 of 2025 seeking interim
relief, including stay of the operation of the Commission’s order dated
25.11.2024, particularly the direction requiring refund of the excess LD amount.
iii. The Appeal, along with the Interim Application, was taken up by the
Tribunal, and notice was issued. Subsequently, when the Interim Application
seeking stay of the Commission’s order came up for consideration before the
Tribunal on 4.7.2025, BRPL stated that it did not wish to press the said
application seeking interim relief for the present and reserved liberty to move
an appropriate application at a later stage, if required. In view of the said
submission, the Tribunal dismissed I.A. No. 2102 of 2025 as not pressed.
Consequently, no interim protection or stay has been granted by the Tribunal
against the operation of the order dated 25.11.2024.
iv. The Petitioner has also filed Appeal No. 91 of 2025 before the Tribunal
challenging certain findings in the order dated 25.11.2024, including the
findings relating to the levy of LD and the issue of GST. The said Appeal is
presently pending adjudication before the Tribunal. However, the pendency of
the appeals does not affect the enforceability of the Commission’s Order in the
absence of any stay granted by the Tribunal.
Order in Petition No. 874/MP/2025 Page 4 of 11

A. There is wilful defiance of the directions of this Commission by BRPL
v. The continued failure of BRPL to comply with the directions contained in
the order dated 25.11.2024 amounts to willful non-compliance with the
directions of the Commission.
B. Power of the Commission to issue directions for non-compliance of
directions in terms of Section 142 of the Electricity Act read with Regulations 65
and 70(2) of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Conduct of
Business) Regulations, 2023 (2023 COB Regulations)
vi. Section 142 of the Electricity Act, 2003, empowers the Commission to
impose a penalty in case of contravention of the provisions of the Act or the
directions issued by the Commission. Reliance has been placed on the
judgment of the APTEL in Bihar State Electricity Board vs CERC (Appeal No.
53 of 2009), wherein it was held that the element of mens rea is not required to
be established for imposing a penalty under Section 142 and that mere
contravention of the directions issued by the Commission is sufficient to attract
the said provision.
C. Direction of the Commission amounts to a money decree
vii. The direction issued by the Commission requiring BRPL to refund the
excess LD amount effectively amounts to a money decree, which is liable to be
executed. In support of this contention, reliance has been placed on the
judgment of the Supreme Court in Malwa Strips (P) Ltd. v. Jyoti Ltd., (2009) 2
SCC 426, wherein it was held that a money decree cannot ordinarily be stayed
without the deposit of the decretal amount. Reliance has also been placed on
the judgment of APTEL in Western Electricity Supply Company Limited v. OCL
Iron & Steel Limited, wherein it was held that the executing forum may
determine the quantum payable even where the decree does not specify the
exact amount.
D. Amounts liable to be refunded and paid to Petitioner
viii. After recomputation of LD on a monthly basis in terms of the order dated
25.11.2024, the amount refundable by BRPL to the Petitioner has been
calculated as ₹1,51,14,117, along with applicable interest, and execution of the
said order has accordingly been sought in the present petition.
Order in Petition No. 874/MP/2025 Page 5 of 11

Hearing dated 25.11.2025
10. The matter was taken up for hearing ‘on admission’ through virtual mode. The
learned counsel for the Petitioner submitted that the Petition had been filed under
Section 142 of the Electricity Act, 2003 read with Regulations 65 and 70(2) of the
2023 COB Regulations, seeking execution of the Commission’s order dated
25.11.2024 passed in Petition No. 75/MP/2022 and initiation of appropriate action on
account of the alleged non-compliance of the directions issued therein.
11. After hearing the learned counsel for the Petitioner, the Commission admitted
the Petition and directed issuance of notice to the Respondents and parties to
complete their pleadings.
Hearing dated 15.1.2026
12. During the hearing, the learned counsel for the Petitioner submitted that no stay
had been granted by APTEL in Appeal No. 22/2025 filed by the Respondents, and
therefore, the present execution petition was maintainable.
13. Despite notice, none appeared on behalf of the Respondents. After hearing the
submissions made on behalf of the Petitioner, the Commission reserved its order in
the Petition.
Additional Affidavit dated 19.1.2026
14. The Petitioner has filed an Additional Affidavit placing on record the updated
computation of the amounts payable by BRPL in terms of the Commission’s order
dated 25.11.2024 in Petition No. 75/MP/2022. As per the affidavit, the total amount
payable by BRPL to JIPL as on 15.1.2026 is stated to be ₹2,52,75,135, comprising
₹1,51,14,117 towards excess amount and ₹1,01,61,018 towards interest. The same
has been taken on record.
Order in Petition No. 874/MP/2025 Page 6 of 11

Analysis and Decision
15. The present petition has been filed by the Petitioner under Section 142 of the
Electricity Act, 2003, read with Regulations 65 and 70(2) of the Central Electricity
Regulatory Commission (Conduct of Business) Regulations, 2023, seeking
execution of the Commission’s order dated 25.11.2024 in Petition No. 75/MP/2022.
16. The dispute between the parties in Petition No. 75/MP/2022 pertained to, inter
alia, the computation of LD for the alleged shortfall in supply of power under the Letter
of Intent dated 13.2.2021 issued by BRPL to TPTCL, with the Petitioner being the
source of supply. The Petitioner and TPTCL had contended that the permissible
deviation of 15% from the contracted energy was required to be computed on a
monthly basis, whereas BRPL computed the LD on a fortnightly basis, resulting in
the deduction of excess amounts from the payments due to the Petitioner. On
25.11.2024, the Commission passed its order in Petition No. 75/MP/2022, partly
allowing the issues raised therein, to the extent of directing that the computation of
LD be undertaken on a monthly basis. The relevant portion of the order dated
25.11.2024 reads as follows:
“[…]
27. In view of the foregoing observations, the levy of the liquidated damages
computed on a fortnightly basis by BRPL cannot be sustained as such computation
has to be on a monthly basis as clearly envisaged in Clause 7(b) of the LoI.
Consequently, the excess amount paid by the Petitioners on account of such
erroneous computation by BRPL shall be refunded by BRPL within 30 days from the
date of this order, along with applicable interest at the rate of surcharge for the delayed
payment as prescribed in the LOI.”
17. The Petitioner has submitted that despite the lapse of considerable time from
the date of the order dated 25.11.2024, BRPL has not refunded the excess amount
deducted from the payments due to the Petitioner. The Petitioner has further
submitted that BRPL had preferred Appeal No. 22 of 2025 before the APTEL,
Order in Petition No. 874/MP/2025 Page 7 of 11

challenging certain findings in the said order, and had also sought interim relief by
way of stay of the operation of the order. However, when the Interim Application
seeking stay came up for consideration before the Tribunal on 4.7.2025, BRPL stated
that it did not wish to press the said application for interim relief, and the Tribunal
dismissed the application as not pressed. Consequently, there is no stay operating
against the order dated 25.11.2024.
18. The Petitioner has also filed Appeal No. 91 of 2025 before the APTEL
challenging certain findings in the order dated 25.11.2024, including the findings
relating to the levy of LD and the issue of GST. As per the latest status placed on
record, it has been represented before the Tribunal that a cross appeal, being Appeal
No. 22 of 2025, has already been included in the List of Finals, and a request has
been made to tag the said appeal with Appeal No. 22 of 2025. The Tribunal has
directed that the appeal be re-included in the List of Finals to be taken up along with
Appeal No. 22 of 2025 in its turn. Thus, both appeals are presently pending
adjudication before the Tribunal.
19. However, it is well settled that the mere pendency of an appeal does not render
the directions of the Commission unenforceable unless the operation of such
directions has been specifically stayed by the appellate forum. In the present case,
no stay has been granted by the Appellate Tribunal against the order dated
25.11.2024, and therefore, the said order continues to remain operative and binding
upon the parties.
20. We observe that despite notice in the present proceedings, BRPL has neither
appeared nor filed any reply rebutting the submissions made by the Petitioner.
Accordingly, the averments made by the Petitioner regarding non-compliance of the
directions contained in the order dated 25.11.2024 remain uncontroverted.
Order in Petition No. 874/MP/2025 Page 8 of 11

21. At this stage, it is also relevant to examine the powers of the Commission in
cases of non-compliance with its orders. Section 142 of the Electricity Act, 2003,
empowers the Commission to take appropriate action where any person contravenes
or fails to comply with the provisions of the Act or any direction issued by the
Commission. Section 142 provides as under:
“Section 142 – Punishment for non-compliance of directions by Appropriate
Commission.
In case any complaint is filed before the Appropriate Commission by any person or if
that Commission is satisfied that any person has contravened any of the provisions of
this Act or the rules or regulations made thereunder, or any direction issued by the
Commission, the Appropriate Commission may after giving such person an opportunity
of being heard in the matter, by order in writing, direct that, without prejudice to any
other penalty to which he may be liable under this Act, such person shall pay, by way
of penalty, which shall not exceed one lakh rupees for each contravention and in case
of a continuing failure with an additional penalty which may extend to six thousand
rupees for every day during which the failure continues after contravention of the first
such direction.”
22. The above statutory provision makes it clear that the Commission is
empowered to take action where a party fails to comply with its directions. The scope
of such power is further reinforced by the 2023 COB Regulations.
23. Regulation 65 of the 2023 COB Regulations preserves the inherent powers of
the Commission and provides as under:
“Regulation 65 – Saving of the inherent power of the Commission
(1) Nothing in these regulations shall be deemed to limit or otherwise affect the inherent
power of the Commission to make such orders as may be necessary for the ends of
justice or to prevent the abuse of the process of the Commission.
(2) Nothing in these regulations shall bar the Commission from adopting in conformity
with the provisions of the Act a procedure that is at variance with any of the provisions of
these Regulations if the Commission, in view of the special circumstances of a matter or
class of matters and for reasons to be recorded in writing, deems it necessary or
expedient for dealing with such a matter or class of matters.
(3) Nothing in these regulations shall, expressly or impliedly, bar the Commission from
dealing with any matter or exercising any power under the Act for which no Regulations
have been framed.”
24. Further, Regulation 70(2) of the 2023 COB Regulations provides that failure to
comply with the provisions of the Act, the Rules, the Regulations issued under the
Order in Petition No. 874/MP/2025 Page 9 of 11

Act or any directions or orders of the Commission shall invite appropriate action
against the concerned party under Section 142 of the Electricity Act, 2003.
25. In this regard, the APTEL in Bihar State Electricity Board v. Central Electricity
Regulatory Commission (Appeal No. 53 of 2009, Judgment dated 31.7.2009) has
clarified that proceedings under Section 142 are civil in nature and that the element
of mens rea is not required to be established for invoking the said provision. The
Tribunal observed that once the Commission is satisfied that its directions have been
violated, appropriate action under Section 142 may be initiated after providing an
opportunity of hearing.
26. It is also pertinent to note that the direction issued by the Commission in the
Order dated 25.11.2024, requiring BRPL to refund the excess amount along with
interest, is in the nature of a money decree. In this regard, the Supreme Court in
Malwa Strips (P) Ltd. v. Jyoti Ltd., (2009) 2 SCC 426, held that ordinarily there cannot
be an unconditional stay of a money decree without deposit of the decretal amount.
In the present case, though BRPL preferred an appeal before the APTEL, no stay
has been granted by APTEL, and BRPL has not deposited any amount towards the
refund directed to be made.
27. Further, APTEL in Western Electricity Supply Company Limited v. OCL Iron &
Steel Limited (E.P. No. 2 of 2013 in Appeal Nos. 171 and 187 of 2010, judgment
dated 2.12.2013) has held that it is not necessary for a decree sought to be executed
to specify the exact amount payable. It is sufficient if the terms of the decree clearly
indicate that payment is required to be made by the judgment debtor, and the
executing forum may determine the quantum payable in the course of execution.
Order in Petition No. 874/MP/2025 Page 10 of 11

28. The Petitioner has also filed an Additional Affidavit dated 19.1.2026, placing on
record the updated computation of the amount payable by BRPL in terms of the order
dated 25.11.2024. As per the said affidavit, the total amount payable by Respondent
No.1 to the Petitioner as on 15.1.2026 is ₹2,52,75,135, comprising ₹1,51,14,117
towards excess amount and ₹1,01,61,018 towards interest, which has not been
contested by BRPL.
29. Having considered the submissions of the Petitioner and the material placed on
record, it is evident that the directions issued in the order dated 25.11.2024 have not
been complied with by BRPL. In the absence of any stay against the said order,
BRPL is bound to comply with the directions contained therein.
30. Accordingly, BRPL is directed to comply with the directions contained in the

the Electricity Act, 2003.
31. The Petitioner is at liberty to revive the matter in case BRPL fails to pay the
abovesaid amount to the Petitioner within the specified period.
32. Petition No. 874/MP/2025 is disposed of in terms of the above.

ORDER
The Petitioner, NHPC Limited, has filed present Petition for truing-up of the tariff
of Kishanganga Hydroelectric Project (3x110 MW) (in short “the generating station”)
for the period 2019-24 in terms of Regulation 13 of the Central Electricity Regulatory
Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2019 (in short “the 2019
Tariff Regulations”) and for the determination of the tariff of the generating station for
the period 2024-29 in terms of the provisions of the Central Electricity Regulatory
Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2024 (in short “the 2024
Tariff Regulations”). The generating station, located in the Bandipora District of
Jammu & Kashmir, is a run-of-the-river with pondage scheme (ROR with pondage)
that envisages the diversion of water from Kishanganga (a tributary of the river
Jhelum) into an underground power house and discharging the tail race water into
Wular Lake. The date of commercial operation of the first unit (Unit I) was 18.5.2018,
and the commercial operation of both Units II & III of the generating station was
24.5.2018.
2. Petition No. 453/GT/2020 was filed by the Petitioner for truing-up of tariff of the
generating station for the period 2014-19 and approval of tariff of the generating
station for the period 2019-24, the Commission, vide its order dated 12.1.2024,
approved the capital cost and annual fixed charges of the generating station for the
period 2019-24 as under;

5. The Petition was heard on 24.6.2025. The Petitioner, in response to the
Commission’s technical validation (TV) letter, has furnished the additional information,
vide affidavit dated 2.7.2025. The Respondents, UPPCL and CSPDCL, have filed their
replies vide affidavit dated 12.9.2025 and 21.7.2025, respectively, and the Petitioner
has filed its rejoinder to the said replies. Pursuant to the hearing dated 9.9.2025, an
order in this Petition was reserved. Based on the submissions and the documents on
record, we proceed to examine the Petitioner's claims, subject to a prudence check
as stated in the subsequent paragraphs.
Capital Cost
6. Regulation 19 of the 2019 Tariff Regulations provides as under:
19. Capital Cost:
(1) The Capital cost of the generating station or the transmission system, as the case may be,
as determined by the Commission after prudence check in accordance with these Regulations
shall form the basis for determination of Tariff for existing and new projects.
(2) The Capital Cost of a new project shall include the following:
(a) The expenditure incurred or projected to be incurred up to the date of commercial operation
of the project;
(b) Interest during construction and financing charges, on the loans (i) being equal to 70% of
the funds deployed, in the event of the actual equity in excess of 30% of the funds deployed, by
treating the excess equity as normative loan, or (ii) being equal to the actual amount of loan in
the event of the actual equity less than 30% of the funds deployed;
Order in Petition No. 624/GT/2025 Page 4 of 77

(c) Any gain or loss on account of foreign exchange risk variation pertaining to the loan amount
availed during the construction period;
(d) Interest during construction and incidental expenditure during construction as computed in
accordance with these Regulations;
(e) Capitalised initial spares subject to the ceiling rates in accordance with these Regulations;
(f) Expenditure on account of additional capitalization and de-capitalisation determined in
accordance with these Regulations;
(g) Adjustment of revenue due to sale of infirm power in excess of fuel cost prior to the date of
commercial operation as specified under Regulation 7 of these Regulations;
(h) Adjustment of revenue earned by the transmission licensee by using the assets before the
date of commercial operation;
(i) Capital expenditure on account of ash disposal and utilization including handling and
transportation facility;
(j) Capital expenditure incurred towards railway infrastructure and its augmentation for
transportation of coal upto the receiving end of the generating station but does not include the
transportation cost and any other appurtenant cost paid to the railway;
(k) Capital expenditure on account of biomass handling equipment and facilities, for co-firing;
(l) Capital expenditure on account of emission control system necessary to meet the revised
emission standards and sewage treatment plant;
(m) Expenditure on account of fulfilment of any conditions for obtaining environment clearance
for the project;
(n) Expenditure on account of change in law and force majeure events; and
(o) Capital cost incurred or projected to be incurred by a thermal generating station, on account
of implementation of the norms under Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) scheme of
Government of India shall be considered by the Commission subject to sharing of benefits
accrued under the PAT scheme with the beneficiaries.
(3) The Capital cost of an existing project shall include the following:
(a) Capital cost admitted by the Commission prior to 1.4.2019 duly trued up by excluding liability,
if any, as on 1.4.2019;
(b) Additional capitalization and de-capitalization for the respective year of Tariff as determined
in accordance with these Regulations;
(c) Capital expenditure on account of renovation and modernisation as admitted by this
Commission in accordance with these Regulations;
(d) Capital expenditure on account of ash disposal and utilization including handling and
transportation facility;
(e)Capital expenditure incurred towards railway infrastructure and its augmentation for
transportation of coal upto the receiving end of generating station but does not include the
transportation cost and any other appurtenant cost paid to the railway;
(f) and Capital cost incurred or projected to be incurred by a thermal generating station, on
account of implementation of the norms under Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) scheme of
Government of India shall be considered by the Commission subject to sharing of benefits
accrued under the PAT scheme with the beneficiaries.
(4) The capital cost in case of existing or new hydro generating station shall also include:
(a) cost of approved rehabilitation and resettlement (R&R) plan of the project in conformity with
National R&R Policy and R&R package as approved; and
(b) cost of the developer’s 10% contribution towards Rajiv Gandhi Grameen Vidyutikaran
Yojana (RGGVY) and Deendayal Upadhyaya Gram Jyoti Yojana (DDUGJY) project in the
affected area.
(5) The following shall be excluded from the capital cost of the existing and new projects:
(a) The assets forming part of the project, but not in use, as declared in the Tariff petition;
(b) De-capitalised Assets after the date of commercial operation on account of replacement or
removal on account of obsolescence or shifting from one project to another project: Provided
that in case replacement of transmission asset is recommended by Regional Power Committee,
such asset shall be decapitalised only after its redeployment; Provided further that unless
shifting of an asset from one project to another is of permanent nature, there shall be no de-
capitalization of the concerned assets.
Order in Petition No. 624/GT/2025 Page 5 of 77

(c) In case of hydro generating stations, any expenditure incurred or committed to be incurred
by a project developer for getting the project site allotted by the State Government by following
a transparent process;
(d) Proportionate cost of land of the existing project which is being used for generating power
from generating station based on renewable energy; and
(e) Any grant received from the Central or State Government or any statutory body or authority
for the execution of the project which does not carry any liability of repayment.
7. Clause (1) of Regulation 19 of the 2019 Tariff Regulations provides that the
capital cost as determined by the Commission, after a prudence check, in accordance
with the Regulation, shall form the basis of the determination of the Tariff of existing
and new projects. Vide order dated 12.1.2024 in Petition No. 453/GT/2020, and, in
accordance with the 2019 Tariff Regulations, the capital cost of Rs. 543047.02 lakh
as on 31.3.2019 was approved. Accordingly, in terms of Regulation 19(1) of the 2019
Tariff Regulations, the capital cost of Rs. 543047.02 lakh has been considered as the
opening capital cost as on 1.4.2019 for the purposes of truing up of Tariff of the
generating station, for the period 2019-24.
Additional Capital Expenditure:
8. Regulations 24 to 26 of the 2019 Tariff Regulations provide as under:
“24. Additional Capitalisation within the original scope and upto the cut – off date
(1) The additional capital expenditure in respect of a new project or an existing project incurred
or projected to be incurred, on the following counts within the original scope of work, after
the date of commercial operation and up to the cut – off date may be admitted by the
Commission, subject to prudence check:
a. Undischarged liabilities recognized to be payable at a future date;
b. Works deferred for execution;
c. Procurement of initial capital spares within the original scope of work, in
accordance with the provisions of Regulation 23 of these Regulations;
d. Liabilities to meet award of arbitration or for compliance of the directions or order
of any statutory authority or order or decree of any court of law;
e. Change in law or compliance of any existing law; and
f. Force Majeure events:
Provided that in case of any replacement of the assets, the additional capitalisation shall be
worked out after adjusting the gross fixed assets and cumulated depreciation of the assets
replaced on account of de-capitalisation.
(2) The generating company or the transmission licensee, as the case may be shall submit the
details of work assets wise/ wise included in the original scope of work along with estimates
of expenditure, liabilities recognised to be payable at a future date and the work deferred
for execution.
25. Additional Capitalisation within the original scope and after the cut – off date:
Order in Petition No. 624/GT/2025 Page 6 of 77

(1) The additional capital expenditure incurred or projected to be incurred in respect of an
existing project or a new project on the following counts within the original scope of work and
after the cut off date may be admitted by the Commission, subject to prudence check:
a. Liabilities to meet award of arbitration or for compliance of the direction or order of any
statutory authority, or order or decree of any court of law;
b. Change in law or compliance of any existing law;
c. Deferred works relating to ash pond or ash handling system in the original scope of
work;
d. Liability for works executed prior to the cut-off date;
e. Force Majeure events;
f. Liability for works admitted by the Commission after the cut-off date to the extent of
discharge of such liabilities by actual payments; and
g. Raising of ash dyke as a part of ash disposal system.
(2) In case of replacement of assets deployed under the original scope of the existing project
after cut – off date, the additional capitalisation may be admitted by the Commission, after
making necessary adjustments in the gross fixed assets and the cumulated depreciation,
subject to prudence check on the following grounds:
a. The useful life of the assets is not commensurate with the useful life of the project and
such assets have been fully depreciated in accordance with the provisions of these
regulations;
b. The replacement of the assets or equipment is necessary on account of change in law
or Force Majeure conditions;
c. The replacement of such assets or equipment is necessary on account of obsolescence
of technology; and
d. The replacement of such assets or equipment has otherwise been allowed by the
Commission.
26. Additional Capitalisation beyond the original scope
(1) The capital expenditure, in respect of existing generating station or the transmission system
including communication system, incurred or projected to be incurred on the following counts
beyond the original scope, may be admitted by the Commission, subject to prudence check:
a. Liabilities to meet award of arbitration or for compliance of order or directions of any
statutory authority, or order or decree of any court of law;
b. Change in law or compliance of any existing law;
c. Force Majeure events;
d. Need for higher security and safety of the plant as advised or directed by appropriate
Indian Government Instrumentality or statutory authorities responsible for national or
internal security;
e. Deferred works relating to ash pond or ash handling system in additional to the original
scope of work, on case-to-case basis:
Provided also that of any expenditure has been claimed under Renovation and
Maintenance (R&M) or repairs and maintenance under O&M expenses, the same shall
not be claimed under these Regulations;
f. Usage of water from sewage treatment plant in thermal generating station.
(2) In case of de-capitalisation of assets of a generating company or the transmission licensee,
as the case may be, the original cost of such asset as on the date of decapitalisation shall be
deducted from the value of gross fixed asset and corresponding loan as well as equity shall be
deducted from outstanding loan and the equity respectively in the year such de-capitalisation
takes place with corresponding adjustments in cumulative depreciation and cumulative
repayment of loan, duly taking into consideration the year in which it was capitalised.”

11. The Respondents, UPPCL and CSPDCL, have submitted that the Petitioner has
claimed that the true-up of tariff for the 2019-24 period is based on inflated figures,
misapplication of regulations, and data inconsistencies, which, if allowed, would
unduly burden the Respondents and end consumers. Further, the Respondents

secure, and efficient operation of the generating station, were beyond the original
Order in Petition No. 624/GT/2025 Page 8 of 77

claims would inflate the capital cost base, increasing depreciation, return on equity,
and interest on loans, thereby raising annual fixed charges and burdening consumers.
The Petitioner, in its rejoinder, has clarified that all claims are strictly in accordance
with the provisions of the 2019 Tariff Regulations, and are supported by the requisite
tariff forms and supporting documents, duly certified by statutory auditors. The data

standards, and verified in line with a prudence check against the requirements
envisaged under the 2019 Tariff Regulations. The matter has been considered. Based

14. The Commission had allowed the ceiling limit of Rs. 3839.73 lakh for the
purchase of initial spares in respect of the Kishanganga power station, vide Order
dated 12.1.2024 in Petition No. 453/GT/2020, which is stated as under:
“14. The matter has been examined. The cut-off date of the generating stations is
31.3.2021. The Plant & Machinery cost as on cut-off date is Rs. 94438.29 lakh. As such,
as per above regulation the permissible limit of initial spares works out to Rs. 3839.73
lakh. Accordingly, the claim of the Petitioner for Rs. 2284.67 lakh being within the ceiling
limit upto the COD of the generating station, the same is allowed. The Petitioner has not
claimed capitalization of initial spares in 2018-19.
15. As regard the prayer for extension of cut-off date till 31.3.2024, we are not in
agreement to extend the cut-off date, however, based on the justification provided by the
Petitioner, the claim of capitalization of initial spares during the period 2019-24, beyond
the cut-off date is being considered, subject to above ceiling limit of Rs.3839.73 lakh.”
15. In view of the directions stated above, a ceiling limit of 3839.73 lakh is fixed for
capitalisation of initial spares, out of which Rs. 2284.67 lakh has been capitalised up
to COD of the station. As such, the balance available for capitalisation of initial spares
as on the station's COD is Rs. 1555.06 lakh (Rs. 3839.73 lakh – Rs. 2284.67 lakh). It
is noted that the Petitioner has claimed Rs. 1737.27 lakh, which exceeds the
remaining balance above. Therefore, the excess amount of Rs. 182.21 lakh (Rs.
1737.27 lakh – Rs. 1555.06 lakh) is not allowed. The remaining balance for
capitalisation of initial spares is “Nil” beyond 2023-24.

transmission system including communication system and run-of river hydro generating station
and at the base rate of 16.50% for the storage type hydro generating stations including pumped
storage hydro generating stations and run-of river generating station with pondage:
“Provided that return on equity in respect of additional capitalization after cut-off date beyond the
original scope, excluding additional capitalization on account of emission control system, shall be
computed at the weighted average rate of interest on actual loan portfolio of the generating station
or the transmission system or in the absence of actual loan portfolio of the generating station or
the transmission system, the weighted average rate of interest of the generating company or the
transmission licensee, as the case may be, as a whole shall be considered, subject to ceiling of
14%”
Provided further that:
i. In case of a new project the rate of return on equity shall be reduced by 1.00% for such period
as may be decided by the Commission if the generating station or transmission system is
found to be declared under commercial operation without Commissioning of any of the
Restricted Governor Mode Operation (RGMO) or Free Governor Mode Operation (FGMO)
data telemetry communication system up to load dispatch centre or protection system based
on the report submitted by the respective RLDC;
ii. in case of existing generating station as and when any of the requirements under (i) above of
this Regulation are found lacking based on the report submitted by the concerned RLDC rate
of return on equity shall be reduced by 1.00% for the period for which the deficiency continues;
iii. in case of a thermal generating station with effect from 1.4.2020:
a) rate of return on equity shall be reduced by 0.25% in case of failure to achieve the ramp
rate of 1% per minute;

b) an additional rate of return on equity of 0.25% shall be allowed for every incremental ramp
rate of 1% per minute achieved over and above the ramp rate of 1% per minute subject to
ceiling of additional rate of return on equity of 1.00%:
Provided that the detailed guidelines in this regard shall be issued by National Load
Dispatch Centre by 30.6.2019.
(3) The return on equity in respect of additional capitalization on account of emission control
system shall be computed at the base rate of one-year marginal cost of lending rate (MCLR) of
theState Bank of India as on 1st April of the year in which the date of operation (ODe) occurs plus

31. Tax on Return on Equity:
(1) The base rate of return on equity as allowed by the Commission under Regulation 30 of these
Regulations shall be grossed up with the effective tax rate of the respective financial year. For
this purpose the effective tax rate shall be considered on the basis of actual tax paid in respect of
the financial year in line with the provisions of the relevant Finance Acts by the concerned
generating company or the transmission licensee as the case may be. The actual tax paid on
income from other businesses including deferred tax liability (i.e. income from business other than
business of generation or transmission as the case may be) shall be excluded for the calculation
of effective tax rate.
(2) Rate of return on equity shall be rounded off to three decimal places and shall be computed
as per the formula given below:
Rate of pre-tax return on equity = Base rate / (1-t)
Where “t” is the effective tax rate in accordance with clause (1) of this Regulation and shall be
calculated at the beginning of every financial year based on the estimated profit and tax to be
paid estimated in line with the provisions of the relevant Finance Act applicable for that financial
year to the company on pro-rata basis by excluding the income of non-generation or non-
transmission business as the case may be and the corresponding tax thereon. In case of
generating company or transmission licensee paying Minimum Alternate Tax (MAT) “t” shall be
considered as MAT rate including surcharge and cess.
Illustration-
(i) In case of a generating company or a transmission licensee paying Minimum Alternate Tax
(MAT) @ 21.55% including surcharge and cess: Rate of return on equity = 15.50/(1-0.2155)
= 19.758%
(ii) In case of a generating company or a transmission licensee paying normal corporate tax
including surcharge and cess:
(a) Estimated Gross Income from generation or transmission business for FY 2019- 20 is Rs.
1000 cr;
(b) Estimated Advance Tax for the year on above is Rs. 240 cr;
(c) Effective Tax Rate for the year 2019-20 = Rs. 240 Crore/Rs. 1000 Crore = 24%;
(d) Rate of return on equity = 15.50/ (1-0.24) = 20.395%.
(3) The generating company or the transmission licensee as the case may be shall true up the
grossed up rate of return on equity at the end of every financial year based on actual tax paid
together with any additional tax demand including interest thereon duly adjusted for any refund of
tax including interest received from the income tax authorities pertaining to the Tariff period 2019-
24 on actual gross income of any financial year. However penalty if any arising on account of
delay in deposit or short deposit of tax amount shall not be claimed by the generating company
or the transmission licensee as the case may be. Any under-recovery or over-recovery of grossed
up rate on return on equity after truing up shall be recovered or refunded to beneficiaries or the
long term customers as the case may be on year to year basis.”

“25. Additional Capitalisation within the original scope and after cut-off date:
(1) The additional capital expenditure incurred or projected to be incurred in respect

cumulative depreciation, subject to prudence check on the following grounds:
(a) Assets whose useful life is not commensurate with the useful life of the project and
such assets have been fully depreciated in accordance with the provisions of these
Regulations;
(b) The replacement of the asset or equipment is necessary on account of a change in
law or Force Majeure conditions;

involved in relation to the renewal of lease of lease hold land on case to case basis.
Provided that any claim of additional capitalisation with respect to the replacement of
assets under the original scope and on account of obsolescence of technology, less than
Rs. 20 lakhs shall not be considered as part of Capital cost and shall be met through
normative O&M expenses.
26. Additional Capitalisation beyond the original scope

transmission system, including the communication system, incurred or projected to be

ORDER
The Petitioner, NTPC Ltd. (“Petitioner”/ “NTPC”), has filed the present Petition
under Section 79 (1) (a) & (k) read with Section 62 of the Electricity Act, 2003 (“the
Act”), seeking expenditure towards procurement and capitalization of wagons for
Kahalgaon Super Thermal Power Station, Stage-I (840 MW) (“Kahalgaon-I”) located
in the State of Bihar. The Petitioner has made the following prayers:
Order in Petition No.424/MP/2025 Page 2 of 20

a) Allow the expenditure of Rs. 454.49 lakh incurred towards 10 wagons for Kahalgaon
Stage-I for the financial year 2014-15 under Regulation 14(3)(x) of the 2014 Tariff
Regulations;
b) Revise the tariff of Kahalgaon Stage-I for the period 2014-19 accordingly; and
c) Pass any other order as it may deem fit in the circumstances mentioned above.
Background of the Case:
2. The Petitioner is a Government Company within the meaning of the
Companies Act, 1956 and a ‘Generating Company’ as defined under Section 2(28) of
the Electricity Act, 2003 (the Act). It operates power stations and projects across
various regions of the country, including Kahalgaon-I, located in the State of Bihar.
3. Prior to filing the instant Petition, the Petitioner had filed a Petition No.
279/GT/2014 before the Commission for the determination of the 2014-19 tariff of
Kahalgoan-I. The Commission, vide order dated 30.7.2016 in Petition No.
279/GT/2014, determined the capital cost and annual fixed charges of the generating
station for the tariff period 2014-19. Aggrieved by the disallowance of Rs. 510 lakh
incurred towards augmentation of the firefighting system, the Petitioner filed Review
Petition No. 46/RP/2016. The Commission, by order dated 21.2.2017, disposed of the
Review Petition, keeping the issue of capitalization of the said expenditure open,
pending submission of the report of the CEA.
4. Subsequently, the Petitioner filed Petition No. 294/GT/2020 dated 30.10.2019
for truing-up of 2014-19 tariff under Regulation 8(1) of the 2014 Tariff Regulations. In
its additional submissions dated 10.5.2022 in the said Petition, the Petitioner claimed
Rs. 454.49 lakh towards procurement of 10 wagons under Regulation 14(3)(x) of the
2014 Tariff Regulations. It was submitted that the expenditure had earlier been claimed
under exclusion since the same was disallowed in the Commission’s order dated
30.7.2016 in Petition No. 279/GT/2014. The Petitioner further referred to a similar
Order in Petition No.424/MP/2025 Page 3 of 20

disallowance in Petition No. 150/2009 (Farakka STPS), which was upheld by the
Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (APTEL) in its order dated 26.3.2014 in Appeal No.
86 of 2012. However, the Hon’ble Supreme Court, in Civil Appeal No. 5990 of 2014,
by judgment dated 9.11.2017, set aside the APTEL order and remanded the matter to
the APTEL for reconsideration.
5. Accordingly, since the issue of wagon capitalization was pending adjudication
before the APTEL, the Commission, vide order dated 19.5.2024 in Petition No.
294/GT/2020 (read with corrigendum dated 15.6.2024), deferred consideration of the
claim while granting liberty to the Petitioner to approach the Commission upon final
adjudication, and pursuant thereto, upon the APTEL’s judgment dated 22.11.2024 in
Appeal No. 86 of 2012 (“APTEL judgment dated 22.11.2024) allowing the claim for
capitalization of wagons, the Petitioner has filed the present Petition seeking
capitalization of 10 wagons amounting to Rs. 454.49 lakh for the year 2014–15 under
Regulation 14(3)(x) of the 2014 Tariff Regulations.
Submissions of the Petitioner:
6. The Petitioner, in support of the relief sought, has mainly submitted the following:
(a) The APTEL judgment dated 22.11.2024 concerning Farakka STPS, allowed the
claim towards capitalization of wagons, holding inter alia that the wagons were
essential for the efficient operation of the generating station and formed an
integral part of the fuel receipt system; that inter-unit transfer of wagons during
exigencies is a permissible and economically prudent practice to ensure
sustained functioning of the generating stations; that replacement of
unserviceable wagons had been duly accounted for through decapitalization;
and that similar inter-unit transfers between Farakka STPS and other NTPC
stations underscored the operational necessity of maintaining an adequate
stock of wagons.
Order in Petition No.424/MP/2025 Page 4 of 20

(b) Regulation 14(3)(x) of the 2014 Tariff Regulations provides for capitalization of
expenditure necessitated on account of modifications in the fuel receiving
system arising due to circumstances not within the control of the generating
station. In the present case, the procurement of wagons was necessitated due
to operational exigencies and the need to replace unserviceable wagons to
maintain the efficiency and reliability of coal transportation. The wagons are
directly linked to the fuel receipt system, which is critical for the operation of the
generating station. This expenditure is, therefore, fully justified under the
provisions of Regulation 14(3)(x) of the 2014 Tariff Regulations.
(c) The wagons in question do not fall under the category of minor assets, tools, or
furniture. The expenditure was incurred for assets of significant operational
importance and is not of a nature that could be covered under Compensation
Allowance or O&M expenses. Thus, the claim for capitalization meets the
regulatory requirements.
(d) The expenditure incurred for the procurement of the aforesaid wagons is
essential for the reliable operation of Kahalgaon Stage-I. The wagons are
utilised for the transportation of coal from mines to the station and are integral
to the functioning of the fuel receipt system. The procurement was necessitated
by the decapitalization of old and unserviceable wagons.
(e) The findings and observations of the APTEL`s judgment dated 22.11.2024
conclusively establish that the expenditure incurred on wagons is a legitimate
claim. Given the similar operational requirements at Kahalgaon Stage-I, the
principles laid down in the said APTEL`s judgment are squarely applicable to
the present case.
(f) The Commission has duly recognised the necessity of wagons for the
generating station in question and has not disallowed the Petitioner’s claim on
this ground. It has appropriately granted the Petitioner liberty to approach the
Commission upon the final adjudication by the APTEL in the remand
proceedings concerning Farakka STPS. The Commission, in a similar context,

allowed claims pertaining to wagons for Farakka STPP Stage-I & II in the truing-

(g) The APTEL`s judgment dated 22.11.2024 further reinforces the legitimacy of

Analysis and Decision
11. We have heard the learned counsels for both the Petitioner and Respondent
No. 1, BSPHCL, and have carefully perused the documents available on record and
Order in Petition No.424/MP/2025 Page 14 of 20

duly considered the submissions advanced by the parties. The issue for our
consideration is whether the additional capital expenditure of Rs. 454.49 lakh incurred
by the Petitioner towards the procurement of 10 railway wagons for Kahalgaon STPS
Stage-I during FY 2014-15 is admissible under Regulation 14(3)(x) of the 2014 Tariff
Regulations.
12. It is noticed that the Petitioner’s claim was earlier deferred by the Commission
in its order dated 19.5.2024 in Petition No. 294/GT/2020, pending final adjudication by
the APTEL on an identical issue relating to Farakka STPS. Pursuant thereto, the
APTEL vide its judgment dated 22.11.2024 allowed capitalization of expenditure
incurred towards procurement of railway wagons, holding that such wagons form an
integral part of the fuel receiving system of a thermal generating station and that the
expenditure is not in the nature of routine O&M or covered under compensation
allowance.
13. The BSPHCL has objected to the claim primarily on the grounds of alleged lack
of documentary evidence, absence of wagon-wise inventory data, and apprehension
of double recovery through O&M expenses or compensation allowance. It has also
been contended that details relating to decapitalization and compliance with the SoP
for declaring wagons unserviceable are insufficient. The Petitioner, on the other hand,
has submitted that a total of 66 wagons were decapitalized during FY 2008-09 to FY
2012-13 and two additional wagons in FY 2016-17, and that the corresponding
decapitalized amounts were duly deducted from the capital cost by the Commission in
the respective tariff orders. The Petitioner has further submitted that the 10 wagons
procured in FY 2014-15 were the first replacement wagons capitalized for the
generating station after a prolonged period of decapitalization, and that the expenditure
Order in Petition No.424/MP/2025 Page 15 of 20

has been duly supported by audited accounts, Form-9Bi, auditor’s certificates, and
third-party certification by RITES Limited.
14. We note that the operational circumstances of Kahalgaon STPS Stage-I are
materially similar to those considered by the APTEL. We observe that the expenditure
is due to decapitalisation of a substantial number of wagons over the years, with
corresponding deductions already effected from the capital cost by the Commission,
and that the procurement of 10 wagons in FY 2014-15 was undertaken on a
replacement basis due to operational exigencies beyond the control of the generating
station.
15. In view of the decision of the APTEL`s judgment dated 22.11.2024 and in terms
of Regulation 14(3)(x) of the 2014 Tariff Regulations, the additional capital expenditure
of Rs. 454.49 lakh incurred towards procurement of 10 railway wagons for Kahalgaon
STPS Stage-I in FY 2014-15 is admissible. Accordingly, the additional capitalization of
Rs. 454.49 lakh is allowed, and the tariff allowed vide order dated 19.5.2024 in Petition
No. 294/GT/2020 read with corrigendum dated 15.6.2024 for Kahalgaon STPS Stage-
I for the period 2014-19 is revised in accordance with the 2014 Tariff Regulations in
subsequent paragraphs.
