Shri Hari Babu Vakada, CTUIL
Shri Yogeshwar, CTUIL
Shri Lashit Sharma, CTUIL
ORDER
The Petitioner, Sembcorp Energy India Limited (SEIL), has instituted the present
Petition seeking recovery of an amount of Rs. 2.26 crore towards interest from the
Respondent, Central Transmission Utility of India Limited (CTUIL), on account of delay in
reimbursement of excess transmission charges of Rs. 19.40 crore, which SEIL had paid
towards Bill of Supply for PoC Bill-1 for the months of October 2020 and November 2020.
The Petitioner has made the following prayers in the present Petition:
“(a) Direct CTUIL to pay Rs. 2.26 Crore (calculated till 08.02.2022) to SEIL towards
interest, for delay in reimbursement of excess transmission charges, paid towards Bill of
Supply for PoC Bill-1 for the month of October 2020 and November 2020
(b) Direct CTUIL to pay interest from 09.02.2022 including interest pendente lite till
actual payment of aforesaid interest amount; and
(c) Pass any other order or direction as this Commission may deem fit in light of facts
and circumstances of the present Petition.”
Order in Petition No. 315/MP/2022
Page 2

Submissions of Petitioner
2. The submissions made by the Petitioner, in support of the above prayers, are as
follows:
a) The Petitioner owns and operates two Thermal Power Projects of 1320 MW
each (Projects P1 and P2). For P1, SEIL has an untied capacity of 170 MW and a
tied-up Long-Term Access (LTA) quantum of 1070 MW.
b) Pursuant to a competitive bidding process, SEIL entered into a Power
Purchase Agreement (PPA) dated 1.4.2013 with the distribution licensees of the
undivided State of Andhra Pradesh for the supply of the 500 MW from Project P1 for
25 years. Post bifurcation of the erstwhile State of Andhra Pradesh, the said PPA
was suitably amended post-bifurcation to segregate capacities for the Andhra
Pradesh Discoms (APCPDCL, APEPDCL, APSPDCL, APNPDCL) and Telangana
Discoms (TSSPDCL, TSNPDCL), with further amendments for name change to
SEIL and the reallocation of contracted capacities.
c) SEIL also entered into a Power Sale Agreement (PSA) dated 18.02.2016
with Telangana Discoms (TS Discoms). Under the PPA and PSA, the respective
Discoms are responsible for payment or reimbursement of transmission charges
(from the injection point onwards) and RLDC/SLDC charges for their contracted
capacities. SEIL paid such charges upfront and sought reimbursement from the
Discoms on proof of payment.
d) SEIL has entered into Long-Term Access and Transmission Agreements
with PGCIL/CTUIL (BPTA dated 24.12.2010, Transmission Agreements dated
24.12.2010 and 23.11.2011, and supplementary agreements reducing quantum),
requiring SEIL to pay the transmission charges, with beneficiaries ultimately bearing
the charges once agreements are signed.
e) On 05.11.2020 and 07.12.2020, PGCIL issued PoC Bill-1 to SEIL for Project
P1 towards untied capacity (170 MW) and tied-up capacity (1070 MW), for the
months of October and November 2020, respectively, in terms of the Central
Electricity Regulatory Commission (Sharing of Inter- State Transmission Charges
and Losses) Regulations, 2010 (in short ‘the Sharing Regulations, 2010’). SEIL paid
these bills and sought reimbursement from AP and TS Discoms.
Order in Petition No. 315/MP/2022
Page 3

f) AP Discoms reimbursed the full amounts paid by SEIL. Telangana Discoms
unilaterally deducted Rs. 18.83 crore, anticipating a reduction in transmission
charges.
g) The Commission, vide Order No. L-1/250/2019/CERC dated 14.02.2021
(“Order dated 14.02.2021”) held that in terms of Regulation 22 of the Central
Electricity Regulatory Commission (Sharing of Inter- State Transmission Charges
and Losses) Regulations, 2020 (in short ‘the Sharing Regulations 2020’), bills for the
transition period of November-December 2020 onwards would be raised as per the
Sharing Regulations 2010, and from January 2021 onwards as per Regulations
2020.
h) This Commission, vide Order No. L-1/44/2010-CERC dated 21.02.2021
(“Order dated 21.02.2021”) notified the revised PoC rates for October 2020 to
November 2020 and directed that bills for the months of November 2020 and
December 2020 shall be based on these revised PoC rates under the Sharing
Regulations, 2010.
i) Pursuant to Order dated 21.02.2021, CTUIL vide Letter dated 22.02.2021
requested Regional Power Committees (RPCs) to issue the revised Regional
Transmission Accounts (RTA) for the month of October 2020 and November 2020.
j) On 23.02.2021, the Southern Regional Power Committee (SRPC) issued the
revised RTA for the months of October 2020 (issued vide SRPC Letter dated
04.11.2020) and November 2020 (issued vide SRPC Letter dated 04.12.2020),
based on the revised PoC rates notified by this Commission in Order dated
21.02.2021.
k) On 31.05.2021, CTUIL issued the Second Bill for the Billing period of
October 2020 to December 2020 to SEIL in terms of the Sharing Regulations, 2020.
CTUIL failed to credit Rs. 19.40 crore in excess transmission charges due to SEIL
as per revised RTAs dated 23.02.2021.
l) SEIL wrote to CTUIL on 02.06.2021, 30.07.2021, 21.09.2021, and 02.11.2021,
highlighting non-consideration of revised RTA credit (~Rs. 10 crore initially noted),
requesting revision of Bill-2, and noting financial prejudice as TS Discoms refused
reimbursement citing the revision.
Order in Petition No. 315/MP/2022
Page 4

m) On 01.12.2021, CTUIL issued the Second Bill for untied capacity (170 MW)
for April-June, 2021. On 02.12.2021, CTUIL issued three Supplementary Second
Bills for tied-up capacity (1070 MW) for the same period, explicitly showing Rs.
19.40 crore as receivable by SEIL (excess charges for October-November 2020),
thereby admitting the liability.
n) On 06.12.2021, SEIL requested direct remittance of Rs. 19.40 crore credit
into its account rather than adjustment in future bills. CTUIL did not comply with the
same.
(o) On 03.01.2022 and 04.01.2022, CTUIL raised Bill-1 and Bilateral Bill for
January 2022. On 07.01.2022, SEIL wrote an e-mail to CTUIL inter alia stating that
SEIL was in receipt of a credit amount of Rs. 19.40 crore towards Project P1
Transmission Charges (Bill-2) for the period from April 2021 to June 2021. On
06.12.2021, SEIL had written to CTUIL requesting that the credit amount be
remitted directly to SEIL’s account instead of being adjusted in monthly bills. On
03.01.2022, SEIL received Bill-1 for the untied quantum from SEIL’s Project P1 and
Project P2 and tied-up quantum for Project P2, amounting to Rs. 15.90 crore. As
there has been a delay in crediting the amount to SEIL, SEIL proposed to adjust
the transmission charges payable by SEIL for the billing month of January 2022.
Accordingly, SEIL sought CTUIL’s confirmation regarding whether Transmission
Charges payable for SEIL’s Project P2 for January 2022 can be adjusted against
the receivable amount qua SEIL Project P1, and whether SEIL is eligible for
availing TDS and rebate on the payable amount while adjusting the amounts
(which is Rs. 15.35 crore). After adjustment of transmission charges for January
2022, the balance amount payable by CTUIL is Rs. 4.05. crore.
(p) On 10.01.2022, CTUIL, in response to SEIL’s e-mail dated 07.01.2022
stating that the adjustment as requested may be made by SEIL against the
credit/receivables, subject to suitable communication and reconciliation. Upon
confirmation from CTUIL vide e-mail dated 10.01.2022, the credit amount of Rs.
19.40 crore due in terms of the revised RTA for October 2020 and November 2020,
was adjusted by CTUIL by 08.02.2022 in the subsequent bills
(q) On 11.02.2022, SEIL wrote to CTUIL, inter-alia stating that:
i. In terms of the Sharing Regulations 2020, CTUIL should have issued
a credit amount of Rs. 19.40 crore, on account of revision in RTA through
Bill-2 issued on 31.05.2021. However, the same was credited vide
Order in Petition No. 315/MP/2022
Page 5

Supplementary Bill-2 dated 02.12.2021 for the period of April 2021 to June
2021.
ii. SEIL had requested CTUIL for remittance of the credit amount to
SEIL vide letter dated 06.12.2021.
iii. As CTUIL did not respond to the said communication, SEIL proposed
an adjustment of the credit amount in the subsequent monthly bills vide e-
mail dated 07.01.2022.
iv. Upon confirmation from CTUIL vide email dated 10.01.2022, the said
credit amount was adjusted by 08.02.2022 in the subsequent bills issued by
CTUIL to SEIL towards Project P1 and Project P2.
v. Accordingly, there has been a delay on the part of CTUIL in returning
the credit amount of Rs. 19.40 crore from 01.06.2021 to 08.02.2022.
vi. Accordingly, SEIL issued a debit note towards interest/Late Payment
Surcharge amounting to Rs. 2,26,33,048/- for the delayed period computed
on the basis of LPS payment methodology mentioned in the Sharing
Regulations 2020.
In view of the above, CTUIL was requested to arrange for remittance of
interest/LPS of Rs. 2,26,33,048/-.
(r) On 15.02.2022, SEIL raised an invoice towards delay in returning excess
transmission charges amount paid by SEIL for the months of October 2020 and
November 2020 for the LTA quantum of 1070 MW. CTUIL was requested to accept
the invoice and make the payment.
(s) On 28.02.2022, CTUIL, in response to SEIL’s e-mail dated 15.02.2022, inter
alia stated that billing has been done as per the extant CERC Regulations, which do
not include any provision for such a surcharge claim. Accordingly, SEIL’s claim was
unacceptable. Further, the necessary credit amount has already been received and
adjusted by SEIL.
(t) On 04.04.2022, SEIL wrote to CTUIL and stated that to date, the interest
amount had not been remitted by CTUIL to SEIL. Accordingly, CTUIL was requested
to pay the interest amount of Rs. 2,26,33,048/- within 15 days. In the event of
CTUIL’s failure to release the aforesaid amount, SEIL would be constrained to
initiate appropriate legal action, and such failure would be construed as non-
compliance with the relevant Regulations and other applicable laws.
Order in Petition No. 315/MP/2022
Page 6

(u) CTUIL was under a contractual and statutory obligation to issue Bills and
adjust the credit amount on account of a revision in RTA through Bill-2 issued on
31.05.2021, in terms of the Sharing Regulations, 2020. Since CTUIL has delayed in
reimbursing/adjusting the credit amount for the months of October 2020 and
November 2020, CTUIL is liable to pay the interest on the delayed reimbursement of
the excess transmission charges paid by SEIL, amounting to Rs. 2.26 crore,
calculated as per the LPS provisions of the Sharing Regulations 2020.
(v) SEIL ought to be compensated and restituted for the delay in
reimbursement/refund/adjustment of excess transmission charges paid to CTUIL.
The Hon`ble Supreme Court in State of Rajasthan vs. J.K Synthetics Ltd.
[reported as (2011) 12 SCC 518] categorically held that even if there is no
provision, the court can direct payment of interest by way of restitution. This principle
was also upheld by the Hon`ble Madras High Court in S. Parameswaran vs. Union
of India and Another [reported as 2006 SCC On Line Mad 455] wherein the
Hon`ble Madras High Court reiterated the decision of the Hon`ble Supreme Court in
Sandvik Asia Ltd. vs. Commissioner of Income Tax I, Pune & Ors. Reported as
[(2006) 2 SCC 508].
(w) Further, even under equity, SEIL is to be granted compensation as it has
established that CTUIL had breached the Sharing Regulations 2020 and ought to
have reimbursed the excess transmission charges earlier to SEIL. In such a
scenario, this Commission ought to direct CTUIL to pay interest to SEIL. This
position has been upheld by the Hon`ble Supreme Court in the case of South
Eastern Coalfields Ltd. vs. State of M.P & Ors. [Reported as (2003) 8 SCC 648].
(x) SEIL been reimbursed the excess transmission charges of Rs. 19.40 crore
at the proper time, it would have been able to utilise the same. Accordingly, SEIL
was not only deprived of the usage of Rs. 19.40 crore but also denied the
opportunity to earn any interest which it would have earned had the same been put
into any instrument/invested. The Hon`ble Supreme Court in Central Bank of India
vs. Ravindra & Ors. [reported as (2002) 1 SCC 637] elaborately laid out the
meaning of interest. The Hon`ble Supreme Court in the case of Indian Council of
Enviro-Legal Action vs. Union of India & Ors. [reported as 2011 (8) SCC 161]
emphasised the importance of the time value of money.
(y) The Commission has the power to direct CTUIL to pay interest to SEIL in
terms of the BCD Procedure issued by CTUIL. Further, without prejudice, the
Order in Petition No. 315/MP/2022
Page 7

Commission has the power to issue directions in exercise of its general regulatory
powers under Section 79 of the Electricity Act, 2003. This position stands confirmed
in terms of the Hon`ble Supreme Court Judgment in Energy Watchdog vs. CERC &
Ors. [Reported as (2017) 14 SCC 80].
(z) In light of the foregoing submissions, the Commission may direct CTUIL to
pay the interest due and payable on account of the delay in reimbursement of the
admitted credit amount of Rs. 19.40 crore, towards Bills of Supply for the months of
October 2020 and November 2020, expeditiously.
Hearing on 14.03.2023
3. The Petition was admitted on 14.3.2023, and notices were issued to the
Respondent to file its reply. Vide Record of Proceedings for the hearing dated 14.3.2026
CTUIL was directed to clarify when CTUIL raised the bill in terms of the Commission`s
order dated 21.02.2021, and the reason for the delay in raising the same.
Submissions of Respondent, CTUIL
4. CTUIL, vide affidavit dated 06.06.2023, has submitted as under:
a) On 21.02.2021, this Commission issued an Order determining the PoC rates
for the period October 2020 and November 2020. Immediately after the passing of
the Order dated 21.02.2021, CTUIL vide its letter dated 22.02.2021 requested all
RPCs to issue a revision to the RTA for the months of October 2020 and November
2020 as per the PoC rates issued for the months of October 2020 and November
2020.
b) On 23.02.2021, 24.02.2021, 25.02.2021, 02.07.2021 and 01.10.2021, the
SRPC, ERPC, NERPC, NRPC and WRPC, respectively, issued the revised RTA for
the months of October 2020 and November 2020 on the basis of PoC rates issued
by the Commission in Order dated 21.02.2021. The last RTA was published by
WRPC on 01.10.2021, and it is only after 01.10.2021 that CTUIL could have issued
the adjustment with reference to the revised RTAs.
c) In terms of Regulation 15 of the Sharing Regulations, 2020, the ISTS
transmission charges and losses are billed to the Designated ISTS Customers
(DICs) and, upon collection, are disbursed by CTUIL to the transmission licensees.
Order in Petition No. 315/MP/2022
Page 8

In this scheme of billing, collection, and disbursement, the regulatory mandate is that
the YTCs of ISTS licensees are fully and exactly recovered. Each RPC Secretariat
issues RTA on a monthly basis, in which transmission charges for the DICs under its
region are published using the PoC slab rates approved by this Commission. The
differential amount due to a revision in transmission charges for a billing period
should be billed by CTUIL to DICs in proportion to their first bill of the relevant
month. The first bill itself is getting revised as per the revised RTAs issued by the
respective RPCs. Thus, in order to take into account the impact of the revised
transmission charges, the revised first bill for all the DICs is needed, which can only
be achieved after receipt of all the revised RTAs.
d) As WRPC issued its revised RTA received only on 01.10.2021, the
differential billing of all the regions has been calculated and billed in the immediate
second bill, i.e., Second bill for April 2021 to June 2021, raised in December 2021 as
per Regulation 15 of the Sharing Regulations, 2020.
e) CTUIL has acted in accordance with the Sharing Regulations (as amended)
and the standard procedure adopted by CTUIL in every case involving RTA revision.
The above claim of the Petitioner, if accepted, would create chaos in settling the
bills/transmission charges by CTUIL and may lead to errors/mismatches in the
recovery of transmission charges of the ISTS licensees to the full & exact.
f) There is no provision in the Sharing Regulations providing for interest to be paid by
CTUIL to the DICs. The Petitioner has based its claim on equity and the basis of
certain judgments, which are not relevant to the present case. Sharing Regulations
provide for a Late Payment Surcharge (LPS) to be levied in the event of delayed
payment of transmission charges by DICs. In this regard, reliance has been placed
on Clause 3.4 of BCD Procedure under Sharing Regulations, 2010, read with
Regulation 59 of the Tariff Regulations, 2019, which provides for LPS. Similarly,
Regulation 18 of the Sharing Regulations, 2020 provides a provision for the Late
Payment Surcharge (LPS). Later, the Ministry of Power notified the Electricity (Late
Payment Surcharge and Related Matters) Rules, 2022, which came into effect from
03.06.2022
g) In such a scenario, the judgments relied upon by the Petitioner to the effect
that ‘if the Statute is silent on payment of interest then interest can be awarded’ has
no application to the present case as the Regulations do provide for interest/LPS in
Order in Petition No. 315/MP/2022
Page 9

certain scenario and has consciously not provided for payment of any interest/LPS in
a case like the present case.
h) Further, CTUIL has a revenue-neutral role, and it has also not made any
default and has fulfilled all its statutory responsibilities in terms of the Sharing
Regulations. Therefore, CTUIL, in its capacity, cannot be saddled with any liability
for payment of interest.
Submissions of Petitioner
5. The Petitioner, vide its rejoinder dated 06.07.2023, mainly has submitted as below:
a) CTUIL’s contention that adjustment is done only after revised RTAs are
issued by all concerned Regional Power Committees is incorrect and ought to be
rejected. CTUIL is obligated to raise the transmission bills in accordance with the
timelines specified under the respective Regulations.
b) Pertinently, prior to the present reply filed by CTUIL, CTUIL did not adopt a
position that RTAs of all the regions were not finalised and wilfully defaulted in
crediting the amount of Rs. 19.40 crore, which remains unpaid/ unadjusted till
08.02.2022. CTUIL is now setting up a completely new case, contending that Bill-2 is
raised after receipt of RTAs from all the regions, which is nothing but an
afterthought.
(c) It is trite law that Regulations framed by the Commission are binding on the
parties, being in the nature of delegated legislation. CTUIL’s contention that it could
have issued Bill-2 only after the receipt of all the RTAs by the other respective RPCs
is arbitrary and ought to be rejected because (i) the RTA (for the DICs) is prepared
by the Secretariat of the respective RPC inter alia basis the DIC-wise transmission
charges for the billing month, as furnished by the Implementing Agency, (ii) The
RPC is to issue the RTA by the end of the month following the billing period, and (iii)
In case of under-recovery or over-recovery due to a revision in transmission
charges, the CTUIL bills DICs the amount in proportion to their first bill in the
relevant billing month. Therefore, the Regulations do not mandate receipt of all the
revised RTAs from the concerned RPCs for issuance of Bill-2 qua adjustment in
variations on the concerned DIC.
(d) Even otherwise and without prejudice to the foregoing submissions, SEIL
cannot be penalised for the delay in issuance of the revised RTA by the WRPC.
Order in Petition No. 315/MP/2022
Page 10

SEIL cannot be denied payment on the basis of failure by CTUIL and WRPC to
issue the revised RTAs and Bills within the stipulated timelines.
(e) Raising of Bill 2 within the prescribed timelines based on the RTA issued by the
concerned RPC and disbursement of the same to the ISTS licensees has no nexus
with the issuance of RTAs by other RPCs. Therefore, CTUIL’s contention that in
order to take into account the impact of the revised transmission charges, the
revised first bill of all DICs is needed, which can only be achieved after the receipt of
all the revised RTAs, ought not be countenanced.
(f) If the contentions advanced by CTUIL are accepted, that Bill 2 is raised only
after the RTAs for all the regions are received, it would make the timelines specified
in the Regulations redundant. Further, without prejudice, if RTAs for all regions were
required as CTUIL is a revenue-neutral body, there would be no need for Regulation
18 of the Sharing Regulations 2020, which provides for the levy of LPS for delay in
making payment to CTUIL. This provision has been inserted to ensure that CTUIL
can raise and disburse amounts in accordance with the prescribed timelines and will
not suffer any financial loss if there is any delay in payment by a DIC. Even
otherwise, there has been a delay of approximately 1 year on the part of CTUIL in
returning the credit of Rs. 19.40 crore, on account of revision in RTA for October
2020 and November 2020, from 23.02.2021 (i.e., when SRPC revised the RTA) to
08.02.2022.
(g) It is settled law that even if there is no provision, the court can direct
payment of interest by way of restitution, as held by the Hon`ble Supreme Court in
the State of Rajasthan v. J.K Synthetics Ltd. [(2011) 12 SCC 518] and South
Eastern Coalfields Ltd. vs. State of M.P & Ors. [Reported as (2003) 8 SCC 648].
(h) As per Regulation 18 of the Sharing Regulations 2020, SEIL is liable to pay
the interest on the delayed payment of transmission charges. However, depriving
SEIL of compensation/interest for delayed reimbursement/adjustment of excess
transmission charges by CTUIL would be grossly unfair and contrary to the
principles of equity.
(i) CTUIL, having failed to issue the Bills within the prescribed timelines under
the Sharing Regulations, cannot be permitted to take advantage of its own wrong
merely on the ground that it’s a neutral entity and thus, cannot be exonerated from
its liability to pay interest.
Order in Petition No. 315/MP/2022
Page 11

Hearing on 11.10.2023
6. Relevant extract of the RoP of hearing dated 11.10.2023 is as under:
“……….
3. After hearing the learned counsel for the Petitioner and the Respondent CTUIL, the
Commission deemed it appropriate to take into account the views of RPCs, particularly
NRPC and WRPC, in the context of delay on their part in issuing the revised RTAs for the
months of October & November, 2020. Accordingly, the Commission ordered as under:
(a) The Petitioner to implead WRPC, NRPC, SRPC, NERPC, and ERPC to the Petition
and file a revised memo of parties within a week; and
(b) The Petitioner to also serve a copy of the Petition to the above RPCs, who shall file
their replies/comments, specifically on the aspect of delay in issuance of revised RTAs for
the months of October & November 2020, after the issuance of the revised PoC rates by
the Commission by order dated 21.2.2021, within three weeks after serving copy of the
same to the Petitioner, who may file its rejoinder within three weeks thereafter.
………………………”
Submission of Petitioner
7. The Petitioner vide reply dated 18.10.2023 has filed “Amended Memo of Parties”
impleading Western Regional Power Committee (WRPC), Northern Regional Power
Committee (NRPC), Southern Region Power Committee (SRPC), North Eastern Regional
Power Committee (NERPC), and Easter Regional Power Committee (ERPC) as parties to
the present Petition.
Submission of Respondent NRPC
8. The Respondent NRPC, vide reply dated 31.10.2023, has submitted as below:
a) Regulation 10 of the Sharing Regulations 2010 provides for the preparation
of Monthly Transmission Accounts by NRPC on the basis of data to be received
from the Implementing Agency in respect of "Approved withdrawal/Injection (MW),
Zonal Point of Connection Charge (Rs/MW/month) and Approved Additional
Medium-Term Withdrawal/Injection (MW)". Revision of the Monthly Transmission
Account is merely the re-issuance of the Monthly Transmission Account with revised
input data.
b) In view of the above provisions, energy accounting software used by NRPC
was designed, incorporating relevant provisions of the Sharing Regulations 2010, to
Order in Petition No. 315/MP/2022
Page 12

prepare the Monthly Transmission Account, viz. Regional Transmission Account
(RTA) for Dedicated ISTS Customers of Northern Region using input data furnished
by the Implementing Agency in a specified format without any further manual
interventions in processing of the said account on a monthly basis. Accordingly, RTA
was prepared by NRPC on a regular basis upon receipt of input data from the
Implementing Agency for a fresh RTA and for any revision thereof.
c) As regard to the revision in RTA for the months of October 2020 and
November 2020 which were issued by NRPC on 02.07.2021, the input data in the
prescribed format was received from Implementing Agency vide its email dated
01.07.2021, subsequently the revisions of RTA for the month of October and
November 2020 were issued immediately on the next day after receipt of input data
from implementing agency, i.e. on 02.07.2021.
Submission of Respondent WRPC
9. The Respondent WRPC vide its reply, filed on 31.10.2023, has submitted similar
submission as submitted by NRPC and has additionally submitted that the input data in
the format for RTA revision of October and November 2020 was received from
Implementing Agency vide their email dated 30.09.2021 and the revisions of RTA
accounts for the month of October and November 2020, were issued immediately on the
next day after receipt of input data from implementing agency.
Submission of Respondent ERPC
10. The Respondent, ERPC vide reply dated 22.02.2024, has submitted that after
issuance of the revised PoC rates for the month of October and November 2020 by the
Commission through its order dated 21.02.2021, ERPC issued the revised RTA for the
said months on 24.02.2021. ERPC further submitted that in light of ERPC’s reply, the
Commission may advise and issue directions as deemed fit.
Order in Petition No. 315/MP/2022
Page 13

Hearing on 02.07.2025
11. During the course, the learned counsels for the parties argued at length, and after

32. In light of the above factual sequence and the regulatory framework, we find that
the alleged delay in adjustment cannot be attributed to any regulatory violation, wilful
default, or actionable lapse on the part of CTUIL. The operative mechanism under the
Sharing Regulations 2020, particularly Regulations 14, 15(2), and 20, casts CTUIL in the
role of a revenue-neutral conduit, tasked with collecting transmission charges strictly on
the basis of finalised RTAs furnished by the RPCs and disbursing the same in full to ISTS
licensees without retaining any surplus. Unilateral refunds or piecemeal adjustments prior
to receipt of comprehensive RTAs from all RPCs would precipitate systemic mismatches.
While the Petitioner might receive a credit (as an over-payer under revised SRPC RTA),
corresponding under-payers or levy-liable DICs in other regions (per NRPC/WRPC RTAs)
would remain unsettled, disrupting the PoC mechanism's foundational principle of full and
exact yearly recovery of transmission charges across the national grid.
33. CTUIL's sequenced handling, provisional billing under Regulation 14, Second Bill
issuance per the quarterly timeline in Regulation 15(2), prompt request to RPCs vide letter
dated 22.02.2021, and eventual adjustment via Supplementary Second Bills once all
RTAs were aligned fully, accords with the statutory mandate. The inherent
interdependence on multiple RPCs for RTA revisions, coupled with documented delays in
input data from implementing agencies (as explained by NRPC and WRPC), underscores

the fact that the timeline was circumscribed not by CTUIL's indiscretion but by the
collective settlement architecture of the inter-State transmission system.
34. In light of the foregoing, the delay in adjustment is not attributable to any regulatory
violation or default by CTUIL, and CTUIL acted in accordance with the Sharing
Regulations 2020. Thus, considering the above discussions, we are of the view that
CTUIL could not have revised the bills prior to the issuance of RTAs by all RPCs, and the
delay in providing the adjustment to the excess transmission charges cannot be attributed
to CTUIL.
B. In view of the answer to A, whether CTUIL can be held liable to pay
interest to the Petitioner towards the delayed adjustment of the excess

35. Although we have answered the sub-issue A in the negative, we do find it
appropriate to examine whether any liability of interest can still be fastened upon CTUIL

36. Regulation 18 of the Sharing Regulations, 2020, which was in effect from
01.11.2021 till 01.10.2023 (effective date of the First Amendment), provided as under:
“18. Late Payment Surcharge
Notwithstanding any provision to the contrary in the applicable Tariff Regulations or
Transmission Service Agreement under tariff based competitive bidding, in case the
payment of any bill for charges payable under these regulations is delayed by a DIC,
beyond the due date, a late payment surcharge at the rate of 1.50% per month shall be
payable by the concerned DIC.”
The aforesaid Regulation was, thereafter, amended vide First Amendment, which
came into effect from 01.10.2023, and provides as under:
“18. Late payment surcharge shall be payable by the concerned DIC as per the LPS Rules
in case the payment of any bill for charges payable under these Regulations is delayed by
a DIC, beyond the due date.”

It is apparent from the above that, under the Sharing Regulations, the Late Payment
Surcharge (LPS) is applicable to the concerned DIC only in the event of a delay in
payment of the charges beyond the due date. The amended Regulation 18 aligns LPS
with the LPS Rules, 2022, and applies only to DIC payment delays.
37. We note that neither the Sharing Regulations 2020 nor the LPS Rule, 2022
provides for payment of any interest on the excess payments, delayed adjustments, or
refunds to DICs or other entities. On the contrary, the regulations only provide for raising
the bill for under-recovery or over-recovery of any amount on account of revision in
transmission charges through the Second Bill on DICs. No provisions under the Sharing

entity, as claimed by the Petitioner, against the transmission charges for any billing
period.

41. The reliance placed by SEIL on South Eastern Coalfields Ltd. Vs. State of M.P. &
Ors. (2003) 8 SCC 648 and other judicial precedents to claim interest on delayed
reimbursement of excess transmission charges is wholly misplaced and legally
unsustainable, as the said judgments arise from materially distinct factual and legal
contexts involving wrongful retention of money or unjust enrichment, or undue financial
advantage gained by one party at the expense of another, circumstances entirely absent
here. The doctrine of restitution as recognised in South Eastern Coalfields, State of
Rajasthan v. J.K. Synthetics Ltd., Sandvik Asia Ltd., and S Parameswaran, applies only
where a party has wrongfully retained money or derived an undue financial benefit,
whereas in the instant matter the collection and adjustment of transmission charges is

governed by a comprehensive statutory and regulatory framework under the Sharing

solely for the collection and disbursement of transmission charges without deriving any
financial gain. The excess amount paid by SEIL was not wrongfully retained by CTUIL but
arose due to system-wide settlement adjustments contingent upon revision of RTAs by
multiple RPCs, which is intrinsic to the collective billing architecture of the inter-State
transmission system.
42. None of the principles laid down by the above precedents finds application in the
instant matter. The so-called "excess" of Rs. 19.40 crore did not arise from any wrongful
appropriation or retention by CTUIL but was an inevitable outcome of the system-wide
revision of RTAs across multiple RPCs, a process intrinsic to the collective, PoC-based
billing architecture of the inter-State transmission system. CTUIL, positioned as a
revenue-neutral intermediary under the Sharing Regulations, does not derive any financial
gain from collections; rather, it merely aggregates charges per finalised RTAs and
disburses them in full to ISTS licensees. The timeline for adjustment was dictated not by
CTUIL's volition but by the sequential receipt of revised RTAs (SRPC on 23.02.2021,
NRPC on 02.07.2021, WRPC on 01.10.2021), ensuring no unilateral refunds disrupt the
delicate balance of national grid charge recovery. Equating this regulated settlement
process to "wrongful retention" stretches the doctrine of restitution beyond recognition.
43. Further, the applicable regulations expressly provide for the levy of LPS in cases of
delayed payment by DICs while consciously omitting any provision for payment of interest
on delayed refund or adjustment, thereby reflecting clear legislative and regulatory intent
that cannot be overridden by equitable doctrines.

44. The Supreme Court in CIT v. Gujarat Fluoro Chemicals Ltd. (2013) has
categorically clarified that Sandvik Asia does not lay down a general principle mandating
payment of interest in the absence of statutory provision but is confined to its tax refund
context, and in Union of India v. Watkins Mayor & Co. (AIR 1966 SC 275), it has been
held that interest is payable only when supported by statute, contract, or recognised
equitable principle. Likewise, Central Bank of India v. Ravindra and Indian Council for
Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India merely explain the conceptual framework of interest
and restitution and do not create an independent enforceable right to claim interest in
regulated tariff matters. Accordingly, in the absence of any express provision under the
Sharing Regulations, BCD Procedure, or contractual framework providing for payment of
interest on transmission charge adjustments, SEIL’s claim for interest is untenable both in
law and in regulatory practice.
45. On the other hand, the facts of the present case attract the ratio laid down in NTPC
v. MPSEB, (2011) 15 SCC 580. In the said case, the beneficiaries of NTPC had claimed
interest on the differential (excess) amounts between the pre-existing tariff, which
continued until this final determination, and the tariff finally determined by the
Commission, which NTPC adjusted in favour of beneficiaries in their subsequent bills.
APTEL allowed this interest on the differential amounts on the grounds of justice, equity
and fair play. The Hon’ble Supreme Court, however, ruled that APTEL could not have
brought in either the principle of justice, equity or fair play or that of restitution to award
the interest in the said case. It noted that it was not the case that the beneficiaries were
made to pay the excess tariff at the instance of NTPC through force, coercion or threat,
and while there was a delay in the process of determination of tariff, NTPC was not in any
way responsible. The tariff charged by NTPC in the interregnum was permitted under the
Commission's notification, and it could not be said that NTPC retained the excess amount
in an unjust manner or to call it unjust enrichment on the part of NTPC. Since the terms of

based on provisional RTAs utilising the PoC rates of July to September 2020. The PoC

and immediately thereafter, CTU requested that all RPCs issue the revised RTAs.

Regulations nor the BCD Procedure provide for payment of interest on the excess amount

under the Sharing Regulations. In such circumstances, CTUIL cannot be held liable to

ORDER
SBSR Power Cleantech Eleven Private Limited (hereinafter referred to as
“SBSR/Petitioner”) (now known as Adani Solar Jaisalmer Two Private Limited) has
filed the instant Interlocutory Application (hereinafter referred to as “IA”) seeking
direction upon the Respondent No. 1 i.e., Solar Energy Corporation of India Limited
(hereinafter referred to as “SECI”) to accept the request of the Petitioner to replace
the existing Performance Bank Guarantee bearing No. 2158001515321 with a new
Performance Bank Guarantee to be furnished by the said applicant/ petitioner,
amongst other reliefs.
2. The Petitioner has made the following prayers in the IA:
a. Direct SECI to accept and acknowledge the new Performance Bank
Guarantee (PBG) bearing No. 03189GPCA2525402 dated 16.09.2025
(with Canara Bank Limited), for all purposes under the PPA dated
20.08.2019;
b. Consequently, direct SECI to return the Performance Bank Guarantee
with Bank of Baroda being BG no. 2158IGP001515321 to Petitioner;
c. Direct SECI to allow and permit the assignment of the Petitioner’s rights
and obligations under Article 15.1 of the PPA (to the extent of present
PPA capacity of 150 MW) in favour of Canara Bank Limited; and
d. Pass any other order or order(s) as this Hon’ble Commission may deem
fit and proper in the facts and circumstances of the present case.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Order in IA No. 126/2025 In Petition No. 192/MP/2021 Page 2 of 4

3. It is stated that Petition No. 192/MP/2021 has been filed by the Petitioner inter
alia seeking a direction that it is not liable to pay any liquidated damages or other
penalties corresponding to reduced capacity of 150 MW which stands commissioned
under the Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) and the short-closed balance capacity
of 150 MW shelved out of PPA on account of the delay which are not attributable to
the Petitioner for both capacities. In the Petition, the Petitioner has also sought relief
for the return of the Performance Bank Guarantee(s) furnished to the Respondent,
SECI. The Pleadings and arguments in the Petition have already been concluded,
and the order was reserved by the Commission on 7.7.2025.
4. The Performance Bank Guarantee furnished by the Petitioner, which is a part
of the Petition, has been issued by the Bank of Baroda. However, in the meantime,
Petitioner has now entered into an arrangement with a new Bank, namely Canara
Bank, and accordingly, it seeks to replace the earlier Performance Bank Guarantee
bearing No. 2158IGP001515321 (issued by Bank of Baroda) with a new
Performance Bank Guarantee issued by Canara Bank, bearing No.
03189GPCA2525402 in favour of SECI. The Petitioner, vide its communication dated
23.9.2025, requested SECI to accept the new Performance Bank Guarantee and
return the old one. However, since the Petition was pending and there was a specific
prayer qua the earlier Performance Bank Guarantee, SECI expressed its difficulty
towards replacing the earlier Performance Bank Guarantee.
5. The IA was listed for hearing on 12.2.2026. During the hearing, the learned
counsel for the Petitioner, while reiterating the submissions made in the IA, pointed
out that the Performance Bank Guarantee issued by Bank of Baroda was valid only
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Order in IA No. 126/2025 In Petition No. 192/MP/2021 Page 3 of 4

up to 15.2.2026, and since the final order in the Petition was yet to be passed, the
Petitioner should be allowed to replace this earlier Performance Bank Guarantee
with the new one.
6. However, in view of the observation of the Commission that the order in the
Petition will be passed before 15.2.2026, the learned counsel fairly stated that, in
that case, the Petitioner does not wish to pursue the reliefs prayed for in the IA.
Subsequently, on 12.2.2026 itself, a common order was passed in Petition Nos.
192/MP/2021 and 235/MP/2023. Accordingly, as stated by the learned counsel for
the Petitioner, the ground for which the IA was moved no longer survives. Thus, the
IA is disposed of as such.
7. IA No.126/2025 in Petition No. 192/MP/2021 is disposed of in terms of the
above.

ORDER
The Petitioner, SLS Power Corporation Limited, has filed the present petition
seeking the following relief(s):
a) Admit the Present Petition;
b) Declare that the action of Respondent No. 1 in rejecting the applications for grant of
short term inter-state open access by the Respondent No. 1 for the capacity of 22 MW
is illegal and contrary to the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Open Access
in Inter-State Transmission) Regulations 2008 and the provisions of the Electricity Act,
2003;
c) Direct the Respondent No. 1 to grant NOC to the Petitioner for sale of power on the
power exchange in terms of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Open
Access in Inter-State Transmission) Regulations 2008 with the exception of there being
any bonafide constraints in the transmission system of Respondent No. 3-
TSTRANSCO which Respondent No. 4 certifies in advance and not otherwise;
d) Pass ad interim orders directing the Respondent No. 1 to grant NOC to the Petitioner
for sale of power on the power exchange in terms of the Central Electricity Regulatory
Commission (Open Access in Inter-State Transmission) Regulations 2008 for the
period from December 2023 onwards unless there are any bonafide constraints in the
transmission system of Respondent No. 3- TSTRANSCO which Respondent No. 4
certifies in advance and not otherwise;
e) Grant necessary compensation to the Petitioner for the losses suffered by it due to non-
grant of NOC by the Respondent No. 1; and
f) Pass such other order or orders as this Hon'ble Court deems fit and proper in the
interest of justice.
2. The Petitioner, a company incorporated under the provisions of the Companies
Act, 1956, has established a 24 MW small hydro power project at Dummaguden
Village and Mandal in Khammam District, Telangana, on the left flank of a branch of
the Godavari River. The generating station achieved synchronization on 9.12.2013
and was declared under commercial operation on 26.1.2014. The Petitioner has been
supplying power through Inter-State Short Term Open Access (STOA) to the Indian
Energy Exchange (IEX) through collective transactions via a trading licensee.
Order in Petition No.385/MP/2023 Page 2 of 4

3. In accordance with Regulation 8 of the Open Access Regulations, 2008 (as
amended by the 5th Amendment, 2018), the Petitioner is required to obtain a ‘No
Objection Certificate’ (NOC) from the concerned State Load Despatch Centre (SLDC)
for availing the STOA. The applications filed by the Petitioner for the period from
January to May 2023 were rejected by Telangana State Load Despatch Centre
(TSLDC) (Respondent No. 1) on the ground of non-availability of distribution corridor.
Aggrieved thereby, the Petitioner approached the Hon’ble High Court of Telangana,
which, by interim orders, directed the Respondents to consider the applications and
grant open access, pursuant to which concurrence was granted up to August 2023.
4. Thereafter, further applications dated 7.5.2023 and 8.6.2023 for the months of
July, August and September 2023 were rejected citing load growth and corridor
constraints. The Petitioner challenged the same in W.P. No. 15975 of 2023, and by
order dated 23.6.2023, the Hon`ble High Court directed issuance of NOC for the
months of July and August 2023. Subsequently, applications dated 11.8.2023 and
12.8.2023 for the months of September, October, and November 2023, were rejected
on 14.8.2023 and 16.8.2023 on the ground of intra-State corridor congestion. The
Petitioner again approached the Hon`ble High Court in W.P. No. 23063 of 2023,
wherein, by order dated 22.8.2023, directions were issued for grant of NOC for the
said period. The applications for December 2023, January 2024 and February 2024,
were also rejected on 3.11.2023 on similar grounds.
5. In the aforesaid background, the Petitioner has filed present Petition. The
matter was listed for admission on 19.1.2024 and admitted on 6.3.2024, with directions
to the Respondents to file their replies. However, the Respondents failed to file any
reply. Thereafter, on 1.5.2024, the learned senior counsel for the Petitioner sought
Order in Petition No.385/MP/2023 Page 3 of 4

leave to effect service of dasti notice upon the Respondents. However, no reply has
been filed till date and the matter has not seen any further progress.
Hearing dated 24.2.2026
6. When the matter was taken up for hearing on 24.2.2026, the learned counsel
for the Petitioner, on instructions, sought permission to withdraw the present Petition.
The learned counsel for the Respondents also did not oppose the Petitioner’s request
for withdrawal of the Petition.
7. Considering the submissions of the learned counsels for the parties, the present
Petition is disposed of as ‘withdrawn’.
8. Accordingly, Petition No. 385/MP/2023 is disposed of as ‘withdrawn’.
Sd/- sd/- sd/-

ORDER
The Petitioner, Greennsure Trading Private Limited (hereinafter referred to as
‘the Petitioner’), incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013, read with Regulation 6
of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Procedure, Terms and Conditions
for the Grant of Trading Licence and other related matters) Regulations, 2020
(hereinafter referred to as “the Trading Licence Regulations”), amended from time to
time, has filed the present Petition for the grant of a Category ‘V’ trading licence for
inter-State trading in electricity in all over India.
Order in Petition No. 46/TD/2026
Page 1 of 6

2. In accordance with sub-Section (2) of Section 15 of the Act read with Clause
(4) of Regulation 6 of the Trading Licence Regulations, notices were published by the
Petitioner on 27.12.2025 in the ‘Indian Express’ (Lucknow, Kolkata, Jaipur, Delhi and
Chandigarh and throughout all the States in North-eastern region of India editions), in
the ‘Financial Express’ (Pune, Mumbai, Lucknow, Kochi, Hyderabad, Delhi, Chennai,
Chandigarh, Bengaluru and Pune editions) and in the E-newspaper of Indian Express
(Belagavi, Bangaluru, Bhubaneshwar, Chennai, Coimbatore, Dharmapuri, Hubbali,
Hyderabad, Kalaburagi, Kuchi, Kozhikode, Maduri, Nagapattinam, Sambalpur,
Shivamogga, Thiruvananthapuram, Tiruchy, Tirunelveli, Vellore, Vijayawada,
Villupuram, Visakhapatnam). The Petitioner has submitted that no objections have
been received in response to the public notices.
3. In accordance with Regulation 3(3) of the Trading Licence Regulations, a
person applying for a Category 'V' trading licence should have a net worth of Rs. Two
crores and should have maintained a minimum current ratio and liquidity ratio of 1:1
as on the date of the Audited Special Balance Sheet accompanying the application.
As per the Audited Balance Sheet submitted by the Petitioner as on 15.12.2025, the
Petitioner possesses the required net worth and current ratio for the grant of a
Category 'V' trading licence. The Commission, vide its order dated 17.2.2026,
concluded that the Petitioner is prima facie qualified for the grant of a Category “V”
licence for inter-State trading in electricity.
4. On the above consideration, the Commission, vide its order dated 17.2.2026,
had proposed to grant a Category 'V' inter-State trading licence to the Petitioner. The
relevant portions of the said order dated 17.2.2026 are extracted as under:
Order in Petition No. 46/TD/2026
Page 2 of 6

“13. In accordance with Clause (2) of Regulation 3 of the Trading Licence
Regulations, the Petitioner should have at least one full-time professional
possessing qualifications and experience in power system operation and the
commercial aspects of power transfer, including finance, commerce and
accounts. With regard to full-time professionals, the Petitioner vide its affidavit
dated 10.2.2026 has submitted that Mr. Mageswaran. N, (Director), MBA
(Marketing), B.Tech. (Energy and Environmental Engineering) has 11 years’
experience in Business Development and possess strong knowledge on
renewable power, open access power facilitation, solar rooftop power
facilitation, Energy auditing, regulatory & Policy infrastructure, etc. and Mr.
Prasanna K., graduate from the Anna University with Degree of Master of
Business Administration (Finance) has more than five years’ experience in the
finance sector. Accordingly, as per the information submitted by the Petitioner,
it fulfils the requirements of Clause (2) of Regulation 3 of the Trading Licence
Regulations.
14. On consideration of the above facts, after a preliminary examination, we
find that the Petitioner meets the requirements as specified in the Trading
Licence Regulations for the grant of a Category 'V' trading licence. In view
thereof, the Commission proposes to grant a Category 'V' trading licence to the
Petitioner. We direct that a notice under Clause (a) of Sub-section (5) of Section
15 of the Act be issued inviting further suggestions or objections to the proposal
of the Commission.”
5. In line with the above-mentioned order dated 17.2.2026, notice under Clause
(a) of sub-Section (5) of Section 15 of the Act was published in all editions of the Indian
Express (English) and Hindustan (Hindi) on 19.2.2026. No suggestions or objections
have been received in response to the Commission’s notice.
6. The case was called out for the hearing on 26.2.2026. During the course of the
hearing, the learned counsel for the Petitioner submitted that no objection had been
received in response to the public notice published by the Commission under sub-
Section (5) of Section 15 of the Act. He further submitted that the Petitioner’s company
would comply with the requirements specified in the Trading Licence Regulations
during the subsistence of the trading licence, i.e., till 25 years, if granted.
7. Clause (9) of Regulation 6 of the Trading Licence Regulations provides as under:
Order in Petition No. 46/TD/2026
Page 3 of 6

“(9) On consideration of further objections or suggestions received and the reply
of the applicant thereto, if any, the Commission may grant the licence or reject
the application, for reasons to be recorded in writing if the application does not
confirm to the provisions of the Act, the rules or regulations or provisions of any
other law for the time being in force:
Provided that no application shall be rejected, unless the applicant has been
given an opportunity of being heard.”
8. On consideration of the materials on record, we are satisfied that the Petitioner
company meets the requirements of the Act and the Trading Licence Regulations for
the grant of an inter-State trading licence for a Category 'V'.
9. The grant of the trading licence to the Petitioner (hereinafter referred to as “the
licensee”) is subject to the fulfilment of the following conditions throughout the period
of subsistence of the licence:
(a) The licensee shall comply with the provisions of the Act, the Rules, and the
Regulations, particularly Trading Licence Regulations, orders, and directions
issued by the Commission, from time to time, and any other law in force;
(b) The licensee shall comply with orders and directions issued by the Commission
from time to time;
(c) The licensee shall not engage in the business of transmission of electricity
during the period of subsistence of the trading licence, i.e., till 25 years;
(d) The licensee shall charge trading margin strictly in accordance with the Trading

ORDER
The instant Petition has been filed by Power Grid Corporation of India Limited
(PGCIL) (hereinafter referred to as “the Petitioner”) for truing up of the transmission tariff
for the 2019-24 tariff period under the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms
and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2019 (hereinafter referred to as “the 2019 Tariff
Regulations”) and the determination of the transmission tariff for the 2024-29 tariff period
under the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff)
Regulations, 2024 (hereinafter referred to as “the 2024 Tariff Regulations”) in respect of
the following transmission asset under “Transmission System for controlling high Short
Circuit Current level at 400kV Thiruvalam S/s” (hereinafter referred to as “the
transmission project) in the Southern Region.

Background
3. The brief facts of the case are as under:
a. The Investment Approval (IA) for the transmission project was accorded by
Page 4 of 41
Order in Petition No. 484/TT/2025

the Petitioner’s Competent Authority vide Memorandum No. C/CP/PA2021-
03-0D-IA004 dated 12.6.2020, at an estimated cost of ₹8839 lakh, including
the Interest During Construction (IDC) of ₹402 lakh based on the December
2019 price level.
b. The transmission project was discussed and agreed upon in the 2nd meeting
of the Southern Region Standing Committee on Transmission (SRSCT) held
on 10.6.2019. The transmission project was also discussed in the 36th SRPC
meeting held on 12.7.2019 and recommended vide letter dated 14.8.2019.
Further, the 4th meeting of the National Committee on Transmission (NCT)
held on 31.7.2019 recommended the implementation of the transmission
project through the Regulated Tariff Mechanism (RTM) route. Further, the
Ministry of Power (MoP), vide its Office Memorandum dated 15.1.2020
approved the implementation of the subject project of the Petitioner under the
RTM route.
c. The scope of the transmission project covered in the instant Petition is as
under:
Sub-station extension at Thiruvalam Sub-station:
i) Installation of 12 Ω, 420 kV fault limiting bus series reactors at Thiruvalam
S/s between:
a) Bus Section-A and Bus Section-B
b) Bus Section-B and Bus Section-C
c) 4 Nos. 400 kV bays for 2 Nos. series bus reactors + 1 No. tie bay (note:
any Sub-station element viz ICTs, bus reactors, switchable line reactors,
etc. require one main bay and one tie bay for their operation. In this case
of each series reactor, 2 main breaker and 2 tie breakers are required
for their reliable operation. Therefore, 4 bays have been considered as
Page 5 of 41
Order in Petition No. 484/TT/2025

main bays (2 main bays per bus reactor) in current scheme)
ii) Opening of one of the bus (other than on which fault-limiting bus series
reactors are being installed) between the above-mentioned bus sections
through suitable arrangement.
iii) By-pass of Kolar-Thiruvalam and Thiruvalam- Sriperumbudur 400 kV S/C
Line to form Kolar-Sriperumbudur 400 kV S/C direct line.
d. The entire scope of the project is completed and covered in the instant
Petition.
e. The Commission vide Order dated 2.8.2024 in Petition No. 34/TT/2023 had
determined the transmission tariff in respect of transmission asset for the
2019-24 tariff period from date of Commissioning.
4. The Respondents are the distribution licensees, transmission licensees and
power departments, mainly beneficiaries of the southern region, which are procuring
transmission services from the Petitioner.
5. The Petitioner has served a copy of the Petition on the Respondents, and the
notice regarding the filing of this Petition have been published in the newspapers in
accordance with Section 64 of the Electricity Act, 2003 (hereinafter referred to as “the
Act”). No comments or suggestions have been received from the general public in
response to the aforesaid notices published in the newspapers by the Petitioner. None
of the Respondents have filed reply in the matter.
6. The hearings in this matter were held on 30.10.2025 and 11.12.2025, and the
Order was reserved.
7. This Order is being passed after considering the submissions made by the
Petitioner vide affidavit dated 7.11.2024. In response to the Commission's letter dated

Treatment of Liquidated Damages (LD):
18. The Petitioner has submitted that in respect of the transmission asset, LD
amounting to ₹295.48 lakh was recovered from the contractor and adjustment from the
capital cost in the year 2022-23. However, while computing tariff for the transmission
asset, LD up to the extent of IDC and IEDC, i.e., ₹ 167.19 lakh disallowed vide Order
dated 2.8.2024 in Petition No. 34/TT/2023 has been added back to the capital cost in
the year 2022-23.
19. We have considered the submissions of the Petitioner. Regulation 21 (4) & 21(5)
of 2019 Tariff Regulation provide as follows:
21. Interest During Construction (IDC) and Incidental Expenditure during Construction
(IEDC)
Xxxx
Xxxxx
(4) If the delay in achieving the COD is not attributable to the generating company or the
transmission licensee, IDC and IEDC beyond SCOD may be allowed after prudence check
and the liquidated damages, if any, recovered from the contractor or supplier or agency shall
be adjusted in the capital cost of the generating station or the transmission system, as the
case may be.
(5) If the delay in achieving the COD is attributable either in entirety on in part to the
generating company or the transmission licensee or its contractor or supplier or agency, in
such cases, IDC and IEDC beyond SCOD may be disallowed after prudence check either in
entirety or on pro-rata basis corresponding to the period of delay not condoned and the
liquidated damages, if any, recovered from the contractor or supplier or agency shall be
retained by the generating company or the transmission licensee, as the case may be.

20. The Commission, vide Order dated 2.8.2024 in Petition No. 34/TT/2023 has
disallowed IDC of ₹ 0.79 lakh and IEDC of ₹166.40 lakh, on account of time over-run not
condoned in respect of the transmission asset.
21. Accordingly, when the time over-run is attributable to the project developer, or its
contractors, the cost of time over-run, i.e., IDC and IEDC has to be borne by the project
developer and LD, if any, recovered can be retained by the Petitioner. In the instant case,
time over-run in respect of the transmission asset was partially condoned and accordingly,
the IDC and IEDC for the period of time over-run not condoned was deducted from the
capital cost. As the amount of the LD recovered has already been reduced by the Petitioner
from the ACE (as certified in the Auditor’s Certificate dated 9.9.2024) for FY 2022-23, as
such, the amount of LD recovered to the extent of the IDC and IEDC disallowed is to be
adjusted in ACE in FY 2022-23.
22. Accordingly, an amount of ₹167.18 lakh of Liquidated Damages recovered to the
extent of IDC and IEDC already disallowed is allowed to be added back to arrive at the
net ACE in FY 2022-23, which is ₹504.60 lakh as claimed by the Petitioner.

33. We have considered the Petitioner’s submissions and have also gone through
the record. We noted that the entities covered under the MAT regime are paying Income
Tax as per the MAT rates notified for the respective financial years under the IT Act,
1961, which is levied on the book profit of the entity computed as per Section 115 JB of
the IT Act, 1961. Section 115 JB (2) of IT Act, 1961 defines book profit as the net profit
in the Statement of Profit and Loss prepared in accordance with Schedule-III of the
Companies Act, 2013, subject to some additions and deductions as mentioned in the IT
Act, 1961. Since the Petitioner has been paying the MAT rates of the respective financial
years, the notified MAT rates for the respective financial year shall be considered as an
effective tax rate for the purpose of grossing up the Return on Equity (RoE) for truing
up of the tariff for the 2019-24 period in terms of the provisions of the 2019 Tariff
Regulations. The Interest imposed on any additional income tax demand as per the
assessment order of the Income Tax Authorities shall be considered on the actual
payment. However, the penalty (for default on the part of the Assessee), if any, imposed
shall not be taken into account for the purpose of grossing up the rate of RoE. Any
under-recovery or over-recovery in the grossed-up rates on the RoE after truing up shall
be recovered from or refunded to the beneficiaries or the long-term customers, as the
case may be, on a year-to-year basis. Therefore, the following effective tax rate based

ORDER
The instant Petition has been filed by Power Grid Corporation of India Limited
(hereinafter referred to as “the Petitioner / PGCIL”) for truing up of the transmission
tariff for the 2019-24 tariff period under the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission
(Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2019 (hereinafter referred to as “the 2019

the transmission asset under “Additional System for Power Evacuation from Generation
Projects pooled at Raigarh (Tamnar) Pool” (hereinafter referred to as “the transmission
project”) in the Western Region.
2. The Petitioner has made the following prayers in the instant Petition:
“a) Approve the trued-up Transmission Tariff for 2019-24 block and transmission tariff
for 2024-29 block for the assets covered under this petition, as per para 12 and 13
above.
b) Admit the capital cost claimed and additional capitalization incurred during 2019-24
and 2024-29.

Charges, on account of Return on Equity due to change in applicable Minimum
Alternate/Corporate Income Tax rate as per the Income Tax Act, 1961 (as amended
from time to time) of the respective financial year directly without making any application
before the Commission as provided in Tariff Regulation 2019 and Tariff regulations 2024
as per para 12 and 13 above for respective block.
d) Approve the reimbursement of expenditure by the beneficiaries towards petition filing
fee, and expenditure on publishing of notices in newspapers in terms of Regulation 94
(1) Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff)
Regulations, 2024, and other expenditure (if any) in relation to the filing of petition.

separately from the respondents in terms of Regulation 94 (3) and (4) Central Electricity
Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2024.
f) Allow the petitioner to bill and adjust impact on Interest on Loan due to change in
Interest rate on account of floating rate of interest applicable during 2024-29 period, if
any, from the respondents.
g) Allow the petitioner to file a separate petition before the Commission for claiming the
overall security expenses and consequential IOWC on that security expenses as
mentioned at para 19 above.
h) Allow the petitioner to file a separate petition before the Commission for claiming the
overall insurance expenses and consequential IOWC on that insurance expenses as
mentioned at para 19 above.
i) Allow the petitioner to file a separate petition before the Commission for claiming the
overall capital spares as mentioned at Para 19 above.

separate petition as mentioned at para 20 above.

authorities shall be allowed to be recovered from the beneficiaries.
and pass such other relief as the Commission deems fit and appropriate under the

Commission’s order dated.28.04.2023 in Petition No. 296/TT/2022. Accordingly, a

submitted that truing-up of the tariff is a statutory exercise undertaken to reconcile the

liabilities crystallised after the close of the tariff period. The add-cap placed on record

ORDER
This Petition has been filed by the Petitioner, Adani Power Limited (in short,
Adani), inter alia, seeking adjudication of the dispute qua PCKL/Karnataka ESCOMs’
illegal, unilateral withholding of energy charges payable to the Petitioner for the months
of June and July 2021. Accordingly, through this petition, the Petitioner has sought
direction against PCKL and the Karnataka ESCOMs to pay for the withheld energy
charges, and associated Late Payment Surcharge (LPS) at the rate of 18%, in
accordance with Regulation 59 of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms
and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2019. The Petitioner has made the following
prayers in the instant Petition:
(a) Admit the Petition.
(b) Direct PCKL/ Karnataka ESCOMs to pay Adani withheld energy charges of INR
67.11 Cr. for June and July 2021 as claimed through Adani’s revised monthly tariff invoice
dated 21.7.2021 for June 2021 and Adani’s monthly tariff invoice dated 7.8.2021 for July
2021;
(c) Direct PCKL/ Karnataka ESCOMs to pay Adani LPS at 18% per annum towards
delay in payment of revised monthly tariff invoice for June 2021 (dated 21.7.2021) and
monthly tariff invoice dated 7.8.2021 for July 2021.
(d) Pass such further order as this Commission may deem just and proper in the facts
and circumstances of the case and in the interest of justice.

Background of the case
2. The Petitioner is a power-generating company in terms of Section 2(28) of the
Electricity Act, 2003 (“Act”) and owns and operates a thermal power station, having an
installed capacity of 1200 MW (2x600 MW). Out of 1200 MW, 1080 MW is being supplied
to the distribution licensees of the State of Karnataka (“Karnataka ESCOMs”) in terms of
the Power Purchase Agreement (“PPA”) dated 26.12.2005. On 29.9.2010, the
Government of Karnataka (GoK) granted approval to the Petitioner for executing a Coal
Supply and Purchase Agreement (CSPA) with Glencore International AG (“Glencore”) for
the supply of 0.5 MTPA coal. The Petitioner, on 2.11.2010, signed a bituminous Coal
Sale and Purchase Agreement (“CSPA”) with M/s. Glencore International AG
(“Glencore”) to procure the 5,00,000 tonnes of coal per annum. Clause 7.02 of the CSPA
with Glencore stipulated that the price of coal from 2016 to 2022 would be based on
Japanese/Australian benchmark prices, with provisional billing allowed using the Global
COAL Newcastle Index (“GC Newc”) when the benchmark was not finalised.
3. Between 13.3.2021 and 24.4.2021, Glencore dispatched six coal shipments to
Adani, which were provisionally billed at Global Coal Newcastle Index prices as the
Japanese benchmark was not finalised then. Adani raised monthly tariff invoices to
Karnataka ESCOMs for the months of April and May 2021 based on provisional Glencore
coal invoices. On 4.6.2021, Glencore issued invoices to Adani, revising the cost of coal
procured from 13.3.2021 to 24.4.2021 for 6 shipments. Similarly, on 7.6.2021, the
Petitioner raised a monthly tariff invoice for May 2021 on Karnataka ESCOMs based on
the provisional coal invoices issued by Glencore.
4. On 14.6.2021, Adani received Glencore’s revised invoices dated 4.6.2021,
reflecting the final benchmark FOB rate of $107.85/MT for all 6 shipments, which was
significantly higher than the earlier provisional rate of $66.04/MT. Adani sent the revised

Glencore invoices for internal verification to its coal desk in Singapore and to the finance
section in Ahmedabad, due to the substantial price variation.
5. On 7.7.2021, Adani raised a monthly tariff invoice upon the Karnataka ESCOMs
for the month of June 2021 based on the provisional invoice of Glencore, and also
enclosed Glencore’s coal cost invoice dated 4.6.2021 (received on 14.6.2021) as part of
this monthly tariff invoice and requested Karnataka ESCOMs’ confirmation/approval on
the same.
6. Following a meeting on 15.7.2021, PCKL advised Adani to submit revised tariff
invoices factoring in the differential cost for the months April to June 2021. On 21.7.2021,
Adani submitted revised monthly invoices to Karnataka ESCOMs for April to June 2021
based on Glencore’s revised coal prices. On 6.8.2021, PCKL denied liability to pay the
revised claims, citing delayed submission by Adani and the alleged incorrect application
of the benchmark index period. In response, Adani, vide its letter dated 9.8.2021,
explained the timeline for receipt and scrutiny of Glencore’s invoice, and clarified that the
CSPA was based on calendar year pricing, not financial year. PCKL reiterated its position
in a letter dated 19.8.2021, emphasising that Adani delayed informing it, and raised
issues regarding the basis of benchmark price applicability. In subsequent
correspondence dated 20.8.2021 and meetings, Adani clarified that shipments with a
March 2021 bill of lading fell under CY2021 rates and the Japanese index applied on a
calendar-year basis as per the CSPA.
7. On 28.3.2022, PCKL, in its 68th Board meeting, agreed to accept the revised coal
rate for April-May 2021 but denied the same for the months June-July 2021. PCKL also
required an undertaking from Adani not to claim the LPS for delayed payment. Adani
rejected PCKL’s partial acceptance and requested full payment as per Glencore’s final
coal invoices and warned of LPS liability under CERC Tariff Regulations. A differential
claim of ₹27.60 crore was raised by Adani, asserting that PCKL wrongly applied a uniform

lower GC Newcastle rate rather than the correct higher rate applicable to May 2021
shipments.
8. Several rounds of communication took place through 2022 and 2023, with Adani
insisting on full settlement and PCKL maintaining that their internal Board decision was
binding and denied further liability.
9. On 22.6.2022, a meeting between Adani, PCKL, and the Additional Chief
Secretary (GoK) took place, where Adani reiterated its claim and clarified that even if the
JPU Index was not accepted, the correct GC Newcastle rate of $86.98/MT for May
shipments must be applied. Despite this, PCKL refused to revise its stance and denied
the differential claim of ₹27.6 crore, later leading to an increased claim of ₹67.11 crore,
including LPS and July 2021 invoices.
10. As PCKL and Karnataka ESCOMs continued to deny full payment and LPS, Adani
has filed the present petition seeking recovery of the outstanding dues in terms of CSPA
and applicable regulations.
