Analysis and Decision
20. We have considered the rival submissions of the parties and perused the
documents available on record. The main issue that arises for our consideration is
whether the Petitioner, Adani Power Limited, is entitled to recovery the revised energy
charges for the months of June and July 2021 arising from the final coal price
communicated by M/s Glencore International under the Coal Supply and Purchase
Agreement (CSPA), and whether such costs are recoverable under the terms of the PPA
and the applicable provisions of the Act, 2003 and CERC Terms and Conditions of Tariff
Regulations, 2019.
Order in Petition No. 220/MP/2024 Page 13 of 27

The Petitioner has submitted that the Respondent, PCKL, has illegally withheld payment
of energy charges of Rs. 67.11 crore and the Late Payment Surcharge (LPS) of Rs. 31.63
crore for the months of June and July 2021. The Petitioner has submitted that valid
invoices for the said months were submitted to the ESCOMs in accordance with the PPA
and applicable Tariff Regulations. However, the Respondent ESCOMs have withheld the
same without lawful justification, thereby causing material cash-flow injury. The
Respondent has submitted that the Petitioner failed to provide the information regarding
the bills dated 14.6.2021 from its fuel supplier, Glencore International, violating prudent
utility practices under Article 4.7 of the PPA. The non-disclosure undermined
transparency in invoicing and resulted in the Petitioner being placed in the Merit Order of
Dispatch, thereby imposing an additional burden of Rs. 67.10 crore on ESCOMs, despite
cheaper alternatives being available.
We have considered the submissions of the Petitioner and Respondent. The tariff of the
generating station is determined by the Commission under Section 62 of the Act. As per
Section 62(4) read with Section 61(a) and (b), the tariff is required to be determined
having regard to the actual cost of generation, including fuel cost, and is subject to
adjustment in accordance with the tariff regulations framed by this Commission.
We deem it proper here to refer to provisions of the PPA and CSPA as under:
21. Article 4.4 of the PPA provides as under:
“4.4, the energy charges for each billing month shall be the sum of recoverable cost
of primary fuel, secondary fuel and lime.”
22. Further, Article 6.2 of the PPA regarding the monthly invoices and despatch
thereon provides as under:
Article 6.2(a): The Seller shall submit to the Principal Buyers a Tariff Invoice for each
Order in Petition No. 220/MP/2024 Page 14 of 27

Billing month setting forth those amounts payable by the Principal Buyers for Monthly
Capacity (fixed) charge amount, Energy charges and Incentive payment wherever
applicable. Along with each monthly bill, the Seller will submit documents as agreed
between Principal Buyers and Seller.
Article 6.2(b): The Seller shall, if necessary, submit to the Principal Buyers
Supplementary Invoices each month for any other payment not included in the Tariff
invoice. Provided that no revision in respect of a Tariff invoice shall be included in a
Supplementary invoice after one month of the expiry of the relevant Tariff period.
Article 6.3(a): The Principal Buyers shall communicate to the Seller and the Bank any
dispute in respect of the Tariff invoice or the Supplementary invoice, within Ten
Business days of the Acknowledgement date. If the Principal Buyers do not
communicate to the Bank and the Seller any such dispute, it shall be construed as
deemed acceptance by the Principal Buyers in respect of the entire amount of such
invoice. The Principal Buyers will forward the invoice copy to the Bank for making
payment to the Seller.
Regulation 43 (1) of the Tariff Regulations 2019 provides as under:
“43. Computation and Payment of Energy Charge for Thermal Generating Stations
(1) The energy charge shall cover the primary and secondary fuel cost and limestone
consumption cost (where applicable), and shall be payable by every beneficiary for the
total energy scheduled to be supplied to such beneficiary during the calendar month on
ex-power plant basis, at the energy charge rate of the month (with fuel and limestone price
adjustment). Total Energy charge payable to the generating company for a month shall
be:
Energy Charges = (Energy charge rate in Rs./kWh) x {Scheduled energy (ex-bus) for the
month in kWh}:
. As per the above provisions, the Energy Charge Rate (“ECR”) is required to be
computed based on the actual landed cost of fuel for the month, subject to prudent utility
practices. As per Regulation 43(1, energy charges shall be payable by the beneficiary for
all the scheduled energy at the energy charge rate computed based on the weighted
average landed price of primary fuel.
Clauses 7.01A and 7.02 of the CSPA provide as under:
“Clause 7.01A deals with ‘Price’ of coal. Further, Clause 7.02 provides that the
methodology adopted to arrive at the FOB price component in article 7.01 shall be
applicable for the first five years of the Term (i.e. 2011 - 2015 inclusive).
Clause 7.02 is extracted as under:
…
7.02 …
Order in Petition No. 220/MP/2024 Page 15 of 27

The FOB price for each calendar year from 2016 until 2022 (inclusive), and for each
calendar year of the Extended Term (if applicable), and for each calendar year of the
Further Extended Term (if applicable), shall be the Japanese/Australian benchmark
yearly price basis 6322 gross as received, with actual calorific value to be adjusted to
6250 gross as received. Such price shall be finalized at least 60 days prior to 1
January of each calendar year (a) from 2016 to 2022 (inclusive), (b) of the Extended
Term, as applicable, and (c) of the Further Extended Term, as applicable.
The FOB price is for multi-origin source of loading/supply of coal which can be either
from Australia, Indonesia, South Africa or Colombia at Seller's option. The FOB price
will still be the Japanese/Australian benchmark FOB price irrespective of the origin
selected by Seller.
The yearly benchmark price finalized for each calendar year from 2016 until 2022
(inclusive), and for each calendar year of the Extended Term (if applicable), and for
each calendar year of the Further Extended Term (if applicable), shall be applicable
for all of the shipments effected during that calendar year, save that, should the yearly
Japanese/Australian benchmark pricing not be finalized for any reason before the
start of the first Quarter or any subsequent Quarter of any calendar year from 2016
until 2022 (Inclusive) or of any calendar year of the Extended Term or the Further
Extended Term (if applicable), the GC Newc price for the Quarter preceding the
Quarter of shipment shall apply until such time as the Japanese/Australian benchmark
price is finalized.
If for any reason the above benchmark Japanese/Australian benchmark price is
discontinued, the FOB price will be set for each Quarter based on the quarterly
average GC Newc price of the Quarter preceding the Quarter of shipment.”
As per the CSPA dated 2.11.2010 executed between the Petitioner and M/s
Glencore International stipulates, from 2016 onwards, the FOB price shall be determined
based on the Japanese/Australian benchmark price, and in the absence of such
benchmark, the Global Coal Newcastle Index price for the preceding quarter shall be
applied until such time the Japanese/Australian benchmark price is finalised.
23. The Respondent, PCKL, has contended that by delaying disclosure of the revised
price, the Petitioner ensured its inclusion in the Merit Order Dispatch (MOD) for the
months of June and July 2021. Under the MOD mechanism of the State Load Dispatch
Centre, this led to UPCL’s power being scheduled ahead of other lower-cost options. Had
the increased fuel cost been disclosed on time, UPCL’s variable cost would have been
₹3.624/unit in June 2021 and ₹4.676/unit in July 2021, placing it at the bottom of the MOD
stack. By comparison, the highest variable cost in June 2021 was ₹3.104/unit (NTPL)
Order in Petition No. 220/MP/2024 Page 16 of 27

and in July 2021, ₹3.081/unit (NTPL). Therefore, UPCL would not have been scheduled
for dispatch in either month.
24. The Petitioner, in its rejoinder, dated 10.2.2025, has submitted that, being a
Section 62 project, it is entitled to a pass-through of actual prudent fuel costs. Accordingly,
PCKL/ESCOMs are bound to pay the energy charges for the months of June and July
2021 based on the revised Glencore invoice. It has been further submitted that as per
Regulation 43 of the Tariff Regulations, 2019, energy charges are payable on the basis
of actual fuel cost, the Merit Order Dispatch (MoD) position has no relevance in
determining the tariff payment.
25. Further, the Commission, vide ROP for the hearing dated 19.2.2025, directed the
Petitioner to submit the following additional information:
(a) Indicate the specific provisions outlined in the Power Purchase Agreement (PPA)
and Coal Supply Purchase Agreement (CSPA) regarding the timeline and process for
communicating information to the Respondents for the revision of coal invoices by
Glencore, particularly following the availability of the Japanese/Australian pricing index?
Specifically, within how many days is such information required to be shared, and what are
the associated obligations for transparency and accuracy in the recalculation process?
(b) Given that the revision in rates was known to the Petitioner on 14th June 2021 but
was communicated to the Respondent only on 7th July 2021, resulting in a delay of 23 days,
what were the underlying reasons for such delay in conveying the information regarding the
revised rates? Whether there were any contractual, operational, or external factors that had
contributed to this lapse, and how does this delay align with the provisions outlined in the
governing PPA for timely communication of such revisions?"
(c) Explain the past practices followed for the intimation of revised rates of the
Japanese/Australian pricing index from Glencore;
(d) What is the procedure for Merit Order Dispatch (MOD) in power scheduling,
considering the variable costs of thermal power stations?
26. In compliance with the above ROP, the Petitioner, vide additional affidavit dated
15.3.2025, has mainly submitted as under:
(a) On PPA and CSPA provisions: There are no specific provisions in the
PPA or CSPA regarding timelines or processes for communicating revised coal
rates linked to the Japanese/Australian pricing index. Adani follows prudent utility
Order in Petition No. 220/MP/2024 Page 17 of 27

practices and submits revised invoices, along with supporting documents as per the
Tariff Regulations, 2019.
(b) On the 23-day delay in communication: The delay was due to internal
scrutiny by Adani’s teams in Singapore and Ahmedabad, considering the significant
rate change. No contractual timeline was breached, and Adani does not benefit from
such delays.
(c) On past practices: There is no prior instance of rate revision based on the
Japanese/Australian index; hence, no past practice exists.
(d) On Merit Order Dispatch (MOD): MOD is prepared by BESCOM on the
7th of each month based on the previous month's invoices and communicated to
SLDC Karnataka for implementation.
27. Since there is no express timeline in the PPA or CSPA for communicating index-
linked coal price revisions, the Petitioner was not strictly contractually obliged to notify
within a fixed number of days. However, the absence of a clause creates a gap because
timely disclosure is required by good commercial practice. The Petitioner has attributed
the 23-day gap to internal scrutiny by Adani’s Singapore coal desk and Ahmedabad
finance department. The absence of any prior precedent for Japanese/Australian-index
revisions means there was no established operational practice to rely on. Further, the
described practice regarding Merit Order Despatch prepared by BESCOM on the 7th of
each month, based on the previous month's invoices forwarded to SLDC, is an
operational arrangement.
On entitlement to revised coal price:
28. As per the provisions of the CSPA, Japanese/Australian benchmark pricing is
required to be adopted for the period from 2016 to 2022. However, in the absence of such
pricing, the Global Coal Newcastle (“GC Newc”) Index price shall be applicable. The
Petitioner issued provisional bills based on Glencore's coal cost invoices, using the
Global Coal Newcastle Index ("GC Newc") price for six shipments from 13.3.2021 to
Order in Petition No. 220/MP/2024 Page 18 of 27

24.4.2021, as the Japanese benchmark pricing for calendar year 2021 had not yet
finalised. Later, on 7.7.2021, the Petitioner issued revised tariff invoices based on
Glencore's coal cost invoices, reflecting the updated Japanese/Australian benchmark
price.
29. On 7.5.2021, the Petitioner raised a monthly tariff invoice for the month of April
2021 on Karnataka ESCOMs based on the provisional coal invoices issued by Glencore.
On 4.6.2021, Glencore issued invoices to Adani for the revised cost of coal procured
during 13.3.2021 to 24.4.2021, for 6 shipments based on the following differences in
index rates:
Shipments Bill of Provisional FOB Final FOB Rate (USD/MT)
(Vessel Name) lading Rate (USD/MT) as as per Japanese/
per GC Newc rate Australian Index
MV AOM Federica 13.3.2021 66.04
MV PS Framura 22.3.2021 66.04
MV LMZ Francisco 29.3.2021 66.04 107.85
MV Bulk Greece 21.4.2021 85.72
MV Ocean Garlic 22.4.2021 86.98
MV JY Atlantic 24.4.2021 85.94
30. The Petitioner has contended that the revised rate claimed by Glencore is
$107.85/MT, while the pre-revised rate applicable for the first three vessels is $66.04/MT,
and the pre-revised rate for the balance 3 vessels is in the range $85.72/MT to
$86.98/MT. The pre-revised rates are based on the Global Coal Newcastle rate under
clause 7.02 of the CSA. However, PCKL has erroneously considered the pre-revised rate
as $66.04/MT for all six vessels.
31. Per contra, the Respondent, PCKL vide affidavit dated 20.1.2025, has submitted
that during the months of April–June 2021, the FOB price for coal procured from Glencore
was USD 66.04/MT for 6200 kcal/kg, based on the GC Newc Index of the preceding
Order in Petition No. 220/MP/2024 Page 19 of 27

quarter. However, the Petitioner’s monthly tariff invoice dated 7.5.2021 did not disclose
or attach Glencore’s actual invoices for April 2021, which reflected a higher rate of USD
86.98/MT as per Clause 7.02 of the CSPA, and the reasons for such non-disclosure are
known only to the Petitioner.
32. The Petitioner, in its rejoinder dated 10.2.2025, has not submitted the clarification
regarding a higher rate of USD 86.98/MT but has clarified that as per Clause 7.02 of the
CSPA, till the finalisation of the yearly Japanese/Australian benchmark price, the GC
Newcastle price for the preceding quarter applies. However, while computing energy
charges for July 2021, PCKL/Karnataka ESCOMs applied the lower GC Newcastle rate
of USD 66.04/MT applicable to March 2021 shipments, instead of the correct rates, i.e.
USD 85.72/MT, USD 86.98/MT, and USD 85.94/MT, corresponding to April 2021
shipments actually consumed during July 2021. Consequently, the Petitioner sought
through the I.A. No. 53 of 2024 an interim direction for payment of ₹27.60 crore (with
LPS) towards the differential energy charges for July 2021, without prejudice to its
broader claim based on the final benchmark price of USD 107.85/MT as per Glencore’s
revised invoice dated 4.6.2021. However, no response has been filed by PCKL in this
regard.
33. It is not in dispute that the Japanese/Australian benchmark price for the relevant
shipments for March and April 2021 was finalised at USD 107.85/MT, significantly higher
than the provisional Global Coal Newcastle rate of USD 66.04/MT applied earlier. The
Petitioner on 7.7.2021 raised a monthly tariff invoice for June, 2021, based on the
provisional invoice and Glencore’s coal cost invoice dated 4.6.2021 received on
14.6.2021. Further, the Petitioner factored in the revised coal cost and raised monthly
invoices for the months of April–June 2021 on 21.7.2021 and for July 2021 on 7.8.2021.
Order in Petition No. 220/MP/2024 Page 20 of 27

34. It is noted that the Coal Supply and Purchase Agreement (CSPA) executed
between Adani and Glencore provides for provisional billing based on the GC Newcastle
Index, subject to adjustment upon finalisation of the Japanese/Australian benchmark
price. It is an undisputed fact that Glencore issued revised invoices dated 4.6.2021,
received by Adani on 14.6.2021, reflecting the finalised benchmark price of USD
107.85/MT. Consequently, the Petitioner, Adani, revised the tariff invoices for the period
from April to June 2021 on 21.7.2021 and issued the tariff invoice for the month of July
2021 on 7.8.2021 in accordance with the said finalised benchmark.
35. Articles 4.4 and 4.7 of the PPA provide as under:
“Article 4.4, the energy charges for each billing month shall be the sum of recoverable
cost of primary fuel, secondary fuel and lime.”
“Article 4.7 Cost of Primary fuel and Secondary fuel
(c) The seller shall use all reasonable efforts at all times during the term to acquire the
Primary and Secondary Fuel on commercially competitive terms consistent with market
conditions.”
36. The Commission notes the Respondent’s contention that the finalisation of the
benchmark price is a recurring annual event and, therefore, could not have been
unforeseen. However, the Commission observes that such contention cannot override
the express contractual framework set out in the Coal Supply and Purchase Agreement
(CSPA) and the Power Purchase Agreement (PPA). The PPA, being a cost-plus
arrangement governed by Section 62 of the Electricity Act, 2003, explicitly allows
recovery of actual and prudently incurred fuel costs as a pass-through in the tariff.
Accordingly, once the fuel supplier issues revised invoices pursuant to the finalisation of
the benchmark price under the CSPA, the corresponding expenditure constitutes a
legitimate fuel cost of the Petitioner, recoverable through the tariff.
Order in Petition No. 220/MP/2024 Page 21 of 27

37. The Respondent, PCKL, has submitted that the Petitioner received the revised
coal invoices from Glencore on 4.6.2021 but failed to share this information with PCKL
or the ESCOMs, which is violative of prudent utility practices under Article 4.7 of the PPA.
It has further been submitted that, as a coal trading entity, the Petitioner was well aware
that Japanese/Australian benchmark prices are settled each year around April–June, and
industry reports on 4.6.2021 had already confirmed the revised benchmark price. Despite
this, the Petitioner withheld the revised bills and supporting documents without any
justification, affecting transparency and accuracy in tariff calculation. This delay kept the
Petitioner in the Merit Order Dispatch, resulting in an avoidable financial burden of ₹67.10
crore on the ESCOMs. In response, the Petitioner has submitted that PCKL’s statements
do not align with one another. The Respondent accepted that Glencore’s revised invoice
is dated 14.6.2021, but still accused Adani of knowing the revised FoB rates on 4.6.2021.
The Petitioner has explained that the time taken from 14.6.2021 to 7.7.2021 was
reasonable because the invoice had to be checked by its coal desk in Singapore and the
finance team in Ahmedabad as part of normal verification before being sent to
PCKL/ESCOMs.
We have considered rival submissions of the parties. It is noted that the Respondent has
already accepted and settled the supplementary invoices raised for the months of April
and May 2021 based on the same revised benchmark price. Such conduct constitutes an
acknowledgement of the validity of Glencore’s benchmark-linked invoicing under the
CSPA. Having accepted the contractual adjustment for the earlier months, the
Respondent’s denial of similar treatment for June and July 2021 is inconsistent and
untenable.
38. The Commission further observes that the PPA does not contain any provision for
disallowance of legitimate fuel costs merely on the ground that the revised invoices were
Order in Petition No. 220/MP/2024 Page 22 of 27

received or communicated at a later stage. Since the adjustment in coal cost arises
directly from the benchmark finalisation process under the CSPA, the resultant revised
fuel price forms part of the actual fuel cost of the generating station. Accordingly, such
costs are recoverable for all months in which the affected coal shipments were
consumed, including June and July 2021.
"The Respondent’s objection regarding the delay in intimation
39. The Respondent has contended that there was a delay of 46 days in furnishing
the revised Glencore invoice, which allegedly enabled the Petitioner to remain in the Merit
Order Dispatch (MOD) stack, resulting in a higher procurement cost for the State. It has
been further submitted that no documentary evidence was placed on record to
demonstrate the due diligence allegedly carried out by the Petitioner during the period
from 4.6.2021 to 21.7.2021, nor has the Petitioner shown that it was prevented from
informing the Respondent of the steps being taken to verify the revised FOB rates. In
response, the Petitioner reiterated that this assertion is incorrect. It has been further
submitted that there was no delay on the part of Adani. Adani received the coal cost
invoice from Glencore on 14.6.2021 and, after undertaking a reasonable and prudent
scrutiny of the claims over a period of 23 days, it shared the revised invoice with the
ESCOMs on 7.7.2021. The time taken for verification was neither excessive nor
unreasonable, and cannot be construed as a lapse that should deny Adani its statutory
and contractual entitlement to recover energy charges on actuals. The Petitioner has
submitted that, as affirmed in the affidavit dated 15.3.2025, there is no provision under
the applicable law or contract prescribing any mandatory timeline for intimating revised
coal cost invoices to PCKL/ESCOMs, nor does any alleged delay disentitle Adani from
recovering the applicable energy charges.
Order in Petition No. 220/MP/2024 Page 23 of 27

40. We have considered the submissions of the parties. It is observed that the PPA
and CSPA do not prescribe a specific time limit for communicating revised coal prices.
The delay of intimation, as explained by the Petitioner, was due to internal verification
given the magnitude of the price change, and such verification, which is consistent with
prudent utility practice under Article 4.7 of the PPA.
Article 4.7 of PPA provides as under-
“4.7 Cost of Primary fuel and Secondary fuel
(a) The cost of Primary fuel shall be the aggregate cost associated with purchasing and
delivering fuel to the Plant Boundary (capacity jetty) and transporting it to the Plant site at
Nandikur. This cost will include the cost of commodity, forex adjustment, royalty, Taxes,
unloading/loading, transportation charges by rail port charges, insurance, for the reliable
supply of the fuel.
(b) The cost of Secondary fuel shall be the aggregate cost associated with purchasing and
delivering fuel to the Plant site at Nadikur. This cost will include the cost of the commodity
and transportation charges by road, for the reliable supply of fuel.”
41. It is noted that the Merit Order Dispatch (MOD) is simply the order in which
generating stations are called upon to supply power based on their variable cost. It is
used to determine which plants are to operate at any given time for system operation and
economics. We have considered the submissions of the Respondent alleging that Adani
intentionally withheld the revised coal cost invoices issued by Glencore with a view to
securing a favourable position in the Merit Order Despatch (MoD). The generating station
is operating under a Section 62 cost-plus tariff regime, in which the energy charge is a
pass-through of the actual fuel cost, subject to a prudence check. However, under
Section 62 cost-plus tariff, a generator’s entitlement to recover charges is not determined
by when or how it was dispatched; it is based on the actual, prudently incurred costs, as
approved by the Commission.
42. As regards the allegation of delayed disclosure, it is noted that Adani had shared
the revised coal cost invoice dated 4.6.2021 with PCKL/ESCOMs on 7.7.2021. Even after
receiving the revised invoice, PCKL/ESCOMs did not consider it when finalising the Merit
Order in Petition No. 220/MP/2024 Page 24 of 27

Order Despatch for the subsequent period. In these circumstances, when the procurers
were already in possession of the relevant information, the allegation of mala fide intent
against Adani is not supported by the material on record. The Commission is of the view
that, although timely disclosure of fuel cost is desirable, the period of 23 days between
receipt of Glencore’s invoice on 14.6.2021 and submission to PCKL on 7.7.2021 does
not constitute such a delay as to vitiate the Petitioner’s claim. The PPA or CSPA does
not prescribe a rigid time limit for such disclosure. From the submissions of the Petitioner,
it is observed that during the financial year 2021-22, the period under consideration, the
Plant Load Factor achieved by the generating station was only 18.04%. At such a low
PLF, a generating company does not derive any commercial benefit from being placed
higher in the Merit Order Dispatch, as incentive benefits accrue only when generation
exceeds the threshold of 85% PLF, which is not the case here. In light of the above
findings, the Commission holds that energy charges based on the revised Glencore coal
invoice dated 4.6.2021 are admissible for the months of June and July 2021 as well,
under Articles 4.4, 6.2, and 6.3 of the PPA. Accordingly, ₹67.11 crore withheld by PCKL
and Karnataka ESCOMs is not justifiable.
On the past acceptance of similar claims
43. It is relevant that the Respondent has accepted and paid the revised energy
charges for the months of April-May 2021 based on the same Glencore benchmark
finalisation. The differential treatment meted out to the months of June and July 2021
invoices, despite arising from the same coal price revision, is inconsistent and not
supported by the contractual framework.
Late Payment Surcharge
44. Regulation 59 of the CERC Tariff Regulations, 2019 provides as under:
Order in Petition No. 220/MP/2024 Page 25 of 27

“59. Late payment surcharge: In case the payment of any bill for charges payable under
these regulations is delayed by a beneficiary or long term customers as the case may
be, beyond a period of 45 days from the date of presentation of bills, a late payment
surcharge at the rate of 1.50% per month shall be levied by the generating company or
the transmission licensee, as the case may be.”
45. From the above, it could be inferred that, if a beneficiary or long-term customer
fails to pay a bill within 45 days of its presentation, the generator or transmission licensee
may charge a late payment surcharge of 1.50% per month on the overdue amount this
surcharge accrues for each month the bill remains unpaid. The charge is intended to
compensate the seller for delayed payment and encourage timely settlement.
46. The Commission has noted the Respondent’s contention that LPS should not
apply since the Petitioner allegedly delayed disclosure. However, the liability to pay the
LPS arises once tariff invoices are raised and remain unpaid beyond the stipulated due
date. The LPS under the Tariff Regulations is a statutory entitlement and cannot be
waived unilaterally. Accordingly, Karnataka ESCOMs are liable to pay the LPS on the
withheld energy charges, calculated in accordance with Regulation 59 of the Tariff
Regulations, 2019.
47. In light of the above findings, we hold as under:
a) The Petitioner, being a Section 62 generating company, is entitled to full
pass-through of actual fuel cost incurred, subject to a prudence check. The revised
FOB rate of USD 107.85/MT as per Glencore’s invoice dated 4.6.2021 shall be
allowed for the computation of energy charges for the months of June and July
2021.
Order in Petition No. 220/MP/2024 Page 26 of 27

b) The Respondent is directed to release the withheld amount of ₹67.11 crore
towards energy charges for the months of June–July 2021, along with LPS, within
30 days from the date of this order.
c) Late Payment Surcharge shall be payable in terms of Regulation 59 of the
Tariff Regulations, 2019, for the period of delay beyond the due date of payment
as per the PPA, until actual payment.
48. Petition No. 220/MP/2024 is disposed of in terms of the above discussions and
findings.
Sd/- Sd/- Sd/- Sd/-
(Ravinder Singh Dhillon) (Harish Dudani) (Ramesh Babu V.) (Jishnu Barua)

CENTRAL ELECTRICITY REGULATORY COMMISSION

for the power procured in the month of December, 2022, in terms of the

The following were present:
Shri Hemant Singh, Advocate, CEPL & ILFS

Order in Petition No. 137/MP/2023
Page 1 of 19

Shri Harshit Singh, Advocate, CEPL & ILFS
Ms. Lavanya Panwar, Advocate, CEPL & ILFS
Shri Chetan Garg, Advocate, CEPL & ILFS
Shri Syed Fazl, Advocate, CEPL & ILFS
Ms. Ankita Bafna, Advocate, CEPL & ILFS
Shri Gyanedra Singh, Advocate, ILFS
Shri Pawan Singh, Advocate, ILFS

Shri Shailendra Singh, Advocate, CEPL
Ms. Anusha Nagarajan, Advocate, TANGEDCO
Shri Rahul Ranjan, Advocate, TANGEDCO
ORDER
On 5.5.2022, the Central Government through Ministry of Power
(hereinafter referred to as “Respondent No. 2 or MoP”) issued directions
under Section 11(1) of the Electricity Act, 2003 (hereinafter referred to as “the
Act”) to all imported coal-based generating stations to generate and supply
electricity to address the extraordinary power crisis arisen due to the impact of
high international coal prices. The Central Government, through the
committee constituted under the directions, issued the benchmark tariff for
payment purposes. The Ministry of Power, through successive directions after
5.5.2022, issued clarifications, modifications, benchmark tariffs and
extensions of validity on a continuous basis (collectively referred to as
“directions”). On 28.9.2022, the Respondent No.2 extended the validity of its
earlier directions dated 5.5.2022 (which were originally applicable until
31.10.2022) till 31.12.2022.
2. The IL&FS Tamil Nadu Power Company Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as
“Petitioner”) entered into a Long-Term Power Purchase Agreement dated
Order in Petition No. 137/MP/2023
Page 2 of 19

12.12.2013 (“PPA”) with Tamil Nadu Generation and Distribution Co. Ltd.
(hereinafter referred to as “Respondent No.1”), for the supply of 540 MW of
power for 15 years, based on imported coal. The Respondent No.1 purchased
the power from the Petitioner as per the terms of the directions issued by the
Respondent No.2.
3. The Petitioner has supplied power as per the terms of the directions from
its effective date. However, about 6 months later, the dispute arose when the
Respondent No.1 issued letters to the Petitioner on 23.11.2022 and
30.11.2022, insisting on supplying power as per the tariff provided under the
PPA rather than the benchmark tariff notified by the Ministry of Power.
Subsequent to the receipt of the aforesaid letters, the Petitioner vide letters
dated 24.11.2022 and 1.12.2022 clarified its intention to continuously abide by
the Section 11 directions issued by the Respondent No.2, including the
payment of Energy Charge Rate (“ECR”) notified by the committee constituted
under said directions.
4. Previously, the Petitioner filed Petition No. 350/MP/2022 before this
Commission to seek directions against the Respondent No.1. In the said
Petition, the Commission vide its order dated 23.12.2022, has directed to
comply with the directions issued by the Respondent No.2 under Section 11 of
the Act and granted liberty to file fresh petition regarding the charges payable
by the Respondent No.1. Relevant para of the said order is as under:-
“10. Insofar as the aspects of TANGEDCO having already scheduled the power
from the Petitioners from 1st December, 2022 onwards and applicable rates for
such supply as raised during the course of arguments, we are of the view that
such aspects are beyond the subject matter of these Petitions and it would not be
Order in Petition No. 137/MP/2023
Page 3 of 19

appropriate to stretch the scope of these cases beyond what have been prayed for
by the Petitioners. In case of the any grievances in relation to the charges to be
payable by/receivable from TANGEDCO for such supply by the Petitioners during
the subsistence of direction of MoP, the Petitioners are at liberty to approach the
Commission with fresh Petitions and contentions of both the sides, on these
aspects, are kept open. However, both parties, the Petitioners and TANGEDCO,
are directed to scrupulously comply with the direction issued by MoP under
Section 11 of the Act read with subsequent clarifications thereto as long as they
are in force.”
5. The Petitioner submits that they raised the invoices for the supply of power
during December, 2022 as per the terms of the directions. According to the
Petitioner, the power was offered by declaring its availability during the month
of December 2022 (from 07.12.2022), along with the remark that the power
was being offered in terms of the directions. Further, the Petitioner submitted
that the Respondent No.1 has scheduled the power without any objections.
Subsequently, the Respondent No.1 objected to the invoices raised by the
Petitioner as per the directions qua benchmark rates. Pursuant to the liberty
granted by the Commission, vide its order dated 23.12.2022, the Petitioner
preferred the instant petition, seeking recovery of Energy Charges of INR
119,97,41,125/- from the Respondent No.1, for the power procured in the
month of December 2022, in terms of the MoP’s notified benchmark tariff. The
Petitioner has made the following prayers:-
(a) “Direct the Respondent No.1 / TANGEDCO to make payment of Energy Charges
of INR 119,97,41,125/- (at Energy Charges of INR 5.98/Kwh- INR 5.77/Kwh, INR
5.78/Kwh, INR 5.77/Kwh for the period 01.12.2022 to 10.12.2022,11.12.2022 to
24.12.2022,25.12.2022 to 31.12.2022 respectively), for the power it procured
from 01.12.2022 till 31.12.2022, in terms of the ECR/ benchmark tariff notified by
the MOP under Section 11 of EA 2003;
(b) Grant liberty to the Petitioner to claim Energy Charges from the Respondent No.

10. The matter was heard on 10.5.2023, 20.3.2024 and 22.8.2024. The
Petition was admitted vide Record of Proceedings of the hearing dated
10.5.2023, and after hearing the submissions of the Petitioner, the
Commission admitted the matter and directed the parties to file their
respective replies and rejoinders, if any. The Respondent No.1, vide its
written submissions dated 13.11.2023, has mainly reiterated its submissions
in its reply; therefore, the same is not repeated . The Petitioner also made its
written submissions on 3.11.2023, reiterating its earlier submissions. The
order in the petition was reserved on 22.8.2024.
Analysis and Decisions
11. We have considered the submissions of the Petitioner and Respondent
No.1 and perused the documents on record. The present petition has been
filed by the Petitioner seeking direction for payment of the electricity supplied
during December 2022 in terms of the liberty granted by the Commission in
Petition No. 350/MP/2022. Respondent No.1 has raised the issue of the
jurisdiction again, which was already settled by the Commission in the order
dated 23.12.2022 in Petition No. 350/MP/2022. Hence, the same is not dealt
with again.
12. In the instant case, the Respondent No.1 has objected to the payment
claimed as per the benchmark tariff decided by the Committee constituted by
the MoP, on the ground that the directions provide options to distribution
companies to purchase the power at the benchmark rates till the Section 11
directions were in force. The Respondent No. 1 advanced their submissions
Order in Petition No. 137/MP/2023
Page 14 of 19

to enforce the tariff as per PPA on the strength of the communication dated
23.11.2022, wherein they informed and clarified to the Petitioner that they
proposed to withdraw their consent for procuring power at the benchmark
rates issued by the MoP. According to the Petitioner, the directions provide
Respondent No.1 with the discretion to either procure or not to procure power
in terms of the said directions. If Respondent No.1 decides to procure power,
it is left with the only option to procure power either at the Energy Charge Rate
notified by the MoP or at a negotiated rate, but not at the PPA rates.
13. The limited issue beforehand is whether the direction dated 5.5.2022
(including subsequent clarifications and amendments) issued by the MoP
obliges the distribution companies to purchase the power at the benchmark
rates during the validity of the Section 11 directions? Alternatively, can
Respondent No. 1 enforce the existing tariff agreed under the PPA during the
operation of the directions?
14. The Commission has partly addressed this issue in the order dated
23.12.2022 in Petition No. 350/MP/2022, wherein the Respondent No.1 itself
admitted that they will not insist upon power supply as per PPA till such time
the directions of MoP are in force. Relevant Paras are extracted below:-
“9. In view of the categorical submissions made by the learned senior counsel for
TANGEDCO including to take on record the clarification made by TANGEDCO before
the Hon’ble High Court of Madras, as recorded in paragraph 11 of the order dated
6.12.2022, i.e. the word ‘shall’ occurring in 3rd paragraph of letters dated 23.11.2022
and 30.11.2022 be read as ‘may’ and that TANGEDCO will not insist upon power supply
as per PPA till the such time the direction of MoP are in force, in the present cases also,
we are of the view that the prayers made by the Petitioners in these Petitions no longer
survive and have become infructuous.
10. Insofar as the aspects of TANGEDCO having already scheduled the power from the
Petitioners from 1st December, 2022 onwards and applicable rates for such supply as
Order in Petition No. 137/MP/2023
Page 15 of 19

raised during the course of arguments, we are of the view that such aspects are beyond
the subject matter of these Petitions and it would not be appropriate to stretch the scope
of these cases beyond what have been prayed for by the Petitioners. In case of the any
grievances in relation to the charges to be payable by/receivable from TANGEDCO for
such supply by the Petitioners during the subsistence of direction of MoP, the
Petitioners are at liberty to approach the Commission with fresh Petitions and
contentions of both the sides, on these aspects, are kept open. However, both parties,
the Petitioners and TANGEDCO, are directed to scrupulously comply with the direction
issued by MoP under Section 11 of the Act read with subsequent clarifications thereto
as long as they are in force.”
15. We have examined the directions issued by the MoP. It is observed from
clauses 4(a) and 4(b) of the said directions, which laid the obligations of the
generating company to operate and generate power to their full capacity,
whereas the distribution companies or the PPA holders have no obligation to
procure the power from the same generating company. The said direction
addresses the cost component of the electricity supplied and its recovery.
Clause 4(f) explicitly provides the framework for determining the electricity
rate, which may be either the benchmark rate worked out by the Committee
constituted by MoP, or a mutually negotiated rate with the generating
company. Clause 4(h) addresses the situation where any distribution company
is not able to enter into mutually negotiated rates with the generating company
and is also not willing to procure power at the benchmark rate worked out by
the Committee constituted by MoP, or is not able to make payment on weekly
basis, then such quantity of power shall be sold in the Power Exchanges.
Relevant paras of the directions are extracted below:-
“4. In the light of the present emergent circumstances, the following directions
issued under Section 11 of the Electricity Act:
a. All imported coal-based power plants shall operate and generate power to
their full capacity. Where the imported coal-based plant is under NCLT, the
Resolution Professional shall take steps to make it functional.
Order in Petition No. 137/MP/2023
Page 16 of 19

b. These plants will supply power in the first instance to the PPA holders. Any
surplus power left thereafter or any power for which there is no PPA will be
sold in the Power Exchanges.
….
…..
f. The PPA holders shall have an option to make payment to the generating
company according to the benchmark rate worked out by the Group or at a
rate mutually negotiated with the generating company.
…
h. Where any DISCOM/State is not able to enter into mutually negotiated rates
with the generating company and is also not willing to procure power at the
benchmark rate worked out by the Committee; or is not able to make weekly
payment then such quantity of power shall be sold in the Power Exchanges.
….”
16. It is clear from the above that in the event of the failure to agree on
mutually negotiated rates or to procure electricity at the benchmark rate or
failure to make payment, the consequence is to sell the power in the open
market. The obligation lies with the generating company to sell in the open
market. Clause 4(f) of the directions provides only two options for the tariff, i.e.
benchmark rate worked out by the Committee constituted by MoP or a rate
mutually negotiated with the generating company. Thus, no option is
contemplated to supply at the PPA rate. The PPA rate can be qualified as
mutually negotiated rates as per the directions provided that both parties
arrive at a fresh consensus dehors the existing PPA after issuance of the
MoP’s directions. Moreover, while laying down the obligations to make the
payment at the benchmark rate or mutually negotiated rate, there are no
corresponding obligations on the Respondent No.1 to purchase the power.
This is consistent with the objective of the directions, which provides that there
is no provision in the existing PPA to pass through the present high cost of
Order in Petition No. 137/MP/2023
Page 17 of 19

imported coal. The framework prescribed in the directions is an overarching
framework over the existing PPA; hence, the provisions of the PPA with
regard to tariff and power supply cannot be enforced during the operation of
the directions. Accordingly, the claim of Respondent No.1 to supply power as
per the tariff provided under the existing PPA instead of the benchmark tariff,
on the strength of their prior communications dated 23.11.2022 and
30.11.2022, does not sustain.
17. Further, the Commission, in its order dated 13.10.2025 in Petition No.
162/MP/2022, has decided the adverse financial impact under Section 11(2)
of the Act, which is also applicable for the power supplied to the Respondent
No.1 during December 2022. The adverse financial impact determined by the
Commission is over and above the rate agreed under the PPA, after
adjustment of the amount received through the benchmark rate. Relevant
Para 35 of the order dated 13.10.2025 in Petition No. 162/MP/2022:
“35. It is clear from the above that the provisions of the Act do not allow the Central Government
to decide the adverse financial impact under Section 11(1) of the Act, at which the distribution
licensees have to make the payment to the generating company. The objective behind the rates
determined by the Committee is limited for the interim period till the Commission decides the
compensation to be given to the generating company for ensuring continued operation of the
plant in terms of the arrangement of working capital since the adverse financial impact under
Section 11(2) of the Act is to be worked out based on actual cost on an ex-post basis. In the
instant case, the benchmark rate decided by the Committee, based on the indicative cost and
paid by Respondent No.1, partially offsets the adverse financial impact on the generating
company. Accordingly, the adverse financial impact determined by the Commission under
Section 11(2) of the Act needs to be adjusted by the payment made by Respondent No.1 over
and above the tariff. This can be represented by the following formulae:-
Adverse financial Impact u/s 11(2) of the Act (ΔP) =
{ Tariff (Pa) (to be assessed based on actual cost ) – Tariff (Pc) (approved by the
Appropriate Commission based on existing arrangement or contract) – Adjustments
Order in Petition No. 137/MP/2023
Page 18 of 19

Adjustment (Adj) = Tariff (Pp)( paid as per the benchmark rate decided by the
Committee of Central Government) - Tariff (Pc) (approved by the Appropriate
Commission as per the existing contract or arrangement )
(ΔP) = (Pa) - (Pc) - Adj.”
The Commission, in the above-mentioned order dated 13.10.2025, has held
that the benchmark rate determined by the Committee was allowed by the
MoP in its directions on an ex-ante basis for the limited purpose to meet the
working capital requirement for sustaining operations of the power plant. This
benchmark tariff partly covers the adverse financial impact, which is to be
further decided by the Commission under section 11(2) of the Act. Since the
Commission, in its above-mentioned order dated 13.10.2025, has already
decided on the adverse financial impact during the period of directions, the
prayer of the Petitioner to enforce the benchmark tariff has become
infructuous. The Petitioner is entitled to raise the bill as per the decision of the
Commission in its order in Petition No. 162/MP/2022, over and above the tariff
as per PPA paid by the Respondent No.1, after adjustment of the payment, if
any, made against the benchmark tariff. In view of the decision of the
Commission in its order in Petition No. 162/MP/2022, the prayer for interim
direction qua 80% of outstanding charges and liberty to claim the differential
amount does not arise.
18. Petition No.137/MP/2023 is disposed of in terms of the above.

The instant Petition has been filed by Power Grid Corporation of India Limited,
for truing up of the transmission tariff for the 2019-24 tariff period under the Central
Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2019
(hereinafter referred to as “the 2019 Tariff Regulations”) and determination of the
transmission tariff under the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and
Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2024 (hereinafter referred to as “the 2024 Tariff
Regulations”) for the 2024-29 tariff period in respect of the following transmission assets
(hereinafter referred to as the “transmission assets/Combined Asset”) under “System
Strengthening – XXVI” (hereinafter referred to as the “transmission project”) in the
Southern Region.
Asset-1: 2 Nos. 220 kV line bays at 400/220 kV Cochin East (pallikkara) Sub-
station for termination of Cochin East (Pallikara) – Aluva 220 kV D/C
line, to be implemented by KSEBL
Asset-2: 2 Nos. 400 kV line bays at Kozhikode (Areakode) Sub-station for
termination of North Trissur (Madakkathara) - Kozhikode (Areakode)
400 kV (Quad) D/C line, to be implemented by KSEBL
(Asset-1 and Asset-2 have been combined as on 1.4.2024 and have been
collectively referred to as "Combined Asset" for the 2024-29 tariff period.)

for 2024-29 block for the assets covered under this petition, as per para 17 and 18
above.

28. We have considered the Petitioner’s submissions and have also gone through
the record. We have noted that the entities covered under the MAT regime are paying
Income Tax as per the MAT rates notified for the respective financial year under the IT
Act, 1961, which is levied on the book profit of the entity computed as per Section 115
JB of the IT Act, 1961. Section 115 JB (2) defines book profit as net profit in the
statement of Profit and Loss prepared in accordance with Schedule-III of the Companies
Act, 2013, subject to some additions and deductions as mentioned in the IT Act, 1961.
Since the Petitioner has been paying the MAT rates of the respective financial year, the
notified MAT rates for the respective financial year shall be considered as an effective

“32. Interest on loan capital: (1) The loans arrived at in the manner indicated in

gross normative loan.

to be equal to the depreciation allowed for the corresponding year or period. In case
of decapitalization of assets, the repayment shall be adjusted by taking into account
cumulative repayment on a pro rata basis, and the adjustment should not exceed
cumulative depreciation recovered up to the date of de-capitalisation of such asset.
(4) Notwithstanding any moratorium period availed of by the generating company or
the transmission licensee, as the case may be, the repayment of the loan shall be
considered from the first year of commercial operation of the project and shall be
equal to the depreciation allowed for the year or part of the year.
(5) The rate of interest shall be the weighted average rate of interest calculated on
the basis of the actual loan portfolio or allocated loan portfolio;
Provided that if there is no actual loan outstanding for a particular year but
the normative loan is still outstanding, the last available weighted average rate of
interest of the loan portfolio for the project shall be considered;
Provided further that if the generating station or the transmission system, as
the case may be, does not have any actual loan, then the weighted average rate of
interest of the loan portfolio of the generating company or the transmission licensee
as a whole shall be considered.

emission control system commissioned subsequent to date of commercial operation
of the generating station or unit thereof, shall be the weighted average rate of
interest of the actual loan portfolio of the emission control system, and in the
absence of the actual loan portfolio, the weighted average rate of interest of the
generating company as a whole shall be considered, subject to a ceiling of 14%;

as the case may be, does not have any actual loan, then the rate of interest for a

Fees and Charges of Central Transmission Utility of India Limited (CTUIL)
69. The Petitioner has submitted that as per Regulation 99 of the 2024 Tariff
Regulations, the fees and charges of the CTUIL may be allowed separately through a
separate regulation. The Petitioner has further submitted that in the absence of such
regulation, the expenses of CTUIL will be borne by the Petitioner, which will be
recovered by the Petitioner as additional O&M Expenses through a separate Petition at

70. It is apt here to refer to Regulation 99 of the 2024 Tariff Regulations, which
provides as under:

(CTUIL): The fee and charges of CTUIL shall be allowed separately by the Commission
through a separate regulation:

of CTUIL shall be borne by Power Grid Corporation of India Ltd. (PGCIL) which shall be
recovered by PGCIL as additional O&M expenses through a separate petition.”
71. We have considered the Petitioner’s submissions and perused Regulation 99 of
the 2024 Tariff Regulations. In view of the explicit provision made under Regulation 99
of the 2024 Tariff Regulations, we permit the Petitioner, i.e., PGCIL, to bear the fees
and charges expenses of CTUIL and recover the same as additional O&M Expenses
through a separate Petition until such regulation is notified and issued by the
Commission.

project are as follows:

ORDER
The instant Petition has been filed by Power Grid Corporation of India Limited
(PGCIL), for truing up of the transmission tariff for the 2019-24 period under the Central
Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2019
(hereinafter referred to as “the 2019 Tariff Regulations”) and for the determination of
the transmission tariff for the 2024-29 period under the Central Electricity Regulatory
Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2024 (hereinafter referred
to as “the 2024 Tariff Regulations”) with respect to the following transmission assets
(hereinafter referred to as the “transmission assets / Combined Assets”) under
“Western Region System Strengthening Scheme-WRSS XXIII ” (hereinafter referred
to as the “transmission project”) in the Western Region.

(During the 2019-24 tariff period the assets are termed as “transmission asset”. The
transmission assets have been combined during the 2024-29 tariff period and for the
2024-29 tariff period the transmission assets are termed as “the Combined Asset”.)
2. The Petitioner has made the following prayers in the instant Petition:
“a) Approve the trued-up Transmission Tariff for 2019-24 block and transmission tariff
for 2024-29 block for the assets covered under this petition, as per para 14 and 15
above.
b) Admit the capital cost claimed and additional capitalization incurred during 2019-
24.
c) Allow the petitioner to recover the shortfall or refund the excess Annual Fixed
Charges, on account of Return on Equity due to change in applicable Minimum
Alternate/Corporate Income Tax rate as per the Income Tax Act, 1961 (as amended
from time to time) of the respective financial year directly without making any
application before the Commission as provided in Tariff Regulations 2019 and Tariff
Regulations, 2024 as per para 14 and 15 above for respective block.
d) Approve the reimbursement of expenditure by the beneficiaries towards petition
filing fee, and expenditure on publishing of notices in newspapers in terms of
Regulation 94 (1) Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions
of Tariff) Regulations, 2024, and other expenditure (if any) in relation to the filing of
petition.
e) Allow the petitioner to bill and recover RLDC fees & charges and Licensee fee
separately from the respondents in terms of Regulation 94 (3) and (4) Central
Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations,
2024.
f) Allow the petitioner to bill and adjust impact on Interest on Loan due to change in
Interest rate on account of floating rate of interest applicable during 2024-29 period,
if any, from the respondents.
g) Allow the petitioner to file a separate petition before the Commission for claiming the
overall security expenses and consequential IOWC on that security expenses as
mentioned at para 21 above.
h) Allow the petitioner to file a separate petition before he Commission for claiming the
overall insurance expenses and consequential IOWC on that insurance expenses
as mentioned at para 21 above.
i) Allow the petitioner to file a separate petition before the Commission for claiming the
overall capital spares as per actual as mentioned at Para 21 above.
j) Allow the petitioner to claim expenses of CTUIL borne by POWERGRID through a
separate petition as mentioned at para 22 above.
k) Allow the Petitioner to bill and recover GST on Transmission Charges separately
from the respondents, if GST on transmission is levied at any rate in future. Further,
any taxes including GST and duties including cess etc. imposed by any
statutory/Govt./municipal authorities shall be allowed to be recovered from the
beneficiaries.
Order in Petition No. 534/TT/2025 Page 3 of 67

and pass such other relief as the Commission deems fit and appropriate under the
circumstances of the case and in the interest of justice.”
Background
3. The brief facts of the case are as follows:
a. The Investment Approval (the IA) and expenditure sanction of the
transmission project was accorded by the Competent Authority of the
Petitioner on 5.5.2021 and communicated vide Memorandum No. C/CP/PA
2122-02-0A-IA001 dated 6.5.2021 at an estimated cost of ₹9234.00 lakh
including an IDC of ₹331.00 lakh based on December, 2020 price level.
b. The scope of the transmission project was discussed and agreed in 2nd
Western Region Standing Committee on Transmission (WRSCT) held on
21.5.2019, and in 1st Western Region Power Committee (WRPCTP)
meeting held on 11.1.2020.
c. The scope of work covered under the transmission project are as follows:
Part-A: Augmentation of ICTs at Wardha and Seoni 400/220 kV Sub-station
of POWERGRID and Morena 400/220 kV Sub-station of CWRTL in
the Western Region:

• All bay equipment already existing at Site for 400 kV bay and 220
kV bay (except surge arrester).
(ii) Seoni 400/220 kV Sub-station:
• 400/220 kV 500 MVA ICT-1 no.
• 400 kV ICT bay-1 no.
• 220 kV ICT bay-1 no.
(iii) Morena 400/220 kV Sub-station:
• 400/220 kV 500 MVA ICT-1 no.
• 400 kV ICT bay-1 no.

4. The Respondents are the distribution licensees and power departments, which
are procuring transmission services from the Petitioner, mainly the beneficiaries of the
Western Region.
5. The Petitioner has served a copy of the Petition on the Respondents, and notice
regarding the filing of this Petition was published in the newspapers in accordance with
Section 64 of the Electricity Act, 2003 (hereinafter referred to as “the Act”). No
comments or suggestions have been received from the general public in response to
the aforesaid notices published in the newspapers by the Petitioner. Madhya Pradesh
Power Management Company Limited (MPPMCL), Respondent No. 1, has filed its
reply vide affidavit dated 18.9.2025 and has raised the issues of grossing-up of Return
on Equity (RoE), Additional Capital Expenditure (ACE), determining the tariff for the
2024-29 period after prudence check, Initial Spares, effect of GST and Sharing of
Transmission Charges, licensee fee and RLDC fees & charges, Interest on Loan (IoL)
and security expenses and consequential IWC. In response, the Petitioner has filed its
rejoinder to the reply of MPPMCL vide affidavit dated 10.11.2025.
6. The hearing in this matter was held on 11.12.2025, and the order was reserved.
This order is passed after considering the submissions made by the Petitioner in the
Petition vide affidavit dated 25.11.2024 and subsequent affidavits dated 10.9.2025,
17.11.2025 and 26.12.2025, MPPMCL’s reply vide affidavit dated 18.9.2025 and the
Petitioner’s rejoinder affidavit dated 10.11.2025 to the MPPMCL’s reply.
7. Further, we noted that MPPMCL has repeatedly raised issues relating to the
allowance of tariff for the 2024-29 tariff period after prudence check, grossing up of
RoE, CGST and sharing of transmission charges in its replies, despite clear findings
of the Commission in various orders including in Petition Nos. 401/TT/2024,
Order in Petition No. 534/TT/2025 Page 6 of 67

25/TT/2025, 1/TT/2025, and 406/TT/2025, etc. Since, the issues raised by MPPMCL
and the clarifications filed by the Petitioner have already been dealt with in the
aforementioned Petitions, the same are not discussed in the instant order. The other
issues raised by MPPMCL have been considered in the succeeding paragraphs of this
order.
8. Having heard the representatives of the Petitioner and perused the material on
record, we proceed to dispose of the Petition in the succeeding paragraphs.

18. The Petitioner has submitted that the excess Initial Spares as deducted by the
Commission in Petition No. 332/TT/2022 have been re-claimed based on the overall
completion cost of the project in line with the APTEL’s judgment dated 14.9.2019 in
Appeal No. 74 of 2017.
Order in Petition No. 534/TT/2025 Page 10 of 67

19. We have considered the Petitioner’s submissions. Regulation 23 of 2019 Tariff
Regulations, provides as follows:
“23. Initial Spares: Initial spares shall be capitalised as a percentage of the Plant and
Machinery cost, subject to following ceiling norms:
……..
(d) Transmission system
(i) Transmission line - 1.00%
(ii) Transmission Sub-station
Green Field- 4.00%
Brown Field - 6.00%
(iii) Series Compensation devices and HVDC Station - 4.00%
(iv) Gas Insulated Sub-station (GIS)
Green Field- 5.00%
Brown Field - 7.00%
(v) Communication system - 3.50%
(vi) Static Synchronous Compensator - 6.00%
Provided that:
i. Plant and Machinery cost shall be considered as the original project cost excluding
IDC, IEDC, Land Cost and Cost of Civil Works. The generating company and the
transmission licensee for the purpose of estimating Plant and Machinery Cost,
shall submit the break-up of head wise IDC and IEDC in its tariff application;
ii. where the generating station has any transmission equipment forming part of the
generation project, the ceiling norms for initial spares for such equipment shall be
as per the ceiling norms specified for transmission system under these
regulations.”

been observed that the Petitioner has considered the expenditure of the civil works for
“Foundation for structures” under the Plant and Machinery Cost for determination of
the Initial Spares in respect of the transmission assets.

were not closed and liabilities were not finalized. However, in instant true up Petition,
ACE has been claimed on the basis of the actual payment made to the contractor after
receipt of the final invoices from the contractor and incorporating the amendments.

variation as the ACE approved by the Commission in Petition No. 322/TT/2022 was based
on the projections. In this regard it may be noted that while projecting the estimated ACE,
the contracts were not closed and the liabilities were not finalized. However, in the instant
true up Petition, the ACE has been claimed on the basis of the actual payments made to
the contractor after receipt of the final invoices from the contractor and incorporating the
amendments. MPPMCL has also submitted that the actual capital expenditure incurred by
the Petitioner after closing of the contract may happen to be higher or lower than the
estimated ACE prepared and submitted. MPPMCL has further submitted that the
payments were made after submission of the invoice and after reconciliation in accordance
with the contractual clause as per the provisions of the contract.
27. In response, the Petitioner has submitted that the ACE claimed is as per the 2019
Tariff Regulations, therefore, the capital cost may be allowed as claimed.

the Companies Act, 2013, subject to some additions and deductions as mentioned in

of the Income Tax Authorities shall be considered on the actual payment. However,

ORDER
The Petitioner, K.P. Energy Limited (hereinafter referred to as ‘the Petitioner’),
incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013, has made the present application
under Sections 14 of the Electricity Act, 2013 (hereinafter referred to as “the Act”)
read with Regulation 6(1) of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission
(Procedure, Terms and Conditions for the Grant of Trading Licence and other related
matters) Regulations, 2020 (hereinafter referred to as “the Trading Licence
Order in Petition No. 868/TD/2025
Page 1 of 6

Regulations”), amended from time to time, has filed the present Petition for the grant
of a Category ‘V’ trading licence for inter-State trading in electricity in the whole of
India.
2. In accordance with sub-Section (2) of Section 15 of the Act read with Clause
(4) of Regulation 6 of the Trading Licence Regulations, notices were published by
the Petitioner on 6.12.2025 in the ‘Business Standard’ (Chandigarh, Ahmedabad,
Jaipur, Mumbai, Pune, Bangalore, Bhubaneshwar, Chennai, Kochi, Kolkata, Delhi,
Lucknow, Guwahati and Bhopal editions) and in “The Financial Express”
(Hyderabad, Bengaluru, Chennai, Chandigarh, Kolkata, Mumbai, Pune, Ahmedabad
(including Gujarati language), Delhi and Lucknow editions). The Petitioner has
submitted that no objections have been received in response to the public notices.
3. In accordance with Regulation 3(3) of the Trading Licence Regulations, a
person applying for a Category 'V' trading licence should have a net worth of Rs. Two
crores and should have maintained a minimum current ratio and liquidity ratio of 1:1
as on the date of the Audited Special Balance Sheet accompanying the application.
As per the Audited Balance Sheet submitted by the Petitioner as on 31.8.2025, the
Petitioner possesses the required net worth and current ratio for the grant of a
Category 'V' trading licence. The Commission, vide its order dated 31.1.2026,
concluded that the Petitioner is prima facie qualified for the grant of a Category “V”
licence for inter-State trading in electricity.
4. On the above consideration, the Commission, vide its order dated 31.1.2026,
had proposed to grant a Category 'V' inter-State trading licence to the Petitioner. The
relevant portions of the said order dated 31.1.2026 are extracted as under:
Order in Petition No. 868/TD/2025
Page 2 of 6

“21. In accordance with Clause (2) of Regulation 3 of the Trading Licence
Regulations, the Petitioner should have at least one full-time professional
possessing qualifications and experience in power system operation and the
commercial aspects of power transfer, including finance, commerce and
accounts. With regard to full-time professionals, the Petitioner vide its affidavit
dated 31.12.2025 has submitted that Dr N Karunamoorthy, as the Director of
the Company, has 30 years of experience in onshore wind power technology
and Ms. Shabana Bajari, as Chief Financial Officer in the Accounts and
Finance Department, has 27 years of experience in financial management,
auditing, and strategic planning. Accordingly, as per the information submitted
by the Petitioner, it fulfils the requirements of Clause (2) of Regulation 3 of the
Trading Licence Regulations.
22. The Memorandum of Association authorises the Petitioner company to
engage in the transmission of electricity. The Petitioner, vide its affidavit dated
15.12.2025, has submitted that it will not carry out the transmission business
without surrendering the trading licence, if granted by the Commission.
23. On consideration of the above facts, after a preliminary examination,
we find that the Petitioner meets the requirements as specified in the Trading
Licence Regulations for the grant of a Category 'V' trading licence. In view
thereof, the Commission proposes to grant a Category 'V' trading licence to
the Petitioner. We direct that a notice under Clause (a) of Sub-section (5) of
Section 15 of the Act be issued inviting further suggestions or objections to
the proposal of the Commission.”
5. In line with the above-mentioned order dated 31.1.2026, notice under Clause
(a) of sub-Section (5) of Section 15 of the Act was published in all editions of the
Hindustan Times (English) and Amar Ujala (Hindi) on 6.2.2026. No suggestions or
objections have been received in response to the Commission’s notice.
6. The case was called out for the hearing on 19.2.2026. During the course of
the hearing, the learned counsel for the Petitioner submitted that no objection had
been received in response to the public notice published by the Commission under
sub-Section (5) of Section 15 of the Act. He further submitted that the Petitioner’s
company would comply with the requirements specified in the Trading Licence
Regulations during the subsistence of the trading licence, i.e., till 25 years, if granted.
Order in Petition No. 868/TD/2025
Page 3 of 6

7. Clause (9) of Regulation 6 of the Trading Licence Regulations provides as
under:
“(9) On consideration of further objections or suggestions received and the
reply of the applicant thereto, if any, the Commission may grant the licence or
reject the application, for reasons to be recorded in writing if the application
does not confirm to the provisions of the Act, the rules or regulations or
provisions of any other law for the time being in force:
Provided that no application shall be rejected, unless the applicant has been
given an opportunity of being heard.”
8. On consideration of the materials on record, we are satisfied that the
Petitioner company meets the requirements of the Act and the Trading Licence
Regulations for the grant of an inter-State trading licence for a Category 'V'.
9. The grant of the trading licence to the Petitioner (hereinafter referred to as
“the licensee”) is subject to the fulfilment of the following conditions throughout the
period of subsistence of the licence:
(a) The licensee shall comply with the provisions of the Act, the Rules, and the
Regulations, particularly Trading Licence Regulations, orders, and directions
issued by the Commission, from time to time, and any other law in force;
(b) The licensee shall comply with orders and directions issued by the
Commission from time to time;
(c) The licensee shall not engage in the business of transmission of electricity
during the period of subsistence of the trading licence, i.e., till 25 years;
(d) The licensee shall charge trading margin strictly in accordance with the
Order in Petition No. 868/TD/2025
Page 4 of 6

Trading Licence Regulations, as amended from time to time;
(e) The licensee shall maintain the net worth as mentioned in the order dated
31.8.2025, and current & liquidity ratio, as prescribed in the Trading Licence
Regulations, at all times.
(f) The licensee shall continue to be governed by the qualifications and
disqualifications specified in Chapter 2 of the Trading Licence Regulations
during the subsistence of the licence;
(g) The licensee shall continue to abide by the terms and conditions of the licence
specified in Chapter V of the Trading Licence Regulations, as amended from
time to time;
(h) The licensee shall regularly pay the annual licence fee in accordance with the
provisions of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Payment of
Fees) Regulations, 2012, as amended from time to time or any subsequent
enactment thereof;
(i) Non-compliance with the provisions of the Act, Rules, Regulations, and the
provisions of the Trading Licence Regulations shall make the licence of the
Petitioner liable for revocation;
(j) If the licensee fails to undertake trading in electricity within a year from the
date of the licence, the licence shall be liable for revocation in accordance
with the provisions of the Act and the Trading Licence Regulations; and
(k) The licensee shall submit all such reports or information as may be required
Order in Petition No. 868/TD/2025
Page 5 of 6

under Trading Licence Regulations or any other regulations of the
Commission or as per the directions of the Commission as may be issued
from time to time.
10. An extract of a copy of this order be sent to the Central Government (the
Ministry of Power) and the Central Electricity Authority in terms of sub-Section (7) of
Section 15 of the Act for their information and record.
11. Petition No. 868/TD/2025 is allowed in terms of the above.

19. Further, we observed that the APTEL vide its judgment dated 14.9.2019 in Appeal
No. 74 of 2017, observed that the Commission for the purpose of prudence check may
restrict the Initial Spares to the cost of the individual asset and later at the time of truing-up
allow Initial Spares as per the ceiling limit on the overall project cost. The relevant portion
of the said judgment is extracted here under:
Page 10 of 52

“18.13. ……… We do not agree with this methodology of restricting initial spares asset /
element wise as adopted by the Central Commission. The Central Commission to have a
prudence check on the initial spares, being restricted based on the individual asset wise
cost initially, but subsequently ought to have allowed as per the ceiling limits on the overall
project cost basis during the true- up.”
20. In terms of the aforementioned judgment, the Initial Spares are to be allowed as per
the prescribed norms on the overall project cost, which can ideally be determined only when
all the transmission assets are combined. However, in the instant Petition, the Petitioner
has combined Asset-I, Asset-II, and Asset-III as Combined Asset and Asset-IV separately
for the 2019–24 tariff period. Accordingly, the admissibility of Initial Spares is required to
be examined separately for the Combined Asset (Asset-I to Asset-III), and for Asset-IV.
21. We are of view that in case the Initial Spares are not required to be re-calculated as
a whole based on the overall project cost in accordance with the APTEL’s judgement dated
14.9.2019 during the 2019-24 tariff period and accordingly, the claim of the Petitioner in
this regard is rejected.

72. Regulation 18 of the 2024 Tariff Regulations provides as under:
“18. Debt-Equity Ratio: (1) For new projects, the debt-equity ratio of 70:30 as on date of

date of each investment:

licensee, as the case may be, while issuing share capital and investment of internal
resources created out of its free reserve for the funding of the project, shall be reckoned as

26. We have considered the Petitioner’s submissions and have also gone through
the record. We noted that the entities covered under the MAT regime are paying Income
Tax as per the MAT rates notified for the respective financial year under the IT Act,
1961, which is levied on the book profit of the entity computed as per Section 115 JB of
the IT Act, 1961. Section 115 JB (2) defines book profit as net profit in the statement of
Profit and Loss prepared in accordance with Schedule-II of the Companies Act, 2013,
subject to some additions and deductions as mentioned in the IT Act, 1961. Since the
Petitioner has been paying the MAT rates of the respective financial year, the notified
MAT rates for the respective financial year shall be considered as an effective tax rate
for the purpose of grossing up the RoE for truing up the 2019-24 tariff period in terms of
the provisions of the 2019 Tariff Regulations. Interest imposed on any additional income
tax demand as per the Assessment Order of the Income Tax Authorities shall be
considered on the actual payment. However, the penalty (for default on the part of the
Assessee), if any, imposed shall not be taken into account for the purpose of grossing
up the rate of RoE. Any under-recovery or over-recovery of the grossed-up rates on the
RoE after truing up shall be recovered or refunded to the beneficiaries or the long-term
customers, as the case may be, on a year-to-year basis. Therefore, the following

of decapitalization of assets, the repayment shall be adjusted by taking into account
cumulative repayment on a pro rata basis, and the adjustment should not exceed
cumulative depreciation recovered up to the date of de-capitalisation of such asset.

the transmission licensee, as the case may be, the repayment of the loan shall be
considered from the first year of commercial operation of the project and shall be
equal to the depreciation allowed for the year or part of the year.
(5) The rate of interest shall be the weighted average rate of interest calculated on
the basis of the actual loan portfolio or allocated loan portfolio;

the normative loan is still outstanding, the last available weighted average rate of
interest of the loan portfolio for the project shall be considered;
