22. We have considered the submissions of the Petitioner, BPC, and CTUIL. The
proviso to Clause 2.15.2 of the RfP provides that “if for any reason attributable to the
BPC, the said activities are not completed by the Selected Bidder within the above
period of ten (10) days as mentioned in this clause, such period of 10 days shall be
extended, on a day-to-day basis till the end of the Bid validity period”. As per the
above provision, the selected bidder was required to complete all the activities,
including the acquisition of the SPVs, by 26.9.2025. Though the LoI was issued on
16.9.2025, BPC, vide its letter dated 16.10.2025, in terms of Clause 2.15.2 of the
RfP, extended the deadline to 16.10.2025 for completion of all activities by the
successful bidder. The selected bidder furnished the Contract Performance
Guarantee in favour of the Nodal Agency (CTUIL) for Rs. Rs. 20 crore on 16.10.2025
and acquired a hundred per cent equity-holding in the applicant company on
16.10.2025 after execution of the Share Purchase Agreement. As per clause 2.15.4
of the RfP, TSP is required to apply to the Commission for the grant of a
transmission licence within five working days of the issuance of the acquisition of the
SPV to the successful bidder. The successful bidder, namely Power Grid
Corporation of India Limited, acquired the SPV on 16.10.2025. Accordingly, the TSP
has filed the instant Petition for the grant of a transmission licence through e-filing on
24.10.2025.
23. Considering the material on record, we are prima facie of the view that the
Petitioner satisfies the conditions for the grant of an inter-State transmission licence
under Section 15 of the Act, read with the Transmission Licence Regulations for

a transmission licence aforesaid. The objections or suggestions, if any, shall be filed

the provisions of the TSA, the applicable provisions of the Electricity Act, 2003, and

25. It is observed that as per Article 5.1.1 of the TSA, the TSP, at its own cost and
expense, shall be responsible for designing, constructing, erecting, testing, and

regard, the Petitioner has submitted that it will implement the Project in accordance
with the provisions of the TSA, including Articles 16.4, 5.1.1, and 5.4 of the TSA. It is
expected that while carrying out the survey, the Petitioner has complied with the

CENTRAL ELECTRICITY REGULATORY COMMISSION
NEW DELHI

ORDER
The Petitioner, K.P. Energy Limited (hereinafter referred to as ‘the Petitioner’),
incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013, read with Regulation 6(1) of the
Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Procedure, Terms and Conditions for the
Grant of Trading Licence and other related matters) Regulations, 2020 (hereinafter
Order in Petition No. 868/TD/2025
Page 1 of 14

referred to as “the Trading Licence Regulations”), amended from time to time, has
filed the present Petition for the grant of a Category ‘V’ trading licence for inter-State
trading in electricity in the whole of India.
Hearing Dated 20.11.2025
2. During the hearing, the learned counsel for the Petitioner reiterated the
submissions made in the Petition. The Petitioner, vide Record of Proceedings
(hereinafter referred to as “RoP’) for the hearing dated 20.11.2025, was directed to
submit the following information on an affidavit:
(i) Audited special balance sheet in place of provisional or unaudited
statement (within 30 days preceding the date of filing of the Petition), along
with Auditor’s certificate/ report, Profit & Loss Statement and Schedules and
notes to accounts etc.,
(ii) Revised Net Worth Certificate based on the audited special balance sheet,
not on a provisional or unaudited statement.
(iii) Demonstrate compliance with the net worth and current & liquidity ratio
requirements as per the Trading Licence Regulations, 2020, by submitting the
necessary audited special balance sheet.
(iv) Rectify the contradictory declaration in Form 1, ensuring that the
statement aligns with the Memorandum of Association, which authorises
transmission activities.
(v) Compliance affidavit in terms of Regulation 6(4) of the Trading Licence
Regulations, 2020.
(vi) Declaration to the effect that the Petitioner does not hold any transmission
licence and that it shall not carry out the business of transmission of electricity
Order in Petition No. 868/TD/2025
Page 2 of 14

during the subsistence of the inter-State trading licence, if granted by the
Commission.
(vii) Clarify whether the profile of professionals submitted in the Petition is full-
time in the Petitioner company as per the requirement of Technical
Qualifications under Regulation 3 of the Trading Licence Regulation, 2020.
3. In compliance with the RoP dated 20.11.2025, the Petitioner vide its affidavit
dated 15.12.2025 has furnished the information regarding (i), (ii), (iv) to (vi) above,
which have been taken on record. With regard to (iii) and (vii) above, the Petitioner
has submitted as under:
a In compliance with the Net Worth, Current Ratio and Liquidity Ratio
requirements in terms of Regulation 9(2) of the Trading Regulations, 2020,
Regulation 9(1) of the Trading Regulations, 2020 mandates that the Current
Ratio and Liquidity Ratio shall be maintained at 1:1 throughout the financial
year. The proviso to Regulation 9(2) stipulates that where a Trading
Licensee’s current ratio or liquidity ratio at the end of the financial year is
below 1:1, the licensee is required to maintain additional Net Worth
equivalent to 100% of the Net Worth mandated for its respective category.
Under Regulation 3(a), a Category V Trading Licensee is required to
maintain a minimum Net Worth of Rs. 2 crore. In the present case, although
the Applicant’s liquidity ratio, as per the Special Balance Sheet, is 0.92, its
Net Worth stands at Rs. 341.4461 crore, which is well in excess of the
additional Net Worth requirement. Accordingly, the Applicant satisfies the
financial eligibility criteria for the grant of a Category-V Trading Licence.
Order in Petition No. 868/TD/2025
Page 3 of 14

b The professionals furnished by the Applicant in its Application are fully
compliant with Regulation 3 of the Trading Regulations, 2020. Further, the
personnel engaged by the Applicant are full-time employees of the Applicant.
Hearing dated 23.12.2025
4. During the hearing, the learned counsel for the Petitioner submitted that the
Petitioner has filed its compliance affidavit dated 15.12.2025 in terms of the RoPs
dated 20.11.2025, furnishing all the requisite information/ clarification ought by the
Commission therein for the grant of a Category ‘V’ trading licence.
5. Vide RoP dated 23.12.2025, the Petitioner was directed to submit the

Das has also been shown as a full-time professional in Petition No.
871/TD/2025 filed by KPI Green Energy Limited. Clarify the above
discrepancy and comply with Regulation 3 of the Central Electricity
Regulatory Commission (Procedure, Terms and Conditions for Grant of
Trading Licence and Other Related Matters) Regulations, 2020 and confirm
that the professionals are fulltime employees of the Petitioner company in

(b) As per Regulation 6(3) Trading Licence Regulations, 2020 the Petitioner is

one economic daily newspaper, within seven days after making the

However, the Petitioner published the notices of its application on 6.12.2025.
Order in Petition No. 868/TD/2025
Page 4 of 14

Reason for non-compliance with the provisions of the Trading Licence
Regulations, 2020.
6. In compliance with the RoP dated 23.12.2025, the Petitioner, vide affidavit
dated 31.12.2025, has submitted as under:
(a) The details of Dr. Alok Das have been unintentionally produced in the
Application of KP Energy Limited in the instant Petition. The Petitioner hereby
annexes the profile of Dr N Karunamoorthy, who is a permanent employee of
K.P. Energy Limited and holds requisite qualification in terms of Regulation
3(2) of Trading Regulations, 2020, i.e., he has a degree in engineering with 30
years of experience in the field.
(b) The Petitioner has clarified that the Applicant waited until the first
hearing was concluded before publishing the notice in newspapers, to ensure
compliance with the regulations. The notice was published in good faith on
6.12.2025 in Business Standard, Financial Express and The Assam Tribune,
and the Applicant submits that the delay has not caused any harm to the
Commission or to the public.
Hearing Dated 21.1.2026
7. During the course of the hearing, the learned counsel for the Petitioner
submitted that the Petitioner company has complied with the requirements of the
Trading Licence Regulations. With regard to the liquidity ratio, the learned counsel
for the Petitioner submitted that the application of the liquidity ratio requirement in the
present case may be relaxed, in exercise of its powers under the Trading Licence
Regulations. In support of the said prayer, learned counsel placed its reliance on
earlier orders passed by the Commission, wherein relaxation of the liquidity ratio
requirement was granted in appropriate cases, having regard to the overall financial
Order in Petition No. 868/TD/2025
Page 5 of 14

strength of the applicant and compliance with other regulatory requirements. After
hearing the learned counsel for the Petitioner, the matter was reserved for Order.
8. We have perused the documents available on record. Regulation 6 of the
Trading Licence Regulations provides for the procedure for the grant of a trading
licence as under:
“6. Procedure for grant of licence
(1) Any person desirous of undertaking inter-State trading in electricity shall
make an application to the Commission for grant of licence in the manner
specified in Form-I appended to these regulations and such application shall
be accompanied by-
(a) Such application fee as prescribed by the Central Government from
time to time and shall be paid as per the procedure specified in Central
Electricity Regulatory Commission (Payment of Fees) Regulations,
2012, as amended from time to time or any statutory re-enactment
thereof.
(b) Copies of the annual reports in case of the persons incorporated
under the Companies Act, 1956 or Companies Act, 2013 including
audited accounts along with the Directors' Report, Auditors' Report, the
Schedules and notes to accounts for one Year immediately preceding
the Year in which the application has been made and the audited
special balance sheet as on any date falling within 30 days immediately
preceding the date of filing the application.
(2) The Applicant shall post complete application along with annexures and
enclosures on its website so as to facilitate access to the application by any
person through internet and shall keep them on the website till the disposal of
the application.
(3) The Applicant shall within 7 days after making such application, publish a
notice of its application, in two daily newspapers in Form II, with the following
particulars, namely:
************
(4) The Applicant shall within 7 days from the date of publication of the notice
as aforesaid submit to the Commission on affidavit the details of the notice
published and shall also file the original complete page of the newspaper in
which the notice has been published.
(5) The Applicant shall allow a period of 30 days to the public to file objections
or suggestions to the notice of application published in the newspapers.
Order in Petition No. 868/TD/2025
Page 6 of 14

(6) The Applicant shall file its reply before the Commission within 30 days
from the last date of receipt of objections or suggestions from the public.
(7) The Commission after consideration of the objections or suggestions
received in response to the notice published by the Applicant and its reply
may reject the application or may propose to grant licence.
(8) When the Commission proposes to grant licence, it shall publish a notice
of its proposal in two daily newspapers, as the Commission may consider
appropriate, stating the name and address of the person to whom it proposes
to issue the licence and with such other details as the Commission considers
appropriate, to invite further objections or suggestions to its proposal.”
9. The Petitioner has submitted the application as per Form I, along with the
requisite fees.
10. The Petitioner has uploaded the application for the grant of a trading licence
on its website in terms of Clause (3) of Regulation 6 of the Trading Licence
Regulations, 2020, and further placed on record the relevant copies of the
newspapers in original in which notice of its application has been published. As per
Regulation 6 (3) of the Trading Licence Regulations, 2020, the Petitioner was
required to publish notices of its application within 7 days of filing, in two daily
newspapers with circulation in each of the five regions, in addition to publications
from Delhi, including one economic daily. However, although the present Petition was
filed on 26.9.2025, the notices were published only on 6.12.2025 with a delay of
approximately two months. In this regard, the Petitioner has submitted that notices
were published in good faith, and the delay has not caused any harm to the
Commission or to the general public. The Petitioner, vide its additional affidavit dated
15.12.2025, has submitted that notices under sub-section (2) of Section 15 of the Act
read with Clause (4) of Regulation 6 of the Trading Licence Regulations, 2020 have
been published by the Petitioner company on 6.12.2025 in the ‘Business Standard’
Order in Petition No. 868/TD/2025
Page 7 of 14

(Chandigarh, Ahmedabad, Jaipur, Mumbai, Pune, Bangalore, Bhubaneshwar,
Chennai, Kochi, Kolkata, Delhi, Lucknow, Guwahati and Bhopal editions) and in “The
Financial Express” (Hyderabad, Bengaluru, Chennai, Chandigarh, Kolkata, Mumbai,
Pune, Ahmedabad (including Gujarati language), Delhi and Lucknow editions). The
Petitioner has submitted that no objections have been received in response to the
public notices. It is noted that the notices were required to be published within seven
days after making the application. In our view, the Petitioner has published the
notices with a delay of two months. However, no prejudice has been caused to the
general public for such a delay. Accordingly, considering the submissions of the
Petitioner, we condone such a delay with direction to the Petitioner to comply with
the provisions of the Trading Licence Regulations, 2020, in a letter and spirit in
future.
11. The Petitioner Company was incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956,
on 8.1.2010 and subsequently the status was changed from private to public limited
company on 11.5.20215. Clauses 1 and 2 of the Memorandum of Association
provide that the Petitioner is authorised to undertake trading in electricity. We note
that trading in electricity is covered under the Memorandum of Association of the
Petitioner. Clauses 1and 2 of the Memorandum of Association of the Petitioner
company read as under:
“1. To manufacture, produce, install, commission, operate, prepare, pay,
import, buy, sell, supply, distribute or otherwise deal in all energy
production and conversion activities in all its form including of various
renewable sources like solar and wind energy, all forms of biomass,
geothermal energy, hydel energy, tidal and wave energy also effective and
efficient utilization of conventional energy forms like coal, oil, gas, electricity
and all equipments at may be associated with such energy related activities.

17. As per the above special audited balance sheet dated 31.8.2025, the
Petitioner fulfills the requirement of net worth for the grant of Category ‘V’ trading
licensee. However, the Petitioner does not meet the requirement of the liquidity ratio
specified in Regulation 3(3)(b) of the Trading Licence Regulations. As per Regulation
9 of the Trading Licence Regulations, the trading licensee is required to maintain the
liquidity ratio of 1:1 at all times. Relevant portion of Regulation 9 of the Trading
Licence Regulations is extracted as under:
“9. Obligations of the Trading Licensee
The Trading Licensee shall be subject to the following obligations, namely: -
Order in Petition No. 868/TD/2025
Page 11 of 14

(1) The Trading Licensee shall comply with the requirements of laws in force
and, in particular, the Act, the Rules and the Regulations, Grid Code, orders
and directions issued by the Commission from time to time and any of the
State Electricity Regulatory Commissions in accordance with law.
(2) The Trading Licensee shall maintain the Net Worth in accordance with
Regulation 3 of these regulations at all times and shall maintain Current Ratio
of 1:1 and Liquidity Ratio of 1:1 at the end of every financial year:
Provided that if the current ratio or the liquidity ratio at the end of the financial
year is less than 1:1, then the Trading Licensee shall be required to maintain
additional Net Worth of 100% of the Net Worth stipulated for the respective
category of trading licence.”
18. Since the Petitioner was not fulfilling the liquidity ratio requirement, the
Commission, vide RoP dated 20.11.2025, directed the Petitioner to demonstrate
compliance with the net worth and current and liquidity ratio requirements under the
Trading Licence Regulations, 2020, by submitting the requisite audited special
balance sheet. The Petitioner, vide affidavit dated 15.12.2025, clarified that it
satisfies the financial eligibility criteria under the proviso to the relevant regulations,
notwithstanding the shortfall in the liquidity ratio. Further, during the course of the
hearing held on 21.01.2026, the learned counsel for the Petitioner prayed that the
liquidity ratio requirement be relaxed, submitting that the Petitioner has
demonstrated adequate financial soundness for undertaking electricity trading and
fulfils all other prescribed criteria.
19. With regard to relaxation of liquidity ratio, the Commission vide order dated
7.7.2025 in Petition No. 557/TD/2025 had relaxed the liquidity ratio requirement, as
the company demonstrated financial soundness in terms of liquidity for conducting
electricity trade and fulfilled all other necessary criteria. The relevant extract of the
Order is extracted as under:
Order in Petition No. 868/TD/2025
Page 12 of 14

“17. The Commission, upon perusal of the submissions, observed that
although the Petitioner does not fulfil the liquidity ratio requirement as
stipulated under the applicable Regulations, the Petitioner possesses a net
worth of ₹4,96,804 lakh, which is several times higher than the minimum net
worth required for a Category-I trading license. In view of the substantial
financial strength demonstrated by the Petitioner, the Commission, in exercise
of its powers under Regulation 17 of the Central Electricity Regulatory
Commission (Procedure, Terms and Conditions for grant of Trading Licence
and other related matters) Regulations, hereby relaxes the requirement of the
liquidity ratio in the present case. However, as specified under Regulation 9(2)
of Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Procedure, Terms and
Conditions for grant of trading licence and other related matters) Regulations,
2020, the Petitioner shall be required to maintain the additional net worth of
100% of the net worth stipulated for the respective category of trading licence.
20. It is noted that although the Petitioner does not fulfil the liquidity ratio
requirement as stipulated under the applicable Regulations, the Petitioner possesses
a net worth of Rs. 341.4461 crore, which is several times higher than the minimum
net worth required for a Category ‘V’ trading licence. In light of the above order dated
7.7.2025 and in view of the substantial financial strength demonstrated by the
Petitioner, the Commission, in exercise of its powers under Regulation 17 of the
Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Procedure, Terms and Conditions for
grant of Trading Licence and other related matters) Regulations, hereby relaxes the
requirement of the liquidity ratio in the present case. However, as specified under
Regulation 9(2) of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Procedure, Terms
and Conditions for grant of trading licence and other related matters) Regulations,
2020, the Petitioner shall be required to maintain the additional net worth of 100% of
the net worth stipulated for the respective category of trading licence.
21. In accordance with Clause (2) of Regulation 3 of the Trading Licence
Regulations, the Petitioner should have at least one full-time professional possessing
qualifications and experience in power system operation and the commercial aspects
Order in Petition No. 868/TD/2025
Page 13 of 14

of power transfer, including finance, commerce and accounts. With regard to full-time
professionals, the Petitioner vide its affidavit dated 31.12.2025 has submitted that Dr
N Karunamoorthy, as the Director of the Company, has 30 years of experience in
onshore wind power technology and Ms. Shabana Bajari, as Chief Financial Officer
in the Accounts and Finance Department, has 27 years of experience in financial
management, auditing, and strategic planning. Accordingly, as per the information
submitted by the Petitioner, it fulfils the requirements of Clause (2) of Regulation 3 of
the Trading Licence Regulations.
22. The Memorandum of Association authorises the Petitioner company to
engage in the transmission of electricity. The Petitioner, vide its affidavit dated
15.12.2025, has submitted that it will not carry out the transmission business without
surrendering the trading licence, if granted by the Commission.
23. On consideration of the above facts, after a preliminary examination, we find
that the Petitioner meets the requirements as specified in the Trading Licence
Regulations for the grant of a Category 'V' trading licence. In view thereof, the
Commission proposes to grant a Category 'V' trading licence to the Petitioner. We
direct that a notice under Clause (a) of Sub-section (5) of Section 15 of the Act be
issued inviting further suggestions or objections to the proposal of the Commission.
24. The Petition shall be listed for a final hearing on 19.2.2026.

ORDER
The Petitioner, Power Grid Corporation of India Limited (PGCIL) has filed this
Petition for the truing up of the transmission tariff for the 2019-24 period under the
Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff)
Regulations, 2019 (hereinafter referred to as “the 2019 Tariff Regulations”) and the
determination of the transmission tariff for the 2024-29 period under the Central
Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2024
(hereinafter referred to as “the 2024 Tariff Regulations”) for the following assets
(hereinafter referred to as the “Combined Assets”) under “Northern Region System
Strengthening Scheme-XVI” in the Northern Region (hereinafter referred to as the
‘transmission project’):
Asset-I: LILO of both circuits of 400 kV D/C Kishenpur Wagoora
Transmission Line along with bays at New Wanpoh and 1 No. 315 MVA,
400/220 kV ICT-I along with associated bays at New Wanpoh and 3 Nos.
220 kV line bays;
Asset-II: 400/220 kV 315 MVA ICT-II along with associated bays at New
Wanpoh Substation;
Asset-III: 400 kV 125 MVAr Bus Reactor along with associated bays at
New Wanpoh Substation;
Asset-IV: 400 kV D/C Kishenpur- New Wanpoh Line along with associated
bays at both ends.
2. The Petitioner has made the following prayers in the instant Petition:
“a) Approve the trued-up Transmission Tariff for 2019-24 block and transmission tariff
for 2024-29 block for the asset covered under this petition, as per para 16 and 17
above.
b) Admit the capital cost claimed and additional capitalization incurred during 2019-24
and projected additional capitalization to be incurred during 2024-29.
c) Allow the petitioner to recover the shortfall or refund the excess Annual Fixed
Charges, on account of Return on Equity due to change in applicable Minimum
Alternate/Corporate Income Tax rate as per the Income Tax Act, 1961 (as amended
from time to time) of the respective financial year directly without making any application
Order in Petition No. 564/TT/2025 Page 3 of 46

before the Commission as provided in Tariff Regulations, 2019 and Tariff Regulations,
2024 as per para 16 and 17 above for respective block.
d) Approve the reimbursement of expenditure by the beneficiaries towards petition filing
fee, and expenditure on publishing of notices in newspapers in terms of Regulation 94
(1) Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff)
Regulations, 2024, and other expenditure (if any) in relation to the filing of petition.
e) Allow the petitioner to bill and recover RLDC fees & charges and Licensee fee,
separately from the respondents in terms of Regulation 94 (3) and (4) Central Electricity
Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2024.
f) Allow the petitioner to bill and adjust impact on Interest on Loan due to change in
Interest rate on account of floating rate of interest applicable during 2024-29 period, if
any, from the respondents.
g) Allow the petitioner to file a separate petition before Hon’ble Commission for claiming
the overall security expenses and consequential IOWC on that security expenses as
mentioned at para 23 above.
h) Allow the petitioner to file a separate petition before Hon’ble Commission for claiming
the overall insurance expenses and consequential IOWC on that insurance expenses
as mentioned at para 23 above.
i) Allow the petitioner to file a separate petition before Hon’ble Commission for claiming
the overall capital spares at the end of tariff block as per actual as mentioned at Para 23
above.
j) Allow the petitioner to claim expenses of CTUIL borne by POWERGRID through a
separate petition as mentioned at para 24 above.
k) Allow the Petitioner to bill and recover GST on Transmission Charges separately from
the respondents, if GST on transmission is levied at any rate in future. Further, any taxes
including GST and duties including cess etc. imposed by any statutory/Govt./municipal
authorities shall be allowed to be recovered from the beneficiaries and
l) Pass such other relief as Hon’ble Commission deems fit and appropriate under the
circumstances of the case and in the interest of justice.”
Background
3. The brief facts of the case are as follows:
a. The Investment Approval (IA) for the transmission project was accorded by
the Board of Directors of the Petitioner vide Memorandum dated 6.7.2010,
with an estimated cost of ₹75264 lakh, including an Interest During
Construction (IDC) of ₹6331 lakh, based on the 1st Quarter 2010 price level.
b. The Revised Cost Estimate-II (RCE-II) of the transmission project was
accorded by the Board of Directors of the Petitioner vide Memorandum
Order in Petition No. 564/TT/2025 Page 4 of 46

dated 31.3.2017 with an estimated cost of ₹75794 lakh, including the IDC of
₹12622 lakh, based on the October 2016 price level.
c. The entire scope of the transmission project is complete and covered under
the instant Petition. The details of the scope of work are as under:
Transmission Lines:
i) LILO of both circuits of Kishenpur-Wagoora 400 kV D/C Line at New
Wanpoh: 8 km;
ii) Kishenpur-New Wanpoh 400 kV Line: 132 km (125 km Double circuit+7
km Multi circuit in Pir Panjal Mountain Range).
Sub-stations:
i) New 2x315 MVA (7x105 MVA Single Phase Units considered), 400/220
kV New Wanpoh Substation;
ii) Extension of 400/220 kV Kishenpur Substation.
Reactive Compensation:
i) 1X125 MVAr Bus Reactor at New Wanpoh.
d. The Commission, vide order dated 9.10.2018 in Petition No.161/TT/2017,
trued-up the transmission tariff in respect of Asset-I from the COD to
31.3.2014 and determined the transmission tariff for the 2014-19 period.
The transmission tariff in respect of Assets-II and III from the COD to
31.3.2019 was approved by the Commission vide order dated 31.3.2016 in
Petition No.111/TT/2013. The transmission tariff in respect of Asset-IV from
the COD to 31.3.2019 was allowed by the Commission vide order dated
7.3.2019 in Petition No.62/TT/2018.
e. The Commission, vide order dated 1.3.2022 in Petition No. 378/TT/2020
trued-up of the transmission tariff with respect to Assets-I, II, III and IV for the
2014-19 period and determined the Annual Fixed Charges (AFC) in respect
Order in Petition No. 564/TT/2025 Page 5 of 46

of the Combined Assets for the 2019-24 tariff period. Further, the
Commission vide its order dated 4.7.2024 in Review Petition No. 6/RP/2023
in Petition No. 378/TT/2020, revised O&M Expenses and IWC which
consequently revised AFC for the 2019-24 tariff period for the Combined
Assets.
4. The Respondents are the distribution licensees, transmission licensees and
power departments, mainly beneficiaries of the Northern Region, which are procuring
transmission services from the Petitioner.
5. The Petitioner has served a copy of the Petition on the Respondents, and
notices regarding the filing of this Petition have been published in the newspapers in
accordance with Section 64 of the Electricity Act, 2003 (hereinafter referred to as “the
Act”). No comments or suggestions have been received from the general public in
response to the aforesaid notices published in the newspapers by the Petitioner.
6. None of the Respondents has filed their reply to the instant Petition.
7. The hearing in this matter was held on 6.11.2025, and the order was reserved.
8. This order is issued considering the submissions of the Petitioner vide affidavits
dated 7.11.2024, 2.9.2025 and 13.11.2025.
9. Having heard the Petitioner’s representatives and perused the material available
on record, we proceed to dispose of the Petition.
Truing-up of the Annual Fixed Charges for the 2019-24 Tariff Period
10. The details of the trued-up transmission charges claimed by the Petitioner for

project cost basis during the true-up.”

ORDER
The present IA has been filed by the Petitioner, Lakadia-Vadodara
Transmission Project Limited (‘LVTPL’) seeking amendment of Petition No.
256/MP/2023 to include various Change in Law and Force Majeure events under the
Transmission Service Agreement dated 23.4.2019 (‘TSA’) and the Electricity (Timely
Recovery of Costs due to Change in Law) Rules, 2021 (‘CIL Rules’), which have
impacted the Project of the Petitioner. Petition No. 256/MP/2023 was filed for seeking
verification of the calculation of the impact due to Change in Law events on the cost
of implementation of the Petitioner’s transmission project, and consequent
adjustment in the monthly transmission charges.
Background
2. Petition No. 256/MP/2023 was filed by the Petitioner, which was heard at
length extensively by the Commission, and the order was reserved on 19.2.2025. The
Petitioner and the Respondents had also filed their respective written submissions in
the matter pursuant to the liberty granted by the Commission.
3. Now, the Petitioner has approached the Commission through the present IA
seeking the amendment to the Petition No. 256/MP/2023. The Petitioner has made
the following submissions in the IA:
(i) The Petitioner had previously approached the Commission on 7.7.2021
Order in IA No. 89/2025 in Petition No. 256/MP/2023 3

vide Petition No. 158/MP/2021 inter alia for the in-principle declaratory reliefs
in view of the Force Majeure and Change in Law events impacting its Project,
and a declaratory relief with respect to the Petitioner’s scope of work. During
the pendency of Petition No. 158/MP/2021, the Change in Law Rules, 2021,
were notified by the Ministry of Power (MoP). Thereafter, a clarification was
issued by the MoP stating that CIL Rules are applicable to Change in Law
events that have occurred on or after the notification of the CIL Rules in the
official gazette, i.e., 22.10.2021. The Clarification Order categorically states
that all changes in Law events that have occurred prior to the notification of the
CIL Rules shall be dealt with in accordance with the prevalent dispensation/
rule position at the time of occurrence of the event.
(ii) The Commission adjudicated upon the issue concerning the Petitioner’s
claim regarding a change in the scope of work, and vide order dated 1.8.2022,
the Petitioner was directed to approach the Commission for all other issues
concerning Force Majeure and Change in Law events after the completion of
the Project. Accordingly, in terms of the liberty granted by the Commission vide
Order dated 1.8.2022 in Petition No. 158/MP/2021, the Petitioner filed the
Petition No. 256/MP/2023 after the commissioning of its Project under CIL
Rules for verification of the impact of the Change in Law events that occurred
after 22.10.2021.
(iii) A plain reading of the CIL Rules indicated, prima facie, that the merits of
such post-CIL Rules, Change in Law claims lay beyond the scope of the
Commission’s jurisdiction under the CIL Rules. It was, therefore, the
Petitioner’s consistent position that the merits of a CIL event are not open to
examination in a Petition filed under Rules 3(7) and 3(8) of the CIL Rules. The
limited test for the grant of relief under these provisions was to establish that
the event contractually fell within the ambit of Article 12 of the TSA.
(iv) The final order was reserved in Petition No. 256/MP/2023 on 19.2.2025.
However, the Commission vide its Order dated 20.04.2025 in Petition No.
131/MP/2024, Mumbai Urja Marg Limited v. Maharashtra State Electricity
Distribution Company Limited & Ors. (MUML Order) held that Rule 3(8) of the
CIL Rules does not restrict the Commission’s power to adjudicate the validity
or merits of a Change in Law event. The Order thus represents a significant
departure from the understanding prevailing at the time of filing of the present
Petition with respect to the remit of the CIL Rules and squarely addresses the
jurisdictional question forming the basis of the Petitioner’s earlier position.
(v) The Order in the MUML case was delivered subsequently on 20.4.2025,
mandating adjudication of Change in Law claims before recovery. Subsequent
to the issuance of the order in the MUML matter, CTUIL, on 1.5.2025 directed
the Petitioner to revise its bills raised from 31.3.2025 onwards. Accordingly,
such recovery has now stopped w.e.f. March 2025. Given that Change in Law
claims are now required to be adjudicated by the Commission, therefore, to
Order in IA No. 89/2025 in Petition No. 256/MP/2023 4

avoid multiplicity of proceedings and ensure wholistic overview of the
uncontrollable events that had impacted the Project, the Petitioner has sought
to include its other/ Force Majeure claims in the present Petition as well.
(vi) The APTEL has very recently adopted a similar approach, as sought by
the Applicant therein, in Bhopal Dhule Transmission Company Limited v.
CERC & Ors., Appeal No. 272 of 2018, vide Order dated 8.7.2025. In the said
Order, the APTEL permitted consideration on merits of the subsequent
developments in a matter that had been reserved for judgment nearly three
months earlier (i.e., on 22.4.2025). The approach taken by the APTEL shows
that, where material legal developments occur after reserving of orders, it is
both permissible and desirable to bring the new developments/ facts on record
and re-hear the matter to ensure complete and effective adjudication.
(vii) In fact, the Commission has also adopted a similar approach in the IA
No. 18 of 2025 filed in Petition No. 227/MP/2022 (ReNew Wind Energy (AP2)
Private Limited & Anr. v. CTUIL & Ors.), wherein the Commission permitted
the Petitioners therein to place on record subsequent judgments of the APTEL
having a material bearing on the outcome of the matter after the final Order
was reserved on 21.1.2025, and to make further submissions thereon on
7.8.2025. In that case, the subsequent decisions of the APTEL in Sarda
Energy and Minerals Ltd. v. CERC & Ors. (Appeal No. 400 of 2017, Judgment
dated 28.01.2025) and Brahmani Thermal Power Pvt. Ltd. v. PGCIL & Ors.
(Appeal No. 235 of 2017, Judgment dated 20.3.2025) were allowed to be
brought on record even after the conclusion of arguments and the final Order
being reserved, given their direct relevance to the issues being adjudicated in
Petition No. 227/MP/2022.
(viii) Thus, the Petitioner seeks to amend the captioned Petition previously
filed to include other claims, details and documents on account of subsequent
regulatory developments, including the Order in the MUML matter passed in
April 2025, subsequent to the final Order in the captioned matter being
reserved in February 2025. The instant IA is in the nature of an application
filed under Regulations 38 read with 26(3)(b) of the Conduct of Business
Regulations, which vests the Commission with the power to permit parties to
modify or alter their pleadings, averments in a petition or the prayers in a
petition or both, at any stage of the proceedings.
Proceedings before the Commission
Hearing dated 23.9.2025
4. The IA was listed for the hearing on 23.9.2025. During the course of the
hearing, the Petitioner submitted that the amendment to Petition No. 256/MP/2023 is
Order in IA No. 89/2025 in Petition No. 256/MP/2023 5

necessitated not only due to events post filing of the Petition but also in light of the
Commission’s order dated 20.4.2025 in Petition No. 131/MP/2024 wherein it was
clarified that Rule 3(8) of the CIL Rules does not curtail the Commission’s jurisdiction
to adjudicate validity or merits of a Change in Law claim, thereby altering the legal
position which existed at the time of the original filing. However, the Respondent,
GUVNL, raised an objection on the maintainability of the IA and sought liberty to file

Hearing dated 10.11.2025
7. During the course of the hearing, both sides made detailed arguments in the
matter, and the IA was reserved for order. Further, the parties were permitted to file

and the Respondent, GUVNL, have filed their respective written submissions in the

Analysis and decision
8. We have considered the submissions made by the parties. The present IA has
Order in IA No. 89/2025 in Petition No. 256/MP/2023 12

been filed by the Petitioner seeking the amendment of Petition No. 256/MP/2023. The
captioned Petition was filed in August 2023 under Rule 3(7) and Rule 3(8) of the CIL
Rules read with Article 12 of the TSA dated 23.4.2019 and Sections 61 and 63 of the
Act seeking verification of the calculation of the impact due to Change in Law events
on the cost of implementation of its Transmission Project and consequent adjustment
in the monthly transmission charges. In the said Petition, the Petitioner had submitted
that after the cut-off date and post the coming into effect of the CIL Rules, i.e.,
22.10.2021, it suffered additional expenditure towards its Project during the
construction phase on account of (i) Additional expenditure for securing RoW, and (ii)
Change in rate of compensation for loss of trees, fruits, and crops. The matter was
heard extensively on several occasions, and after the conclusion of the final hearing,
it was reserved for order on 19.2.2025. Thereafter, the Petitioner has moved the
present IA seeking amendment of the Petition, seeking to include its Force Majeure
claims and pre-CIL Rules Change in Law claims along with the corresponding reliefs.
9. In view of this, the only issue that arises for our consideration is whether the
present IA seeking amendment of Petition No. 256/MP/2023 deserves to be allowed
or not. The IA has been filed under Regulation 38, read with Regulation 26(3)(b) of
the Conduct of Business Regulations, 2023. The relevant clauses of these
Regulations are reproduced below:
“26. Interlocutory Applications
(3) An interlocutory application shall be filed to seek any of the following
reliefs:
….
(b) Amendment of the averments in a petition or the prayers in a
petition or both;
….
38. Amendment of Pleadings
The Commission may, at any stage of the proceedings in a petition, allow
Order in IA No. 89/2025 in Petition No. 256/MP/2023 13

either party to alter or amend its pleadings in such manner and on such
terms as may be considered appropriate, and all such amendments shall
be made as may be necessary for the purpose of determining the real
issues in controversy between the parties:
Provided that no application for amendment shall be allowed after
commencement of the final hearing of the petition, unless the
Commission is of the opinion that, in spite of due diligence, the party
could not have raised the matter before the commencement of the final
hearing:
Provided further that no application for amendment shall be entertained
after the conclusion of the final hearing and order is reserved in the
petition”.
10. Regulation 26(3)(b) is an enabling provision which provides that the Party
intending amendment of the averments in Petition or prayers in Petition or both shall
file an IA. Whereas Regulation 38 is a substantive provision governing the powers of
this Commission to allow the amendment of the Pleadings. The main provision of the
said Regulation provides that the Commission may allow either party to alter or
amend its pleadings, necessary for the purpose of determining the real issues in
controversy, in such a manner and on such terms as may be considered appropriate
at any stage of proceedings in a Petition. However, this main provision is qualified by
two provisos restricting the discretion that may be exercised under the main
provision. The first proviso stipulates that no application for amendment shall be
allowed after the commencement of the final hearing of the Petition, unless the
Commission is of the opinion that, in spite of due diligence, the party could not have
raised the matter before the commencement of the final hearing. The second proviso
goes a step further and stipulates that no application for amendment shall be
entertained after the conclusion of the final hearing and reserving of the Order in the
Petition. In other words, even the plea of “due diligence”, as available under the first
proviso, cannot come to the aid of a Party seeking amendment of the Pleadings after
the conclusion of the final hearing and reserving of the Order.
Order in IA No. 89/2025 in Petition No. 256/MP/2023 14

11. Under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, the amendment of Pleadings is
governed by Order VI Rule 17, which states as follows:
“17. Amendment of pleadings.
The Court may at any stage of the proceedings allow either party to alter or
amend his pleadings in such manner and on such terms as may be just, and all
such amendments shall be made as may be necessary for the purpose of
determining the real questions in controversy between the parties:
Provided that no application for amendment shall be allowed after the trial has
commenced, unless the Court comes to the conclusion that in spite of due
diligence, the party could not have raised the matter before the commencement
of trial”.
As per the above, pleadings can be amended at any stage of the proceedings if,
in the view of the Court, the amendments are necessary for the purpose of
determining the real questions in controversy between the parties. The proviso to the
said rule stipulates that no application for amendment shall be allowed after the trial
has commenced unless the Court concludes that, in spite of due diligence, the party
could not have raised the matter before the commencement of the trial. The
provisions of Regulation 38, except for its second proviso, are in pari materia with the
above Rule. This Rule does not contain any express stipulation similar to the second
proviso to Regulation 38. Can it then be averred that the above Rule permits the filing
of an amendment application even after the conclusion of the hearing and reservation
of the judgment?
12. In this regard, our attention has been drawn to the settled position in law that
there is no hiatus between the reservation of judgment and the pronouncement of
judgment in a matter, and as such, the proceedings cannot be reopened nor can new
issues or evidence be brought on record. In this regard, we may gainfully refer to the
judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Andhra Pradesh Southern Power
Distribution Power Co. Ltd. v. Hinduja National Power Corpn. Ltd, [(2022) 5 SCC
Order in IA No. 89/2025 in Petition No. 256/MP/2023 15

484]+, wherein it has been observed as under:
“95. It can be seen that this Court in Arjun Singh case [Arjun Singh v. Mohindra
Kumar, AIR 1964 SC 993 : (1964) 5 SCR 946] has held that CPC contemplates
two stages of the trial in the suit : (1) where the hearing is adjourned; and (2)
where the hearing is completed. It has been held that where the hearing is
completed, the parties have no further rights or privileges in the matter and it is
only for the convenience of the court that Order 20 Rule 1 permits judgment to be
delivered after an interval after the hearing is completed. It has been held that
there is no hiatus between the two stages of reservation of judgment and
pronouncing the judgment so as to make it necessary for the court to afford to the
party the remedy of getting orders passed on the lines of Order 9 Rule 7.”
As per the above, where the hearing is completed, the parties have no further
rights or privileges in the matter, and it is only for the convenience of the Court that
Order 20 Rule 1 permits judgment to be delivered after an interval after the hearing is
completed. There is no hiatus between the two stages of the reservation of judgment
and pronouncing the judgment, so as to make it necessary for the court to afford to
the party the remedy of getting orders passed on the lines of Order 9 Rule 7.
13. Be that as it may, it appears that several High Courts have opined that the
expression “at any stage of proceedings” would also include the stage up to the
pronouncement of judgment and even after filing the appeal [Ref. Om Rice Mill v.
Banaras State Bank Ltd., [1999 SCC OnLine All 966], Laxman Marotirai Paunikar v.
Keshaorao Rambhau Paunikar, [2000 SC OnLine Bom 169], and BDR Developers
Pvt. Ltd. v. Narsingh Shah alias Narsingh Sah, [2021:DHC:2283]. Additionally, the
Petitioner has sought to rely and invoke the inherent power of the Commission/
Court, principles laid down in the Anil Rai Judgment, and the settled principles
governing the amendment of Pleadings. Hence, we deem it appropriate to test the
maintainability of this application against the above propositions.
14. Assuming that, unlike Regulation 38 of Conduct of Business Regulations,
Order VI Rule 17 of CPC permits the Petitioner to move an application seeking
Order in IA No. 89/2025 in Petition No. 256/MP/2023 16

amendment of the Pleadings even after the conclusion of the final hearing and the
reservation of the Order in the Petition. This, however, does not dispense with the
requirement of satisfying the test of due diligence and demonstrating that the
Petitioner could not have sought such an amendment before the commencement of
trial in spite of due diligence. In the present case, the Petitioner has sought to amend
the Petition to incorporate all its Force Majeure and Change in Law claims and the
corresponding reliefs under Articles 11 and 12 of the TSA, read with the Change in
Law Rules. It is not even the case of the Petitioner that the above claims could not
have been incorporated before the conclusion of the final hearing and reservation of
the order in the matter. The only ground advanced by the Petitioner justifying the
amendment at this belated stage is the change in regulatory position by the
Commission’s MUML Order, which came to be passed after the caption Petition was
reserved for order.
15. As per the Petitioner, the MUML Order represents a significant departure from
the understanding prevailing at the time of filing of the present Petition with respect to
the remit of Change in Law Rules and addresses the jurisdictional question forming
the basis of the Petitioner’s earlier position. It is submitted that in the MUML Order,
the Commission for the first time clarified that it possesses full adjudicatory
jurisdiction while considering the claims under Rule 3(8) of the Change in Law Rules
and since such a regulatory view on the interpretation of Rule 3(8) did not exist
before April 2025, the Petitioner could not have predicted such a shift or acted upon
at the time when the arguments in the present Petition were concluded. However, we
find the Petitioner’s reliance on the MUML Order is entirely misplaced. Nowhere in
the said Order has the Commission held that it can adjudicate or examine the
merits/validity of the Change in Law claims under Rule 3(8) of the Change in Law
Rules. In fact, this very same argument as advanced by the Respondents therein has
Order in IA No. 89/2025 in Petition No. 256/MP/2023 17

been rejected in the said Order. The Order observes that the Change in Law Rules
do not cover a scenario where the parties are not in agreement with each other as to
whether the event constitutes a Change in Law event or not under the TSA, and this
conclusion was based on the findings of the APTEL in judgment dated 5.4.2022
passed in OP No.1 of 2022 and Ors., wherein the APTEL had already examined the
scope/ scheme of the Change in Law Rules. The Order also notes that in the said
case, the Petitioner’s Change in Law claims were already disputed by the LTTCs and
since the Petitioner had also invoked Article 12 of the TSA, the Commission was, as
per Article 12 read with Article 16.3 of the TSA, empowered to look into the merits of
such claim and adjudicate upon the disputes that had arisen between the parties.
Thus, to argue that the above Order altered the regulatory regime prevailing at the
time of filing of the Petition is misconceived. As noted, the APTEL, after examining
the scheme of Change in Law Rules, had already expressed, way back in April 2022,
that the said Rules do not appear to cover a scenario where the parties are at dispute
as to whether an event so claimed constitutes a Change in Law event and in such
cases, the Commission is required to exercise its dispute resolution jurisdiction.
Failure on the part of the Petitioner to take necessary recourse in light of the APTEL’s
above decision at the relevant point in time clearly reflects the lack of ‘due diligence’
on its part. Resultantly, the MUML Order cannot be relied upon by the Petitioner to
justify the filing of the amendment application after the conclusion of the hearing and
reservation of the order in this Petition.
16. Assuming, arguendo, that the MUML Order represents a significant departure
from the understanding prevailing at the time of filing of the present Petition with
respect to the remit of Change in Law Rules as averred by the Petitioner, there is no
explanation as to how the said Order can be the basis of incorporating its all Force
Majeure claims and corresponding reliefs under Article 11 of the TSA at this stage as
Order in IA No. 89/2025 in Petition No. 256/MP/2023 18

sought to be incorporated by way of this IA. The MUML Order only addressed the
Change in Law claims raised by the Petitioner therein and not any Force Majeure
claims. Hence, the Petitioner cannot in any manner rely upon the said Order to
incorporate its claims of Force Majeure and the corresponding reliefs at this stage of
proceedings.
17. The Petitioner has also argued that this IA seeking amendment of the Petition
squarely satisfies the settled principles governing the amendment of Pleadings as
crystallised by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in LIC v. Sanjeev Builders Private Limited
& Anr., [2022 SCC OnLine SC 1128], since the amendment sought is necessary for
proper and effective adjudication of real controversy between the parties and to avoid
multiplicity of proceedings. The application also does not introduce any time-barred
causes of action, as the Project was commissioned only in January 2023. Also, the
application neither withdraws any admission conferring a right on the opposite party
nor takes away any valid defence nor alters the fundamental nature of the Petition
nor causes irreparable prejudice to the Respondents.
18. There cannot be any quarrel with the settled law that all amendments are to be
allowed which are necessary for determining the real question in controversy,
provided it does not cause injustice or prejudice to the other side. Pertinently, some
of the relevant factors that need to be taken into consideration while dealing with the
application for amendment have been succinctly summarised by the Hon’ble
Supreme Court in Revajeetu Builders and Developers v. Narayanaswamy & Sons,
[(2009) 10 SCC 84], which include (i) Whether the amendment sought is imperative
for the proper adjudication of the case; (ii) Whether the application for amendment is
bona fide or mala fide; (iii) The amendment should not cause such prejudice to the
other side which cannot be compensated adequately in terms of money; (iv) Refusing
Order in IA No. 89/2025 in Petition No. 256/MP/2023 19

amendment would in fact lead to injustice or lead to multiple litigation; (v) Whether the
proposed amendment constitutionally or fundamentally changes the nature or
character of the case; and (vi) As a general rule, the court should decline
amendments if a fresh suit on the amended claims would be barred by limitation on
the date of application.
19. However, examining an application for amendments against the above
principles is significant where the application has been filed before the
commencement of a trial or the final hearing. However, when such an application is
filed after the commencement of a trial or the final hearing, the ‘due diligence’ test
assumes greater significance than the above principles as it takes away the court’s
jurisdiction to allow such applications unless this condition precedent is satisfied, viz.,
the court must come to a conclusion that in spite of due diligence the party could not
have raised the matter before the commencement of trail. In the foregoing
paragraphs, we have already concluded that the amendments sought to be
incorporated by this IA do not stand the test of due diligence, as the Petitioner could
very well have raised them before the commencement of trial or the final hearing in
the matter and that its attempt to attribute the need for these amendments to the
MUML Order is completely misplaced. In view of this, we are not even required to
examine the amendments sought by the Petitioner against the above-mentioned
factors. Nonetheless, even a cursory reading of the amendments sought to be
incorporated by the Petitioner indicates that they fail to meet several of the above-
mentioned factors. Incorporation of its Force Majeure claims along with the
corresponding reliefs under Article 11 of the TSA in the present Petition cannot be in
any way held to be necessary or imperative for proper adjudication of the present
case. Further, incorporation of such claims would substantially alter the basic nature
or character of the Petition filed for seeking the reliefs for the Change in Law events.
Order in IA No. 89/2025 in Petition No. 256/MP/2023 20

Thus, even otherwise, the present application for amendment of the Pleadings does
not pass the muster of the relevant factors/ principles that need to be considered
while dealing with such applications.
20. Likewise, we also do not find any merit in the Petitioner’s plea to allow this IA
by exercising the inherent powers under Regulation 65 of the CB Regulations. It is
well-settled law that the inherent powers may be exercised ex debito justitiae in those
cases where there is no express provision and cannot be exercised in contravention
of, or in conflict with, or ignoring the express and specific provisions of law. Hence, in
the present case, we are unable to accede to the plea of allowing this IA by exercise
of the Commission’s inherent powers, especially when the IA, as noted above, fails to
meet the several thresholds for allowing the amendments to the Pleadings. Further,
the Petitioner has also sought to point out that the Commission and the APTEL have,
in several cases, allowed the consideration of subsequent developments on merits in
reserved matters. However, the said cases are clearly distinguishable as they are not
cases in which the parties sought to amend their appeals/petitions after the
conclusion of the final hearing and reservation of judgment/order.
21. The Petitioner has also contended that in Anil Rai v. State of Bihar, [(2001) 7
SCC 318], the Hon’ble Supreme Court has stressed on the fact that the
pronouncement of judgments in civil cases should not be permitted go beyond 2
months from the date of conclusion of oral hearing and if the pronouncement of
judgment is delayed beyond 6 months, either party shall have the right to file an
application seeking a fresh hearing. Accordingly, the Petitioner has submitted that, as
per the Anil Rai principle, the Petitioner is entitled to seek a fresh hearing of the
matter for bringing on record critical developments in the regulatory regime post-
reservation of the judgment that go to the root of the matter and are crucial to
Order in IA No. 89/2025 in Petition No. 256/MP/2023 21

determine the real controversy and do complete justice between the parties. It is also
submitted that if re-hearing is permitted, the matter reverts to the pre-reservation
stage and the amendments become undeniably maintainable. However, we do not
find any merit in the aforesaid submissions of the Petitioner. Firstly, the Petitioner has
not made any application for a fresh hearing of the matter in terms of the Anil Rai
Judgment and hence, cannot simply presume the matter to be at the pre-reservation
stage to justify its prayer for amendment. Secondly, in the foregoing paragraphs, we
have already concluded that the amendments sought to be incorporated by the
Petitioner fail on several counts and cannot be allowed even at the pre-reservation
stage.
22. In view of the above findings and observations, the IA No. 89/2025 seeking
amendment of Petition No. 256/MP/2023 stands rejected.
Sd/- Sd/- Sd/- Sd/-
