ORDER
Adani Power Limited has filed the instant petition under Sections 79(1)(b) and (f)
of the Electricity Act, 2003 (“Act”) read with Article 7.2 of the Power Purchase
Agreement (“PPA”) dated 26.12.2005 seeking adjudication of dispute qua Power
Company of Karnataka Limited (PCKL)/ Electricity Supply Companies in Karnataka
(“ESCOM’s”) illegal unilateral withholding of differential energy charges payable to the
Petitioner for the period 1.4.2016 to 31.3.2019 and clarification of a finding in order
dated 13.1.2023 in Petition No. 155/MP/2019. PCKL, Respondent No. 1, is the nodal
agency for power procurement in the State of Karnataka and acts on behalf of
Respondent Nos. 2 to 6, the ESCOMs.
2. The Petitioner has made the following prayers:
“(a) Clarify that the benchmark energy charges formula laid down at Para 137 of the
Original Order applies to coal procurement through spot purchase from ‘sister
companies’ only and is NOT applicable to Adani’s coal procurement through spot
purchase from ‘entities other than sister companies’.
(b) Direct PCKL/ Karnataka ESCOMs to pay Adani, the withheld differential energy
charges and corresponding Carrying Cost to the tune of Rs. 100 Cr. towards spot
procurement of coal during 01.04.2016 to 31.03.2019.
Order in Petition No. 238/MP/2024
Page 2 of 27

(c) Direct PCKL/Karnataka ESCOMs to pay Adani, the LPS to the tune of Rs. 15.23
Cr. (as of 30.04.2024) and until the date of payment, towards spot procurement of coal
during 01.04.2016 to 31.03.2019 for the delay by PCKL/ ESCOMs in payment of
withheld differential energy charges and corresponding Carrying Cost to Adani.
(d) Pass such order(s) as this Ld. Commission may deem fit and proper in facts and
circumstances of the present case.”
3. The petition was admitted on 7.10.2024, and a notice was issued to the
Respondents. In response, PCKL has filed its reply vide affidavit dated 4.1.2025, and
the Petitioner has filed its rejoinder vide affidavit dated 10.2.2025. Further, the
Petitioner and PCKL filed their written submissions dated 12.8.2025 and 21.8.2025,
respectively.
Brief facts
4. The brief facts of the matter are as follows:
a. To meet the coal requirement for operating its imported coal-based power
project (“Project”) at an average PLF of 85%, the Petitioner entered into a long-
term contract for the supply of coal with (i) Adaro for 1.2 MTPA, (ii) Banpu for
0.5 MTPA and (iii) Glencore for 0.5 MTPA. The cumulative coal quantity
available under the said contracts was 2.2 MTPA, as against the total annual
coal requirement of 3.635 MTPA. However, as per PCKL’s advice on 26.9.2013,
the Petitioner terminated the long-term coal contracts with PT Adaro and
Banpu.
b. The Petitioner’s agreement with Glencore for procuring 0.5 MTPA out of
3.635 MTPA only subsists, and the remaining coal requirement is met by spot
procurement of coal.
c. In PCKL’s 46th Board of Directors’ meeting on 15.2.2017, it was resolved that
the spot procurement of coal by the Petitioner till March 2016 would be allowed
on the condition of self-certification by the Petitioner, certifying that ClF prices
for spot coal procurement till March 2016 were not more than weighted average
price of coal as per the terms of long-term coal supply contracts with Indominco,
PT Adaro and Glencore, which were in force till March 2016.
d. PCKL informed the Petitioner on 16.11.2018 that in its 53rd Board of Directors’
meeting held on 25.8.2018, it was resolved that the methodology decided in the
Order in Petition No. 238/MP/2024
Page 3 of 27

46th Board of Directors’ meeting shall continue for spot purchases of coal for
2016-17 and onwards.
e. PCKL’s 55th Board of Directors’ meeting held on 28.12.2018 resolved, with
respect to Petitioner’s coal procurements on a spot basis, as follows:
(a) Disallowance of the dead freight component of the long-term
contract for comparison with the spot procurement price of coal.
(b) Comparison of CIF cost on spot purchases with long-term contract
on ship-to-ship basis instead of cumulative basis from November 2010 to
November 2018.
f. In response, the Petitioner on 6.2.2019 wrote to PCKL informing the actual
landed cost of coal incurred and highlighted that any disallowance in the
landed cost of coal would lead to a reduction in assured RoE, which would be
contrary to the letter and spirit of the Tariff Regulations.
g. On 27.2.2019, PCKL responded to the Petitioner’s letter dated 6.2.2019,
reiterating that PCKL’s Board took a decision to consider CIF of spot
purchases at a rate which shall not be more than the weighted average price
of coal on long-term coal supply agreements.
h. On 11.3.2019, the Petitioner responded to PCKL’s letter dated 27.2.2019,
stating that PCKL’s conclusion with regard to acceptance of the mechanism
for allowance of CIF cost on an individual shipment basis without
consideration of Dead Freight was incorrect and that the coal cost should be
allowed on an actual landed cost basis as per the Tariff Regulations.
i. On 30.4.2019, PCKL responded, reiterating its decision and denying the cost
of dead freight.
j. Due to non-consideration of actual landed cost of coal for computation of
energy charges for the period 1.4.2016 to 31.3.2019 by ESCOMs, the
Petitioner filed Petition No. 155/MP/2019 on 22.5.2019 seeking directions to
ESCOMs to allow the cost of coal incurred by Adani on an actual basis and to
allow the resultant amount of ₹336 crore incurred on spot procurement of coal.
k. PCKL objected to the Petitioner’s claim of actual landed coal cost, as the
Petitioner was procuring coal from sister companies through spot procurement
without any transparency.
l. Taking into consideration the submissions of the Petitioner and PCKL, the
Commission prescribed a formula in an order dated 13.1.2023 for the
calculation of the base CIF price of coal procured on a spot basis from
Order in Petition No. 238/MP/2024
Page 4 of 27

countries other than Indonesia and the base CIF price for coal imported from
Indonesia, in line with the formula prescribed in the CSPA with Glencore.
m. On 27.2.2023, Adani raised an invoice on PCKL/ ESCOMs in terms of the
findings/ observations in order dated 13.1.2023, claiming ₹101 crore towards
differential energy charges and ₹80 crore towards Carrying Cost on the
differential energy charges.
n. On 10.4.2023, PCKL disputed the Petitioner’s claim on the premise that the
benchmark energy charges formula in the order dated 13.1.2023 applies to
coal procurement from ‘sister companies’ and also to coal procurement from
‘entities other than the sister companies’.
5. The gist of the submissions made by the Petitioner in support of its claims is as
follows:
a. The Petitioner supplies 1080 MW of the installed capacity of 1200 MW to
the distribution licensees of the State of Karnataka (“ESCOMs”) in terms of
the PPA, for which the annual coal requirement is 3.635 MTPA. During the
period under dispute, i.e. 1.4.2016 to 31.3.2019, the Petitioner was procuring
0.5 MTPA of 3.635 MTPA from Glencore International AG (“Glencore”)
through a long-term contract, viz., bituminous Coal Sale and Purchase
Agreement (“CSPA”), and the remaining coal requirement was met by spot
procurement of coal.
b. The Petitioner filed the Petition No. 155/MP/2019 seeking adjudication of
dispute between the Petitioner and ESCOMs relating to payment of (a)
capacity charges, (b) energy charges for the period from November 2010 to
March 2019 and (c) Carrying Cost for the difference between provisional, final
and revised tariff based on various orders of the Commission and APTEL. As
regards the energy charges with respect to Petitioner’s claim for actual landed
cost of coal procured through spot procurement, the Commission, in an order
dated 13.1.2023, pegged the Petitioner’s entitlement to a benchmark energy
charges formula.
c. The Petitioner raised an invoice on 27.2.2023 against the Respondents in
terms of the findings of the Commission in order dated 13.1.2023, wherein a
claim was made for ₹101 crore towards differential energy charges and ₹80
crore towards Carrying Cost on the differential energy charges. The
Order in Petition No. 238/MP/2024
Page 5 of 27

Respondents admitted and paid ₹81 crore (of ₹181 crore) i.e., (i) ₹33.59 crore
towards differential energy charges (ii) ₹47.38 crore towards Carrying Cost in
September 2023. The Respondents unilaterally and illegally withheld the
remaining payment of ₹100 crore (of ₹181 crore) i.e. (i) ₹67.41 crore towards
differential energy charges (ii) ₹33.62 crore towards Carrying Cost.
d. Such withholding of payment of energy charges by Respondents is based
on the ground that the benchmark energy charges formula laid down in the
order dated 13.1.2023 applies to Petitioner’s coal procurement through spot
procurement (a) from ‘sister companies’ and (b) from ‘entities other than the
sister companies.
e. As per the Petitioner, the benchmark energy charges formula specified in
the order dated 13.1.2023 applies only to coal procurement through spot
procurement from ‘sister companies’ and does not apply to the Petitioner’s
coal procurement from ‘entities other than the sister companies’. This
interpretation aligns with the pleadings by the parties in Petition No.
155/MP/2019 and with the observations and findings of the Commission in the
order dated 13.1.2023. Therefore, the Petitioner is constrained to seek
clarification that the benchmark energy charges formula applies to the
Petitioner’s coal procurement through spot procurement from ‘sister
companies’ only and is not applicable to coal procurement through spot
procurement from ‘entities other than the sister companies’.
f. The dispute between the Petitioner and PCKL in Petition No. 155/MP/2019
was regarding computation of energy charges and it was primarily qua
disallowance of ‘actual landed coal cost’ incurred by the Petitioner towards
spot procurement of coal, which is contrary to Regulation 21 of the Central
Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff)
Regulations, 2009 (“2009 Tariff Regulations”) and Regulation 30 of the
Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff)
Regulations, 2014 (“2014 Tariff Regulations”).
g. The main objection of PCKL is that the Petitioner was procuring coal from
‘sister companies’ at higher prices and without any transparent process.
Therefore, the Commission, in an order dated 13.1.2023, aligned the coal
purchase price through 'spot procurement from ‘sister companies’ with the
benchmark price notified by the Government of Indonesia every month.
Order in Petition No. 238/MP/2024
Page 6 of 27

h. The Commission modified the provision regarding coal pricing under
CS&PA between the Petitioner and Glencore and laid down a benchmark
energy charges formula for settlement of disputes between the parties with
regard to the spot procurement of coal during the disputed period of 1.4.2016
to 31.3.201. The Commission further considered it appropriate to bifurcate the
benchmark energy charges into two parts, viz. ‘Base CIF price of coal
procured on spot basis from countries other than Indonesia’ and ‘Base CIF
price for coal imported from Indonesia’.
i. Evidently, there was no dispute whatsoever regarding the Petitioner’s coal
procurement from ‘entities other than sister companies’ in Petition No.
155/MP/2019. Therefore, the benchmark energy charges formula is not
applicable for the Petitioner’s coal procurement from ‘entities other than the
sister companies’.
j. The Respondents’ interpretation of the order dated 13.1.2023 to apply the
benchmark energy charges formula to Petitioner’s coal procurement from
‘entities other than the sister companies’ is erroneous. Placing reliance on the
Hon’ble Supreme Court judgements in Zee Telefilms Ltd. v. Union of India,
(2005) 4 SCC 649 (Para 254) and Goan Real Estate and Construction Ltd. &
Anr. v. Union of India (2010) 5 SCC 388 (Para 31), the Petitioner has
submitted that a judgment ought to be read in its context, and any
observations made during the course of reasoning in a judgment should not
be read divorced form the context in which it was used.
k. A Judgment cannot be interpreted to have rendered a finding on a fact/issue
which was not raised in the pleadings. Applying this legal principle to the facts
of this case, since PCKL/ ESCOMs had raised no aspersions regarding
Adani’s coal procurement from ‘entities other than the sister companies’, the
benchmark energy charges formula laid down cannot be read to apply to the
Petitioner’s coal procurement from ‘entities other than the sister companies’.
The Petitioner placed its reliance on P.S. Sathappan vs. Andhra Bank Ltd.
(2004) 11 SCC 672 (Para 147) and Bacchaj Nahar v. Nilima Mandal, (2008)
17 SCC 491 (Para 17).
l. The Petitioner is entitled to LPS for the delay in payment of differential
energy charges. The Petitioner, on 27.2.2023, raised an invoice on the
Respondents for ₹101 crore towards differential energy charges and ₹80 crore
towards Carrying Cost on the differential energy charges in terms of the
Order in Petition No. 238/MP/2024
Page 7 of 27

directions in order dated 13.1.2023. However, the Respondents paid only ₹81
crore (out of ₹181 crore), i.e., (i) ₹33.59 crore towards differential energy
charges, (ii) ₹47.38 crore towards Carrying Cost in September 2023. The
Respondents withheld the remaining payment of ₹100 crore on the pretext
that the benchmark energy charges formula applies both to coal procurement
from ‘sister companies’ and also to coal procurement from ‘entities other than
the sister companies’.
m. As per Regulation 59 of the 2019 Tariff Regulations, the Respondents are
liable to pay LPS at the rate of 18% per annum to the Petitioner. The non-
obstante clause under Article 6.4(a) of the PPA rules out any right conferred
on the ESCOMs to delay payments. It is no longer res integra that for any
delay in payment by the Respondents, the Respondents are liable to pay LPS
at the rate specified in terms of the applicable Tariff Regulations. In this regard,
the Petitioner placed reliance on the judgment of APTEL dated 2.11.2020 in
Appeal No. 10 of 2020 and batch in PCKL & Ors. v. CERC & Ors., wherein,
while considering the same PPA between the same parties, APTEL held that
PCKL’s argument that the rate of interest must be in terms of the PPA
approved rate (SBI PLR) and not as per the provisions of the Tariff Regulations
is contrary to the settled law that the Tariff Regulations have over-riding effect
over the PPAs executed between the parties. The APTEL further held that the
provision of LPS is a compensatory provision under the PPAs and the
ESCOMs, having violated the provisions of the PPA with respect to the
payment of dues, cannot seek to take advantage of the rate stipulated for
interest under the PPA. The said judgement of APTEL was also upheld by the
Hon’ble Supreme Court vide order dated 8.2.2022 in Civil Appeal (PCKL &
Ors. v. CERC & Ors. in C.A. No. 838 of 2021) filed by the Respondents.
Accordingly, the Respondents ought to pay ₹15.23 crore (up to 30.4.2024)
towards LPS for the delay by the Respondents in payment of withheld
differential energy charges to Adani.
n. The Petitioner filed Appeal DFR No. 265/ 2024 before APTEL against the
Commission’s order dated 13.1.2023 in Petition No.155/MP/2019, and it is
pending disposal.
6. PCKL, Respondent No. 1, filed its reply vide affidavit dated 4.1.2025, and the
gist of the submissions made by PCKL is as follows:
Order in Petition No. 238/MP/2024
Page 8 of 27

a. The present petition is a gross abuse of the process of law, and it is not
maintainable and deserves to be dismissed.
b. The Petitioner has filed multiple cases in respect of the order dated
13.1.2023, and they are:
(a) DFR 265/ 2024 pending before the APTEL, challenging the order
dated 13.1.2023 and also seeking payment of over ₹350 crore.
(b) Petition No. 151/MP/2024 filed before this Commission seeking
execution of the order dated 13.1.2023 and seeking payment of ₹566
crore.
(c) Petition No.238/MP/2024 (the instant petition) purportedly seeking
clarification of the order dated 13.1.2023 and also seeking payment of
over ₹115 crore.
c. Section 79(1)(b) of the Act is not attracted to the present case, since the
relevant tariff has already been determined by this Commission. Further,
Section 79(1)(f) is also not attracted, since the dispute between the parties has
already been adjudicated by the Commission in an order dated 13.1.2023 in
Petition No. 155/MP/2019. The Commission has become functus officio insofar
as the said dispute is concerned. The Petitioner is seeking a modification of the
order dated 13.1.2023. In any event, the present petition has been filed after a
gross delay of about 1.5 years after the order dated 13.1.2023, purely as an
afterthought.
d. The order dated 13.1.2023 is clear and suffers from no ambiguity. It applies
to all the coal obtained by the Petitioner from the spot market. The parties have
also implemented the said order by undertaking a detailed reconciliation of the
accounts, pursuant to which, payments totalling ₹419.70 crore have already
been made by the Escoms to the Petitioner in installments by September, 2023,
in full compliance with the order dated 13.1.2023.
e. The Commission has no power to issue clarifications in respect of its orders.
If the Petitioner was aggrieved with the order dated 13.1.2023, the remedy
available to the Petitioner is to file a review petition in terms of Section 94(1)(f)
of the Act or to file an appeal before APTEL under Section 111 of the Act.
f. The Petitioner has filed an appeal, being DFR No. 265/ 2024, before APTEL
seeking a declaration that the Petitioner is entitled to energy charges for the
coal procured through spot procurement during 1.4.2016 to 31.3.2019 as per
the actual landed cost of coal without being pegged to any benchmark energy
Order in Petition No. 238/MP/2024
Page 9 of 27

charges formulae. The Petitioner is seeking the same relief in the present
petition. Having elected to file an appeal, the Petitioner cannot simultaneously
maintain another petition before this Commission seeking clarification of the
same order and claiming further alleged dues and LPS. Further, since the
remedy of review is also grossly time-barred, the Petitioner has filed this
petition, under the pretext of seeking clarification, but effectively seeking a
substantive modification/ review of the order, purely with a view to overcoming
the aspect of limitation.
g. In this regard, the Respondents placed reliance on the judgment of the
Hon’ble Supreme Court, in Jaipur Vidyut Vitran Nigam Ltd. & Ors. v. Adani
Power Rajasthan Ltd. & Anr., 2024 SCC On Line SC 313, wherein after the
disposal of the main appeal, the Petitioner had filed an application seeking a
direction to the Rajasthan Discoms to make a payment of ₹1376.35 crore
towards LPS, even though it had not preferred any review of the order. The
Hon’ble Supreme Court, after referring to a plethora of judgments, held as
follows:
“25. We felt it necessary to examine the question about maintainability of the
present application as we are of the view that it was necessary to spell out the
position of law as to when such post-disposal miscellaneous applications can be
entertained after a matter is disposed of. This Court has become functus officio
and does not retain jurisdiction to entertain an application after the appeal was
disposed of by the judgment of a three-Judge Bench of this Court on 31.08.2020
through a course beyond that specified in the statute. This is not an application for
correcting any clerical or arithmetical error. Neither it is an application for extension
of time. A post disposal application for modification and clarification of the order of
disposal shall lie only in rare cases, where the order passed by this Court is
executory in nature and the directions of the Court may become impossible to be
implemented because of subsequent events or developments. The factual
background of this Application does not fit into that description.”
h. Therefore, the present petition is nothing but an abuse of the process of law,
is not maintainable, and has been filed by the Petitioner purely with the ulterior
objective of unjustly enriching itself. The Petition therefore deserves to be
dismissed with exemplary costs in favour of the Respondents.
i. In Petition No. 155/MP/2019, Issue No. 6 “Whether UPCL is entitled to
recover actual landed cost of coal procured from spot market?” is framed in
general terms and is not restricted to procurement only from the sister
companies of the Petitioner. Similarly, the findings are also general and apply
to all spot purchases of coal, irrespective of which party it is purchased from.
Order in Petition No. 238/MP/2024
Page 10 of 27

j. The prayer (d) in Petition 155/MP/2019 is couched in general terms as
follows: “Allow energy charges for the coal cost incurred by Udupi Power on
account of spot procurement of coal, amounting to ₹336 crore, without any
deductions/ future adjustment on account of PCKL’s proposed disallowances/
differences in computation”. The Commission disallowed this prayer of the
Petitioner and on the contrary, has deemed it fit to fix a formula/ benchmark for
all spot purchases during the relevant period. There is no observation or finding
in the order dated 13.1.2023 which permits the Petitioner to recover the actual
cost in case of spot purchases made from entities other than the related parties.
Allowing the same would defeat the entire purpose of having a formula/
benchmark, which is to regulate the cost of spot purchases and prevent the
ESCOMS and consumers at large from being burdened with high costs.
k. The findings on Issue No. 6 give a clear picture that the order was not
restricted merely to spot purchase from sister companies of the Petitioner, but
applies to all spot purchases of coal, irrespective of from which party it is
purchased. The same is clear from the following:
(a) The parties had agreed that the Petitioner could carry out spot
procurement as long as the CIF price of each shipment did not exceed the
weighted average price of coal as per the long-term contracts. However,
the Petitioner subsequently insisted that the weighted average cost of all
spot purchases, as opposed to the CIF price of each shipment, ought to be
considered. In para 133, the Commission has succinctly captured the

of coal on a spot basis is from the group companies of the Petitioner without any
transparency in pricing, specified a formula for the computation of the base CIF price
for coal. While doing so, the Commission took into consideration the “Amended and
Restated Bituminous Coal Sale Agreement” dated 2.11.2010 between the Petitioner
and Glencore for the supply of coal, which has provisions for pricing of coal in respect
of coal from the country of origin, except Indonesia and coal imported from Indonesia.
On similar lines, the Commission specified a formula for computing “Base CIF price of
coal procured on spot basis from countries other than Indonesia” and “Base CIF price
for Coal imported from Indonesia”. The Commission specified the formula, taking into
consideration the existing contract between the Petitioner and Glencore, which had
the consent of PCKL. The Commission did not restrict the applicability of the formula
specified in the order dated 13.1.2023 only to the coal procured through spot
purchases from “sister companies”. If the intention of the Commission was to restrict
the findings in the order dated 13.1.2023 to “sister companies”, then the Commission
would have clearly specified so, as it has specified distinctly in the case of coal
procured on the spot market from countries other than Indonesia and coal imported
from Indonesia.
17. If the contention of the Petitioner, that the benchmark energy charges formula
specified in order dated 13.1.2023 applies only to “sister companies” and not
applicable to “entities other than the sister companies”, is accepted, then it would
amount to allowing the actual landed cost of coal in case of the coal procured on spot
basis from “entities other than the sister companies”. That was not the Commission's
intention. As no distinction was made in the order dated 13.1.2023 between the coal
procured on a spot basis from the “sister companies” and the “entities other than the
Order in Petition No. 238/MP/2024
Page 24 of 27

sister companies”, the formula specified is applicable to all procurements of coal made
by the Petitioner. Therefore, the order is clear, and there is no ambiguity in the order
dated 13.1.2023, and the Petitioner cannot read what was not envisaged in the said
order.
18. The Petitioner referring to the Hon’ble Supreme Court judgements in Zee
Telefilms Ltd. v. Union of India, (2005) 4 SCC 649 (Para 254) and Goan Real Estate
and Construction Ltd. & Anr. v. Union of India (2010) 5 SCC 388 (Para 31), has
submitted that a judgment ought to be read in its context, and any observations made
during the course of reasoning in a judgment should not be read divorced form the
context in which it was used. The Petitioner has submitted that there is no ambiguity
that the energy charges formula specified is applicable only to the Petitioner’s “sister
companies” and not to coal procurement from “entities other than the sister
companies”. We have considered the Petitioner's contention. It appears that the
Petitioner is referring to the reference made by the Commission, in order dated
13.1.2023, to PCKL’s submission that the cost of coal procured by the Petitioner from
its “sister companies” is more than the market prices, to claim that the formula
specified by the Commission is only applicable to the coal procured from its “sister
companies”. The Commission has specified the formula for the computation of the
base CIF price, taking into consideration the existing agreements of the Petitioner and
not mainly on the submissions of PCKL that the cost of coal procured from the “sister
companies” of the Petitioner is higher. Therefore, the reliance placed by the Petitioner
on the above-referred judgements of the Hon’ble Supreme Court to claim that the
Commission’s findings are applicable only to the coal procured from its “sister
companies” is misplaced.
19. Further, placing reliance on the Hon’ble Supreme Court judgements in P.S.
Sathappan v. Andhra Bank Ltd. (2004) 11 SCC 672 (Para 147) and Bacchaj Nahar v.
Order in Petition No. 238/MP/2024
Page 25 of 27

Nilima Mandal, (2008) 17 SCC 491 (Para 17), the Petitioner has submitted that a
judgment cannot be interpreted to have rendered a finding on fact/ issue which was
not raised in pleadings. Applying this legal principle to the facts of this case, since
Respondents had raised no aspersions regarding the Petitioner’s coal procurement
from ‘entities other than the sister companies’, the benchmark energy charges formula
laid down cannot be read to apply to the Petitioner’s coal procurement from ‘entities
other than the sister companies’. We have considered the Petitioner’s submissions.
We have already made it clear (in paragraph 17) that the Commission’s findings in the
order dated 13.1.2023 are applicable to the coal procured from the Petitioner’s “sister
companies” and “entities other than the sister companies” and there is no distinction
made on the basis of the source of coal. Therefore, the Petitioner’s claim that, as no
aspersions were cast on the coal procured from ‘entities other than sister companies’,
the formula specified cannot be made applicable to the Petitioner’s coal procurement
from ‘entities other than the sister companies’ does not hold good.
20. Allowing the contention of the Petitioner that the formula specified by the
Commission would only apply to its “sister companies” and not to “entities other than
the sister companies” would amount to modification of the order dated 13.1.2023, as
contended by PCKL, which is impermissible in the instant petition, which is filed
seeking clarification of the order dated 13.1.2023.
21. In view of the above discussion, the Petitioner’s prayers for directions to the
Respondents to pay the withheld differential energy charges and corresponding
Carrying Cost of ₹100 crore towards spot procurement of coal during 1.4.2026 to
31.3.2019 and the consequent LPS of ₹15.23 crore have become infructuous.
Order in Petition No. 238/MP/2024
Page 26 of 27

22. The Petition No. 238/MP/2024 is disposed of in terms of the above.

ORDER
The present petition has been filed by Haryana Power Purchase Centre (HPPC),
Uttar Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam Limited (UHBVN), Dakshin Haryana Bijli Vitran Nigam
(DHBVN) and Haryana Vidyut Prasaran Nigam Limited (HVPNL) (hereinafter collectively
referred to as ‘Petitioners’) for their claims against sharing of the transmission charges and
losses related to ±500 KV Bipole Mundra-Mohindergarh HVDC Transmission Line
(hereinafter referred as “Mundra-Mohindergarh HVDC Line”) connected to the generating
units of the Mundra Power Project of Adani Power (Mundra) Limited (hereinafter referred as
“APML”) under Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Sharing of Inter-State
Transmission Charges and Losses) Regulations 2010 (hereinafter referred to as ‘the 2010
Sharing Regulations’) read with orders of the Commission. The Petitioner has made the
following prayers:
(a) Admit the present petition;
(b) Declare that the Petitioners are not liable to pay any POC charges or make any adjustment for
losses in regard to the transmission of power from Mundra generating stations in Kutch Gujarat
to Mohindergarh in Haryana through the 500 kV HVDC line of Adani Power including for
injection of 1 MW for the purpose of intervening AC network as claimed by the Respondents 1
to 5 or on account of socialization of cost accounted with 500 KV DC line otherwise;
Order in Petition No. 627/MP/2020 Page 2

(c) Direct Respondents 1 to 5 to take immediate steps to re-compute and render accounting of
the loss/charges and give refund to the Petitioner of the amount collected from the Petitioners
with interest;
(d) Alternatively hold Adani Power (Mundra)Limited to pay the amount collected by Respondents
No. 1 to 5 towards transmission charges and Compensation for the losses adjusted both with
interest.
(e) Award cost of the present petition; and
(f) Clarify that the POC regulations notified on 04.05.2020 will be implemented considering the
exemption made for Haryana subject to which transmission licence was granted under Hon’ble
Commission’s orders dated 08.06.2013 and 29.07.2013.
(g) Pass such further order or orders as may be deemed just and proper to give justice to the
Petitioners.
Submissions of the Petitioner:
2. The Petitioners have mainly submitted as follows:
(a) HPPC is responsible for all power purchases, long term as well as short term, from within
and outside the State of Haryana, including trading of power for the two distribution
companies UHBVN and DHBVN. UHBVN and DHBVN are collectively referred to as
‘the Haryana Utilities’.
(b) Pursuant to a competitive bid for the procurement of power for consumers in the State
of Haryana, APML was selected as the successful bidder based on the tariff quoted for
the delivery of power at the nearest STU sub-station in Haryana. Haryana Utilities
entered into Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) both dated 07.08.2008 with APML
where APML has agreed to undertake generation and supply of electricity of the
contracted capacity aggregating to 1424 MW from Unit 7, Unit 8 and Unit 9 of the Mundra
Power Project located at Kutch District in the State of Gujarat and for delivery of
electricity at the delivery point at State periphery of Haryana through a dedicated
transmission system to be established by APML entirely at its own cost, expense and
risk.
(c) APML was selected as the successful bidder based on the tariff quoted for the delivery
of power at the nearest STU substation in Haryana, for injection of power in the State
Grid/Network of Haryana. The obligation for delivering electricity in the State of Haryana
being of APML, the Haryana Utilities were not concerned with the arrangement for the
use of any inter-State transmission system or otherwise any transmission line or system
of any other person or licensee for effecting such delivery, and the same were entirely
at the cost, responsibility and risk assumed by APML.
Order in Petition No. 627/MP/2020 Page 3

(d) The bid given by APML under the competitive bid was clearly based on the fact that
there would be no direct or indirect costs related to the transmission system till the
nearest STU sub-station, associated with the purchase of power from APML, to be borne
by the Haryana Utilities.
(e) The Haryana Utilities have factored the quantum as well as the tariff at which the
quantum of power shall be available for the Haryana Utilities at the Haryana periphery
for long term power purchase planning and procurement without there being any
additional charges to be paid for inter-state or intra-state transmission from Mundra to
Haryana Periphery at STU substation at Dhanoda.
(f) For wheeling of electricity from the generating facility of APML at Mundra to Haryana
periphery, i.e. STU sub-station at Dhanonda, a dedicated HVDC line (Mundra-
Mohindergarh HVDC Line) was constructed by APML in lieu of its offer/bid. The Mundra-
Mohindergarh HVDC Line was constructed with the vision of maintaining a reliability
margin in case one circuit is unavailable. The HVDC Line has a total capacity of carrying
2500 MW of electricity if both bipoles of the HVDC line are in regular operation and are
fully available, i.e. each bipole of the HVDC Line is capable of evacuating and carrying
1250 MW. If one of the bipoles is backed down or otherwise not in operation for any
reason, including scheduled maintenance and forced outages, etc., the capacity that
could be evacuated from the other pole would be only 1250 MW. Accordingly, on the
basis of the optimum capacity requirement for evacuation of 1424 MW from the Mundra
Power Station to Mohindergarh in Haryana, both poles of the HVDC Line are required
to be available in a dedicated manner at all times, and for the above quantum, there is
no extra or redundant capacity available for carrying any other power on a long term
committed basis.
(g) The ± 500KV Bipole Mundra- Mohindergarh HVDC transmission line from Unit 7,8&9 of
Mundra power project to Mohindergarh of Adani Power did not meet the contingency
outage planning criteria of Grid Code since with the tripping of one pole, the available
pole having capacity of 1250 MW was not able to carry 1424 MW of power without load
shedding or rescheduling of generation during Steady State Operation, as per
requirement of PPAs.
(h) The HVDC Line was envisaged to be developed as a dedicated transmission line
primarily for evacuation and supply of power to Haryana Utilities at the delivery point at
Order in Petition No. 627/MP/2020 Page 4

nearest STU sub-station or in common parlance of electricity terminology, it was an
extended bus of the generating units and such use of the transmission line having
dedicated nature for evacuation and delivery of 1424 MW needs to be given an absolute
priority without any reservation. The consideration of setting up the dedicated line while
quoting tariff was a suitable and beneficial proposition at relevant point of time to APML
on the premise of avoidance cost towards transmission charges of Western Region,
Northern Region and WR-NR Inter-regional link and transmission losses of Western
Region and Northern Region under the then prevailing Postage Stamp Transmission
Pricing in order to edge out other competing bidders and the same was clearly provided
by APML in the letter dated 10.04.2008.
(i) Despite the above, APML filed Petition No. 44/TL/2012 before the Commission under
Section 15 of the Electricity Act, 2003, for the grant of an inter-State transmission licence
for the said HVDC Line. The Haryana Utilities opposed the grant of a licence for such a
transmission line. The Commission, considering the submissions of the parties, vide
orders dated 08.06.2013 and dated 14.06.2013, had inter-alia granted in-principle
approval for transmission licence for 400 kV DC Mundra-Dehgam Transmission Line
and the HVDC Line, including associated 400 kV lines.
(j) By order dated 29.07.2013, passed in Petition No. 44/TL/2012, this Commission
decided on the grant of an inter-state transmission line to Adani Power for the above
500 KV Bipole Mundra – Mohindergarh HVDC Transmission Line along with its
associated facilities.
(k) On 1.4.2015, the Commission notified the Third Amendment to the 2010 Sharing
Regulations whereby the said HVDC transmission system was covered vide Clause
(4)(3)(iii) of Regulation 11 of the 2010 Sharing Regulations.
(l) The Commission in its orders dated 08.06.2013 and 29.07.2013 had, inter alia, secured
the interest of Haryana Utilities considering the Regulations in vogue. In paragraph 60
of the order dated 08.06.2013, the Commission had categorically observed that under
the circumstances, the question of any additional liability, direct or indirect, on Haryana
Utilities cannot arise.
(m) Further, in terms of paragraph 45.22 of the Statement of Reasons dated 26.10.2015,
Haryana Utilities, as drawl DIC, were not required to pay the transmission charges or
bear the transmission losses in regard to the said HVDC Line. The actual drawl by
Order in Petition No. 627/MP/2020 Page 5

Haryana Utilities has been from the Dhanonda 400 kV sub-station of the HVPNL, which
is connected to the Mohindergarh sub-station of APML.
(n) Despite the above clear provisions, the Respondent, NLDC proceeded to compute the
POC (point of connection) charges and losses as the liability to/ account for by Haryana
Utilities purported to be based on the maximum withdrawal, involving the HVDC Line
approved by the Validation Committee by increasing the demand in each node by 1 MW
and thereby assuming the usage of the said transmission system by Haryana Utilities.
(o) In the above circumstances, by letter dated 11.06.2018, HVPNL approached the
Chairman of the Validation Committee for redressal of the dispute regarding payment of
the transmission charges and for meeting the losses in regard to the said 500 kV HVDC
Line. In the said letter, HVPNL also specifically placed on record that the amount being
collected by NLDC constitutes a double payment, as Haryana Utilities are already
paying the tariff to APML, inclusive of admissible transmission charges and adjustment
for losses, in terms of the PPAs; therefore, NLDC should stop the recovery.
(p) In the meeting of the Validation Committee held on 20.06.2018, wherein the issues
raised by HVPNL were discussed, after due deliberations, it was conveyed that the
Validation Committee is not the right forum to seek such relief. The Validation
Committee advised approaching the Commission on the matter.
(q) A meeting was scheduled with the officers of the Commission on 20.08.2018, in which
concerns of Haryana Utilities on double billing under POC mechanism in lieu of 1424
MW power through the HVDC Line were deliberated, and it was decided that Haryana
Utilities needs to substantiate their argument with the system studies, for which options
may be as follows:
i) Treat 1424 MW flow on the HVDC Line as an internal generator at Mohindergarh
(STU side) - HVDC set point to be reduced by 1424 MW and APL generation to be
reduced by 1424 MW.
ii) Reduce 1424 MW demand from Haryana and equivalent reduction at APML HVDC
generation side, and reduce the set point of HVDC accordingly.
(r) In pursuance of the above, a study was undertaken by NLDC, and the result of the study
was communicated to the Validation Committee. Upon receiving the study report, by
letter dated 29.05.2019, HVPNL approached the Chief (Engineering) of CERC, who was
Order in Petition No. 627/MP/2020 Page 6

Chairman of the Validation Committee, for necessary modifications in the computation
of POC charges and losses qua the said HVDC Line.
(s) Despite the above, the Petitioners’ grievance has not been redressed, and the
Petitioners are being subjected to double charging as set out in the said letters dated
11.06.2018 and dated 29.05.2019 to the serious prejudice of the Petitioners. The
Petitioners, through HPPC vide its letter dated 06.03.2020, requested the Chief
(Engineering) of CERC for appropriate amendments and revisions to ensure that
conversion of the HVDC Line to ISTS has no direct or indirect financial impact on
Haryana.
(t) There is no cause or justification for imposing the liability of POC charges and losses
under the 2010 Sharing Regulations effective from 01.04.2015 on Haryana Utilities on
the assumption of marginal participation of Haryana Utilities on account of increasing
the load on intervening AC network and for the said purpose increasing the generation
at Mundra by one MW particularly, when the load meant for Haryana and flow of the
quantum of power to Haryana Utilities with delivery point at Haryana remains constant.
The usage of one MW power for the intervening AC network cannot lead to fastening of
the liability to pay any transmission charges or losses on the Haryana Utilities contrary
to the entire scheme considered in the 2010 Sharing Regulations and the third
amendment to the 2010 Sharing Regulations, etc. dealing specifically with the HVDC
Line, in the light of conditions subject to which the transmission licence itself was granted
by the Commission.
(u) In terms of the study conducted by NLDC on behalf/ direction of CERC, the loss
computed for the quarter of July 2018 to Sept 2018 is as under:

(v) The above study report has been sent to the Commission vide Letter dated 29.05.2019.
A similar study would have to be conducted for the entire period from 01.10.2013. In this
Order in Petition No. 627/MP/2020 Page 7

regard, the NLDC/RLDC may be directed to conduct a study and render an accounting
of loss/double payment by Haryana Utilities.
(w) The study conducted on behalf of CERC is based on the scientific methodology. The
study indicated that the methodologies adopted for allocating transmission charges are
detrimental to Haryana’s interests and have resulted in charging twice to Haryana, as
claimed by HVPNL.
(x) The Petitioners are entitled to refund of amount paid towards double payment and
losses on account of 1424 MW power from the HVDC Line since 01.10.2013 (date of
deemed CoD), attributed to POC mechanism along with interest and further monetary
compensation with interest for the losses adjusted either by appropriate adjustments by
Respondents 1 to 3 in the pool account or in the alternative recover the same from
APML.
(y) Besides the above, the Petitioner is required to share the cost of 1005 MW indirectly, as
the cost of this part is included in the POC calculations by scaling up the Yearly
Transmission Charges of AC lines on an all-India basis. Considering the fact that the
total cost of the HVDC Line constructed to supply power to the State of Haryana under
the PPA has already been factored into the tariff quoted by APML, any recovery for the
remaining capacity of 1005 MW is impacting the Haryana Utilities adversely. The
Haryana Utilities are required to bear the socialised charges on account of 1005 MW in
lieu of the POC mechanism in vogue.
(z) The Commission vide Notification dated 04.05.2020, has specified the Central Electricity
Regulatory Commission (Sharing of Inter-State Transmission Charges and Losses)
Regulations, 2020. However, despite submissions from Haryana, the interest of
Haryana as per the Commission orders dated 08.06.2013 and dated 29.07.2013 has
not been secured, and the situation is more or less the same in the revised POC regime,
whereby Haryana will be impacted indirectly with the inclusion of the HVDC Line as
ISTS.
Hearing dated 20.04.2021:
3. The matter was heard on 20.04.2021 through video conferencing. During the course of
the hearing, the senior counsel for the Petitioners reiterated the submissions made in the
Petition. In response to the Commission's specific query regarding nature of the reliefs
Order in Petition No. 627/MP/2020 Page 8

sought, the senior counsel submitted that the Petitioners have, inter-alia, sought a
declaratory relief under Sections 79(1)(c) and 79(1)(d) of the Act on account of being
aggrieved by NLDC's wrong interpretation of the provisions of the 2010 Sharing
Regulations and the Commission's order dated 08.06.2013 in Petition No. 44/TL/2012.
It was further submitted that the Petitioners are neither contesting the provisions of the
2010 Sharing Regulations nor that the present Petition contains any dispute under the
PPAs dated 07.08.2008. After hearing the senior counsel for the Petitioners, the
Commission reserved the order on the admissibility of the matter.
Interim Order dated 24.01.2022:
4. The relevant extract of the order dated 24.01.2022 is as under:
“Maintainability of the Petition
5. We have considered the submissions of the Petitioners. The Petitioners have mainly
argued on liability of transmission charges and losses on Haryana Utilities due to grant of
license to APML for the HVDC Line as part of ISTS. The Petitioners have submitted that the
HVDC Line was developed by APML as dedicated transmission line for evacuation and
supply of 1424 MW power to Haryana Utilities under Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs)
dated 07.08.2008 and that the Commission, while granting in-principle approval for grant of
transmission license in respect of the HVDC Line (whereby it became part of ISTS), vide its
orders dated 08.06.2013 and dated 29.07.2013 in Petition No. 44/TL/2012, had observed
that APML shall have the obligation to supply power to Haryana Utilities in accordance with
the terms and conditions of the PPAs, without any extra burden of transmission charges on
them.
6. The Petitioners have contended that despite the fact that the Commission in its orders
dated 08.06.2013 and 29.07.2013 had secured the interest of Haryana Utilities considering
the Regulations in vogue, NLDC computed the POC charges and losses involving the HVDC
Line as approved by the Validation Committee and thereby assuming the usage of the HVDC
Line by Haryana Utilities.
7. In view thereof, the Petitioners have claimed that despite clear decision of the Commission
vide orders dated 08.06.2013 and 29.07.2013, the Haryana Utilities are being billed and
charged transmission charges for the HVDC Line twice – one, as part of the PPAs with APML
(wherein it has been agreed that no direct or indirect cost would be levied on the Haryana
Utilities) and the other, being charged through the PoC mechanism. The Petitioners have
contended that they are entitled for refund of amount paid since 01.10.2013 (date of deemed
CoD of the HVDC Line) towards double payment on account of 1424 MW power from the
HVDC Line, along with interest.
8. The Petitioners have also submitted that the Haryana Utilities are also required to share
the cost of 1005 MW indirectly as the cost of this part is included in the PoC calculation by
scaling up Yearly Transmission Charges of AC lines on all-India basis. Considering the fact
that the total cost of the HVDC Line constructed for supplying power to the State of Haryana
against the PPAs has already been factored in tariff quoted by APML, any recovery for the
remaining capacity of 1005 MW is adversely impacting the Haryana Utilities.
9. The issue for our consideration at this stage is whether the present Petition is maintainable
in the present form.
Order in Petition No. 627/MP/2020 Page 9

10. The Petitioners have placed reliance on the order of the Commission dated 08.06.2013
in Petition No. 44/TL/2012 while according in-principle approval granting transmission license
to APML for the HVDC Line. We note that the Commission had considered the concerns of
Haryana Utilities and, inter alia, observed as under:
“60. One specific concern of Haryana is regarding levy of transmission charges. The
petitioner has already accepted that its delivery point for the contracted power is STU,
Haryana and it will bear all the open access charges for the power to be delivered up to
the delivery point. Therefore, once the dedicated transmission lines are converted into
licensed lines, the petitioner shall be treated as a long-term customer for the quantum to
be supplied under PPAs with UHBVNL/DHBVNL. It is made clear that the petitioner shall
have the obligation to supply power to UHBVNL/DHBVNL in accordance with the terms
and conditions of PPAs, without any extra burden on them for the mere fact that the
petitioner has been granted transmission licence for Mundra–Mohindergarh HVDC bi pole
transmission line. Therefore, under the circumstances, the question of any additional
liability, direct or indirect, on UHBVNL/DHBVNL cannot arise”
…..
14. From the above-mentioned submissions of the Petitioners, we note that the Petitioners
are contesting alleged double billing and charging on account of granting the HVDC Line a
status of ISTS which was initially envisaged as a dedicated line. They have placed reliance
on the orders of the Commission dated 08.06.2013 and 29.07.2013 in Petition No.
44/TL/2012 and submitted that in those orders, the Commission had specifically held that no
additional charges would be levied on account of the HVDC Line becoming part of ISTS.
15. Therefore, we are of the view that the petition to the extent that there is alleged double
billing or charging of transmission charges in the calculations done by NLDC allegedly in
contravention to the provisions of the 2010 Sharing Regulations and in violation of orders
dated 08.06.2013 and 29.07.2013 in Petition No. 44/TL/2012, is maintainable.
16. We note that the 2010 Sharing Regulations has since been repealed and the 2020
Sharing Regulations has come into effect from 01.11.2020. Relevant provision of Regulation
3 of the 2020 Sharing Regulations provides as follows:
“(3) National Component-HVDC shall comprise of the following:
.
(c) Yearly Transmission Charges of Mundra–Mohindergarh 2500 MW HVDC transmission
system corresponding to 1005 MW capacity:
Provided that Yearly Transmission Charges corresponding to 1495 MW for the said
transmission system shall be borne by M/s Adani Power (Mundra) Limited or its successor
company; and
...”
17. We note from above-quoted extract that proviso to Regulation 3(c) of the 2020 Sharing
Regulations provides that the liability for payment of transmission charges for 1495 MW
capacity of the HVDC Line is with APML while transmission charges corresponding to 1005
MW is part of the National Component-HVDC.
18. It is also observed that the Statement of Reasons dated 10.08.2020 for the 2020 Sharing
Regulations mentions as follows:
“73.2.1 HVPN has suggested that the 2010 Sharing Regulations mentions the treatment
of HVDC lines as under: “Treatment of HVDC: Flow of HVDC systems is regulated by
power order and remains constant for marginal change in load or generation. Hence
Order in Petition No. 627/MP/2020 Page 10

marginal participation (MP) of HVDC systems is zero”. This results in increase of PoC
charges of Haryana as Haryana is receiving power from M/s Adani through a dedicated
HVDC Mundra- Mohindergarh HVDC transmission line. Under Marginal Participation
method, an increase in 1 MW of load in Haryana has to be compensated by a
corresponding increase in generation at the slack buses at Mundra end, but as stated
above, HVDC line doesn’t respond in the marginal participation. Hence, power flows
through alternate AC transmission lines which results in increase in the PoC charges for
the State of Haryana. However, the Draft 2019 Sharing Regulations are silent about
treatment of HVDC transmission line.
73.3 Analysis and Decision
73.3.1 Marginal participation of HVDC system is zero since its flow is regulated by power
order. The Statement of Reasons for the 3rd amendment to the 2010 Sharing Regulations
had clearly recognised this, when it was noted that “As tariff of HVDC links cannot be
allocated with marginal participation method, a separate treatment is unavoidable.” The
treatment of HVDC system is provided for in the Regulations under NC-HVDC and RC
components.”
19. In the present petition, the Petitioners have also submitted that in the 2020 Sharing
Regulations, despite submissions from Haryana, the interest of Haryana as per the
Commission orders dated 08.06.2013 and dated 29.07.2013 have not been secured. Any
contention of the Petitioner that it is aggrieved with any of the provisions of the 2020 Sharing
Regulations cannot be entertained or dealt with in this petition. Any amendment of the
Regulations in the garb of rectification in the computation of transmission charges is not
maintainable.
20. In light of the foregoing discussions, we find that the present petition is maintainable to
the limited extent for examining whether the transmission charges as calculated by NLDC
are in contravention to the provisions of the 2010 Sharing Regulations and in violation of the
Commission’s order dated 08.06.2013 and 29.07.2013 in Petition No. 44/TL/2012 and
consequently, there is any double billing and charging of transmission charges, as alleged
by the Petitioner.”
As per above, the Commission vide order dated 24.01.2022 held that the present petition
is maintainable to the limited extent for examining whether the transmission charges as
calculated by NLDC are in contravention to the provisions of the 2010 Sharing
Regulations and in violation of the Commission’s order dated 08.06.2013 and 29.07.2013
in Petition No. 44/TL/2012 and consequently, whether there is any double billing and
charging of transmission charges, as alleged by the Petitioner.

Analysis and decision:
14. The Petitioners in the instant petition have submitted that Haryana Discoms (UHBVN
and DHBVN) have entered into Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) dated 07.08.2008
with APML for 1424 MW from its Mundra Power Project located in the State of Gujarat.
For wheeling of electricity from its Mundra Power Project to Haryana’s State Periphery,
i.e. STU sub-station at Dhanonda, the HVDC Line with a total capacity of 2500 MW was
constructed by APML. APML filed Petition No. 44/TL/2012 before this Commission for
the grant of an inter-State transmission licence for the HVDC Line, and Commission vide
Order dated 08.06.2013 granted in-principle approval for the transmission licence,
observing that the question of any additional liability, direct or indirect, on
UHBVNL/DHBVNL cannot arise.
15. Petitioners have disputed the methodology of calculation of POC charges and losses
carried out by NLDC. Petitioners submitted that it is incorrect to impose the liability of
PoC charges and losses on the basis of marginal participation of the Petitioners on
account of increasing the load on intervening AC network and for the said purpose
increasing the generation at Mundra by one (1) MW particularly when the load is meant
for Haryana and the flow of power quantum to the Petitioners with delivery point at
Haryana remains constant. Petitioner had conducted a study by NLDC during 2018-19
under the following options, where the slab rates for Haryana changed subsequent to
the exercise:
(a) Treat 1424 MW flow on the HVDC Line as an internal generator at
Mohindergarh (STU side) - HVDC set point to be reduced by 1424 MW and
APL generation to be reduced by 1424 MW.
(b) Reduce 1424 MW demand from Haryana and equivalent reduction at APML
HVDC generation side, and reduce the set point of HVDC accordingly.
16. Respondent NLDC has submitted that vide the directions issued by the Commission in
its Order in Petition No. 44/TL/2012 dated 08.06.2013 and 29.07.2013, the transmission
charges corresponding to the capacity of 1424 MW had been billed to Adani Power
Limited in terms of the PPA dated 07.08.2008 with Haryana Utilities. Accordingly, the
transmission charges for ±500 KV Bipole Mundra- Mohindergarh HVDC Transmission
Line corresponding to 1424 MW had been excluded from recovery under the PoC
mechanism. Since the transmission charges of the Mundra-Mohindergarh HVDC system
corresponding to 1495MW capacity had been excluded from the recovery under the PoC
Order in Petition No. 627/MP/2020 Page 22

mechanism, there is no double billing and charging of transmission charges
corresponding to 1424 MW, as alleged by the Petitioner.
17. In light of the submissions, the following issues arise for our consideration:
Issue No.1 : Whether the Implementing Agency, NLDC, was carrying out
calculations under the 2010 Sharing Regulations and the 2020 Sharing
Regulations in contravention of the provisions of the said Regulations and various
Orders issued by the Commission? Whether any directions required to be issued
to Respondents 1 to 5 to recompute POC charges? Consequently whether
Petitioners are entitled to any refund with interest?
Issue No2 : Whether any directions are required to be issued to hold APML to pay
the amount collected by Respondents No. 1 to 5 towards transmission charges
and compensation for the losses adjusted both with interest;
18. The issues are dealt with together in subsequent paragraphs.
19. Petitioners have submitted that the 500 KV Bipole Mundra - Mohindergarh HVDC
transmission line was developed by APL as a dedicated transmission line for the
evacuation and supply of 1424/1495 MW power to Haryana Utilities under Power
Purchase Agreements (PPAs) dated 7.8.2008. The tariff quoted under the said PPAs was
after factoring in the cost of the said HVDC line. Subsequently, APL filed a Petition
bearing No.44/TL/2012 for the grant of an inter-State transmission licence for the
aforesaid HVDC line, which was not opposed by the Haryana Utilities. However, the
Commission, while granting in-principle approval for grant of transmission licence, in its
order dated 8.6.2013, inter-alia, observed that APL shall have the obligation to supply
power to Haryana Utilities in accordance with the terms and conditions of the PPAs,
without any extra burden on them and that the question of any additional liability, direct
or indirect, on Haryana Utilities cannot arise.
20. Petitioner has mainly challenged the POC calculations carried out by NLDC stating that
Dispatch Centre (NLDC) proceeded to compute the POC (point of connection) charges
and losses as the liability to/ account for by Haryana Utilities purported to be based on
the maximum withdrawal, involving the HVDC Line by increasing the demand in each
node by 1 MW and thereby assuming the usage of the said transmission system by
Haryana Utilities.
21. Petitioners have got sample studies done by NLDC for Q2 of 2018-19 i.e. July 2018 to
September 2018 under two scenarios (i)Treat 1424 MW flow on the HVDC Line as
internal generator at Mohindergarh (STU side) - HVDC set point to be reduced by 1424
Order in Petition No. 627/MP/2020 Page 23

MW and APL generation to be reduced by 1424 MW, (ii) Reduce 1424 MW demand from
Haryana and equivalent reduction at APML HVDC generation side and reduce set point
of HVDC accordingly. Under the sample studies, the slab rate for Haryana was reduced.
On account of the incorrect methodology adopted by NLDC, as opposed to the two
scenarios for transmission cost allocation considered in the Study Report dated
09.04.2019, there is a difference in the slab rate, leading to a reduction of Rs. 30-40
Crores per quarter in the transmission network usage cost.
22. Petitioners have prayed that they are entitled for refund of amount paid towards double
payment and losses on account of 1424 MW power from the HVDC Line since 01.10.2013
(date of deemed CoD), attributed to POC mechanism along with interest and further
monetary compensation with interest for the losses adjusted either by appropriate
adjustments by Respondents 1 to 3 in the pool account or in the alternative recover the
same from Adani Power.
23. Respondent NLDC has submitted that transmission charges of the Mundra-Mohindergarh
HVDC system corresponding to 1495 MW capacity had been excluded from the recovery
under the PoC mechanism, and no cost of HVDC is considered in the base case. Haryana
uses the HVDC system at no cost to receive power from Mundra TPS, as per the PPA.
There is no double-billing or charging of transmission charges corresponding to 1424
MW, as alleged by the Petitioner. The computation of PoC charges was carried out by
the NLDC as per the extant 2010 Sharing Regulations and amendments thereof. There
was no provision in the said regulation, nor was it discussed in the Validation Committee
meetings, to compute the charges of the states as proposed by Haryana in the study.
24. Respondent NLDC has further submitted that the path of power flow (contract path)
envisaged as per the terms and conditions of the Power Purchase Agreement signed
between the two parties may not be the same as the actual electrical path, which follows
the laws of physics. In a meshed network, power flows depend on factors such as load
and generation in a control area, load and generation in nearby control areas, availability
of transmission lines, etc. All these factors may vary for different scenarios considered
for the computation of transmission charges.
25. NLDC had also conducted additional studies for the period from January 2019 to March
2019 (Q4 of 2018-19), where the following assumptions were taken:
“Scenario A
Order in Petition No. 627/MP/2020 Page 24

a. Assumptions:
• Reduction of 1000 MW set point at Mundra-Mohindergarh HVDC transmission line
to zero.
• Reduction of generation of 1000 MW at APL Mundra generating station.
• Equivalent generation of 1000 MW modelled at Mohindergarh (STU side).
• Demand of Haryana has been considered as 6333 MW.
b. The HVDC set point of Mundra-Mohindergarh HVDC transmission line and Demand
of Haryana in the study have been considered as 1000 MW and 6333 MW respectively
as finalized by the Validation Committee during the computation of sharing of
transmission charges for January 2019 to March 2019.
Scenario B
a. Assumptions:
• Reduction of 1000 MW set point at Mundra- Mohindergarh HVDC transmission
line to zero.
• Reduction of generation of 1000 MW at APL Mundra generating station.
• Equivalent reduction of demand for Haryana of 1000 MW.
• Demand of Haryana has been considered as 5333 MW (6333 less 1000 MW).
b. The HVDC set point of Mundra-Mohindergarh HVDC transmission line and Demand
of Haryana was considered as 1000 MW and 6333 MW respectively as finalized by
the Validation Committee during the computation of sharing of transmission charges
for January 2019 to March 2019.”
In one scenario, there is no change in slab rate, and in another scenario, the slab
rate has changed from the fifth slab from the fourth slab.
26. NLDC has submitted that in view of the reduction in transmission charges for Haryana with
the above study scenarios, transmission charges for other DICs in the country will increase
due to scaling of transmission charges for complete recovery of the total monthly
transmission charges.
27. We have considered the submissions of Petitioners and Respondents. Commission vide
Interim Order dated 24.01.2022 in the instant Petition observed as follows:
“20. In light of the foregoing discussions, we find that the present petition is maintainable to
the limited extent for examining whether the transmission charges as calculated by
NLDC are in contravention to the provisions of the 2010 Sharing Regulations and in
violation of the Commission’s order dated 08.06.2013 and 29.07.2013 in Petition No.
44/TL/2012 and consequently, there is any double billing and charging of transmission
charges, as alleged by the Petitioner.”
As per the above, the instant Petition was held maintainable to the extent of examining
whether the transmission charges, as calculated by NLDC are in contravention of the
provisions of the 2010 Sharing Regulations and Orders of the Commission.
Order in Petition No. 627/MP/2020 Page 25

28. Let us peruse the methodology of calculation of PoC charges to determine if NLDC was
calculating PoC charges in contravention of the 2010 Sharing Regulations and 2020 Sharing
Regulations. We observe that Petitioner has alleged that the calculation needs to be revised
from 1.10.2013, when the said HVDC line was included in PoC. Petitioner has also referred
to the 2020 Sharing Regulations, praying for a revision in the methodology for calculating
PoC Charges.
29. Petitioner has mainly challenged the POC calculations with respect to the methodology of
increasing the demand in each node by 1 MW and thereby assuming the usage of the said
transmission system by Haryana Utilities. Petitioner is suggesting an alternative
methodology for which it had the NLDC conduct sample studies as (a) Treat 1424 MW flow
on the HVDC Line as internal generator at Mohindergarh (STU side) - HVDC set point to be
reduced by 1424 MW and APL generation to be reduced by 1424 MW, (b) Reduce 1424
MW demand from Haryana and equivalent reduction at APML HVDC generation side and
reduce set point of HVDC accordingly.
30. In light of this, the methodology needs to be analysed for the 2010 Sharing Regulations and
the 2020 Sharing Regulations. We have perused relevant provisions of the 2010 Sharing
Regulations quoted as under:
“2.1.1 NODAL GENERATION AND DEMAND INFORMATION
Data Required for Annual process of determination of transmission charges based on Hybrid
Methodology:
The DICs will provide forecast injection/withdrawal information {MW and MVAR (or an assumption about
the power factor to be used)} at all the nodes or a group of nodes in a zone (identified a-priori by the
Implementing Agency (IA) in the Network. “Typical” injection/withdrawal data based on maximum
injection/withdrawal as defined in these regulations shall be provided to the Implementing Agency by the
DICs for each of the application period.
DICs shall also provide injection and withdrawal data for the corresponding quarter of last three years.
The data provided by the DICs shall be as per the formats prepared by the IA and duly approved by the
Commission under the relevant provisions of these Regulations.
Information provided by the DICs shall be vetted by the Implementing Agency as per the provisions of the
Regulations and Detailed procedure notified by Implementing Agency.
Methodology for calculation of forecasted maximum generation/withdrawal of DICs for vetting by
Implementing Agency
For Demand data:
The projected maximum withdrawal figures provided by DICs will be vetted by Implementing Agency based
on the following:
a. Monthly peak demand met for each State/UT in the last 3 years for the period corresponding to the
Application Period shall be considered.
b. The average of monthly peak demand met for each State/UT in each of the last 3 years for the period
corresponding to the Application Period shall be calculated.
c. The average peak demand met for each State/UT for the Application Period shall be projected based on
last 3 year’s average of monthly peak demand met figures.
Order in Petition No. 627/MP/2020 Page 26

d. Similarly All India peak demand met in last 3 years shall be averaged for the period corresponding to
the Application Period. This shall be projected for the ensuing Application Period. The projected peak
demand of each State/UT thus arrived shall be normalized with the projected All-India peak demand met
of the Application Period under consideration for the current year.
…..
2.4 Computation: Hybrid Method for the determination of transmission charges
Any usage based methodology attempts to identify how much of power that flows through each of the
lines in the system is due to the existence of a certain network user, in order to charge it according
to the adopted measure of utilization. To do so, the Hybrid Method analyzes how the flows in the grid
are modified when minor changes are introduced in the production (or consumption) of agent i, and
it assumes that the relationship of the flow through line j with the behaviour of the agent i can be
considered to be linear. For each of the considered blocks of months and, the procedure can be
described as follows:
1. Marginal participation sensitivities are obtained that represents how much the flow through
each network branch j increases when the injection/ withdrawal in a bus is increased by 1
MW. Flow variation in each network branch j incurred by 1 MW injection / withdrawal at
each bus is computed for each scenario.
2. Due to the Kirchoff’s laws, any 1 MW increase in generation (or load) at node i has to be
compensated by a corresponding increase in load (or generation) at some other node or nodes
(after adjusting for incremental system losses). Thus the calculation of how much an injection
(or withdrawal) at a certain bus affects the flows in the network depends on the decision of
which is the node that responds, and the answer that is demanded from the method is heavily
conditioned by an assumption that it needs as an input. The methodology used for the selection
of the distributed slack buses is explained above.
3. Once the flow variation in each line incurred by each agent is obtained, it is possible to
compute a usage index for each network user. This index is computed according to equation
given below. It can be seen that only positive increments in the direction of the power flow in
the base case are considered. This implies that increments which reduce burden on lines are
neither given any credit nor charged for use of the system. This is essentially because of
practical reasons where it could be difficult to pay grid connected entities for being connected
to the grid. Further, there could be times (with strictly positive chance) when these entities
need to use certain network branches along the direction of the main flow, though such times
may not be the times which coincide with [maximum injection/ maximum withdrawal]1
considered in the load flow studies. This is also a standard international practice followed in
countries where such pricing mechanisms are used.

2.5 Computation: Determination of Sharing of YTC and Transmission Losses
The simulations will be carried out by the IA by using a software duly approved by the CERC.
The following steps shall be followed:
“1. Converged AC Load Flow data for the all India Grid shall be used directly for the implementation
of the Hybrid Methodology.”
2. Treatment of HVDC: Flow on HVDC systems is regulated by power order and remains constant
for marginal change in load or generation. Hence, marginal participation (MP) of HVDC systems is
zero. Since the HVDC systems were specifically set up for transfer of bulk power to specific Region,
the DICs of the Region shall share the cost of HVDC systems. HVDC system also helps in controlling
voltages and power flow in inter-regional lines and some benefits accrue to all DICs by virtue of
HVDC system. Accordingly, 10 % of the MTC of these systems be recovered through Reliability
Support Charges. The balance amount shall be payable by Withdrawal DICs of the Region in
proportion to their Approved Withdrawal. In case of Injection DICs having Long Term Access to
target region, it shall be payable in proportion to their Approved Injection.
Where transmission charges for any HVDC system line are to be partly borne by a DIC (injecting
DIC or withdrawal DIC, as the case may be) under a PPA or any other arrangement, transmission
charges in proportion to the share of capacity in accordance with PPA or other arrangement shall
be borne by such DIC and the charges for balance capacity shall be borne by the remaining DICs by
scaling up of YTC of the AC system included in the PoC.”
As per the above, it is observed that the entire methodology of calculation of PoC charges
has been provided in detail in the Regulations . As per the above methodology, forecasted
withdrawal data is to be furnished only by DICs. Further marginal participation is calculated
by imposing a 1 MW variation in injection and drawal for each network branch at each node
as per above. HVDCs charges have been covered under Paragraph 2.5 which clearly
provides that “Where transmission charges for any HVDC system line are to be partly borne
by a DIC (injecting DIC or withdrawal DIC, as the case may be) under a PPA or any other
arrangement, transmission charges in proportion to the share of capacity in accordance with
PPA or other arrangement shall be borne by such DIC”.

31. NLDC has submitted that the Path of power flow (contract path) envisaged as per the terms
and conditions of the Power Purchase Agreement signed between the two parties may not
be the same as the actual electrical path, which follows the laws of physics. In a meshed
network, power flows depend on factors such as load and generation within a control area,
load and generation in nearby control areas, and the availability of transmission lines, etc.
All these factors may vary for different scenarios considered for the computation of
transmission charges. Further, NLDC has confirmed that transmission charges for 1495 MW
are being billed directly to APML, as per the directions of Order 44/TL/2012 and the
provisions of the 2010/2020 Sharing Regulations.
32. We note that sample studies were carried out by Petitioners with NLDC, where the basic
network was modified to either treat 1424 MW as an internal generator at Mohindergarh or
to reduce 1424 MW demand from Haryana and modify the HVDC set point. We have
carefully considered the submissions of Petitioner and NLDC as well as the provisions of
the 2010 Sharing Regulations. We note that NLDC has carried out calculations of POC
charges strictly in accordance with the 2010 Sharing Regulations. The prayer of Petitioner
to modify the base case of POC and consequent POC calculations, which have been carried
out in terms of the 2010 Sharing Regulations in a way to reduce its slab rates, is not
acceptable. We note that, since the transmission charges for 1495 MW are being billed
directly to APML, the Petitioners' contention that it is being billed double charges does not
hold water. We note that the options proposed by Petitioners to modify the base case are
not at all provided for in the 2010 Sharing Regulations.
33. We have perused the provisions of the 2020 Sharing regulations quoted as under:
“5.Components and sharing of National Component (NC)
….
(c)Yearly Transmission Charges of Mundra–Mohindergarh 2500 MW HVDC transmission
system corresponding to 1005 MW capacity:
Provided that Yearly Transmission Charges corresponding to 1495 MW for the said
transmission system shall be borne by M/s Adani Power (Mundra) Limited or its successor
company; and..”
…
Annexure-I

(A) Data acquisition;
(B) Computation of load flows on the Basic Network;
(C) Identification of slack node(s);
(D) Determination of transmission charges; and
(E) Determination of sharing of transmission charges
(A) DATA ACQUISITION: INPUTS TO THE MODEL
5.2 The transmission pricing model requires a set of inputs for peak block of the month as
follows:
• Generation information at nodes;
• Demand information at nodes;
• Transmission circuits between these nodes and their electrical characteristics
required for load flow analysis, the associated lengths of these transmission lines
and their capacity and Yearly Transmission Charges (YTC) of each transmission
line; and
• Identification of reference node(s).
5.3 The DICs will provide actual generation and actual drawal {MW and MVAR at each
node in the Basic Network. The data provided by the DICs shall be as per the formats
stipulated by the Implementing Agency. All drawee DICs shall also submit generation
from their own generating stations for the peak block during the billing period to the
Implementing Agency to prepare the Base Case for load-generation balance.
5.4 Information provided by the DICs shall be verified by the Implementing Agency as per
the detailed procedure stipulated by the Implementing Agency.
5.5 Inter-State transmission licensees, intra-State transmission licensees whose
transmission system are included in Yearly Transmission Charges, and the DICs shall
supply network data for the existing network, in the format stipulated by the
Implementing Agency.
5.6 The Basic Network shall contain all the power system elements including generating
station and transmission line at. 110 kV and above. Power flow into a lower voltage
system from the voltage levels indicated in the definition of the Basic Network shall be
considered as load at that sub-station. Power flow from a lower voltage system into the
electricity systems at the voltage levels shall be considered as generation at that sub-
station.

(D) DETERMINATION OF TRANSMISSION CHARGES
5.15 Hybrid Methodology analyzes the modifications in power flows in the grid when minor
changes are introduced in the production (or consumption) of agent i, and it assumes
that the relationship of the flow through line j with the behaviour of the agent i can
be considered to be linear. The procedure is as under:
5.15.1 Marginal participation sensitivities are obtained that represent the increase in power
flow through each network branch j when the injection or drawal in a bus is increased
by 1 MW. Flow variation in each network branch j incurred by 1 MW injection or
drawal at each bus is computed for each scenario, e.
5.15.2 As already stated at Clause 5.14 of this Annexure, due to the Kirchoff’s laws, any 1
MW increase in generation (or load) at node i has to be compensated by a
corresponding increase in load (or generation) at some other node(s) (after adjusting
for incremental system losses). Thus, the calculation of quantum of injection (or
drawal) at a certain bus affecting the power flows in the Basic Network depends on
Order in Petition No. 627/MP/2020 Page 30

the choice of the node(s) that responds. The methodology used to identify such node
shall be distributed slack buses as explained above at Clause 5 (C).
5.15.3 Once the power flow variation in each transmission line incurred by each agent is
obtained, it is possible to compute a usage index for each network user. This index
is computed according to equation given below. Only positive increments in the
direction of the power flow in the base case are considered while increments which
reduce burden on transmission lines are neither given any credit nor charged for
use of the system.
