Minimum Paid Up Share Capital to be held by Project Promoter in
accordance with provisions stipulated under Clause 6.15 of RfS Document.
The WPD shall provide information about its promoters and their
shareholding in the Company before signing of PPA with SJVN.
13.0 The WPD shall commence the supply of Wind Power of full Contracted
Capacity within 24 months from the Effective Date of the PPA in accordance
with the provisions stipulated under Clause 6.8.2 of RfS and relevant articles
of PPA, including subsequent amendment (if any).
14.0 All disputes arising out of and/or in connection with the selection of WPD
under this RfS and execution of PPA thereto shall be governed by laws of
India and shall be subject to the jurisdiction of Courts of New Delhi.
15.0 Project implementation will be governed in line with the provisions of the RfS
and PPA.
16.0 This Letter of Award is being issued to you in duplicate. You are requested
to kindly return the duplicate copy of the same duly signed and stamped on
each page by the authorized signatory of your firm as a proof of
acknowledgement and confirmation of your unequivocal acceptance within
07 days from the date of issuance of this Letter of Award (LOA).
26. As per the Wind Guidelines, the Evaluation Committee is required to certify
that the bidding process and the evaluation have been conducted in conformity with
the provisions of the RfS document. In compliance with the above, the Petitioner has
furnished the conformity certificates on record. As per the conformity certificate dated
13.06.2025, the Petitioner has certified that the aspects of the bid evaluation and
adopted price are in conformity with the competitive bidding guidelines and aligned
with the prevailing market tenders. The relevant extract of the aforesaid conformity
certificate is as under:
“CONFORMITY CERTIFICATE
Order in Petition No 582/AT/2025 Page 17

The bidding process and evaluation criteria as specified in the RfS document
has been strictly complied with and the entire process of evaluation has been
transparent.”
27. The Petitioner has submitted that it is in active discussions with the end
procurer and after finalisation of the PSA with the end procurer(s), the PPAs shall be
signed with the successful bidders to whom LOA has been issued.
28. The Petitioner has stated that it is in the process of executing the Power
Supply Agreement (PSA) with the Bihar Discoms, and the approval of the same is
pending before the Bihar Electricity Regulatory Commission.
29. We have considered the submissions made by the parties. In the past, the
Commission has adopted tariffs only to the extent that the awarded capacity has
been committed under the PPAs and PSAs with the successful bidders/developers
and the distribution licensees, respectively. In the present case, the Petitioner is in
the process of executing the Power Supply Agreement (PSA) with the Bihar
Discoms, and the approval of the same is pending before the Bihar Electricity
Regulatory Commission. However, keeping in view the overall emphasis of the
Guidelines on the expeditious adoption of the tariff, we consider it appropriate to
proceed with its adoption without waiting for the tying up of the entire awarded
capacity under the PPAs and PSAs.
30. In view of the aforesaid discussions, it emerges that the selection of the
successful bidders has been made, and the tariff of the Wind Power Projects has
been discovered by the Petitioner, SJVN, through a transparent process of
competitive bidding in accordance with the Guidelines issued by the Ministry of
Power, Government of India. Therefore, in terms of Section 63 of the Act, the
Commission adopts the individual tariff for the Wind Power Projects, as agreed to by
Order in Petition No 582/AT/2025 Page 18

the following successful bidders, subject to the Petitioner tying up the capacity under
the PPAs and PSAs:

31. Prayer (a) of the Petitioner is answered in terms of paragraph 30 above.
Moreover, as soon as the awarded capacity is tied up under the PPAs and PSAs,
the Petitioner shall place on record the copies of such PPAs and PSAs in the present
case. Also, if the awarded capacity does not fructify into PPAs and PSAs, the
Petitioner shall also place on record such development(s) in the file of the present
case.
32. The Petitioner has also prayed to approve the trading margin of Rs . 0.07/kWh
to be paid by the distribution companies/buying entities(s) as specified in the RfS
document and specified in the Guidelines.
33. In this regard, Regulation 8(1)(d) of the Trading Licence Regulations dealing
with trading margin provides as under:
“For transactions under long term contracts, the trading margin shall be as
mutually decided between the Trading licensee and the seller:…”
34. The above provision gives a choice to the contracting parties to mutually
agree on a trading margin for long-term transactions. However, proviso to
Regulation8(1)(d) of the Trading Licence Regulations provides as under:
“8(1)(d) *************
Order in Petition No 582/AT/2025 Page 19

Provided that in contracts where escrow arrangement or irrevocable,
unconditional and revolving letter of credit as specified in clause (10) of
Regulation 9 is not provided by the Trading Licensee in favour of the seller,
the Trading Licensee shall not charge trading margin exceeding two (2.0)
paise/kWh.”
35. Regulation 8(1)(f) of the Trading Licence Regulations provides as under:
“For transactions under Back to Back contracts, where escrow arrangement
or irrevocable, unconditional and revolving letter of credit as specified in
clause (10) of Regulation 9 is not provided by the Trading Licensee in favour
of the seller, the Trading Licensee shall not charge trading margin exceeding
two (2.0) paise/kWh.”
36. The above two provisions are exceptions to the main provision as regards the
trading margin. In the present case, awarded capacity is yet to be tied up with the
distribution licensees, and accordingly, the trading margin shall be as per the
provisions of the PSAs to be entered into between SJVN and the distribution
licensees and with due regard to the provisions of the Payment Settlement
Mechanism in the Guidelines/PPA, and be subject to the provisions of the Trading
License Regulations. Further, in case of failure of the SJVN to provide an escrow
arrangement or an irrevocable, unconditional, and revolving letter of credit to the
wind solar power generators, the trading margin shall not exceed Rs. 0.02/kWh
specified in Regulation 8(1)(d) and Regulation 8(1)(f) of the Trading Licence
Regulations.
37. Prayer (b) of the Petitioner is answered accordingly.
38. Accordingly, Petition No. 582/AT/2025 is disposed of in terms of the above.

ORDER
The instant Petition has been filed by Power Grid Corporation of India Limited
(hereinafter referred to as “PGCIL/ the Petitioner”), a deemed transmission licensee, for
truing up of the transmission tariff for the 2019-24 tariff period under the Central
Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2019
(hereinafter referred to as “the 2019 Tariff Regulations”) and the determination of the
transmission tariff under the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and
Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2024 (hereinafter referred to as “the 2024 Tariff
Regulations”) for the 2024-29 tariff period with respect to the following transmission
assets (hereinafter referred to as “the transmission assets/Combined Asset”) under
“Augmentation of Transformation capacity at existing Hiriyur and Kochi Sub-stations”
(hereinafter referred to as “the transmission project” in the Southern Region.
Asset-1: 1 x 500 MVA, 400/220 kV Transformer along with associated bays at
the Hiriyur Sub-station
Asset-2: 1 x 500 MVA, 400/220 kV Transformer along with associated bays at
the Kochi Sub-station
***The Petitioner has combined both the transmission assets and collectively referred to
as “the Combined Asset” (comprising of Asset-1 and Asset-2) and has claimed the
transmission tariff for the 2024-29 tariff period.
2. The Petitioner has made the following prayers in the instant Petition:
“a) Approve the trued-up Transmission Tariff for 2019-24 block and transmission tariff for
2024-29 block for the assets covered under this petition, as per Para 17 and 18 above.

b) Admit the capital cost claimed and additional capitalization incurred during 2019-24
and also allow the projected additional capitalization during 2024-29.
c) Allow the petitioner to recover the shortfall or refund the excess Annual Fixed
Charges, on account of Return on Equity due to change in applicable Minimum
Alternate/Corporate Income Tax rate as per the Income Tax Act, 1961 (as amended
from time to time) of the respective financial year directly without making any application
before the Commission as provided in Tariff Regulations,2019 and Tariff
Regulations,2024 as per Para 17 and 18 above for respective block.
d) Approve the reimbursement of expenditure by the beneficiaries towards petition filing
fee, and expenditure on publishing of notices in newspapers in terms of Regulation 94(1)
of Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff)
Regulations, 2024, and other expenditure (if any) in relation to the filing of petition.
e) Allow the petitioner to bill and recover RLDC fees & charges and Licensee fee
separately from the respondents in terms of Regulation 94(3) and 93(4) of Central
Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2024.
f) Allow the petitioner to bill and adjust impact on Interest on Loan due to change in
Interest rate on account of floating rate of interest applicable during 2024-29 period, if
any, from the respondents.

overall security expenses and consequential IOWC on that security expenses as

authorities shall be allowed to be recovered from the beneficiaries.
and pass such other relief as the Commission deems fit and appropriate under the
circumstances of the case and in the interest of justice.”
Background
3. The brief facts of the case are as under:
a) The matter of non-compliance of N-1 criteria of 2x315 MVA, 400/220 kV ICTs
at the Hiriyur Sub-station was discussed in the 1st SRSCT meeting held on
Page 4 of 50
Order in Petition No. 559/TT/2025

7.9.2018, 2nd SRSCT meeting held on 10.6.2019 and 1st SRPC(TP) meeting
held on 16.12.2019.
b) In the 2nd SRPC (TP) meeting held on 1.10.2020, the issue of overloading of
2x315 MVA, 400/220 kV ICTs at the Hiriyur Sub-station was discussed.
Accordingly, implementation of the instant transmission project comprising
1x500 MVA, 400/220 kV 3rd ICT was agreed upon as a Regional System
Strengthening Scheme. It was also discussed in the same meeting that, with
the execution of the Tirunelveli-Kochi 400 kV (quad) D/C line, loadings on
2x315 MVA, 400/220 kV ICTs at the Kochi Sub-station have increased
significantly. Both ICTs are loaded to about 80-90% of their transformation
capacity and do not comply with the N-1 criteria. Further, it was discussed
that the ICTs at the Kochi Sub-station are highly loaded, and the loadings are
expected to increase further with the commissioning of the 2000 MW, ±320
kV Pugalur-Trichur VSC-based HVDC system. Accordingly, the
augmentation by 1x500 MVA, 400/220 kV 3rd ICT at the Kochi Sub-station
was agreed for implementation as a Regional System Strengthening
Scheme.
c) The Investment Approval (the IA) for the transmission project was accorded

ORDER
The Petitioner, Warora Kurnool Transmission Limited (hereinafter referred to as
‘the Petitioner/ WKTL’), has been granted a transmission licence under Section 14 of
the Electricity Act, 2003 (hereinafter referred to as ‘the Act’) to establish the
transmission system for the “Additional inter-Regional AC link for import into Southern
Order in Petition No. 855/MP/2025 Page 2

Region i.e. Warora – Warangal and Chilakaluripeta – Hyderabad – Kurnool 765kV
link” (hereinafter referred to as ‘the Transmission System’ or ‘Project’), the details of
which are specified in the schedule attached to the licence issued vide order dated
29.9.2016 in Petition No. 111/TL/2016. The Transmission System was commissioned
on 28.9.2023.
2. According to the Petitioner, for the purpose of financing the project, the
Petitioner had earlier approached the lender, namely, State Bank of India (SBI)
(hereinafter referred to as ‘Original Lender’), for a term loan facility of Rs. 2368 crore
to meet a part of the construction cost of the transmission system and re-finance the
then existing debt facilities. Accordingly, the Petitioner had approached the
Commission for approval of creating a security interest of Rs. 2,368 crore over the
Transmission System in favour of the SBICAP Trustee Company Limited (“SBI
Trustee”) under sub-sections (3) and (4) of Section 17 of the Act. The Commission,
vide its order dated 31.8.2021 in Petition No. 135/MP/2021 accorded in-principle
approval allowing the Petitioner to create security interest only with respect to loan
facility of Rs. 2,254 crore and excluded Performance Bank Guarantee (“BG facility”) of
Rs. 110 crore and Hedging facility of Rs. 4 crore in favour of SBI Trustee. Aggrieved
by the said order, the Petitioner filed a Review Petition No. 25/RP/2021 seeking
limited review of the Order dated 31.8.2021 in Petition No. 135/MP/2021. The
Commission, vide its order dated 28.2.2022 in Review Petition No. 25/RP/2021
accorded in-principle approval to the Petitioner to create the security interest in
respect of the entire loan facilities of Rs.2,368 crore which includes a term loan facility
of Rs.2,254 crore, BG facility of Rs.110 crore, and Hedging facility of Rs.4 crore in
favour of Security Trustee, namely, SBI Trustee.
3. The Petitioner has submitted that it has substituted the existing lender with new
Order in Petition No. 855/MP/2025 Page 3

lender i.e. HDFC Bank Limited and appointed Catalyst Trusteeship Limited as a
Security Trustee for the benefit of secured party i.e. HDFC Bank Ltd. as per the
Facility Agreement dated 29.04.2025 and the Security Trustee Agreement dated
29.04.2025. Accordingly, the Petitioner is seeking approval for assignment of the
transmission licence by way of security in favour of Security Trustee and creation of
security interest by way of mortgage, hypothecation, charge or assignment over all
movable and immovable assets including over rights, title, interest, claims, demands,
benefits under mortgage properties, project assets, clearance, project documents, and
agreements in favour of the Security Trustee, Respondent No.14 i.e., Catalyst
Trusteeship Ltd.. The Petitioner has made the following prayers:
“(a) Allow the present Petition;
(b) Take on record the New Lender i.e. HDFC Bank Ltd. and the
appointment of Catalyst Trusteeship Limited acting as Security Trustee for the
benefit of secured party i.e., HDFC Bank Ltd. as per Facility Agreement dated
29.04.2025 and Security Trustee Agreement dated 29.04.2025;
(c) Grant in principle approval for creation of security over all movable and
other immovable assets of WKTL (including over WKTL’s benefits, rights, title
and interest under the Transmission Service Agreement dated 06.01.2016, the
transmission license dated 29.09.2016 and other Transmission System
documents) by execution of relevant security creating documents in favour of
Catalyst Trusteeship Ltd. acting as Security Trustee for the benefit of secured
lenders including HDFC Bank Ltd. and any other lender (banks or financial
institutions) to which the rights and/ or obligations of all or any one or more of
the aforementioned Lenders are assigned, novated and/ or transferred, as per
Facility Agreement dated 29.04.2025 and Security Trustee Agreement dated
29.04.2025; and
(d) Pass such other and further orders as may be deemed fit under the facts
and circumstance of the present case.”
Background
4. The Petitioner has mainly submitted as under:
(a) The Petitioner is an inter-State transmission licensee under Section 14
of the Act. The Petitioner executed a Transmission Service Agreement with
Long-Term Transmission Customers (hereinafter referred to as ‘Respondents
No. 1-13’) on 6.1.2016 for availing the transmission services under the
Order in Petition No. 855/MP/2025 Page 4

Transmission System. Respondent No. 14 i.e., Catalyst Trusteeship Limited,
is a company incorporated under the Companies Act, and acting as a
Security Trustee for the purpose of holding securities on behalf of or for the
benefit of the new lenders.
(b) The Petitioner had executed a Facility Agreement with the State Bank of
India on 30.1.2021, to meet a part of the construction cost of the Transmission
System and to re-finance the then existing debt facilities. Pursuant to the
execution of the said Facility Agreement, the State Bank of India agreed to
provide the financial assistance in the form of a Term Loan Facility amounting
to Rs.2,254 crore with a Letter of Credit Facility (as a sub-limit of the Term
Loan Facility) amounting to Rs.1,300 crore Performance Bank Guarantee up
to Rs.110 crore/- and Hedging Facility of up to Rs.4 crore for the construction,
development, and implementation of the Transmission Project, on the terms
and conditions set out in the said Agreement.
(c) The Petitioner and the State Bank of India had appointed SBI Trustee,
as a Security Trustee by entering into a Security Trustee Agreement dated
7.4.2021 for the benefit of the lender, as defined under the Facility Agreement
dated 30.1.2021, and to execute all relevant financing documents. Vide order
dated 31.8.2021 in Petition No. 135/MP/2021, the Commission allowed
creation of security interest only with respect to loan facility of Rs. 2,254 crore
and excluded BG facility and Hedging facility. Aggrieved by the said order, the
Petitioner filed a Review Petition 25/RP/2021 seeking limited review of the
order dated 31.8.2021. The Commission, thereafter, vide its order dated
28.2.2022, accorded the in-principle approval to create the security interest in
respect of the entire loan facility of Rs. 2,368 crore, including term loan of Rs.
2,254 crore, BG facility of Rs. 110 crore and Hedging facility of Rs. 4 crore.
Order in Petition No. 855/MP/2025 Page 5

(d) The Petitioner approached HDFC Bank for financial assistance to pre-
pay the existing loan from the State Bank of India, under the Facility
Agreement dated 30.1.2021. Pursuant to the Petitioner’s request, HDFC
Bank, vide sanction letter dated 24.3.2025, sanctioned a total facility of Rs.
2,960 crore to the Petitioner, subject to the terms and conditions set forth in
the said sanction letter.
(e) Subsequently, on 29.4.2025, the Petitioner executed a Facility
Agreement with HDFC Bank substituting the State Bank of India. Pursuant to
the said Facility Agreement, the new lender (HDFC Bank) has agreed to
provide the Petitioner with term loan facilities aggregating to Rs. 2,910 crore
(hereinafter referred to as the ‘Facility’) (against the sanctioned amount of
2,960 crore), on the terms and conditions set out in the Agreement. As per
Schedule IA of the Facility Agreement, the new loan facility includes Rupee
Loan Facility 1 of Rs. 2,180 crore and Rupee Loan Facility 2 of Rs. 730 crore
including a BG Facility of Rs. 110 crore (as a sub-limit for Rupee Loan Facility
2).
(f) As per Clause 2.2 (Purpose) of the Facility Agreement dated 29.4.2025,
the New Loan Facility will be utilised by the Petitioner in the following manner:
“Rupee Facility 1 - Towards repayment of dues of the Existing Project
Lenders to the extent of the outstanding amounts of the Existing Project
Lenders existing as on the date of execution of this Agreement;
Rupee Facility 2 - Towards payment of capital creditors, if any, and
repayment of the monies infused by the Promoter in the Borrower which
was used for incurring capital expenditure of the Project (“Refinanced
Sub-debt”); and
BG Facility - Towards guarantee to be provided in favour of the
Beneficiary-BG.”
Order in Petition No. 855/MP/2025 Page 6

(g) As per Clause 3.1 of the Facility Agreement dated 29.4.2025, the loan
obligations under the said agreement and/or the other documents entered/to be
entered into in relation to the Original Loan Facility shall be secured by first pari
passu security interest on the movable and immovable assets of the
Petitioner/Transmission System in favour of the Security Trustee (for the benefit
of HDFC).
5. Accordingly, on 29.4.2025, the Petitioner, HDFC Bank and Catalyst
Trusteeship Limited have executed a Security Trustee Agreement authorising Catalyst
Trusteeship Limited to act as the New Security Trustee in relation to the New Loan
Facility (as sanctioned by HDFC) for the benefit of the HDFC/ secured party pursuant
to the trust created under the said Agreement.
6. The Petitioner has submitted that pursuant to the terms of the Facility
Agreement, the secured obligations are secured by,
(i) a first mortgage and charge on all the immovable properties (owned
and/or leased) of the Borrower pertaining to the Project, together with all
structures and appurtenances thereon, whether owned or leased (both present
and future) pertaining to the Project, in the form satisfactory to the Lenders/
Lenders’ Agent;
(ii) a first charge by way of hypothecation on all the tangible moveable
assets of the Borrower pertaining to the Project, including but not limited to
movable plant and machinery, machinery spares, tools and accessories,
furniture, fixtures, vehicles and all other movable assets pertaining to the
Project, both present and future;
(iii) a first charge by way of hypothecation on all current assets and
intangibles of the Borrower pertaining to the Project, including but not limited to,
book-debts, Receivables, operating cash flows, commissions, revenues of
whatsoever nature and wherever arising, goodwill, intellectual property rights,
uncalled capital and undertaking pertaining to the Project, both present and
future;
Order in Petition No. 855/MP/2025 Page 7

(iv) a first charge by way of hypothecation over all accounts of the Borrower,
including but not limited to the Account and the Sub-Accounts (including the
DSRA) (or any account in substitution thereof) that may be opened in
accordance with the Transaction Documents pertaining to the Project and in all
funds from time to time deposited therein (including the reserves), all non-fund
based reserves maintained by way of letters of credit / bank guarantees or
otherwise including DSR Instrument, and the Permitted Investments credited to
the Account;
(v) a first charge by way of hypothecation of:
A. all the right, title, interest, benefits, claims and demands whatsoever of
the Borrower in, to and under all the Project Documents including the
Transmission Services Agreement, duly acknowledged and consented to by the
counter parties to the Project Documents, all as amended, varied or
supplemented from time to time;
B. rights, title, interest, benefits, claims and demands of the Borrower in, to
and under all the Clearances pertaining to the Project;
C. all the right, title, interest, benefits, claims and demands whatsoever of
the Borrower in, to and under any letter of credit, guarantee including contractor
guarantees and liquidated damages, consent agreements, side letters and
performance bond provided by any party to the Project Documents, both
present and future; and
D. all the right, title, interest, benefits, claims and demands whatsoever of
the Borrower in, to and under all Insurance Contracts (obtained by the Borrower
or by any Contractor for the benefit of the Project or favouring the Borrower)
and Insurance Proceeds pertaining to the Project, both present and future
(vi) Pledge (in dematerialised form) over the 51% (fifty one percent) Equity
Share Capital and Preference Share Capital held by the Promoter, free from
any Security Interest, so as to maintain the Required Cover….”
7. The Petitioner has submitted that as per Articles 15.2.2 and 15.2.4 of the
Transmission Service Agreement (hereinafter referred to as ‘the TSA’) dated
6.1.2016, the Petitioner is required to take prior approval of the Commission, before
creating any encumbrance over all or part of the receivables, letter of credit or other
assets of the Transmission System, in favour of its lenders or the lender’s
representative. Upon receiving approval of the Commission, the Petitioner shall enter
Order in Petition No. 855/MP/2025 Page 8

into relevant security creating document(s) with Catalyst Trusteeship Limited to create
a first ranking security interest on the movable and immovable properties of WKTL/
Transmission System in favour of the Catalyst Trusteeship Ltd. (acting as the Security
Trustee) for the benefit of the secured party i.e. HDFC.
8. Accordingly, the Petitioner has filed the present Petition under Section 17 of the
Act, and Article 15 of the TSA, seeking prior approval of the Commission for the
creation of a Security Interest over all assets including the movable and immovable
assets for the Project in favour of the Security Trustee pursuant to the Security
Trustee Agreement and the Facility Agreement and for bringing on record the change
of existing lender viz. State Bank of India with the new lender i.e. HDFC Bank.
Hearing dated 6.11.2025
9. The Petition was called out for the hearing on 6.11.2025 after notice to the
Respondents. Vide Record of Proceedings (hereinafter referred to as “RoP”) for the
hearing dated 6.11.2025, the Respondents were granted the opportunity to file their
respective replies and the Petitioner was directed to implead the lender(s) as a party
to the Petition and further to file the details of application and source of funds as on
date of filing of this Petition and a No Due Certificate from the previous lender. In
compliance, the Petitioner has Petitioner has filed the information called for.
Hearing dated 16.12.2025
10. During the course of the hearing, the learned counsel for the Petitioner
submitted that the Petitioner has filed its compliance affidavit placing on record the
additional information sought vide RoP dated 6.11.2025. He further submitted that
neither any reply has been filed by the Respondents nor was anyone present on
Order in Petition No. 855/MP/2025 Page 9

behalf of the Respondents during the hearing, despite notice. Considering the
submissions of the Petitioner, the matter was reserved for order.
Analysis and Decision
11. We have considered the submissions made by the Petitioner and perused the
documents placed on record. The Petitioner initially approached the State Bank of
India (“Original Lender”) for the purpose of securing financial assistance of Rs. 2,368
crore for the implementation of the Transmission Project and to refinance the debt
availed from the then existing lenders. The State Bank of India, vide Sanction Letter
dated 11.8.2020 sanctioned Rs. 2,368 crore (Term loan facility of Rs. 2,254 crore, BG
facility of Rs. 110 crore and Hedge Facility of Rs. 4 crore) in favour of the Petitioner.
Further, the Original Lender entered into a Facility Agreement dated 30.1.2021 with
the Petitioner and agreed to provide the above-mentioned facilities to the Petitioner
amounting to Rs. 2,368 crore. In terms of the Facility Agreement, Rs. 508 crore was to
be utilised towards repayment of the sustainable debt portion of the loan obligations to
then existing lenders as full and final settlement. The balance facility of Rs. 1,746
crore sanctioned by the SBI is the additional debt available for drawdown for
completion of the Transmission System. As per the said Facility Agreement, the
estimated project cost was Rs. 3,220 crore and the SCOD was 1.1.2022, thus, the
project were under commissioning.
12. The Commission, vide Order dated 31.8.2021 in Petition No. 135/MP/2021,
accorded in-principle approval allowing the Petitioner to create a security intertest in
favour of SBICAP Trustee Company Limited (“SBI Trustee”) only against the term
loan facility of Rs. 2,254 crore, excluding BG Facility and Hedging Facility. Aggrieved
by the said exclusion, the Petitioner filed a Review Petition - 25/RP/2021 seeking
limited review of the Order dated 31.8.2021. Further, vide Order dated 28.2.2022, the
Order in Petition No. 855/MP/2025 Page 10

Commission accorded in-principle approval to the Petitioner to create the security
interest in respect of entire Original Loan Facility of Rs. 2,368 crore (which include
term loan facility of Rs. 2,254 crore, BG facility of Rs.110 crore and Hedging facility of
Rs. 4 crore). Accordingly, the Petitioner entered into a Security Trustee Agreement on
7.4.2021 with SBI and SBI Trustee.
13. Subsequently, the Petitioner approached the lender, namely, HDFC Bank (New
Lender) for refinancing the original loan facility availed from the SBI. The New Lender
has agreed to sanction the same vide its sanction letter dated 24.3.2025 in favour of
the Petitioner. Consequently, the Petitioner entered into a Facility Agreement on
29.4.2025 with the New Lender, HDFC to provide a New Loan Facility of Rs. 2,910
crore including Rupee Loan Facility 1 of Rs. 2,180 crore, Rupee Loan Facility 2 of Rs.
730 crore and BG Facility of Rs. 110 crore (as a sublimit for Rupee Loan Facility 2).
Consequently, the Petitioner entered into a Security Trustee Agreement on 29.4.2025
with HDFC Bank and Catalyst Trusteeship Limited. The Date of Commercial
Operations of the project as mentioned in the Facility Agreement dated 29.4.2025 is
28.09.2023.
14. The Facility Agreement dated 29.4.2025 under which a New Loan Facility was
agreed to be extended, includes Rupee Loan Facility -1 of Rs 2,180 crore, to be
utilised for repayment of existing project lenders’ dues and Facility- 2 of Rs 730
crores, and a Bank Guarantee Facility of Rs. 110 crore as a sublimit under Facility 2
for payment to capital creditors, and reimbursement of promoter funds infused for the
project capital expenditure. The Petitioner has submitted the following details for
utilization of disbursement received from HDFC Bank of Rs 2800 crore.
1. Towards repayment of dues of the Existing Project Rs 2180 crore
Lenders - State Bank of India
2. Towards repayment of Inter-corporate Deposits Rs 620 crore
Order in Petition No. 855/MP/2025 Page 11

Additionally, a Bank Guarantee Facility of Rs. 110 crore.
15. The Petitioner, vide affidavit dated 12.12.2025, has also submitted the following
Financing Plan and the details of Contribution as on the date of filing of the Petition,
i.e., 29.09.2025 :
Schedule II
PART A
FINANCING PLAN
Particulars Amount in crore (Rs.)
Contributions 1483.97
Facility 2762.16
PART B
DETAILS OF CONTRIBUTION
Particulars Amount in crore (Rs.)
Subscription to Equity Share Capital 537.00
Subscription to OCD 186.07
Subordinate Loan 760.90
16. The transmission projects are capital intensive projects requiring large capital
investment. These projects are financed through loans. It is normal practice followed
by financial institution/ banking industry to ask for sufficient security from the borrower
to back the loan in order to mitigate the credit risk of the lenders. In the instant case,
the new lender (HDFC) has agreed to provide rupee term loan Rs. 2,910 crore and for
the said purpose has entered into a Facility Agreement dated 29.4.2025 with the
Petitioner for, inter-alia, refinancing of the existing loan. In addition, the Petitioner, in
compliance with the RoP dated 6.11.2025, has submitted the ‘No Due Certificate’
issued by the existing lender (State Bank of India) dated 15.10.2025, confirming that
there is no outstanding amount against the credit facilities of Rs. 2,254 crore availed
by the Petitioner/ Warora Kurnool Transmission Limited. The relevant portion of the
letter dated 15.10.2025 is extracted as under:
“This is with reference to your Term loan of Rs. 2254,00,00,000 (Rupees Two
Thousand Two Hundred and Fifty-Four Crore Only) and NFB Limit of Rs.
Order in Petition No. 855/MP/2025 Page 12

114,00,00,000 (Rupees One hundred and Fourteen Crore only) in the name of
M/s Warora Kurnool Transmission Limited with our Bank. We would like to
inform that the Term Loan Account and NFB has been fully repaid and closed
on 01.05.2025 and 06.10.2025 and there are no dues outstanding in the loan
account as on date.”
17. The Petitioner has submitted that, in terms of the Financing documents, the
Petitioner is required to create a Security Interest on a first charge basis for the lender.
The Petitioner has submitted that under the Financing Agreements and on
enforcement of a security interest, it shall be lawful for the lender and its assigns
transferees, and novates to enter into and take possession of the assets/ properties
mortgaged/ hypothecated/ charges assigned for their benefits and substitute
themselves or any one of them or its nominees for the Petitioner under any or all of the
project document(s). Article 15.2.2 of the TSA provides as under:
“15.2.2 However, the TSP may create any encumbrance over all or part of the
receivables, Letter of Credit or the other assets of the Project in favour of the
Lenders or the Lenders’ Representative on their behalf, as security for amounts
payable under the Financing Agreements and any other amounts agreed by the
Parties.
Provided that:
i. the Lenders or the Lenders’ Representative on their behalf shall have
entered into the Financing Agreements and agreed in writing to the
provisions of this Agreement; and
ii. any encumbrance granted by the TSP. in accordance with this Article
15.2.2 shall contain provisions pursuant to which the Lenders or the
Lender’s Representative on their behalf agrees unconditionally with the
TSP to release from such encumbrances upon payment by the TSP to the
Lenders of all amounts due under the Financing Agreements.”
In accordance with the above provision, the Transmission Service Provider has
been allowed to create an encumbrance over all or part of the receivables, Letters of
Credit, or other assets of the Project in favour of the lenders or the lenders’
representatives or their representatives, as security for amounts payable under the
Financing Agreements and any other amounts agreed by the parties.
18. Article 15.3 of the TSA provides as under:
Order in Petition No. 855/MP/2025 Page 13

“15.3 Substitution Rights of the Lenders:
15.3.1 The TSP would need to operate and maintain the Project under the
provisions of the Transmission License granted by the Appropriate Commission
and the provisions of this Agreement and can not assign the Transmission
License' or transfer the Project or part thereof to any person by sale, lease,
exchange or otherwise, without the prior approval of the Appropriate
Commission.
15.3.2 However, in the case of default by the TSP in debt repayments, the
Appropriate Commission may, on an application from, the Lenders, assign the
Transmission License to the nominee of the Lenders subject to the fulfilment of
the qualification requirements and provisions of the Central Electricity
Regulatory Commission (Procedure, terms and Conditions for grant of
Transmission License and other related matters) Regulations, 2006 or as
amended from time to time.”
19. Sub-sections (3) and (4) of Section 17 of the Act provides as under:
“17. (3) No licensee shall any time assign his licence or transfer his utility, or
any part hereof, by sale, lease, exchange or otherwise without the prior
approval of the Appropriate Commission.
(4) Any agreement relating to any transaction specified in sub-section (1) or
sub-section (3), unless made with the prior approval of the Appropriate
Commission, shall be void.”
As per the above provisions, a licensee is required to obtain approval of the
Commission for assigning its licence or transferring its utility or any part thereof by
way of sale, lease, exchange or otherwise and entering into an agreement relating to
any of these transactions.
20. Accordingly, we accord approval for substitution of new lender, who has agreed
to refinance the projects/ transmission assets and accord in-principle approval for
creation of security interest in favour of Security Trustee, namely, Catalyst Trusteeship
Limited for the benefit of the lender. In this regard, the Petitioner has placed on record
the relevant documents pertaining to the involvement of HDFC Bank as the new
lender and the creation of a security interest in favour of Catalyst Trusteeship Limited,
acting as the Security Trustee on behalf of the new lender, have been duly placed on
record.
Order in Petition No. 855/MP/2025 Page 14

21. This approval is being granted with the condition that the transmission licence
granted by the Commission to the Petitioner cannot be assigned in favour of the
Security Trustee or nominee of the lender without prior approval of the Commission at
the time of creating rights in favour of such a nominee. Before agreeing to the
assignment of the licence and the assets of the Petitioner to the nominee of the
lender, the Commission will evaluate such a nominee’s expertise in the development
design, construction, operation, and maintenance of the transmission lines and its
ability to execute the Project and undertake the transmission of electricity. The
licensee, lender, security trustee, and nominee, accordingly, shall be jointly required
to approach the Commission to seek approval. This will allow the Commission to
satisfy itself of the circumstances necessitating such a transfer.
22. This decision of ours is in accordance with Regulation 8 of the Central
Electricity Regulatory Commission (Procedure, Terms and Conditions for grant of
Transmission Licence and other related matters) Regulations, 2024, which reads as
under:
“8. Assignment of Licence: In case of default by the licensee in debt
repayment, the Commission may, on an application made by the lenders of the
licence, assign the licence to a nominee of the lenders.”
23. In the event of default by the licensee regarding debt repayment, the
Commission may, upon a joint application submitted by the licensee, lender, Security
Trustee, and their nominee, grant approval for the assignment of the licence to a
nominee, contingent upon the satisfactory completion of due diligence procedures.
Consequently, it is imperative to obtain explicit prior approval from the Commission for
the assignment of the licence to the nominee of the Security Trustee or for the transfer
of any assets to them. Finally, the Petitioner is required to submit the financial
Order in Petition No. 855/MP/2025 Page 15

documents and statements in accordance with the directives issued by the
Commission.
24. Petition No. 855/MP/2025 is disposed of in terms of the above.

CENTRAL ELECTRICITY REGULATORY COMMISSION
NEW DELHI

Date of Order: 17th January, 2026
In the matter of
Petition under Section 79(1)(f) of the Electricity Act, 2003, seeking relief on account of
Force Majeure and Change in Law events under the Power Purchase Agreements
dated 22.12.2021 and 24.12.2021 executed between the Petitioner and Respondent
No. 1 and Respondent No. 2, respectively.
And
In the matter of
MB Power (Madhya Pradesh) Limited,
Laharpur, Jaithari, Anuppur,
Madhya Pradesh – 484330 …Petitioner
Vs.
1. PTC India Limited,
2nd Floor, NBCC Tower,
15 Bhikaji Cama Place,
New Delhi-110066
2. Torrent Power Limited,
Samanvay, 600 Tapovan,
Ambawadi, Ahmedabad-380015
Gujarat
…Respondents
Parties Present:
Shri Amit Kapur, Advocate, MBPMPL
Shri Akshat Jain, Advocate, MBPMPL
Shri Shikhar Verma, Advocate, MBPMPL
Shri Abhishek Gupta, MBPMPL
Shri Shubham Batia, MBPMPL
Shri Ravi Kishore, Advocate, PTCIL
Shri Singh, Advocate, PTCIL
Ms. Deepa Chawan, Senior Advocate, TPL
Order in Petition No. 71/MP/2023
Page 1 of 15

Ms. Swapna Seshadri, Advocate, TPL
Ms. Reshamarani, Advocate, TPL
Ms. Aishwarya Subramani, Advocate, TPL
ORDER
The Petitioner, MB Power (Madhya Pradesh) Limited (‘MBPMPL’), a generating
company, has developed a 1200 MW (2x600 MW) coal-based thermal power project
in District Anuppur, Madhya Pradesh (the ‘Project’). In light of the guidelines issued by
the Ministry of Power dated 30.3.2016, Respondent No. 2/ Torrent Power Limited
(‘TPL’) floated a tender on 8.12.2021 for the procurement of power for short-term (i.e.,
for the period from 1.4.2022 to 30.9.2022) through a tariff-based competitive bidding
process. Respondent No. 1/ PTC participated in the bid on behalf of the Petitioner,
emerged as a successful bidder and was issued a Letter of Award (LoA) on 22.12.2021
for the supply of 50 MW power to TPL. Eventually, on 22.12.2021, Respondent No. 1/
PTC India Limited (‘PTC’) entered into a Power Purchase Agreement with TPL (‘PTC
PPA’) for the supply of the 50 MW power to TPL from the Project for the period from
1.4.2022 to 30.9.2022. Subsequently, on 24.12.2021, the Petitioner entered into a
Power Purchase Agreement with PTC (‘MB Power PPA’) on a back-to-back basis for
the supply of the 50 MW power to TPL through PTC from the Project. Unit-1 and Unit-
2 of the Project achieved Commercial Operation Date (‘COD’) on 20.5.2015 and
7.4.2016, respectively. The Petitioner is seeking discharge from the MB Power PPA
dated 24.12.2021 on account of impossibility and frustration of the contract due to the
force majeure events which have rendered supply under the PPA impossible. Further,
the Petitioner has submitted that the MB Power PPA is not in conformity with the short-
term guidelines issued by the MoP. The Petitioner has made the following prayers:
“(a) Hold and declare that the Power Purchase Agreements dated 24.12.2021
executed between MB Power and PTC is not in conformity with the MoP Short-
Term Guidelines and GERC Guidelines;
Order in Petition No. 71/MP/2023
Page 2 of 15

(b) Declare and hold that MB Power PPA dated 24.12.2021 stands frustrated w.e.f.
31.03.2022, due to supervening impossibility on account of subsistence of Force
Majeure Events;
(c) Hold and declare that CIL Circular dated 01.03.2022 issued pursuant to CCEA’s
decision dated 26.02.2022 constitutes a Force Majeure event for MB Power in
terms of Article 6 of the MB Power PPA to the extent that it has resulted in shortfall
in availability of sufficient and compatible coal required to generate and supply the
Contracted Capacity of 50 MW to PTC;
(d) Hold and declare that CIL Circular dated 01.03.2022 issued pursuant to CCEA’s
decision dated 26.02.2022 constitutes a Change in Law event for MB Power in
terms of Article 6 of the MB Power PPA read with Change in Law Rules 2021 to
the extent of increase in the cost of procurement of coal;
(e) Declare that PTC is not entitled to seek any liquidated damages and/or
replacement power cost and/or any open access charges from MB Power or levy
any penalty on MB Power on account of non-supply of 50 MW power to PTC;
(f) Quash the Invoices/Debit Notes issued by PTC on MB Power as being unlawful;
(g) Direct PTC to refund the amount illegally, unjustifiably and arbitrarily deducted
from MB Power’s payments to be made by PTC for supply of 361 MW to Uttar
Pradesh Power Corporation Ltd. through PTC under the operational Long Term
PPA till date along with the late payment surcharge/carrying cost;
(h) Direct PTC not to make any such illegal, unjustifiable and arbitrary deductions
in future from MB Power’s payments to be made by PTC for supply of 361 MW to
Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Ltd. through PTC under the operational Long
Term PPA;
(i) Direct PTC to make the payments of Rs. 24,91,27,471/- against the power
supplied to PTC [approximately 37 Million Units (MUs)] to PTC for the period
between 01.05.2022 to 31.05.2022 and 08.09.2022 to 09.09.2022 along with the
applicable carrying cost/ late payment surcharge;
(j) In the interim, direct the Respondents to not take any coercive actions against
MB Power on account of non-supply of 50 MW power to PTC; and
(k) Pass any such other and further reliefs as this Commission deems.”
Proceedings before the Commission
2. The Petition was admitted on 16.5.2023. After the completion of pleadings, the
matter was again listed for hearing, wherein the Petitioner made detailed submissions.
However, the matter remained part-heard. During the course of the hearing, the
learned counsel for the Petitioner submitted that in light of the APTEL’s judgment dated
28.8.2024 in Appeal No. 309 of 2019 titled as Madhya Pradesh Power Management
Co. Ltd. v. DVC and Anr. (‘DVC judgement’), as upheld by the Hon’ble Supreme Court
Order in Petition No. 71/MP/2023
Page 3 of 15

in the Civil Appeal No. 10480/2023 dated 23.9.2024 (‘SC Order’), the present matter
needs to be referred to the arbitration by the Commission. On the contrary, the
Respondents in the matter have vehemently contested such averments of the
Petitioner. Subsequently, both sides were permitted to file their respective submissions
on the above aspect and were extensively heard, as noted below.
Hearing dated 11.2.2025
3. Learned counsel for the Petitioner submitted that since the primary issue in the
matter pertains to the validity of the Power Purchase Agreement dated 24.12.2021, the
matter requires arbitration in light of the DVC judgment as well as the SC Order.
Learned senior counsel for the Respondent TPL submitted that there is no arbitration
agreement between the Petitioner and TPL, and in the absence thereof, no reference
can be made to the arbitrator. Learned senior counsel further submitted that while there
is an arbitration clause in the agreement entered into between the Respondents, TPL,
and PTC, PTC has entered into the said agreement in the capacity of a merchant
trader. In fact, the Petitioner's various prayers relate only to the Agreement entered
into by the Petitioner with PTC. After considering the submissions of the parties, the
parties were directed to file their notes of arguments on the aspect of arbitrability of the
dispute.
4. Pursuant to the directions of the Commission issued vide Record of Proceedings
dated 11.2.2025, the Petitioner and the Respondents, PTC and TPL, have filed their
respective submissions on the aspect of arbitrability of the dispute in the Petition.
Hearing dated 16.9.2025
5. During the course of the hearing, both sides made detailed submissions and
Order in Petition No. 71/MP/2023
Page 4 of 15

concluded their respective arguments on the arbitrability of the dispute involved in the
matter. After hearing both sides, the Commission reserved the matter for order on the
arbitrability of the disputes. Further, the Commission directed the parties to file their
respective written submissions/ notes of argument in the matter. The Petitioner and the
Respondents have filed their respective written submissions on the aspect of
arbitrability of the dispute(s). The gist of the submissions of the parties is as under:
Submissions of the Petitioner/ MBPL
6. The Petitioner has mainly submitted as under:
Re: The present Petition primarily pertains to a non-tariff dispute
(i) The findings of the DVC judgment and SC Order are squarely applicable
to the present matter. As per the DVC Judgment, non-tariff disputes involving
a generating company or a distribution licensee do not fall within the ambit of
clause (f) of Section 79(1) of the Electricity Act and are arbitrable. However,
disputes relating to termination or breach of contract, which do not impact the
tariff either directly or indirectly, are considered as non-tariff related disputes
and can be resolved through arbitration.
(ii) The primary prayer in the present Petition seeking declaration that the
PPA dated 24.12.2021 executed between the Petitioner and PTC is not in
conformity with the MoP Short-Term Guidelines and GERC Guidelines.
Therefore, the primary prayer sought by MB Power in the present Petition
pertains to the question of whether the PPA is a valid document or not. Thus,
the primary prayer in the present Petition first ought to be decided by arbitration
as the subsequent prayers sought in the Petition pertain to
ancillary/consequent reliefs.
(iii) In the DVC judgment, the APTEL itself divided the reliefs sought
thereunder to identify a ‘main issue’, i.e., the issue of termination of the PPA,
which it held to be a non-tariff issue. The Cause of Action in the present Petition
has not sought to be split by the Petitioner, but the Commission ought to
identify that the primary relief sought by the Petitioner pertains to whether the
PPA is a valid document or not. Since the primary issue pertains to the validity
of the PPAs entered into between the parties and does not relate to tariff or
regulation of tariff, the same ought to be referred to arbitration.
Re: Agreement between the parties to enter into Arbitration under Section 7 of
the Arbitration and Conciliation Act
(iv) PTC PPA contains a valid Arbitration Clause in writing, which mandates
that all disputes other than tariff/tariff-related disputes are to be resolved by
way of arbitration. In terms of Clause 3 of the MB Power PPA, all risks, titles
Order in Petition No. 71/MP/2023
Page 5 of 15

and obligations as per the PTC PPA shall be applicable mutatis mutandis to
MB Power. Further, Clause 4 of the MB Power PPA states that the PTC PPA
is an integral part of the MB Power PPA. Therefore, it is not a case of merely
annexing the PTC PPA, but makes the PTC PPA an integral part of the MB
Power PPA. On a conjoint reading of Section 8 of the Arbitration & Conciliation
Act and the arbitration clause of the PPA, it is clear that any and all non-tariff
related disputes amongst MB Power, PTC and TPL shall be essentially
resolved by way of the arbitration.
Re. MB Power invoked arbitration in terms of Section 8 of the Arbitration and
Conciliation Act
(v) As held by the Hon’ble Supreme Court in its judgment dated 13.03.2008
titled Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Ltd. v. Essar Power, [(2008) 4 SCC 755], in
case there is a conflicting provision between the Electricity Act and the
Arbitration and Conciliation Act, the provisions of the Electricity Act will prevail.
Since the language in Section 79(1)(f) of the Electricity Act does not impose
any embargo regarding the stage at which the parties can approach this
Commission to refer the dispute to arbitration, Section 79(1)(f) of the Electricity
Act will override Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act.
Re. The MB Power PPA and PTC PPA are Back-to-Back Agreements
(vi) It is a settled position of law that when a trading licensee such as PTC,
is not functioning as a merchant trader, i.e. without taking upon itself the
financial and commercial risks but passing on the all the risks to the purchaser
under re-sale, then there is clearly a link between the ultimate distribution
company and the generator with the trader acting as only an intermediary
linking company.
(vii) TPL was already aware from the beginning that the entire transaction
under the PPAs shall encompass the supply of the 50 MW power by MB Power
to TPL through PTC. In terms of Clause 3 of the MB Power PPA, all risks, titles
and obligations as per the PTC PPA shall be applicable mutatis mutandis to
MB Power. The terminology used in Clause 3 of the MB Power PPA is ‘risks,
titles and obligations’, meaning that all the risks, including the arbitration clause
in the PTC PPA will be applicable mutatis mutandis to the MB Power PPA. In
this regard, reliance has been placed on the Order of the Commission dated
25.4.2024 in Petition No. 48/MP/2023 titled as Jaiprakash Power Ventures Ltd.
v. PTC India Ltd. & Torrent Power Ltd’.
Re. This Commission’s power to ‘Regulate’ under Section 79 being guided by
MoP’s Short-Term Guidelines
(viii) The Commission has the power under Section 79(1)(b) of the Electricity
Act to ‘Regulate’ tariff of the generating companies which are not
owned/controlled by the Central Government, if such generating companies
enter into or otherwise have a composite scheme for the generation and sale
of electricity in more than one State. Further, the present dispute is covered by
MoP’s ‘Guidelines for short-term (i.e., for a period of more than one day to one
year) Procurement of Power by Distribution Licensees through Tariff Based
Bidding Process’ dated 20.03.2016 (“Short Term Guidelines”) issued under
Order in Petition No. 71/MP/2023
Page 6 of 15

Section 63 of the Electricity Act. In terms of the Energy Watchdog Judgment,
the Commission’s power to regulate under Section 79(1) is subject to and
guided by the Short-Term Guidelines as the situation pertaining to arbitrability
of the present dispute is squarely covered thereunder and this Commission
must exercise its regulatory functions, albeit under Section 79(1)(b) of the
Electricity Act, only in accordance with those guidelines.
(ix) Further, the CERC (Code of Business) Regulations, 2023, also envisage
the Reference of a dispute to arbitration. Regulation 49 provides that the
Commission has the power to nominate arbitrators where the Commission
decides to refer the matter to arbitration by a person or persons.
Submissions of Respondent No. 2/ TPL
7. The Respondent TPL has submitted on the aspect of arbitrability of the dispute
in question as under:
(i) The plea regarding arbitration appears to have been raised inter alia for
two oblique purposes, namely delaying the proceedings, and forum shopping
mid-way through the proceedings and sitting on the fence till delivery of the
DVC judgment by the APTEL. The same plea is untenable as the Commission
has already addressed this in a similar matter in its Order dated 25.4.2024 in
Petition No. 48/MP/2023 titled ‘Jaiprakash Power Ventures Ltd. v. PTC & Anr.’
The Commission in the said order has interpreted a comparable PPA and held
that any third-party sale outside the terms of the contract would necessitate the
reimbursement of the additional costs incurred by the Procurer, in arranging
for replacement power.
(ii) DVC Case clearly incorporated and specified an arbitration clause. Thus,
both the parties in the said judgment had agreed to proceed for arbitration in
the event of differences arising between the parties and failure of settlement
initiatives, contemplated under the PPA. However, in the present case, there
is no arbitration agreement between TPL and the Petitioner. Further, there is
no signed document by either parties nor exchange of any letter, telex,
telegram or any communication relating to submission to arbitration between
the parties. In the present case, TPL has a PPA with PTC, and there are no
claims inter se. Any arbitration between third parties cannot bind the TPL, and
the TPL has no contractual arrangement with the Petitioner and thus cannot
be made subject to any arbitration with the Petitioner. The arbitration
agreement between TPL and PTC is an agreement which is to be treated as
different from the underlying transaction for which the contract is entered into
between both parties.
(iii) As per the DVC case, the fundamental basis for mandatory reference to
arbitration is the applicability of the conditions contained in Section 8 of the
Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (A&C Act). Thus, the reference to
arbitration must occur at the first instance at the stage of pleadings. Reliance
in this regard has been placed on the judgments in Booz Allen & Hamilton Inc.
v. SBI Home Finance Ltd., and P Anand Gajapathi Raju and Ors. vs. P V G
Raju (Dead) and Ors. However, the pleadings are completed in the present
Order in Petition No. 71/MP/2023
Page 7 of 15

matter, and the arguments on behalf of the Petitioner have also been
completed in the matter without raising any issue of the matter being arbitrable.
In fact, the Petitioner, merely relying on the annexing of the Agreement dated
22.12.2021 between TPL and PTC to its agreement dated 24.12.2021 with
PTC does not hold that an arbitration is entered between MBP and TPL.
(iv) The Petitioner has wrongfully asserted that its independent PPA dated
24.12.2021 between PTC incorporates the words “Mutatis Mutandis” in relation
to the contents of the PPA dated 22.12.2021 between TPL and PTC.
(v) Section 7 of the Arbitration & Conciliation Act sets out that there has to
be an interest between the parties by a document signed between the parties,
or exchange of letters or any other means of communication recording the
intention of the parties for an arbitration. However, the earlier interest and
conduct of parties reveal that the claim was never understood to be covered
by the arbitration clause. In fact, in the DVC judgment, there was an Arbitration
agreement between the parties. The DVC judgment relied on Section 8 of the
Arbitration & Conciliation Act and had nothing to do with Section 7 thereof,
which is crucial in the present case.
(vi) Further, the PPAs in their entirety cannot be treated as a ‘statutory
contract’ merely because the PPA is entered into in exercise of enabling power
conferred by a statute, i.e. in the present case pursuant to Section 63 of the
Electricity Act. Even if the contention of the Petitioner that these were back-to-
back arrangements, then the nature of the contract would be a contract under
the Sale of Goods Act read with the Indian Contract Act and would not ipso
facto become a contract executed under Section 63 of the Electricity Act. Even
otherwise, Section 7 of the Arbitration & Conciliation Act, 1996 applies to the
statutory contracts, necessitating adherence by the parties to the ingredients
of an arbitration agreement.
(vii) In the DVC judgment, the APTEL has concluded that where there is an
arbitration agreement between the generating company and the procurer and
the dispute is not related to the regulatory functions/tariff disputes, namely
disputes having an impact on tariff directly or indirectly, the same ought to be
referred to arbitration by the Commission. DVC case has only clarified the
position of law that even the Commission is bound by Section 8 of the
Arbitration Act, in cases wherein an arbitration agreement exists. However, it
does not create a new route for the parties to a matter pending before the
Commission to transfer such matters to arbitration at an advanced stage of a
proceeding and that to without the existence of an arbitration agreement.
Further, the factual matrix of the DVC judgment differs from that of the present
matter.
(viii) There is no arbitration agreement between the Petitioner and TPL and
hence there can be no plea for arbitration. PTC has a PPA with the Petitioner
wherein TPL is not a party hand therefore there is no question of back-to-back
contract. Multi-party arbitration is not contemplated within the scheme of the
Arbitration Act unless all the parties to the suit / petition are parties to the
arbitration agreement.
Order in Petition No. 71/MP/2023
Page 8 of 15

(ix) The Petitioner had in April 2021 initially raised issues of change in law
and force majeure without invoking arbitration. Despite the same, it filed a Writ
Petition before the Hon`ble High Court, Madras, challenging the Commission’s
Open Access Regulations, which had been operative for nearly thirteen (13)
years. The ex-parte stay in favour of the Petitioner passed by the Hon`ble High
Court, Madras was vacated by the Hon`ble Supreme Court. The Petitioner
after filing the present Petition and after completion of pleadings on merits in
Case No. 71 of 2023 willingly participated in the hearing of the present case
on 09.10.2023. The Petitioner was fully heard on 09.10.2023 in support of its
Petition. During the hearing held on 16.09.2025, the Petitioner argued in
support of its oral request dated 11.02.2025 for referring the matter for
arbitration on the specious plea of the pronouncement of the DVC judgment by
the APTEL. The Petitioner cannot contend that subsequent judgments give it
the right to raise an issue of arbitration. Judicially, the doctrine of sitting on the
fence is a recognised concept.
(x) The prayers of the Petitioner reveal that the primary dispute relates to
compensation for the amounts charged by the PTC on account of diversion of
power supply by the Petitioner. The Petitioner has sought to be exempted from
paying such compensation and sought a declaration of certain events as
change in law. The same falls directly within the category of tariff disputes set
out in the DVC judgment. In the present case, there is no relief sought by the
Petitioner against TPL.
(xi) The Hon’ble Supreme Court in the judgment of Sukanya Holdings (P)
Ltd. vs Jayesh H. Pandya has settled that there can be no splitting of cause of
action in order to determine the issue of arbitration. Thus, the entire subject
matter of the petition filed should be covered by the arbitration agreement, and
further, the entire suit should be arbitrable. There can be no bifurcation of the
cause of the subject matter, i.e., one part to be decided by the arbitral tribunal
and the other by the civil court/the Commission in the present case.
(xii) The dispute involved in the matter is not arbitrable under the A&C Act in
view of the several parties involved in the matter. In adjudication, disputes
involving several parties can be heard and decided in one petition. However,
there will be several arbitrations if the dispute is to be referred to arbitration
under each PPA separately and decided separately, with the possibility of
conflicting decisions.
(xiii) The Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Gujarat Urja Vikas Nigam Ltd.
Vs. Essar Power Ltd., (2008) 4 SCC 755, has held that Section 79 (1) (f) and
Section 86 (1) (f) of the Electricity Act are pari materia. In GUVNL’s case, there
was an arbitration provision in the agreement between the parties. However,
in the present case, there is no agreement between the Petitioner and TPL.
(xiv) The Hon’ble Supreme Court, while considering the DVC judgment, has
passed a summary order upholding the DVC judgment on the prima facie
difference in language between Section 79 (1) (f) & Section 86 (1) (f).
Therefore, the SC Order has to be read with the DVC Judgment of the APTEL.
All that the DVC Judgment does, as stated before, is to carve out an exception
for non-tariff disputes, albeit where an arbitration agreement exists between
the parties. The dismissal of the Civil Appeal by the Hon’ble Supreme Court
Order in Petition No. 71/MP/2023
Page 9 of 15

does not amount to upholding the law propounded in the decision challenged
through the Civil Appeal.
(xv) TPL is not agreeable to the plea of arbitration put forth by the Petitioner
orally, mid-way through the proceedings in the matter and thus the
Commission may decide the matter being the tariff related disputes.
Submissions of Respondent No. 1/ PTC
(i) On 22.12.2021, the LoA was issued by TPL to PTC, which was duly
accepted by the Petitioner. On 21.12.2021, PTC and TPL signed the PPA, and
the Petitioner and PTC signed the PPA on 24.12.2021. The Petitioner was duly
aware of all the terms and conditions of the tender and also accepted the same.
On 31.3.2022, the Petitioner sent a letter informing that the change in policy
regarding allocation of coal will be a Change in Law event. Subsequently, the
Petitioner took a position that a change in policy regarding the allocation of
coal is a Force Majeure event under Article 6 of the Power Purchase
Agreement dated 24.12.2022.
(ii) In the present petition, the Petitioner had taken a stand that the PPA
dated 24.12.2021 executed between the Petitioner and Respondent No.1 is
not in conformity with the MoP Short-Term Guideline and GERC Guidelines.
(iii) The Commission vide order dated 25.4.2024 in Petition No. 48/MP/2023
has held that PPA and PSA are on a back-to-back basis and Respondent No.
2 has a privity of contract with the Petitioner. The present PPA and PSA are in
regard to the same tender floated by PTL.
(iv) The Commission has the power under Section 79(1)(f) of the Act, to
adjudicate the disputes, if the same falls under Clauses (a) to (d). Clauses (a)
to (d) of Section 79 of the Act, invariably uses the word “regulate” the tariff,
inter State transmission of electricity etc. Section 79(1) (a) to (d) does not
primarily deals with matters related to only tariff, which is a pure number. The
words being used in the aforesaid Sections are “regulate” which has a much
wider connotation. The Hon’ble Supreme Court in catena of judgments has
elaborated the meaning of “regulate” in contest of the Electricity Act, wherein
the term “regulate’ used is very wide.
(v) The APTEL in the matter of Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd Vs.
CERC & Anr and also on the BSES Rajdhani Power Limited vs Delhi Electricity
Regulatory Commission & Anr., has held that the word “regulate” has much
wider connotation as used in Section 79 of the Act and the powers of the
Commission under Section 79(1) (f) will definitely include power to adjudicate
disputes which will include the billing, the payment, the consequences of delay
in the payment by way of surcharge, rebate for payment within a specified
period, termination or suspension of supply, payment security mechanism etc.
(vi) In DVC judgment, the issue before the APTEL was termination of the
PPA and the judgment has to be viewed in the facts and circumstances of that
case. The Civil Appeal of the same has been dismissed in limine by the Hon’ble
Supreme Court and no detailed orders/reasoning has been given while
Order in Petition No. 71/MP/2023
Page 10 of 15

dismissing the appeal. The judgment of Hon’ble Supreme Court may not
please be considered as applicable to all the cases.
(vii) In a similar matter regarding termination of the PPA, the Hon’ble
Supreme Court in its Order dated 1.4.2025 in SLP (C) No. 5276/2023 has
granted leave and also recognised that the word ‘regulate’ has much wider
connotation. From the order of the Hon’ble Supreme Court, it is evident that
the suit pending before the Hon’ble Delhi High Court has been stayed with the
direction that only pleadings are to be completed. The above matter/SLP
pertains to the Petition filed by PTC challenging the order of Hon’ble Delhi High
Court rejecting the application of PTC under Order 7 Rule 11 of the CPC. The
Application under Order 7 Rule 11 was filed by PTC in Petition filed by MBPL
being Petition No. CS (COMM.) 282/2022. In the said Petition, issue also
pertained to the termination of the PPA. The said application was dismissed by
the Hon’ble Delhi High Court.
(viii) The issue before the Commission in the present petition pertains to
various issues regarding change in law/ events of Force Majeure/ alleged non-
approval of the PPA by GERC/ non-supply of power, and consequently
covered under Section 79(1) (b) and (c) of the Act. Therefore, such issues need
to be adjudicated by the Commission and not under arbitration as prayed by
the Petitioner.
Analysis and Decision
8. We have considered the submissions made by the parties and perused the
documents made available on record. The primary issue that arises for our
consideration is whether the disputes involved in this case are, as explained in the DVC
Judgment, tariff disputes or non-tariff disputes? Further, both sides have also raised
certain additional issues, such as the existence/ non-existence of an arbitration
agreement between the Petitioner and TPL, the stage at which an arbitration can be
invoked/ compliance with Section 8 of the A & C Act 1996, the scope and meaning of
the term “Mutatis Mutandis”, etc., as noted above. However, the need to examine these
issues would arise only once we conclude that the disputes in the matter are non-tariff
and are mandatorily required to be referred to arbitration. Hence, these issues will be
addressed in the latter part of the order, if so required.
9. The Petitioner has submitted that, as per the DVC Judgment, the non-tariff
disputes involving a generating company or a distribution licensee do not fall within the
Order in Petition No. 71/MP/2023
Page 11 of 15

ambit of clause (f) of Section 79(1) of the Electricity Act and are arbitrable. All matters
which would have a bearing upon the tariff for a generating company would constitute
‘tariff disputes. However, disputes relating to termination or breach of contract, which
do not impact the tariff either directly or indirectly, are considered as non-tariff related
disputes and can be resolved through arbitration. It is submitted that the primary prayer
in the present Petition seeks a declaration that the PPA dated 24.12.2021 executed
between MB Power and PTC is not in conformity with the MoP Short-Term Guidelines
and GERC Guidelines. Therefore, the primary prayer sought by the Petitioner pertains
to the question of whether the PPA is a valid document or not, which does not relate to
tariff or regulation of tariff in terms of the DVC Judgment and ought to be referred to
the arbitration. It is also submitted that the subsequent prayers sought in the Petition
are merely ancillary/ consequential reliefs. Whereas, the Respondent, PTC, has
submitted that the disputes in the present Petition pertain to the various issues
regarding Change in Law/ Force Majeure events, alleged non-approval of the PPA,
non-supply of power and consequently, are covered under Section 79 (1)(b) and (c) of
the Act. Similarly, the Respondent, TPL, has also submitted that the primary dispute
concerns compensation for the amounts charged by Respondent No. 1 on account of
the alleged diversion of power supply by the Petitioner. Further, the Petitioner has
sought to be exempted from paying such compensation and sought a declaration that
certain events constitute a Change in Law, which falls directly within the category of
tariff disputes set out in Para 25 of the DVC Judgment.
10. Before examining the nature of disputes involved in this case, it would be
apposite to refer to the relevant portions of the DVC Judgment. While deliberating upon
what constitutes “tariff disputes” and “non-tariff disputes”, the DVC Judgment holds as
under:
Order in Petition No. 71/MP/2023
Page 12 of 15

“25. At this juncture, we would again revert to Section 79(1) of the Electricity Act, 2003.
Section 79(1) empowers the Commission to adjudicate upon the disputes relating to
regulation of tariff for the generating companies as well as inter-state transmission of
Electricity and to determine tariff inter-state transmission of electricity as provided under
clause (1) to (d) therein. We wonder how the dispute relating to termination of PPAs would
be regarded as a dispute relating to tariff or regulation of tariff of the generating companies,
as held by the Commission in the impugned order. To understand this aspect, it is
necessary to determine what constitutes tariff and non-tariff disputes. In our considered
opinion, all the matters which would have a bearing upon the tariff for a generating
company would constitute “tariff disputes” namely disputes related to Change in Law,
delayed completion of projects, invocation of Force Majeure events etc. Such matters
impact the tariff for a generating company directly and, therefore, fall solely within the
jurisdiction of the Central Commission under Section 79(1) of the Electricity Act, 2003.
However, the disputes related to termination or breach of contract which do not impact the
tariff either directly or indirectly, can be considered as non-tariff related disputes referable
to arbitration.”
As per the above, all the matters which would have a bearing upon the tariff for a
generating company would constitute “tariff disputes”, namely, disputes related to
Change in Law, delayed completion of projects, invocation of Force Majeure events,
etc. Such matters impact the tariff for a generating company directly and therefore fall
solely within the jurisdiction of the Central Commission under Section 79(1) of the Act.
Whereas disputes related to termination or breach of contract, that do not impact the
tariff either directly or indirectly, can be considered as non-tariff related disputes
referable to arbitration.
11. Upon examining the various prayers (supra) made by the Petitioner along with
the grounds urged in support thereof, we find that the primary disputes involved in the
matter are whether or not the Cabinet Committee on Economic Committee’s decision
dated 26.2.2022 and Coal India Limited’s Circular dated 1.3.2022, which changed the
mechanism for allocation of non-linkage coal to the power sector, would qualify as
Change in Law and Force Majeure events under the MB Power PPA. In fact, the
Petitioner, at Paragraph 97(c) and (b), has specifically prayed for a declaration of both
these events as Change in Law events to the extent of increase in the cost of
Order in Petition No. 71/MP/2023
Page 13 of 15

procurement of coal and as Force Majeure events to the extent they resulted in shortfall
in the availability of the sufficient and compatible coal required to generate and supply
the contracted capacity. Both of these events/ pleas affect the tariff agreed under the
MB Power PPA for the supply of the contracted capacity. Also, even the declaration
that the MB Power PPA stands frustrated w.e.f. 31.3.2022 due to supervening
impossibility on account of the subsistence of Force Majeure events is premised on the
recognition and declaration of these as Force Majeure events. Furthermore, various
prayers made by the Petitioner at Paragraph 97(e) to (i) appear to be merely
consequential reliefs necessitated on account of the actions taken by the Respondent,
PTCIL, consequent to its refusal to accept the Petitioner’s above Change in Law and
Force Majeure claims. As held by the DVC Judgment, the disputes relating to Change
in Law, invocation of Force Majeure, etc., are tariff disputes and fall solely within the
jurisdiction of this Commission.
12. It is true that the Petitioner, at Paragraph 97(a), has also prayed for a declaration
that the MB Power PPA is not in conformity with the MoP Short-Term Guidelines and
GERC Guidelines. However, this prayer alone cannot dictate the nature of the primary
disputes as sought to be argued by the Petitioner. It is not the case of the Petitioner
that the rest of the prayers/grounds are mere alternatives to the above principal
prayer/ground. In any case, whether or not the MB Power PPA conforms to the MoP
and GERC Guidelines, and the consequences are not simpliciter disputes arising out
of the contractual arrangement between the parties. Where the Guidelines vest the
power to approve any deviations therefrom in the Commission, the Commission would
also have the necessary power to examine the dispute arising from the alleged non-
compliance with/deviations from the Guidelines and the effects/ consequences of such
non-compliance/deviation. These aspects, in our view, concern the Commission's
Order in Petition No. 71/MP/2023
Page 14 of 15

regulatory functions and, as held by the DVC Judgment itself, the Commission is not
bound to refer such disputes to arbitration.
13. In view of the above, we hold that the primary disputes involved in the present
case are tariff disputes and/or concern the regulatory function of the Commission and
therefore, they are not required to be referred to arbitration in terms of the DVC
Judgment. Having held so, we do not find it necessary to examine the other issues
raised by both sides, as noted above.
14. The Petition will be listed for further hearing on merits in due course, for which
a separate notice shall be issued.

submitted that the 29th NCT MOM dated 05.05.2025 clarified that the extended timeline
approved by NCT would not apply to the present asset, as it was awarded prior to the
issuance of the NCT minutes, and the extension would only be applicable for the
projects planned after the issuance of the MoM of the 28th NCT meeting.
60. In the first instance, we should deal with whether 3 months extension granted by
the 28th NCT is applicable or not.

implementation of the projects under RTM:
i. Bay extension works - 18 months,
ii. ICT augmentation works - 21 months, and
iii. GIS extension works - 24 months.

Act, 1961. Section 115 JB(2) of the IT Act, 1961, defines book profit as net profit in the
statement of Profit and Loss prepared in accordance with Schedule-III of the Companies
Act, 2013, subject to some additions and deductions as mentioned in the IT Act, 1961.

notified MAT rates for the respective financial year shall be considered as an effective
