Filing Fee and Publication Expenses
69. The Petitioner has claimed reimbursement of the fee it paid for filing the Petition
and for publication expenses. The Petitioner has further submitted that it is entitled to
reimbursement of the filing fee and the expenses incurred on publication of notices in
the application for approval of tariff, directly from the beneficiaries or the long-term
customers, as the case may be, in accordance with Regulation 94(1) of the 2024 Tariff
Regulations.
70. We have considered the Petitioner's submissions. The Petitioner is entitled to
reimbursement of the fee paid for filing the Petition and of publication expenses incurred
on this count, in accordance with Regulation 94(1) of the 2024 Tariff Regulations,
directly from the beneficiaries or long-term customers, as the case may be.
Fees and Charges of Central Transmission Utility of India Limited (CTUIL)
71. The Petitioner has submitted that, as per Regulation 99 of the 2024 Tariff
Regulations, the fees and charges of the CTUIL may be allowed separately through a
separate regulation. The Petitioner has further submitted that, in the absence of such a
regulation, the expenses of the CTUIL will be borne by the Petitioner and recovered by
the Petitioner as additional O&M Expenses through a separate Petition at the end of the
tariff period.
72. MPPMCL has submitted that the expenses of CTUIL borne by the Petitioner
cannot be passed on to the beneficiaries unless such costs are approved by the
Order in Petition No. 601/TT/2025 Page 36 of 41

Commission and duly allocated as per regulatory norms. Accordingly, MPPMCL has
submitted that this request is not maintainable.
73. It is apt here to refer to Regulation 99 of the 2024 Tariff Regulations, which
provides as under:
“99. Special Provisions relating to Central Transmission Utility of India Ltd.
(CTUIL): The fee and charges of CTUIL shall be allowed separately by the Commission
through a separate regulation:
Provided that until such regulation is issued by the Commission, the expenses
of CTUIL shall be borne by Power Grid Corporation of India Ltd. (PGCIL) which shall be
recovered by PGCIL as additional O&M expenses through a separate petition.”
74. We have considered the submissions of the parties and perused Regulation 99
of the 2024 Tariff Regulations. In view of the explicit provision under Regulation 99 of
the 2024 Tariff Regulations, we permit the Petitioner, i.e., PGCIL, to bear the fees and
charges incurred by CTUIL and recover the same as additional O&M Expenses through
a separate Petition until such regulation is notified and issued by the Commission.
Licence Fee and RLDC Fees and Charges
75. The Petitioner has claimed reimbursement of the licence fee, RLDC fees and
charges.
76. MPPMCL has submitted that the Petitioner may be directed to bear the costs
associated with licence fees and RLDC fees, since the Petitioner is already recovering
such costs from end-consumers, which should be sufficient to meet these expenses. It
has further been submitted that these expenses are covered under the normative
parameters of AFC, and therefore, may not be allowed additionally by the Commission.
77. We have considered the submissions of the parties. Since there is provision for
the reimbursement of the licence fee, the Petitioner is accordingly allowed the
reimbursement of the licence fee strictly in accordance with Regulation 94(4) of the
Order in Petition No. 601/TT/2025 Page 37 of 41

2024 Tariff Regulations for the 2024-29 tariff period. The Petitioner is also allowed to
recover the RLDC fee and charges from the beneficiaries in terms of Regulation 94(3)
of the 2024 Tariff Regulations for the 2024-29 tariff period.
Goods and Services Tax
78. The Petitioner has submitted that the transmission charges claimed herein are
exclusive of GST, and in case GST is levied in the future, the same shall be additionally
paid by the Respondents and be charged and billed separately by the Petitioner. It is
also prayed that additional taxes, if any, are paid by the Petitioner on account of the
demand from the Government/ statutory authorities, and the Commission may allow the
same to be recovered from the beneficiaries.
79. MPPMCL has submitted that the transmission of electricity is exempted from the
levy of GST as per Notification No. 12/2017 Central Tax dated 28.06.2017, issued under
the Goods and Services Tax Act 2017. Therefore, no GST is levied on transmission
charges, and there is no occasion for the Petitioner to bill or recover GST separately
from the beneficiaries. Hence, MPPMCL has prayed that the Commission may reject
this claim as it is beyond the scope of the existing tax regime and contrary to the
statutory notification.
80. We have considered the submissions of the parties. Since GST is not levied on
the transmission service at present, we are of the view that the Petitioner’s prayer on
this count is premature.
Security Expenses, Insurance and Capital Spares
81. The Petitioner has submitted that, as per Regulation 36(3)(d) of the 2024 Tariff
Regulations, security expenses and capital spares exceeding ₹10 lakh, and insurance
Order in Petition No. 601/TT/2025 Page 38 of 41

expenses arrived through the competitive bidding for the transmission system and
associated communication system, shall be allowed separately after a prudence check.
82. Regarding the security expenses of the assets, the Petitioner has submitted that
it shall file a separate Petition for the true-up of security expenses from 1.4.2019 to
31.3.2024 under Regulation 35(3)(c) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations and for the recovery
of security expenses from 1.4.2024 to 31.3.2029 under Regulation 36(3)(d) of the 2024
Tariff Regulations. According to the Petitioner, the security expenses regarding the
Combined Assets are not claimed in the instant Petition.
83. The Petitioner has also submitted that it has not claimed insurance expenses in
the instant Petition and that it shall file a separate Petition to claim the overall insurance
expenses and consequential Interest on Working Capital (IWC) on the same,
considering the actual insurance expenses incurred by it for FY 2023-24, after
escalating the same at 5.25% per annum to arrive at the estimated insurance expense
for FY 2024-25, FY 2025-26, FY 2026-27, FY 2027-28, and FY 2028-29.
84. MPPMCL has submitted that the request to file a separate Petition for security
expenses and the associated IOWC is not justified, as security-related expenses are
already covered under normative O&M Expenses prescribed in the tariff regulations.
Allowing such a separate claim would amount to double recovery, and therefore it
should be rejected.
85. The Petitioner has not claimed capital spares for the Combined Assets in the
instant Petition for the 2024-29 tariff period. According to the Petitioner, it shall file a
separate Petition for the capital spares consumed and the consequential IWC thereon,
on an actual basis, for the 2024-29 tariff period, as per the 2024 Tariff Regulations. The
Petitioner has also submitted that it has filed Petition No. 45/MP/2024, claiming capital
spares for the 2019-24 tariff period as per the 2019 Tariff Regulations.
Order in Petition No. 601/TT/2025 Page 39 of 41

86. We have considered the submissions of the parties and have perused the record.
We deem it proper here to refer to Regulation 36(3) (d) of the 2024 Tariff Regulations
which provides as follows:
“36(3)
(d) The Security Expenses, Capital Spares individually costing more than Rs. 10
lakh and Insurance expenses arrived through competitive bidding for the
transmission system and associated communication system shall be allowed
separately after prudence check:
Provided that in case of self insurance, the premium shall not exceed
0.12% of the GFA of the assets insured;
Provided that the transmission licensee shall submit the along with
estimated security expenses based on assessment of the security requirement,
capital spares and insurance expenses, which shall be trued up based on details
of the year-wise actuals along with appropriate justification for incurring the same
and along with confirmation that the same is not claimed as a part of additional
capitalisation or consumption of stores and spares and renovation and
modernization.”
87. On perusal of Regulation 36(3)(d) of the 2024 Tariff Regulations and considering
the Petitioner’s submissions, the Petitioner is allowed to file a single consolidated
Petition comprising security expenses, capital spares individually costing more than ₹10
lakh, and insurance expenses, estimated on an estimated basis, as per the 2024 Tariff
Regulations for the 2024-29 tariff period.
Sharing of Transmission Charges
88. The Petitioner has submitted that the truing-up of the tariff for the 2019-24 tariff
period shall be recovered on a monthly basis in accordance with Regulation 57 of the

recovered on a monthly basis in accordance with Regulation 78 of the 2024 Tariff
Regulations and shall be shared by the beneficiaries and long-term transmission
customers as per the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Sharing of Inter State
Transmission Charges and Losses) Regulations, 2020 (2020 Sharing Regulations).

Act, 1961, which is levied on the book profit of the entity computed as per Section 115
JB of the IT Act, 1961. Section 115 JB (2) defines book profit as net profit in the
Statement of Profit and Loss prepared in accordance with Schedule-III of the
Companies Act, 2013, subject to some additions and deductions as mentioned in the IT
Act, 1961. Since the Petitioner has been paying the MAT rates of the respective financial
year, the notified MAT rates for the respective financial year shall be considered as an
effective tax rate for the purpose of grossing up the RoE for truing up the 2019-24 tariff

expenses for one month.

(2) ……

considered at the Reference Rate of Interest as on 1.4.2024 or as on 1st April of the
year during the tariff period 2024- 29 in which the generating station or a unit thereof
or the transmission system including communication system or element thereof, as the
case may be, is declared under commercial operation, whichever is later:
Provided that in case of truing-up, the rate of interest on working capital shall be
considered at Reference Rate of Interest as on 1st April of each of the financial year
during the tariff period 2024-29.
(4) Interest on working capital shall be payable on a normative basis, notwithstanding
that the generating company or the transmission licensee has not taken a loan for
working capital from any outside agency.”
67. The Petitioner has considered the rate of IWC as 11.90% as on 1.4.2024. The
IWC has been worked out in accordance with Regulation 34 of the 2024 Tariff
Regulations. The ROI considered is 11.90% (SBI 1-year MCLR applicable as on
1.4.2024 of 8.65% plus 325 basis points) for the FY 2024-25 to FY 2028-29.

Filing Fee and Publication Expenses
70. The Petitioner has claimed reimbursement of the fee paid by it for filing the
Petition and publication expenses. The Petitioner has further submitted that it is entitled
to the reimbursement of the filing fee and the expenses incurred on publication of
notices in the application for approval of tariff directly from the beneficiaries or the long-
term customers, as the case may be, in accordance with Regulation 94(1) of the 2024
Tariff Regulations.
71. We have considered the Petitioner's submissions. The Petitioner is entitled to
reimbursement of the fee paid for filing the Petition and publication expenses incurred
on this count directly from the beneficiaries or long-term customers, as the case may
be under Regulation 94(1) of the 2024 Tariff Regulations. Accordingly, we allow the
Petitioner to recover filing fee and the publication expenses from the beneficiaries.
Fees and Charges of Central Transmission Utility of India Limited (CTUIL)
72. The Petitioner has submitted that as per Regulation 99 of the 2024 Tariff
Regulations, the fees and charges of the CTUIL may be allowed separately through a
separate regulation. The Petitioner has further submitted that in the absence of such
regulation, the expenses of CTUIL will be borne by the Petitioner, which will be
Order in Petition No. 596/TT/2025 Page 36 of 40

recovered by the Petitioner as additional O&M Expenses through a separate Petition at
the end of the tariff period.
73. It is apt here to refer to Regulation 99 of the 2024 Tariff Regulations, which
provides as under:
“99. Special Provisions relating to Central Transmission Utility of India Ltd.
(CTUIL): The fee and charges of CTUIL shall be allowed separately by the Commission
through a separate regulation:
Provided that until such regulation is issued by the Commission, the expenses
of CTUIL shall be borne by Power Grid Corporation of India Ltd. (PGCIL) which shall be
recovered by PGCIL as additional O&M expenses through a separate petition.”
74. We have considered the Petitioner’s submissions and perused Regulation 99 of
the 2024 Tariff Regulations. In view of the explicit provision made under Regulation 99
of the 2024 Tariff Regulations, we permit the Petitioner, i.e., PGCIL, to bear the fees
and charges expenses of CTUIL and recover the same as additional O&M Expenses
through a separate Petition until such regulation is notified and issued by the
Commission.
Licence Fee and RLDC Fees and Charges
75. The Petitioner has claimed reimbursement of the licence fee, RLDC Fees and
Charges. The Petitioner is allowed the reimbursement of the license fee in accordance
with Regulation 94(4) of the 2024 Tariff Regulations for the 2024-29 tariff period. The
Petitioner is also allowed to recover the RLDC fee and charges from the beneficiaries
in terms of Regulation 94(3) of the 2024 Tariff Regulations for the 2024-29 tariff period.
Goods and Services Tax
76. The Petitioner has submitted that the transmission charges claimed herein are
exclusive of GST, and in case GST is levied in the future, the same shall be additionally
paid by the Respondents and be charged and billed separately by the Petitioner. It is
also prayed that additional taxes, if any, are paid by the Petitioner on account of the
Order in Petition No. 596/TT/2025 Page 37 of 40

demand from the Government/ statutory authorities, and the Commission may allow the
same to be recovered from the beneficiaries.
77. We have considered the submissions of the Petitioner submissions. Since GST
is not levied on the transmission service at present, we are of the view that the
Petitioner’s prayer on this count is premature.
Security Expenses, Insurance and Capital Spares
78. The Petitioner has submitted that a separate Petition will be filed for truing up of
Security Expenses from 1.4.2019 to 31.3.2024 under Regulation 35(3)(c) of the 2019
Tariff Regulations and recovery of security expenses from 1.4.2024 to 31.3.2029 under
Regulation 36(3)(d) of the 2024 Tariff Regulations. According to the Petitioner, the
Security Expenses regarding the Combined Asset are not claimed in the instant Petition.
79. The Petitioner has also submitted that it has not claimed Insurance Expenses in
the instant Petition and has submitted that it will file a separate Petition for claiming the
overall Insurance Expenses and consequential IWC on the same, considering the actual
Insurance Expenses incurred by it for the FY 2023-24 after escalating the same at
5.25% per annum to arrive at the estimated Insurance Expense for the FY 2024-25, FY
2025-26, FY 2026-27, FY 2027-28, and FY 2028-29.
80. The Petitioner has not claimed Capital Spares for the Combined Asset in the
instant Petition for the 2024-29 tariff period. Accordingly, the Petitioner has submitted
that it will file a separate Petition for the capital spares consumed and consequential
IWC thereon on an actual basis for the 2024-29 tariff period as per the 2024 Tariff
Regulations. The Petitioner has also submitted that it has filed Petition No. 45/MP/2024,
claiming therein Capital Spares for the 2019-24 tariff period as per the 2019 Tariff
Regulations.
Order in Petition No. 596/TT/2025 Page 38 of 40

81. We have considered the Petitioner’s submissions and have perused the record.
We deem it proper here to refer to Regulation 36(3)(d) of the 2024 Tariff Regulations
which provides as under:
“36(3)
(d) The Security Expenses, Capital Spares individually costing more than Rs. 10 lakh
and Insurance expenses arrived through competitive bidding for the transmission
system and associated communication system shall be allowed separately after
prudence check:
Provided that in case of self insurance, the premium shall not exceed 0.12% of
the GFA of the assets insured;
Provided that the transmission licensee shall submit the along with estimated
security expenses based on assessment of the security requirement, capital spares and
insurance expenses, which shall be trued up based on details of the year-wise actuals
along with appropriate justification for incurring the same and along with confirmation
that the same is not claimed as a part of additional capitalisation or consumption of
stores and spares and renovation and modernization.”
82. On perusal of Regulation 36(3)(d) of the 2024 Tariff Regulations and considering
the Petitioner’s submissions, the Petitioner is allowed to file a single consolidated
Petition comprising security expenses, capital spares individually costing more than ₹10
lakh and insurance expenses on the estimated basis as per the 2024 Tariff Regulations
for the 2024-29 tariff period.
Sharing of Transmission Charges
83. The Petitioner has submitted that the trued-up tariff for the 2019-24 tariff period
will be recovered on a monthly basis in accordance with Regulation 57 of the 2019 Tariff
Regulations and will be shared by the beneficiaries and long-term transmission
customers. Further, the tariff for the 2024-29 tariff period will be recovered on a monthly
basis in accordance with Regulation 78 of the 2024 Tariff Regulations and will be shared
by the beneficiaries and long-term transmission customers as per the 2020 Sharing
Regulations.
Order in Petition No. 596/TT/2025 Page 39 of 40

84. We have considered the Petitioner’s submissions. The billing, collection, and
disbursement of the transmission charges for the Combined Asset shall be recovered
in terms of provisions of the Sharing Regulations as provided in Regulation 57 of the
2019 Tariff Regulations for the 2019-24 tariff period and Regulation 78 of the 2024 Tariff
Regulations for the 2024-29 tariff period.

Filing Fee and Publication Expenses
74. The Petitioner has claimed reimbursement of the fee paid by it for filing the
Petition and publication expenses. The Petitioner has further submitted that it is entitled
to the reimbursement of the filing fee and the expenses incurred on publication of
notices in the application for approval of tariff directly from the beneficiaries or the long-
term customers, as the case may be, in accordance with Regulation 94(1) of the 2024
Tariff Regulations.
75. We have considered the Petitioner's submissions. The Petitioner is entitled to
reimbursement of the fee paid for filing the Petition and publication expenses incurred
on this count directly from the beneficiaries or long-term customers, as the case may
be Regulation 94(1) of the 2024 Tariff Regulations. Accordingly, we allow the Petitioner
to recover the filing fee and publication expenses from the beneficiaries.
Fees and Charges of Central Transmission Utility of India Limited (CTUIL)
76. The Petitioner has submitted that as per Regulation 99 of the 2024 Tariff
Regulations, the fees and charges of the CTUIL may be allowed separately through a
separate regulation. The Petitioner has further submitted that in the absence of such
Regulation, the expenses of CTUIL will be borne by the Petitioner, which will be
Order in Petition No. 590/TT/2025 Page 39 of 44

recovered by the Petitioner as additional O&M Expenses through a separate Petition at
the end of the tariff period.
77. It is apt here to refer to Regulation 99 of the 2024 Tariff Regulations, which
provides as under:
“99. Special Provisions relating to Central Transmission Utility of India Ltd.
(CTUIL): The fee and charges of CTUIL shall be allowed separately by the Commission
through a separate regulation:
Provided that until such regulation is issued by the Commission, the expenses
of CTUIL shall be borne by Power Grid Corporation of India Ltd. (PGCIL) which shall be
recovered by PGCIL as additional O&M expenses through a separate Petition.”
78. We have considered the Petitioner’s submissions and perused Regulation 99 of
the 2024 Tariff Regulations. In view of the explicit provision made under Regulation 99
of the 2024 Tariff Regulations, we permit the Petitioner, i.e., PGCIL, to bear the fees
and charges expenses of CTUIL and recover the same as additional O&M Expenses
through a separate Petition until such Regulation is notified and issued by the
Commission.

Fees and Charges of Central Transmission Utility of India Limited (CTUIL)
68. The Petitioner has submitted that, as per Regulation 99 of the 2024 Tariff
Regulations, the fees and charges of the Central Transmission Utility of India Limited
(CTUIL) may be allowed separately through a separate regulation. The Petitioner has
further submitted that in the absence of such regulation, the expenses of CTUIL will be
borne by the Petitioner, which will be recovered by the Petitioner as additional O&M
Expenses through a separate Petition at the end of the tariff period.
69. It is apt here to refer to Regulation 99 of the 2024 Tariff Regulations, which
provides as under:
“99. Special Provisions relating to Central Transmission Utility of India Ltd.
(CTUIL): The fee and charges of CTUIL shall be allowed separately by the Commission
through a separate regulation:
Provided that until such regulation is issued by the Commission, the expenses
of CTUIL shall be borne by Power Grid Corporation of India Ltd. (PGCIL) which shall be
recovered by PGCIL as additional O&M expenses through a separate petition.”
70. We have considered the Petitioner’s submissions and perused Regulation 99 of
the 2024 Tariff Regulations. In view of the explicit provision made under Regulation 99
of the 2024 Tariff Regulations, we permit the Petitioner, i.e., PGCIL, to bear the fees
and charges of CTUIL and recover the same as additional O&M Expenses through a
separate Petition until such regulation is notified and issued by the Commission.
License Fee and RLDC Fees and Charges

that the additional taxes, if any, are paid by the Petitioner on account of the demand
from the Government/ Statutory Authorities, the same may be allowed to be recovered

count is premature.

Time overrun
18. The Petitioner in the instant truing up Petition has submitted that the Commission
vide its order dated 27.5.2022 in Petition No. 675/TT/2020 did not condone the time
overrun of Asset-4 and directed the Petitioner to submit relevant documentary evidence
related to the time overrun at the time of truing up. Accordingly, the requisite
documentary evidence and supporting documents have been submitted by the
Petitioner.
19. We have considered the Petitioner’s submissions. The Commission vide its order
dated 27.5.2022 in Petition No. 675/TT/2020, observed that the Petitioner had not
submitted any supporting documents with respect to the denial of shutdown, and
accordingly, did not condone the time overrun of 242 days with respect to Asset 4
(referred to therein as Asset- III). The Commission also granted liberty to the Petitioner
to submit the relevant documentary evidence related to time overrun claimed at the time
of truing up. The relevant extract of the aforesaid order is reproduced as under for
reference:
“41. As regards Asset-III, the Petitioner has submitted that shut-down of 400 kV Patna-
Balia line-1, 400 kV bus-2, 500 MVA ICT at Patna was approved from 1.5.2019 to
15.5.2019 but BSEB did not approve the shut-down due to excessive loading at Patna
Sub-station. The Petitioner has not submitted any letter or documentary evidence to show
that BSEB had rejected or denied the shut-down. In the absence of valid documentary
evidence in support of shut-down, time over-run of 242 days is not condoned. However,
the Petitioner is at liberty to provide all necessary documents at the time of truing up of
tariff in support of delay of 242 days and the claim for time over-run with reference to
Asset-III shall be considered on merit.”

20. We have perused the supporting documents submitted by the Petitioner in the
instant truing up Petition. It is observed that the Petitioner has submitted various letters,
e-mails exchanged between the Petitioner and the concerned authorities regarding the
approval of shutdown. The Petitioner has also provided the relevant portions of the
158th, 160th and 161st OCC meetings as supporting documents. It is also noted that the
letters dated 27.5.2019, 31.5.2019, 7.6.2019, 26.6.2019 and emails dated 17.5.2019,
4.7.2019, pertain to the shutdown requirement for jumpering the work from the dead-
end tower to Gantry with respect to the 400 kV D/C Patna-Barh-I Transmission Line and
other works of associated bays. The aforesaid letters and e-mails are not concerned
with the shutdown deferment by BSEB due to excessive loading, with respect to the 80
MAVR Switchable Line Reactor.
21. However, it is noted that ERLDC vide e-mail dated 16.8.2019, deferred the
shutdown requested by the Petitioner from 20.8.2019 to 23.8.2019 for Commissioning of
the instant transmission asset on account of the forced outage of the 400 kV D/C Motihari-
Gorakhpur Transmission Line. Therefore, we are of the view that based on the supporting
documents submitted in the instant truing up Petition, The Petitioner has substantiated
the deferment of shutdown only for a period of 3 days. Accordingly, we condone the time
overrun of 3 days with respect to the instant transmission, i.e., Asset-4.

44. We have considered the Petitioner’s submissions and have also gone through
the record. We noted that the entities covered under the MAT regime are paying Income
Tax as per the MAT rates notified for the respective financial year under the IT Act,
1961, which is levied on the book profit of the entity computed as per Section 115 JB of
the IT Act, 1961. Section 115 JB(2) defines book profit as net profit in the Statement of
Profit and Loss prepared in accordance with Schedule-II of the Companies Act, 2013,
subject to some additions and deductions as mentioned in the IT Act, 1961. Since the
Petitioner has been paying the MAT rates of the respective financial year, the notified
MAT rates for the respective financial year shall be considered as an effective tax rate

be considered on the actual payment. However, the penalty (for default on the part of
the Assessee), if any, imposed shall not be taken into account for the purpose of
grossing up of the rate of RoE. Any under recovery or over-recovery of the grossed-up

ORDER
The instant Petition has been filed by Power Grid Corporation of India (PGCIL)
(hereinafter referred to as “the Petitioner”) for the true-up of the transmission tariff for
the 2019-24 period under the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and
Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2019 (hereinafter referred to as “the 2019 Tariff
Regulations”), and for the determination of the transmission tariff for the 2024-29
period under the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of
Tariff) Regulations, 2024 (hereinafter referred to as “the 2024 Tariff Regulations”), in
respect of the following assets (hereinafter referred to as “the Combined Assets”)
under “Line Bays and Reactor Provisions at POWERGRID Substations associated
with System Strengthening common for Western Region and Northern Region"
(hereinafter referred to as “the transmission project”):

Substation for 765 kV S/C Jabalpur-Bina ckt-III (IPTC);
Asset-2: 765 kV Line Bay and 240 MVAr Line Reactor (Non-switchable) at Bina
Substation for 765 kV S/C Jabalpur-Bina ckt-III (IPTC);
Asset-3: 765 kV Line Bay and 240 MVAr Line Reactor at Jabalpur PS and 765 kV
Line Bay and 330 MVAr Switchable Line Reactor at Dharamjaygarh Substation for ckt.
3 of 765 kV D/C (ckts. 3 and 4) Dharamjaygarh-Jabalpur PS Transmission Line (IPTC);
and
Asset-4: 765 kV Line Bay and 240 MVAr Line Reactor at Jabalpur PS and 765 kV
Line Bay and 330 MVAr Switchable Line Reactor at Dharamjaygarh Substation for ckt.
4 of 765 kV D/C (ckt. 3 and 4) Dharamjaygarh-Jabalpur PS Transmission Line (IPTC).
2. The Petitioner has made the following prayers in the instant Petition:
“a) Approve the trued-up Transmission Tariff for 2019-24 block and transmission tariff
for 2024-29 block for the assets covered under this petition, as per para 12 and 13
above.
b)Admit the capital cost claimed and additional capitalization incurred during 2019-
24 and 2024-29 tariff block for the assets covered under this petition.
c)Allow the petitioner to recover the shortfall or refund the excess Annual Fixed
Charges, on account of Return on Equity due to change in applicable Minimum
Alternate/Corporate Income Tax rate as per the Income Tax Act, 1961 (as amended
from time to time) of the respective financial year directly without making any
application before the Commission as provided in Tariff Regulation 2019 and Tariff
regulations 2024 as per para 12 and 13 above for respective block.
d)Approve the reimbursement of expenditure by the beneficiaries towards petition
filing fee, and expenditure on publishing of notices in newspapers in terms of
Regulation 94 (1) Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions
of Tariff) Regulations, 2024, and other expenditure (if any) in relation to the filing of
petition.
e)Allow the petitioner to bill and recover Licensee fee and RLDC fees & charges,
separately from the respondents in terms of Regulation 94 (3) and (4) Central
Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations,
2024.
f)Allow the petitioner to bill and adjust impact on Interest on Loan due to change in
Interest rate on account of floating rate of interest applicable during 2024-29 period,
if any, from the respondents.
g)Allow the petitioner to file a separate petition before Hon’ble Commission for
claiming the overall security expenses and consequential IOWC on that security
expenses as mentioned at para 19 above.

h)Allow the petitioner to file a separate petition before Hon’ble Commission for
claiming the overall insurance expenses and consequential IOWC on that insurance
expenses as mentioned at para 19 above.
i)Allow the petitioner to file a separate petition before Hon’ble Commission for
claiming the overall capital spares as mentioned at Para 19 above.
j)Allow the petitioner to claim expenses of CTUIL borne by POWERGRID through a
separate petition as mentioned at para 20 above.
k)Allow the Petitioner to bill and recover GST on Transmission Charges separately
from the respondents, if GST on transmission is levied at any rate in future. Further,
any taxes including GST and duties including cess etc. imposed by any
statutory/Govt./municipal authorities shall be allowed to be recovered from the
beneficiaries.
and pass such other relief as Hon’ble Commission deems fit and appropriate under
the circumstances of the case and in the interest of justice.”

reimbursement of the fee paid for filing the Petition and the publication expenses
incurred on this count, directly from the beneficiaries or long-term customers, as the
Order in Petition No. 386/TT/2025 Page 36 of 42

case may be. Accordingly, we allow reimbursement of the filing fee and publication
expenses to the Petitioner, in terms of Regulation 94(1) of the 2024 Tariff Regulations.
Fees and Charges of Central Transmission Utility of India Limited (CTUIL)
79. The Petitioner has submitted that, as per Regulation 99 of the 2024 Tariff
Regulations, the fees and charges of the Central Transmission Utility of India Limited
(CTUIL) may be allowed separately through a separate regulation. It is submitted that,
in the absence of such a regulation, the expenses of CTUIL will be borne by the
Petitioner, which will be recovered by the Petitioner as additional O&M Expenses
through a separate Petition at the end of the tariff period.
80. It is apt here to refer to Regulation 99 of the 2024 Tariff Regulations, which
provides as under:
“99. Special Provisions relating to Central Transmission Utility of India Ltd.
(CTUIL): The fee and charges of CTUIL shall be allowed separately by the Commission
through a separate regulation:
Provided that until such regulation is issued by the Commission, the expenses
of CTUIL shall be borne by Power Grid Corporation of India Ltd. (PGCIL) which shall be
recovered by PGCIL as additional O&M expenses through a separate petition.”
81. We have considered the Petitioner’s submissions and perused Regulation 99 of
the 2024 Tariff Regulations. In view of the explicit provision under Regulation 99 of the
2024 Tariff Regulations, we permit the Petitioner, i.e., PGCIL, to bear the fees and
charges of CTUIL and recover the same as additional O&M Expenses through a
separate Petition until such regulation is notified and issued by the Commission.
License Fee and RLDC Fees and Charges
82. The Petitioner has claimed reimbursement of the license fee and RLDC fees and
charges.
Order in Petition No. 386/TT/2025 Page 37 of 42

83. In its reply, MPPMCL has submitted that the Petitioner may be directed to bear
the license fee and RLDC fees, as it is actively recovering costs from the end customers,
which is more than sufficient to cover these expenses, and that these fees are covered
under the normative parameters of the AFC, hence they may not be allowed
additionally.
84. In response, the Petitioner has submitted that the objections of MPPMCL are
untenable. It is submitted that these objections have been repeatedly raised by the
beneficiaries and rejected by the Commission. It is further submitted that the Petitioner’s
claims are squarely covered by the applicable Tariff Regulations.
85. We have considered the submissions of the parties. The Petitioner is allowed the
reimbursement of the license fee in accordance with Regulation 94(4) of the 2024 Tariff
Regulations for the 2024-29 tariff period. The Petitioner is also allowed to recover the
RLDC fee and charges from the beneficiaries, in terms of Regulation 94(3) of the 2024
Tariff Regulations for the 2024-29 tariff period.
Goods and Services Tax
86. The Petitioner has submitted that the transmission charges claimed herein are
exclusive of the Goods and Services Tax (GST), and in case GST is levied on
transmission of electricity in the future, the same shall be additionally paid by the
Respondents, and be charged and billed separately by the Petitioner. It is prayed that
the additional taxes, if any, are paid by the Petitioner on account of the demand from
the Government/Statutory Authorities, the same may be allowed to be recovered from
the beneficiaries.
87. MPPMCL, in its reply, has submitted that the demand of the Petitioner is
premature and need not be considered at this juncture.
88. In response, the Petitioner has reiterated its submissions made in the Petition.
Order in Petition No. 386/TT/2025 Page 38 of 42

89. We have considered the submissions of the parties. Since GST is not levied on
the transmission services at present, we are of the view that the Petitioner’s prayer on
this count is premature.
Security Expenses, Insurance and Capital Spares
90. The Petitioner has submitted that a separate Petition shall be filed for truing up
of the security expenses from 1.4.2019 to 31.3.2024 under Regulation 35(3)(c) of the
2019 Tariff Regulations and recovery of the security expenses from 1.4.2024 to
31.3.2029 under Regulation 36(3)(d) of the 2024 Tariff Regulations. It is submitted that
the security expenses regarding the Combined Assets are not claimed in the instant
Petition.
91. The Petitioner has also submitted that it has not claimed the insurance expenses
in the instant Petition and that it shall file a separate Petition to claim the overall
insurance expenses and consequential IWC on the same, considering the actual
insurance expenses incurred by it for the FY 2023-24, after escalating the same at
5.25% per annum to arrive at the estimated insurance expense for the FYs 2024-25,
2025-26, 2026-27, 2027-28 and 2028-29.
92. The Petitioner has further submitted that it has not claimed the capital spares
for the Combined Assets in the instant Petition for the 2024-29 tariff period. It is
submitted that the Petitioner shall file a separate Petition to claim the capital spares
consumed and the consequential IWC thereon, on an actual basis, for the 2024-29 tariff
period, as per the 2024 Tariff Regulations. It is further submitted that the Petitioner has
filed Petition No. 45/MP/2024, claiming the capital spares for the 2019-24 tariff period
as per the 2019 Tariff Regulations.
93. In its reply, MPPMCL has submitted that these expenses are premature and
unwarranted, as the 2019 Tariff Regulations and the 2024 Tariff Regulations do not
Order in Petition No. 386/TT/2025 Page 39 of 42

allow the same. Further, the request of the Petitioner to file a separate Petition for
claiming the capital spares is infructuous and may be denied, as the same is sub-judice
before the Commission in Petition No. 45/MP/2024.
94. In response, the Petitioner has submitted that the allegations denying the
admissibility of these expenses are incorrect. Both the 2019 Tariff Regulations and the
2024 Tariff Regulations provide for the recovery of these expenses.
95. We have considered the submissions of the parties and have perused the record.
We deem it proper here to refer to Regulation 36(3) (d) of the 2024 Tariff Regulations
which provides as follows:
“36(3)
(d) The Security Expenses, Capital Spares individually costing more than Rs. 10
lakh and Insurance expenses arrived through competitive bidding for the
transmission system and associated communication system shall be allowed
separately after prudence check:
Provided that in case of self insurance, the premium shall not exceed
0.12% of the GFA of the assets insured;
Provided that the transmission licensee shall submit the along with
estimated security expenses based on assessment of the security requirement,
capital spares and insurance expenses, which shall be trued up based on details
of the year-wise actuals along with appropriate justification for incurring the same
and along with confirmation that the same is not claimed as a part of additional
capitalisation or consumption of stores and spares and renovation and
modernization.
Provided that the self-insurance premium shall be transferred to a
separate fund for utilization to meet the claims, and the expenditure incurred or
amount utilized from the self-insurance fund shall be made available to the
Commission as and when directed.”
96. On perusal of Regulation 36(3)(d) of the 2024 Tariff Regulations, the Petitioner
is allowed to file a single consolidated Petition comprising security expenses and capital
spares individually costing more than ₹10 lakh and insurance expenses on the
estimated basis as per the 2024 Tariff Regulations for the 2024-29 tariff period.
Order in Petition No. 386/TT/2025 Page 40 of 42

CENTRAL ELECTRICITY REGULATORY COMMISSION
NEW DELHI
Petition No. 211/TT/2024
Coram:
Shri Jishnu Barua, Chairperson

Date of Order: 16.01.2026
In the matter of:
Approval under Regulation 23 of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission
(Conduct of Business) Regulations, 2023 and the Central Electricity Regulatory
Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2019 for determination of
transmission tariff from the COD to 31.3.2024 for Asset:1: 420 kV 63 MVAR Lower
Subansiri-2 line reactor (to be used as Bus Reactor) along with associated bays &
equipment at Biswanath Chariali (POWERGRID), Asset-2: Lower Subansiri - Biswanath
Chariali (POWERGRID) 400 kV D/C line-1 with twin Lapwing conductor along with
associated bays & equipment at Biswanath Chariali (POWERGRID), Asset-3: Lower
Subansiri - Biswanath Chariali (POWERGRID) 400 kV D/C line-2 with twin Lapwing
conductor along with associated bays & equipment at Biswanath Chariali
(POWERGRID) & Asset-4: 420 kV 63 MVAR Lower Subansiri-4 line reactor (to be used
as Bus Reactor) along with associated bays & equipment at Biswanath Chariyali
(POWERGRID) under the transmission system associated with “North East –
Northern/ Western Inter-connector – I Project” in the North-Eastern Region.
And in the matter of:

Parties Present: Ms. Swapna Seshadri, Advocate, PGCIL
Shri Utkarsh Singh, Advocate, PGCIL
Ms. Rupinder Kaur, Advocate, PGCIL
Shri Venkatesh, Advocate, NHPC
Shri Ashutosh K. Shrivastava, Advocate, NHPC
Shri Akash Lamba, Advocate, NHPC

Shri Zafrul Hasan, PGCIL
Shri Vijay G, PGCIL

INTERIM ORDER
The instant Petition has been filed by Power Grid Corporation of India Limited for
determination of tariff under the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and
Interim order in Petition No.211/TT/2024 Page 2 of 51

Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2019 (hereinafter referred to as “the 2019 Tariff
Regulations”) of the period from COD to 31.3.2024 in respect of the following assets
under North East-Northern/Western Interconnector-I Project in the North-Eastern
Region.
Asset
Asset-1:420 kV 63 MVAR Lower Subansiri-2 line reactor (to be used as Bus Reactor) along
with associated bays & equipment at Biswanath Chariyali (POWERGRID)
Asset-2: Lower Subansiri – Biswanath Chariyali (POWERGRID) 400 kV D/C line-1 with twin
Lapwing conductor along with associated bays & equipment at Biswanath Chariyali
(POWERGRID)
Asset-3: Lower Subansiri – Biswanath Chariyali (POWERGRID) 400 kV D/C line-2 with twin
Lapwing conductor along with associated bays & equipment at Biswanath Chariyali
(POWERGRID)
Asset-4: 420 kV 63 MVAR Lower Subansiri-4 line reactor (to be used as Bus Reactor) along
with associated bays & equipment at Biswanath Chariyali (POWERGRID)
2. The scheduled date of commercial operation (SCOD), the date of commercial
operation (COD) claimed by the Petitioner and time over-run in case of the instant
transmission are assets as follows:
Asset SCOD COD Time over-run
Asset 1 12.8.2022 3451 days
Asset 2 2.4.2023* 3684 days
1.3.2013
Asset 3 26.3.2024* 4043 days
Asset 4 3.11.2023 3899 days
*The Petitioner has claimed COD for Asset-2 and Asset-3 under Regulation 5(2)
of the 2019 Tariff Regulations.
3. The Petitioner has claimed the COD for Asset-2 and Asset-3 under Regulation
5(2) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations, as the interconnected generating station, i.e., Lower
Subansiri Hydro-Electric Power Project, being implemented by NHPC, was not ready.
The Petitioner also prayed for the grant of interim relief under Regulation 13(3) of the
2019 Tariff Regulations.
4. The Commission vide order dated 5.12.2025 approved 70% of the AFC claimed
as an interim tariff for Asset-1 and Asset-4 under Regulation 10(3) of the 2019 Tariff
Regulations. However, no interim tariff was approved for Asset-2 and Asset-3 as they
have not been put into commercial operation, due to the non-readiness of the
Interim order in Petition No.211/TT/2024 Page 3 of 51

interconnected generation under the scope of NHPC, and their COD was claimed under
Regulation 5(2) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations. The relevant portions of the
Commission’s order dated 5.12.2025 are extracted hereunder:
“6. We have considered the Petitioner’s submissions and prayer for the grant of an
interim tariff. The rival contentions will be considered only at the time of the final tariff
order. Therefore, the same are not deliberated in the instant interim order.
7. Regulation 5 (2) of the 2019 Tariff Regulation provides as under:
“In case the transmission system or element thereof executed by a transmission licensee
is ready for commercial operation but the interconnected generating station or the
transmission system of other transmission licensee as per the agreed project
implementation schedule is not ready for commercial operation, the transmission licensee
may file petition before the Commission for approval of the date of commercial operation
of such transmission system or element thereof.”
8. As we are not deliberating in detail in this interim order, the prayer for the grant of
COD under Regulation 5(2) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations shall be considered in the
final order.”
“10. As the Petitioner has filed the application in pursuance of Regulation 9(1) of the
2019 Tariff Regulations for the grant of interim tariff for its new transmission project under
Regulation 10(3) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations, this interim tariff is being granted to the
Petitioner after carrying out a preliminary prudence check of the Annual Fixed Cost
(AFC) claimed by the Petitioner and taking into consideration the time over-run in case
of the instant transmission assets, which shall be looked into in detail at the time of grant
of the final tariff order. Accordingly, the interim tariff @ 70% of the AFC claimed in Asset-
1 and Asset-4 in the instant Petition shall be allowed for the 2022-23 and 2023- 24 tariff
period in terms of Regulation 10(3) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations. However, the
Commission is not inclined to allow an interim transmission tariff for Asset-2 and Asset-
3 as the assets have not been put into commercial operation due to delay in
commissioning of generation asset under the scope of NHPC, and the tariff has been
claimed under Regulation 5(2) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations and hence, the same shall
be dealt with in the final tariff order.”
5. We understand that NHPC has commissioned a 250 MW Unit on 23.12.2025,
and Asset-2 and Asset-3 are put into use w.e.f. 23.12.2025, i.e. after the issue of order
dated 5.12.2025 allowing interim tariff for Asset-1 and Asset-4. The Petitioner has not
been able to recover any transmission charges for Asset-2 and Asset-3, which are of
high capital cost and have been put to use, in the absence of approval of any tariff by
this Commission. Taking into consideration that the issue of final order in the matter
would take some more time, we decide to grant an interim tariff for Asset-2 and Asset-
3 under Regulation 10(3) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations.
6. Regulation 10(3) and 10(6) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations provide as follows:
Interim order in Petition No.211/TT/2024 Page 4 of 51

“10. Determination of tariff
………
(3) If the information furnished in the petition is in accordance with these regulations and
is adequate for carrying out prudence check of the claims made, the Commission may
consider granting interim tariff in case of new projects.
………
(6) The Commission may hear the petitioner, the respondents and any other person
permitted including the consumers or consumer associations while granting interim or
final tariff.”
7. As per Regulation 10(3) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations, the Commission may
grant an interim tariff, if the information furnished by the Petitioner is adequate for
carrying a prudence check of the claims made, after hearing the parties concerned as
provided in Regulation 10(6) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations. In the instant case, we have
heard the Petitioner and NHPC.
COD of Asset- 2 and Asset-3
8. For granting an interim tariff, we need to first approve the COD of the Asset-2
and Asset-3. The Petitioner has claimed the COD of Asset-2 and Asset-3 as 2.4.2023
and 26.3.2024, respectively, under Regulation 5(2) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations due
to the non-readiness of the interconnected generating station under the scope of NHPC.
In support of the COD of Asset-2 and Asset-3, the Petitioner has submitted the CEA
Energisation Certificate, RLDC Trial Run Certificates of Idle Charging Operation
(without electrical load), and the CMD certificate.
9. NHPC, in its affidavits dated 24.6.2025 and 15.9.2025, has contested the
Petitioner’s claim for approval of COD of Asset-2 and Asset-3 as 2.4.2023 and
26.3.2024, respectively, under Regulation 5(2) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations. The gist
of the submissions made by NHPC is as follows:
a. The Petitioner has failed to coordinate effectively with NHPC regarding the
synchronisation of its Asset-2 and Asset-3 with NHPC and did not establish any
fixed timelines or obligations for this alignment. Further, the Petitioner advanced
the construction of these transmission elements independently, based solely on
Interim order in Petition No.211/TT/2024 Page 5 of 51

its internal grid planning approvals, without engaging NHPC to agree on their
scope, timeline, or purpose. Therefore, the Petitioner's unilateral communications
claiming deemed COD for Asset 2 as 2.4.2023 and Asset-3 as 26.3.2024 prior to
the grant of final connectivity to NHPC by CTUIL show that the Petitioner planned
its assets as per its own convenience. The start date of connectivity was notified
as follows:
i. Connectivity for Unit-1 for 250 MW with a start date of connectivity as
17.2.2024.
ii. Connectivity for Unit-2 for 250 MW with a start date of connectivity as
29.2.2024
iii. Connectivity for grant of 1500 MW (Units 3 to 8) with a start date of
connectivity as 31.3.2024.
b. The letters issued under Regulation 5(2) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations are not
as per the start date of connectivity. Thus, the Petitioner cannot insist on any
liability on NHPC prior to the start date of connectivity granted by CTUIL, as it is
against the 2020 Sharing Regulations and the 2022 GNA Regulations.
c. The Petitioner has not complied with Regulation 5(2) of the 2019 Tariff
Regulations on the following counts:
i. The Petitioner has failed to coordinate effectively in statutory meetings
regarding the alignment of commissioning schedules for its assets and
NHPC's assets. The minutes of the 19th JCC Meeting dated 22. 9.2023
indicate a lack of coordination between the parties. The Petitioner is
responsible for the initial commissioning, and proper coordination was
expected.
ii. The Petitioner also failed to document the relevant JCC meetings
during which NHPC updated the status of its generating station. This
omission suggests that the Petitioner’s failure to record these statutory
meetings disentitles them from claiming COD.
Interim order in Petition No.211/TT/2024 Page 6 of 51

d. Non-Compliance of Regulation 27(1)(c)(i) of the Indian Electricity Grid Code
(IEGC) Regulations, 2023, (2023 IEGC Regulations). The unilateral declaration of
COD by the Petitioner contradicts the fourth proviso of Regulation 27(1)(c)(i) of the
2023 IEGC Regulations.
e. The Petitioner declared COD for Asset-2 on 2.4.2023 and Asset-3 on
26.3.2024 without the CTUIL certificate or the Commission’s approval, relying on
certificates from the Grid Controller, which is legally untenable. The Grid
Controller’s role is limited to operational monitoring and cannot certify COD for
cost recovery. Thus, the fourth proviso to Regulation 27(1)(c)(i) of the 2023 IEGC
Regulations, unequivocally mandates that the COD of a transmission element or
system shall not take effect unless approved by the Commission, and such
approval must be founded upon a certificate issued by the CTUIL confirming the
successful completion of trial operation and readiness of the asset. This
requirement is not a procedural nicety but a statutory safeguard, designed to
ensure that:
(a) The transmission elements are grid-compliant and technically ready.
(b) The operationalisation is validated by the CTUIL, the designated
statutory authority, and
(c) No financial burden is shifted onto the generators or beneficiaries
without regulatory approval.
f. The Grid Controller’s certificate cannot replace CTUIL’s statutory certification
under the fourth proviso of Regulation 27(1)(c) of the 2023 IEGC Regulations.
Without CTUIL certification, the Petitioner's unilateral COD declaration has
no legal effect and cannot impose YTC on NHPC. The attempt to rely on the
Grid Controller’s certification bypasses the statutory procedures and should
be rejected.
Interim order in Petition No.211/TT/2024 Page 7 of 51

10. In response, the Petitioner vide affidavit dated 8.7.2025 and 22.9.2025 has made
the following submissions:
a. NHPC's claim of no coordination is incorrect. NHPC responded to both the
notices issued by the Petitioner under Regulation 5(2) of the 2019 Tariff
Regulations, participated in the meetings with regard to the trial operation and was
made aware of the provisions of the Tariff Regulations as well as the IEGC with
regard to the mismatch. NHPC’s objections are untenable, as the facts with regard
to the charging and trial operation of both Assets 2 and 3 speak for themselves.
NHPC was kept informed at all stages. Therefore, the allegation that there was
lack of coordination on the part of the Petitioner is not correct.
b. Non-Compliance of IEGC Regulation 27(1)(c)(i)
NHPC’s reliance upon the fourth proviso to Regulation 27(1)(c)(i) of the 2023 IEGC
Regulations with regard to claiming COD of the transmission elements or system/
Assets is misplaced. The declaration of COD of Asset-2 and Asset-3 was
undertaken strictly in accordance with the 2019 Tariff Regulations. There is also
no inconsistency between the 2019 Tariff Regulations and the IEGC for the IEGC
to override the issue of deemed COD declaration, if sought by a transmission
licensee. NHPC has selectively relied upon the fourth proviso to Regulation
27(1)(c)(i) of 2023 IEGC Regulations, while ignoring that the COD of Asset-2
(2.4.2023) was declared prior to the coming into force of the 2023 IEGC
Regulations. Therefore, the requirement of the CTUIL certificate cannot be applied
to Asset-2. Further, the fourth proviso to Regulation 27(1)(c)(i) of 2023 IEGC
Regulations does not nullify or over-ride the scheme of Regulation 5(2) of the 2019
Tariff Regulations which empowers a transmission licensee to declare COD where
its asset is ready but the generating station is delayed, and such a declaration is
always subject to the approval of the Commission.
Interim order in Petition No.211/TT/2024 Page 8 of 51

c. Asset-3 was ready on 26.3.2024, which is after the notification of the 2023 IEGC
Regulations, and the CTUIL certificate has been furnished.
d. NHPC’s contention that no CTUIL certificate has been placed on record, even
though deemed COD has been claimed, ignores that the Petitioner has placed on
record the CTUIL Certificate towards completion of Asset-3 in compliance with the
fourth proviso of Regulation 27(1)(c) (i) of the 2023 IEGC Regulations.
11. We have considered the submission of the Petitioner and NHPC.
12. Regulation 5 of the 2019 Tariff Regulations provides as follows:
“5. Date of Commercial Operation: (1) The date of commercial operation of a
generating station or unit thereof or a transmission system or element thereof and
associated communication system shall be determined in accordance with the
provisions of the Grid Code.
(2) In case the transmission system or element thereof executed by a transmission
licensee is ready for commercial operation but the interconnected generating station or
the transmission system of other transmission licensee as per the agreed project
implementation schedule is not ready for commercial operation, the transmission
licensee may file Petition before the Commission for approval of the date of commercial
operation of such transmission system or element thereof:
Provided that the transmission licensee seeking the approval of the date of commercial
operation under this clause shall give prior notice of at least one month, to the generating
company or the other transmission licensee and the long-term customers of its
transmission system, as the case may be, regarding the date of commercial operation:
Provided further that the transmission licensee seeking the approval of the date of
commercial operation of the transmission system under this clause shall be required to
submit the following documents along with the petition:
(a) Energization certificate issued by the Regional Electrical Inspector under
Central Electricity Authority;
(b) Trial operation certificate issued by the concerned RLDC for charging element
with or without electrical load;
(c) Implementation Agreement, if any, executed by the parties;
(d) Minutes of the coordination meetings or related correspondences regarding
the monitoring of the progress of the generating station and transmission
systems;
(e) Notice issued by the transmission licensee as per the first proviso under this
clause and the response;
(f) Certificate of the CEO or MD of the company regarding the completion of the
transmission system including associated communication system in all respects.
13. NHPC has mainly contended that the Petitioner’s unilateral communications
claiming deemed COD for Asset-2 as 2.4.2023 and Asset-3 as 26.3.2024 prior to the
Interim order in Petition No.211/TT/2024 Page 9 of 51

final grant of connectivity granted to NHPC by CTUIL shows that PGCIL planned its
asset as per its own convenience and the letters issued under Regulation 5(2) of the
2019 Tariff Regulations are not as per the start date of connectivity. In response, the
Petitioner has submitted that NHPC responded to both the notices issued by the
Petitioner under Regulation 5(2) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations, participated in the
meetings with regard to trial operation and was informed of the provisions of the Tariff
Regulations as well as the IEGC with regard to the mismatch.
COD of the Asset-2
14. The Petitioner has claimed the COD of the Asset -2 as 2.4.2023 under Regulation
5(2) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations due to the delay in commissioning of the generation
asset under the scope of NHPC. The 2023 IEGC Regulations were notified after
2.4.2023; therefore, the Petitioner has to comply with the requirements of Regulation
5(2) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations. The Petitioner may file a petition for approval of the
COD of the transmission system through a petition under Regulation 5(2) of the 2019
Tariff Regulations and submit the applicable documents mentioned in the second
proviso to Regulation 5(2) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations. The Petitioner has submitted
the following documents in support of its claim:
a. Energisation certificate issued by the Regional Electrical Inspector:
The Petitioner has submitted CEA energisation certificate dated 8.2.2023 and
6.10.203, and the same are as follows:
Interim order in Petition No.211/TT/2024 Page 10 of 51

Interim order in Petition No.211/TT/2024 Page 11 of 51

b. Trial operation certificate issued by the concerned RLDC for charging
element with or without electrical load;
NERLDC vide letter dated 25.8.2023 has issued an idle charging certificate for
400 kV BNC - Lower Subansiri ckt-1, along with associated line bays at BNC,
and the same is as follows:
Interim order in Petition No.211/TT/2024 Page 12 of 51

Interim order in Petition No.211/TT/2024 Page 13 of 51

c. Notice issued by the transmission licensee as per the first proviso to
Regulation 5(2) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations
Interim order in Petition No.211/TT/2024 Page 14 of 51

15. We have perused the above-mentioned documents. The Petitioner has furnished
the documents required for the approval of the COD of the Asset-2 under Regulation
5(2) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations. Taking into consideration the CEA energisation
certificate dated 6.10.2023 and 8.2.2023, Idle Charging Operation Certificate dated
25.8.2023 issued by the Grid Controller of India and the Notices dated 5.10.2023 issued
by the Petitioner under Regulation 5(2) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations, the COD of the
Asset-2 is approved as 2.4.2023 under Regulation 5(2) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations.
Interim order in Petition No.211/TT/2024 Page 15 of 51

charges under Regulation 13(7) of the 2020 Sharing Regulations apply only from
Interim order in Petition No.211/TT/2024 Page 38 of 51

the connectivity start date via the existing ISTS infrastructure. Transmission
charges can only be imposed in accordance with the connectivity start dates under
Regulation 13(7) of the 2020 Sharing Regulations, and not beforehand. NHPC has
submitted that Assets 2 and 3 were not solely for the Lower Subansiri HEP of
NHPC. The Lower Subansiri Transmission Project was created as a common
infrastructure to evacuate power from multiple hydroelectric projects, including the
Siang Middle HEP (1000 MW). The Petitioner has submitted that, as per the Final
Grant of Connectivity, the Biswanath Chariali (Twin Lapwing) 2 x D/C lines under
ISTS are the evacuation system for the Lower Subansiri HEP. The Petitioner has
further submitted that there is no question of the applicability of Regulation 13(7)
of the 2020 Sharing Regulations, when the primary question of charges qua mis-
match has to be considered. The liability of NHPC to bear 100% liability of the
transmission charges from the COD of Asset–2 and Asset-3 is consistent with the
Commission’s regulations and the Grant of Connectivity by CTUIL, which was
never challenged by NHPC.
35. We have considered the submission of the Petitioner and NHPC. The Regulation
13(7) of 2020 Sharing Regulation provides as follows:
"(7) Where a Connectivity grantee other than a Renewable Power Park
Developer has been granted Connectivity through existing transmission system
and no augmentation of transmission system has been undertaken for such
Connectivity, transmission charges at the rate of ₹3000/MW/month shall be
payable by the Connectivity grantee from the start date of Connectivity, till
operationalization of Long-Term Access."
36. It is observed that the “400kV Lower Subansiri - Biswanath Chariali (Twin
Lapwing) 2 x D/C transmission lines” were planned to be implemented for immediate
evacuation of power from Lower Subansiri HEP, in the 6th TCC and 6th NERPC meeting
held on 7th and 8th August 2008. Further, CTUIL in its Final Grant of Connectivity vide
letter dated 10.10.2023 had mentioned that the dedicated transmission system for
evacuation of power from Lower Subansiri HEP, i.e. 400 kV Lower Subansiri -
Interim order in Petition No.211/TT/2024 Page 39 of 51

Biswanath Chariali (Twin Lapwing) 2 x D/c transmission lines, as existing ISTS, as the
1st D/C line was already charged and the 2nd D/C was expected to be ready by
December 2023. It is quite clear that the 400 kV Lower Subansiri - Biswanath Chariali
(Twin Lapwing) 2 x D/c transmission lines were planned only for the immediate
evacuation of power from Lower Subansiri HEP owned by NHPC, and just mentioning
of said line as existing ISTS in the final grant of connectivity by CTUIL does not change
the purpose of implementation of aforementioned transmission line.
37. CTUIL intimated the in-principle grant of 250 MW Connectivity to NHPC vide
letter dated 31.8.2023, and it is extracted hereunder:
Interim order in Petition No.211/TT/2024 Page 40 of 51

ORDER
The Petitioner, KPI Green Energy Limited (hereinafter referred to as ‘the
Petitioner’), incorporated under the Companies Act, 2013, read with Regulation 6(1)
of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Procedure, Terms and Conditions
for the Grant of Trading Licence and other related matters) Regulations, 2020
Order in Petition No. 871/TD/2025
Page 1 of 11

(hereinafter referred to as “the Trading Licence Regulations”), amended from time to
time, has filed the present Petition for the grant of a Category ‘IV’ trading licence for
inter-State trading in electricity in the whole of India.
Hearing Dated 20.11.2025
2. During the course of the hearing, the learned counsel for the Petitioner
reiterated the submissions made in the Petition and submitted that the Petitioner
company has complied with the provisions of the Trading Licence Regulations. The
Petitioner, vide Record of Proceedings (hereinafter referred to as “RoP’) for the
hearing dated 20.11.2025, was directed to submit the following information on an
affidavit:
(i) Audited special balance sheet in place of provisional or unaudited
statement (within 30 days preceding the date of filing of the Petition), along
with Auditor’s certificate/report, Profit & Loss Statement and Schedules and
notes to accounts, etc.
(ii) Revised Net Worth Certificate based on the audited special balance sheet,
not on a provisional or unaudited statement.
(iii) Demonstrate compliance with the net worth and current & liquidity ratio
requirements as per the Trading Licence Regulations, by submitting the
necessary audited special balance sheet.
(iv) Compliance affidavit in terms of Regulation 6(4) of the Trading Licence
Regulations.
(v) Declaration stating that the Petitioner does not hold any transmission
licence and that it shall not carry out the business of transmission of electricity
during the subsistence of the inter-State trading licence, if granted by the
Order in Petition No. 871/TD/2025
Page 2 of 11

Commission. (vi) Clarify whether the profile of professionals submitted in the
Petition is full-time in the Petitioner company as per the requirement of
Technical Qualifications under Regulation 3 of the Trading Licence
Regulations, 2020.
(vii) Under which provisions, two applications have been made for the grant of
the inter-State trading licences by the two companies of the same group
company, where the shareholders of the companies are the same.
3. In compliance with the RoP dated 20.11.2025, the Petitioner vide its affidavit
dated 16.12.2025 has furnished the information regarding (i) to (v) above, which
have been taken on record. With regard to (vi) and (vii) above, the Petitioner has
submitted as under:
(a) The professionals furnished in the instant Application are in compliance
with Regulation 3 of the Trading Regulations, and the personnel engaged are
full-time employees of the Applicant company. The details of the technical
qualifications of the key personnel, namely, Mr. Alok Das (Group CEO), Mr.
Surinder Kumar Negi (Chief Operating Officer), Mr. Venu Birappa (Non-
Executive Independent Director), Mr. Salim Suleman Yahoo (Chief Financial
Officer), and Mr. Akshit Pacchigar (Chartered Accountant and Head of Finance
& Accounts), have been placed on record which have been discussed in the
later part of the order.
(b) In response to the provisions under which two applications have been
made for the grant of inter-State trading licences by two companies of the same
group having common shareholders, each application has been filed under
Section 14 of the Act, read with the Trading Licence Regulations. Both
Applicant Companies are separate legal entities and have applied under
Order in Petition No. 871/TD/2025
Page 3 of 11

different licence categories (Category IV and Category V). Each Applicant
independently meets the prescribed net worth, creditworthiness, past
performance, and other eligibility criteria, and has an independent corporate
identity, governance structure, and financial statements. Accordingly, the filing
of separate licence applications by two distinct companies of the same group is
stated to be in compliance with Regulations 3 and 4 of the Trading Licence
Regulations, and there is no statutory or regulatory restriction on group
companies or companies with common shareholding from applying for or
holding trading licences, provided each satisfies the regulatory requirements
individually.
Hearing dated 23.12.2025
4. During the hearing, the learned counsel for the Petitioner submitted that the
Petitioner has filed its compliance affidavit dated 16.12.2025 in terms of Record of

5. Vide RoP dated 23.12.2025, the Commission observed that, in terms of
