CENTRAL ELECTRICITY REGULATORY COMMISSION
NEW DELHI
Review Petition No. 14/RP/2025
in
Petition No. 87/AT/2025
Coram:
Shri Jishnu Barua, Chairperson
Shri Ramesh Babu V., Member
Shri Harish Dudani, Member
Shri Ravinder Singh Dhillon, Member
Date of Order: 15th January, 2026
In the matter of
Review of the order dated 19.06.2025 passed by the Commission in Petition No.
87/AT/2025 titled as ‘NHPC Limited vs. M/s. Jevargi Solar Power Private Limited and
Ors.’
And
In the matter of
NHPC Limited,
(a Govt. of India Enterprise)
NHPC Office Complex, Sector-33,
Faridabad (Haryana)- 121003. …Petitioner
Vs.
1. M/s Jevargi Solar Power Private Limited,
6th Floor, Imperia Mindspace,
Golf Course extension Road,
Sector-62, Gurugram-122001.
2. M/s Juniper Green Energy Private Limited,
Plot No. 18, First Floor, Institutional Area,
Sector – 32, Gurugram-122001.
3. M/s Avaada Energy Private Limited,
C-11, Sector-65, Noida- 201301.
4. ACME Solar Holdings Limited,
Plot No.-152, Sector-44,
Gurugram-12202. …Respondents
Parties Present:
Shri Akshay Goel, Advocate, NHPC
Shri Jagpal Singh, Advocate, NHPC
Shri Harsh Tandon, Advocate, NHPC
Order in Petition No. 14/RP/2025 1

Shri Binwant Goel, Advocate, NHPC
Shri Tabrez Malawal, Advocate, ACME Solar
Shri Syed Hamza, Advocate, ACME Solar
Shri Sourajit Sarkar, Advocate, ACME Solar
Shri Rupali Jain, Advocate, ACME Solar
ORDER
The instant Review Petition has been filed by the Review Petitioner, NHPC
Limited (NHPC), seeking a review of the Commission’s order dated 19.6.2025 in
Petition No. 87/AT/2025 (the ‘impugned order’), whereby the Commission approved
the tariff for the supply of the 1200 MW power from Inter-State Transmission System
(“ISTS”) connected Firm and Dispatchable Power (“FDRE”) from Renewable Energy
Power Generators (“RE-PG”) with Energy Storage Systems (“ESS”) selected through
competitive bidding process. The prayers urged in the present Review Petition are as
under:
“(a) Admit the present Petition.
(b) Adopt the Tariff discovered in the Competitive Bidding Process under
“Greenshoe Option” for individual Power Projects as listed in Table at Para 5 above, in
addition to the tariff already adopted by the Commission in its order dated 19.06.2025
in Petition No. 87/AT/2025, on terms and conditions contained in the PPA to be signed
with RE-Power Generators being Respondent Nos 1 to 4 and a Trading Margin of Rs
0.07/kWh in addition to above Tariff is to be recovered from buying Utilities /Distribution
Licensee/DISCOM(s) in terms of the PSA to be signed between NHPC & Utilities/
Distribution Licensee.
(c) Issue amendment to Para 31 of order dated 19.06.2025 in petition No.
87/AT/2025.
(d) Pass such other and further order / orders as are deemed fit and proper in the
facts and circumstances of the case.”
2. The Review Petitioner has submitted that the Commission, while passing the impugned
order dated 19.6.2025, has inadvertently failed to adopt the tariff pertaining to an additional
quantum of 1150 MW, being the ‘Greenshoe Option’. The Review Petitioner has further
contended that the Commission has failed to adopt the said tariff despite having acknowledged
the Letters of Award (LOA) dated 30.1.2025 issued to the successful bidder and other material
on record, which clearly exhibits the existence of the factum of the ‘Greenshoe Option’.
Order in Petition No. 14/RP/2025 2

Therefore, there is an error apparent on the face of the record which merits exercise of review
jurisdiction under Section 94 (1) (f) of the Electricity Act, 2003 (hereinafter referred to as ‘Act’).
Submissions of the Review Petitioner:
3. The Review Petitioner/ NHPC has mainly made the following submissions:
(a) NHPC is a Government of India company within the meaning of the
Companies Act, 1956 and a ‘generating company’ within the meaning of Section
2 (28) of the Act. NHPC has been designated by the Ministry of New and
Renewable Energy (MNRE), Government of India, as an Intermediary procurer/
Renewable Energy Implementing Agency (REIA) for the purpose of the Act, and
the Guidelines dated 9.6.2023 for Tariff-based Competitive Bidding Process for
Procurement of Firm and Dispatchable Power from Grid-connected Renewable
Energy Power Projects with Energy Storage Systems.
(b) NHPC floated a tender on 28.6.2024 in terms of the Request for Selection
(RfS) for inviting bids from stakeholders for the supply of the 1200 MW FDRE
projects. In response, 5 bids were received from the bidders who subsequently
participated in the e-reverse auction (E-RA) on 10.12.2024. As a result of the
same, the 1200 MW FDRE capacity was allocated to the following four entities,
along with a ‘Greenshoe’ quantum at the corresponding tariff discovered
through the E-RA:
S.No. Name of REPGs Allocated Tariff Greenshoe Tariff
Capacity capacity (MW)
(MW)
1. Jevargi Solar Power Private 150 4.48 - -
Limited
2. Juniper Green Energy 200 4.56 300 4.48
Private Limited
3. Avaada Energy Private 600 4.56 600 4.48
Limited
4. Acme Solar Holdings 250 4.56 250 4.48
Limited
Total 1200 1150
Order in Petition No. 14/RP/2025 3

(c) Pursuant to the competitive bidding process and the discovery of tariff,
NHPC issued Letters of Award (LOAs) to the successful bidders for supply of
1200 MW FDRE from ISTS-connected RE power projects coupled with ‘ESS’
under the tariff-based competitive bidding process, with a ‘Greenshoe Option’
of additional capacity of 1150 MW.
(d) Subsequently, NHPC filed Petition No. 87/AT/2025 seeking adoption of the
tariff discovered from the E-RA conducted in terms of the Ministry of Power
Guidelines. In response to the Commission`s query dated 19.2.2025, NHPC
also furnished additional information/ clarifications vide affidavit dated 6.3.2025.
After hearing the parties, the Commission reserved the matter for orders on
2.4.2025. Subsequently, the Commission vide order dated 19.6.2025 adopted
the tariff for the base FDRE quantum of 1200 MW. However, the tariff for the
additional ‘Greenshoe option’ quantum was not adopted.
(e) The Commission failed to adopt the tariff pertaining to the ‘Greenshoe
Option’ quantum, despite acknowledging the LOAs dated 30.1.2025 and the
factum of allocation of additional ‘Greenshoe option’ quantum to the successful
bidders in Paragraph 27 of the impugned order.
(f) During the course of the hearings dated 19.2.2025 and 2.4.2025, the
Review Petitioner apprised the Commission regarding the adoption of the tariff
pertaining to 2350 MW (1200 MW FDRE and 1150 MW ‘Greenshoe Option’
quantum) discovered from the E-RA conducted in accordance with the TBCB
guidelines.
Submissions of the Respondents:
4. Respondent No. 4, ACME Solar Holdings Limited (ASHL) has submitted as
Order in Petition No. 14/RP/2025 4

under:
(a) AHSL is one of the successful bidders of the E-RA conducted by NHPC
and has been awarded an LOA for the supply of the FDRE along with the
‘Greenshoe option’ quantum at the discovered tariff. ASHL has accordingly
supported the submissions and the prayers of NHPC in the captioned Review
Petition.
b) The Commission in the impugned order dated 19.6.2025 has
acknowledged the existence of ‘Greenshoe Option’.
(c) The ‘Greenshoe Option’ is in furtherance of public interest since it would
ensure the injection and availability of a significant quantum of renewable energy.
The tariff discovered for the ‘Greenshoe option’ quantum was in accordance with
the Guidelines issued by the Ministry of Power, thereby satisfying the statutory
mandate under Section 63 of the Act.
5. The matter was heard on 27.11.2025. After hearing the parties, the matter was
reserved for order.
Analysis and Decision
6. The instant Review Petition has been filed under Section 94(1) of the Act read
with Section 114 and Order 47 Rule 1 of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908 (hereinafter
referred to as ‘CPC’) and Regulation 52 (2) (B) of the Central Electricity Regulatory
Commission (Conduct of Business) Regulations, 2023 (hereinafter referred to as
“CBR, 2023”) seeking review of the order dated 19.6.2025 passed by the Commission
in Petition No. 87/AT/2025. Regulation 52(2) of the CBR, 2023 provides that an
aggrieved party can seek review of a direction, decision or order of the Commission,
which is akin to the grounds provided in Order 47 Rule 1 of the CPC. The Review
Order in Petition No. 14/RP/2025 5

Petitioner has submitted that at paragraphs 31 & 32 of the impugned Order, the
Commission only adopted the tariff for allocated capacity to the respective bidders but
not the capacity allocated under the Greenshoe Option to such bidders despite having
acknowledged the same.
7. We have examined the submissions made by the parties and have perused the
record, including the impugned order.
8. Regulation 52(2) of the CBR, 2023 provides as under:
“52. Review of Orders, Decisions and Directions
“(1) The Commission shall exercise jurisdiction to review its own orders, decisions, and
directions in accordance with Clause (f) of sub-section (1) of Section 94 of the Act read
with Section 114 and Order 47 of the Civil Procedure Code.
(2) Any person aggrieved by a direction, decision, or order of the Commission, from
which no appeal has been preferred, may file a review petition on the 34 following
grounds within forty days of the making of such decision, direction, or order:
(a) Upon the discovery of new and important matter or evidence that, after the
exercise of due diligence, was not within his knowledge or could not be produced
by him at the time when the direction, decision, or order was passed or;
(b) On account of some mistake or error apparent from the face of the record, or;
(c) If there is any other sufficient reason to review the matter. ………………….”
9. It is noted that the Review Petitioner had filed Petition No. 87/AT/2025 along
with the following prayers:
“(a) Admit the present Petition.
(b) Adopt the Tariff discovered in the Competitive Bidding Process for
individual Power Projects as listed in Table-1 at paragraph 9 above on terms
and conditions contained in the PPA to be signed with RE-Power Generators being
Respondent Nos. 1 to 5 and a Trading Margin of Rs. 0.07 / kWh in addition to above
Tariff is to be recovered from buying Utilities /Distribution Licensee/DISCOM(s) in
terms of the PSA to be signed between NHPC & Utilities/ Distribution Licensee.
(c ) Pass such other and further order / orders as are deemed fit and proper in the
facts and circumstances of the case.”
[emphasis supplied]
10. A plain reading of the prayers reveals that the prayers are narrowly tailored to
the tariffs for the base capacities listed in the table below, with no reference, express
Order in Petition No. 14/RP/2025 6

or implied, to any additional quantum, i.e. Greenshoe option. Accordingly, the
Commission adopted the following capacities and their tariff as under:
S. Name of RE-PGs Allocated Tariff
No. Capacity (MW) (Rs/kWh)
1 Jevargi Solar Power Private Limited 150 4.48
2 Juniper Green Energy Private Limited 200 4.56
3 Avaada Energy Private Limited 600 4.56
4 Acme Solar Holdings Limited 250 4.56
Total 1200
11. A careful examination of the record irrefutably establishes that the Review
Petitioner, NHPC, neither prayed for adoption of the tariff pertaining to the ‘Greenshoe
Option’ quantum discovered during the e-Reverse Auction (E-RA) conducted by NHPC
on 10.12.2024 nor advanced any submissions on this aspect during the hearings in
Petition No. 87/AT/2025. The prayers for the adoption of the tariff are clearly restricted
to the adoption of the tariff without the ‘Greenshoe Option’ quantum.
12. Therefore, the Review Petitioner has failed to incorporate any specific prayer
seeking the relief now claimed in the Review Petition. It is a cornerstone of procedural
jurisprudence that no court or tribunal possesses the inherent power to grant a relief
not expressly pleaded or prayed for, as this would deny counter-parties a fair
opportunity to address the claim and imperil the adversarial process. The Hon’ble
Supreme Court in the case of Bharat Amratlal Kothari v. Dosukhan Samadkhan Sindhi
[(AIR 2010 SC 475)] has held that a tribunal cannot grant relief not prayed for,
disregarding established norms governing the grant of relief.
13. It is apposite to note that the power of the Commission to review its order is
concededly restricted and can be exercised only in certain specific circumstances and
is limited to errors that are self-evident, without requiring elaborate arguments or
interpretation. The Review Petitioner has invoked the provisions of Section 94(1)(f) of
the Act and Regulation 52 of the CBR, 2023, on the ground of an ‘error apparent on
Order in Petition No. 14/RP/2025 7

the face of the record’ in the impugned order for failing to adopt the tariff pertaining to
the ‘Greenshoe option’ quantum. However, as seen above, the order passed by the
Commission was confined to the prayers specifically sought by NHPC during the
hearing of Petition No. 87/AT/2025. No such patent error has been demonstrated by
the Review Petitioner.
14. For the reasons aforementioned, we find no merit in the submissions advanced
by the Review Petitioner so as to warrant the entertainment of the present Review
Petition. The Review Petition does not disclose any error apparent on the face of the
record that merits exercise of review jurisdiction under Section 94(1)(f) of the Act read
with Regulation 52 of the CBR, 2023. Accordingly, the Review Petition is rejected.
However, considering the important nature of the matter which pertains to green power,
the Petitioner is granted liberty to file a fresh Petition specifically seeking adoption of
the ‘Greenshoe Option’ quantum, and the same shall be considered in accordance with
law.
15. Review Petition No. 14/RP/2025 is accordingly disposed of.
Sd/- sd/- sd/- sd/-
(Ravinder Singh Dhillon) (Harish Dudani) (Ramesh Babu V.) (Jishnu Barua)
Member Member Member Chairperson

3. The Commission, after considering the application of the Petitioner in light of
the provisions of the Act and the Transmission Licence Regulations, in its order dated
26.12.2025, prima facie proposed to grant a transmission licence to the Petitioner. The
relevant extracts of the order dated 26.12.2025 are extracted as under:
“23. Considering the material on record, we are prima-facie of the view that
the Petitioner satisfies the conditions for the grant of inter-State transmission
licence under Section 15 of the Act read with the Transmission Licence
Regulations for construction, operation, and maintenance of the transmission
system as described in para 1 of this order. We, therefore, direct that a public
notice in two daily digital newspaper and on the Commission`s website under
clause (a) of sub-section (5) of Section 15 of the Act be published to invite
suggestions or objections to the grant of transmission licence aforesaid. The
objections or suggestions, if any, be filed by any person before the Commission
by 9.1.2026.”
4. A public notice under Sub-section (5) of Section 15 of the Act was published in
all editions of the Hindustan Times (English) and Amar Ujala (Hindi) on 1.1.2026. No
suggestions/ objections have been received from members of the public in response
to the public notice.
Hearing dated 13.1.2026
5. The matter was called out for the hearing on 13.1.2026. During the course of
the hearing, the learned counsel for the Petitioner submitted that no objection had
been received in response to the public notice published by the Commission under
sub-section (5) of Section 15 of the Act. He prayed to be granted a transmission
licence. The representative of the CTUIL submitted that CTUIL has already complied
with the provisions of the Transmission Licence Regulations.
Order in Petition No. 860/TL/2025
Page 14

6. As regards the grant of a transmission licence, Clauses (13) and (14) of
Regulation 5 of the 2024 Transmission Licence Regulations provide as under:
“(13) The Commission may, after consideration of the further suggestions
and objections, if any, received in response to the public notice in terms of
Clause (12) of this Regulation, grant licence to the applicant in Form-III
appended to these regulations or for reasons to be recorded in writing, reject
the application.
(14) The Commission shall before granting licence or rejecting the application
under the provisions of this Regulation provide an opportunity of hearing to
the applicant, CTUIL, the concerned DICs, or the person who has filed
suggestions and objections, or any other interested person.”
7. In our order dated 26.12.2025, we had proposed to grant a transmission licence
to the Petitioner company and directed the issue of public notice. In response to the
public notice, no suggestions/objections have been received. CTUIL, in its letter dated
24.10.2025, has recommended the grant of a transmission licence to the Petitioner.
We find that the Petitioner company meets the requirements of the Act and the
Transmission Licence Regulations, 2024, for the grant of a transmission licence for
the subject Transmission System mentioned in paragraph 1 of this order. Considering
the submissions of the Petitioner and CTUIL, we direct that a transmission licence be
granted to the Petitioner, ‘Rajgarh Neemuch Power Transmission Limited, for
“Evacuation of Power from RE Projects in Rajgarh (1500 MW) SEZ in Madhya
Pradesh-Phase III and Evacuation of Power from RE Projects in Neemuch (1000 MW)
SEZ in Madhya Pradesh-Phase II” on a Build, Own, Operate and Transfer basis as
per the details given in paragraph 1 above.
8. The grant of the transmission licence to the Petitioner (hereinafter referred to
as “the licensee”) is subject to the fulfilment of the following conditions throughout the
period of the licence:

ORDER
The Petitioner, Mundra I Transmission Limited, has filed the present Petition under
Section 63 of the Electricity Act, 2003 read with Section 79(1) (c) & (d) of the Electricity
Act, 2003 (hereinafter referred to as “the Act”) seeking the adoption of transmission
tariff discovered through the tariff based competitive bidding process for the purpose
of selection of bidder as the Transmission Service Provider (TSP) to establish the
Order in Petition No. 440/AT/2025
Page 2

Inter-State Transmission System for “Transmission System for supply of power to
Green Hydrogen/ Ammonia manufacturing potential in Mundra area of Gujarat under
Phase-I: Part B1 scheme (3 GW at Navinal S/s)” on a Build, Own, Operate and
Transfer Basis (hereinafter referred to as “BOOT Basis”). The Petitioner has made
the following prayers:
“(1) Adopt Transmission Charges for the Project discovered through
competitive bidding process.
(2) Allow the Transmission Charges of “Transmission system for supply of
power to Green Hydrogen/Ammonia manufacturing potential in Mundra area of
Gujarat under Phase-I: Part B1 scheme (3 GW at Navinal S/s)” to be part of
POC pool under CERC (Sharing of Inter-state Transmission Charges and
Losses Regulations) Regulation, 2020 and its amendment thereof issued from
time to time by Hon’ble Commission.
(3) Condone any inadvertent errors omissions/errors/shortcomings and permit
the Petitioner to add/change/modify/alter these filings and make further
submissions as may be required at a future date.
(4) Pass any such other order / orders, as may be deemed fit and proper in the
facts and circumstances of the case.”
2. On receipt of the present Petition, the Bid Process Coordinator (hereinafter
referred to as “the BPC”), PFC Consulting Limited (hereinafter referred to as
“PFCCL”), vide letter dated 5.5.2025, was directed to submit the relevant documents
regarding the complete process of the competitive bidding. The necessary details
have been filed by the BPC under an affidavit dated 14.5.2025.
Hearing dated 20.5.2025, 20.6.2025, and 17.7.2025
3. Notice was issued to the Respondents vide Record of Proceedings (hereinafter
referred to as “RoP”) dated 20.5.2025 to file their respective replies. However, no reply
has been received from the Respondents despite notice. Accordingly, the matter was
reserved for orders vide RoP dated 17.7.2025.
Order in Petition No. 440/AT/2025
Page 3

Analysis and Decision
4. We have considered the submissions of the Petitioner and the Respondents
and perused the documents available on record. The Petitioner has filed the instant
Petition under Section 63 of the Act for the adoption of the Inter-State Transmission
System for “Transmission System for supply of power to Green Hydrogen/Ammonia
manufacturing potential in Mundra area of Gujarat under Phase-I: Part B1 scheme (3
GW at Navinal S/s)”.
5. The Ministry of Power, Government of India, vide its Gazette Notification No.
CG-DL-E-13092024-257122 dated 12.9.2024, has notified the PFCCL as the Bid
Process Coordinator for the purpose of selection of bidder as the Transmission
Service Provider to establish the Inter-State Transmission System for “Transmission
System for supply of power to Green Hydrogen/Ammonia manufacturing potential in
Mundra area of Gujarat under Phase-I: Part B1 scheme (3 GW at Navinal S/s)” on a
Build, Own, Operate and Transfer Basis through a tariff based competitive bidding
process.
6. Mundra I Transmission Limited was incorporated on 26.12.2024 under the
Companies Act, 2013 as a wholly owned subsidiary of PFCCL with the objective to
establish the inter-State Transmission System for the “Transmission System for supply
of power to Green Hydrogen/Ammonia manufacturing potential in Mundra area of
Gujarat under Phase-I: Part B1 scheme (3 GW at Navinal S/s)” and to act as the
Transmission Service Provider after being acquired by the successful bidder.
7. The BPC prepared the bidding document (RfP) in accordance with the Standard
Bid Documents issued by the Ministry of Power, Government of India. The BPC started
Order in Petition No. 440/AT/2025
Page 4

the process of selection of the successful bidder with the publication of a Global
Invitation for Qualification for the selection of a developer on a BOOT basis for the
Project. The notice for the RfP was published in National/International newspapers
on 15.10.2024, with the last date of submission of response to the RfP as 18.12.2024.
Intimation regarding the initiation of the bid process was given to this Commission on
21.10.2023, in accordance with Clause 4.2 of the Guidelines dated 10.8.2021.
8. The scope of the Project as per the Request for Proposal and
the Transmission Service Agreement is as under:

9. The RfP was issued on 15.10.2024. At the RfP (Technical and Financial) stage,
three bidders, namely, (i) Power Grid Corporation of India Limited; (ii) Sterlite Grid 32
Limited, and (iii) Adani Energy Solutions Limited (Formerly known as Adani
Transmission Limited) submitted their offers. The RfP (Technical) bids of the bidders
were opened by the Bid Opening Committee at the Central Electricity Authority on
9.1.2025 in the presence of a representative of the bidders. Based on the
recommendation of the Bid Evaluation Committee (BEC), the RfP (Financial) Bids-
Initial Price Offer of the bidders were opened on 27.1.2025. The Lowest Initial Price
Offer discovered (Best Deal) on the MSTC portal was Rs. 3,700.00 million per annum.
10. As per the provisions of the RfP documents, BEC recommended that the three
qualified bidders participate in the e-reverse auction stage and submit their final offer.
Order in Petition No. 440/AT/2025
Page 6

The e-reverse auction among the three qualified bidders was conducted on the MSTC
portal on 28.1.2025 and concluded on 29.1.2025 after intimating the bidders regarding
the lowest initial price offer. However, of the three shortlisted bidders, only the two
bidders, namely, Adani Energy Solutions Limited and Power Grid Corporation of India
Limited, participated in the e-reverse auction.
11. Based on the e-reverse bidding, BEC, in its meeting held on 3.2.2025,
recommended Adani Energy Solutions Limited, with the lowest transmission charges
of Rs. 3,081.73 million per annum, as the successful bidder. The Letter of Intent was
issued by the BPC on 6.2.2025 to the successful bidder, i.e., Adani Energy Solutions
Limited. In accordance with Clause 12.3 of the Guidelines, the BPC has hosted on the
website of PFCCL the final result of the evaluation of the bids for the selection of a
developer for the Project.
12. In accordance with the provisions of the bid documents and upon the issuance
of the LoI to the successful bidder (Adani Energy Solutions Limited) and acquisition of
the SPV (the Petitioner) by the successful bidder, the Petitioner has prayed for the
adoption of transmission charges for the Project, which has been discovered through
the competitive bidding process.
13. It is noted that the Petitioner had filed a separate application along with the
instant Petition for the grant of a transmission licence for the subject transmission
system. The Commission, vide its order dated 30.10.2025 in Petition No. 441/TL/2025,
has observed that it is premature to consider the grant of a transmission licence for the
instant transmission scheme, as it does not fulfil the requirement prescribed under
Section 38(2)(c) of the Act, and accordingly, referred the matter to NCT for
Order in Petition No. 440/AT/2025
Page 7

reconsideration on the basis of its likely utilisation and impact on the consumers, in the
absence of any application for its use by the bulk consumers. The relevant extract of
the order dated 30.10.2025 is as under:
“25. The Act mandates that the inter-state transmission system be developed in
an efficient and economical manner. However, the instant transmission scheme
may lead to a redundant transmission asset without any visibility of its utilization.
Therefore, we are of the considered view that it is premature to consider the
grant of a transmission licence for the instant transmission scheme, as it does
not fulfil the requirement under section 38(2)(c) of the Act. We find it appropriate
to refer the proposal for the instant transmission scheme back to the NCT for
reconsideration on the basis of its likely utilization and impact on the consumers
in the absence of any application for its use by the bulk consumers. Accordingly,
we direct the Petitioner and the CTUIL to approach the NCT with the
observations as made in this Order. After the decision of the NCT, the Petitioner
may approach the Commission if so advised.
26. The Petition No. 441/TL/2025 is disposed of in terms of the above.”
14. In view of the above, the question of adoption of transmission charges of the
subject transmission scheme does not arise at this stage, and no purpose would be
served to keep the instant adoption Petition pending any further when the decision of
the NCT is pending in the subject transmission scheme. Accordingly, the Petition is
disposed of, with liberty to the Petitioner to approach the Commission for the adoption
of transmission charges after the NCT takes a decision on the subject transmission
scheme. The filing fee paid in the instant Petition shall be adjusted against the adoption
Petition, if any, to be filed by the Petitioner for the subject transmission scheme in
future.
15. Petition No. 440/AT/2025 is disposed of in terms of the above.

आदेश/ ORDER
The Petitioner, M/s NTPC Ltd. (NTPC), has developed a 90 MW Anta Solar PV Project in the
existing vacant land in the station premises of the ‘Anta Gas based Power Station’, Baran, in the
State of Rajasthan. The Guidelines for Tariff-Based Competitive Bidding Process for Procurement
of Power from Grid-Connected Solar PV Power Projects were issued by the Ministry of Power on
03.08.2017. Pursuant to these Guidelines, the Request for Selection (RfS) was issued by Kerala
State Electricity Board Limited (KSEBL) on 18.09.2020. The Corrigendum to the RfS was issued
on 06.10.2020, modifying certain clauses in the RfS and the PPA. NTPC submitted its bid on
20.10.2020. The non-financial bids of the tender were opened on 20.10.2020, and only two bidders
submitted the bids, viz. NTPC for 90 MW and M/s Tata Power Company Ltd. (TPCL) for 200
MW. The evaluation committee reviewed the offers and documents on 04.11.2020 and
recommended opening the financial bid on 12.11.2020 along with an e-Reverse auction on the
same day. The final allotted quantum and the price are as follows:
i) NTPC - 90 MW @ Rs. 2.97/kWh; and
ii) Tata Power Company Ltd. - 110 MW @ Rs. 2.97/kWh.
Kerala State Electricity Regulatory Commission (KSERC), in its order dated 18.12.2020 in OP.
No. 39 of 2020 adopted the tariff of Rs. 2.97/kWh for the procurement of power. KSEBL issued
the Letter of Award (LoA) to NTPC on 06.01.2021 at a final tariff rate of Rs. 2.97 per kWh for the
awarded capacity of 90 MW for a Solar PV Power Project. Subsequently, KSEBL filed a Petition
bearing OP No. 39 of 2020 before KSERC seeking the adoption of a Tariff of Rs. 2.97/kWh for
the procurement of 90 MW of Solar Power from NTPC. On 05.02.2021, KSEBL and NTPC signed
the initialled PPA for the procurement of 90 MW of Solar power for the purpose of submitting the
same before the KSERC for approval. On 08.02.2021, KSEBL filed OP No. 11 of 2021 before
KSERC for approval of the initialled PPA. On 21.06.2021, KSERC approved the initialled PPA.
Order in Petition No. 417/MP/2024 Page 2 of 33

On 06.07.2021, NTPC requested KSEBL to indicate the date for signing of the PPA. During the
pendency of OP No. 11 of 2021, on 12.11.2021, KSEB issued a letter to NTPC, requesting it to
reduce the tariff from Rs. 2.97/kWh to Rs. 2.44/kWh in the light of lowering of tariff by another
generator, which was also allowed subject to the condition that the rate change due to change in
law, including BCD, shall be governed by Clause 5.7 of the TBCB Guidelines. On 21.06.2022, in
response to the letter dated 12.11.2021 issued by KSEBL, NTPC proposed that KSEBL reduce
the tariff to Rs. 2.77/kWh for the Project in good faith and in furtherance of the interest of the
Project. However, while proposing the revised tariff, NTPC made it clear that any implication
arising from any change in law event post the last date of bid submission, i.e., 20.10.2020, shall
be payable additionally by KSEBL to NTPC. On 05.07.2022, KSERC vide Order in O.P. No. 73
of 2021 reduced and revised the tariff to Rs. 2.77/kWh by amending Clause 9.1 of the draft
initiated PPA, thereby allowing the procurement of 90 MW of solar power for a period of 25 years
from the Scheduled Commissioning Date (SCoD) from NTPC. NTPC executed the Power
Purchase Agreement (PPA) with Kerala State Electricity Board Limited on 24.08.2023. As per the
PPA dated 24.08.2023, the Scheduled Commercial Operation Date (SCoD) is 24.02.2025 (18
months from the date of execution of the PPA (24.08.2023). The project was commissioned on
31.05.2024. NTPC is seeking approval of a change in law and consequential determination of
quantum and mechanism of compensation on account of the change in law events
2. The Respondent No. 1, Kerala State Electricity Board Limited (KSEBL), is the successor entity
of Kerala State Electricity Board, which was constituted by the Government of Kerala under the
Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948, for carrying out the business of Generation, Transmission, and
Distribution of electricity in the State of Kerala.
3. NTPC has made the following prayers:
a) Declare the Finance Act, 2022 dated 30.03.2022 issued by the Parliament read with
OM dated 09.03.2021 issued by MNRE as a Change in Law event in terms of Article 12
of the PPA;
b) Declare Notification No. 8/2021-Central Tax (Rate) dated 30.09.2021 issued by
Ministry of Finance as a Change in Law event in terms of Article 12 of the PPA;
c) Consequently direct KSEBL to pay to NTPC change in law compensation of Rs.
117,48,23,761/- along with carrying cost applicable from the date the aforesaid amount
becomes payable till the actual date of payment, towards compensation for such Change
in Law events to the Petitioner for the period from 14.04.2022 till 29.05.2024;

d) Grant liberty to NTPC to approach this Hon’ble Commission for seeking appropriate
remedy towards additional financial impact for the post COD period invoices which
remain due to be paid.
e) Pass any further order(s)/direction(s) that this Hon’ble Court may deem fit in nature of
the facts and circumstances of the present case.

5. The present petition was filed on 05.10.2024. The petition was listed for hearing on 21.01.2025,
wherein the Commission, after hearing the submissions of NTPC, admitted the Petition. On
25.03.2025 & 08.05.2025, none appeared on behalf of KSEBL. Hence, the Commission adjourned

Submissions of NTPC:
7. Briefly, NTPC has submitted as under:
a. The 2022 BCD Notification and the 2021 GST Notification, having been issued post the

12. We have heard the learned counsels for the Petitioner and the Respondents and have carefully
perused the records.
13. The main issues that arise for consideration before the Commission in the present matter are as
under:
Issue No. I: Whether the imposition of an increased rate of basic customs duty vide the

the Ministry of Finance, Government of India amounts to Change in Law events under Article

24.08.2023, towards additional expenditure on account of the Change in Law events?

14. Before going to the main issue, we feel it is pertinent to deal with the preliminary issues raised by
KSEBL. KSEBL has argued that the Change in Law claim is not maintainable. KSEBL has
submitted that the PPA dated 24.08.2023 clearly states that any claim of “Change in Law” shall
be adjudicated by the Appropriate Commission (Clause 12.2.1). Further, the Appropriate
Commission has been defined in the Agreement as the Kerala State Electricity Regulatory
Commission (KSERC). NTPC, a signatory to the PPA, is also bound by its terms, and the present
Petition filed by NTPC before this Commission is not maintainable and deserves to be rejected.

15. We observe that Section 79(1) of the Electricity Act, 2003 (the Act, 2003) stipulates as under:
Section 79. (Functions of Central Commission): --- (1) The Central Commission shall
discharge the following functions, namely:-
(a) to regulate the tariff of generating companies owned or controlled by the Central
Government;
(b) to regulate the tariff of generating companies other than those owned or
controlled by the Central Government specified in clause (a), if such generating
companies enter into or otherwise have a composite scheme for generation and
sale of electricity in more than one State;
(c) to regulate the inter-State transmission of electricity;
(d) to determine tariff for inter-State transmission of electricity;
(e) to issue licenses to persons to function as transmission licensee and electricity
trader with respect to their inter-State operations;
(f) to adjudicate upon disputes involving generating companies or transmission
licensee in regard to matters connected with clauses (a) to (d) above and to refer
any dispute for arbitration;
(g) to levy fees for the purposes of this Act;
(h) to specify Grid Code having regard to Grid Standards;
(i) to specify and enforce the standards with respect to quality, continuity and
reliability of service by licensees;
(j) to fix the trading margin in the inter-State trading of electricity, if considered,
necessary;
(k) to discharge such other functions as may be assigned under this Act.
16. In this context, the Appellate Tribunal, in its judgment dated 04.09.2012 in Appeal Nos. 94 and
95 of 2012 (BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd. v. Delhi Electricity Regulatory Commission and Ors.) has
also held as under:
“32. Sections 61 and 79 not only deal with the tariff but also deal with the terms and
conditions of tariff. The terms and conditions necessarily include all terms related to
tariff. Determination of tariff and its method of recovery will also depend on the terms and
conditions of tariff. For example, interest on working capital which is a component of tariff
will depend on the time allowed for billing and payment of bills. This will also have an
impact on terms and conditions for rebate and late payment surcharge. Similarly, billing
and payment of capacity charge will depend on the availability of power station. Therefore,
the scheduling has to be specified in the terms and conditions of tariff.
33. Accordingly, the billing, payment, consequences of early payment by way of grant of
rebate, consequences of delay in payment by way of surcharge, termination or
suspension of the supply, payment security mechanism such as opening of the Letter of
Credit, escrow arrangement etc. are nothing but terms and conditions of supply.
34. Section 79(1)(f) of the Electricity Act, 2003 provides for adjudication of disputes
involving a generating company or a transmission licensees in matters connected with
clauses (a) to (d) of Section 79. Thus, anything involving a generating station covered
under clauses (a) and (b) as to the generation and supply of electricity will be a matter
governed by Section 79(1)(f) of the Act.”
Order in Petition No. 417/MP/2024 Page 11 of 33

17. The Appellate Tribunal, in its judgment dated 13.08.2024 in Appeal No. 414 of 2022 titled SECI
vs KSERC & Anr. has held that KSERC could not adjudicate disputes arising from interstate
transactions, as these fall under the exclusive jurisdiction of this Commission. The extract of the
judgment is as under:
20. The operations of the Central Commission and the State Commission are prescribed
in Sections 79 and 86 of the Electricity Act, 2003 respectively. Bare reading of these
Sections would reveal that they operate in different fields and are totally independent of
each other. It would be advantageous to note the comparative provisions of these two
Sections by way of the table mentioned below:-
…
…
21. Section 79(1)(f) of the Act empowers the Central Commission to adjudicate upon the
disputes involving generating companies or transmission licensees in the mattes connected
with clauses (a) to (d) of the said Section. Therefore, any dispute involving a generating
station or a transmission licensee covered under Clauses (a)(b) & (c) will fall within the
jurisdiction of the Central Commission. It appears that since the generating companies
owned by Central Government and the generating companies having a composite scheme
for generation and sale of Electricity in more than one State have Pan India presence, the
Parliament found it proper and prudent to subject such companies to a special treatment
and, therefore, have been brought under the jurisdiction of the Central Commission vide
Section 79 of the Act. The primary object for such exercise appears to be uniformity of
tariff amongst more than one State beneficiaries and prescribing uniform terms and
conditions of supply of electricity to more than one State.
22. It is notable that Clauses (a) (b) & (c) of Section 79 (1) of the Act begin with the
expression “to regulate”. It is only the clause (d) which begins with the term “to
determine tariff”. “Regulation of Tariff” is totally distinct from “Determination of
tariff”. Regulation of Tariff includes all the necessary terms and conditions relating to the
tariff such as billing, consequences of delay in payment of electricity charges, rebate,
termination, suspension of electricity supply, payment of security, etc.
23. Section 86(1)(b) of the Act, provides for regulating the role of Distribution Licensees
in the procurement of power and 86(1)(f) relates to adjudication upon the disputes between
the licensees and generating companies by the State Commission. These are general
provisions and have to be read subject to Section 79(1) (a) to 79(1)(d) of the Act. In so far
as the generating companies who have a composite scheme for generation and sale of
electricity in more than one State, the role of the State Commission would be only to
decide whether the PPA to be entered into by them and a distribution company for
sales/purchase of electricity at the tariff determined by Central Commission, has to be
approved or not. In doing so, the State Commission would take into consideration
various factors including the availability of power from other sources at a cheaper or in
a more economical manner to be supplied to the consumers in the State. Thus, the State
Commission has a limited role to play with regards to the sale of electricity under a
composite scheme and it has no power to suggest any modifications to the terms and
conditions of the PPA/PSA to be executed between a generating company, a distribution
company and an inter-mediary.
Order in Petition No. 417/MP/2024 Page 12 of 33

24. In view of the scheme of the Act, as specified more particularly in Section 79 & 86,
it would be anomalous to permit State Commission to claim concurrent jurisdiction
along with the Central Commission in any dispute arising out of a composite scheme for
generation and sale of electricity in more than one State, which is covered by Section
79(1) (b) of the Act. The jurisdiction of the Central Commission would be only in respect
of the matters other than those which fall within the jurisdiction of the State Commission
under Section 79 of the Act. In other words, if any matter falls under the scheme of
79(1)(a) to 79(1)(d) of the Electricity Act, 2023, the provisions of Section 86(1)(f) are of
no application. In this context, we find it apposite to quote the observations of the Hon’ble
Supreme Court in Energy Watchdog Vs. CERC & Ors., (2017) 14 SCC 80.
“24. The scheme that emerges from these sections is that whenever there is inter-
State generation or supply of electricity, it is the Central Government that is
involved, and whenever there is intra-State generation or supply of electricity, the
State Government or the State Commission is involved. This is the precise scheme
of the entire Act, including Sections 79 and 86. It will be seen that Section 79(1)
itself in clauses (c), (d) and (e) speaks of inter-State transmission and inter-State
operations. This is to be contrasted with Section 86 which deals with functions of
the State Commission which uses the expression “within the State” in clauses (a),
(b) and (d), and “intra-State” in clause (c). This being the case, it is clear that the
PPA, which deals with generation and supply of electricity, will either have to be
governed by the State Commission or the Central Commission. The State
Commission's jurisdiction is only where generation and supply takes place within
the State. On the other hand, the moment generation and sale takes place in more
than one State, the Central Commission becomes the appropriate Commission
under the Act. What is important to remember is that if we were to accept the
argument on behalf of the appellant, and we were to hold in the Adani case that
there is no composite scheme for generation and sale, as argued by the appellant,
it would be clear that neither Commission would have jurisdiction, something
which would lead to absurdity. Since generation and sale of electricity is in more
than one State obviously Section 86 does not get attracted. This being the case,
we are constrained to observe that the expression “composite scheme” does not
mean anything more than a scheme for generation and sale of electricity in more
than one State. ……………………….
26. Even otherwise, the expression used in Section 79(1)(b) is that generating
companies must enter into or otherwise have a “composite scheme”. This makes it
clear that the expression “composite scheme” does not have some special meaning
— it is enough that generating companies have, in any manner, a scheme for
generation and sale of electricity which must be in more than one State.”
….
27. On the other hand, the jurisdiction of the State Commission under Section 86(1)(b)
of the Act refers only to initial stage where approval is to be granted or not to be granted
to the Power Purchase Agreement providing for purchase of power at the price and other
terms and conditions specified therein. This provision does not empower the State
Commission to regulate implementation of Power Purchase Agreement for all times to
come in future also and to adjudicate upon the disputes arising between the parties
therein. Holding otherwise would tantamount to permit the State Commissions to make
inroads with the functioning of the Central Commission which would militate against
the very scheme of Act, as discussed hereinabove.”
18. From the above, we find that Section 79(1)(a) has a wider scope and is not merely confined to the
Order in Petition No. 417/MP/2024 Page 13 of 33

determination of tariff. It would also involve the adjudication of disputes arising from the
implementation, application or interpretation of the provisions of the PPA and the terms and
conditions of supply in cases involving Central Government-owned generating companies.
19. In the instant petition, we note that the Petitioner is a generating company wholly owned and
controlled by the central government. The dispute is regarding seeking compensation due to
increase in costs on account of Change in Law events, viz. basic customs duty vide the Finance
Act, 2022 dated 30.03.2022 issued by Government of India read with MNRE OM No. 283/3/2018-
GRID SOLAR dated 09.03.2021 and Notification No. 8/2021- GST issued by the Ministry of
Finance, Government of India amounts to Change in Law events under Article 12 of the PPA dated
24.08.2023. It is pertinent to mention that Article 12 of the PPA dated 24.08.2023 stipulates that,
in the event of a change in law that has an adverse effect on the project, the Petitioner is required
to approach the Appropriate Commission for appropriate relief. This involves implementation,
application and interpretation of the PPA and is clearly covered under the ambit of this
Commission under section 79(1) of the Electricity Act.

21. KSEBL has argued that, as per the PPA dated 24.08.2023, it has been agreed upon by the
contracting parties that the rate change due to a change in law shall be as per Article 12 of the
Change in Law of the PPA to be decided by the Appropriate Commission, which means the
KSERC.
22. We note that it is a well-settled principle of law that the parties, by their agreement, can neither
confer jurisdiction upon a forum that does not have the jurisdiction under the law nor can the
parties, by their agreement, oust the jurisdiction of the forum vested under the law.
23. In this context, we observe that the Hon’ble Supreme Court judgement in the matter of A.B.C
Laminart Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs. A.P. Agencies, (1989) 2 SCC 163 has held as under:
“….where the parties to a contract agreed to submit the disputes arising from it to a
particular jurisdiction which would otherwise also be a proper jurisdiction under the law
their agreement to the extent they agreed not to submit to other jurisdictions cannot be
said to be void as against public policy. If on the other hand the jurisdiction they agreed
to submit to would not otherwise be proper jurisdiction to decide disputes arising out of
the contract it must be declared void being against public policy.”
24. We also observe that the Hon’ble Supreme Court judgement in the matter of New Moga Transport
Co. vs. United India Insurance Co. Ltd. & Ors. (2004) 4 SCC 677 has held as under:
Order in Petition No. 417/MP/2024 Page 15 of 33

“By a long series of decisions it has been held that where two Courts or more have under
the CPC jurisdiction to try a suit or proceeding an agreement between the parties that the
dispute between them shall be tried in any one of such Courts is not contrary to public
policy and in no way contravenes Section 28 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. Therefore,
if on the facts of a given case more than one Court has jurisdiction, parties by their consent
may limit the jurisdiction to one of the two Courts. But by an agreement parties cannot
confer jurisdiction to a Court which otherwise does not have jurisdiction to deal with a
matter.”
25. In the light of the above position of law, we are of the view that merely because the PPA mentions
adjudication of the dispute in a specific manner, it cannot oust the jurisdiction of this Commission,
which flows from the provisions of the Act. Hence, we hold that adjudication involving the parties
will be governed by this Commission under Section 79 (1)(f), read with Section 79(1)(a) of the
Act. However, we would like to observe that the Petitioner should have exercised prudence before
executing the PPA with KSEBL. The Petitioner was well aware about the applicability of Section
79(1)(a) of the Electricity Act, 2003 which confers jurisdiction upon CERC to regulate the
generating companies owned/controlled by the Central Government and should have raised this
issue of jurisdiction at the RfS stage itself and more so at the time of signing the PPA, which it did
not do so, leading to avoidable confusion about the jurisdiction. We expect the Petitioner to be
more responsible in the future and to make its position clear at the outset when it participates in
such state-specific bids. Accordingly, we hold that the matter is covered within the jurisdiction of
the Central Commission as per Section 79(1)(a) read with Section 79(1)(f) of the Electricity Act,
2003.

Re. Issue No. I:
Whether the imposition of an increased rate of basic customs duty vide the Finance Act, 2022,
dated 30.03.2022, issued by the Government of India, read with MNRE OM No. 283/3/2018-
GRID SOLAR dated 09.03.2021 and Notification No. 8/2021- GST issued by the Ministry of
Finance, Government of India amounts to Change in Law events under Article 12 of the Power
Purchase Agreement dated 24.08.2023? AND whether the Petitioner is entitled to compensation
in terms of Article 12 of the Power Purchase Agreement dated 24.08.2023, towards additional
expenditure on account of the Change in Law events?
32. NTPC has submitted that on account of a change in position in light of the 2022 BCD Notification
and 2021 GST Notification, NTPC has incurred additional expenditure of Rs 117,48,23,761/-.
Per contra, KSEBL has submitted that the impugned events do not constitute CIL events. Also,
NTPC has to prove that (i) the said costs incurred were prudent costs and (ii) that NTPC took

every step to mitigate the additional expenditure incurred. Further, the LoA was issued by the
KSEBL to NTPC on 06.01.2021. The 2022 BCD Notification was issued on 09.03.2021(w.e.f.
01.04.2022), i.e., more than 15 months after the issuance of the LoA to NTPC. In other words,
NTPC had more than 15 months to import the solar modules without incurring any BCD. NTPC
has voluntarily chosen to import solar modules after 01.04.2022, i.e., the date on which the
imposition of BCD came into force. Similarly, the 2021 GST Notification came into effect on
01.10.2021, and NTPC had nearly 9 months to avoid the imposition of GST, however, it failed
to do so as its own voluntary commercial decision. In such facts and circumstances, NTPC itself
took the voluntary commercial decision to wait for many months before importing the solar
modules – the provision of Article 12, i.e., “Change in Law” (which envisages an involuntary
financial burden on account of a new/modified law, etc.) would not have any applicability. The
claims and contentions of NTPC that it ought to be granted relief as “Change in Law” by taking
into consideration the 2022 BCD Notification dated 30.03.2022 and 2021 GST notification dated
30.09.2021 – would not be sustainable and would deserve to be rejected on this ground as well.
33. We observe that the Petitioner submitted the bid on 20.10.2020. Whereas the MNRE issued the
BCD O.M. on 09.03.2021, the Ministry of Finance, GOI issued the 2022 BCD Notification on
30.03.2022, and the 2021 GST notification was issued on 30.09.2021. We are of the view that
since the bid was submitted prior to the imposition of the notifications mentioned above, there
was no way the Petitioner could have anticipated the levy of future taxes/duties and incorporated
them into the bid. Also, as per the PPA dated 24.08.2023, the SCoD was 24.02.2025 (viz. 18
months from the date of execution of the PPA dated 24.08.2023). NTPC commissioned its project
on 31.05.2024. We have seen in the past that the developers claiming Change in Law
compensation have argued that to optimise costs, they generally procure/import solar panels
closer to the actual CoD, and the Commission has also allowed Change in Law compensation
based on the taxes prevalent as on or closer to the actual CoD. We also observe that NTPC has
achieved early commissioning; as such, the argument of KSEBL that the Petitioner has not taken
due care to import the equipment prior to the date of effect of the GST and BCD notifications
does not sustain.

entitled to approach the Commission which shall “provide relief” in relation to the
impact of the change in law event if it has resulted in “any additional recurring /non-

Duty on Imports, as the case may be) would come from the date of enforcement of the
new laws, the relief intended to be afforded under the contracts cannot be complete
unless the said burden is allowed to be given a pass through from the date of imposition
of the levy. Unlike the PPA in UHBVNL (supra) wherein the phraseology of change-in-
law provision was exhaustive, the words “provide relief” in present PPAs are open
ended, not qualified in any manner so as to be given a restrictive meaning in order to
treat the date of adjudication of the claim by the regulatory authority as the effective
date or to justify denial of carrying cost burden for the period anterior thereto. In our

reading, the expression “provide relief” is of widest amplitude and cannot be read to
limit its scope the way the contesting respondents seek to propagate or the way the

Appeal no. 275 of 2022 (Parampujya Solar Energy Pvt. Ltd. &Anr. v. CERC &Ors.) -
deserve to be allowed. We order accordingly directing the Central Electricity Regulatory
Commission to take up the claim cases of the Solar Power Projects Developers herein
for further proceedings and for passing necessary orders consequent to the findings
recorded by us in the preceding parts of this judgment, allowing Change in Law (CIL)
compensation (on account of GST laws and Safeguard Duty on Imports, as the case may
be) from the date(s) of enforcement of the new taxes for the entire period of its impact,
including the period post Commercial Operation Date of the projects in question, as
indeed towards Operation & Maintenance (O&M) expenses, along with carrying cost
subject, however, to necessary prudence check.”
52. In view of the above, even in the absence of a specific restitution clause in the PPA, this
Commission holds that NTPC, in the instant petition, shall be eligible for carrying costs starting
from the date when the actual payments were made to the authorities until the date of issuance of
this Order, at the actual rate of interest paid by NTPC for arranging funds (supported by Auditor’s
Certificate) or the rate of interest on working capital as per the applicable RE Tariff Regulations
prevailing at that time or the late payment surcharge rate as per the PPA, whichever is the lowest.
Once a supplementary bill is raised by NTPC in terms of this order, the provision of Late Payment
Surcharge in the PPA would kick in if the payment is not made by KSEBL on or before the due
date.
53. Accordingly, the Commission hereby directs the contracting parties to carry out the reconciliation
of additional expenditure along with carrying cost by exhibiting a clear and one-to-one correlation
with the projects and the invoices raised, supported with an auditor certificate. The Commission
further directs that the KSEBL is liable to pay NTPC all the above-reconciled claims.
54. The Hon’ble Supreme Court, in its Order dated 12.12.2022, in Civil Appeal no. 8880/2022 in the
case of “Telangana Northern Power Distribution Co. Limited & Anr. Vs. Parampujya Solar
Energy Pvt. Limited & Ors.” (and in similar Orders dated 03.01.2023 and 23.01.2023) has held as
under:
Order in Petition No. 417/MP/2024 Page 31 of 33

“Pending further orders, the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC) shall
comply with the directions issued in paragraph 109 of the impugned order dated 15
September 2022 of the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity. However, the final order of the
CERC shall not be enforced pending further orders.”
55. Therefore, in view of the Hon’ble Supreme Court Order dated 12.12.2022, as quoted above, the
directions issued in this Order so far as they relate to compensation for the period post Commercial
Operation Date of the projects in question as also towards carrying cost (pre-COD & post-COD)
shall not be enforced and shall be subject to further orders of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in Civil
Appeal No. 8880/2022 in Telangana Northern Power Distribution Company Limited & Anr. V.
Parampujya Solar Energy Pvt. Limited & Ors, and connected matters.
56. The issue is decided accordingly.
57. The summary of our findings is as follows:
a) The 2022 BCD Notification, increase in social welfare surcharge on the import of
machinery and auxiliary equipment, and increase in the quantum of IGST levied in
addition to the basic customs duty on the import of machinery and auxiliary equipment are
events of Change in Law as per Article 12 of the PPA dated 24.08.2023. The 2021 GST
Notification is also a Change in Law event in terms of Article 12 of the PPA dated
24.08.2023.
b) NTPC is entitled to compensation on account of a Change in Law as per the terms of
Article 12 of the PPA dated 24.08.2023, due to the 2022 BCD Notification, increase in
social welfare surcharge on the import of machinery and auxiliary equipment, increase in
the quantum of IGST levied in addition to the basic customs duty on the import of
machinery and auxiliary equipment and 2021 GST Notification. The contracting parties to
carry out reconciliation on account of additional expenditure as per Article 12 of the PPA
dated 24.08.2023 by exhibiting clear and one to one correlation with the projects and the
invoices raised supported with auditor certificate on account of 2022 BCD Notification,
increase in social welfare surcharge on the import of machinery and auxiliary equipment,
increase in the quantum of IGST levied in addition to the basic customs duty on the import
of machinery and auxiliary equipment and 2021 GST Notification.
c) Compensation is to be paid at the discount rate of 10.65% and an annuity period of 15
years. The liability of KSEBL for ‘Monthly Annuity Payment’ starts from the 60th
(sixtieth) day from the date of this order or from the date of submission of claims by NTPC,
Order in Petition No. 417/MP/2024 Page 32 of 33

whichever is later. The provision of a late payment surcharge in the respective PPA/PSA
shall kick in if the monthly annuity payment is not made by the Respondents within the
due date.
d) NTPC shall also be eligible for carrying cost starting from the date when the actual
payments were made to the Authorities till the date of issuance of this Order, at the actual
rate of interest paid by NTPC for arranging funds (supported by Auditor’s Certificate) or
the rate of interest on working capital as per applicable RE Tariff Regulations prevailing
at that time or the late payment surcharge rate as per the PPA, whichever is the lowest.
Once a supplementary bill is raised by NTPC in terms of this order, the provision of a Late
Payment Surcharge in the PPA would kick in if the payment is not made by the
Respondents within the due date.
e) The directions issued in this Order so far as they relate to compensation for the period post
Commercial Operation Date of the projects in question as also towards carrying cost (pre-
COD & post-COD) shall not be enforced and shall be subject to further orders of the
Hon’ble Supreme Court in Civil Appeal No. 8880/2022 in Telangana Northern Power
Distribution Company Limited & Anr. V. Parampujya Solar Energy Pvt. Limited & Ors.,
and connected matters.
58. The Petition no. 417/MP/2024 is disposed of in terms of the above.

CENTRAL ELECTRICITY REGULATORY COMMISSION

Regulation 32 of Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Grant Of Connectivity, Long

Regulations, 2009 along with Regulation 24 and 111 of the Central Electricity Regulatory

Parties Present:
Shri Basava Prabhu Patil, Sr. Advocate, SESPL
Shri Sumant Nayak, Advocate, SESPL
Shri Tushar Srivastava, Advocate, SESPL
Shri Rohit Subramaniam, Advocate, SESPL

ORDER
The present petition has been filed by Srijan Energy Systems Private Limited
(hereinafter to be referred as the “Petitioner”/ “SESPL”) under Section 79(1)(c) and
Section 79(1)(f) of the Electricity Act, 2003 read with Regulation 32 of the Central
Electricity Regulatory Commission (Grant of Connectivity, Long Term And Medium Term
Open Access In Inter State Transmission And Related Matters) Regulations, 2009
(“Connectivity Regulations, 2009”) along with Regulation 24 and 111 of the Central
Electricity Regulatory Commission (Conduct of Business) Regulations, 1999 (“CoB
Regulations”) challenging inter alia the levy of relinquishment charges by Central
Transmission Utility Limited (CTUIL) vide its letter dated 24.12.2021 (“Impugned Letter”)
as being patently illegal and being issued without any basis in law and in complete
contravention, as well as violation of the principles laid down by this Commission in the
case tiled as Power Grid Corporation of India Limited v. Kerala State Electricity Board
and Ors. bearing Petition No. 92/MP/2015. The Petitioner has made the following
prayers:
Main Prayers:
(a) Hold and declare that the Petitioner is not liable to pay any relinquishment charges towards
surrender of Original LTA, as the said LTA was relinquished and re-applied for the same
quantum on account of change in the target region and relinquishment charges are not to
be paid for a change in target region in terms of the principles laid down by this Hon’ble
Commission in Petition No. 92/MP/2015.
(b) Hold and declare that the Petitioner is not liable to pay any interim relinquishment charges
for the period starting from the relinquishment of Original LTA and the date of grant of
Revised LTA or any relinquishment charges due to non-availability of stranded capacity in
the transmission system on which the Original LTA was granted;
Order in Petition No. 372/MP/2022 along with 71/IA/2024 Page 2

(c) Hold and declare that as a consequence of termination of the Power Purchase Agreement
dated 25.03.2019 executed with NTPC, LTA Agreement for 50 MW dated 24.12.2019 was
rendered impossible to be performed by the Petitioner;
(d) Hold and declare that the Petitioner is not liable to pay any transmission charges for LTA
quantum of 35 MW, as the 50 MW LTA stood frustrated due to termination of PPA with
NTPC and 125 MW was realigned to be utilized by the sister concern of the Petitioner viz.
CTN and further, that there is no stranded capacity for the said LTA’s;
(e) Issue appropriate order(s) / direction(s) to set aside / quash the letter and the computation
for Determination of Stranded Capacity and Relinquishment Charges issued by the
Respondent No. 1/ CTU on 24.12.2021, respectively, inter alia in accordance with the
directions under order dated 08.03.2019 issued in Petition No. 92/MP/2015.
(f) Issue appropriate direction(s) / order (s) to the Respondents to return / release forthwith the
Performance Bank Guarantees No: 0393BGFD002420 for Rs 15 crores respectively issued
in its favour by the Petitioner;
Interim Prayers:
(a) Issue ex-parte ad interim orders/ directions to the Respondents not to act in any prejudicial
manner to the rights and interest of the Petitioner, including, but not limited to:
i. Encashment of the CBG issued by the Petitioner in favour of the Respondent No. 2 (in its
erstwhile capacity of CTU);
ii. Abstain itself from taking coercive and/ or precipitative actions pursuant to letters dated
03.09.2021 and 24.12.2021 herein till final disposal of the petition; and/or
(b) Pass any such further / other orders that this Hon’ble Commission may deem fit in the
interest of equity and justice.
2. The Petitioner has also filed an IA bearing No. 71/IA/2024, seeking a stay on the
invoices dated 12.03.2024, vide which CTUIL has claimed the relinquishment charges
as calculated vide its letter dated 24.12.2021. The Petitioner has made the following
prayers:
(a) Grant an ad-interim stay on the Impugned Bills dated 12.03.2024 bearing Bill of Supply No.
MI0636120162 and Billy of Supply No. MI0636120173 imposing relinquishment charges on
the Petitioner for a sum of INR 39,74,00,000 (Thirty-Nine Crores Seventy-Four Lacs Only)
and a sum of INR 2,88,00,000 (Two Crores Eighty-Eight Lacs Only), respectively;
(b) Direct the Respondents to not issue any other bills to the Petitioner towards stranded
capacity and relinquishment charges concerning the 300 MW AND 35 MW LTA relinquished
by the Petitioner;
(c) Direct the Respondent to delete the Impugned Bills from the PRAAPTI e-portal.
(d) Pass any such further/ other Orders as this Hon’ble Commission may deem fit in the interest
of equity and justice.
3. The Commission during the hearing dated 05.09.2024, after considering the
submissions of the Petitioner, directed the CTUIL shall not proceed to any take any
coercive/precipitative action against the Petitioner in connection to the said invoices,
Order in Petition No. 372/MP/2022 along with 71/IA/2024 Page 3

provided the Petitioner deposit 25% of the amount within two weeks and such payment
by the Petitioner shall be subject to the order of the Commission in the matter.
Submission by the Petitioner:
4. The Petitioner has mainly submitted as follows:
(a) The Petitioner is a generating company and is setting up a wind power project with a
proposed capacity of 600 MW at Kutch, Gujarat. The Petitioner had, for the purposes of
connectivity of its Project, divided the said Project into two phases, being Phase 1 and
Phase 2, each of 300 MW.
(b) The Petitioner has executed a PPA with SECI in the name of its subsidiary, being
Continuum Power Trading (TN) Pvt Ltd. (“CTN”), for 250 MW.
(c) The Petitioner also participated in the NTPC auction and secured an additional 50MW
on 19.10.2018 and executed a PPA dated 25.03.2019 in the name of its subsidiary Kutch
Windfarm Development Pvt. Ltd.
(d) In relation to Phase 1 of the Project, the Petitioner had applied for a grant of
connectivity and the same was granted connectivity by the CTUIL on 29.07.2016 at the
existing Bhuj pooling station in terms of the Connectivity Regulations 2009. A
connectivity performance bank guarantee of Rs 15 crores was also deposited by the
Petitioner with the CTU on 10.10.2017 (“CBG”). Further, the Petitioner was also
allocated two bays, being Bay Nos. 219 and 222 for its project, and signed the Bay
Implementation Agreement with CTUIL on 19.05.2017 for the two allotted bays, and paid
the corresponding fee of Rs 1.38 Crore as early as 14.06.2017.
(e) The Petitioner vide its application dated 27.04.2016 had applied for the grant of the
LTA for the transfer of power from the 300 MW Project to the target Western Region
(“WR”), Northern Region (“NR”) and Southern Region (“SR”), and accordingly, an LTA
Agreement dated 11.07.2017 was executed between the parties.
(f) On the 11.07.2017, the CTUIL, in response to a request from the Petitioner for revision
of the start date, granted the extension of the start date of LTA to 31.03.2019 or the
availability of the transmission system, whichever was later, instead of 31.03.2018.
Order in Petition No. 372/MP/2022 along with 71/IA/2024 Page 4

(g) The details pertaining to the Original LTA are as under:
