(h) After the Original LTA was granted to the Petitioner, this Commission modified the
detailed procedure for the grant of connectivity to renewable energy systems and issued
a Detailed Procedure in May 2018. The revised Detailed Procedure required either a
Letter of Award issued under a competitive bid or possession of at least 50% of the land
required for the project for the grant of Stage II connectivity. In view of the earlier grant
of connectivity to the Petitioner and execution of the Bay Implementation Agreement
executed by the Petitioner, the Petitioner was recognised as a deemed stage II grantee
and was required to provide the details of the Letter of Award for a PPA or possession
of land for actual grant of Stage II connectivity.
(i) The Petitioner won a bid for a 250 MW wind project under tranche IV of wind competitive
bids invited by SECI and submitted the Letter of Award to CTUIL for the grant of Stage
II Connectivity. Under this PPA, the distribution utility/beneficiaries to which the
electricity was to be supplied was at the discretion of SECI and, therefore, the earlier
Order in Petition No. 372/MP/2022 along with 71/IA/2024 Page 5

regions notified by the Petitioner in the Original LTA were no longer valid and within the
control of the Petitioner.
(j) After the operationalisation of the Original LTA, the Petitioner had issued a letter dated
26.08.2019 whereby the Petitioner relinquished the Original LTA, inter alia, to align the
beneficiary firm up and the resultant change in the target region. Pursuant to the
relinquishment of the Original LTA, the Petitioner was again granted LTA for a capacity
of 300 MW.
(k) Thereafter, the 125 MW LTA was revoked by the CTUIL vide its letter dated 05.08.2020
due to non-fulfilment of regulatory requirements. The 50 MW LTA (NR for supply of
power to UPPCL under NTPC PPA) was relinquished by the Petitioner vide its letter
dated 22.05.2020. For 125 MW LTA (WR for supply of power to MPPMCL under SECI
PPA), the Petitioner relinquished the same vide its letter dated 30.03.2021, and the
relinquishment of the said LTA was accepted w.e.f. 30.03.2021 by the CTU vide its letter
dated 11.05.2021.
(l) Post relinquishment of 125 MW LTA and 50 MW LTA, the sister concern of the
Petitioner, CTN, re-applied for a fresh LTA for a quantum of 140 MW. The said LTA was
granted to CTN on the same transmission corridor as shared by the 125 MW LTA and
the 50 MW LTA.
(m) Subsequently, CTUIL had issued the impugned Letter along with the computation
sheet for the determination of stranded capacity and relinquishment charges and has
sought to impose a relinquishment charge amounting to Rs. 39.74 Crore for Original
LTA and Rs. 2.88 Crore for 35 MW LTA. The CTU allegedly computed the
relinquishment charges in accordance with the directions under Petition No.
92/MP/2015. CTUIL in the aforesaid computation sheet has determined the
relinquishment charges by taking the following into consideration:
(i) For the Original LTA: The notice period date and relinquishment date are
considered as 29.08.2019, and Bhuj-Banaskantha-Chittorgarh 765kV D/c corridor,
2X500MVA 400/220kV ICTs at Bhuj, Banaskantha-Sankhari 400kV D/c line and
Chittorgarh-Chittorgarh (RVPN) D/c line have been considered for determining the
stranded capacity. The YTC of FY 2019-20 is based on the approved tariff for FY
Order in Petition No. 372/MP/2022 along with 71/IA/2024 Page 6

2018-19, corresponding to the above system, which has been considered for the
calculation of relinquishment charges.
(ii) For the Revised LTA: The CTU relied on paragraph 161 (g) of the Order dated
8.3.2015 in Petition No. 92/MP/2015 and has sought to impose relinquishment
charges for 35 MW LTA after taking into consideration that the 140 MW LTA was
granted to CTN on the same corridor as that of the Revised LTA. Thus, the
relinquishment of the Petitioner for the remaining 175 MW LTA was to the tune of
35MW [i.e., 175 MW – 140 MW].
However, the calculation of the stranded capacity charges as 66% of the NPV for a
period falling short of 12 years, as well as notice period charges, i.e., 66% of NPV for
the period falling short of one year, has been calculated by the CTU wrongfully, and
in contravention of the principles laid down by this Commission in Petition no.
92/MP/2015.
(n) Thus, in view of the erroneous imposition of relinquishment charges in the letter dated
24.12.2021, the Petitioner issued a letter seeking clarifications from the CTU on
29.03.2022. In response to the aforesaid Letter dated 29.03.2022 issued by the
Petitioner, the CTU had, on 29.04.2022, provided further clarification on the mode of
calculations.
(o) After a review of the Letter dated 24.12.2021 and response letter dated 29.04.2022, it
is submitted that the CTU has failed to adhere to the principles laid down by this
Commission in Petition No. 92/MP/2015, as the CTU completely failed to consider the
following:
Illegal imposition of Relinquishment Charges for the original LTA
(p) After firming up the beneficiary in terms of the SECI PPA and NTPC PPA, the Petitioner
issued a letter dated 08.10.2018 to the CTUIL calling upon it to, inter alia, issue the
revised 300 MW LTA (revised for change in the beneficiaries as determined by SECI
and NTPC, respectively, in their discretion and the revised timelines as per the PPAs to
the Petitioner.
(q) However, the CTUIL vide its response dated 14.11.2018 rejected the request of the
Petitioner seeking the grant of a revised LTA on account of a change of target region.
CTUIL issued a response dated 17.01.2019, once again denying the grant of a revised
Order in Petition No. 372/MP/2022 along with 71/IA/2024 Page 7

LTA and stating that the earlier LTA granted to the Petitioner shall be made effective
from 31.03.2019.
(r) In view of the order passed by this Commission in petition No. 07/MP/2019, the
Petitioner proceeded to apply for the Revised LTA based on the firmed-up regions. It is
imperative to note that the entire quantum of Original LTA was reallocated to the target
region under the SECI PPA and NTPC PPA, thereby causing no loss in capacity
utilisation of CTU infrastructure.
(s) Thereafter, on 29.11.2019, the Respondent No. 2 issued three letters granting LTAs for
the supply of 125 MW power from the Project to MPPMCL, WR, 125 MW power from
the Project to WR and 50 MW power from the Project to UPPCL, NR.
(t) On 24.12.2019, the Petitioner entered into three LTA Agreements with the Respondent
No. 2 for the supply of power from the Project of a quantum of 125 MW to MPPTCL,
Madhya Pradesh (WR), 125 MW to WR and 50 MW to UPPCL.
(u) This Commission, in its Order passed in Petition No. 92/MP/2015, categorically
observed at paragraph 143 that no relinquishment charges shall be imposed on the LTA
grantee for a change in the target region. However, the only exception carved out by
this Commission to the said principle is the applicability of transmission charges for
stranded capacity for the interim period starting from the effective date of LTA as per the
fresh application for the new region and the date of relinquishment in the previous region
and only for the capacity for which LTA to the changed region has not been effective.
(v) However, it is noted that the effective date of LTA as per the fresh application for new
beneficiary basis change in the target region and the date of relinquishment of the
Original LTA, i.e. from 29.08.2019 to 30.09.2019. In view of the above, in terms of the
Order passed by this Commission in Petition No. 92/MP/2015, relinquishment charges
by the CTU can at best be only imposed upon the Petitioner for the said interim period,
if there is any stranded capacity in that period. It is also worthwhile to note that the
transmission charges from 14.04.2019 to 26.08.2019 for the Original LTA of Rs.
1,21,07,582/- have already been paid by the Petitioner.
(w) CTU acted in an arbitrary and illegal manner by computing the relinquishment charges
towards surrender of Original LTA, as 66% of the NPV of the transmission asset for the
Order in Petition No. 372/MP/2022 along with 71/IA/2024 Page 8

period of 12 years, as contemplated in Paragraph 139 of the Order passed in
92/MP/2015.
The Petitioner is not liable to bear any relinquishment charges or the Interim
Charges towards the Original LTA
(x) CTN had applied for and was granted an LTA quantum of 140 MW.
(y) Reference be made to the 55th Meeting of the WR Constituents regarding Connectivity/
LTA Applications convened on 21.01.2021. It is noteworthy that as on 21.01.2021, 1712
MW capacity of Bhuj PS already stood operationalised. The said quantum of 1712 MW
already operationalised, did not include the 125 MW LTA granted to the Petitioner.
Further, after the utilisation of 1712 MW capacity of the Bhuj PS, the remaining LTAs
were suggested to be operationalised on the margins of 488 MW available at the Bhuj
PS while ignoring the requirement of N-1 contingency. Therefore, 125 MW LTA of the
Petitioner, the said LTA was intended to be operationalised on the margins available at
Bhuj PS. Therefore, as the LTA was to be operationalised on the margins, it is evident
that the CTU was already positioned to recover the entire capital cost towards the
establishment of Bhuj PS from other long-term transmission consumers (LTTCs) and
any subsequent operationalisation of LTA was completely premised on the margins
available at the Bhuj PS. Hence, the question of stranded capacity at Bhuj PS does not
arise in the present case. Accordingly, the imposition of relinquishment charges on the
Petitioner towards Original LTA, as well as for the interim period in terms of Petition No.
92/MP/2015, is completely illegal and is only an attempt on the part of the CTU to gain
an undue benefit.
(z) Petitioner has referred to the 56th Meeting of the Western Region Constituents on
26.02.2021 and the 57th Meeting of Western Region Constituents on 31.03.2021, where
the issue pertaining to the grant of 90 MW LTA to CTN was deliberated upon. It can be
established that, due to the lack of system capacity at Bhuj PS, the fresh two LTAs of
125 MW each and one LTA of 50 MW granted to Petitioner on a different transmission
system from that of the Original LTA were only due to the non-availability of system
capacity. However, the Respondent, by adopting a contradictory stand in its letter dated
29.04.2022, is trying to create a new principle from that evolved by this Commission in
Petition No. 92/MP/2015.
Order in Petition No. 372/MP/2022 along with 71/IA/2024 Page 9

(aa) Further, in the 58th meeting of Western Region Constituents on 28.04.2021, the
request for surrendering 125 MW LTA and 50 MW LTA granted to the Petitioner was
considered and allowed. It is also important to mention herein that the margin available
at Bhuj PS, as indicated in the said meeting, was only 210.7 MW. Therefore, it is
necessary to point out that the margin availability at the Bhuj PS already stood
exhausted. Therefore, the question of imposing relinquishment charges or interim
transmission charges for a change in the target region upon the Petitioner due to the
availability of stranded capacity does not arise in the present case.
(bb) On 09.08.2021, a meeting was convened between CEA, CTU, POSOCO, SECI and
various LTA Grantees at Bhuj PS regarding the operationalisation of 40 MW LTA (out
of the 90 MW LTA mentioned above) granted to CTN based on available margins at
Bhuj PS. In this regard, CTU categorically informed the following:
(i) Currently, 2410 MW LTA is operational at Bhuj PS, out of which about 1825 MW
capacity has been commissioned, and an additional 585MW capacity is expected by
Dec'21.
(ii) About 600MW capacity is also envisaged to come up at Radhanesda Solar Park
(700MW) by Oct'21, which is also expected to get operationalised shortly (System is
ready).
(iii) System studies indicate that a total of 2410 MW capacity can only be evacuated
from Bhuj PS (considering 75% wind dispatch at Bhuj PS as well as 100% dispatch
from Radhanesda Solar Park).
(iv) The limiting constraint is observed to be the Banaskantha -Sankhari 400kV D/C line
(~1100MW under N-1).
(v) To further enhance evacuation capacity from Bhuj complex, either the LILO of Zerda
- Ranchhodpura 400kV line at Banaskantha (WRSS-XIX: Sterlite- anticipated by
Jul'22) or Lakadia -Vadodara 765kV D/C line (WRSS-21 Part B by Sterlite- anticipated
by Dec'21) shall be required.
(vi) No further margins were available for transfer of power under Long Term Access
from Bhuj PS, and the applicants, including CTN, were asked to explore transfer of
power under short term open access, depending upon available margins in the
system.
Order in Petition No. 372/MP/2022 along with 71/IA/2024 Page 10

dated 15.11.2023, the Hon’ble CESTAT allowed the Appeal filed by Respondent No.1
and held that any invoices for relinquishment charges raised by the then unified
POWERGRID were beyond the scope of Section 66E (e) of the Finance Act, 1994,
and as such, neither any service tax nor any GST could be charged on it. It followed
that Respondent No.1 could now raise invoices in terms of the Order dated 8.3.2019
without any deposit of GST upfront and as such could fulfil its statutory duty. It was
only after the above Order dated 15.11.2023 passed by the Hon’ble CESTAT that
Respondent No.1-CTUIL was able to raise the invoices towards relinquishment
charges, including on the present Petitioner.
“Net relinquishment” of the Petitioner’s LTA:
(f) As per the directions laid down in para 161(g) of the Order dated 8.3.2019 passed in
Petition No.92/MP/2015, which stated that “….In case there are applicant for LTA for
the same corridor as being relinquished, the relinquishment charges shall be
calculated for the number of years (period) till the effective date of LTA of incoming
customer”, the above 140 MW LTA granted to the sister concern of the Petitioner was
Order in Petition No. 372/MP/2022 along with 71/IA/2024 Page 23

not considered for computation of relinquishment charges. Therefore, the remaining
capacity of 35 MW was considered as the “net relinquishment” for the purpose of
computation of the relinquishment charges payable by the Petitioner.
(g) Term “net relinquishment” refers to the quantum of relinquished LTA, after taking into
account certain adjustments such as overlapping LTAs, grants made on the same
transmission corridor or the presence of other customers who have been granted LTA
for the same transmission corridor for which relinquishment charges are to be
computed. In the present case, the capacity of 175 MW was not considered for
calculating the relinquishment charges; rather, 35 MW was considered to have been
relinquished after taking into account of the 140 MW LTA granted to M/s Continuum
Power Trading (TN) Pvt. Ltd. (CPTPL) through the same corridor in terms of the Order
dated 8.3.2019 passed in Petition No.92/MP/2015.
Analysis and Decision
14. We have considered the submission of the Petitioner and the Respondents.
15. The present petition has been filed by the Petitioner challenging the calculation of
relinquishment charges by Central Transmission Utility Limited vide its letter dated
24.12.2021. Petitioner has submitted that it was granted LTA vide CTUIL intimation
dated 31.03.2017 for 300 MW (divided into three regions viz. 90 MW-Western Region,
150 MW- Norther Region and 60 MW-Southern Region) (Original LTA) with a start date
of 31.03.2019. Pursuant to the grant of the Original LTA, the Petitioner firmed up the
beneficiary and finalised the target region. Accordingly, the Petitioner, keeping in view
the ultimate beneficiary, requested the CTUIL to revise the Original LTA in view of the
changed target region. The Petitioner's request was not accepted by the CTUIL.
Petitioner, not being able to change the target region, was thereafter constrained to
relinquish the original LTA of 300 MW on 29.08.2019.
16. The Petitioner has further submitted that, subsequent to the relinquishment of the
Original LTA, the Petitioner had applied for and was granted another LTA for 300 MW
(Revised LTA) on 29.11.2019. The Revised LTA was for the supply of 125 MW-Western
Region, 125 MW- Southern Region, and 50 MW- Northern Region. Further, the revised
LTA to the quantum of 125 MW (WR) was revoked due to non-fulfilment of regulatory
requirements and the balance 125 MW, and the 50 MW LTA were to be operationalised
by 30.11.2020 and 30.12.2020, respectively. However, even before they were
Order in Petition No. 372/MP/2022 along with 71/IA/2024 Page 24

operationalised, the same were relinquished on 30.03.2021 and 22.05.2020
respectively. The Petitioner’s sister concern CTN then applied for and was granted an
LTA for 140 MW, and accordingly, three LTA agreements were executed between CTN
and the CTU on 07.01.2021 for 50 MW, 19.04.2021 for 40 MW and 30.04.2021 for 50
MW.
17. The Petitioner has also submitted that in the present case, the CTU itself admitted that
at the time of relinquishment of 125 MW LTA, no further margin was available at the
Bhuj PS, and the Banaskantha-Sankhari 400 kV D/C line was undergoing system
constraints as 2410 MW quantum of LTAs were already operationalised by the CTU.
Therefore, from the said fact, it can be established that no margins are available in the
transmission corridor in which the Original LTA was granted to the Petitioner and no
capacity was stranded.
18. The Petitioner has also stated that CTU vide its letter dated 24.12.2021 is claiming
relinquishment charges for the original LTA quantum of 300 MW and the relinquishment
charges for the difference between 175 MW and 140 MW, i.e., 35 MW. Relinquishment
charges in respect of the Original LTA could, if at all and at the most , be applied only
for the period between 29.08.2019 and 30.09.2019 (interim period only). That is also
subject to the condition that there was stranded capacity due to the relinquishment of
the Original LTA. Moreover, the liability for relinquishment charges for the 35 MW LTA
does not arise at all in view of the frustration of the 35 MW LTA due to the frustration
of the PPA executed with NTPC. The Petitioner is also seeking the return of the
Construction Phase Bank Guarantee of Rs. 15 crores submitted in October 2017.
19. CTUIL, in its reply, submitted that as per the order dated 08.03.2019 in Petition
No.92/MP/2015, no compensation is payable by a relinquishing LTA grantee for a
change in target region under two conditions: (i) If the effective start date of LTA in the
new region matches the date of relinquishment in the original region; and (ii) If the
change in region applies to the entire capacity relinquished. 300MW LTA was granted
through Bhuj-Banaskantha-Chittorgarh 765kV D/c corridor along with Bhuj ICTs,
whereas 175MW LTA (125MW and 50MW) was granted through Bhuj PS – Lakadia –
Vadodara 765kV D/c corridor, which were two different corridors with separate LTA
applications. Stranded capacities of the above relinquishments by M/S SESPL have
been determined accordingly: 12 years for a 300 MW quantum and 35 MW net
relinquishment for the LTA applied later.
Order in Petition No. 372/MP/2022 along with 71/IA/2024 Page 25

20. CTUIL has also submitted that the 300 MW LTA granted to the Petitioner was
operationalised w.e.f 14.4.2019, upon commissioning of the Bhuj-Banaskantha-
Chittorgarh corridor as well as 2x500 MVA 400/220 kV ICTs at the Bhuj pooling station.
For the 125 MW+50 MW LTAs (aggregating to 175 MW), at the time of determination,
relinquishment charges were levied for 35 MW since for the remaining 140 MW, LTA
had been granted to M/s Continuum Power Trading (TN) Pvt. Ltd., through the same
Bhuj PS – Lakadia – Vadodara 765kV D/c corridor, as per Paragraph 161 (g) of the
Order dated 8.3.2019 passed in Petition No.92/MP/2015.
21. Considering the submission of Petitioner and Respondent, the following issues
arise for our consideration:
Issue No.1: What shall be the relinquishment charges for the Petitioner? Whether
the CTUIL letter dated 24.12.2021 and the computation for Determination of Stranded
Capacity and Relinquishment Charges issued by the CTUIL are liable to be set aside
in terms of the principles laid down by this Commission in Petition No. 92/MP/2015?
Issue No.2: Whether termination of PPA with NTPC would have any effect on
relinquishment charge?
Issue No 3: Whether margins in the existing system would have an effect on the
relinquishment charge for the Petitioner?
Issue No.4: Whether any direction is to be issued with regard to the return/release
of the Performance Bank Guarantees of Rs. 15 crores furnished by the Petitioner?
22. The above issues are being dealt with in the succeeding paragraphs.
Issue No.1: What shall be the relinquishment charges for the Petitioner? Whether
the CTUIL letter dated 24.12.2021 and the computation for Determination of Stranded
Capacity and Relinquishment Charges issued by the CTUIL are liable to be set aside
in terms of the principles laid down by this Commission in Petition No. 92/MP/2015?
23. The Petitioner was granted the original LTA of 300 MW on a target region basis (90
MW-Western Region, 150 MW- Northern Region and 60 MW-Southern Region) vide
CTUIL intimation dated 31.03.2017. The snapshot of the LTA grant is as under:
Order in Petition No. 372/MP/2022 along with 71/IA/2024 Page 26

“Sub: Relinquishment of LTA for 300 MW
Dear Sir,
This is with reference to the 300 MW LTA granted for the Wind Power Project of M/s Srijan

Hon’ble CERC, in its order dated 6.8.2019 on Petition No 7/MP/2019, has not considered
our prayer to revise the LTA and aligning it with the beneficiaries and the timelines as per
Wind Power project awarded by SECI/NTPC, and has instead directed us to file for a fresh

Under the sequence of circumstances explained above, the implementation of our 250 MW

We are undertaking detailed re-assessment of our project execution plan and shall

Accordingly, we hereby relinquish our LTA as per the details tabulated below. We

3 Quantum of LTA to be relinquished 300 MW
4 Date from which relinquishment is sought 28-Aug-2019
As per above, the Petitioner relinquished its original LTA of 300 MW with effect from

26. Subsequent to the relinquishment of the original LTA of 300 MW, Petitioner applied for

As per the above, the Petitioner relinquished the LTA of 50 MW with effect from

The said relinquishment was accepted by CTUIL vide its letter dated 03.07.2020. The

The above relinquishment in LTA quantum is subject to payment of applicable

As per the above, the CTUIL accepted the relinquishment of 50 MW LTA, subject to

31. The Petitioner also relinquished the balance 125 MW LTA vide its letter dated

In view of the above-mentioned developments, SESPL is not able to utilize the 125MW

We hereby relinquish LTA for 125 MW vide C/CTU/W/07/LTA/1200002251 dated 29-

of the LTA being relinquished are as summarized below-

As per the above, the Petitioner relinquished the 125 LTA w.e.f. 30.03.2021. The
Petitioner also undertook to pay the applicable relinquishment charges. The said
relinquishment was accepted by CTUIL vide its letter dated 11.05.2021. The relevant
extract of the letter dated 11.05.2021 is as under:
“……
Further, the LTA quantum of 125MW granted for application no. 1200002251 vide intimation

32. We note that the CTUIL vide letter dated 24.12.2021 calculated the stranded capacity

given below have been calculated as per the methodology specified in the above order and
the same is enclosed at Annexure-I.
1) Aug’19: 300 MW relinquishment by Srijan Energy Systems Pvt Ltd (SESPL) at Bhuj

• For calculation of relinquishment charges of 300MW relinquishment by SESPL, the notice

at Bhuj, Banaskantha-Sankhari 400kV D/c line and Chittorgarh-Chittorgarh (RVPN) D/c line

As per the above, CTUIL has calculated the following charges for the petitioner:

(aggregating to 175 MW) relinquished, considering that at the time of

determination, 140 MW LTA had been granted to M/s Continuum Power Trading

the order passed by this Commission in Petition No. 92/MP/2015, relinquishment
charges by the CTU can at best be only imposed upon the Petitioner for the said interim

34. Commission vide order dated 08.03.2019 in Petitioner no. 92/MP/2015 regarding the
treatment of cases where Long Term Customers have sought relinquishment with a
change in the Target Region, observed as under:
“….
139. Cases with treatment of notice period under alternative scenarios, namely, (i)LTA
relinquishment prior to date of start of LTA, and (ii)LTA relinquishment after date of start of
LTA are analysed below with illustrative examples.
(a)LTA relinquishment prior to date of start of LTA
Suppose, Customer A's scheduled date of start of LTA was 1.1.2014. However, the
associated transmission system was commissioned on 1.12.2014. So, the effective
date of start of LTA is 1.12.2014. Customer A issues notice to CTU on 1.4.2013
relinquishing its entire LTA without specifying any notice period. Thus, the notice
date is 1.4.2013. However, relinquishment charges shall be calculated only from
1.12.2014, as on the effective date of start of LTA. In such case, since the
transmission charge liability for such customer does not arise till date effective date
of LTA i.e. 1.12.2014, no transmission charges shall be paid for the notice period
falling short of 1 year i.e. for 1.4.2013 to 31.3.2014. Relinquishment charges shall
be calculated from 1.12.2014 as per the specified methodology in this Order.
(b)LTA relinquishment after date of start of LTA
Suppose, Customer A issues relinquishment notice on 1.12.2014, wishing to
relinquish with effect from 1.12.2014 itself. In such case, it shall be liable to pay 66%
of the estimated transmission charges (net present value) for one (1) year. The
estimated transmission charges shall be as per the prevailing mechanism of POC
charges. Further, it shall be liable to pay transmission charges for stranded capacity
for 12 years as per the specific methodology in this Order.
Suppose, Customer A relinquishes LTA as per notice dated 1.12.2014 with
relinquishment effective from 1.12.2015. In this case, it shall pay POC charges for
period from 1.12.2014 to 30.11.2015 since relinquishment starts from 1.12.2015.
Since it has availed transmission facility for 1 year from 1.12.2014 to 30.11.2015,
the relinquishment charges for stranded capacity shall be calculated for 11 years
period starting 1.12.2015 as Notice period and availing of LTA for one year have run
concurrently from 1.12.2014 to 1.12.2015.
……
Treatment of cases where Long Term Customers have sought relinquishment with
change in Target Region
Order in Petition No. 372/MP/2022 along with 71/IA/2024 Page 38

...
142. We observe that in case a long term customer who had sought LTA in a particular
region seeks to shift its LTA to a different region, it relinquishes its LTA in original region
and applies afresh in the changed region. We note that in case of change in Target
Region, the liability of a long term access customer to pay transmission charge
continues. The transmission charges by a long term customer are payable as
calculated under Sharing Regulations. These Regulations calculate point of connection
charges on the basis of usage of ISTS by a DIC and the methodology is based on load flow
studies. In case of long term customers (viz. generators) with LTA to Target Region, point
of connection charges in case LTA is without PPA are calculated at generation end only
and generator is not liable to pay any Target Region charges. Hence, irrespective of the
Target Region, charges on the basis of calculation at generation end shall continue.
The same analogy can be extended for cases of change in Target Region. This implies that
the charges shall remain same even if generator changes its Target Region. This can be
explained through an example below:-
Example 1: Suppose a generator “A” is located in Western region. It has LTA
to Northern Region effective from 1.4.2016. Suppose he relinquishes its LTA to
Northern Region w.e.f. 1.6.2016 and seeks LTA to Southern Region starting from
1.12.2016. For the period starting 1.4.2016, the generator shall pay transmission
charges as per POC methodology at its point of connection till 31.5.2016. From
1.6.2016 to 30.11.2016, it shall pay relinquishment charges in terms of methodology
given in this Order. Starting from 1.12.2016, the generator shall start paying
transmission charges calculated at its point of connection.
Example 2: Suppose generator A relinquishes 1000 MW in NR w.e.f. 1.6.2016 and
seeks only 600 MW in SR w.e.f. 1.12.2016, relinquishment charges for 400 MW
shall be payable w.e.f. 1.6.2016 for the entire period of relinquishment in addition to
relinquishment charges for 600 MW from 1.6.2016 to 30.11.2016 in terms of
methodology given in this Order.”
143. In the light of the above discussion, we are of the view that there shall be no
relinquishment charges for change in Target Region, if the effective date of start of LTA in
the changed region is the same as date of relinquishment in original region and the change
in region is sought for entire capacity relinquished. If there is a gap between effective date
of LTA as per fresh application for new region and relinquishment in previous region,
transmission charges for stranded capacity shall be levied for such interim period and for
such capacity for which LTA to changed region has not been effective.”
As per above, in case of a change in the Target Region, if there is a gap between the
effective date of the start of LTA as per the fresh application for the new region and the
relinquishment date in the previous region, relinquishment charges for the stranded
capacity shall be levied for such an interim period.
35. We observe that the methodology to be followed to calculate the relinquishment
charges on relinquishment sought by the LTA Customer, where relinquished capacity
has been reallocated or is likely to be reallocated to new LTA applicants, has been
elaborated in an order dated 8.3.2019 in Petition No. 92/MP/2015. Relevant extract of
the Order is quoted below:
Order in Petition No. 372/MP/2022 along with 71/IA/2024 Page 39

“Treatment of cases where relinquished capacity has been reallocated or is likely to
be reallocated to new LTA applicants
151. Respondent No. 6 (KSK Mahanadi Power Ltd.) and PEL Power Limited have submitted
that even in cases where LTA is granted with augmentation, there will not be any stranded
capacity, if there are pending LTA applications in queue seeking LTA for the same corridor.
152. We have considered submission of Respondents. We are of the view that in case there
are applicants for grant of LTA against the relinquished capacity in the same corridor, the
relinquishment charges shall be calculated for the period starting with the date of
relinquishment of LTA till the effective date of LTA of new LTA customer depending on its
quantum of LTA.
Summary of Decisions
161. The summary of our decisions is as under:
…..
(g) In case there are applicants for LTA for the same corridor as being relinquished, the
relinquishment charges shall be calculated for the number of years (period) till the effective
date of LTA of incoming customer.”
As per the above, if there is another LTA applicant in the same corridor, the
relinquishment charges are to be calculated considering the incoming customer.

ORDER
The present Petition has been filed by NLC India Limited (NLCIL) for approval
of recovery of “Mineral Bearing Land Tax” levied under the Tamil Nadu Mineral
Bearing Land Tax Act, 2024 and the Tamil Nadu Mineral Bearing Land Tax Rules,
2025 as a “statutory charge” read with Regulation 50 and under Regulation 77 of the
Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff)
Regulations, 2024 (2024 Tariff Regulations).
2. The Petitioner has made the following prayers in the petition:
“(a) To take on record of the details and prayers as submitted by the Petitioner through
this affidavit;
(b) Declare and hold that imposition of Mineral Bearing Land Tax which has resulted in
increase in input price of Lignite and consequent energy charges of the Petitioner as
a change in law;
(c) Permit the Petitioner to bill the Tax paid as “Statutory Charges” in the input price of
lignite and recover the same from its beneficiaries through landed cost of lignite as
energy charge component of tariff of linked Thermal Stations;
(d) To grant the interim relief for recovery of the same through monthly billing till issue
of the final order;
(e) To grant carrying cost if there is any difference between the date of payment of the
tax by the Petitioner and its recovery from the beneficiaries at the rate of interest
applicable as per Tariff regulations 2024-29 for the Tariff difference;
(f) To pass any other order(s) as deems fit.”

Analysis and Decision
9. We have considered the submissions made by the Petitioner and TANGEDCO
and perused the documents available on record. The Government of Tamil Nadu
notified the 2024 Act on 20.2.2025, and it came into effect on 4.4.2025.
Simultaneously, the Government of Tamil Nadu issued the 2025 Rules on 4.4.2025,
which specify the procedures for assessing, collecting, and enforcing the land tax
across the State. As per the Schedule to the 2024 Act, the Petitioner is liable to pay to
the State Government Land Tax of ₹250/- per Metric Ton for the lignite excavated from
the Petitioner’s mines before its despatch. The Petitioner has submitted that the land
tax leviable under the 2024 Act is a Statutory Charge under Regulation 3(77) and it is
a Change in Law event under Regulation 3(12) of the 2024 Tariff Regulations. Lignite
is the Primary Fuel for the pit head thermal generating stations, and the Land Tax
imposed on the lignite extracted is payable by the Petitioner to the Government of
Tamil Nadu. The Petitioner has claimed the Land Tax as part of the Input Price through
Energy Charges of the generating stations and recovery of the same from the
beneficiaries linked to the concerned generating stations. The Petitioner has submitted
that the impact of the Land Tax would be around ₹625 crore per annum, and the
Petitioner has already paid ₹25.81 crore of Land Tax for the period from 4.4.2025 to
30.4.2025. The Petitioner has also sought monthly recovery of the Land Tax as an
interim relief. TANGEDCO has not opposed the recovery of the Land Tax as part of
the Input Price of lignite. TANGEDCO has, however, submitted that it should be
allowed prospectively from the actual date of levy of the Land Tax, and the Petitioner’s
claims should be supported by monthly details of tax actually paid, duly audited
computations, half-yearly and annual statutory returns for verification of the claims
Order in Petition No. 763/MP/2025 Page 9 of 16

made by the Petitioner. TANGEDCO has further submitted that any penalty, interest,
or additional liability arising due to disputes or non-compliance should not be allowed
as a pass through. TANGEDCO has also submitted that the relief should be limited to
the certified expenditure proportionate to the scheduled or actual generation,
whichever is lower. In its rejoinder, the Petitioner has clarified that the Land Tax is paid
by the Petitioner prospectively from 4.4.2025 and penalty, interest, or additional liability
would be passed on to the Respondents. The Petitioner has further clarified that
operational efficiencies are passed on to the beneficiaries and inefficiencies or
ancillary operations are not passed to the beneficiaries, and therefore, TANGEDCO’s
contention that the Land Tax liability should be limited to lignite consumption based on
the lower of actual or scheduled generation does not arise.
10. The Petitioner has claimed that the land tax is a Statutory Charge and it is a
Change in Law event under Regulations 3(77) and 3(12) of the 2024 Tariff
Regulations. The Statutory Charges are defined in Regulation 3(77) of the 2024 Tariff
Regulations, and they are as follows:
“(77) ‘Statutory Charges’ means and includes taxes, cess, duties, royalties and other
charges levied through Acts of the Parliament or State Legislatures or by Indian
Government Instrumentality under relevant statutes;”
11. As per the above definition, Statutory Charges include taxes, duties, royalties
and other charges levied through Acts of Parliament or State Legislatures or by an
Indian Government Instrumentality under a statute. It is a compulsory payment
imposed by law through an Act, rule, or government notification. In the instant case,
the Government of Tamil Nadu has notified the Land Tax on 20.2.2025 and has made
it operational with effect from 4.4.2025, which means the Land Tax is imposed under
a specific statute and the rules notified by the State Government of Tamil Nadu,
making it a mandatory levy applicable to lignite-bearing land and linked to the
extraction/ despatch of lignite. Further, the land tax under the 2024 Act is levied
Order in Petition No. 763/MP/2025 Page 10 of 16

specifically on the quantity of lignite anticipated to be extracted from the Neyveli Mines,
constituting the taxable event, and it is the Petitioner's statutory liability to the
Government of Tamil Nadu. Therefore, the land tax imposed by the State Government
of Tamil Nadu under the 2024 Act is a Statutory Charge as defined under Regulation
3(77) of the 2024 Tariff Regulations.
12. The term “Change in Law” is defined in Regulation 3(12) of the 2024 Tariff
Regulations, and it is as follows:
“(12) 'Change in Law' means the occurrence of any of the following events:
(a) enactment, bringing into effect or promulgation of any new Indian law; or
(b) adoption, amendment, modification, repeal or re-enactment of any existing Indian
law; or
(c) change in interpretation or application of any Indian law by a competent court,
Tribunal or Indian Governmental Instrumentality which is the final authority under law
for such interpretation or application; or
(d) change by any competent statutory authority in any condition or covenant of any
consent or clearances or approval or licence available or obtained for the project; or
(e) coming into force or change in any bilateral or multilateral agreement or treaty
between the Government of India and any other Sovereign Government having
implications for the generating station or the transmission system regulated under
these regulations.”
13. Regulation 3(12) of 2024 Tariff Regulations defines Change in Law to include
the enactment or bringing into effect of any new law by Parliament or State Legislature.
Change in Law refers to any legal or regulatory development that alters the existing
framework applicable to a generating station or transmission system. It covers a wide
spectrum of events, including, the introduction of a new law, amendments,
modifications, repeal, or re-enactment of existing laws, new judicial or governmental
interpretations that are binding, changes in conditions of statutory approvals,
clearances, or licenses, and the coming into effect or modification of international
treaties or agreements entered into by the Government of India which have an impact
on the project. In essence, it is any authoritative change in the legal, regulatory, or
policy environment that materially affects the rights, obligations, or costs associated
with the Project. The 2024 Act, notified vide Gazette Notification dated 20.2.2025 and
Order in Petition No. 763/MP/2025 Page 11 of 16

brought into effect through Gazette Notification dated 4.4.2025, is a new enactment
by the State Legislature. Accordingly, in terms of Regulation 3(12)(a) of the 2024 Tariff
Regulations, the said levy qualifies as a ‘Change in Law’ event and is admissible for
consideration under the applicable regulatory framework.
14. Further, Regulation 77 of the 2024 Tariff Regulations provides for the recovery
of Statutory Charges, and it is as follows:
“77. Recovery of Statutory Charges: The generating company shall recover the
statutory charges imposed by the State and Central Government, such as electricity duty
and water cess, by considering normative parameters specified in these regulations. In
case the electricity duty is applied to the auxiliary energy consumption, such amount of
electricity duty shall apply to the normative auxiliary energy consumption of the
generating station (excluding colony consumption) and apportioned to each of the
beneficiaries in proportion to their scheduled dispatch during the month.”
15. The above regulation clearly specifies that any statutory charges levied by the
Central or State Government, like the Land Tax in the instant case, are recoverable
by the generating company through tariff on the basis of the normative parameters
fixed by the Commission.
16. The Petitioner has claimed that the Land Tax, being a Statutory Charge, should
be allowed as an Input Price of lignite under Regulation 38 of the 2024 Tariff
Regulations, which provides as follows:
“38. Input Price of coal or Lignite: (1) Input price of coal or lignite from the integrated
mine(s) shall be determined based on the following components:
I) Run of Mine (ROM) Cost; and
II) Additional charges:
a. crushing charges;
b. transportation charge within the mine up to the washery end or coal handling plant
associated with the integrated mine, as the case may be;
c. handling charges at mine end;
d. washing charges; and
e. transportation charges beyond the washery end or coal handling plant, as the case
may be, and up to the loading point:
Provided that one or more components of additional charges may be applicable in the
case of the integrated mine(s), based on the scope and nature of the mining activities;
Provided further that the input price of lignite shall be computed based on Run of Mine
(ROM) based on the technology such as bucket excavator-conveyor or belt-spreader
or its combination and handling charges, if any.
Order in Petition No. 763/MP/2025 Page 12 of 16

(2) Statutory Charges, as applicable, shall be allowed.”
17. As per Regulation 38 of the 2024 Tariff Regulations, the Input Price of coal or
lignite from an integrated mine is to be calculated by adding the Run of Mine (ROM)
cost and applicable additional charges such as crushing, internal transportation,
handling, washing, and transportation up to the loading point, depending on the nature
of mining operations. Further, the statutory charges from the integral mines shall also
be included for computing the Input Price of coal or lignite.
18. Regulation 50 of the 2024 Tariff Regulations provides for the recovery of Input
Charges, and as per the said regulation, Input Charges are equal to the Input Price
multiplied by the quantity of lignite plus the applicable Statutory Charges. The
Regulation 50 of the 2024 Tariff Regulations provides as follows:
“50. Recovery of Input Charges: (1) The input charges of coal or lignite shall be
recovered as under:
Input Charges = [Input Price x Quantity of coal or lignite supplied] + Statutory
charges, as applicable;
Provided that where the energy charge rate based on the input price of coal
from integrated mine(s) exceeds 20% of the energy charge rate based on the price of
alternative coal available to the station in a given month, the generating company shall
obtain prior consent from the beneficiary(ies);.
Provided further that where such consents of beneficiaries are not available,
the input price of coal from such integrated mine(s) shall be so fixed that the energy
charge rate based on the input price of coal from integrated mine(s) does not exceed
by more than 20% of the energy charge rate based on the price of alternative coal
available to the station in a given month;
Provided also that the energy charge rate based on the input price of coal does
not lead to a higher energy charge rate throughout the tenure of the power purchase
agreement than that which would have been obtained as per terms and conditions of
the existing power purchase agreement.
Explanation: The alternative coal for the generating station will be the sourcing of coal
from an arrangement that could have been made by the generating company in case
of a shortage or non-availability of coal from the linked integrated mine and offers the
least cost arrangement in comparison to all other available options.
(2) The generating company shall work out the comparative energy charge rate based
on the input price of coal and notified price of Coal India Limited for the commensurate
grade of coal for every month from the date of commercial operation of integrated
mine(s) and share the same with beneficiaries.”
Order in Petition No. 763/MP/2025 Page 13 of 16

19. Regulation 58 of the 2024 Tariff Regulations specifies the Landed Fuel Cost of
Primary Fuel, and it is as follows:
“58. Landed Fuel Cost of Primary Fuel: The landed fuel cost of primary fuel for
any month shall consist of the base price or input price of fuel corresponding to the
grade and quality of fuel and shall be inclusive of statutory charges as applicable,
washery charges, transportation cost by rail or road or any other means and loading,
unloading and handling charges:
Provided that procurement of fuel at a price other than Government notified
prices may be considered if it is based on competitive bidding through a transparent
process;
Provided further that the landed fuel cost of primary fuel shall be worked out
based on the actual bill paid by the generating company, including any adjustment on
account of quantity and quality;
Provided also that in the case of coal-fired or lignite based thermal generating
station, the Gross Calorific Value shall be measured by third party sampling, and the
expenses towards the third party sampling facility shall be reimbursed by the
beneficiaries.”
20. As per Regulation 58 of the 2024 Tariff Regulations the landed cost of the
primary fuel for a given month is the total delivered cost of the fuel at the power station,
comprising the approved base or input price for the relevant grade and quality of fuel,
together with all applicable statutory charges, washery charges, transportation costs
(by rail, road, or other modes), and loading, unloading, and handling expenses.
21. Hence, the levy of Land Tax at ₹250/MT, being a statutory charge, shall form
part of the Input Price of lignite like other statutory levies like royalty, DMF, NEMT,
GST etc. and forms part of energy charges rate of the linked thermal generating station
and is recoverable through the landed cost of lignite as part of energy charge.
22. The Petitioner has sought recovery of Land Tax from the linked thermal
generating stations as part of energy charges on a monthly basis as interim relief and
carrying cost in case of delayed recovery. TANGEDCO has submitted that the 2025
Rules were notified by the Government of Tamil Nadu on 28.3.2025, and that land tax
can be considered only prospectively in the 2024-29 tariff period. TANGEDCO has
further submitted that the Petitioner should submit detailed audited computations
Order in Petition No. 763/MP/2025 Page 14 of 16

along with its monthly regular or supplementary bills of change in law claims and also
furnish monthly details of tax actually paid, along with half-yearly and annual statutory
returns, to enable proper verification and reconciliation of the claim.
23. We have considered the submissions of the Petitioner and TANGEDCO. The
Land Tax is statutory in nature and is fixed at ₹250/ton of lignite extracted, through a
Gazette notification. The levy is prospective and directly linked to lignite dispatch, and
is already being paid by the Petitioner. Disallowing interim recovery would result in
recovery of the accumulated amount later, along with interest and carrying cost on the
issue of the final tariff order, imposing additional burden of carry cost on the
beneficiaries. Considering the nature of the levy and immediate liability upon the
Petitioner, we allow the monthly recovery of the same from beneficiaries on a
provisional basis, until the determination of the tariff of the Petitioner for the 2024-29
tariff period.
24. The Petitioner has also sought carrying cost, if there is any difference between
the date of payment of the tax by the Petitioner and its recovery from the beneficiaries,
as per the 2024 Tariff Regulations for the difference in the tariff.
25. We have considered the submissions of the Petitioner regarding carrying cost,
and we are of the view that it is premature and hence it is not allowed in this order.
26. We have allowed the principal amount of the statutory charge of Land Tax as a
pass-through as part of the Input Price of lignite. The Petitioner has not furnished the
impact of the said levy on the Input Price of lignite in this petition. The same is also
not reflected in the Petitioner’s tariff petition for the 2024-29 tariff period under the
2024 Tariff Regulations. Since the tariff for the 2024-29 tariff period has not yet been
approved, the Petitioner may amend the tariff petition by duly incorporating the impact
of the Land Tax in the 2024-29 tariff period, if so advised. The issue of grant of carrying
Order in Petition No. 763/MP/2025 Page 15 of 16

cost, if any, will be examined in that petition in accordance with the applicable Tariff
Regulations, after due prudence check.
27. In the light of the foregoing, the Commission directs as follows:
(a) The Mineral Bearing Land Tax levied under the Tamil Nadu Mineral Bearing
Land Tax Act, 2024, is a Statutory Charge under Regulation 3(77) of the

Analysis and Decision
13. In view of the above, we now proceed to consider the prayer of the Petitioner
as regards the Petition under Section 63 of the Electricity Act 2003 for Adoption of
Tariff for the ISTS Grid connected Solar Power projects of 1200 MW with 600 MW /
1200 MWh Energy storage system (ESS) and with additional capacity up to 1200
MW with “Greenshoe Option” selected through Competitive Bidding Process under
Tariff Based Competitive Bidding Guidelines issued by the Ministry of Power, Govt.
of India on 09.06.2023 and its amendments thereof.
14. Section 63 of the Act provides as follows:
“Section 63: Determination of tariff by bidding process: Notwithstanding anything
contained in Section 62, the Appropriate Commission shall adopt the tariff if such
tariff has been determined through transparent process of bidding in accordance with
the guidelines issued by the Central Government.”
15. Thus, in terms of Section 63 of the Act, the Commission is required to adopt
the tariff, on being satisfied that the transparent process of bidding in accordance
with the guidelines issued by the Central Government has been followed in
determining such tariff.
16. The Ministry of Power, Government of India, has notified the guidelines under
Section 63 of the Act vide Resolution No. 23/03/2023-R&R on 09.06.2023 for the
procurement of firm and dispatchable power from grid-connected renewable
energy power projects with energy storage systems. The salient features of the
guidelines are as under:
i) The specific objectives of the guidelines are: a) to provide firm and
dispatchable power to distribution companies (DISCOMs) from renewable
energy sources, b) facilitate renewable capacity addition and fulfilment of
Renewable Purchase Obligation (RPO)/ Storage Power Obligations (SPO)
Order in Petition No 310/AT/2025 Page 7

requirements, provide a transparent, fair, c) to provide standardized
procurement framework based on open competitive bidding with appropriate
risk-sharing between various stakeholders, and d) to provide a framework for
the Inter-State/ Intra-State, long-term, sale purchase of power as a further
measure to de-risk the sector. The guidelines require the bid documents to
be prepared in accordance with the guidelines and seek approval from the
Government for deviations in the draft RfS, draft PPA, and draft PSA (if
applicable) from these Guidelines and/or SBDs.
ii) The Renewable Energy Supply (RfS) outlines the requirements for a
project's commencement of supply, including land acquisition, connectivity,
and regular reporting requirements. The generator must supply firm and
dispatchable renewable energy power, with peak hours declared by the
DISCOM as specified in the RfS. The generator must offer 100% renewable
energy but can source up to 5% from green market sources/bilateral
agreements.
iii) The developer must combine the renewable energy generating system
with energy storage to achieve the required availability against demand profile
and performance criteria. A single tariff for supply of firm and dispatchable
renewable energy power is quoted by the bidders at the CTUIL
interconnection point. Bids are invited in Power Capacity (MW) terms, with a
minimum quantum of 50MW for economies of scale. A maximum of 50% of
bid capacity can be allocated to a single bidder in a tender.
iv) The bidding evaluation parameter is the tariff per unit supply of firm
and dispatchable renewable energy power, fixed for the entire term of the
PPA. The bidder must submit separate technical and price bids, provide an
Earnest Money Deposit (EMD), and meet eligibility criteria set out in the RfS
document. The minimum number of qualified bidders is two, and any
deviation from the tender conditions is rejected. The detailed procedure for
evaluation of bids and selection of bidders is provided in the RfS document.
v) The Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) is a document involving the
purchase of power from a generator. It outlines the PPA period, which can be
20 years or 25 years, and the power procurement terms. The generator must
ensure supply meets specified conditions, such as RTC, load profile, and
number of hours. The summation of generation schedules from multiple
sources cannot exceed the contracted capacity. The generator can supply
power beyond the contracted capacity to third parties or power exchanges
without a No-Objection Certificate (NOC). Developers with untied capacity
may participate in the bid and receive a longer PPA period. If there is a
shortfall in project availability due to the generator, the generator must pay a
penalty, which is equal to one and a half times the tariff for the number of units
not supplied. The generator is responsible for scheduling and punching at
Order in Petition No 310/AT/2025 Page 8

different Regional Load Dispatch Centers. The Deviation Settlement
Mechanism (DSM) applies for deviations from the schedule, and charges are
settled by the generator.
vi) The Electricity (Late Payment Surcharge and Related Matters) Rules,
2022, outline the provisions for payment security and force majeure. The
generator must inform the procurer of a force majeure within 15 days and
respond within 15 days. The Procurer may be constrained from scheduling
power due to transmission infrastructure or grid unavailability. Compensation
for offtake constraints is provided for generators who fail to meet the
forecasting and scheduling process.
vii) For claiming compensation, generators must sell their power in the
power exchange as a price taker, with compensation limited to the difference
of actual generation up to declared capacity. If a generator defaults, the
procurer may terminate the PPA and pay damages equivalent to 24 months
or the balance PPA period whichever is less. If the generator assigns or
innovates rights or obligations contrary to the terms of the PPA, the procurer
may recover the damages through forfeiture of bank guarantee.
viii) The lenders may exercise their rights of substitution in the event of a
generator's default, but if lenders cannot substitute the defaulting generator
within the stipulated period, the procurer may terminate the PPA. If the
procurer/intermediary procurer is in default due to failure in timely payment or
repudiation of the PPA, the generator may terminate the PPA at its discretion.
ix) The Electricity (Timely Recovery of Costs due to Change in Law)
Rules, 2021, have been notified by the Ministry of Power. The bidding process
for the project will adopt a single stage, two-part (Technical Bid & Financial
Bid) electronic mode. The Procurer will invite the generators to participate in
the RfS for installation of the Renewable Energy Power Plants and supply of
the RE Power with Energy Storage System. The developers, who have
already set up capacity or have spare untied capacity, may also participate in
the bid.
x) The procurer will prepare bidding documents, including the RfS and
draft PPA, in accordance with these guidelines and any SBDs. The RfS notice
will be published in at least two national newspapers and its own website for
wide publicity. Pre-bid conferences and written interpretation of the tender
documents will be provided to the bidders.
xi) The Request for Selection (RfS) document will include bid
responsiveness, technical criteria, financial criteria, liquidity, and the
Quantum of the Earnest Money Deposit (EMD). The net worth requirement
should be at least 20% of the estimated 'RE Project' cost or other criteria
Order in Petition No 310/AT/2025 Page 9

specified in the RfS. If a foreign company is selected as the successful bidder,
it must comply with all the laws and provisions related to Foreign Direct
Investment in India.
xii) The Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) between the RE Project and
procurer/intermediate procurer must clearly indicate the SCSD and quantum
of supply. The procurement committee will evaluate the RfS bids and certify
that the bidding process is conducted in conformity with the provisions of the
RfS document. The evaluation authority has the right to reject all price bids if
the rates quoted are not aligned with the prevailing market prices.
xiii) For transparency, the Procurer shall publicly disclose the names of the
successful bidder(s) and the tariff quoted by them, along with their breakup
into components, for at least 30 days. If the distribution licensee or
Intermediary Procurer does not decide on the adoption of tariffs within 60
days of submission or 120 days from the date of Power Sale Agreement
(PSA), the procurer(s) may grant appropriate extension of time in SCSD to
the generators.
xiv) Generators must provide bank guarantees/corporate
guarantees/letters of undertaking to pay to the procurer in terms of the RfS.
These include Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) and "Payment on Order
instrument"/ Letter of Undertaking. The damages/dues recovered by the
intermediary procurer by encashment of the PBG upon default will be credited
to the Payment Security Fund maintained by the Intermediary Procurer.
xv) The successful bidder must ensure that its shareholding in the
SPV/project company executing the PPA does not fall below 51% at any time
prior to one year from the SCSD, except with the prior approval of the
Procurer. In case of generator default, the lenders are entitled to undertake
"Substitution of Promoter" in concurrence with the Procurers.
xvi) The Renewable Energy (RE) Power Generation Scheme aims to
ensure fairness and transparency in procurement by promoting
standardization and uniformity in processes. Delays in power supply beyond
the Supply Cycle Support System (SCSD) can result in penalties for the
generator, such as encashment of the Performance Bank Guarantee (PBG)
or alternate instruments. For delays beyond six months, the contracted
capacity will be reduced to the project capacity that has commenced supply
within the SCSD plus six months, and the PPA for the balance contracted
capacity will stand terminated.
xvii) Part Commencement of supply of power is accepted by the Procurer
subject to the minimum capacity of 50 MW. However, the SCSD will not be
altered due to the part-commencement of supply of power. If a component is
Order in Petition No 310/AT/2025 Page 10

ready for injection but the remaining component is unable to commence
supply, the generator may commence supply from the component outside the
PPA, with the first right of refusal vested with the end Procurer.
xviii) The Procurers must promote commercially established and
operational technologies to minimize technology risk and achieve timely
commencement of supply. Technical specifications for Solar PV/Wind/Hybrid
Power Projects are specified by the Ministry of New & Renewable Energy.
xix) Dispute resolution is subject to the Appropriate Commission, CERC,
or SERC/JERC. If difficulties arise in giving effect to any provision of these
Guidelines or interpretation of the Guidelines, the Ministry of Power is
empowered to do so with the approval of the Ministry, New & Renewable
Energy. Renewable energy components, including Energy Storage System
(ESS) components charged with RE sources, are eligible for RPO
compliance.”
17. The guidelines outline a system for buying reliable and RE power at a price
set through a transparent bidding process by the buyers from RE power projects that
are 50 MW or larger. These projects are expected to contribute significantly to the
transition towards a more sustainable energy landscape. By ensuring transparency
in the bidding process, stakeholders can foster competition and drive down costs,
ultimately benefiting consumers and the environment alike. The guidelines provide
that the generator shall supply firm and dispatchable RE power with the prescribed
availability to meet the procurer’s demand profile, such that 100% of the annual
energy corresponds to RE power. However, generators can source up to 5% of their
power (in energy terms) on an annual basis from green market sources. The
guidelines further provide that the developer shall combine the RE-generating
system with energy storage to ensure it achieves the required availability against the
demand profile.
Order in Petition No 310/AT/2025 Page 11

18. As per the guidelines, the Petitioner, NHPC, in the capacity of intermediary
procurer, invites bids under the TBCB process, enters into the PPAs with developers
at the tariff discovered in the competitive bid process, and enters into the PSAs with
the distribution licensees to enable them to procure a firm and dispatchable RE
power.
19. Accordingly, NHPC invited proposals for the selection of Solar Power
Developers for setting up the 1200 MW with 600 MW/1200MWh ESS and with
additional capacity up to 1200 MW with “Greenshoe Option”. Under the
arrangements, NHPC is to procure power by entering into PPAs with the successful
bidder, with back-to-back PSAs for the sale of power to the distribution
licensees/Buying Utilities.
20. In terms of the provisions of Section 63 of the Act, we have to examine
whether the process outlined in the Guidelines has been followed in the present case
to arrive at the lowest tariff and for the selection of the successful bidder.
21. The key milestones in the present bidding process were as under:

28. The Commission observes that Clause 3.1 of the RfS document provides that
the extra capacity under the “Green shoe Option” will only be given to the winning
bidders at the lowest (L1) price found through the competitive bidding. Capacity
under the Green shoe option can be offered to such bidders, depending upon
availability and the bidder’s willingness. The petitioner also stated that, according to

is no deviation, departure, or dilution in terms of qualification, ranking, or capacity
allocation under Green shoe vis-à-vis the Base Bid.
29. The Petitioner provided additional capacity of up to 1200 MW through the
‘Greenshoe Option’ to the successful bidder(s) who are willing to execute PPAs with
the Petitioner at the lowest tariff (L1 rate) discovered under the Completive Bidding

capacity or higher quantum in case any of the successful bidders does not accept

accordance with the process as stated above, as well as the subsequent

remained unallocated has been allocated to M/s NTPC Renewable Energy Limited,

pursuant to the Green Shoe option, the BEC resolved to allocate the unallocated
capacity of 70 MW, as indicated in the table above, to M/s NTPC Renewable Energy
Limited. The allocation results in a total capacity of 670 MW (300 MW base capacity
+ 370 MW additional capacity under the Green Shoe Option).
42. The Commission notes that the Guidelines issued by the Central Government
under Section 63 of the Act do not expressly provide for or define the "Greenshoe
Option”. However, the Commission observes that NHPC Limited, acting as the
implementing agency, incorporated the provisions relating to the Greenshoe Option
in the original Request for Selection (RfS) document issued for the procurement of
power through tariff-based competitive bidding.
43. While the implementing agency may have included enabling provisions in the
RfS to facilitate such allocation, the Commission is of the view that the enhanced
allotment beyond the originally allotted capacity might raise concerns regarding
Order in Petition No 310/AT/2025 Page 22

transparency, consistency, and equal treatment of bidders under the Green Shoe
allocation, particularly in light of the requirement to ensure a level playing field and
maintain fairness in the competitive bidding framework.
44. The Commission notes that Section 63 of the Electricity Act, 2003 mandates
that the procurement of electricity by the distribution licensees shall be undertaken
through a transparent process of competitive bidding in accordance with the
guidelines issued by the Central Government. Clause 2.4 of these Guidelines
provides for the enhancement of tendered capacity under the same bidding
framework, subject to the condition that such enhancement is of a similar nature and
governed by identical terms and conditions as those of the original Request for
Selection (RfS). It is, however, observed that the term “Greenshoe Option” is not
defined or specifically provided for in the said Guidelines issued by the Ministry of
Power. The mechanism adopted by NHPC under the “Greenshoe Option” appears
to mirror the technical specifications, commercial terms, and bidding parameters of
the original capacity; however, the Commission feels it is desirable to include an
explicit provision in the Guidelines for such a mechanism.
45. In this regard, reference is invited to Order No. 79/AT/2024 dated 01.08.2024
in the matter of M/s SJVN Limited, wherein this Commission, upon a detailed
examination of the bidding process, had observed that the selection of successful
bidders and the discovery of tariffs were undertaken through a transparent process
of competitive bidding in consonance with the “Guidelines for Tariff Based
Competitive Bidding Process for Procurement of Firm and Dispatchable Power from
Grid Connected Renewable Energy Power Projects with Energy Storage Systems”
dated 09.06.2023, issued by the Ministry of Power under Section 63 of the Electricity
Act, 2003. In the said case, the Commission, ex abundanti cautela, permitted the
Order in Petition No 310/AT/2025 Page 23

allocation of additional capacity to certain developers after taking into consideration
the purported “Greenshoe Option” proposed by the implementing agency. It has now
come to the notice of the Commission that NHPC has been applying and
operationalising the “Greenshoe Option” in subsequent bidding exercises as a
matter of routine administrative practice, de hors any explicit provision or prior
sanction under the Guidelines issued by the Ministry of Power. Such continued
invocation of a mechanism not expressly recognised in the extant Guidelines may
prima facie be viewed as inconsistent with the ratio legis of Section 63 of the Act,
which underpins transparency and fair competition in tariff-based procurement.
46. While the approach adopted by NHPC under the purported Greenshoe Option
may have been intended to enable procurement of additional capacity of a similar
nature within the same bidding process and to ensure tariff efficiency, the absence
of a clear basis of guidelines or prior approval for such a mechanism leaves its
consistency with the statutory framework open to interpretation.
47. Therefore, in terms of Section 63 of the Act, the Commission adopts the
individual tariff for the Firm and Dispatchable RE power in terms of LoAs dated
13.03.2025 by restricting the allocation of additional capacity of NTPC Renewable
Energy Ltd. to 300MW as per the first round under the Greenshoe Option. The
Commission has limited the total capacity to the base capacity of 300 MW, resulting
in an allowed total capacity of 600 MW (300 MW base capacity + 300 MW additional
capacity under the Green Shoe Option) for NTPC Renewable Energy Ltd.

48. In view of the foregoing, and keeping in mind the principles of transparency,
fairness, and equal opportunity, the Commission directs all REIAs including NHPC
to approach the Ministry of Power, Government of India, for a clarification on the
Greenshoe option, including the manner/ specificity of allocation of additional
capacity under the Greenshoe Option including limiting the allocation under
Greenshoe option up to 50% of the originally allocated capacity, particularly where
excess capacity arises due to non-acceptance by other bidders. Such clarification
from the Ministry will ensure uniform incorporation of Greenshoe Option provisions
across schemes, safeguard competitive neutrality, and provide regulatory certainty
to all stakeholders in future bidding processes.

50. Clause (10) of Regulation 9 of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission
(Procedure, Terms and Conditions for grant of trading licence and other related
matters) Regulations, 2020 (hereinafter referred to as “the Trading Licence
Regulations”) provides as under:
“9. (10) The Trading Licensee shall make payment of dues by the agreed
due date to the seller for purchase of the agreed quantum of electricity
through an escrow arrangement or irrevocable, unconditional and
revolving letter of credit in favour of the seller. Such escrow arrangement
or irrevocable, unconditional and revolving letter of credit in favour of the
seller shall be equivalent to:
a. one point one (1.1) times the average monthly bill amount
(estimated average of monthly billing amounts for three months or
actual monthly billing amount for preceding three months as the case
may be) with a validity of one year for long term contracts;
b. one point zero five (1.05) times of contract value for short term
contracts.”
51. The above provisions provide for the payment security mechanism to be
complied with by the parties to the present petition. Accordingly, the provisions of
Articles 10.3 and 10.4 of the PPAs and Clause (10) of Regulation 9 of the Trading
Licence Regulations shall be complied with by the concerned parties to the present
petition.
52. The Petitioner, NHPC, has also prayed to approve the trading margin of Rs .
0.07/kWh to be recovered from buying utilities /Distribution Licensee/DISCOM(s) in
Order in Petition No 310/AT/2025 Page 26

terms of the PSA to be signed between NHPC & buying Utilities/Distribution
Licensee.
53. In this regard, Clause (1)(d) of Regulation 8 of the Trading Licence
Regulations provides as under:
“For transaction under long term contracts, the trading margin shall be
decided mutually between the Trading Licensee and the seller:”
The above provision gives the contracting parties the option to mutually agree
on the Trading Margin for long-term transactions.
54. The above provision gives the choice to the contracting parties to mutually
agree on a trading margin for long-term transactions. However, proviso to Regulation
8(1)(d) of the Trading Licence Regulations provides as under:
“8(1) (d) * * * * * Provided that in contracts where escrow arrangement
or irrevocable, unconditional and revolving letter of credit as specified
in clause (10) of Regulation 9 is not provided by the Trading Licensee
in favour of the seller, the Trading Licensee shall not charge trading
margin exceeding two (2.0) paise/kWh.”
55. Regulation 8(1)(f) of the Trading Licence Regulations provides as under:
“For transactions under Back to Back contracts, where escrow
arrangement or irrevocable, unconditional and revolving letter of credit
as specified in clause (10) of Regulation 9 is not provided by the Trading
Licensee in favour of the seller, the Trading Licensee shall not charge
trading margin exceeding two (2.0) paise/kWh.”
56. The above two provisions are exceptions to the main provision as regards
trading margin. In the present case, PSAs have not yet been signed by the
distribution licensees. Once the PSAs are signed with the distribution utilities, the
trading margin shall be in accordance with the provisions of such PSAs, to be
entered into between NHPC and the respective distribution licensee. However, in
Order in Petition No 310/AT/2025 Page 27

case of failure by NHPC to provide an escrow arrangement or an irrevocable,
unconditional, and revolving letter of credit to the wind-solar hybrid power
generators, the trading margin shall be subject to a ceiling of Rs.0.02/kWh specified
in Regulation 8(1)(d) and Regulation 8(1)(f) of the Trading Licence Regulations.
57. In view of the above, the prayer of the petitioner on Trading Margin is
answered accordingly.
58. The Petition No. 310/AT/2025 is disposed of in terms of the above.

आदेश/ ORDER
The Petitioner, Thar Surya 1 Private Limited (TS1PL), is a generating company that has setup
a 300 MW Solar Power Generating System (SPGS) (the Project) in Bikaner District, Rajasthan.
Solar Energy Corporation of India Limited (SECI) issued a Request for Selection (RfS) dated
20.03.2020, inviting proposals for development of 2000 MW ISTS connected solar power
projects. TS1PL submitted its bid on 22.06.2020, and the e-Reverse auction took place on
30.06.2020. TS1PL was a successful bidder having quoted the tariff of INR 2.37/kWh for a
capacity of 300 MW. Thereafter, SECI issued a Letter of Award (LoA) in the name of M/s
Avikiran Surya India Private Limited (parent company of the Petitioner) on 15.07.2020.
Pursuant to the LoA, TS1PL executed a Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) with SECI on
20.08.2021 with effective date as 27.07.2021 under a composite scheme for the generation and
supply of power to BSES Rajdhani Power Limited (BRPL) and BSES Yamuna Power Limited
(BYPL). The Project was commissioned on 24.11.2022. TS1PL has filed the present Petition
seeking relief on account of a Change in Law event under Article 12 of the PPA dated
20.08.2021, specifically the increase in the rate of Goods and Services Tax (GST) qua the
Order in Petition No. 78/MP/2023 Page 2 of 31

issuance of Notification No. 8/2021 Central Tax (Rate) and Notification No. 8/2021 Integrated
Tax (Rate) dated 30.09.2021 by the Ministry of Finance, Government of India, and Notification
No. 8/2021 State Tax (Rate) by the Department of Finance, Government of Rajasthan.
2. Respondent No. 1, Solar Energy Corporation of India Limited (SECI), is under the
administrative control of the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) to facilitate the
implementation of Jawaharlal Nehru National Solar Mission (JNNSM) for the development,
promotion, and commercialisation of solar energy technologies in the country and to achieve
targets set out in the JNNSM. SECI is acting as an intermediary procurer and holds a power
trading license.
3. Respondent Nos. 2 and 3, BRPL and BYPL, are distribution licensees in the National Capital
Territory of Delhi. BRPL and BYPL have executed Power Sale Agreements (PSAs) dated
20.07.2021 with SECI for the sale of 210 MW and 90 MW power, respectively, generated from
the Petitioner’s Project.
4. The Petitioner has made the following prayers:
a) Declare that the issuance of Notification No. 8/2021 Central Tax (Rate) and
Notification No. 8/2021 Integrated Tax (Rate) dated 30.09.2021 by the Ministry of
Finance, Government of India and Notification No. 8/2021 State Tax (Rate) by the
Department of Finance, Government of Rajasthan, are Change in Law events under
Article 12 of the Power Purchase Agreement dated 20.08.2021;
