ORDER
Background facts
The Petitioner, Maithon Power Limited (in short ‘MPL’), is a joint venture between
Tata Power Company Limited (TPCL) and Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC), holding
74% and 26% equity, respectively. The Petitioner owns and operates the Maithon Right
Bank Thermal Power Project, having a capacity of 1050 MW (2 x 525 MW) (in short,
‘the generating station’), located in the Dhanbad District of the State of Jharkhand. The
commercial operation (COD) dates of Unit-I and Unit-II are 1.9.2011 and 24.7.2012,
respectively.
2. The Respondent, DVC and the Respondent, KSEBL, have executed long-term
PPAs with the Petitioner for the supply of 150 MW and 300 MW, respectively. The
Respondent TPDDL and the Respondent WBSEDCL have executed long term Power
Supply Agreement with the Petitioner for the supply of 300 MW each through the
Respondent, TPTCL. On 29.4.2016, the Commission, vide 4th Amendment to the
Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Indian Electricity Grid Code) Regulations,
2010 (IEGC) introduced Regulation 6.3B, viz., ‘Technical Minimum Schedule for
operation of CGS / ISGS’, whose tariff is either determined or adopted by Commission,
wherein, the RPCs were directed to work out a compensation mechanism for the
Station Heat Rate and Auxiliary Energy Consumption, for low unit loading.
Subsequently, on the recommendation of the RPCs, the Commission, vide its order
Order in Petition No. 67/MP/2024 Page 2 of 31

dated 5.5.2017, issued the compensation mechanism for part-load operation of the
generating station. Thereafter, the Commission vide Suo motu order dated 31.1.2019
in Petition No. 2/ SM/2019, introduced the Pilot on Security Constrained Economic
Dispatch (SCED) mechanism for ISGS that are regional entities, and whose tariff is
determined or adopted by this Commission for their full capacity. It further stipulated
compensation for part-load operation, as certified by RPEC, in accordance with the
provisions of IEGC, and instructed POSOCO to frame the detailed procedure within a
month to operationalise the scheme and submit the same for information. On
29.3.2019, POSOCO notified the final procedure for the pilot on SCED for ISGC Pan
India, in compliance with the Commission’s order dated 31.1.2019. On 12.6.2019, the
Petitioner was included in the RRAS and SCED mechanisms, in light of the discussions
held by it with ERPC, NLDC, and ERLDC on 8.5.2019. The SCED mechanism provided
for compensation to the generating stations, for part load operations (for a decrement
in the schedule) as certified by RPC, as per provisions of IEGC read with para 6(i) and
(ii) of Appendix-II of the order dated 5.5.2017.
3. While so, Petition No. 221/MP/2021 was filed by the Petitioner before this
Commission, under Section 79 of the Electricity Act, 2003 (‘Act’) read with Part 7 of the
IEGC 2010, seeking clarification on the compensation methodology notified under
Regulation 6.3B of IEGC 4th Amendment Regulations and the mechanism for
compensation dated 5.5.2017 and also to direct the Respondent ERPC to consider the
approved Heat Rate of 2326.03 kCal/kWh for the purposes of part load compensation
and to issue the revised compensation statements for the years 2019-20 and 2020-21.
The Commission, by order dated 12.1.2023, disposed of the said petition, with the
following directions:
“22. In our considered view, the percentage (%) shares of the generating station can be
computed from the contracted capacities, as the ratio of the gross contracted capacity to
the installed capacity of the generating station of the Petitioner. In the above background
Order in Petition No. 67/MP/2024 Page 3 of 31

and keeping in view the methodology adopted by the WRPC for IPPs of the Western
Region, we direct ERPC to determine the beneficiary wise compensation in line with the
‘Mechanism for Compensation for Degradation of Heat Rate, Aux Consumption and
Secondary Fuel Oil Consumption, due to part load operation and Multiple Start / Stop of
units’ issued by the Commission vide order dated 5.7.2017. Also, considering the fact
that the Commission vide its order dated 8.1.2022 in Petition No.408/GT/2020 had
approved the Station Heat Rate of 2326.03 kcal/kWh, from 1.4.2019 onwards, instead of
the SHR of 2375 kcal/kwh considered earlier, we direct ERPC to revise the total
compensation statements for the generating station, including the compensation
associated with each beneficiary, for the period from 2019-20 onwards, considering the
revised SHR approved as above. The prayers of the Petitioner, is disposed of in terms of
the above.”
Present Petition
4. In the above background, the Petitioner, MPL, has filed the present petition
seeking the following reliefs:
“a) Direct Respondent No. 1/ERPC to issue the revised compensation statements with
regard to SCED in terms of the Order dated 12.1.2023 in Petition No. 221/MP/2021
passed by this Hon’ble Commission.
(b) Direct Respondent No. 1/ERPC to include the applicable carrying cost for the
delayed recovery of the legitimate entitlement of the Petitioner;
(c) Direct Respondent Nos 2, 3 and 4 to release carrying cost on the part load
compensation in terms of the revised ERPC statement dated 10.05.2023 and the
Debit Notes dated 21.12.2023 issued by the Petitioner;
(d) Pass any such further Order(s) as this Hon’ble Commission may deem fit and proper
in the facts and circumstances of the case.”
Submissions of the Petitioner
5. In support of the above prayers, the Petitioner, MPL, has submitted the following:
(a) ERPC issued the compensation statement on 10.10.2019 for the months of
May 2019 to July 2019 for the Eastern Region, including the Petitioner, as per
Regulation 6.3B of the IEGC, 2010, read with the compensation mechanism
and the SCED mechanism. Thereafter, the Petitioner pointed out certain
errors in the compensation statement issued. ERPC issued the revised
compensation statement on 16.10.2019, for the Petitioner, for the months of
June, 2019 and July, 2019. In the said statement, ERPC provided the overall
compensation due to the Petitioner for the months of June 2019 to July 2019,
thereby making it difficult for the Petitioner to recover the compensation due
to lower requisition from the beneficiaries, who were responsible for unit
loading lower than 85 % as envisaged in IEGC, 2010. On 27.4.2020 and
22.7.2021, ERPC published the compensation statement for the periods
2019-20 and 2020-21, based on the earlier SHR of 2375 kCal/kWh.
(b) The Petitioner filed Petition No. 221/MP/2021, seeking necessary clarification
regarding the methodology of compensation for part load operation of its
Order in Petition No. 67/MP/2024 Page 4 of 31

generating station and also sought a direction against the ERPC to consider
the approved heat rate of 2326.03 kCal/kWh (as determined by the order
dated 8.1.2022 in Petition No.408/GT/2020 for the purposes of compensation,
(on account of part load) and to issue the revised compensation statements
in this respect for the period 2019-20 and 2020-21. This petition was allowed
by the Commission’s order dated 12.1.2023.
(c) In terms of the said order, the Petitioner requested ERPC for the publication
of the revised compensation statement. Pertinently, on 10.5.2023, ERPC
issued the beneficiary-wise revised compensation statements for the
Petitioner on account of a degradation in heat rate and auxiliary consumption
due to part load operation for the months from April, 2019 to March, 2022.
However, ERPC, in total disregard and violation of the said order dated
12.1.2023, failed to publish the compensation receivable from the SCED Pool
to the Petitioner.
(d) The Petitioner also issued debit notes on 31.5.2023 to the Respondents 2, 3
and 4 for payment of the compensation amount as reflected in the said
revised compensation statement dated 10.5.2023. On 5.6.2023, the
Petitioner requested ERPC to correct the compensation statement dated

generating company from lenders/promoters/accruals is to be paid by way of

fixed according to commercial principles, but is only a compensation for the
money denied at the appropriate time.

Analysis and Decision
15. Based on the submission of the parties, the issues which emerge for
consideration are the following:

issued vide Commission’s order dated 12.1.2023 in Petition No. 221/MP/2021?

Issue No. (A): Whether the Respondent ERPC has complied with the directions
issued vide Commission’s order dated 12.1.2023 in Petition No. 221/MP/2021? If
not, the relief to be granted to the Petitioner
16. The Petitioner has pointed out that ERPC, on 10.5.2023, while issuing the revised
beneficiary-wise compensation statements, on account of the degradation of heat rate
and auxiliary power consumption due to part load operation, for the months of April
2019 to March 2022, failed to consider the SCED compensation, which is a clear

ERPC, while confirming that the SCED compensation attributable to Petitioner was not
considered in the revised compensation statement dated 10.5.2023, has clarified that
the same was on account of considering that (i) SCED schedule was allowed to

SCED to optimise the despatch of generation resources (ii) as per clause 7.9 of the

as deemed delivered with no retrospective changes in SCED schedules’ (iii) revision in
post-facto SHR, the ECR also changes and compensation may also be revised and (iv)
defeats the very purpose of SCED, which aims to optimise the scheduling and despatch
of the generation resources and reduce the overall cost of production of electricity. The
Respondent WBSEDCL submitted that the ERPC has correctly issued the revised
Order in Petition No. 67/MP/2024 Page 17 of 31

compensation statement on 10.5.2023 in compliance with the order dated 12.1.2023.
WBSEDCL also submitted that the Petitioner's averment that the ERPC has not
complied with the said order is erroneous and baseless.
17. We have examined the rival submissions. We note that in Petition No. 221/MP/
2021 filed by the Petitioner, it sought clarification on the methodology for sharing
compensation for the ISGS having capacity contracted in megawatt and not under any
predetermined percentage allocation, as per sub clause (xiv) of clause 4.1 of the part
load compensation mechanism. The said relief sought was in the context of the
compensation statements dated 27.4.2020 and 22.7.2021 published by ERPC, for the
generating station of the Petitioner for the years 2019-20 and 2020-21, based on the
then prevailing SHR of 2375 kcal/kWh. In fact, the said petition was filed by the
Petitioner, based on the advice of ERPC, seeking clarification from this Commission
with regard to the methodology for compensation from IPP stations. Be that as it may,
we note that during the pendency of this petition and pursuant to the Commission’s
tariff order dated 8.1.2022 in Petition No. 408/GT/2020, wherein, the SHR was revised
to 2326.03 kcal/kWh, the Petitioner filed IA No. 53/2022 (in Petition No.221/MP/2021)
bringing on record the subsequent developments. However, the said IA was disposed
of on 29.7.2022, with a direction to approach the Commission with a separate petition.
Subsequently, the order dated 29.7.2022 was recalled in order dated 12.1.2023, as
under:
“15………However, during the pendency of this petition, the Commission issued tariff order
dated 8.1.2022 in Petition No. 408/GT/2020 in respect of the generating station of the
Petitioner, wherein, the SHR was revised to 2326.03 kcal/kWh. Though the above facts
were placed on record by the Petitioner in its rejoinder dated 8.4.2022, it had also filed IA
No.53/2022 bringing the subsequent developments, which was disposed of, with a direction
to approach the Commission, with a separate petition, as stated in para 13 above. Though
the IA was disposed of as aforesaid, in our view, the computation of compensation
considering the revised SHR based on Commission’s order dated 8.1.2022 (instead of the
prevalent SHR), is necessary for proper determination of the tariff and further it will not cause
any prejudice to the Respondents. Accordingly, the order of the Commission in the hearing
dated 29.7.2022, disposing of the IA, is recalled. Therefore, the IA No. 53/2022 filed by the
Petitioner, is restored on record and the submissions made therein have been considered
Order in Petition No. 67/MP/2024 Page 18 of 31

along with the main petition, for final disposal.”
18. Accordingly, Petition No.221/MP/2021 was disposed of by order dated 12.1.2023,
wherein, ERPC was directed to revise the total compensation statement, including the
compensation associated with each beneficiary, for the period 2019-20 onwards,
considering the revised SHR, as under:
“22. ……, we direct ERPC to determine the beneficiary wise compensation in line with
the ‘Mechanism for Compensation for Degradation of Heat Rate, Aux Consumption and
Secondary Fuel Oil Consumption, due to part load operation and Multiple Start / Stop of
units’ issued by the Commission vide order dated 5.7.2017. Also, considering the fact
that the Commission vide its order dated 8.1.2022 in Petition No.408/GT/2020 had

associated with each beneficiary, for the period from 2019-20 onwards, considering the

19. Thus, in terms of the observations/directions of the Commission, ERPC was
mandated to consider the SCED compensation associated with each beneficiary for
the period from 2019-20 onwards, based on the revised SHR of 2326.03 kcal/kWh.
Admittedly, ERPC, in the present case, though had worked out the SCED
compensation considering the revised SHR of 2326.03 kcal/kWh, did not, however,
include the same in the beneficiary-wise revised compensation statement issued by it
on 10.5.2023, which fact has been acknowledged by it, in its reply filed in the matter.
On a specific query of the Commission as to the reasons for not issuing the
compensation statement attributable to the Petitioner on account of SCED for the
period under dispute, ERPC clarified the reasons (as indicated in para 16 above) for
the non-revision of the said compensation statements, considering the SCED
compensation. In our considered view, the reasons furnished by ERPC for the non-
revision of the compensation statement with regard to SCED are an afterthought and
cannot be accepted. One of the clarifications furnished by ERPC is that clause 7.9 of
the Procedure for Pilot on Security Constrained Economic Despatch for ISGS pan India
provides that SCED schedules would be treated as deemed delivered, and there would
Order in Petition No. 67/MP/2024 Page 19 of 31

be no retrospective changes in the SCED schedules. It is pertinent to mention that the
Commission, while recalling its order dated 29.7.2022 (IA No. 53/2022 in this petition),
observed that the compensation computation, considering the revised SHR of 2326.03
kcal/kWh (based on the Commission’s order dated 8.1.2022 in Petition No.480/GT/
2020) is necessary for the proper determination of tariff and the same will not cause
any prejudice to the Respondents. Accordingly, the Commission in the said order dated
12.1.2023, directed the ERPC to revise the compensation statements, including the
SCED compensation attributable to the Petitioner. None of the parties, including ERPC,
had challenged the order dated 12.1.2023 before any appropriate forum. Thus, the
order dated 12.1.2023 directing ERPC to issue the total compensation statements
(including the SCED compensation) had attained finality. In case ERPC felt that the
issue of retrospectivity was not considered or that the revision of the SCED
compensation statements would involve a retrospective revision of the schedules,
nothing prevented it from challenging the said order dated 12.1.2023 by seeking review
or filing an appeal before the appropriate forum. Having not done so, and the order
dated 12.1.2023, having attained finality, ERPC cannot now be permitted to raise the
issue of retrospectivity, citing clause 7.9 of the procedure for pilot on SCED, to deny
the SCED compensation to the Petitioner. Agreeing to the contention of ERPC that no
retrospective revision is possible would, at this stage, result in the order dated
12.1.2023 being reviewed, which is not permissible. In this regard, it is noteworthy to
extract the observations of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of Commissioner,
Karnataka Housing Board v. C. Muddaiah (2007) 7 SCC 689, which is as under:
“…once a direction has been issued by a competent court, it has to be obeyed
and implemented without reservation; the order of the court cannot be rendered
ineffective on the specious plea that no such direction could have been given by
the court. A party, though perceiving an order to be erroneous, allowing it to attain
finality by reason of acceptance thereof cannot escape the rigours of compliance.
He has to pursue his appellate or other remedy to escape the consequences that
can visit him, should the high court hold him guilty of contempt. Such a compliance
is insisted upon for securing the majesty, dignity and prestige of the court.
Order in Petition No. 67/MP/2024 Page 20 of 31

20. Further, the Hon’ble Supreme Court in its judgement dated 28.11.2008 in C.A.
No.6903/2008 (K.A. Ansari & anr v Indian Airlines Ltd), held as under:
“18…...It is manifest that in direction No. (ii), the learned Single Judge had clearly directed
that the writ petitioners would be entitled to be posted to a post equivalent scale held by
them when the letter dated 23rd April 2003 was issued. The respondent -Indian Airlines
was obliged to obey and implement the said direction. If they had any doubt or if the order
was not clear; it was always open to them to approach the court for clarification of the
said order. Without challenging the said direction or seeking clarification, Indian Airlines
could not circumvent the same on any ground whatsoever. Difficulty in implementation of
an order passed by the Court, howsoever, grave its effect may be, is no answer for its
non-implementation.”
21. Even if the objective of SCED is to optimise the despatch of the generation
resources at inter-state level and to reduce the overall variable charges for production
of electricity, as contended by ERPC, the same cannot be a ground for it to deny the
rightful claims of the Petitioner, which is based on the directions of this Commission to
revise the total compensation statement. To us, the conduct of ERPC, admitting that it
had not revised the compensation statement with regard to SCED, in the teeth of the
Commission’s directions in the order, is highly objectionable and therefore, ERPC
cannot be permitted to act in contravention of the directions of this Commission and to
deny the legitimate relief to the Petitioner. In the above backdrop, ERPC, while issuing
the revised compensation statement dated 10.5.2023, should also have included the
SCED compensation claim of the Petitioner in the revised statement. Thus, there has,
admittedly, been a non-compliance by ERPC of our order dated 12.1.2023 on this
count. It is pertinent to note that in Petition No.166/MP/2021 filed by NTPC seeking
payment of compensation due to part load operation, some of the Respondents therein,
including SRPC, had objected to the said claim, stating that the compensation
mechanism does not envisage any retrospective settlement. Rejecting the said
contentions, the Commission vide its order dated 14.11.2023 held that NTPC was
entitled to a retrospective revision of the part load compensation in terms of the
Compensation Mechanism dated 5.5.2017. The relevant portion of the order is
Order in Petition No. 67/MP/2024 Page 21 of 31

extracted below:
“19…. These Regulations also provide for retrospective adjustment of the tariff recovered
by the Petitioner as against those allowed by the Commission. The Petitioner, pursuant
to the said order, had revised its earlier invoices and refunded an amount of Rs 54.48
crore, to the Respondent beneficiaries. To us, the Compensation mechanism of IEGC
2010, do not bar the retrospective adjustment of compensation due to degradation of
operational parameters. Even otherwise, Regulation 7(3) of the IEGC 2010, as quoted in
para 14 above, provide the Commission with the power to deal with any matter or
exercise any power as deemed fit, in the interest of justice.”
22. Thus, ERPC having not complied with our directions in the order dated 12.1.2023,
the relief(s), which the Petitioner is entitled to, are discussed below.

28. We have examined the rival submissions. The Petitioner, based on the revised
compensation statements (principal amounts) for degradation of Heat Rate and
Auxiliary consumption, issued by the ERPC on 30.5.2023 in terms of the Commission’s

14.11.2023 (in Petition No.166/MP2021), the Petitioner, on 21.12.2023, claimed the

inadvertently missed. While the Respondents DVC and TPDDL have failed to response

Order in Petition No. 67/MP/2024 Page 27 of 31

considered view, the submissions of the Respondent are not acceptable. As regards
the contention that the NTPC’s order dated 14.11.2023 is not applicable to the present

based on the ERPC advice to approach this Commission for seeking necessary
clarification regarding the methodology of compensation for IPP stations, keeping in
view that the share allocation of the Petitioner’s project is based on the fixed LTA
quantum (in MW) to beneficiaries. Similar to the case of an NTPC Plant (CGS), whose
allocation is done by the MOP, GOI (on a percentage basis), the Petitioner’s generating
station (though an IPP) has long-term PPAs with the beneficiaries (on MW basis) and
the tariff of the same is being determined by this Commission. ERPC has been issuing
total compensation statements for CGS, including the SCED compensation
recoverable from each beneficiary. The Petitioner’s generating station was included
under SCED from 12.6.2019. In the above background and keeping in view the
methodology adopted by the WRPC for IPPs of the Western Region, the Commission
vide its order dated 12.1.2023 directed the ERPC to determine the beneficiary wise
compensation due to part load operation including the consideration of the revised SHR
of 2326.03 kcal/kWh, based on the tariff order dated 8.1.2022 in Petition No.
408/GT/2020 in respect of the Petitioner’s generating station. It is pertinent to mention
that the Commission, vide its 4th Amendment dated 29.4.2016 to IEGC, introduced
Regulation 6.3B viz Technical Minimum for operation of CGS/ISGS, whose tariff is
determined by this Commission or adopted by this Commission. Thus, as decided in
the case of NTPC, the compensation for the degradation of heat rate, in the present
case, is based on the provisions of the Grid Code and the Tariff Regulations notified
by this Commission. Even otherwise, we note that NTPC in its Petition (166/MP/2021)
had not claimed any carrying cost, but the Commission, evidently, following the
principles of restitution and time value of money and in terms of the provisions of the
Order in Petition No. 67/MP/2024 Page 28 of 31

Tariff Regulations, directed the payment of the part load compensation along with
simple interest. It is pertinent to mention that the 2019 Tariff Regulations consider the
interest component while considering the expenses qua the over recovery or under
recovery for the generating company or the transmission licensee, as the case may be.
In this background, we hold that the order in the NTPC case granting carrying cost is
squarely applicable to the present case of the Petitioner. As regards the contention of
the Respondent WBSEDCL that it has paid the principal amount without delay, and
therefore, it is not liable to pay the ‘carrying cost’, we clarify that the carrying cost is not
a penal charge, but is only a compensation for the money denied to the Petitioner at
the appropriate time [Ref: judgment of APTEL dated 20.1.2019 in Appeal No. 308/2017
(LAPL v HERC & ors)]. In our view, the interest or carrying cost claimed is in terms of
the Tariff Regulations for the delayed recovery of tariff and with the settled financial
principle that whenever the recovery of cost is deferred, the gap in cash flow is to be
paid by way of carrying cost.

earlier Petition and thus had relinquished the same. Order II Rule 2 stipulates that every
suit shall include the whole of the claim which the plaintiff is entitled to make in respect
of the cause of action; but a plaintiff may relinquish any portion of his claim in order to
bring the suit within the jurisdiction of any Court. As stated earlier, Petition No. 221/
MP/2021 was filed by the Petitioner seeking clarification on the methodology of sharing
of the part load compensation in terms of the Compensation mechanism dated
5.5.2017, while the present petition has been filed seeking directions against ERPC to
issue the revised compensation statements in terms of the order dated 12.1.2023 and
to make payment of the carrying cost. Thus, the reliefs claimed in both petitions filed
Order in Petition No. 67/MP/2024 Page 29 of 31

by the Petitioner arise from a different cause of action. In other words, Order II Rule 2
would not be applicable, where the second suit is based on a different and distinct
cause of action. The contentions of the Respondent are therefore rejected.
30. One more objection of the Respondent WBSEDCL is that the carrying cost was
never raised by the Petitioner in the original petition; and also, no directions were given
in the Commission’s order dated 12.1.2023 for payment of carrying cost by the
beneficiaries. As stated, the allowance of carrying cost is based on the restitutionary
principle and is based on compensation towards the time value of money. In this regard,
we note that APTEL in its judgment dated 6.8.2021 in Appeal No. 43/2020 & batch
(UPPCL v UPERC & ors), as relied upon by the Petitioner, has held that the interest
payable and receivable, being a statutory right, need not be prayed for and pleaded
for. The relevant portion of the order is extracted below:
“339. Another related issue in this regard is with respect to the carrying cost. The
generators, whose tariffs are determined by the Central/ State Commissions under
Section 62 are determined are statutorily entitled for or liable for interest or carrying on
the under or over recovered amount of tariff. The relevant UPERC Tariff Regulation
provide interest at the applicable bank rates as on 1st day of April of the relevant year.
We further observe that lots of judicial time is spent by the generators and judicial
authorities on discussing the carrying cost in about 62 cases of generators, whereas the
cardinal principle that arises is that where there is an under or over recovery of tariff, an
interest payable or receivable, which being a statutory right, need not be prayed for and
pleaded for.”
31. In line with the above and considering the fact that the claim of the Petitioner for
carrying cost vide revised debit notes, is in terms of the provisions of the statute, the
applicable Tariff Regulations and the various orders/judgments of the Supreme Court /
APTEL (as referred to by the Petitioner), we hold that the Petitioner is entitled to the
carrying cost (on the principal amounts paid by the Respondents towards the part load
compensation statements), in terms of the revised debit note of the Petitioner dated
21.12.2023 and the Tariff Regulations. It is pertinent to mention that the Petitioner has
claimed carrying cost (on the principal amounts paid by the Respondents) only till
31.5.2023 (date of raising the original debit note) and not till 21.12.2023 (date of raising
Order in Petition No. 67/MP/2024 Page 30 of 31

the revised debit note). The total carrying cost for the period 2019-21, claimed by the
Petitioner from the date of invoice (as per Annexure-B of the additional submissions
dated 6.12.2024), is Rs 17.49 crore till 31.5.2023, calculated under the 2019 Tariff
Regulations. None of the Respondents has pointed out any discrepancy in the
calculation of this amount. Accordingly, we hold that the Petitioner is entitled to the
recovery of carrying cost for the delayed recovery of the part load compensation from
the Respondents, including the Respondent WBSEDCL, at the simple interest rate
equal to the bank rate as on 1st April of the respective years till the date of payment, in
terms of Regulation 10(7) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations, except for the period from
31.5.2023 till 21.12.2023 (when the revised debit note was raised by the Petitioner).
The said carrying cost shall be paid by these Respondents, within 30 days from the
date of this order. Needless to state, the non-payment of these amounts (including
those in para 24 above) within the timelines mentioned therein, shall result in the
payment of LPS by the beneficiaries. Issue No. (B) is disposed of as above.
32. Petition No. 67/MP/2024 is disposed of in terms of the above discussions and
findings.

ORDER
The Petitioner, TP Gopalpur Transmission Limited (erstwhile ERSS – XXXIX
Power Transmission Limited (hereinafter referred to as “ERSS XXXIX”), has filed the
present Petition under Section 63 read with Section 79(1)(c) & (d) of the Electricity
Act, 2003 (hereinafter referred to as “the Act”) seeking the adoption of transmission
tariff discovered through the tariff based competitive bidding process for the purpose
Order in Petition No. 514/AT/2024
Page 2

of selection of the Bidder as the Transmission Service Provider (hereinafter referred
to as “TSP”) to establish the Inter-State Transmission System namely the “Eastern
Region Expansion Scheme – XXXIX” on a Build, Own, Operate and Transfer Basis
(hereinafter referred to as “BOOT Basis”). The Petitioner has made the following
prayers:
“(a) Adopt the Transmission Charges of Rs. 2897.29 million up to the validity/
expiry of TSA discovered through a transparent competitive bidding process
pursuant to the RFP dated 16.03.2024, for “Eastern Region Expansion
Scheme – XXXIX” comprising of the elements/ assets as detailed in the
executed Transmission Service Agreement dated 14.11.2024;
(b) Approve the Transmission Service Agreement dated 14.11.2024 and other
Project Documents including the RFP issued on 16.03.2024 along with all
amendments/communications/ clarifications forming part of Project
Documents for the “Eastern Region Expansion Scheme – XXXIX” and direct
that the recovery of transmission charges shall be in accordance with the
terms of the Transmission Service Agreement dated 14.11.2024 executed
between the parties and the CERC (Sharing of Inter-State Transmission
Charges and losses) Regulations 2020 and its amendments;
(c) Condone any inadvertent errors/ omissions/ shortcomings and permit the
Petitioner to add/change/modify/alter these filings and make further
submissions as may be required at a future date; and
(d) Pass any such other order/orders, as may be deemed fit and proper in the
facts and circumstances of the case.”
2. On receipt of the present Petition, the Bid Process Coordinator (BPC), REC
Power Development and Consultancy Limited (hereinafter referred to as
“RECPDCL”), vide letter dated 8.1.2025, was directed to submit the relevant
documents regarding the complete process of competitive bidding. The necessary
details have been filed by the BPC vide affidavit dated 15.1.2025.
Hearing Dated 28.1.2025
3. On 28.1.2025, the Petition was admitted, subject to just exceptions. Vide
Record of Proceedings (hereinafter referred to as “RoP”) for the hearing dated
28.1.2025, the Petitioner was directed to implead PGCIL as a party to the Petition
Order in Petition No. 514/AT/2024
Page 3

and to file a revised memo of parties. In compliance with the RoP dated 28.1.2025,
the Petitioner, vide its affidavit dated 3.2.2025, has impleaded Power Grid
Corporation of India Limited as a party to the Petition and has filed a revised memo
of parties.
Hearing Dated 19.2.2025
4. During the course of the hearing, the learned counsel for the Petitioner
submitted that the Petitioner has complied with all the directions issued vide Record
of Proceedings for the hearing dated 28.1.2025. He further submitted that the name
of the company has been changed from ‘ERES-XXXIX Power Transmission Limited’
to ‘TP Gopalpur Power Transmission Limited’, and sought permission to place on
record the certificate in support thereof. Vide RoP dated 19.2.2025, the Petitioner
was directed to file an appropriate application for change of name and place on
record, and to submit the supporting documents in this regard. In compliance with
the RoP dated 19.2.2025, the Petitioner submitted the relevant documents in support
of the change of name on 22.2.2025.
Hearing Dated 4.3.2025, 20.3.2025 and 22.4.2025
5. Vide RoP dated 4.3.2025, the Commission deemed it appropriate to list the
present Petition along with similar matters, i.e., Petition Nos. 424/TL/2024 and
426/TL/2024. During the hearing on 22.4.2025, the learned counsel appearing for
the Petitioner submitted that, pursuant to the CTUIL meeting, one bulk consumer
was initially impleaded as a party to the Petition. However, in its subsequent affidavit,
CTUIL has indicated the names of two additional bulk consumers. Accordingly, the
Petitioner sought permission to file a revised memo of parties to implead the said
additional bulk consumers.
Order in Petition No. 514/AT/2024
Page 4

6. Vide RoP dated 22.4.2025, the Petitioner was directed to file an amended
memo of parties to implead the additional bulk consumers as indicated by CTUIL.
Further, all the bulk consumers in the instant case, including the additional bulk
consumers to be impleaded as above, were directed to file their respective replies, if
not filed already. In compliance with the said direction, the Petitioner, vide affidavit
dated 5.5.2025, filed the revised memo of parties, which has been taken on record.
Hearing Dated 20.5.2025 and 7.7.2025
7. During the course of the hearing on 20.5.2025, the learned counsel for the
Respondent, Bihar State Power Holding Company Limited (hereinafter referred to as
“BSPHCL”) submitted that insofar as issues with respect to time overrun and cost
overrun are concerned, the Commission may kindly observe that these issues would
be adjudged on their own merits as and when they arise. During the course of the
hearing on 7.7.2025, after hearing the learned counsels for the Petitioner, the
Respondent, i.e., OPTCL, and the representative of CTUIL, an order was reserved
in the matter.
Analysis and Decision
8. We have considered the submissions of the Petitioner and the Respondents
and perused the documents available on record. The Petitioner has filed the instant
Petition under Section 63 of the Act for the adoption of the Inter-State Transmission
System to establish the “Eastern Region Expansion Scheme – XXXIX (ERES-
XXXIV).
9. The Ministry of Power, Government of India, vide its Gazette Notification No.
943 [F. No. 15/3/2018- Trans-Part(l)] dated 1.3.2024 has notified the RECPDCL
Order in Petition No. 514/AT/2024
Page 5

Limited as the BPC for the purpose of selection of a bidder as the Transmission
Service Provider to establish a transmission system for evacuation of power from
“Eastern Region Expansion Scheme-XXXIV (ERES-XXXIV)” on a Build, Own,
Operate and Transfer Basis through a tariff based competitive bidding process.
10. ERES-XXXIX Power Transmission Limited (now known as TP Gopalpur
Transmission Limited) was incorporated on 27.3.2024 under the Companies Act
2013 as a wholly owned subsidiary of RECPDCL with the objective to establish
“Eastern Region Expansion Scheme-XXXIV (ERES-XXXIV) on Build, Own, Operate
and Transfer Basis” and to act as the Transmission Service Provider after being
acquired by the successful bidder.
11. BPC prepared the bidding document (RfP) in accordance with the Standard
Bid Documents issued by the Ministry of Power, Government of India. BPC started
the process of selection of the successful bidder with the publication of a Global
Invitation for Qualification for the selection of a developer on a BOOT basis for the
Project. The notice of the RfP was published in National/International newspapers on
16.3.2024, with the last date of submission of response to the RfP as 20.5.2024.
Intimation regarding the initiation of the bid process was given to this Commission on
18.3.2024 in accordance with Clause 4.2 of the Guidelines dated 10.8.2021.
12. The scope of the Project as per the Request for Proposal and
the Transmission Service Agreement is as under:

3000 m

400 kV D/c (Quad) line in two different diameters. Utilisation of other 2

c) OPTCL shall provide space at under implementation Gopalpur
(OPTCL) 400/200 kV GIS S/s for implementation of 2 nos. of 400 kV
GIS line bays for termination of Gopalpur (ISTS) – Gopalpur (OPTCL)

be established.
d) POWERGRID shall provide space at Angul (POWERGRID)
765/400 kV S/s for implementation of 2 nos. of 765 kV line bays (along
with space for future switchable line reactor) along with bus extension
in GIS for termination Angul (POWERGRID) – Gopalpur 765 kV D/c
line.
Order in Petition No. 514/AT/2024
Page 8

13. The RfP was issued on 16.3.2024. At the RfP (Technical and Financial) stage,
four bidders, namely, (i) Power Grid Corporation of India Limited; (ii) The Tata Power
Company Limited; (iii) Adani Energy Solutions Limited and (iv) Sterlite Grid 32 Limited
submitted their offers. The RfP (Technical bids) of the bidders were opened by the
Bid Opening Committee at the Central Electricity Authority on 3.10.2024 in the
presence of representatives of the bidders. Based on the recommendation of the Bid
Evaluation Committee (hereinafter referred to as “BEC”), the RfP (Financial) Bids
Initial Price Offer of the bidders were opened on 3.10.2024. The Lowest Initial Price
Offer discovered (Best Deal) on the MSTC portal was Rs. 3,750.00 million, which was
the initial ceiling for quoting the final offer during the e-Reverse Auction.
14. As per the provisions of the RfP documents, BEC recommended that the four
qualified bidders participate in the e-reverse auction stage and submit their final offer.
The e-reverse auction was conducted on the MSTC portal on 4.10.2024 and
concluded on 5.10.2024 after intimation to the bidders regarding the lowest initial price
offer. Among the four qualified bidders, only two bidders, namely, The Tata Power
Company Limited and Power Grid Corporation of India Limited, participated in the e-
reverse auction and submitted their bids.
15. Based on the e-reverse bidding, BEC, in its meeting held on 8.10.2024,
recommended The Tata Power Company Limited, with the lowest transmission
charges of Rs. 2897.29 million, as the successful bidder. The Letter of Intent was
issued by the BPC on 15.10.2024 to the successful bidder, i.e., The Tata Power
Company Limited. In accordance with Clause 12.3 of the Guidelines, the BPC has
hosted on the website of RECPDCL the final result of the evaluation of the bids for
the selection of a developer for the Project.
Order in Petition No. 514/AT/2024
Page 9

16. In accordance with the provisions of the bid documents and upon the issuance
of LoI to the successful bidder (The Tata Power Company Limited) and acquisition of
SPV (the Petitioner) by the successful bidder, the Petitioner has prayed for the
adoption of transmission charges for the Project, which has been discovered through
the competitive bidding process.
17. It is noted that the Petitioner had filed a separate application along with the
instant Petition for the grant of a transmission licence for the subject transmission
system. The Commission, vide its order dated 18.12.2025 in Petition No.
513/TL/2024, has observed that it is premature to consider the grant of a transmission
licence for the instant transmission scheme, as it does not fulfil the requirement
prescribed under Section 38(2)(c) of the Act, and accordingly, referred the matter to
NCT for reconsideration on the basis of its likely utilization and impact on the
consumers, in the absence of any application for its use by the bulk consumers. The
relevant extract of the order dated 18.12.2025 is as under:
“34. The Act mandates that an inter-State transmission system is required to
be developed in an efficient and economical manner. However, the instant
transmission scheme may result in a redundant transmission asset without
any visibility of its utilisation. Therefore, we are of the considered view that it
is premature to consider the grant of a transmission licence for the instant
transmission scheme, as it does not fulfil the requirement prescribed under
Section 38(2)(c) of the Act. Therefore, we find it appropriate to refer the
proposal for the instant transmission scheme back to the NCT for
reconsideration on the basis of its likely utilisation and impact on the
consumers in the absence of any application for its use by the bulk
consumers. Accordingly, we direct the Petitioner and the CTUIL to approach
the NCT with the observations as made in this Order. After the decision of
the NCT, the Petitioner is granted liberty to approach the Commission, if so
advised.
35. Petition No. 513/TL/2024 is disposed of in terms of the above.”
Order in Petition No. 514/AT/2024
Page 10

18. In view of the above, the question of adoption of transmission charges of the
subject transmission scheme does not arise at this stage, and no purpose would be
served to keep the instant adoption Petition pending any further when the decision of
the NCT is pending in the subject transmission scheme. Accordingly, the Petition is
disposed of, with liberty to the Petitioner to approach the Commission for the adoption
of transmission charges after the NCT takes a decision on the subject transmission
scheme. The filing fee paid in the instant Petition shall be adjusted against the
adoption Petition, if any, to be filed by the Petitioner for the subject transmission
scheme in future.
19. Petition No. 514/AT/2024 is disposed of in terms of the above.
Sd/- sd/- sd/- sd/-
(Ravinder Singh Dhillon) (Harish Dudani) (Ramesh Babu V.) (Jishnu Barua)

A. The Commission is statutorily empowered to execute orders
(i) As per Section 142 of the Act and Regulation 70(2) of CBR 2023, read with
Section 94 of the Act and Sections 42, 47, and Order XXI Rule 10 of CPC, this
Commission is statutorily empowered to execute orders. It is no longer res
integra that a statutory tribunal (in this case, Commission), which has been
conferred with the power to adjudicate a dispute and pass necessary orders,
also has the power to implement its order and make its order effective. Reliance
Order in Petition No. 151/MP/2024 Page 4 of 30

is placed on the Hon’ble Supreme Court’s decision in State of Karnataka v.
Vishwabharathi House Building Coop. Society, (2003) 2 SCC 412.
(j) Since the Act confers jurisdiction on this Commission to execute its order, it
must be held to have also granted all such powers, and to employ all such acts,
as are necessary for its execution, including but not limited to issuing a time-
bound direction to the Karnataka ESCOMs to release the outstanding dues
towards carrying cost payable to Adani. In this regard, reliance is placed on the
Hon’ble Supreme Court’s judgment in Union of India v. Paras Laminates (P) Ltd.,
(1990) 4 SCC 453.
B. The Commission has ‘wide regulatory powers’ to execute orders
(k) Being a sector expert, this Commission has wide regulatory powers to take
all actions necessary for the execution of orders, including issuing a time-bound
direction to the Karnataka Discoms to release the outstanding dues towards
carrying cost payable to APL. The judgments of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in
Transmission Corporation of AP Ltd. v. Rain Calcining Ltd., 2019 SCC OnLine
SC 1537 and Energy Watchdog v. CERC (2017) 14 SCC 80 are noteworthy
regarding the wide regulatory powers of this Commission.
(l) In the absence of any prohibition on embargo, and in view of the wilful
disobedience of the judgments/orders of APTEL and this Commission from time-
to-time by the Karnataka ESCOMs, it is prayed that this Commission may
exercise its ‘wide regulatory powers’ and issue a time bound direction to the
Karnataka ESCOMs to release the outstanding dues towards carrying cost
payable to APL.
C. The Commission has the ‘inherent power’ to execute orders
(m) As per Regulation 65 of the CERC (Conduct of Business) Regulations, 2023
and Section 151 of the Civil Procedure Code, 1908, the inherent powers of this
Commission are saved. Such powers are plenary in nature, and the same can
be exercised concerning an area where the Act or Rules are silent. The
judgments of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in GUVNL v. Solar Semiconductor
Power Co. (India) (P) Ltd (2017) 16 SCC 498, and UPPCL v NTPC Ltd (2009) 6
SCC 235 are noteworthy.
(n) In view of the above, it is prayed that this Commission may invoke its
inherent powers and issue a time-bound direction for the immediate release of
outstanding carrying cost dues payable to APL.
D. Adani is statutorily entitled to payment of carrying cost
(o) As per the 2009 Tariff Regulations and the 2014 Tariff Regulations, APL is
entitled to charge interest on delayed payments. Evidently, the Tariff Regulations
have consistently recognised the entitlement of parties to recover carrying costs
in the event of delayed payments. The aforesaid provisions are based on the
principle that the affected party is compensated for the time value of money. This
Order in Petition No. 151/MP/2024 Page 5 of 30

Commission, in its order dated 13.1.2023 in Petition No. 155/MP/2019, already
recognised that the same principle is applicable in the event where the tariff
subsequently approved results in a revision of the tariff that is in deviation from
the tariff approved earlier for the same period.
(p) Therefore, APL is entitled to carrying cost on the differential amounts from
the date of the respective orders of this Commission determining and/or revising
the tariff [including the orders passed pursuant to APTEL’s interim order dated
3.6.2014 in IA No.199/2014 in Appeal No. 108/2014 to the date of actual
payment. As per the reliefs granted by this Commission till date, leading to a
revision in tariffs, APL is entitled to receive the carrying cost, as per APL’s invoice
dated 27.2.2023.
E. Carrying Cost is a consequential relief in case of delayed payment
(q) APL’s entitlement to carrying cost flows from its right to recover the time
value of money [Ref: UHBVNL v. Adani Power (Mundra) Limited, (2023) 2 SCC
624 (paras 20-24) and APTEL’s judgment in M/s. SLS Power Ltd. v. APERC &
Ors., (Appeal No. 38/2012-Paras 35.5 and 35.6)]. Carrying Cost is a
consequential relief that is ought to be paid to the affected party from the date
such entitlement accrued, and the payment became due. It is a settled position
of law that payment of interest is consequential when the Court has already
awarded the principal sums to be paid to a party [Ref: SECCL v State of M.P
(2003) 8 SCC 648 (para 28) and MSEDCL vs. MERC & ors. (2022) 4 SCC 657
(paras 195-198)].
(r) In terms of this Commission’s orders, APL is entitled to carrying costs on
differential tariffs. Despite a clear and settled position of law with respect to the
entitlement of carrying cost, Respondent PCKL/ESCOMs have failed to comply
with the same till date. It is a trite law that where there is no stay of the directions
of the judgment of the court of first instance or appellate court, the directions of
the court of first instance or appellate court are in operation and binding. [Ref:
Bhopal Sugar Industries Ltd. v. ITO Bhopal, AIR 1961 SC 182 (Paras 7, 8, 10 &
12), RBF Rig Corporation, Mumbai v. Commissioner of Customs (Imports)
Mumbai, (2011) 3 SCC 573 (Paras 17 to 19 & 23 to 27)]
3. In view of the above, the Respondents PCKL/ESCOMs ought to be directed to
pay the carrying cost as per APL’s invoice dated 27.2.2023.

by the Commission in accordance these regulations:
Provided that where the tariff provisionally billed exceeds or falls short of the final
tariff approved by the Commission under these regulations, the generating company
or the transmission licensee, as the case may be, shall refund to or recover from the
beneficiaries or the transmission customers, as the case may be, within six months
along with simple interest at the rate equal to short-term Prime Lending Rate of State
Bank of India on the 1st April of the concerned/respective year.
17. Regulations 6(5) of the 2009 Tariff Regulations and Regulation 8(13) of the
2014 Tariff Regulations provides as under:
Regulation 6(5)
“Where after the truing up, the tariff recovered is less than the tariff approved by the
Commission under these regulations, the generating company or the transmission
licensee, as the case may be, shall recover from the beneficiaries or the transmission
customers, as the case may be, the under-recovered amount along with simple
interest at the rates specified in the proviso to this regulation.”
Regulation 8(13)
“The amount under-recovered or over-recovered, along with simple interest at the
rate equal to the bank rate as on 1st April of the respective year, shall be recovered
or refunded by the generating company or the transmission licensee, as the case
may be, in six equal monthly instalments starting within three months from the date
of the tariff order issued by the Commission.”
18. It is evident that the Tariff Regulations have consistently recognized the
entitlement of the parties to recover the carrying cost in case of delayed payments,
based on the principle that the affected party is compensated for the time value of
money. This principle has also been recognised and made applicable by this
Commission in its order dated 13.1.2023 in Petition No. 155/MP/2019 (UPCL v PCKL
& ors) in the event where the tariff subsequently approved results in the revision of
Order in Petition No. 151/MP/2024 Page 24 of 30

the tariff in deviation of the tariff approved earlier, for the same period. Though the
Respondent PCKL/Discoms have paid the Principal amount, in installments, in line
with the above directions/orders of the APTEL and this Commission’s order dated
13.1.2023, they have, unilaterally withheld the payment of the carrying cost, by not
considering its impact arising from the APTEL’s order dated 3.6.2014, and restricting
the claims till the date the provisional tariff order/final tariff order/revised tariff orders
of this Commission. The Respondents have contended that para 142 of the order
dated 13.1.2023, only directs the payment of interest/carrying cost from the date of
provisional tariff or final tariff or revised tariff determined by the Commission, and
since the APTEL’s interim order dated 3.6.2014, is not a determination by this
Commission, the claim for interest/ carrying cost is not permissible.
19. The above submissions of the Respondents are misconceived. As noted,
Regulation 5(3) of the 2009 Tariff Regulations does not limit itself to provisional tariff
orders /final tariff orders/truing up tariff orders, but also applies to revisions in tariff,
made subsequently, based on the orders/judgments passed by APTEL or higher
Courts. In fact, the APTEL interim orders were provisional tariff orders that modified
the tariff orders of this Commission and were subject to a final decision in the appeals
and to the re-determination of the tariff by this Commission on that basis. We note
that the Commission, vide paras 141 to 143 of the order dated 13.1.2023 (quoted
under para 12 above), had specifically directed the Respondent discoms to pay the
carrying cost, considering the revisions in tariff by APTEL. Admittedly, the APTEL,
vide its interim order dated 3.6.2014, had revised the tariff approved by this
Commission vide order dated 20.2.2014 for the period November 2010 to January,
2013. In other words, the Petitioner APL did not receive the tariff under, the order
dated 20.2.2014, for the said period. The carrying cost computation by the
Order in Petition No. 151/MP/2024 Page 25 of 30

Respondents, considering the tariff of Rs. 4.47/kWh for the period November 2010
to January 2013, is erroneous, as the same was never considered for payment
during the said period. It is only on the basis of the Commission’s consequential
revised tariff order dated 10.7.2015 (based on APTEL’s judgment dated 15.5.2015)
that the Respondents became liable to pay the differential tariff along with the
carrying cost. We also note that in the Review Petition (14/RP/2014) filed by the
Petitioner against the Commission’s order dated 20.2.2024 on certain grounds, the
Commission, while considering the prayer of the Petitioner for a direction to the
Respondents to pay the applicable interest as per Regulation 5(3) of the 2009 Tariff
Regulations on the difference between the provisional tariff paid by the Respondents
and the tariff determined by the said order, held, vide order dated 3.6.2014, as under:
“As stated, the generating station of the petitioner was granted provisional tariff for
Unit-I of the generating station from 11.11.2010 (COD) till 31.3.2014 by order dated
24.12.2012 which was partially modified by the interim order of the Tribunal in I.A.
No. 38/2013 in Appeal No.18/2013. Since the tariff for Units I & II of the generating
station has been finally determined by the Commission by order dated 20.2.2014,
the difference between the tariff provisionally billed and tariff finally determined is
required to be adjusted in terms of the said proviso to Regulation 5(3) of the 2009
Tariff Regulations. Absence of a direction in this regard cannot be considered as
error apparent on the face of record.”
20. In our view, the denial of the legitimate claim of the Petitioner vide invoice dated
27.2.2023, towards the carrying cost on the differential amounts paid by the
Respondents, relating to the period from November, 2010 to January 2013, is
erroneous and is contrary to APTELs’ interim order dated 3.6.2014 and Regulation
5(3) of the 2009 Tariff Regulations read with paras 141-143 of the Commission’s
order dated 13.1.2023. The Hon’ble Supreme Court, in Central Bank of India v.
Ravindra, (2002) 1 SCC 367, referred to its earlier judgement in Secy., Irrigation
Deptt., Govt. of Orissa v. G.C. Roy: (1992) 1 SCC 508, wherein, the Constitution
Bench of the Supreme Court had opined that a person deprived of the use of money
to which he is legitimately entitled has a right to be compensated for the deprivation,
Order in Petition No. 151/MP/2024 Page 26 of 30

call it by any name; it may be called interest, compensation or damages. In Sham
Lal Narula (Dr) v. CIT: AIR 1964 SC 1878, the Hon’ble Supreme Court held that
‘interest’ is paid for the deprivation of the use of the money; the general idea is that
he is entitled to compensation for the deprivation; the money due to the creditor was
not paid, or, in other words, was withheld from him by the debtor after the time when
payment should have been made, in breach of his legal rights, and interest was a
compensation whether the compensation was liquidated under an agreement or
statute. Also, APTEL, vide its judgment dated 19.12.2024 in Appeal No. 211/2021
(Amr Power Private Limited v MESCOM), held that interest can be granted even if
not specifically provided under the contract. In the light of the above, the contentions
of the Respondents with regard to pay the carrying cost on the differential tariff to
petitioner stand rejected and we hold that the Respondents are liable to pay carrying
cost to the Petitioner APL, to be computed in accordance with Regulation 5(3) of the
2009 Tariff Regulations and Regulation 8(13) of the 2014 Tariff Regulations, which
provide for simple interest at the applicable bank rate for under-recovery/refund
situations arising from provisional/final/truing-up tariff determination. We direct
accordingly. Issue No. (A) is disposed of as above.
Issue No (B): Whether the Respondent PCKL/Discoms are liable to pay the LPS
on the carrying cost?
21. The Petitioner APL has submitted that in terms of para 143 of the order dated
13.1.2023, the Respondents are liable to pay the Late Payment Surcharge (LPS) for
the delay in paying the monthly instalments (of carrying cost). It has submitted that
by unilaterally withholding the payment of Rs 566 crore, out of Rs 786 crore, payable
in terms of paras141-143 of the order dated 13.1.2023, the Respondents ought to
pay LPS as directed by this Commission, in the said order. Placing reliance on the
APTEL judgment dated 2.11.2020 in cross Appeal Nos 10/2020 & batch (PCKL &
Order in Petition No. 151/MP/2024 Page 27 of 30

ors v CERC & ors), the Petitioner has submitted that the Respondents are liable to
pay LPS as per the rate specified in terms of the applicable Tariff Regulations. Per
contra, the Respondents, PCKL/Discoms, have argued that the claim for interest on
a compounding basis (interest on interest) is entirely outside the scope of the order
dated 13.1.2023. They have also pointed out that para 142 of the said order
categorically stipulates that ‘simple interest’ shall be payable, and para 143 provides
for LPS only if the payment is not made in 6 monthly instalments.
Analysis and Decision
22. We have considered the submissions of the parties. It is pertinent to note that
while the Commission in para 144(g) of the order dated 13.1.2023 held that the
Petitioner shall be entitled to the carrying cost on the arrears of fixed charge and
energy charge in accordance with para 142 of this order. However, para 143 of the
said order, which provides for the recovery of arrears of fixed charges, energy
charges and carrying cost in six monthly instalments also provides for the late
payment surcharge to the Petitioner, as per the applicable Tariff Regulations, in case
the arrears are not paid as stipulated above, by the Respondents. In Uttar Haryana
Bijli Vitran Nigam Ltd. (2023) 2 SCC 624, the Hon’ble Supreme Court held that
‘interest on carrying cost’ is nothing but a time value for money and the only manner
in which a party can be afforded the benefit of restitution in every which way. On
Compound interest, the Hon’ble Supreme Court, in Indian Council for Enviro-Legal
Action v. Union of India, (2011) 8 SCC 161, observed that to do complete justice,
prevent wrongs, remove incentive for wrongdoing or delay, and to implement in
practical terms the concepts of time value of money, restitution and unjust
enrichment noted above-or to simply levelise-a convenient approach is calculating
interest; here interest has to be calculated on compound basis-and not simple-for
Order in Petition No. 151/MP/2024 Page 28 of 30

the latter leaves much uncalled for benefits in the hands of the wrongdoer; some of
our statute law provide only for simple interest and not compound interest; however,
the power of the Court to order compound interest by way of restitution is not fettered
in any way. In terms of the settled legal position, as above, we hold that the
Respondents are liable to pay LPS on the outstanding carrying cost allowed to the
Petitioner as above, subject to adjustment of LPS, if any already paid, in terms of the
applicable tariff Regulations. Issue No (B) is disposed of in terms of the above.
Conclusion
23. As stated, the Petitioner has raised an invoice dated 27.2.2023 on the
Respondent PCKL/Discoms inter alia claiming Rs 786 crore (Rs 423 crore towards
carrying cost plus Rs 363 crore towards interest on interest). The Respondents after
admitting and paying carrying cost to the tune of Rs 220 crore between May, 2023
and September 2023, had unilaterally withheld the balance amount towards carrying
cost, i.e., Rs 566 crore (Rs 203 crore towards carrying cost plus Rs 363 crore
towards Interest on carrying cost), without considering the impact of carrying cost
arising from the directions of APTEL’s interim order dated 3.6.2014. However, the
Respondent has contended that after a reconciliation process, in which the officers
of APL also participated and provided factual inputs, the amount payable as per the
Commission’s order dated 13.1.2023, has been worked out as Rs 419.70 crore,
which includes the carrying cost on differential tariff for Rs 215.86 crore. This has
been refuted by the Petitioner, who states that though APL participated in the
reconciliation process, no reconciliation statement was signed by APL, and the
amount of Rs 419.70 crore was unilaterally worked out by the Respondent PCKL.
Referring to its letter dated 18.8.2023 addressed to the Respondents, APL has
pointed out that without prejudice to its entire claim, it had insisted on the payment
Order in Petition No. 151/MP/2024 Page 29 of 30

of at least the entire admitted amount by the Respondents, to avoid any
consequences in terms of the MOP, LPS Rules.
24. We have examined the submissions. From the computation statements filed by
the Respondents, it is evident that the impact of the carrying cost arising out of the
APTEL’s interim order dated 3.6.2014 has not been considered by the Respondents
in terms of the Tariff Regulations, as submitted by the Petitioner and discussed in
para 19 above. We have, in paras 20 and 22 of this order, concluded that the
Respondents are liable to pay the carrying cost on the differential amounts arising
out of the APTEL/CERC order, along with LPS on the carrying cost, in terms of the
applicable Tariff Regulations. Accordingly, we direct the Respondents PCKL /
Discoms to pay the outstanding dues for carrying costs, along with LPS, within 45
days from the date of this order.
25. Petition No. 151/MP/2024 is disposed of in terms of the above.
Sd/- Sd/- Sd/-

ORDER
The instant Petition has been filed by Power Grid Corporation of India Limited
(hereinafter referred to as ‘PGCIL’ / ‘the Petitioner’), a deemed transmission licensee,
for truing up of the transmission tariff for the 2019-24 tariff period under the Central
Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2019
(hereinafter referred to as “the 2019 Tariff Regulations”) and the determination of the
transmission tariff under the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and
Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2024 (hereinafter referred to as “the 2024 Tariff

along with associated bays at the Navsari GIS and 400 kV D/C Kakrapar APP-Vapi
Transmission Line along with associated bays at the Vapi Sub-station (hereinafter
referred to as “the transmission asset”) under the transmission system associated with
Kakrapar Atomic Power Project 3 & 4 in the Western Region (hereinafter referred to as
“the transmission system / transmission project”):
2. The Petitioner has made the following prayers in the instant petition:
“a)Approve the trued-up Transmission Tariff for 2019-24 block and transmission tariff
for 2024-29 block for the asset covered under this petition, as per para 14 and 15
above.
b)Admit the capital cost claimed and additional capitalization incurred during 2019-
24.
c)Allow the petitioner to recover the shortfall or refund the excess Annual Fixed
Charges, on account of Return on Equity due to change in applicable Minimum
Alternate/Corporate Income Tax rate as per the Income Tax Act, 1961 (as amended
from time to time) of the respective financial year directly without making any
application before the Commission as provided in Tariff Regulations 2019 and Tariff
Regulations, 2024 as per para 14 and 15 above for respective block.
d)Approve the reimbursement of expenditure by the beneficiaries towards petition
filing fee, and expenditure on publishing of notices in newspapers in terms of
Regulation 94 (1) Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions
of Tariff) Regulations, 2024, and other expenditure (if any) in relation to the filing of
petition.
e)Allow the petitioner to bill and recover RLDC fees & charges and Licensee fee
separately from the respondents in terms of Regulation 94 (3) and (4) Central
Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations,
2024.f)Allow the petitioner to bill and recover RLDC fees & charges and Licensee fee,
separately from the respondents in terms of Regulation 94 (3) and (4) Central
Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations,
2024.

Interest rate on account of floating rate of interest applicable during 2024-29 period,
if any, from the respondents.

Background
3. The brief facts of the case are as under:
a) The Investment Approval (the IA) for the transmission system was accorded
by the Board of Directors (BoD) of the Petitioner on 26.2.2014 vide their
Memorandum No. C/CP/Investment/KAPP 3 & 4 dated 4.3.2014 with an
estimated cost of ₹37871 lakh including Interest During Construction (IDC) of
₹2425 lakh based on the December 2013 price level.
b) The scope of work covered under the transmission system is as under:
Transmission Line:
i. Kakrapar APP-Navsari 400 kV D/C line;
ii. Kakrapar APP-Vapi 400 kV D/C line.
Sub-station:
i. Extension of 400/220 kV Navsari GIS Sub-station;
ii. Extension of 400/220 kV Vapi Sub-station.
c) The transmission asset was scheduled to be put into commercial operation
on 26.10.2016. However, it was put into commercial operation on 29.6.2017

condoned. The Commission vide its order dated 3.10.2018 in Petition No.
118/TT/2017 allowed the tariff of the transmission asset for the period from
COD to 31.3.2019.
d) As per the agreement signed between the Petitioner and NPCIL dated
13.12.2004, Kakrapar Atomic Power Plant (KAPP-3&4; 2X700 MW) was
scheduled to be implemented by NPCIL and the components of associated
transmission system (ATS) for KAPP-3&4 were to be implemented by the
Petitioner. NPCIL vide its letter dated 10.5.2016 intimated the Petitioner that
KAPP-3 is scheduled to be put into commercial operation by November, 2017
and KAPP-4 thereafter. As per the 41st SCM (Standing Committee Meeting)
held on 21.12.2016, it was agreed that charging of Vapi-Kakrapar (KAPP)-
Navsari 400 kV D/C line (using Kakrapar generation switchyard) could be
taken up by the Petitioner after COD of the lines and switchyard bays at
Kakrapar. Accordingly, as a contingency arrangement, the Petitioner charged
the Vapi-Kakrapar (KAPP)-Navsari 400 kV D/C line (using Kakrapar
generation switchyard).
e) The Commission, vide its order dated 15.2.2021 in Petition No. 15/TT/2020,
truing-up of transmission tariff for the 2014-19 tariff period and determined of
transmission tariff for the 2019-24 tariff period with respect to the instant
transmission asset.

tariff for the 2019-24 tariff period and the determination of the transmission
tariff for the 2024-29 tariff period for the following transmission
asset implemented under Western Region:

Profit and Loss prepared in accordance with Schedule-II of the Companies Act, 2013,
subject to some additions and deductions as mentioned in the IT Act, 1961. Since the

ORDER
The instant Petition has been filed by Power Grid Corporation of India Limited, a
deemed transmission licensee, for truing up of the transmission tariff for the 2019-24
tariff period under the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions
of Tariff) Regulations, 2019 (hereinafter referred to as “the 2019 Tariff Regulations”) and
the determination of the transmission tariff under the Central Electricity Regulatory
Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2024 (hereinafter referred to
as “the 2024 Tariff Regulations”) of the 2024-29 tariff period with respect to the
Combined Asset under “Northern Region Strengthening Scheme-XXII” in the Northern
Region (hereinafter referred to as the ‘transmission project/transmission system’’).
2. The Petitioner has made the following prayers in the instant Petition:
a) “Approve the trued-up Transmission Tariff for 2019-24 block and transmission
tariff for 2024-29 block for the asset covered under this petition, as per para 16 &
17 above.

24.
c) Allow the petitioner to recover the shortfall or refund the excess Annual Fixed
Charges, on account of Return on Equity due to change in applicable Minimum
Alternate/Corporate Income Tax rate as per the Income Tax Act, 1961 (as
amended from time to time) of the respective financial year directly without
making any application before the Commission as provided in Tariff Regulations,
2019 and Tariff Regulations, 2024 as per para 16 & 17 above for respective block.
d) Approve the reimbursement of expenditure by the beneficiaries towards petition
filing fee, and expenditure on publishing of notices in newspapers in terms of
Regulation 94 (1) Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and
Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2024, and other expenditure (if any) in relation
to the filing of petition.
e) Allow the petitioner to bill and recover RLDC fees & charges and Licensee fee,
separately from the respondents in terms of Regulation 94 (3) and (4) Central
Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations,
2024.
f) Allow the petitioner to bill and adjust impact on Interest on Loan due to change in
Interest rate on account of floating rate of interest applicable during 2024-29
period, if any, from the respondents.
g) Allow the petitioner to file a separate petition before Hon’ble Commission for
claiming the overall security expenses and consequential IOWC on that security
expenses as mentioned at para 23 above.
h) Allow the petitioner to file a separate petition before Hon’ble Commission for
claiming the overall insurance expenses and consequential IOWC on that
insurance expenses as mentioned at para 23 above.
i) Allow the petitioner to file a separate petition before Hon’ble Commission for
claiming the overall capital spares at the end of tariff block as per actual as
mentioned at Para 23 above.
j) Allow the petitioner to claim expenses of CTUIL borne by POWERGRID through
a separate petition as mentioned at para 24 above.
k) Allow the Petitioner to bill and recover GST on Transmission Charges separately
from the respondents, if GST on transmission is levied at any rate in future.

statutory/Govt./municipal authorities shall be allowed to be recovered from the
beneficiaries.
and pass such other relief as Hon’ble Commission deems fit and appropriate under
the circumstances of the case and in the interest of justice.”

Income Tax as per the MAT rates notified for the respective financial year under the IT
Act, 1961, which is levied on the book profit of the entity computed as per Section 115
JB of the IT Act, 1961. Section 115 JB (2) defines book profit as net profit in the
statement of Profit and Loss prepared in accordance with Schedule-II of the Companies
Act, 2013, subject to some additions and deductions as mentioned in the IT Act, 1961.
Since the Petitioner has been paying the MAT rates of the respective financial year, the
notified MAT rates for the respective financial year shall be considered as an effective
tax rate for the purpose of grossing up the RoE for truing up the 2019-24 tariff period in

additional income tax demand as per the Assessment Order of the Income Tax
Authorities shall be considered on the actual payment. However, the penalty (for default
on the part of the Assessee), if any, imposed shall not be taken into account for the
purpose of grossing up of the rate of RoE. Any under recovery or over-recovery of the

“21. Considering the material on record, we are prima-facie of the view that

website under clause (a) of sub-section (5) of Section 15 of the Act be
published to invite suggestions or objections to the grant of a transmission
licence aforesaid. The objections or suggestions, if any, shall be filed by any
person before the Commission by 31.12.2025.”

in all editions of The Hindu (English) and Hindustan (Hindi) on 18.12.2025. No
suggestions/ objections have been received from members of the public in response
to the public notice.

regarding the change in the name of the Company. The Petitioner, vide its affidavit
dated 1.1.2026 has submitted that the name of the Petitioner company has been

change of name from ‘Mandsaur I RE Transmission Limited’ to ‘POWERGRID
Mandsaur Augmentation Transmission Limited’ dated 31.12.2025, issued by the
Registrar of Companies, Manesar, Haryana, has been placed on record.
Accordingly, the name of the Petitioner has been changed to ‘POWERGRID
Mandsaur Augmentation Transmission Limited’ and the same has been taken on
record.

application under the provisions of this Regulation provide an opportunity of
hearing to the applicant, CTUIL, the concerned DICs, or the person who
has filed suggestions and objections, or any other interested person.”
8. In our order dated 15.12.2025, we had proposed to grant a transmission
licence to the Petitioner company and directed the issue of public notice. In response
to the public notice, no suggestions/objections have been received. CTUIL, in its
letter dated 31.10.2025, has recommended the grant of a transmission licence to the
Petitioner. We find that the Petitioner company meets the requirements of the Act
and the Transmission Licence Regulations, 2024, for the grant of a transmission
licence for the subject Transmission System mentioned in paragraph 1 of this order.
Considering the submissions of the Petitioner and CTUIL, we direct that a
transmission licence be granted to the Petitioner, ‘POWERGRID Mandsaur
Augmentation Transmission Limited’, to establish the “Augmentation of
transformation capacity and Implementation of line bays at Mandsaur S/s for RE
Interconnection” on a Build, Own, Operate and Transfer basis as per the details
given in paragraph 1 above.
Order in Petition No. 869/TL/2025

9. The grant of the transmission licence to the Petitioner (hereinafter referred to
as “the licensee”) is subject to the fulfilment of the following conditions throughout
the period of the licence:
(a) The transmission licence shall, unless revoked earlier, remain in force for
a period of 25 years from the date of issue;
(b) The transmission licensee shall comply with the provisions of the Central
Electricity Regulatory Commission (Procedure, Terms, and Conditions for
grant of Transmission Licence and other related matters) Regulations,
2024 or any subsequent enactment thereof during the period of
subsistence of the licence;
(c) The licensee may make an application, two years before the expiry of the
initial licence period, for the grant of the transmission licence for another
term in accordance with Regulation 9 (2) of the 2024 Transmission
Licence Regulations, which shall be considered by the Commission in
accordance with law;
(d) The licensee shall not enter into any contract for or otherwise engage in
the business of trading in electricity during the period of subsistence of
the transmission licence;
(e) The licensee shall have the liability to pay the license fee in accordance
with the provisions of the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission
(Payment of Fees) Regulations, 2012, as amended from time to time or
any subsequent enactment thereof. Delay in payment or non-payment of

the licence fee or a part thereof for a period exceeding sixty days shall be

(f) The licensee shall comply with the directions of the National Load

Despatch Centre under sub-section (3) of Section 28 or sub-section (1) of

(g) The licensee shall remain bound by the provisions of the Central

and Regulations framed thereunder, in particular the 2024 Transmission

ORDER
The instant Petition has been filed by Power Grid Corporation of India Limited, a
deemed transmission licensee, seeking truing-up of the transmission tariff for the 2019-
24 period under the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions
of Tariff) Regulations, 2019 (hereinafter referred to as “the 2019 Tariff Regulations”) and
determination of the transmission tariff for the 2024-29 period under the Central
Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2024
(hereinafter referred to as “the 2024 Tariff Regulations”) in respect of “Raipur Pooling
Station-Wardha 765 kV 2nd Double Circuit line along with bay extension and equipment
at 765 kV Raipur Pooling Station and Wardha Sub-station” (hereinafter referred to as
“the transmission asset”) under “System Strengthening in Raipur-Wardha Corridor for
IPP Projects in Chhattisgarh (IPP-F)” (hereinafter referred to as “the transmission
project”) in the Western Region.
Order in Petition No. 635/TT/2025
Page 2 of 46

2. The Petitioner has made the following prayers in the instant Petition:
“a) Approve the trued-up Transmission Tariff for 2019-24 block and transmission tariff
for 2024-29 block for the assets covered under this petition, as per para 14 and 15
above.
b) Admit the capital cost claimed and additional capitalization incurred during 2019-24.
c) Allow the petitioner to recover the shortfall or refund the excess Annual Fixed
Charges, on account of Return on Equity due to change in applicable Minimum
Alternate/Corporate Income Tax rate as per the Income Tax Act, 1961 (as amended
from time to time) of the respective financial year directly without making any application
before the Commission as provided in Tariff Regulations 2019 and Tariff Regulations,
2024 as per para 14 and 15 above for respective block.
d) Approve the reimbursement of expenditure by the beneficiaries towards petition filing
fee, and expenditure on publishing of notices in newspapers in terms of Regulation 94
(1) Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff)
Regulations, 2024, and other expenditure (if any) in relation to the filing of petition.
e) Allow the petitioner to bill and recover RLDC fees & charges and Licensee fee
separately from the respondents in terms of Regulation 94 (3) and (4) Central Electricity
Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2024.
f) Allow the petitioner to bill and adjust impact on Interest on Loan due to change in
Interest rate on account of floating rate of interest applicable during 2024-29 period, if
any, from the respondents.
g) Allow the petitioner to file a separate petition before Hon’ble Commission for claiming
the overall security expenses and consequential IOWC on that security expenses as
mentioned at para 21 above.
h) Allow the petitioner to file a separate petition before Hon’ble Commission for claiming
the overall insurance expenses and consequential IOWC on that insurance expenses
as mentioned at para 21 above.
i) Allow the petitioner to file a separate petition before Hon’ble Commission for claiming
the overall capital spares as per actual as mentioned at Para 21 above.
j) Allow the petitioner to claim expenses of CTUIL borne by POWERGRID through a
separate petition as mentioned at para 22 above.
k) Allow the Petitioner to bill and recover GST on Transmission Charges separately from
the respondents, if GST on transmission is levied at any rate in future. Further, any taxes
including GST and duties including cess etc. imposed by any statutory/Govt./municipal
authorities shall be allowed to be recovered from the beneficiaries.
and pass such other relief as Hon’ble Commission deems fit and appropriate under the
circumstances of the case and in the interest of justice.”
Background
3. The brief facts of the case are as follows:
a. The Investment Approval (IA) and expenditure sanction for the transmission
project were accorded by the Board of Directors of the Petitioner in its 266th
meeting held on 23.1.2012, vide Memorandum dated 24.1.2012, at an
estimated cost of ₹142285 lakh, including an IDC of ₹8756 lakh, based on 3rd
Order in Petition No. 635/TT/2025
Page 3 of 46

Quarter 2011 price levels. The Revised Cost Estimate (RCE) for the
transmission project was accorded by the Board of Directors of the Petitioner,
vide Memorandum dated 11.3.2016, at RCE of ₹187513 lakh, including an IDC
of ₹20562 lakh (based on August, 2015 price levels).
b. The scope of work covered under the transmission project is as follows:
