4. The determination of the transmission tariff for the transmission asset from COD
to 31.3.2019 was initially filed under Petition No. 218/TT/2016. The Commission, after
taking into consideration the indicative cost submitted by the Central Transmission
Utility (CTU) for the computation of Point of Connection (PoC) charges, restricted the
capital cost of the transmission lines to ₹3.90 crore/km on a provisional basis and
granted the tariff for the transmission asset vide order dated 18.9.2017 in Petition No.
218/TT/2016.
5. The Petitioner, aggrieved by the aforementioned order dated 18.9.2017 in
Petition No. 218/TT/2016, filed Review Petition No. 42/RP/2017. Subsequently, the
Commission, vide order dated 11.7.2018 in Review Petition No. 42/RP/2017, directed
the Petitioner to file a fresh Petition for determination of the transmission tariff for the
transmission asset for the 2014-19 tariff period.
6. The relevant extracts of the aforementioned order are reproduced below:
Order in Petition No. 635/TT/2025

“14. ….. The Commission has sought certain information/documents in para 18 of the
impugned order. Therefore, we direct the Review Petitioner to file a fresh petition
including all relevant information for determination of tariff of the instant assets in terms
of the directions in this order.”
7. In compliance with the directions in Petition No. 42/RP/2017, the Petitioner filed
Petition No. 30/TT/2019, under which the Commission, vide order dated 28.1.2020,
determined the transmission tariff for the transmission asset from COD to 31.3.2019.
Thereafter, vide order dated 31.12.2021 in Petition No. 27/TT/2021, the Commission
trued up the transmission tariff from COD to 31.3.2019 and determined the transmission
tariff for the 2019-24 tariff period.
8. The Respondents are distribution licensees, transmission licensees, and power
departments, procuring transmission services from the Petitioner, mainly beneficiaries
of the Western Region.
9. The Petitioner has served the Petition on the Respondents, and notice of the
filing of this Petition was published in the newspapers in accordance with Section 64 of
the Electricity Act, 2003. No comments or suggestions have been received from the
general public in response to the notices published in the newspapers by the Petitioner.
10. Madhya Pradesh Power Management Company Limited (MPPMCL),
Respondent No.1, filed its reply vide affidavit dated 15.9.2025, and the Petitioner filed
its rejoinder thereto vide affidavit dated 24.9.2025. In response to the Record of
Proceedings (RoP) dated 30.9.2025, the Petitioner filed an affidavit dated 8.10.2025,
furnishing the requisite information and supporting documents.
11. The hearing in this matter was held on 30.9.2025, and the order was reserved.
This order is issued considering the submissions made by the Petitioner vide affidavits
dated 25.11.2024, 24.9.2025, and 8.10.2025, and the MPPMCL’s submissions made
vide affidavit dated 15.9.2025.

25. MPPMCL, in its reply has submitted that the ACE claimed for FY 2019-20 is
under Regulations 24(1)(a) and 24(1)(b) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations while for the
remaining years of the control period (FY 2020-21 to FY 2023-24), the ACE has been
claimed under Regulation 25(1)(d) of the 2019 Tariff Regulations. It is submitted that
the ACE approved earlier by the Commission in Petition No. 27/TT/2021 for the 2019-
24 tariff period was based on projected costs, whereas the Petitioner is now claiming
ACE based on final invoices and actual payments. MPPMCL prayed that such claims
be scrutinised strictly and be allowed only to the extent admissible under the
Order in Petition No. 635/TT/2025
Page 10 of 46

Regulations. MPPMCL has further submitted that an IDC of ₹29.41 lakh was previously
disallowed by the Commission in the aforementioned order.
26. In response, the Petitioner has submitted that all ACE claims have been made
strictly in accordance with the applicable tariff regulations, and prayed that the same
may be allowed after a prudence check by the Commission.
27. We have considered the submissions of the parties. The ACE claimed during the
2019-24 tariff period on account of undischarged liabilities towards final payment or
withheld payment due to contractual exigencies, and for works executed prior to the
cut-off date, i.e. 31.3.202019 and undischarged liabilities recognized to be payable at a
future date is accordingly permissible for the purpose of tariff under Regulation 25(1)(d)
of the 2019 Tariff Regulations.
28. It is noted that the Liquidated Damages (LD) amounting to ₹271.68 lakh in FY
2021–22, and ₹48.90 lakh in FY 2022-23 were recovered from the contractor. The
Petitioner has submitted that these amounts have already been deducted from the ACE
claimed for the respective years.
29. We are of the view that when the time over-run is attributable to the project

Regulatory Commission (Grant of Connectivity, Long Term Access and Medium-Term

directions in respect of alleged LTOA of 144 MW granted to PTC India Limited in respect
of ‘Free Power’ Share of Government of Sikkim from 1200 MW Teesta-III Hydroelectric

ORDER
PTC India Limited has filed the instant petition under Section 79(1)(f) of the
Electricity Act, 2003 (hereinafter referred to as the “Act”) read with Central Electricity
Regulatory Commission (Grant of Connectivity, Long Term Access and Medium-Term
Open Access in Inter-State Transmission and related matters) Regulations, 2009,
(hereinafter referred to as the “2009 Connectivity Regulations”) seeking for an order that
no LTOA was granted to PTC in respect of the 144 MW free power share of Government
of Sikkim from Teesta-III Hydro Electric Project (hereinafter referred to as the “THEP”) and
to set aside CTUIL’s demand for relinquishment charges in respect of the 144 MW free
power share of Government of Sikkim.
2. The Petitioner is an inter-State trading licensee. Power Grid Corporation of India
Limited (hereinafter referred to as “PGCIL”), Respondent No.1, is a state-owned electricity
utility company in the business of transmission of power and was also performing the
functions of the CTU till CTUIL was notified by the Ministry of Power, Government of India.
Teesta Urja Limited (hereinafter referred to as “TUL”), Respondent No.2, is a generating
company which owns and operates a 1200 MW (2X600MW) HEP located on the Teesta
River in the North District of Sikkim. Government of Sikkim, Respondent No.3, is the State
where the THEP is located and is entitled for 12% free power for the first 15 years and 15%
free power from the 16th to 35th year of THEP. Central Transmission Utility of India Limited
(hereinafter referred to as the “CTUIL”), Respondent No.4, is the Central Transmission
Utility (hereinafter referred to as the “CTU”), as defined in Section 38 of the Act.
Order in Petition No. 699/MP/2020 Page 2

3. The PGCIL was performing the functions of the CTU when the instant petition was
filed by PGCIL. However, during the proceedings in the matter, the Ministry of Power,
Government of India, on 9.3.2021, notified the CTUIL, a Government Company, as the
Central Transmission Utility. Therefore, CTUIL has been impleaded as Respondent No.4
in the matter.
4. The Petitioner has made the following prayers:
“a) Pass an Order that the LTOA was neither granted nor applicable to the Petitioner in
respect of 144 MW free power share of State of Sikkim from Teesta-III HEP;
b) Pass an Order setting aside the demand of the RESPONDENT NO.1 towards
relinquishment charges in respect of the 144 MW free power share of Government of
Sikkim;
c) Pending disposal of the present Petition pass an ad-interim Order restraining the
RESPONDENT NO.1 from taking any coercive action in this regard; and
d) Pass such other and further Order(s) as this Hon’ble Commission may deem fit and
proper under the facts and circumstances of the present case and in the interest of
justice.”
5. The Petition was admitted on 28.5.2021, and notice was issued to the parties. TUL
filed its reply to the petition vide affidavit dated 23.6.2021. PGCIL/ CTU filed its reply to the
petition vide affidavit dated 10.9.2021, and rejoinder to the PGCIL/ CTU’s reply was filed
by the Petitioner vide affidavit dated 11.1.2022. The Department of Power Sikkim, filed its
reply dated 15.6.2023 to the petition. The Petitioner and PGCIL/ CTU were directed to file
certain information vide the RoP dated 29.5.2023. The Petitioner filed the information
sought vide affidavit dated 4.7.2023 and PGCIL/ CTU vide affidavit dated 9.8.2023. The
Petitioner filed written submissions and additional written submissions dated 27.3.2024
and 21.11.2024. The PGCIL/ CTU filed its written submissions dated 16.4.2024.
6. The gist of the submissions made by the Petitioner is as follows:
a. The Petitioner and TUL entered into a Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) on
28.7.2006 for the sale of the entire saleable capacity and electricity generated from
THEP, excluding the auxiliary consumption, free power, transmission and
transformation losses up to the Delivery Point for a period of 35 years from COD
of the project. As per the PPA, the Petitioner was to tie up 70% of the Contracted
Order in Petition No. 699/MP/2020 Page 3

Capacity on a long-term basis through Power Sale Agreements (PSAs) and the
balance 30% of the Contracted Capacity was to be traded by PTC on a short-term
basis, i.e. Merchant Trading.
b. The Petitioner entered into back-to-back PSAs with State Utilities of Punjab (340
MW), Haryana (200 MW), Uttar Pradesh (200 MW) and Rajasthan (100 MW),
whereby 70% of the Contracted Capacity of the Project was tied-up on a long-term
basis in September 2006.
c. The Petitioner on 10.11.2006 made an application to PGCIL/ CTU for LTOA for 35
years for 1032 MW for the first 15 years and 996 MW for the 16th to 35th years. The
LTOA quantum of 1032 MW excludes the 2% auxiliary consumption and 12% (144
MW) of the free power share of the State of Sikkim, as detailed below:
Peak Load to Year 1-15 Year 16 -35
be 1032 MW (after considering 12% 996 MW (after considering 15%
Transferred free power to Sikkim and 2% for free power to Sikkim and 2% for
Auxiliary Consumption & Tie Line Auxiliary Consumption & Tie Line
Losses) Losses)
Name(s) of 1. PSEB – 340 MW
drawee utility 2. HPGCL – 200 MW
3. UPPCL – 200 MW
4. Rajasthan Discoms – 100 MW
5. Balance for Merchant Trading in NR & WR.
d. PGCIL/ CTU on 2.1.2007 informed the Petitioner that the quantum of power to be
transmitted has been indicated as 1032 MW. However, as the full power would be
injected into the grid for onward transmission, the transmission line capacity should
be planned to cater to 1200 MW of power from THEP. Therefore, PGCIL/ CTU is
going ahead with processing the application for long-term open access for the
transfer of 1200 MW to the beneficiaries specified in the application.
e. The Petitioner, vide letter dated 25.1.2007, confirmed that PGCIL/ CTU may take
up detailed studies for identifying the strengthening of the transmission system for
the transfer of power from the Project to Punjab, Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and
Rajasthan Discoms in the Northern Region.
f. The PGCIL/ CTU on 26.5.2009 issued a letter providing LTOA for 25 years to the
Petitioner and nine other Open Access Applicants for generation projects located
in Sikkim.
g. The Petitioner, vide letter dated 30.10.2009, informed PGCIL/ CTU that the
beneficiaries have been finalised in the Northern Region and agreements have
been signed for 840 MW power, and the balance power would be sold on a
Order in Petition No. 699/MP/2020 Page 4

merchant basis in NR and WR. The details of the drawee utilities were furnished
in the LTOA application dated 10.11.2006.
h. The Government of Sikkim, on 19.2.2010, wrote to PGCIL/ CTU stating that after
commissioning of the THEP, it is entitled to avail 12% of free power for the first 15
years and 15% free power from the 16th year till the 35th year. It also stated that
the Government of Sikkim proposes to export free power from THEP to other
regions of the country through PGCIL’s transmission network \. The Government
of Sikkim further stated that it is prepared to enter into a Supplementary Agreement
with PGCIL for transmission of free power from THEP and also requested that a
copy of the draft Supplementary Agreement be provided for execution on a date
convenient to PGCIL.
i. In response, PGCIL/ CTU, on 5.3.2010, sent the draft Agreement to the
Government of Sikkim for execution.
j. PGCIL/ CTU, the Petitioner and the six LTOA applicants of the Sikkim generation
projects entered into a BPTA on 24.2.2010, wherein it was stated that of 1200 MW,
the Petitioner has signed a PPA with State utilities for 840 MW. A separate BPTA
is signed by PGCIL/CTU, and the concerned State utilities and Sikkim will sign a
separate BPTA with PGCIL/CTU for 144 MW. Thus, it was clear to PGCIL/CTU
that it was to sign a separate BPTA with Sikkim for 144 MW of free power.
k. The PGCIL/ CTU, Department of Power of Sikkim and the Petitioner signed a
BPTA on 27.4.2010, wherein the Department of Power of Sikkim agreed to share
and pay the transmission charges directly to PGCIL/ CTU in proportion to their
allocation from THEP and also agreed to provide L/C to PGCIL/ CTU.
l. The Commission, in an order dated 8.2.2016 in Petition No.292/TT/2013, observed
that PGCIL, on affidavit, has stated that the LTOA quantum for THEP is 840 MW.
m. PGCIL/ CTU in its agenda for 12th Connectivity and LTA Meeting of ER dated
21.07.2017 stated that the LTOA quantum for Teesta-III project is 1200 MW. The
Petitioner vide letter dated 28.7.2017, while explaining the sequence of events in
detail, requested PGCIL/ CTU to correct the LTOA quantum for THEP in the
agenda items to 840 MW instead of 1200 MW. In response, PGCIL/CTU, vide letter
dated 6.4.2018, reiterated that the LTOA granted to the Petitioner is 1200 MW and
upon completion and operationalisation of the associated transmission system, the
Petitioner is liable to pay the applicable transmission charges.
n. The Petitioner on 10.10.2018 wrote to the Department of Power of Sikkim with a
copy to PGCIL/ CTU stating that the Teesta-III - Kishanganj 400 kV D/C (Quad)
Order in Petition No. 699/MP/2020 Page 5

line is expected to be commissioned by 30.11.2018, and with commissioning of
this line, the LTA of various beneficiaries of THEP, including Department of Power
of Sikkim will be made effective from 1.12.2018 as per applicable Regulations. The
PGCIL/ CTU was also requested to directly communicate with Sikkim in terms of
the BPTA dated 27.4.2010. On 10.10.2018, PGCIL/CTU wrote to the Petitioner,
with a copy to Sikkim, stating that Sikkim is required to open a confirmed,
irrevocable, unconditional and revolving L/C amounting to ₹148 lakh towards a
payment security mechanism in respect of the 144 MW LTA granted by THEP for
the transfer of power to Sikkim.
o. The Petitioner on 25.10.2018 wrote to PGCIL/ CTU, with a copy to Sikkim, that in
terms of BPTA dated 27.4.2010, PGCIL/ CTU is required to directly communicate
with Sikkim for fulfilling the requirements of LC, etc. The Petitioner further
requested PGCIL/ CTU to take up the matter with Sikkim, as Sikkim is liable to
open the LC and make all payments towards transmission charges for free power
directly to PGCIL/CTU, and PTC has no obligation towards the same. Thereafter,
PGCIL/ CTU on 12.12.2018 wrote to Sikkim to open a confirmed, irrevocable,
unconditional and revolving LC amounting to ₹148 lakh towards payment security
mechanism in respect of 144 MW of LTA granted from THEP for transfer of power
to Sikkim and also informed that the LTA is likely to be made effective from
1.1.2019 upon commissioning of Teesta-III-Kishanganj 400 KV D/C (Quad) line.
p. PGCIL/ CTU on 21.2.2019 wrote to Petitioner with a copy to Sikkim that with the
commissioning of the Teesta-III- Rangpo - Kishanganj line, the entire LTA,
including 144 MW LTA allocated to Sikkim, will be operationalised from 23.2.2019.
The Petitioner, on 21.2.2019, wrote to PGCIL/ CTU with a copy to Sikkim, stating
that in relation to 144 MW LTA for Sikkim, PGCIL/ CTU is already aware that the
corresponding LTA is for Sikkim’s share of free power for which Sikkim has signed
the BPTA with PGCIL. Hence, PTC has no role in the 144 MW LTA in terms of the
BPTA signed with Sikkim. However, as an abundant precaution and without
prejudice to its rights and contention, the Petitioner requested the release of the
unutilized transmission corridor from its side.
q. The PGCIL/ CTU on 6.3.2019 informed PTC that at the request of PTC, the LTOA
grantee, the LTOA of 383 MW, which includes 144 MW of Sikkim, is relinquished
and PTC shall be liable for the payment of relinquishment charges. It further stated
that the Commission, in an order dated 8.3.2019 in Petition No. 92/MP/2015, while
determining the stranded capacity and relinquishment charges, held that the
Order in Petition No. 699/MP/2020 Page 6

relinquishment charges are in the nature of transmission charges. As per the
directions given in order dated 8.3.2019, PGCIL/ CTU on 20.5.2019 published the
details of the stranded capacity and relinquishment charges for various projects,
wherein the relinquishment charges in respect of 144 MW LTA allocated to Sikkim
has been shown in the name of PTC and a compensation amounting to ₹33.04
crore (part of ₹87.88 crore for 383 MW relinquished capacity) has been shown in
the name of PTC.
r. On 30.05.2019, the Petitioner informed Sikkim about the relinquishment charges
of ₹33.04 crore corresponding to the 144 MW LTA allocated to Sikkim and its
obligation to pay the relinquishment charges to PGCIL/ CTU. PGCIL/ CTU
informed the Petitioner on 27.12.2019 that the Petitioner is liable to pay an amount
of ₹209.39 crore towards relinquishment charges for THEP and Budhil HEP.
s. The Petitioner, on 15.1.2020, wrote to PGCIL/ CTU refusing their claim and
reiterated that PTC has no right or obligation over 144 MW of Sikkim’s share of
free power, as it never applied for the LTA of this free power. PGCIL/ CTU, through
its letter dated 12.3.2020, informed that the demand notice dated 27.12.2019 is in
accordance with the Commission’s orders dated 8.3.2019 in Petition No.
92/MP/2015 and 11.12.2019 in Petition No. 252/MP/2019. However, PGCIL/ CTU
did not respond or refute the factual position that the Petitioner never applied for
the LTA Sikkim’s free power share of Sikkim and the Petitioner does not have any
right or obligation over the 144 MW of Sikkim’s share of free power.
t. The LTOA was neither granted nor applicable to the Petitioner in respect of the
144 MW, which was a free power share of Sikkim. Further, the demand of PGCIL/
CTU for relinquishment charges raised vide notice dated 27.12.2019 is totally
arbitrary and illegal.
7. The TUL in its reply stated that the Petitioner entered into a PPA dated 28.7.2006
with TUL for the purchase of the entire 1200 MW saleable power from THEP for its further
sale, after adjusting for auxiliary consumption and free power share of Sikkim. In terms of
Clause 4.2(ix) of the PPA, the Petitioner has undertaken to enter into Long Term Power
Supply Agreements for at least 70% of the contracted capacity. Further, Clause 4.2(x) of
the PPA provides that the Petitioner may enter into Long Term or Short-Term Power Sale
Agreements for the balance of the Contracted Capacity. As per the PPA, it is the obligation
Order in Petition No. 699/MP/2020 Page 7

of PTC to obtain the requisite open access from the ‘Delivery Point’ for supply of the
saleable power to the beneficiaries.
8. The gist of the submissions made by PGCIL/ CTU in its reply is as follows:
a. To evacuate power from the generation projects planned in Sikkim, a comprehensive
transmission system of 2162 MW to the Northern Region and Western Region was
planned. The THEP was one of the generation projects implemented by TUL under
the aforementioned scheme, for which TUL entered into an Agreement with the
Government of Sikkim on 18.7.2005, agreeing to supply a specified percentage of
power to the Government of Sikkim.
b. The Government of Sikkim was responsible for theevacuation of power from the
generating station to the point of consumption as agreed in clause 3.9 read with
clause 4.18 of the above Agreement and to make necessary arrangements. The
evacuation arrangement was permitted on the basis of direct connectivity of the
generating station to the nearest grid sub-station in the State for the supply of free
power from the project to the Government of Sikkim. However, such a system was
never put in place, and the entire power from the project was injected into PGCIL’s
system.
c. Sale of power to be generated from the project was decided to be undertaken
through an intermediate trading licensee, i.e. the Petitioner. Accordingly, the
Petitioner entered into a PPA dated 28.7.2006 with TUL wherein, it was agreed to
purchase at the ‘delivery point’, the entire electricity generated from the THEP
excluding the auxiliary consumption, free power transmission and transmission
losses incurred upto the delivery point i.e. the point of inter-connection with
Government of Sikkim from where open access into the inter-State transmission
system (ISTS) was available as per applicable Regulations.
d. The Petitioner, as a power trader, was to purchase the entire billable power
generated from THEP for onward sale to other entities, which power was to be
delivered at the interconnection point of PGCIL or a transmission licensee and from
there, it was to be carried by the Petitioner or its purchasers through the use of ISTS.
e. Accordingly, the Petitioner on 10.11.2006, approached PGCIL/ CTU for grant of
LTOA into the ISTS for a period of 35 years from the date of commencement of open
access in accordance with the then prevailing Open Access Regulations, i.e. the
Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Open Access in Inter-state
Transmission) Regulations, 2004 (hereinafter referred to as the “2004 Open Access
Order in Petition No. 699/MP/2020 Page 8

Regulations”]. As per the application, the quantum of power to be transmitted during
the entire LTOA period was bifurcated into 2 parts i.e. 1032 MW (for year 1-15 after
considering 12% free power to Sikkim and 2% for auxiliary consumption and tie line
losses) and 996 MW (for year 16-35 after considering 15% free power to Sikkim and
2% for auxiliary consumption and tie line losses). The power was to be injected into
the pooling station of PGCIL at Rangpo/Kishanganj through an integrated
transmission system and was to be drawn by the following utilities in the following
ratio:
(i)Punjab State Electricity Board – 340 MW
(ii)Haryana Power Generation Corporation Ltd. – 200 MW
(iii)Uttar Pradesh Power Corporation Ltd. – 200 MW
(iv)Rajasthan Discoms – 100 MW
(v)balance power for merchant trading in the Northern Region and the
Western Region.
f. The Petitioner also entered into back-to-back PSAs with the drawee utilities. The
2004 Open Access Regulations neither stipulated any provision nor placed any
embargo on the grant of LTOA to a trading licensee on a merchant basis. Fully aware
of this regulatory position, the Petitioner had applied for LTA by including the power
to transact on a merchant basis.
g. PGCIL/ CTU reviewed the Petitioner’s LTOA application and informed that though
the application specified 1032 MW and 996 MW for different periods, the
transmission system has to be planned for the full 1200 MW capacity from THEP
and that the existing grid infrastructure was insufficient and requested confirmation
from the Petitioner to proceed with detailed studies for necessary transmission
system upgrades. After this, the Petitioner confirmed the need for such studies and
paid the required fees. On the basis of the Petitioner’s unequivocal confirmation, the
PGCIL/ CTU conducted detailed system studies and held several meetings
confirming that the system would support the entire 1200 MW. The confirmation is a
clear acknowledgement on the part of the Petitioner that though the LTOA applied
for is 1032MW/996MW, LTOA was required to be granted for the entire 1200 MW.
h. The PGCIL/ CTU on 26.5.2009 granted LTOA to the Petitioner and other LTOA
applicant generators and requested them to give an undertaking to sign the requisite
BPTA for sharing of transmission charges corresponding to their share of power
transfer at the earliest. The LTOA grant clearly stipulated that the LTOA granted to
the Petitioner was for 1200 MW, which included 840 MW for power transfer to the
identified beneficiaries. The transmission system strengthening to be undertaken as
Order in Petition No. 699/MP/2020 Page 9

the dedicated part by generation developers and the common system strengthening
by PGCIL/ CTU was also recorded in the intimation dated 26.5.2009.
i. The LTOA grantees are liable to pay transmission charges and the relinquishment
charges, if any, in accordance with the Regulations. The Petitioner, being the LTOA
grantee for 1200 MW, is responsible for paying all applicable charges, including the
relinquishment charges, and the Petitioner cannot be permitted to resile from the
same.
j. The TUL and the Government of Sikkim agreed that on commissioning of the THEP,
the Government of Sikkim would be entitled to avail free power of 144 MW for the
first 15 years and 180 MW from the 16th to 35th years. The Government of Sikkim
proposed to export the said free power to other regions of the country through the
transmission network of PGCIL and stated that the required transmission charges as
approved by the Commission, and for which it agreed to execute a Supplementary
Agreement with PGCIL/ CTU. PGCIL/ CTU, vide letter dated 5.3.2020, confirmed the
signing of a Supplementary Agreement for payment of transmission charges for
export of free power from THEP to other regions through the use of the PGCIL’s
transmission network.
k. After grant of LTOA to the Petitioner, PGCIL entered into a BPTA with the Petitioner
and six other generators in Sikkim on 24.2.2010, wherein PGCIL/ CTU agreed to
provide open access for a period of 25 years on payment of transmission charges.
The Note in Annexure-1 specifically stated that the total quantum of LTOA granted
to Petitioner was 1200 MW, and out of this 1200 MW, a quantum of 840 MW
corresponded to the tentative beneficiaries with whom the Petitioner had signed
PPAs and that a separate BPTA for 144 MW (out of the 1200MW) was being signed
with the Government of Sikkim.
l. There was thus a categorical contractual recording in the 24.2.2010 BPTA that the
Petitioner was required to pay transmission charges for the LTA quantum of 1200
MW till the said charges are directly paid by the concerned beneficiaries to PGCIL/
CTU. Thus, the Petitioner, being the LTOA grantee, is responsible for paying the
transmission charges, and the said responsibility also extends to payment of
relinquishment charges in accordance with clause 5 of the BPTA. The Agreements
signed by project beneficiaries are to be seen in the context of the above unequivocal
provisions in clause 2, whereunder the Petitioner continues to be liable to discharge
all payment obligations under the BPTA till the charges are paid by the beneficiaries.
The relinquishment charges are payable by the LTOA grantee, i.e., the Petitioner
Order in Petition No. 699/MP/2020 Page 10

and the transmission charges in case of identified beneficiaries who had signed
BPTAs with PGCIL/ CTU are payable by the said beneficiaries.
m. The clause 10.0 read with clause 2.0(a) of the BPTA only recorded a mechanism
adopted for ease of payment of transmission charges, where power sale was taking
place through a power trader like the Petitioner, who had also obtained open access
into the ISTS. The liability to pay transmission charges to PGCIL/ CTU continued to
be the Petitioner’s as the LTOA grantee, and when the beneficiaries sign the BPTAs
with PGCIL/ CTU, the said liability became joint and several, with the primary liability
continuing to be that of the Petitioner as the LTOA grantee. As such, when the LTOA
rights were relinquished, and there was no longer any onward power sale to take

t. The Petitioner was granted LTOA in May 2009 (before the notification of the 2009

22. In response, the Petitioner vide letter dated 30.10.2009 informed PGCIL/ CTU that
the beneficiaries have been finalised in the Northern Region and agreements have been
signed for 840 MW power, and the balance power would be sold on a merchant basis in
NR and WR. The Petitioner also submitted that the details of drawee utilities were
furnished in the LTOA application dated 10.11.2006.
23. A BPTA was entered into by the PGCIL/CTU and seven LTTCs, including the
Petitioner, on 24.2.2010. The BPTA states that the Petitioner applied for a grant of LTOA
of 1200 MW and was granted 840 MW for NR. It is also stated that every LTTC shall share
and bear the applicable transmission charges as decided by the Central Electricity

BPTA are extracted hereunder:
Order in Petition No. 699/MP/2020 Page 26

“E) Each of the project developers i.e. the Long term transmission customer has agreed
to share and bear the applicable transmission charges as decided by Central Electricity
Regulatory Commission of the total transmission scheme as per Annexure-3 from the
scheduled date of commissioning of respective generating units, corresponding to the
capacity of power contracted from the said generation project through open access as
indicated at Annexure- I irrespective of their actual date of commissioning.
xxx

shall pay the applicable transmission charges from the date of commissioning of the

24. The BPTA dated 4.6.2010 between PGCIL/ CTU, the beneficiary Discoms (PSEB,
HPPCL, Rajasthan Discoms and UPPCL), and PTC also states that the capacity is for
1200 MW and gives the details of the beneficiaries from NR (840 MW), Sikkim (144 MW)
and the Petitioner (216 MW). The relevant extract of the BPTA is as follows:
“And whereas PTC is a licensee and is desirous to avail Long Term Open Access
in accordance with CERC (Open Access in Inter-State Transmission) Regulation,
2004 dated 30.1.2004 and Electricity Act 2003 to the transmission system of

(200 MW), Rajasthan DISCOMS (100 MW),

25. A BPTA was entered into between the PGCIL/ CTU, the Department of Power of
Sikkim and the Petitioner on 27.4.2010, and it provides as follows:
Order in Petition No. 699/MP/2020 Page 27

“Name of the Generating Station: Teesta III (Teesta Urja Ltd.) in Sikkim
Capacity : 1200 MW
Beneficiaries : - PSEB (340 MW)
- HPPC (200 MW)
- UPPCL (200 MW)
- Rajasthan DISCOMS (100 MW)
- SIKKIM - 144 MW (12% fee power) for the first 15
years and 180 MW (15% free power) from the 16th
year onwards.
- PTC (Balance 216 MW for the first 15 years and
180 MW from the 16th year onwards)”
26. The PGCIL/ CTU has contended that the Petitioner was aware since 2007 that the
Petitioner was granted LTOA for 1200 MW and has not contested the same, and for the
first time in 2017, vide letter dated 28.7.2017, contended that the Petitioner was granted
LTOA only for 840 MW. PGCIL/ CTU has further contended that the Petitioner, vide its
letter dated 21.2.2019, relinquished the LTOA in respect of the free power granted to
Sikkim; therefore, the Petitioner is liable to pay the relinquishment charges. Per contra,
the Petitioner has contended that it cannot be granted LTOA for a quantum which was not
applied for by the Petitioner. In this regard, the Petitioner has placed reliance on the
Commission’s orders dated 16.10.2015 in Petition No.210/MP/2014, 20.11.2019 in Petition
No. 265/MP/2018 and 23.3.2017 in Petition No.76/MP/2014.
27. PGCIL/ CTU has contended that the Petitioner has relinquished the LTOA of 144 MW
of free power to Sikkim and therefore is liable to pay the relinquishment charges. In
response, the Petitioner has submitted that in view of the PGCIL/ CTU’s persistent
assertion regarding the grant of LTOA to the Petitioner and as a precautionary measure, it
requested PGCIL/ CTU to release the 144 MW LTOA from its end on the transmission
corridor. The Petitioner further submitted that this does not mean that the Petitioner is liable
to bear the transmission charges for the said quantum of LTOA.
28. CTUIL has also submitted that the Commission, in an order dated 5.4.2022 in Petition
No.394/MP/2018, has already held that the Petitioner was granted 1200 MW of LTA, which
includes 216 MW of merchant power and 144 MW of free power to Sikkim. The Petitioner
has submitted that there was no such clear finding in the order dated 5.4.2022.
Order in Petition No. 699/MP/2020 Page 28

29. We have considered the submissions made by the Petitioner and PGCIL/ CTU and
perused the order dated 5.4.2022 in Petition No.394/MP/2018. The Commission, in order
dated 5.4.2022, while dealing with the issue of whether the Petitioner was granted LTOA
for the balance quantum of 216 MW, taking into consideration the sequence of events and
the various BPTAs entered into by the Petitioner and the PGCIL/ CTU, held that the
Petitioner applied for LTOA for 1200 MW, which included the free power to Sikkim for which
a separate BPTA was signed on 27.4.2010. The relevant portions of the Commission’s
order dated 5.4.2022 are as follows:
“41. Perusal of above BPTA dated 24.2.2010 reveals that the Petitioner had applied
LTOA for 1200 MW and PPAs signed by PTC with state utilities were for 840 MW for which
separate BPTAs were to be signed by PSEB, HPGCL, UPPCL, Rajasthan Discoms and
Sikkim.”
42. BPTA dated 4.6.2010 signed by the Petitioner with the CTUIL and the beneficiaries
(PSEB, HPPCL, Rajasthan Discoms and UPPCL) provides as under:
“And whereas PTC is a licensee and is desirous to avail Long Term Open Access
in accordance with CERC (Open Access in Inter-State Transmission) Regulation,
2004 dated 30.1.2004 and Electricity Act 2003 to the transmission system of
POWERGRID as per the following details:
Name of the Generating Station: Teesta III (Teesta Urja Ltd.) in Sikkim
Capacity: 1200 MW
Beneficiaries:PSEB (340 MW), HPPC (200 MW), UPPCL (200 MW),
Rajasthan DISCOMS (100 MW), SIKKIM (144 MW), Balance
(216 MW) – PTC
Open Access is granted for a period of 25 years.”
43. Further, a separate BPTA was signed between the Petitioner, CTUIL and Power
Department of Sikkim on 27.4.2010. The relevant extract of the said BPTA dated
27.04.2010 is as under:
“Name of the Generating Station: Teesta III (Teesta Urja Ltd.) in Sikkim
Capacity: 1200 MW
Beneficiaries: - PSEB (340 MW)
- HPPC (200 MW)
- UPPCL (200 MW)
- Rajasthan DISCOMS (100 MW)
- SIKKIM - 144 MW (12% fee power) for the first 15 years and
180 MW (15% free power) from 16th year onwards.
- PTC (Balance 216 MW for the first 15 year and 180 MW for
16th year onwards)
Open Access is granted for a period of 25 years.”
44. We observe that in the above mentioned LTOA grant and the BPTAs signed, the
Order in Petition No. 699/MP/2020 Page 29

LTOA granted was for 1200 MW, which also included free power to Sikkim for which
separate BPTA was signed on 27.04.2010.”
30. In view of the above finding in the order dated 5.4.2022, we hold that the Petitioner
applied for 1200 MW and was allotted LTOA for 1200 MW, including 144 MW of the free
power allotted to Sikkim.
31. The Department of Power of Sikkim has submitted that the 2009 Connectivity
Regulations are applicable in its case, according to which no LTOA could be granted
without disclosing information in the LTOA application regarding the entity to whom the
electricity was to be supplied under the 2009 Connectivity Regulations. It has been further
submitted that Sikkim bears no financial responsibility for the grant or the relinquishment
of LTOA, as it has neither applied for LTOA nor relinquished any LTOA.
32. We have considered the submissions of the Department of Power, Sikkim. The
Commission, in an order dated 5.4.2022 in Petition No.394/MP/2018, held that the
Petitioner was granted LTOA under the 2004 Open Access Regulations. Therefore,
Sikkim’s contention that the Petitioner was granted open access under the 2009
Connectivity Regulations is not correct. The relevant portion of the order dated 5.4.2022 is
as follows:
“51. It is evident from the Clause 22.3 of the Detailed Procedure that the said
provision is applicable to the new applications being made under the Connectivity
Regulations on or after the same has come into force and is not applicable to
petitioner who was granted LTOA under 2004 Open Access Regulations.”
33. As regards the transmission charges and relinquishment charges in respect of the
free power allotted to Sikkim, the Department of Power of Sikkim, the Government of
Sikkim on 19.2.2010 wrote to PGCIL/ CTU stating that after commissioning of the THEP,
it is entitled to avail 12% of free power for first 15 years and 15% free power from the 16th
year till the 35th year and it proposes to export the free power from THEP to other regions
of the country through the transmission network of PGCIL. The Government of Sikkim
further stated that it is prepared to enter into a Supplementary Agreement with PGCIL for
Order in Petition No. 699/MP/2020 Page 30

1. (a) SIKKIM shall share and pay the transmission charges including FERV, incentive,
taxes ULDC/NLDC charges including charges for interregional links (if any) etc. of
the system strengthening scheme (indicated at Encl. 2) for above Open Access in
proportion to their allocation from Teesta-III Project from its date of commercial
operation in accordance with the norms/notifications/terms and conditions issued by
CERC from time to time.
(b) SIKKIM shall also share and pay the applicable regional transmission charges
of concerned region(s) including Inter-regional links if any, for above Open Access
in proportion to their allocation from Teesta-III Project.”
35. It is clear on perusal of the Government of Sikkim’s letter dated 19.2.2010 and the
subsequent BPTA between the Department of Power, Sikkim, the Petitioner and PGCIL/
CTU dated 27.4.2010, that Sikkim has unequivocally consented to bear the transmission
charges, including FERV, incentive, taxes, ULDC/ NLDC charges in respect of the open
access in proportion to the free power allocation to it from THEP from the date of
commercial operation of the transmission system, directly to PGCIL/ CTU in accordance
with the Commission’s orders.
36. The Commission, in an order dated 8.3.2019 in Petition No.92/MP/2015, held that the
relinquishment charges are in the nature of transmission charges. The relevant portion of
the order dated 8.3.2019 is as follows:
“84. Regulation 15 provides that the grantee of the long term access would be required to
sign a long term access agreement with the CTU if LTA is granted by CTU. A tripartite long
term access agreement is required to be signed with the CTU and inter-State transmission
licensee where the long term access to the transmission system of the inter-State licensee is
involved. Regulation 9 (2) provides that the medium term open access shall be granted if the
resultant power flow can be accommodated in the existing transmission system or the
transmission system under execution. Regulation 26 of the Connectivity Regulations
provides that the transmission charges for the use of the inter-State transmission system
shall be recovered from the long term customers and medium term customers in accordance
with the terms and conditions of the tariff specified by the Commission from time to time. It is
evident from the above that on receipt of the application for long term access, CTU is required
to carry out a system study to ascertain the requirement for system augmentation. The long
term access can be granted to the applicant either with the available transmission system or
with such addition to the existing transmission system as is required. Further, the applicant
who is granted long term access is required to pay the transmission charges for the use of
the ISTS throughout the term of the long term access as either the existing transmission
capacity is earmarked or the new capacity is augmented for the applicant. Whenever a long
term transmission customer relinquishes the long term access rights and obligations, it
ceases to pay the transmission charges for the use of the ISTS. Therefore, Regulation 18
requires that upon such relinquishment, the transmission charges at the specified rates are
payable for servicing of the transmission assets. Relinquishment charges are therefore, in
the nature of transmission charges which the relinquishing long term customer would have
paid had it continued as long term customer of ISTS under the access rights availed by it.
The relinquishment charges in effect is an accelerated payment of the share of the
transmission charges by the relinquishing long term customers to service the transmission
Order in Petition No. 699/MP/2020 Page 32

assets of the ISTS. Therefore, Regulation 18 is inconformity with the provisions of Section 38
(2) (d) (i) and Section 40 (c) of the Act which categorically provides for non-discriminatory
open access to the transmission system of CTU and other inter-State transmission licensees
on payment of transmission charges. The contention of some of the respondents that
Regulation 18 of the Connectivity Regulations is de-hors the provisions of Section 38 (2) (d)
(i) and Section 40 (c) of the Act is clearly misplaced and is liable to be rejected.”
37. In view of the above discussion, we are of the view that the Energy and Power
Department, Government of Sikkim, is liable to pay the relinquishment charges, which are
akin to transmission charges, with respect to the open access for free power allocated to
Sikkim from THEP to PGCIL/ CTU. However, the Commission has already held that the
LTA of 1200 MW was allotted to the Petitioner. Therefore, the Petitioner is liable to pay the
relinquishment charges in respect of 144 MW free power share of the Government of
Sikkim to CTU, and the same will be reimbursed by the Energy and Power Department,
Government of Sikkim, to PTC. The Commission has approved a similar procedure for the
payment of relinquishment charges, initially by PTC and subsequently reimbursed by
Haryana Discoms (one of the beneficiaries of THEP), as per the order dated 22.11.2022
in Petition No. 110/MP/2019. The relevant portion of the order dated 22.11.2022 is as
follows:
“Issue No.(C): Whether the Petitioner PTC is liable for payment of all charges including
relinquishment charges to Respondent PGCIL?
xxxx
57. The Petitioner, PTC has relied upon the above clauses to contend that the beneficiaries
are liable to pay the transmission charges etc., directly to PGCIL in proportion to their
allocation. This has been objected to by the Respondent PGCIL stating that the Petitioner
PTC, as LTA grantee, on behalf of the Respondent Haryana Utilities, is primarily responsible
for the payment of transmission/ relinquishment charges. It is noticed that in the present
case, the Respondent PGCIL, based on the application of the Petitioner PTC, had granted
LTA on 26.5.2009, with a request to sign the BPTA for sharing of transmission charges
corresponding to their share of power. Though, in terms of the BPTA dated 4.6.2010, the
beneficiaries had undertaken to open LC and also pay the transmission charges etc., is
noticed that the Petitioner PTC, vide its letter dated 22.2.2019 sought to relinquish the
subject LTA and the same was accepted by the Respondent PGCIL vide its letter dated
6.3.2019, with accompanied liability towards the payment of relinquishment charges. In this
background and keeping in view that the Petitioner PTC, as an LTA grantee has
relinquished the subject LTA, we hold that the Petitioner, PTC is liable to pay the
relinquishment charges to the Respondent PGCIL for the subject LTA for 200 MW.
58. …..It is pertinent to mention that the Commission vide its order dated 8.3.2019 in Petition
No. 92/MP/2015 had held that the relinquishing long-term customers are liable to pay
Order in Petition No. 699/MP/2020 Page 33

compensation (relinquishment charges) as per methodology specified in the said order. The
relevant portion of the said order is extracted below:
“160. The relinquishing LTA customers are directed to deposit the relinquishment
charges calculated and billed by CTU, within a period of three months of raising the
bill by CTU. CTU is directed to calculate the stranded capacity and the
compensation (relinquishment charges) payable by each relinquishing long-term
customer as per methodology specified in this Order respectively within one month
of date of issue of this Order and publish the same on its website.”
59. The Commission in the said order had clarified that the relinquishment charges are in
the nature of transmission charges. Therefore, the Petitioner cannot absolve itself of its
liability to pay the relinquishment charges. Having said so, we notice that Clause 9.1.1 (iv)
of the PSA, as quoted below, provides that the Purchasers shall pay to Petitioner PTC,
amounts, amongst others, transmission charges, RLDC/SLDC charges or other applicable
charges that may be payable by PTC for use of the transmission system from the Delivery
Point to the Purchasers point of drawl for selling purchaser Contracted Power to the
Purchaser.
“9.1 GENERAL
9.1.1 The Purchasers shall pay to PTC, the payments comprising: xxxxx (ii) Xxxxx;
and (iii) Any transmission open access charges pursuant to CERC inter-state
transmission Regulations viz., transmission charges, RLDC/SLDC charges or other
applicable charges that may be payable by PTC for use of the transmission system
from the Delivery Point to the Purchasers point of drawl for selling purchaser
Contracted Power to the Purchaser.
Xxxxx “
60. Similarly, Clause 4.2 (iii) of the PSA (as stated in para 35 above) obligates the
Purchasers to pay the amounts for obtaining and maintaining long term open access for the
transmission of power. On a harmonious reading of the provisions of the PPA /PSA and the
orders of this Commission, it is evident that the responsibility of making payment of the
transmission charges, including relinquishment charges to the Respondent PGCIL, in
respect of the subject LTA, is with the Petitioner PTC. Needless to say, the charges paid by
the Petitioner PTC, shall however be reimbursable by the Respondent Haryana Utilities, as
the subject LTA obtained by the Petitioner PTC, is on behalf of the Purchaser(s). We direct
accordingly. Issue (C) is disposed of accordingly.”
38. Accordingly, the Petitioner’s prayer for setting aside PGCIL/ CTU’s demand for
relinquishment charges in respect of the 144 MW free power share of the Energy and
Power Department, Government of Sikkim, is rejected. PTC shall pay the relinquishment
charges as worked out by PGCIL in accordance with the methodology specified by the
Commission in the order dated 8.3.2019 in Petition No.92/MP/2015 to PGCIL, and the
same shall be reimbursed by the Energy and Power Department, Government of Sikkim,
to PTC.
Order in Petition No. 699/MP/2020 Page 34

39. Accordingly, Petition No. 699/MP/2020 is disposed of in terms of the above.

ORDER
The instant Petition has been filed by Power Grid Corporation of India Limited
(PGCIL), a deemed transmission licensee, for truing up the transmission tariff for the
2019-24 tariff period under the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and
Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2019 (hereinafter referred to as “the 2019 Tariff
Regulations”) and for the determination of the transmission tariff for the 2024-29 tariff
period under the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of
Tariff) Regulations, 2024 (hereinafter referred to as “the 2024 Tariff Regulations”) in
Page 3 of 39

respect of the following assets (hereinafter referred to as the “Combined Assets”) under
“Transmission System associated with Meja TPS” in the Northern Region (hereinafter
referred to as “the transmission project”):
Asset-1(a): 400 kV Meja-Allahabad Line-I along with 01 number 400 kV
Allahabad bay; and
Asset-1(b): 400 kV Meja-Allahabad Line-II along with 01 number 400 kV
Allahabad bay;
2. The Petitioner has made the following prayers in the instant petition:
“a) Approve the trued-up Transmission Tariff for 2019-24 block and Transmission
Tariff for 2024-29 block for the assets covered under this petition, as per para 15
and 16 above.
b) Admit the capital cost claimed and additional capitalization incurred during 2019-
24.
c) Allow the petitioner to recover the shortfall or refund the excess Annual Fixed
Charges, on account of Return on Equity due to change in applicable Minimum
Alternate/Corporate Income Tax rate as per the Income Tax Act, 1961 (as
amended from time to time) of the respective financial year directly without
making any application before the Commission as provided in Tariff Regulations,
2019 and Tariff Regulations, 2024 as per para 15 and 16 above for respective
block.
d) Approve the reimbursement of expenditure by the beneficiaries towards petition
filing fee, and expenditure on publishing of notices in newspapers in terms of
Regulation 94 (1) Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and
Conditions of Tariff) Regulations, 2024, and other expenditure (if any) in relation
to the filing of petition.
e) Allow the petitioner to bill and recover RLDC fees & charges and Licensee fee
separately from the respondents in terms of Regulation 94 (3) and (4) Central
Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations,
2024.
f) Allow the petitioner to bill and adjust impact on Interest on Loan due to change in
Interest rate on account of floating rate of interest applicable during 2024-29
period, if any, from the respondents.
g) Allow the petitioner to file a separate petition before Hon’ble Commission for
claiming the overall security expenses and consequential IOWC on that security
expenses as mentioned at para 22 above.
h) Allow the petitioner to file a separate petition before Hon’ble Commission for
claiming the overall insurance expenses and consequential IOWC on that
insurance expenses as mentioned at para 22 above.
i) Allow the petitioner to file a separate petition before Hon’ble Commission for
claiming the overall capital spares as per actual as mentioned at Para 22 above.

ORDER
Background
Petition No.15/2010 was filed by the Petitioner, NLC India Limited (in short’
NLCIL), seeking the Commission`s intervention and direction to the Respondent
KSEBL, to clear the outstanding income tax dues amounting to Rs. 119.09 crore, as
on 31.3.2009, and the Commission, by its order dated 20.9.2012, disposed of the
same, as under:
“16. NLC has claimed that it availed of the benefit of tax holiday under Section 80 IA
of the IT Act with effect from the year 2007-08 and passed on the benefit to KSEB as
mandated by the regulations. In view of this claim of NLC, no income-tax liability
accrues on KSEB for the years 2007-08 and 2008-09. Therefore, the question of
recovery of income-tax dues for these two years also does not-arise. We conclude
our findings by stating that income-tax liability in respect of TPS-I Expansion did not
accrue for the years 2003-04, 2004-05, 2005-06 and 2006-07 for want of taxable
income and for the years 2007-08 and 2008-09 because of availing the tax holiday
benefit. In view of these findings, the question whether NLC was obligated to avail
the benefit of Section 80 IA from the date of commissioning of TPS-I Expansion does
not survive for our examination.
17. During the course of hearing it was submitted on behalf of NLC that even though
the tax benefit has already been passed on by NLCIL to the beneficiaries, the
Order in Petition No. 2/MP/2014 (on remand) Page 2 of 34

assessing officer in his assessment order dated 28.12.2010 has disallowed its claim
for tax benefit under Section 80 IA in respect of TPS-I Expansion for the financial
year 2007-08 on the ground that the generating station was only an expansion of the
then existing capacity and could not be considered as a separate undertaking as
provided under Section 80 IA (4) (iv) of the IT Act. In case, NLC becomes liable to
pay income-tax on account of unavailability of benefit under Section 80 IA, it shall be
entitled to recover from KSEBL the income-tax along surcharge, interest etc paid to
the Income-tax Department.
18. We have held that NLC is not entitled to recovery of income-tax dues in respect
of TPS-I Expansion up to 31.3.2009. In view of this, there is justifiably no reason for
KSEB to withhold income-tax dues for TPS-IL NLC has alleged that KSEB has been
withholding income-tax dues in respect of TPS-II amounting to ` 57.00 crore included
in the total amount of 119.0935 crore. We direct that KSEB shall release such
withheld income-tax dues amounting to 57.00 crore pertaining to TPS-II along with
interest at the rate of 9% per annum from June 2007 within 30 days upon NLC
furnishing the claim, duly supported by the statutory auditors' certificate.
19. We have held that NLC is not entitled to recovery of income-tax dues in respect
of TPS-I Expansion up to 31.3.2009. In view of this, there is justifiably no reason for
KSEB to withhold income-tax dues for TPS-II. NLC has alleged that KSEB has been
withholding income-tax dues in respect of TPS-II amounting to `57.00 crore included
in the total amount of Rs.119.0935 crore. We direct that KSEB shall release such
withheld income-tax dues amounting to `57.00 crore pertaining to TPS-II along with
interest at the rate of 9% per annum from June 2007 within 30 days upon NLC
furnishing the claim, duly supported by the statutory auditors’ certificate.”
2. Aggrieved by the order dated 20.9.2012, NLCIL filed Appeal No.250/2012 before
the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity (in short ‘APTEL’), and the APTEL vide its
judgment dated 3.7.2013 disposed of the said appeal, as under:
“19. Even if the Appellant has availed tax benefit under Section 80-I A in respect of
TPS-I Expansion from FY 2007-08, there was no taxable income for TPS-I
Expansion during 2004-05 to 2006-07. Thus, the tax paid by the Appellant during
these years as generating company could not be distributed to TPS-I Expansion for
recovery from the beneficiaries of TPS-I Expansion as per the Tariff Regulations.
20. The Appellant might have set off the profit of its other generating station during
the period 2004-05 to 2006-07 for computing its tax liability under the Income Tax
Act for payment of tax as a generating company, but the total tax has to be
distributed amongst the various generating stations as per the Tariff Regulations i.e.
as per the station-wise profit before tax. Since there was no profit in TPS-I Expansion
in the years from 2003-04 to 2006-07 in view of the huge accumulated loss in FY
2003-04, there is no question of any income tax being apportioned to TPS-I
Expansion during this period.”
3. Pursuant to the above APTEL judgment, the liability of the Respondent
beneficiaries to reimburse the tax, as per the provisions of Regulation 7 of the 2024
Tariff Regulations, was to be determined, taking in into account the applicability of the
tax holiday, provided under Section 80IA of the Income Tax Act, 1961 (in short ‘IT Act’)
Order in Petition No. 2/MP/2014 (on remand) Page 3 of 34

for TPS-I Expansion Project, for the period 2003-04 to 2006-07. Accordingly, NLCIL
vide its letter dated 28.11.2013, reworked the amount to be reimbursed by the
Respondents, including KSEBL, on the basis of the APTEL’s judgment, to the extent
the same related to TPS-I Expansion Project. However, the Respondent, KSEBL vide
letter dated 7.12.2013, disputed the claim of NLCIL with regard to the determination of
the amount due to KSEBL of Rs 20.31 crore, stating that the same was not in
compliance with the Commission’s decision, as upheld vide APTEL’s judgment. In this
backdrop, NLCIL has filed the present Petition under Section 79(1)(f) of the Electricity
Act, 2003 seeking (i) adjudication of the disputes raised by KSEBL with regard to the
implementation of the Commission’s order and upheld by APTEL vide its judgment
dated 3.7.2013; and (ii) a declaration that KSEBL and other Respondents are entitled
to the adjustment of an amount of Rs 5829.27 lakh and in the proportion, as contained
therein. However, the Commission vide its order dated 9.9.2016, disposed of the said
Petition as under:
“13. The difference between the original claim and the revised claim drawn up in
compliance with the Commission's order and judgement of Appellate Tribunal,
amounting to 5829.26 lakh (97570.78 lakh-91741.52 lakh) was appropriated between
the beneficiaries according to their allocation of power.
14. In view of the above, in our opinion the points raised by KSEB and other
respondents do not warrant any intervention as the same is in line with APTEL
judgement dated 03.07.2013 in Appeal No. 250/2012 Accordingly, the parties should
act in accordance with Revised IT reimbursement claim duly certified by auditor as
submitted by the petitioner.”
4. Aggrieved by the Commission’s order dated 9.9.2016, the Respondent KSEBL
filed an appeal (Appeal No. 138/2017) before the APTEL, and APTEL vide its judgment
dated 26.3.2025, observed as under.
“18. It is, therefore, evident that in the final analysis of the case, the Commission
neither referred to the contentions raised by the beneficiaries including Appellant-
KSEB nor discussed the same. It has, after reiterating the submissions of the NLC,
merely stated in one line that in the opinion of the Commission, the points raised by
the KSEB Land other respondents do not warrant any intervention. We find that the

h) Without prejudice to the above, in the event that there is bar placed on the

core business can be recovered from the beneficiaries. Further, the first Proviso

such other income shall be payable by the generating company.

u) It is clear that post-amendment, the term ‘any industrial undertaking’ is no longer
broad or open to interpretation. The benefit under Section 80 IA was therefore
restricted to the eligible business of generation or generation and distribution of
power, as specified under clause (iv) of Section 80IA (4). Therefore, NLCIL has
rightly not claimed Section 80 IA deduction for Mine I Expansion, which was
commissioned during the year 2004-05, after the amendment came into effect, as
the deduction was not allowable only against an undertaking engaged in
generation or generation and distribution of power.
v) The income tax assessment order dated 28.12.2010, for the assessment year
2008-09, rejected the claim for Section 80 IA deduction for TPS-I power project.
As regards the ITAT order dated 11.4.2012 in DCIT v NLC, relied upon by KSEBL,
the same has no applicability to the facts of the present case as (i) the said order
is for the integrated mine of TPS Stage -II (commissioned during 1993) and not for
TPS-I Expansion (commissioned during 2003-after amendment), (ii) the issue
dealt with was to the appeal filed by the Revenue Dept for re-assessment of the
year 2002-03, which was not allowed. Moreover, the issue as to whether Section
80 IA benefits are applicable to the mining component or not was never decided
in the above matter. Hence, no reliance can be placed by KSEBL on the said
decision.
Analysis and Decision
Re: Jurisdiction
10. KSEBL has contended that the disputes pertaining to mining activities fall within
the domain of the MoC, GoI and therefore, the issues surrounding the reimbursement
of income tax from mining activities also sought to be instituted before the appropriate
forum, i.e., the MoC and not before the authorities presiding over Electricity matters.
While pointing out that the income tax reimbursement in lignite mining is distinct from
that for power generation, KSEBL has argued that NLCIL ought to have agitated its
claims falling under the former category before the appropriate authority. Accordingly,
KSEBL has submitted that this Commission lacks the jurisdiction to pass an order in a
matter purely related to mining activity. Per contra, NLCIL has contended that till the
Order in Petition No. 2/MP/2014 (on remand) Page 16 of 34

year 2019, the lignite transfer price was computed in terms of the MoC guidelines and
the same was duly placed before this Commission, which then passed appropriate
orders for its recovery from the beneficiaries during the tariff determination/truing up
process. Referring to Section 79(1)(a) of the Electricity Act 2003, NLCIL has submitted
that the Central Commission is competent to adjudicate the tariff-related disputes
involving the generating companies owned and controlled by the Central Government,
and therefore, the present dispute falls within the scope of this Commission.
11. We have examined the rival submissions. It is an admitted fact that the lignite
transfer price was decided by the Board of Directors of NLCIL and approved by the
MoC, the nodal Ministry. Though the Commission, vide its order dated 4.1.2000 in
Petition No.2/1999, recognised that the mining activities fall under the regulatory
jurisdiction of the MoC, GoI, it had, vide order dated 21.12.2000 in Petition No.4/2000,
while considering the norms for fixation of energy charges, felt the need to review the
transfer price mechanism on the premise that the ultimate cost of power charged to
the consumer is fair and reasonable and also directed NLCIL to furnish the details of
the transfer price mechanism for the Commission’s examination. The relevant portion
of the order is extracted below:
“5.2.2 The situation is different in the case of NLC wherein they operate an integrated
lignite mine. NLC has explained that lignite can neither be stored in large quantities
nor can it be transported over long distances. Accordingly, the mining operations are
totally matched with the requirements of the thermal power stations which are
located very close to the mines. This being so, NLC is following a transfer price
mechanism for arriving at the variable charge. In view of the peculiar situation in
which NLC is operating, the Commission would have liked to review the transfer
price mechanism so that the ultimate cost of power charged to the customer is fair
and reasonable.
5.2.3 In the meantime, the present system of transfer price mechanism may continue
to be followed. The Commission intends to examine the same in future and directs
NLC to furnish the details of transfer price mechanism for the Commission’s
examination at the time of submission of tariff petition.”
12. Thereafter, the Commission vide its order dated 3.5.2005 in Petition No.5/2002
(relating to the tariff of NLCIL TPS-II for the period 2001-04) observed as under:
Order in Petition No. 2/MP/2014 (on remand) Page 17 of 34

“5. The petitioner is the producer of lignite and also the generator of electricity
using this lignite. The Commission is mandated by law to ensure transparency in its
operations. The Commission, in the matter of fixation of tariff for sale of power is also
guided by the consumer interest under Section 61(d) of the Electricity Act. Therefore,
its is not only desirable, but also essential to consider the aspect of the transfer price
of lignite, used as an input for power generation by the petitioner itself…”
13. However, as the disagreement over the lignite transfer price persisted even after
NLCIL worked out the lignite transfer price, based on the principles decided by MoC,
the Commission vide its order dated 25.4.2006, had constituted a one-member Bench
to consider the question of lignite transfer price and make appropriate
recommendations to the Commission for its consideration. Accordingly, after
considering the recommendations dated 8.1.2007 of the Bench on various issues
connected with the determination of the lignite transfer price, and the objections/
comments of the parties, the Commission, vide order dated 23.3.2007 in Petition
No.5/2002, worked out the lignite transfer price for the period 2001-04. The lignite
transfer price computed by NLCIL in terms of the MoC guidelines is placed before this
Commission during the tariff determination process for the NLCIL stations, and orders
are passed by this Commission for the recovery of the same from the beneficiaries,
including KSEBL. Thus, while the mining activities themselves are regulated by MoC
GoI, the determination and approval of the lignite transfer price, including income tax
and other related costs incurred on mining, form part of the input cost to power
generation and accordingly fall within the jurisdiction of this Commission. In other
words, the Commission does not regulate or interfere with the mining operations, but
has the authority to decide on tariff-related components, of which the transfer price of
lignite is a key element. Further, Section 79(1)(a) of the Electricity Act stipulates that
the Central Commission shall regulate the tariff of generating companies owned or
controlled by the Central Government. Section 178 of the Electricity Act confers power
on the Central Commission to frame regulations. Accordingly, this Commission, in
exercise of the said power, notified the 2001 Tariff Regulations and the 2004 Tariff
Order in Petition No. 2/MP/2014 (on remand) Page 18 of 34

Regulations, applicable for the periods 2001-04 and 2004-09 respectively. In terms of
Regulation 2.12 of the 2001 Tariff Regulations, tax on income from the core activity of
the generating company, if any, is to be computed as an expense and shall be
recoverable by the generating company from the beneficiaries. Similarly, Regulation
10 of the 2004 Tariff Regulations, NLCIL is entitled to recover income tax and FERV
from the beneficiaries without making any application before the Commission.
However, in case of any objection by the beneficiaries to the amounts claimed on
account of Income Tax, NLCIL can make an appropriate application before the
Commission for its decision. It is noticed that KSEBL had filed Petition No.
532/MP/2020 before this Commission seeking intervention on the Lignite Transfer
Price fixed by NLCIL for the period 2019-24 (since MoC vide letter dated 24.6.2019
intimated that NLCIL’s Board can, in consultation with the stakeholders decide the
Lignite Transfer Pricing with effect from 1.4.2019) and had prayed, amongst others,
for a direction on NLCIL to strictly follow the guidelines of MoC for fixing the Lignite
Transfer Price for 2019-24, including a direction to follow the Lignite Transfer Price of
2018-19 till the Lignite Transfer Prices are re-fixed by this Commission. This Petition
was disposed of by this Commission directing NLCIL to keep the MoC guidelines in
abeyance and to continue to consider the Lignite Transfer Price based on the MoC
Guidelines dated 2.1.2015, till the regulations for Lignite Transfer Price are notified.
Thus, KSEBL, having acknowledged the jurisdiction of this Commission, cannot now
argue that the dispute regarding the income tax reimbursement cannot be adjudicated
by this Commission. We also note that the question of this Commission having no
jurisdiction to adjudicate the Income Tax related issues came up for consideration in
the Writ Appeal No. 3699/2024 filed by TNPDCL before the Hon’ble High Court of
Madras and the Hon’ble Court, after relying upon the provisions of the Regulation 2.12
of the 2001 Tariff Regulations and Regulation 10 of the 2004 Tariff Regulations,
Order in Petition No. 2/MP/2014 (on remand) Page 19 of 34

Section 79(1)(a) of the Electricity Act and the APTEL judgment dated 10.9.2010 in
Appeal No. 49/2010 (TNEB vs. NLC), vide its order dated 9.4.2025, upheld the
jurisdiction of this Commission to adjudicate the Income Tax disputes, as extracted as
under:
“18. Moreover, the power of CERC is traceable, in view of Sections 79 and 178 of
the Electricity Act and under the Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (Terms
and Conditions of Tariff) Regulations. Income tax claim is a component of tariff and
therefore the CERC is empowered to adjudicate the tax related issues, which is
falling under Section 79(1)(a) of the Electricity Act. Thus the power of CERC is
traceable and the petition already filed by the N.L.C. India Limited was disposed
of merely on the ground that the writ petitions are pending before various High
Courts. Pertinently, liberty was granted to the second respondent to file a fresh
petition. That being so, the apprehension of the appellant is unnecessary and the
TANGEDCO is at liberty to participate in the process of adjudication, if any petition
has been instituted by the generating company and resolve the issues in the
manner known to law.
19. Beyond the grounds, disputed facts of this nature require elaborate
adjudication by the CERC. The High Court may not be in a position to conduct
roving enquiry, since it requires adjudication of facts with reference to the
documents and evidences. Even under the scheme of the Electricity Act and the
Regulations framed by the CERC, tax related claims are the components of tariffs
and thus the writ Court is right in relegating the parties to approach the CERC for
effective adjudication and to resolve the issues in the manner known to law. In the
event of filing any petition by the generating company, the CERC is requested to
dispose of the same by affording opportunity to the parties, as expeditiously as
possible, considering the fact that the income tax claim is relating to several
assessment years and the claim is pending for long period.”
14. In the light of the above discussion, we reject the contentions of KSEBL and hold
that this Commission has the jurisdiction to adjudicate the issues relating to Income
tax reimbursement in the present case.
Re: Deduction under Section 80 IA of the IT Act
15. KSEBL has submitted that, as per proviso 3 to Regulation 7(2) of the 2004 Tariff
Regulations, the benefit of a tax holiday as applicable under the Act shall be passed
on to the beneficiaries. Pointing out that under Section 80 IA (4) of the IT Act, the
various categories of businesses eligible for the benefits, have been identified, under
which an undertaking setup for generation of power has been included, KSEBL has
contended that during the tax holiday period, NLCIL is exempt from tax on profits from
electricity produced using lignite from its own mine, in relation to TPS -I Expansion and
Order in Petition No. 2/MP/2014 (on remand) Page 20 of 34

the linked Mine-I Expansion. Referring to ITAT order dated 11.4.2012 (DCIT vs NLCIL)
supra, KSEBL has argued allowing the claim of Section 80 IA deductions to NLCIL’s
mining activity was upheld and reopening of assessment was found to be
unsustainable. TNPDCL has submitted that the language of Section 80 IA (4) makes
it clear that the ‘undertaking as a whole’, is entitled to a tax holiday, not isolated sub-
components of its operations. Thus, NLCIL being an undertaking, established for
power generation qualifies for the tax holiday benefit under the said section. Per
contra, NLCIL has submitted that the benefit under Section 80 IA was restricted post
2000 Amendment of the Act, only to power generation undertakings and no longer to
mining activities. NLCIL has pointed out that it had not claimed Section 80 IA
deductions for Mine-I Expansion commissioned post the Amendment, consistent with
the amended provision.
16. We have examined the submissions. Regulations 7(1) and 7(2) of the 2004 Tariff
Regulations provides as under:
7. Tax on Income: (1) Tax on the income streams of the generating company or the
transmission licensee, as the case may be, from its core business, shall be computed
as an expense and shall be recovered from the beneficiaries.
(2) Any under-recoveries or over-recoveries of tax on income shall be adjusted every
year on the basis of income-tax assessment under the Income-Tax Act, 1961, as
certified by the statutory auditors.
Provided that tax on any income stream other than the core business shall not
constitute a pass-through component in tariff and tax on such other income shall be
payable by the generating company or transmission licensee, as the case may be.
xx.
Provided further that the benefits of tax-holiday as applicable in accordance with the
provisions of the Income-Tax Act, 1961 shall be passed on to the beneficiaries.
xxx
xxxx

company from its core business is to be computed as an expense and recovered from
the beneficiaries, and Regulation 7(2) provides for the adjustment of over recoveries
and under recoveries, on income tax, as certified by statutory auditors. While the first
Order in Petition No. 2/MP/2014 (on remand) Page 21 of 34

proviso to the said regulation provides that the tax on income other than core business
cannot be made a pass-through in tariff and is payable by the generating company,
the third proviso provides that the benefits of the tax holiday shall be passed on to the
beneficiaries. In other words, the income tax streams of the generating company, only
from its ‘core business’, are recoverable from the beneficiaries, and the benefit of the
tax holiday in accordance with the provisions of the IT Act shall be passed on to the
beneficiaries. While the submissions of the parties on the term ‘core business’ of the
generating company, are being examined under a separate head below, the
submissions of the Respondents that NLCIL is exempt from tax on profits from
electricity produced using lignite from its own mine and that in terms of the third proviso
to the said regulations, the ‘undertaking as a whole’ is entitled to tax holiday, is being
examined under this head. Section 80 IA of the IT Act, prior to the 2000 Amendment,
states as under:
80-IA. Deductions in respect of profits and gains from industrial undertakings or
enterprises engaged in infrastructure development, etc.
(1) Xxx
xxx
(3) This section applies to any industrial undertaking which fulfils the following
conditions…...
