2000, replaced the term ‘any industrial undertaking’ with ‘an industrial undertaking’
referred to in Clause (iv) of sub section (4) is extracted below:
80-IA. Deductions in respect of profits and gains from industrial undertakings or
enterprises engaged in infrastructure development, etc.
(1) xxx
xxx
xxx
(3) This section applies to an industrial undertaking referred to in clause (iv) of sub-
section (4) which fulfils al the following conditions,
(4) (iv) an undertaking which, —
(a) is set up in any part of India for the generation or generation and distribution of
power, if it begins to generate power at any time during the period beginning on the 1st
day of April, 1993 and ending on the 31st day of March, 2017;
xxx
Order in Petition No. 2/MP/2014 (on remand) Page 22 of 34

19. It is evident from the above that post the 2000 amendment of Section 80 IA of
the IT Act, the term ‘any industrial undertaking’ has been replaced by ‘an industrial
undertaking’ wherein, the benefit under Section 80 IA of the IT Act, has been restricted
to the eligible business of the generation and distribution of power, as specified under
clause (iv) of Section 80 IA (4). Mine-I Expansion was commissioned during the year
2004-05, post the amendment and therefore, the benefit of tax holiday under Section
80 IA was allowable only in respect of an ‘undertaking’ engaged in the generation and
distribution of power of NLCIL generating station (viz TPS-I Expansion) and not to ‘any
mining activity’. In terms of this, the benefit of the tax holiday was applicable only to
the generation business of NLCIL and not to its mining activity. We note that in the
Commission’s order dated 20.9.2012 in Petition No. 15/2010, which was upheld by
APTEL vide its judgment dated 3.7.2013, it was observed that NLCIL had no liability
to pay income tax for TPS-I Expansion during the years 2004-07 (as no taxable income
accrued for it in the said station) and that it had availed the benefit of tax holiday under
Section 80 IA of the IT Act, for the period 2007-09 to 2008-09. It was against this
background that the Commission, in the said order, directed that NLCIL was not
entitled to recover income tax dues in respect of TPS-I Expansion up to 31.3.2009. By
no stretch of imagination can this order be extended to hold that the ‘mining activity’ of
NLCIL is covered under the tax holiday benefit under Section 80 IA of the IT Act,
pursuant to the 2000 amendment of the IT Act, as aforesaid. The definition of
‘undertaking’, having undergone a change pursuant to the 2000 amendment to Section
80 IA, as mentioned, the submission of KSEBL that NLCIL’s undertaking as a whole,
includes various other categories of business (including mining) and is eligible for a
tax holiday, is not tenable. As regards the submission of KSEBL that the ITAT order
dated 11.4.2012, wherein Section 80 IA deduction to NLCIL’s mining activity was
upheld, and the re-opening of assessment was found to be unsustainable, we notice
Order in Petition No. 2/MP/2014 (on remand) Page 23 of 34

that there was no conclusive finding of ITAT with regard to Section 80 IA deduction
being made applicable to the mining activity of NLCIL. In fact, the ITAT in the said
order while rejecting the arguments of the Revenue department for re-assessment,
took note that the Assessing officer was satisfied with regard to the claim of deduction
under Section 80 IA of the IT Act, in respect of the electricity produced by the Assesee
(NLCIL) at the time of original assessment, while having doubt with regard to the claim
for deduction in respect of mining of lignite. The said doubt, however, has not been
addressed by the ITAT in the said order. Hence, the reliance placed by KSEBL on the
said ITAT order to argue that Section 80 IA deduction is applicable to NLCIL’s mining
activity is misconceived. In light of the above, the submissions of KSEBL and TNPDCL
stand rejected.
Re: Core Business
20. KSEBL has contended that in the event there is a bar placed on mining activity
under Section 80 IA, that itself is a testimony to the fact that mining activity does not
form the ‘core business’ and thus, no tax liability for the same can be passed on to the
beneficiaries. Referring to the provisions of the 2001 and 2004 Tariff Regulations,
which provide for tax on income streams of the generating company from its core
activity to be recovered from the beneficiaries, KSEBL has argued that while the mining
activities are undertaken by NLCIL to source lignite, that business has no privity with
KSEBL, whose contract with NLCIL, is only for supply of power and not in relation with
lignite mining. According to KSEBL, the applicable Tariff Regulations allow ‘pass
through’ components in tariff, treating NLCIL purely as a power generation company
and not a mining company and therefore, mining being a non-core business, insofar
as the contract between KSEBL and NLCIL is concerned, the income tax arising out
of the same cannot be imposed on KSEBL. TNPDCL has submitted that the agreement
between TNPDCL and NLCIL is focused on the procurement of power and pertains
Order in Petition No. 2/MP/2014 (on remand) Page 24 of 34

24. Reverting back to the submissions of the Respondents on the term ‘core
business’, it is noticed that Regulation 6 of the 2004 Tariff Regulations defines ‘core
business’ as the regulated activities of the generating company and does not include
any other business activities like consultancy, telecommunications of the generating
company. As stated, Regulation 7(1) of the 2004 Tariff Regulations provides that tax
on the income streams of the generating company only from its core business, can be
recovered from its beneficiaries. Further, the first proviso to Regulation 7(2) specifically
stipulates that tax on any income streams, other than the ‘core business’, shall not
constitute a pass-through component on tariff, and tax on such other income shall be
payable by the generating company. In our view, the lignite mine is an integrated mine
with the generating station, and its operations are closely dependent upon the
operation of the generating station, due to the specific characteristics of lignite. Though
the MoC, GOI regulates the mining activities and issues guidelines for the fixation of
transfer price of lignite, from time to time, in case of NLCIL, the same is examined
based on the details furnished by NLCIL and subsequently approved by the
Commission, which forms the input cost, in the tariff determined for the generating
stations of NLCIL, by this Commission. Therefore, being a regulated activity as such,
the mining activity of NLCIL cannot be termed as a ‘non-core business’, as contended
by the Respondents. Merely because the ‘mining activity’ is not included under the
definition of ‘undertaking’ post Section 80 IA amendment (as stated above), it cannot
be argued that the ‘mining activity’ does not form the ‘core business’ of NLCIL. In this
backdrop, the contentions of the Respondents stand rejected.
Re: Res Judicata and estoppel

Petition No. 15/2010) and APTEL judgment dated 3.10.2013 (Appeal No. 250/2012),
came to the categorical conclusion that NLCIL was not entitled to any reimbursement

of Income tax dues from KSEBL in relation to TPS-I Expansion Project till 31.3.2009.
Accordingly, it has submitted that the entire tax reimbursement liability of Rs. 62.08
crores raised by NLCIL on KSEBL was set aside by the Commission and APTEL.
Pointing out that the issue of income tax from power generation activities and mining
activities has been rejected by the Commission and APTEL, and thus having attained
finality, NLCIL is barred from raising the very same issue already agitated by them in
the earlier proceedings. TNPDCL has also submitted that NLCIL is estopped from
claiming that the mining component be excluded from the tax holiday benefits, as the
Commission’s order dated 20.9.2012 and the APTEL judgment dated 3.7.2013
confirming the same, have attained finality. Accordingly, it has submitted that the

dated 20.9.2012, which specifically held that NLCIL is entitled to recover the

tax liability incurred for Mine-I Expansion is contrary to the binding directions of this

26. We have considered the rival submissions. Section 11 of the Code of Civil
Procedure, 1908, which encompasses the principle of res judicata, provides as under:
“11. Res judicata—No Court shall try any suit or issue in which the matter directly and
substantially in issue has been directly and substantially in issue in a former suit
between the same parties, or between parties under whom they or any of them claim,
litigating under the same title, in a Court competent to try such subsequent suit or the
suit in which such issue has been subsequently raised, and has been heard and finally
decided by such Court.
…
Order in Petition No. 2/MP/2014 (on remand) Page 28 of 34

19. We have here to advert to another principle of caution referred to by Mulla (p. 105): “It
is not to be assumed that matters in respect of which issues have been framed are all of
them directly and substantially in issue. Nor is there any special significance to be attached
to the fact that a particular issue is the first in the list of issues. Which of the matters are
directly in issue and which collaterally or incidentally, must be determined on the facts of
each case. A material test to be applied is whether the court considers the adjudication of
the issue material and essential for its decision.”
37. Adverting to the decision in Mahant Pragdasji Guru Bhagwandasji (supra) and two
earlier decisions, the Court held that these were instances where in spite of adverse
findings in an earlier suit, the finding on that specific issue was not treated as res judicata
as it was purely incidental, auxiliary or collateral to the main issue in each of these cases
and not necessary in the earlier case.
38. In another decision in Gram Panchayat of Village Naulakha v. Ujagar Singh, it has
been held that the decision in an earlier suit for an injunction, where no question of title
was adjudicated upon will not be binding on the question of title:
“10. We may also add one other important reason which frequently arises under Section 11
CPC. The earlier suit by the respondent against the Panchayat was only a suit for injunction
and not one on title. No question of title was gone into or decided. The said decision cannot,
therefore, be binding on the question of title. See in this connection Sajjadanashin Sayed v.
Musa Dadabhai Ummer [(2000) 3 SCC 350] where this Court, on a detailed consideration
of law in India and elsewhere held, that even if, in an earlier suit for injunction, there is an
incidental finding on title, the same will not be binding in a later suit or proceeding where title
is directly in question, unless it is established that it was “necessary” in the earlier suit to
decide the question of title for granting or refusing injunction and that the relief for injunction
was founded or based on the finding on title. Even the mere framing of an issue on title may
not be sufficient as pointed out in that case.”
However, in Sajjadanashin Syed (supra), an earlier judgment in Sulochana Amma
(supra) and the Madras High Court’s judgment in Vanagiri were referred to in order to
lay emphasis on the unique facts of each case and its importance for determination of
whether the issue was substantially decided. In both the referred cases, the issue was
whether the finding of title in an injunction suit would operate as res judicata to a
subsequent suit for declaration of title. While in Sulochana Amma, it was held that by the
doctrine of res judicata, the finding would bar the subsequent suit, in Vanagiri, it was
held that the title was not conclusively decided and that the subsequent suit would not
be barred. It was observed that the twin tests of necessity and essentiality might lead to
different conclusions on suits of a similar nature based on the facts and circumstances
in each of them.
39. In a more recent decision in Nand Ram (Dead) Through Legal Representatives v.
Jagdish Prasad (Dead) Through Legal Representatives, a Bench of two judges
reiterated the principle that if a matter has only collaterally or in an auxiliary manner been
in issue or decided in an earlier proceeding, the finding would not ordinarily be res
judicata in a later proceeding where the matter is directly and substantially in issue.
Justice Hemant Gupta (writing for a two judge bench) noted that the material test to be
applied is whether the adjudication of the issue is material and essential for the decision.
In Nand Ram, the land leased by the plaintiffs to the defendants was acquired under the
Land Acquisition Act, 1894. A dispute arose on the apportionment of the compensation.
The suit was decided against the defendant on the ground that defendant did not pay
the lease rent for more than 12 months and thus according to the lease agreement, the
lease had come to an end. It was thus held that the defendant would not be entitled to
the compensation. Subsequently, the plaintiff filed an eviction suit asserting that the
defendant was in possession of the land that was not included in the lease deed. The
High Court in the second appeal held that the subsequent suit was barred by res judicata
since the former suit had conclusively decided on the title of the suit property. On appeal,
Order in Petition No. 2/MP/2014 (on remand) Page 30 of 34

the statutory auditors’ certificate. The procedure adopted by NLC is contrary to that

I Expansion does not survive for our examination.
18. During the course of hearing it was submitted on behalf of NLC that even though
the tax benefit has already been passed on by NLC to the beneficiaries, the assessing
officer in his assessment order dated 28.12.2010 has disallowed its claim for tax
benefit under Section 80 IA in respect of TPS-I Expansion for the financial year 2007-
08 on the ground that the generating station was only an expansion of the then existing
capacity and could not be considered as a separate undertaking as provided under
Section 80 IA (4) (iv) of the IT Act. In case, NLC becomes liable to pay income-tax on
account of unavailability of benefit under Section 80 IA, it shall be entitled to recover
from KSEB the income-tax along surcharge, interest etc paid to the Income-tax
Department.
19. We have held that NLC is not entitled to recovery of income-tax dues in respect of
TPS-I Expansion up to 31.3.2009. In view of this, there is justifiably no reason for
KSEB to withhold income-tax dues for TPS-II. NLC has alleged that KSEB has been
withholding income-tax dues in respect of TPS-II amounting to `57.00 crore included
in the total amount of `119.0935 crore. We direct that KSEB shall release such
Order in Petition No. 2/MP/2014 (on remand) Page 32 of 34

withheld income-tax dues amounting to `57.00 crore pertaining to TPS-II along with
interest at the rate of 9% per annum from June 2007 within 30 days upon NLC
furnishing the claim, duly supported by the statutory auditors’ certificate.”
30. It is evident from the above that KSEBL had, in Petition No. 15/2010, raised
amongst others the issue of NLCIL not availing the tax holiday benefit under Section
80 IA of the Act, in respect of mines, which, according to it, were part of the generating
stations of NLCIL. In response, NLCIL clarified that after the restructuring of Section
80 IA with effect from 1.4.2000, mining is not covered under Section 80 IA of the IT
Act, apart from the fact that the assessing officer in his assessment order dated
28.12.2010, had disallowed the claim for tax benefits under Section 80 IA. The
Commission, in its order dated 20.9.2012, while observing that NLCIL was not entitled
to the recovery of the income tax dues in respect of TPS-I Expansion up to 31.3.2009,
held that there was no reason for KSEBL to withhold income tax dues for TPS-II. This
was subsequently upheld by APTEL in its judgment dated 3.7.2013. However, in the
said order, no discussion or a specific finding/decision was rendered by the
Commission on whether the mining activity of NLCIL is to be excluded from the tax
holiday benefit or not under Section 80 IA. In other words, this issue was not ‘direct
and substantial’ in the aforesaid petition, culminating in the order dated 20.9.2012 and
later affirmed by APTEL. As laid down in the said judgment supra (para 26 above), if
a matter was only ‘collaterally or incidentally’ in issue and decided in the earlier
proceedings, the finding therein would not ordinarily be res judicata in a latter
proceeding, where the matter is directly and substantially in issue. Apart from this issue
being ‘collateral or incidental’, there was also no specific finding/decision on the same
in the earlier proceedings. In view of this, the issues raised by NLCIL in the present
Petition, seeking the reimbursement of the taxes actually paid by it during the relevant
years in respect of the mining component (Mine-I Expansion), cannot be said to be hit
by the principles of res judicata and estoppel. Merely because the IT assessment order
Order in Petition No. 2/MP/2014 (on remand) Page 33 of 34

dated 28.12.2010 was not challenged by NLCIL, for any reason whatsoever, the same
cannot be a ground for KSEBL to deny the income tax reimbursement to NLCIL. In
light of the above, the submissions of the Respondents are rejected, and we hold that
KSEBL is liable to reimburse NLCIL the revised income tax reimbursement claims in
the Petition, duly certified by an auditor, as submitted by NLCIL.
31. It is pertinent to mention that the Respondent, TNPDCL, had adopted the
submissions of KSEBL in the present case. It has, however, been submitted that
payments have been made to NLCIL, on the mistaken belief that the amounts claimed
were legally admissible in accordance with the order of the Commission and other
competent authorities, but in the light of the correct interpretation of the regulatory
framework and the binding findings of the Commission and APTEL, the claim of NLCIL
is not sustainable. Accordingly, TNPDCL has prayed that the amounts paid to NLCIL
are liable to be refunded along with applicable interest from the date of payment till the
date of refund, to compensate for the time value of money. Considering the fact that
the submissions of TNPDCL, which are in line with the submissions of KSEBL, have
been rejected as above, in terms of our findings, the prayer of TNPDCL for a refund of
the IT amounts already paid to NLCIL cannot be entertained and is accordingly
rejected.
32. Petition No. 2/MP/2014, on remand, is disposed of in terms of the above. With
this, the directions contained in the APTEL judgment dated 26.3.2025 in Appeal No.
138/2017 stand implemented.
Sd/- Sd/- Sd/- Sd/-
(Ravinder Singh Dhillon) (Harish Dudani) (Ramesh Babu V.) (Jishnu Barua)

ORDER
The instant petition has been filed by the Petitioner, AD Hydro Power Limited under
Section 79(1)(c), 79(1) (f) and 79(1)(k) of the Electricity Act, 2003 inter alia challenging
firstly, the computation of relinquishment charges determined by Central Transmission
Utility; and secondly, the methodology published by CTU for determining relinquishment
charges pursuant to order dated 8.3.2019 in 92/MP/2015.
The Petitioner has made the following prayers:
(a) Allow the present Petition;
(b) Set aside the determination of relinquishment charges by Respondent no.1 vide its
letter dated 24.12.2021 and the notification dated 22.12.2021;
(c) Hold that the petitioner is not liable to pay relinquishment charges;
(d) In the event of rejection of prayer (c), hold that the petitioner is liable to pay
relinquishment charge on the basis of the All India Minimum POC rate under the CERC
Sharing Regulations, 2010 or the AC-UBC component determined under the CERC
Sharing Regulations, 2020 as applicable to the petitioner and by considering maximum
stranding at 56 MW;
(e) Hold that the petitioner is not liable to pay notice period charges;
(f) Pass such other/further Order(s)/directions(s) as this Hon’ble Commission may deem
fit in the facts and circumstances in the present case.
The Petitioner has made following prayers in 15/IA/2022:
(a) Stay the operation of the impugned letter dated 24.8.2021;
(b) Direct respondent no.1 not to precipitate the matter or in any manner coerce the
petitioner for making payment towards the impugned demand; and/or
(c) Pass any other order(s) in the interest of justice as this Hon’ble Commission deems fit
in the facts of the case.
The Petitioner has made following prayers in 68/IA/2024:
(a) Stay the operation of bill of supply for relinquishment charges dated 12.3.2024 issued
by CTUIL until final adjudication;
(b) Direct respondent no.1 not to precipitate the matter or in any manner coerce the
petitioner for making payment towards the impugned demand; and/or
(c) Pass any other order(s) in the interest of justice as this Hon’ble Commission deems fit
in the facts of the case.
Order in Petition No. 97/MP/2022 Page 3

Submissions of the Petitioner:
2. The Petitioner has mainly submitted as follows:
(a) On 22.02.2001, an Implementation Agreement was signed between the Government
of Himachal Pradesh and Rajasthan Spinning & Weaving Mills Limited for the
development and operation of a 192 MW Allain Duhangan Hydro Electric Project in
Prini, Manali, District Kullu, HP for a period of 40 years (later transferred to AD Hydro
Power Limited vide Quadripartite Agreement dated 05.11.2005, a SPV for the
Project) on BOOT basis.
(b) On 20.8.2002, Central Electricity Authority (CEA) accorded Techno-Economic
Clearance for setting up a Hydro Electric Project in Prini, District-Kullu (Himachal
Pradesh), along with a dedicated double circuit line for evacuation of power
generated by the petitioner up to Nalagarh (ISTS pooling station) for further
transmission.
(c) On 18.07.2005, Petitioner made an application to PGCIL, seeking long-term open
access as per the then prevailing CERC Regulations, 2004, for the injection of power
at Panarasa/ Nalagarh.
(d) Between 18.07.2005 and the first quarter of 2007, there were various deliberations
and discussions between Petitioner, CTU, PGCIL and CEA, etc., regarding the most
suitable evacuation arrangement for the Petitioner’s project. It was finally decided
that the Petitioner’s project shall be connected to the Nalagarh sub-station of CTU
through its 220-kV double-circuit dedicated transmission line and 2 nos. of 220 kV
base at the Nalagarh sub-station.
(e) On 26.04.2007, PGCIL granted long term open access (LTOA) to the Petitioner at
Nalagarh Sub-station of PGCIL, subject to the signing of BPTA.
(f) On 11.09.2009, a Bulk Power Transmission Agreement [BPTA] was signed between
the Petitioner and PGCIL.
(g) On 16.09.2010, the Petitioner’s project, along with its Dedicated Transmission Line
up to Nalagarh, was commissioned. On 16.04.2011, a Connection Agreement in
terms of the CERC (connectivity) Regulations, 2009, was executed between PGCIL
Order in Petition No. 97/MP/2022 Page 4

and the Petitioner. On 03.08.2011, a Transmission Service Agreement (TSA) was
executed between PGCIL and the Petitioner in terms of the CERC Sharing
Regulations 2010.
(h) This Commission has been approving the transmission charges and losses
applicable to each region and the slab rate applicable to entities operating in these
regions. However, until 14.07.2015, when this Commission determined POC
charges, reliability support charges and HVDC Charges for May-June 2015, the
Petitioner’s charges were not determined. Thus, though NLDC was required to
compute POC charges for the Petitioner and seek approval from the commission
thereupon, it was done for the first time only vide order dated 14.07.2015. It is also
worth noting that POC charges, HVDC charges and reliability support charges have
been determined separately, as they are different components of transmission
charges.
(i) On 08.03.2019, this Commission, taking note of the difficulties faced in implementing
Regulation 18 of the CERC Connectivity Regulation 2009, laid down a detailed
procedure for computing stranded capacity and relinquishment charges. It was held
that though determination of stranded capacity is a sine qua non for applying
relinquishment charges, the same cannot be determined in cases where LTA has
been granted on existing system margins. Therefore, this Commission deemed it just
and proper to hold that in cases where LTA has been granted on an existing system,
only the ‘All India Minimum POC rate’ shall be applied instead of the total
transmission charges applicable to such relinquishing entity. It is relevant to note that
the POC charge is one out of the three components of transmission charges and is
distinct from the reliability support charge and HVDC charge, which form the other
two components.
(j) Even with respect to the relinquishment of LTAs, which were granted upon system
augmentation, it is only 66% of the NPV of the transmission charges of such
augmented lines/substation, which is payable. If such an augmented
system/specified system under the relinquished LTA includes an HVDC asset, only
in such a case, the transmission charge towards such HVDC asset will be included
while calculating relinquishment charges.
Order in Petition No. 97/MP/2022 Page 5

(k) The aforesaid order dated 08.03.2019, passed in 92/MP/2015, has been assailed by
several entities before the APTEL in several appeals amongst Appeal No.(s) 171,
250 and 251 of 2019. Amongst others, one of the issues pending adjudication before
APTEL is whether there could be any stranding in the system due to relinquishment
of LTA by those entities that were granted LTA on existing system margins.
(l) In the Appeal No. 251/2019 titled SKS Power Generation (Chhattisgarh) Limited vs.
CERC and Ors, APTEL vide its order dated 08.10.2020, was pleased to restrain the
PGCIL from issuing any invoice towards relinquishment charges during the pendency
of appeals before the APTEL.
(m) On 11.12.2019, this Commission vide its order in 252/MP/2019 directed CTU to
ensure that all the data which was relied upon to calculate relinquishment charges
must necessarily be furnished to the relinquishing entity.
(n) CTU thereafter published on its website a detailed procedure for determining
relinquishment charges. The procedure notified on 20.5.2019 did not deal with the
relinquishment of the LTA granted on existing margins; however, the procedure dated
9.8.2021 provides for the same. The said procedure dated 9.8.2021, applies not only
to All India Minimum POC charges but also reliability support charges in case of
relinquishment by DICs who have been granted LTA on the existing system, i.e.
without any system augmentation.
(o) On 4.5.2020, this Commission issued the CERC (Sharing of Inter-State Transmission
Charges and Losses) Regulations, 2020. The said regulation superseded the CERC
Sharing Regulations, 2010, and laid down an altogether new methodology for
determining the transmission charges. The new sharing regulation came into effect
from 1.11.2020; however, in terms of the ‘transition provision’ under the Sharing
Regulation 2020, the transmission charges for November and December 2020 are
required to be determined under the CERC Sharing Regulation, 2010. The CERC
Sharing Regulation, 2020 has done away with the POC methodology, but it has
saved all acts done under the earlier regulations. The CERC Sharing Regulations,
2020 provides for the following four components of transmission charges:
i. National component
Order in Petition No. 97/MP/2022 Page 6

ii. Regional component
iii. Transformer Component
iv. AC system Component
(p) On 21.2.2021, this Commission approved the transmission charges and losses for
the month of October-November, 2020, based on the CERC Sharing Regulations,
2010. It was also held that the transmission charges and losses payable from January
2021 onwards shall be in terms of the CERC Sharing Regulations, 2020.
(q) In September 2020, Power Research and Development Consultants Pvt. Ltd., being
the consultant appointed by the petitioner before the relinquishment of LTA,
submitted a report to the Petitioner on the future load flow study in the system due to
the relinquishment of the petitioner’s LTA. The said report concludes that the
maximum reduction in load flow on all ISTS lines directly connecting Nalagarh sub-
station and other sub-stations in the northern region is only 56 MW, and that too in
the off-peak season.
(r) On 23.08.2021, the Petitioner sent a notice to CTU, thereby relinquishing the entire
LTA with immediate effect, as the Petitioner had been and is continuing to sell power
in the inter-state on a short-term basis to the power exchange.
(s) On 27.08.2021, the CTU accepted the request for relinquishment of the entire LTA
of 168.96 MW w.e.f. 24.8.2021. Further, the CTU made it clear that the
relinquishment is subject to payment of transmission charges as per the order dated
8.3.2019 passed in 92/MP/2015. CTU did not state in the aforesaid letter that the
relinquishment is subject to payment of All India minimum transmission charges
under the CERC Sharing Regulation 2020.
(t) On 24.12.2021, the CTU vide its letter to the Petitioner stated that the relinquishment
charges towards Petitioner’s relinquishment are calculated at Rs. 58.33 crores under
CTU’s notification dated 22.12.2021. In the aforesaid notification, CTU has calculated
relinquishment charges on the entire LTA capacity of 168.96 MW. Instead of applying
‘all India minimum POC charges’ as per order dated 8.3.2019, it had erroneously and
arbitrarily applied ‘All India minimum transmission charges’ purportedly published on
the NLDC website.
Order in Petition No. 97/MP/2022 Page 7

(u) On 06.01.2022, the Petitioner addressed a letter to CTU, disputing the calculation
stated in the letter dated 24.12.2021. The Petitioner requested CTU to withdraw the
letter dated 24.12.2021, which was not in terms of the order dated 8.3.2019 and also
requested CTU to refer the matter to CERC instead of demanding self-imposed and
arbitrary charges. The said letter has not been replied by CTU.
(v) As on the date of the relinquishment, the petitioner has paid total LTOA charges of
Rs. 385.92 crores approximately.
(w) In the case of the relinquishment of LTAs granted on the existing system, and that
too without having any identified beneficiary, there could be no stranding in the
system. The entire sale of power by the Petitioner, being on a short-term basis
through bilateral/ IEX, is always subject to the lowest priority compared to any other
long-term or medium-term customers having tied up power with an identified
beneficiary. The Petitioner was granted LTA only on the existing margin, and in the
event of a system constraint, the Petitioner’s power will carry the least priority
amongst the LTA holders having tied-up PPAs. Thus, the Petitioner has used the
spare system margins at all times. In other words, the ‘right’ of open access granted
to the Petitioner was restricted and conditional upon the availability of spare margin
in the system. Thus, it is submitted that in such circumstances, it cannot be said that
the Petitioner’s relinquishment of LTA causes any stranding in the system. This
aspect was not considered by this Commission while rendering the decision in
92/MP/2015.
(x) In the case of DICs, which have been granted LTA on an existing system, the system
already had a spare margin, and the existing DICs were already paying for such a
system, including the spare margin, before the LTA was granted. By granting the
LTA on such a spare margin, the new DIC contributes to the system, thereby
lowering the burden on existing DICs. Thus, if such DIC (like the Petitioner)
relinquishes the LTA later, it cannot be said to cause any stranding in the system or
create any burden on the other DICs. The Petitioner herein was also granted LTA on
the system already existing in the region, the cost of which was borne by the existing
DICs. In fact, the Petitioner had to carry out an uphill task to connect its station to the
PGCIL’s Nalagarh station by drawing a dedicated line in one of the most difficult
terrains. No system strengthening was carried out by PGCIL for the Petitioner’s
Order in Petition No. 97/MP/2022 Page 8

power, and hence, there could be no stranding in the system for the reason explained
above.
(y) This issue is presently pending consideration before APTEL in appeals filed against
the order dated 8.3.2019 in 92/MP/2015. Thus, all grounds urged in the present
appeal are without prejudice to this primary submission.
(z) The current regulatory framework governing the methodology for determination of
relinquishment charges is the order dated 8.3.2019, read with regulation 18 of the
CERC Connectivity Regulations, 2009. In the absence of any amendment in the
aforesaid regulatory framework, CTU ought to have applied the same. Even if the
CTU was of the view that there is some regulatory gap on the methodology of
determining relinquishment charges after the issuance of CERC Sharing
Regulations, 2020, the CTU, being a statutory body, ought to have approached this
Commission for necessary clarity instead of arbitrarily applying some charge contrary
to the order dated 8.3.2019 in petition 92/MP/2015.
(aa) Without prejudice and assuming that the CERC Sharing Regulation, 2020 is
applicable to relinquishment under Regulation 18, it is submitted that only the AC-
UBC component as applicable to the petitioner ought to be applied. Under the order
dated 8.3.2019 in 92/MP/2015, this commission, by applying the minimum POC
charge (being the charge for the usage of the system), excluded the assets not in
use thereby excluding the other two components under the CERC Sharing
Regulations, 2010, viz. HVDC Charge and Reliability support charge. Thus, it has
been this commission’s intent that the HVDC charge must not be applied in case of
relinquishment of the LTA where no system augmentation/strengthening has taken
place. The same intent must also carry forward while deciding the applicability under
the CERC Sharing Regulations, 2020. In view thereof, the national component and
the regional component, which includes the cost towards HVDC assets and reliability
support assets largely, ought not to be considered while determining relinquishment
charges.
(bb) Ideally, the relinquishment charge is based on 66% of the transmission charges
payable for the relinquished asset multiplied by the stranded capacity. Thus, the
relinquishing entity has to pay the transmission charges for the system for which it
Order in Petition No. 97/MP/2022 Page 9

was granted an LTA. However, in the case of LTAs granted on the existing system,
no specific system in use by the DIC is identified, and thus, it is difficult to ascertain
which system the DIC should pay for in case of relinquishment. Thus, this
Commission applied the ‘All India minimum POC Charge’ to overcome such
shortcomings. The POC charge under the 2010 regulations was based on usage and
was sensitive to distance, direction and quantum of power. Under the CERC Sharing
Regulations, 2020, the AC-UBC component determines charges based on the usage
of the AC System by each entity, thereby making it a usage-based charge. Under the
CERC Sharing regulations, 2020, the AC-UBC charge is most reflective of distance,
direction and quantum of flow. The AC-UBC determined by NLDC for the petitioner
reflects the transmission charges towards the AC system actually used by the
petitioner for the sale of power under the LTA granted to it for the Target Region
(Northern Region). Thus, in the event of the relinquishment of LTA, only the AC-UBC
charge could have been applied to the petitioner.
(cc) This Commission, in the statement of reasons issued for CERC Sharing
Regulations, 2020, expressly made it clear that the said regulation does not apply to
relinquishment charges. Such being the legislative intent, clearly expressed in the
statement of reasons, the CTU ought not to have acted contrary to it.
(dd) Assuming that there is stranding in the system due to relinquishment of the LTA
granted on the existing system, such stranding ought to be determined by comparing
the system margin as it existed before the grant of LTA versus the system margins
post relinquishment of LTA. The changes in load flow in the ISTS lines connected to
the ISTS Sub-station, where the petitioner is connected, would demonstrate the real
stranding in the system. It is submitted that the load flow study report prepared by
the petitioner’s consultant, analyzed the load flow in all the ISTS lines directly
connected to Nalagarh sub-station and other sub-station in northern region (Patiala
and Mohali) and concluded that the maximum decrease in load flow is 56 MW by way
of line loading and that too in the lines from Nalagarh to Mohali and Nalagarh to
Patiala during off-peak season.
(ee) In the absence of an amendment to the order dated 8.3.2019 and Regulation 18 of
the CERC Connectivity regulations, 2009, the NLDC, being the implementing
agency, should have continued to calculate the POC charges for the purpose of
Order in Petition No. 97/MP/2022 Page 10

applying the said charges to the relinquishing DICs who have been granted LTA on
the existing system.
(ff) The Petitioner has submitted that it is not allowed to sell power in the State of
Himachal Pradesh where its plant is located for its entire O&M period therefore, it
continues to avail and pay for short-term open access in inter-state on the same
injecting point and the same target region as the LTA. Thus, to the extent the
Petitioner is paying the STOA charges in the system, the same are utilised to reduce
the LTOA charges, thereby reducing the overall impact on the other DICs. This
charge must therefore be accounted for while calculating the liability towards
relinquishment charges. It is submitted that the Petitioner transmits around 550
million units annually through the ISTS system (excluding free power component and
transmission losses). As of today, the prevailing STOA charge is Rs. 0.51 / unit,
which, if paid for the period falling short of 12 years, comes to about Rs. 28 crores. If
the same charge is paid for the remaining 29 years, the same comes to about 812
crores. Thus, to this extent, the Petitioner will continue to serve the system, thereby
reducing stranding due to relinquishment.
(gg) The ‘notice period charge’ must not be applied to the Petitioner since the Petitioner
has relinquished its LTA in the 11th year. The scheme of Regulation 18 is such that
relinquishment charges are payable until the 12th year and not beyond. Thus, the
Petitioner herein was only left with one year until completion of 12 years, and hence
it must not be liable to pay notice period charges in the given facts of the case, as it
would lead to payment for two years beyond the 11th year, while relinquishment
charges are not payable beyond the 12th year. It would, in effect, be tantamount to
charging for 13 years, which is not the scheme envisaged under Regulation 18 of
the CERC Connectivity Regulations, 2009.
(hh) This Commission, in an order dated 8.3.2019, passed in 92/MP/2015, expressed
its intention to provide an incentive for LTA customers to relinquish LTAs, if required,
before the expiry of the full term. The application of ‘all India Minimum transmission
charges’ on the petitioner completely takes away such an incentive and makes
relinquishment burdensome and unreasonable.
Order in Petition No. 97/MP/2022 Page 11

(ii) CTU has taken a completely inconsistent stand in relation to the applicability of the
order dated 8.3.2019, passed in petition no. 92/MP/2015. The CTU, vide its letter
dated 28.8.2021, whereby it accepted the request for relinquishment stated in clear
terms that the relinquishment charge shall be calculated in accordance with the
methodology specified in the order dated 8.3.2019 passed in 92/MP/2015. Also, in
its letter dated 24.12.2021, the CTU has again relied upon the order dated 8.3.2019
in petition 92/MP/2015. However, in its notification dated 22.12.2021, the CTU has
ignored the order dated 8.3.2019 on the pretext that ‘after the effectiveness of CERC
Sharing Regulations, 2020, slabs for POC rates are not available’. Petitioner cannot
be made liable to pay relinquishment charges in excess of the All India Minimum
POC rate.
Submissions of the Petitioner in I.A. No. 15/2022:
3. The Petitioner in IA No. 15/2022 has prayed for a stay on the operation of the impugned
letter dated 24.8.2021 and also sought a direction to the Respondent, CTUIL, not to
precipitate the matter or in any manner coerce the Petitioner to make payment towards
the impugned demand.
Hearing dated 05.08.2022
4. The Learned counsel for the Respondent, CTUIL, accepted the notice and sought time
